Title
Stabilizing stress‑persistent gastric cholinergic topology to prevent neurogenic gastritis: imaging‑guided identification and probiotic actuation

Rationale and significance
- Acute psychological stress suppresses vagal output and shifts gastric physiology toward lower mucosal perfusion, reduced mucus/bicarbonate secretion, and barrier compromise. Vagal reflexes and neuropeptide/NO‑linked mechanisms counteract this by sustaining blood flow and cytoprotection; vagotomy abolishes these defenses, indicating a necessary role for vagal circuits in gastric mucosal protection. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK53093/?utm_source=openai))
- Presynaptic cholinergic terminal density can be quantified in vivo with [18F]-FEOBV PET via binding to VAChT in peripheral organs, establishing a feasible, repeatable window on cholinergic innervation outside the CNS. Stomach handling of this tracer includes early luminal secretion, a known quantification confound to be addressed by kinetic modeling and ROI placement outside the lumen. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8975951/?utm_source=openai))
- Vagal afferents innervating the stomach express functional GABAB receptors; local GABA dampens gastric mechanosensory drive and shapes vagal reflexes. GABAergic control at the NTS–DMV interface increases cholinergic efferent outflow to the stomach. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11705755/?utm_source=openai))
- Activity‑dependent genetic tagging (FosTRAP) has recently been used to label functionally defined vagal sensory populations in the nodose ganglion, enabling causal dissection of gut‑to‑brain pathways. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12830305/?utm_source=openai))
- Probiotic chassis can be engineered to produce high levels of GABA via the glutamate decarboxylase (gad) system, offering a chronic, mucosa‑proximal actuator to bias vagal afferent signaling. Vagus‑dependent behavioral effects of a GABA‑active Lactobacillus strain support pathway engagement. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33990858/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question (atomic strategy)
If a subset of gastric cholinergic circuits maintains presynaptic integrity during acute stress, then identifying individuals/regions where this “stress‑persistent cholinergic topology” is strongest and chronically biasing vagal afferent input toward those same patterns will stabilize mucosal protection and prevent stress‑induced gastritis. Does imaging‑defined persistence of VAChT‑positive terminals under stress predict gastric cytoprotection, and can a stomach‑tropic GABA‑producing probiotic durably increase this persistence and its physiological correlates?

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define and validate a stress‑persistent gastric cholinergic topology.
- 1a (mouse): Use FosTRAP2 to tag neurons active during resilience epochs (maintenance of gastric perfusion/barrier during restraint). Quantify trapped ensembles across nodose, NTS/DMV, and gastric enteric plexuses. Causally test whether reactivation (chemogenetic CRISPRa of ChAT/VAChT or DREADDs) preserves mucosal blood flow and barrier during repeated stress. Outcomes: laser‑speckle perfusion, FITC‑dextran permeability, mucus layer thickness.
- 1b (human method development): Establish [18F]-FEOBV PET/CT protocol for upper abdominal/vagal field-of-view. Use dynamic modeling with blood input and multiparametric ROIs (distal esophageal and subdiaphragmatic vagal trunks; perigastric plexus; gastric wall segments away from lumen) to compute a Stress Persistence Index (SPI = percent change in VAChT‑binding parameter from baseline to acute psychological stressor). Address luminal tracer secretion by excluding mucosal ROIs with early luminal activity and emphasizing extra‑luminal cholinergic targets (vagal trunks, celiac plexus). Feasibility endpoints: test–retest variability, motion robustness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8975951/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build a stomach‑tropic GABA‑producing probiotic to bias vagal afferent signaling toward protective reflexes.
- Engineer a Lactococcus/Lactobacillus chassis with high‑flux gadB/gadC and export optimization to produce micromolar GABA at the gastric surface; encapsulate for gastric release. Titrate secretion to engage mucosal GABAB on vagal afferents without depressing gastric motility. Validate dependence on vagus and GABAB using selective deafferentation or antagonists; measure afferent firing, NTS activity, DMV‑driven cholinergic output, and mucosal perfusion/barrier in stressed mice. Benchmarks: in situ mucosal GABA microdialysis, nodose/NTS Ca2+ imaging, gastric physiology readouts. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11705755/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Translational test of probiotic actuation on imaging‑defined topology and gastric protection.
- Conduct a double‑blind, randomized, crossover pilot in stress‑prone adults with recurrent dyspeptic/gastritic symptoms and no H. pylori. Two 8‑week periods: engineered GABA‑probiotic vs matched non‑GABA control. Primary endpoint: change in SPI on [18F]-FEOBV PET during a standardized acute stress paradigm. Secondary endpoints: gastric permeability (lactulose:mannitol), symptom diary, and safety; exploratory: heart‑rate variability, serum inflammatory markers. Prediction: probiotic increases SPI (greater preservation/expansion of VAChT‑positive topology under stress) and improves physiological/symptom measures.

Study design and methods
- Resilience tagging (Aim 1a). Define “resilience epoch” by concurrent maintenance of gastric perfusion and barrier during standardized stress. Time‑lock tamoxifen to capture active nodes. Profile trapped cells for cholinergic/nitrergic/peptidergic markers and projections; re‑activate selectively to test causal protection. Expected linkage: trapped ensembles will map to vagal reflex arcs and submucosal cholinergic/nitrergic effectors that mediate CGRP/NO/PG‑linked cytoprotection. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK53093/?utm_source=openai))
- PET protocol (Aim 1b, Aim 3). Two scan sessions: resting baseline and acute stress. Dynamic 0–60 min acquisition with arterialized venous sampling; kinetic modeling (2‑tissue or reference‑region where appropriate). ROIs emphasize extra‑luminal cholinergic structures to avoid stomach lumen confounds; sensitivity analyses exclude segments with early luminal activity. Compute SPI per ROI; aggregate into a composite gastric‑vagal SPI. Reliability assessed by short‑interval test–retest. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8975951/?utm_source=openai))
- Probiotic engineering (Aim 2). Construct strains with modular gad expression and pH‑responsive promoters; incorporate metabolic edits to increase intracellular glutamate and proton motive force to drive GadC exchange. Use in vitro gastric simulators to tune output, then validate in rodents for mucosal GABA levels and pharmacodynamics on vagal afferents and DMV cholinergic tone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33990858/?utm_source=openai))

Endpoints and analyses
- Primary mechanistic endpoint (preclinical): with reactivation of trapped ensembles or probiotic dosing, preservation of gastric perfusion and barrier during repeated stress vs controls.
- Primary translational endpoint: ΔSPI (probiotic − control) in vagal/epigastric ROIs; hypothesized positive shift indicates stabilization/expansion of presynaptic cholinergic terminals active under stress.
- Secondary endpoints: changes in permeability, symptoms, and HRV; correlations between ΔSPI and physiological outcomes.
- Powering: pilot effect sizes from preclinical SPI analogs and human test–retest variability guide adaptive sample sizing in the crossover trial.

Risk mitigation and alternatives
- Tracer luminal secretion may obscure gastric wall VAChT. Mitigation: prioritize extra‑luminal ROIs (vagal trunks/celiac plexus), late‑frame analyses, and kinetic separation of vascular, nonspecific, and specific compartments; validate with phantom and large‑animal studies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8975951/?utm_source=openai))
- Off‑target GABA effects on motility: enforce dose‑finding with telemetry and barostat readouts; if needed, shift to lower‑output strains or timed dosing (evening).
- If probiotic fails to shift SPI, re‑examine engagement via mucosal GABA microdialysis and consider adding low‑intensity vagal stimulation during dosing as a rescue experiment.

Expected outcomes and impact
- A validated SPI as an imaging biomarker of stress‑persistent gastric cholinergic topology; preclinically, FosTRAP shows that this topology is causal for mucosal protection. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12830305/?utm_source=openai))
- A living, chronic actuator (GABA‑probiotic) that biases vagal afferent input to maintain DMV cholinergic drive and mucosal defense, shifting SPI and improving physiological measures in stress‑prone individuals. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3179073/?utm_source=openai))
- A generalizable framework: use state transitions (stress) as calibration to discover protective circuit topology, then reinforce it—rather than blocking “harmful” signals—creating a self‑maintaining defense for neurogenic gastritis.

Title
Phase-coherent vagal control to preempt stress-induced gastric microvascular failure

Hypothesis–Question
Do stress-evoked decouplings between cardiorespiratory rhythms and gastric microvascular vasomotion precede mucosal injury, and can brief, phase-locked vagus nerve stimulation restore coherence rapidly enough to prevent stress gastritis? If “yes,” can a tiny, repeated thermal pulse sensed at the mucosa provide a stable readout of this phase state for chronic closed-loop control? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9895103/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat the gastric submucosal network as a driven oscillator whose phase/coherence with respiration and cardiac rhythms reflects upstream autonomic drive. Detect impending injury as a shift in phase/coherence of microvascular flow relative to respiration/cardiac cycles; immediately deliver brief, respiration-gated or cardiac-synchronized vagus nerve stimulation to re-entrain vasomotion and preserve perfusion, aborting the cascade to epithelial injury. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2017.00749/full?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish a phasor biomarker of harmful autonomic drive in gastric microcirculation.
2) Build a minimally perturbative thermal-tracer sensor to estimate submucosal perfusion dynamics and phase in vivo, repeatedly.
3) Test phase-corrective, gated VNS to restore coherence and prevent stress gastritis compared with open-loop VNS and sham.

Rationale and prior
- Earliest peripheral events in stress gastric injury are microvascular: seconds-scale flow stasis or dysregulated vasodilation precede overt lesions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2945748/?utm_source=openai))
- Gastric microvascular tone is under autonomic control; vagal stimulation can dilate submucosal arterioles via noncholinergic mechanisms, while hypothalamic–vagal drive can also produce mucosal damage if dysregulated. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3706527/?utm_source=openai))
- Respiratory/cardiac rhythms couple to microvascular oscillations; wavelet/phase coherence reveals central–peripheral coupling changes in disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9895103/?utm_source=openai))
- Respiratory- or cardiac-gated aVNS/cVNS is feasible in humans/animals and modulates brainstem cardiovagal responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6592731/?utm_source=openai))
- Thermal diffusion flowmetry provides quantitative perfusion from tiny heat perturbations and is compatible with repeated use. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3345808/?utm_source=openai))

Study design

Models and groups
- Rat water-immersion restraint stress and hypothermic restraint stress models; n≥12/group for power to detect 25% reduction in lesion index.
- Groups (randomized, blinded outcome assessment):
  A) Sham stimulation + sensing only.
  B) Open-loop VNS (tonic).
  C) Closed-loop phase-corrective VNS (respiration-gated).
  D) Closed-loop with reversible conduction block “resets” (brief LFAC/kHz bursts) only when phase error persists >30 s. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8243469/?utm_source=openai))

Sensors and signals
- Gastric mucosal thermal-tracer pad: 5×5 mm, flexible, with microheater (<10 mW, 100–300 ms) and two NTC micro-thermistors spaced 2–3 mm. Every 10 s, deliver a millikelvin thermal pulse; fit transit time, dispersion, and amplitude to infer local flow speed and effective radius. Extract instantaneous phase of the perfusion signal by bandpassing at respiratory (0.15–0.4 Hz) and myogenic (0.06–0.15 Hz) bands, and compute wavelet phase coherence with concurrently recorded respiration and ECG. Safety: temperature rise <0.1°C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3345808/?utm_source=openai))
- Validation optics in a subset: ultrathin endoscopic OCT angiography/Doppler OCT sessions to map submucosal microvasculature and confirm flow/diameter dynamics and coherence signatures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4285613/?utm_source=openai))

Phasor biomarker
- Define ΦR = circular mean phase difference between respiratory cycle and thermal-tracer perfusion oscillation; CR = wavelet phase coherence over sliding 60 s.
- Stress-harm state H(t) flagged when: CR drops below the 5th percentile of baseline for ≥10 s and ΦR drifts >π/4 from baseline mean, or thermal transit time lengthens by ≥20% with increased dispersion—whichever occurs first. Ground truth: Laser Doppler flowmetry and mucosal PO2/tonometry in a subset. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9895103/?utm_source=openai))

Intervention logic
- On H(t) flag:
  1) Deliver exhalation-gated aVNS (300 μs, 20–25 Hz, 30 s) to re-entrain vasomotion with respiration. If ΦR error persists, iterate phase offset to minimize instantaneous phase error (PMU-style correction).
  2) If CR remains low and transit time continues to worsen after two gated attempts, deliver a brief LFAC/kHz cervical burst (1–5 s) to transiently block efferent volleys, then resume phase-locked aVNS to reconstitute coherent drive. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6592731/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
Primary
- Prevention of microvascular failure: sustained restoration of CR and ΦR to within baseline ±1 SD within 60 s of trigger; maintenance of thermal transit metrics within 10% of baseline during stress epochs.
- Reduction in mucosal injury: lesion index and hemorrhage score at 3–6 h; epithelial permeability (51Cr-EDTA flux) and histology. ([citeseerx.ist.psu.edu](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=c3657dd1ba648435a4f6a305c57939f606930637&repid=rep1&type=pdf&utm_source=openai))

Secondary
- Gastric mucosal blood flow by laser Doppler; OCT-A flow density; mast-cell degranulation; acid output; HRV. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7705551/?utm_source=openai))

Statistical/analytical plan
- Mixed-effects models for repeated CR, ΦR, and transit metrics across stress epochs; time-to-restoration Kaplan–Meier with log-rank; lesion index ANOVA with Dunnett correction. Pre-registered decision thresholds for H(t) to avoid p-hacking.

Milestones and falsifiable predictions
M1: Stress induces an early drop in CR and ΦR drift before any macroscopic lesion; thermal transit time lengthens with increased dispersion. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2945748/?utm_source=openai))
M2: Exhalation-gated aVNS restores CR and ΦR faster than tonic VNS and reduces lesion index by ≥40%. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6592731/?utm_source=openai))
M3: When gating fails acutely, a 1–5 s LFAC/kHz block resets phase and accelerates re-entrainment without bradycardia/hypotension. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8243469/?utm_source=openai))

Engineering notes and safety
- Thermal pulses: duty-cycled to keep ΔT<0.1°C; cumulative thermal dose below Arrhenius injury thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3345808/?utm_source=openai))
- aVNS parameters within human-safe ranges; respiratory gating by nasal thermistor/diaphragm EMG. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306452224006547?utm_source=openai))
- Cervical block delivered via bipolar cuff in animals only, with onset-response mitigation (LFAC or pre-conditioning ramp). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8243469/?utm_source=openai))

Translational path
- Human feasibility in endoscopy suites: endoscopic thermal-tracer pad with suction adhesion for 30–60 min monitoring during stress provocation (cold pressor, mental arithmetic). Outcome: demonstration that coherence indices shift with stress and normalize under exhalation-gated aVNS, plus OCT-A confirmation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4285613/?utm_source=openai))

Potential failure modes and contingencies
- If coherence indices are unstable due to motion, add robust wavelet-coherence estimators and respiration-synchronous artifact rejection; cross-validate with OCT-A segmentations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9895103/?utm_source=openai))
- If aVNS fails to re-entrain, evaluate cardiac-synchronized timing as alternate reference or adjust frequency to optimize DMV/NTS engagement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9637096/?utm_source=openai))
- If thermal sensing sensitivity is insufficient, increase inter-sensor spacing modestly (improves time-of-flight precision) or reduce pulse width with higher SNR thermistors while maintaining ΔT safety.

Impact
This proposal reframes stress gastritis prevention as phase control of neurovascular coupling, replacing amplitude-only monitoring with coherence-targeted intervention. If validated, it provides a repeatable, mechanism-grounded, closed-loop therapy that interrupts the brain-to-stomach stress pathway before tissue injury forms. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-023-00866-z?utm_source=openai))

Title
Causal neuro-epithelial drivers of barrier microdomain failure in atopic dermatitis mapped by Patch‑seq and impedance‑resolved skin‑on‑chip

Hypothesis–question
Do defined pruriceptor excitability states, conditioned by type‑2 cytokines and microbial products, causally precede and localize epidermal barrier microdomain failure that then recruits and programs immune cells in atopic dermatitis? If so, can targeted neuromodulation or microbe‑derived metabolites reverse the sequence and normalize barrier and immune single‑cell states?

Atomic strategy
Treat barrier dysfunction as a spatiotemporal readout of an upstream neuro‑epithelial circuit. Use Patch‑seq to capture neuron firing/transcriptome states while simultaneously tracking barrier microdomain integrity with high‑density impedance spectroscopy and aligning those phenotypes to matched single‑cell states of adjacent keratinocytes and immune cells under controlled microbial conditions.

Rationale
- IL‑4/IL‑13 suppress keratinocyte barrier gene programs and lipids, linking type‑2 inflammation to barrier weakness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11909353/?utm_source=openai))
- IL‑31 acts via IL‑31RA on sensory neurons to drive pruritus and contributes to AD pathology; clinical IL‑31RA blockade is now approved in AD, establishing targetability of the neuro‑immune node. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3960328/?utm_source=openai))
- S. aureus secreted proteases/toxins activate/primes pruriceptors and damage tight junctions, providing a microbial path to neurogenic itch and barrier loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10669764/?utm_source=openai))
- Commensal AHR‑ligand metabolites can restore keratinocyte barrier programs, suggesting a microbiome‑to‑epithelium counter‑axis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))
- Patch‑seq links electrophysiology to single‑cell transcriptomes in DRG neurons, but has not been used to couple pruriceptor states to barrier failure and immune recruitment in skin. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8578708/?utm_source=openai))
- High‑density microelectrode impedance arrays resolve epithelial barrier heterogeneity at high spatial/temporal resolution and are compatible with organ‑on‑chip. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724121/?utm_source=openai))
- Neuron–keratinocyte organ‑on‑chip co‑cultures exist, enabling human‑relevant innervation with real‑time electrophysiology. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/doi/d5lc00867k?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build a human innervated, immune‑competent, microbiome‑tunable skin‑on‑chip with impedance‑resolved barrier readout.
- Components: primary human keratinocytes and fibroblasts (patient‑derived where available), iPSC‑derived human sensory neurons enriched for pruriceptors, and autologous PBMCs (enriched for ILC2/T cells). Establish air–liquid interface epidermis.
- Sensors: integrate a CMOS high‑density impedance microelectrode array under the epidermis to map barrier microdomains continuously.
- Microbial control: apply defined inputs—S. aureus protease‑rich supernatant/α‑toxin; commensal consortia; purified metabolites (e.g., indolelactic acid).
- Outputs: baseline and perturbed barrier impedance maps; live imaging for scratch‑like mechanical insults (controlled microrubbing).

Aim 2. Link pruriceptor excitability states to immediate epithelial and immune single‑cell programs that precede barrier failure.
- Perturbations: IL‑31, IL‑4/IL‑13, PAR1/2 agonists, staphylococcal proteases; commensal AHR ligands.
- Patch‑seq: perform whole‑cell recordings from identified neuronal fibers/varicosities projecting into the epidermal compartment; immediately harvest the recorded neuron for scRNA‑seq from the same cell.
- Time‑locking: when local impedance drops below a predefined threshold (onset of microdomain failure), micro‑biopsy the corresponding region for scRNA‑seq/spatial transcriptomics of keratinocytes and immune cells.
- Readouts: neuronal intrinsic excitability metrics and neuropeptide/cytokine receptor transcription; keratinocyte junction/lipid synthesis stress programs; immune activation/chemokine modules; ligand–receptor edges reconstructed with temporal ordering.

Aim 3. Mechanism‑based intervention tests targeted to the earliest causal node identified in Aim 2.
- Neuronal node: TRPA1/TRPV1 antagonists; NK1R antagonism if substance‑P signatures dominate; IL‑31RA blockade proxy (nemolizumab‑equivalent Fc fragment) for validation of axis dependence. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK200927/?utm_source=openai))
- Epithelial node: AHR agonist metabolites (e.g., indolelactic acid) or PPAR agonists if junction/lipid programs are primary; protease inhibitors if proteolysis precedes failure. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbial node: antistaphylococcal biologics or phage if staphylococcal factors temporally precede impedance collapse; add‑back of commensals that restore barrier signatures.
- Success criteria: reversal of local impedance minima (magnitude and kinetics), normalization of keratinocyte/immune single‑cell states, reduced neuronal excitability signatures.

Model and methods
- Organ‑on‑chip: multilayer PDMS or thermoplastic device with apical air interface; embedded CMOS HD‑MEA beneath a porous ECM‑coated membrane supporting the epidermis; perfused dermal channel with immune cell access.
- Neurons: hiPSC‑derived pruriceptors matured 6–8 weeks; confirm expression of IL31RA, TRPV1/TRPA1, Mrgpr receptors; axonal guidance into epidermis via microgrooves.
- Microbiome: sterile baseline; then add defined S. aureus strains or commensal mixes; deliver purified metabolites.
- Electrophysiology: targeted whole‑cell recordings of intraepidermal fibers; current‑clamp ramps and pruritogen applications; post‑record aspiration for Patch‑seq library prep.
- Single‑cell profiling: 10x multiome for keratinocyte/immune micro‑biopsies adjacent to recorded neurons; spatial RNA with targeted junction/immune panels.
- Data integration: causal inference via time‑aligned datasets—neuron firing → keratinocyte early genes → immune modules → impedance trajectory; ligand–receptor with temporal constraints.

Primary outcomes and decision rules
- Causality: neuronal excitability/neuropeptide transcriptional state must rise before local impedance decline and before epithelial stress/chemokine induction to infer an initiating neuronal driver. Conversely, epithelial stress preceding neuron changes indicates epithelial initiation.
- Microbial modulation: shifts in neuronal excitability and barrier signatures attributable to microbial inputs define a neuron–microbiome axis; AHR‑metabolite rescue defines an epithelial metabolic lever.
- Therapeutic selection rules: choose the earliest perturbed node per context; test single‑agent and minimal combinations; advance only if impedance recovery and single‑cell state normalization co‑occur.

Validation and translatability
- Cross‑check neuronal findings with published DRG Patch‑seq features to ensure pruriceptor identity mapping. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8578708/?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmark impedance phenotypes against established HD‑MEA epithelial barrier mapping. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724121/?utm_source=openai))
- Pharmacologic face validity using IL‑31RA pathway blockade and TRP antagonists; clinical relevance supported by approvals/late‑phase data. ([dailymed-beta.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed-beta.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=e9229ef1-ac60-4c24-afb6-009d3c781687&type=display&utm_source=openai))

Potential results and interpretations
- Finding A: IL‑31 raises pruriceptor excitability that temporally precedes barrier dips and chemokine induction; rescue by IL‑31RA blockade or TRPA1 antagonism implies a neuron‑first loop in susceptible microdomains. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3960328/?utm_source=openai))
- Finding B: S. aureus proteases trigger PAR‑dependent neuronal activation with concurrent tight‑junction transcript loss; protease inhibition or PAR1 antagonism restores barrier, revealing a microbe‑to‑neuron‑to‑barrier path. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10669764/?utm_source=openai))
- Finding C: Commensal AHR ligands reduce neuronal hyperexcitability indirectly and restore junction/lipid programs; topical AHR‑metabolite therapy is prioritized. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Month 6: chip assembled; stable impedance baselines and epidermal stratification achieved.
- Month 12: Patch‑seq throughput of ≥20 neurons/condition with matched micro‑biopsies; first causal chains resolved for IL‑31 and S. aureus inputs.
- Month 18: Intervention screen completed; mechanism‑based responders defined; candidate topical neuromodulators/metabolites nominated.

Risk management
- Low Patch‑seq yield: adopt optimized protocols and pre‑enrichment of target fibers; fallback to juxtacellular MEA‑triggered capture with snRNA‑seq. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/65482?utm_source=openai))
- Neuronal maturation variability: batch QC by transcriptomic and functional markers; use donor‑matched iPSCs where possible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11974934/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbial overgrowth: use flow‑controlled inocula and short‑pulse exposures; include toxin/protease‑defined inputs to isolate mechanisms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6409874/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanism‑based therapeutic outputs
- Patient/context‑specific algorithms: if neuron‑first signature detected, prioritize IL‑31 pathway inhibitors, TRP/NK1R modulators; if epithelial‑first, prioritize AHR/PPAR agonists and barrier peptides; if microbe‑first, deploy antistaphylococcal or protease‑targeted strategies. ([dailymed-beta.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed-beta.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=e9229ef1-ac60-4c24-afb6-009d3c781687&type=display&utm_source=openai))

Impact
This platform closes the loop among the four AD domains—barrier, immune, neuro‑immune, and microbiome—by time‑locking neuronal states to barrier microdomain failure and immune recruitment, enabling direct, mechanism‑anchored therapeutic selection and de‑risked translation.

Title
A tunable extracellular “delay line” at the skin interface governs the barrier-versus-disease decision in atopic dermatitis

Central hypothesis-question
Does loss or remodeling of the apical extracellular matrix’s glycosaminoglycan (GAG) filtering convert identical immune, microbial, and neuronal inputs into pathogenic temporal waveforms that flip keratinocytes and cutaneous sentinels into atopic dermatitis (AD) attractor states—and can restoring this filtering veto disease initiation?

Rationale
- AD emerges from coupled barrier dysfunction, type‑2 immune skewing, neuro-immune pruritus circuits, and dysbiosis; IL‑4/13 suppress keratinocyte barrier programs; IL‑31/TRP channel pathways and neuropeptides drive itch–inflammation loops; Staphylococcus aureus predominance and its products aggravate disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8119845/?utm_source=openai))
- Heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) and related GAGs at cell surfaces and basement membranes bind and sequester many cytokines and chemokines, shaping their spatial–temporal profiles (“signal buffering”). Changes in HS abundance/sulfation and heparanase activity modulate retention, gradient formation, and release, thereby altering cell signaling kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9097616/?utm_source=openai))
- Current AD skin-on-chip models largely impose disease via exogenous cytokines; few treat the apical interfacial matrix as a tunable signal router whose kinetics determine downstream fate. This gap constrains mechanistic attribution and therapeutic discovery. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8878506/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat the barrier’s extracellular interface as a computational filter. By tuning its GAG content, charge density, and porosity, we reshape the delivery kinetics (not dose) of type‑2 cytokines, neuropeptides, and microbial factors to target cells. If disease arises when specific signals arrive too fast, too prolonged, or in a pathologic order, then restoring the interface’s “slow‑pass” filter should veto transition to AD states despite unchanged total input.

Platform
Human immuno‑neuro‑epidermal skin‑on‑a‑chip with a tunable apical GAG-rich diffusion layer (primary platform; satisfies the model constraint). Confirmatory ex vivo tests with human skin equivalents.

Specific aims and methods

Aim 1. Build a human skin-on-chip that encodes a tunable extracellular delay line and supports all four AD axes.
- Architecture
  - Apical channel: stratified human keratinocyte epidermis at air–liquid interface over a replaceable hydrogel interlayer (the “delay line”) whose HS/CS content, 6‑O‑sulfation, and crosslink density are programmable; optional heparanase-sensitive crosslinks. Basal dermal fibroblast matrix with microvascular flow.
  - Immune axis: perfused compartment with human Langerhans-like DCs/monocyte-derived DCs and ILC2/T cells; efferent channel connected to a microengineered lymphoid module to emulate skin–node crosstalk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13005681/?utm_source=openai))
  - Neuro axis: iPSC-derived human TRPV1/TRPA1+ pruriceptors interfaced basally; optogenetic or capsaicin/AITC stimulation to deliver defined firing patterns. Neuroimmune relevance in AD is established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9082890/?utm_source=openai))
  - Microbiome axis: apical colonization with defined S. aureus strains and protective commensals (e.g., Cutibacterium acnes) to model dysbiosis and competition. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37232427/?utm_source=openai))
- Verification
  - The delay line’s transport properties quantified by FRAP and tracer proteins; measurement of effective diffusion coefficients and reversible binding capacities for IL‑4, IL‑13, chemokines, and alarmins.
  - Baseline chip recapitulates IL‑4/13‑induced AD-like molecular features (e.g., reduced FLG/LOR/IVL, pSTAT6 activation). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8119845/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test whether kinetics imposed by the delay line, rather than input dose, determine disease-state transitions.
- Experimental design
  - Deliver identical integrated doses of: (a) IL‑4/13 ± IL‑31; (b) neurogenic bursts (TRPV1/TRPA1 activation); (c) S. aureus supernatant/toxins; (d) scratch mimetics. Vary only the delay line’s parameters (HS density/sulfation, degradability, pore size) to reshape temporal profiles at the basal membrane without changing total exposure.
  - Readouts across time: multi-compartment scRNA‑seq/CITE‑seq of keratinocytes, DCs/ILC2/T cells, and neurons; phospho-proteomics (STAT, NF‑κB, MAPK, YAP/TAZ); barrier metrics (TEER, lipidomics); microbial load and AMP expression.
  - Causal inference: perturb-sequence experiments (e.g., microbe→neuro vs neuro→Th2) under “fast” vs “slow” filters to see which sequence flips keratinocyte states first; compute “veto power” of each axis from early-response magnitudes and state-transition probabilities.
- Mechanistic expectations
  - Increasing HS content/sulfation lengthens residence times and promotes gradient formation, reducing rapid spikes at receptors; heparanase-sensitive gels release bound ligands, converting steps into pulses. If the AD transition requires a fast sustained STAT6 or pruritogen waveform, high‑HS filters should veto it. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4554917/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Map minimal control switches and nominate mechanism‑directed therapies that restore kinetic filtering.
- Identify cell-intrinsic switches: early keratinocyte attractor transitions (loss of differentiation genes; alarmin upshift) under “fast” vs “slow” delivery. Link to immune (DC activation, ILC2 cytokines) and neuro (peptide release) states.
- Therapeutic tests on‑chip
  - Interface reparatives: topical HS-mimetic hydrogels or ECM‑glycan formulations to reconstitute apical buffering and gradient shaping; test heparanase inhibitors to preserve HS scaffolds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11115568/?utm_source=openai))
  - Canonical pathway comparators: IL‑4Rα blockade/JAK inhibition, TRPA1/TRPV1 antagonists, and microbiome modulation (commensal add-back) to benchmark efficacy and synergy with interface repair. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S266702672200039X?utm_source=openai))
- Decision criterion
  - A therapy is “mechanism‑concordant” if it restores slow‑pass filtering metrics and prevents state transitions under unchanged total inputs more effectively than receptor blockade alone.

Key measurements and analytics
- Temporal deconvolution: cytokine/neuropeptide time–concentration curves measured above/below the delay line; integrate with single‑cell state trajectories to estimate thresholded “waveform–state” transfer functions.
- Spatial mapping: spatial indexing/scRNA‑seq to link apical micro-colonies of S. aureus and local HS density to underlying cell states.
- Cross-axis coupling: quantify how neurogenic bursts alter DC/ILC2 activation when the filter is tight vs leaky.

Validation and boundary testing
- Ex vivo HSEs with tunable GAG coatings to replicate filter effects. Compare to immunocompetent skin-on-chip literature to ensure external validity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13136756/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes
- Mechanistic proof that kinetic filtering at the barrier interface is a veto node for AD initiation.
- A quantitative atlas linking ligand waveforms to keratinocyte/immune/neural state transitions.
- A therapeutic class: interface‑centric glycan biomaterials that restore physiological signal kinetics and synergize with existing cytokine or neuromodulatory blockers.

Feasibility and innovation
- HSPG/GAG control of cytokine gradients and retention is well supported; altering HS content/sulfation is a practical engineering handle in gels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4554917/?utm_source=openai))
- AD skin chips exist but typically induce pathology via cytokine cocktails; repositioning the extracellular interface as the primary control dial is a conceptual and technical advance directly tied to disease mechanisms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8878506/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- Year 1: Fabricate chips; calibrate delay-line kinetics; reproduce IL‑4/13 barrier suppression and neurogenic responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8119845/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Establish dose–waveform dissociation; identify waveform thresholds that trigger AD attractor transitions by scRNA‑seq.
- Year 3: Demonstrate that HS-mimetic interface repair prevents transitions under pathogenic inputs and outperforms or synergizes with IL‑4Rα/JAK or TRPA1/TRPV1 blockade.

Mechanistic guardrails
- The proposal does not assume novel biology; it leverages established HSPG–ligand binding principles and known AD circuits while reframing the interface as a kinetic controller. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9097616/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Healthy-neighbor backup signals as developmental stabilizers in atopic dermatitis: a patterned skin-on-chip to discover and time-lock paracrine, mechanical, and microbial cues that prevent lifelong immune and neuronal imprinting

Integrated hypothesis and goal
Keratinocytes in healthy microdomains emit a small, conserved set of stabilizing cues—paracrine metabolites/cytokines, mechanotransductive adhesion/tension states, and microbiota-metabolite outputs—that keep local ILC2s, dendritic cells, and sensory neurites plastic during a brief postnatal window. Failure of these “backup” cues adjacent to barrier-impaired keratinocytes locks in hyperinnervation and type-2–skewed immunity, predisposing to chronic AD. Discovering these cues and their timing will enable barrier-agnostic, neonatal interventions that prevent the durable pathogenic programming of immune and nerve circuits. Early-life ILC2 priming by keratinocyte TSLP under microbiome influence supports a defined developmental window; AD features increased intraepidermal nerve density with reduced repulsive Sema3A from keratinocytes; keratinocyte mechanotransduction via YAP/TAZ integrates barrier stress and inflammatory outputs. Dysbiosis with Staphylococcus aureus overgrowth amplifies this loop. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38198924/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Reconstruct side-by-side WT and AD-mutant keratinocyte microdomains with deterministic edges on an innervated, immune-competent, microbiome-colonized skin-on-chip, then (i) quantify how WT edges maintain immune/neuronal plasticity in adjacent AD domains, and (ii) identify the minimal edge-delivered cue set that substitutes for “healthy-neighbor” function when provided during the neonatal-equivalent window.

Model systems
- Primary platform: Patterned, innervated, microbiome-ready skin-on-chip with microcontact-printed hydrogel niche arrays that tile isogenic WT and AD-mutant keratinocytes in repeating microdomains at air–liquid interface; microcontact printing provides precise keratinocyte adhesion geometry and edge control. DRG neuron axons are compartmentalized to innervate the epidermal face. Defined microbial consortia colonize the stratum corneum. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2693873/?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo timing/translation: Photoactivatable Cre transgenic mice (DiLiCre or ePA-Cre) crossed to keratinocyte reporters/conditional AD alleles enable spatial–temporal induction of mutant keratinocyte patches at P0–P7 to validate timing and region specificity of candidate cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9616875/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build a side-by-side WT/AD keratinocyte skin-on-chip that quantitatively reports barrier, immune, neuronal, and microbiome states at microdomain edges.
- Engineering: Use microcontact printing to deposit ECM stripes/dots (fibronectin/laminin) on PEG-based hydrogels to seed alternating WT and AD-mutant (e.g., FLG−/− or DSG1−/−) keratinocyte microdomains from isogenic lines, generating standardized edges of 50–200 μm. Maintain ALI differentiation. Patterned DRG axons project into WT/AD regions via microgrooves; introduce a six-strain human skin commensal consortium ± S. aureus to test dysbiosis. TEER and lipidomics quantify barrier; bacterial 16S/metatranscriptomics quantify colonization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2693873/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts (single-cell required): scRNA-seq of keratinocytes, ILC2s/DCs, and neurons from WT vs AD domains and “edge bins,” with feature barcoding for domain-of-origin. Markers: barrier (FLG/LOR/ceramide enzymes), alarmins (TSLP/IL33), YAP/TAZ targets, axon-guidance (SEMA3A/NGF), itch/neuropeptide pathways (IL31RA/TRPA1; SP/CGRP), ILC2 activation (GATA3/IL5/IL13), and DC states; spatial transcriptomics validates edge gradients. Outcomes: Identify WT-edge factors and mechanical states that correlate with suppressed ILC2 priming and restrained neurite growth in adjacent AD microdomains. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37326015/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Causal mapping of “backup” cues by edge-localized delivery and mechanical tuning.
- Candidate paracrine cues guided by Aim 1 and prior biology: controlled AHR agonism (low-dose tapinarof or commensal-derived ligands) to normalize keratinocyte programs and dampen Th2 cross-talk; Sema3A to cap neurite ingrowth; transient EGF-family pulses to resolve stress keratinocyte states. Immobilize candidates at edges via click chemistry or heparin-binding domains versus soluble delivery to distinguish short-range stabilization from bulk effects. Mechanically tune edges by modulating ECM ligand density and stiffness to reduce pathologic YAP/TAZ activation in AD domains. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42057395/?utm_source=openai))
- Measurements: Edge-resolved scRNA-seq/ATAC-seq for keratinocyte/immune/neuron state changes; live Ca2+ imaging of DRG endings and optogenetic activation to measure excitability; neurite density/branching; ILC2 cytokines (IL-5/IL-13) and DC activation; commensal retention versus S. aureus expansion. Success criterion: A minimal, two- to three-component cue set that, when confined to edges during the maturation window, simultaneously (i) reduces ILC2 priming and DC alarmin signatures, (ii) limits neurite overgrowth and excitability, (iii) maintains commensal dominance under S. aureus challenge, and (iv) improves TEER/lipid metrics in adjacent AD domains.

Aim 3. Developmental timing and prevention in vivo.
- Strategy: Induce keratinocyte AD patches neonatally (P0–P7) by light-gated Cre to define the window when alarmin and neurite programs become persistent. Deliver the minimal cue set identified in Aim 2 using a neonatal, skin-adherent patch that releases edge-targeted factors (e.g., tapinarof microdose + Sema3A) over 48–72 h. Outcomes at weaning and adulthood after standardized epicutaneous challenges (e.g., MC903 or allergen): skin scRNA-seq (keratinocytes/immune), TRM and ILC2 pools, intraepidermal nerve density/excitability, and spontaneous S. aureus expansion. Success criterion: Neonatal, barrier-agnostic intervention prevents durable type-2 imprinting and hyperinnervation despite persistent barrier gene defects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9616875/?utm_source=openai))

Key experimental details

- Keratinocyte genotypes: human or mouse isogenic lines harboring FLG−/−, DSG1−/−, or SPINK5−/− edits; domain identity encoded by fluorescent barcodes to link scRNA-seq cells to microdomain of origin.
- Immune modules: neonatal-equivalent ILC2s and cDC2s added basally; measure ILC2 priming states and DC IL-23/TSLP responsiveness in line with early-life programming. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38198924/?utm_source=openai))
- Neuronal modules: hiPSC-derived DRG-like neurons or primary mouse DRG in compartmentalized chips; microgrooves standardize innervation density; quantify TRPV1/TRPA1 responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10023681/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbiome modules: commensal consortium (e.g., S. epidermidis/Cutibacterium/Corynebacterium) ± S. aureus to model dysbiosis known in AD; monitor shifts and host AMP expression. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2023.1151527/full?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanotransduction metrics: YAP/TAZ nuclear localization at edges; ROCK–Rho sensitivity to mechanical tuning; correlation with alarmin expression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9986521/?utm_source=openai))

Data integration and analysis
- Edge-centric multi-omics: deconvolve gradients of transcripts and chromatin states from WT to AD across the edge; infer ligand–receptor signaling (NicheNet/CellChat) linking keratinocytes to ILC2s/neurons; couple with microbial metatranscriptomes to identify host–microbe metabolite interactions.
- Causality tests: perturb candidate cue nodes with edge-immobilized ligands/antagonists and mechanical tuning; assess necessity/sufficiency by loss/gain at edges.

Therapeutic translation
- Product concept: neonatal “edge-mimetic” patch delivering a minimal cue set (e.g., low-dose AHR agonist and Sema3A) for 2–3 days during the defined window; intent is to preemptively stabilize immune–neuronal set points without correcting barrier genetics. Clinical plausibility is supported by the safety and efficacy of topical AHR agonism in AD, and by data implicating Sema3A in controlling epidermal hyperinnervation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42057395/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision points
- M1 (Months 0–9): Functional patterned chip with reproducible WT/AD edges; baseline multi-omic atlas linking WT edges to reduced ILC2 priming and neurite growth. Go/No-Go: reproducible edge effects across donors/genotypes.
- M2 (Months 9–18): Minimal cue set identified that rescues ≥3 of 4 domains (barrier, immune, neuro-immune, microbiome) in AD domains when edge-delivered. Go/No-Go: effect size ≥30% improvement vs vehicle.
- M3 (Months 18–30): In vivo window defined by light-gated induction; neonatal patch prevents durable TRM/ILC2 expansion and hyperinnervation after later challenge. Go/No-Go: sustained reduction in ILC2/Th2 signatures and nerve density with maintained commensal balance.

Anticipated outcomes and impact
This proposal yields (i) a mechanistic, edge-resolved map of how healthy keratinocyte microdomains keep immune and neuronal circuits flexible during early life; (ii) a minimal, actionable cue set that substitutes for “healthy neighbor” signals; and (iii) a barrier-agnostic, time-limited neonatal intervention concept to prevent chronic AD programming across all four pathophysiological domains. If successful, it reframes AD prevention as restoration of developmental stabilizers rather than repair of the barrier alone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38198924/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Tempo-gated microbiome control of epidermal fate and neuroimmune activation in atopic dermatitis

Unified hypothesis–question
Do the tempo and quorum-sensing (QS) state of early skin colonization instruct epidermal cell-state trajectories and neuroimmune circuits that culminate in atopic dermatitis (AD), and can temporally targeted microbiome and neuromodulatory interventions prevent this disease trajectory? This posits that QS-driven virulence programs in Staphylococcus aureus and commensal-derived aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) ligands are upstream instructors of keratinocyte differentiation, IL-31–centered itch circuits, and type 2 inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7426015/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Control the history (tempo) and QS-state of microbial exposure in gnotobiotic, AD‑prone mice and treat the experiment as an unbroken causal chain. Continuously measure interstitial mediators and neural activity while resolving cell-state transitions with scRNA‑seq and spatial transcriptomics. Infer and validate directed edges from microbe→keratinocyte→immune→neural and intervene at tempo-defined inflection points.

Rationale
- S. aureus Agr-QS regulates virulence (e.g., δ-toxin, PSMs) that damages barrier and activates mast cells and keratinocyte alarmins; Agr activity in infant skin predicts later AD. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6658404/?utm_source=openai))
- Commensal metabolites (e.g., indolelactic acid) activate keratinocyte AHR, upregulate filaggrin/loricrin/tight junctions, and suppress alarmins. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))
- IL‑31 is a validated neuroimmune pruritogen in AD; its blockade reduces itch and inflammation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1645095/full?utm_source=openai))
- Dermal microdialysis enables continuous interstitial cytokine/metabolite sampling; peripheral sensory activity can be recorded in vivo; vagus/peripheral stimulation modulates skin inflammation and itch. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6456961/?utm_source=openai))

Model systems
- Gnotobiotic, transgenic AD-prone mice (e.g., filaggrin-deficient) with dorsal skin windows.
- Optional parallel skin-on-chip from the same genotype for spatially patterned, within-chip colonization.

Colonization programs (tempo and QS design)
- Pathogenic ramp: S. aureus (Agr+) delivered as a slow exponential ramp to matched area under the curve (AUC) as “fast-bolus” exposure; an Agr– isogenic strain controls for QS. Include arms with QS quenchers (e.g., solonamide B or CoNS AIPs) to dissociate density from virulence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6093339/?utm_source=openai))
- Protective ramp: commensal-first consortium (Cutibacterium acnes strain producing indolelactic acid; CoNS that quorum‑quench Agr) introduced gradually before any S. aureus challenge. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))

Longitudinal readouts (treated as one continuous experiment)
- Interstitial microdialysis via dermal probe: 15–30 min fractions for cytokines/chemokines (TSLP, IL‑33, IL‑31, IL‑4/IL‑13), protease activity, staphylococcal toxins/PSMs, AHR‑ligand surrogates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6456961/?utm_source=openai))
- Peripheral neural activity: repeated in vivo DRG GCaMP6 imaging epochs aligned to skin events; optional peri‑saphenous nerve cuff recordings during sampling epochs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36847407/?utm_source=openai))
- Barrier physiology: transepidermal water loss, pH, lipidomics of stratum corneum.
- Single‑cell/spatial omics: serial skin scRNA‑seq (keratinocytes, Langerhans/DCs, ILC2/Th subsets, mast/eosinophils, fibroblasts), with spatial transcriptomics to map niches.
- Microbiome state: metagenomics for community and Agr‑activity reporter strain luminescence/RT‑qPCR for RNAIII as a temporal QS marker. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140505/?utm_source=openai))

Causal inference and analysis
- Construct dynamic Bayesian/state‑space models linking QS markers and metabolite/alarmin streams to cell‑state transitions (pseudotime) and neural spikes.
- Identify tempo thresholds (“bifurcation points”) where:
  1) Keratinocyte differentiation diverges toward FLG/LOR-high vs KRT6/16/SPR-high stress states. AHR target induction used as barrier‑stabilizing marker. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7432778/?utm_source=openai))
  2) IL‑31 module emergence precedes/prioritizes C‑fiber activation and Th2 polarization. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1645095/full?utm_source=openai))
  3) Agr‑dependent protease/toxin surges precede alarmin upswings (IL‑1α/IL‑36α) and IL‑17/Th2 crosstalk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12162026/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Demonstrate that colonization tempo and QS-state instruct keratinocyte fate.
- Compare slow‑ramp Agr+ vs Agr– vs QS‑quenched S. aureus on keratinocyte trajectories by scRNA‑seq and spatial maps; quantify AHR target gene induction vs stress/proliferation modules. Predicted: slow commensal‑first ramp stabilizes AHR/EDC programs; Agr+ ramps shift to protease‑injury states. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7432778/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Resolve the directed microbe→alarmin/IL‑31→neural pathway.
- Align interstitial IL‑31/TSLP/IL‑33 dynamics to DRG activity; test temporality with Granger causality. Perturb with anti‑IL‑31R dosed only at predicted surge windows; expect attenuation of neural bursts and downstream Th2 signatures with minimal overall exposure. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1645095/full?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Validate QS as an upstream control node of the AD network.
- Apply QS inhibitors (e.g., solonamide B) or commensal AIPs during identified pre‑bifurcation windows without changing S. aureus load; assess barrier, immune, and neural outcomes. Prediction: preventing Agr activation prevents the IL‑31/pruriceptor/Th2 cascade even when bacterial burden matches Agr+ arms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6093339/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Test neuromodulatory interruption of the itch–inflammation loop at tempo‑defined inflection points.
- Closed‑loop peripheral or auricular vagus stimulation when neural spikes exceed model thresholds; measure effects on interstitial cytokines and cell states. Prediction: neuromodulation blunts IL‑31‑linked activity and reduces inflammatory modules, validating directionality. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42281200/?fc=None&ff=20260613031052&v=2.20.0&utm_source=openai))

Key measurements and endpoints
- Barrier domain: FLG/LOR/IVL and lipid synthesis gene modules; TEWL; tight junction markers; AHR target induction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7432778/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune domain: Th2 (IL‑4/IL‑13), alarmins (TSLP, IL‑33), IL‑17/IL‑22 modules; antigen‑presenting cell activation states.
- Neuro‑immune domain: IL‑31/IL‑31RA expression across cell types; DRG activity metrics; pruriceptor channel expression (TRPA1/TRPV1) and neuropeptides (SP/CGRP). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7027518/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbiome domain: Agr activity (RNAIII), toxin/protease profiles, commensal metabolite signatures; community composition.

Experimental controls
- Load‑matched S. aureus arms differing only in QS state (Agr+ vs Agr– vs QS‑quenched).
- Commensal‑first vs S. aureus‑first priority effects under identical total AUC.
- Vehicle vs targeted timing of biologics/neuromodulation.

Mechanism‑based intervention prototypes
- Tempo therapy: commensal‑first seeding with AHR‑ligand producers (e.g., C. acnes strains producing indolelactic acid) to pre‑install barrier‑stabilizing programs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))
- QS‑targeting: topical delivery of Agr inhibitors (solonamide B; commensal AIPs; small‑molecule Agr blockers) during pre‑bifurcation windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6093339/?utm_source=openai))
- Biomarker‑timed anti‑IL‑31R: dose only when interstitial IL‑31 rises and DRG activity forecasts a surge. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1645095/full?utm_source=openai))
- Adjunct neuromodulation: closed‑loop taVNS/peripheral nerve stimulation at predicted inflection points to suppress cytokine peaks and neural sensitization. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42281200/?fc=None&ff=20260613031052&v=2.20.0&utm_source=openai))

Statistical and computational plan
- Power for repeated‑measures mixed models on interstitial cytokines and neural metrics; scRNA‑seq differential state analysis with pseudobulk and lineage trajectory inference.
- Causal discovery with time‑lagged Bayesian networks; validation by perturbation (QS inhibitors, anti‑IL‑31R, neuromodulation) and do‑calculus contrasts.
- Pre‑registered primary outcomes: 1) divergence in keratinocyte differentiation trajectory scores attributable to QS/tempo; 2) directionality from IL‑31→DRG activity→Th2 module; 3) prevention of AD‑like pathology by time‑locked QS inhibition without changing S. aureus burden.

Feasibility notes
- Cutaneous microdialysis for cytokines is established; DRG in vivo calcium imaging is routine; Agr reporting and QS inhibitors have in vivo precedent; commensal AHR‑ligand effects on barrier are validated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6456961/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision gates
- M1: Establish matched‑AUC colonization ramps and confirm separable QS trajectories (RNAIII). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140505/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Detect a tempo‑dependent bifurcation in keratinocyte trajectories linked to AHR targets.
- M3: Show IL‑31 rise precedes DRG bursts; anti‑IL‑31R blocks bursts and downstream Th2 modules on a just‑in‑time schedule. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1645095/full?utm_source=openai))
- M4: Demonstrate that QS inhibition during the pre‑bifurcation window prevents AD‑like pathology without reducing S. aureus load. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6093339/?utm_source=openai))
- Go/No‑Go: If no directed edges are validated, pivot to organ‑on‑chip spatial heterogeneity platform to amplify contrasts while preserving tempo control.

Anticipated outcomes and impact
- Mechanistic proof that early microbial tempo and QS state program epidermal and neuroimmune trajectories toward or away from AD.
- A minimal control set—commensal AHR‑ligand provision, QS‑state suppression, and biomarker‑timed anti‑IL‑31/neuromodulation—constituting a preventive, mechanism‑based therapy stack for AD that targets upstream instructive events rather than downstream inflammation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42335903/?utm_source=openai))

Compliance with constraints
- Transgenic gnotobiotic mice; optional skin‑on‑chip.
- scRNA‑seq central to analysis with spatial transcriptomics and proteomics.
- Mechanism focus across barrier, immune, neuro‑immune, microbiome axes.
- Therapeutic proposals grounded in validated mechanisms and timed by causal readouts.

text:
Title
Edge-state tipping points govern natural remission in atopic dermatitis and can be identified and locked in with event-triggered, minimal-dose interventions

Integrated hypothesis–question
Does spontaneous remission in atopic dermatitis (AD) occur when local microenvironments at lesion margins cross discrete, coupled thresholds in barrier integrity, type-2 inflammation, pruriceptor excitability, and Staphylococcus aureus quorum activity—and can precisely timed, spatially restricted micro-interventions at these crossings push the system into a stable remission basin? This asks whether remission is a thresholded, multi-axis state transition rather than a gradual continuum. Evidence that type-2 cytokines impair barrier lipids and differentiation; that IL-31/IL-4/IL-13 sensitize pruriceptors and amplify itch–scratch; and that S. aureus agr-controlled virulence fuels inflammation supports this framing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Instrument AD lesions to detect imminent threshold down-crossings (barrier: TEWL; immune: IL-4/IL-13 reporter signal; neuro: neurite Ca2+ burst rate; microbiome: S. aureus bioluminescence as a quorum/bioburden proxy). Sample immediately before/after each event with scRNA-seq and spatial multi-omics to identify the minimal concurrent cell-state changes that predict durable local remission, then deliver brief, localized “lock-in” pulses (barrier lipid metabolism agonists, neuromodulators, and targeted anti-staphylococcal measures) only at those windows. This minimizes dose and exploits system hysteresis. Continuous TEWL/pruritus wearables and bacterial reporters make the event triggers feasible; IL-4/IL-13 dual-reporter mice and organ-on-chip models render immune and neuronal transitions observable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12528383/?utm_source=openai))

Model systems, constraints, and readouts
- In vivo longitudinal mouse platform: Dorsal skinfold chamber on inducible reporter/conditional mice permits repeated imaging and micro-biopsies. Use IL-4/IL-13 dual-reporter (4C13R) background; optionally add keratinocyte-specific Ahr or Elovl perturbations (K14-CreER). Colonize skin with bioluminescent S. aureus (LAC::lux or similar) to track bacterial burden/quorum with IVIS. Mount micro-TEWL sensors over the window and image cutaneous sensory axons (Pirt-GCaMP) for Ca2+ event rates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9270450/?utm_source=openai))
- Human-relevant chip: Spatial multi-omics skin-on-a-chip with iPSC-derived sensory neurons and commensal microbiota. Induce AD-like states with IL-4/IL-13 and dryness; integrate TEER/optical TEWL proxies and microvalves for event-triggered sampling and drug/microbe pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8878506/?utm_source=openai))
- Omics core: Event-triggered spatially registered scRNA-seq/snATAC-seq of epidermis, immune, and neuronal-associated niches; 16S/shotgun on swabs; targeted lipidomics (ceramide chain-length) and proteomics on matched micro-samples. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Detect and map local threshold crossings during natural lesion improvement.
- Barrier: Define TEWL down-crossing events and corresponding increases in differentiation markers and long-chain ceramides in edge keratinocytes. Expect recovery of FLG/LOR, ELOVL1/3/6, and SREBP/PPAR programs as barriers reseal. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune: Track real-time IL-4/IL-13 dynamics (4C13R reporters) and keratinocyte/immune scRNA-seq signatures around TEWL crossings; test whether immune downshift lags barrier resealing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9437001/?utm_source=openai))
- Neuro-immune: Quantify pruriceptor Ca2+ burst rate and density versus local IL-31/TSLP axes; test whether reductions precede barrier resealing at edges. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13555-023-01081-0?utm_source=openai))
- Microbiome: Monitor S. aureus bioluminescence decline and commensal recovery near edges; relate to agr-linked virulence and host AMPs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3553733/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Identify minimal multi-axis driver sets sufficient for irreversible local remission.
- Event-triggered perturbations: Immediately before anticipated down-crossings, deliver single, low-dose, localized pulses:
  - Barrier pulse: topical nanoparticle PPAR/AHR agonists plus ceramide/cholesterol precursors to accelerate lipid program activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4077953/?utm_source=openai))
  - Neuro pulse: peripherally restricted kappa-opioid agonist (difelikefalin micro-dose gel) or TRP-channel antagonist micro-gel to transiently suppress itch circuitry without systemic exposure. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37453614/?utm_source=openai))
  - Microbiome pulse: a short, localized antibacterial directed at S. aureus (e.g., lysin/lantibiotic) at bioluminescence down-crossing to ensure quorum collapse; optionally follow with commensal consortium patch to stabilize colonization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8052297/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: Post-pulse, sample at +6 h, +24 h, +72 h for scRNA-seq/spatial multi-omics to test whether a specific triad—edge keratinocyte lipid-differentiation module up; pruriceptor excitability down; S. aureus burden below quorum proxy—predicts sustained local suppression of IL-4/IL-13 reporters and durable TEWL normalization. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Build a causality-preserving trajectory model oriented by thresholded events and spatial gradients.
- Construct a multi-layer graph linking ligand–receptor directionality (immune↔keratinocyte↔neuron), physical constraints (lipid stoichiometry vs TEWL), and timed perturbations. Use spatial position (edge→core) as an ordering prior only when triggers are absent, exploiting established wound-edge propagation analogs but validating in AD lesions. Quantify minimal-change driver sets that move tissue across separatrix into remission. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10843988/?utm_source=openai))
- Validate on human skin-on-chip by recreating threshold crossings with continuous TEER/neurite Ca2+ monitoring and single-cell/spatial profiling. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2026/lc/d5lc00867k?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
- Mouse AD induction: Employ established eczematous models (e.g., MC903), then allow spontaneous improvement under controlled humidity to enrich for natural remission events. Implant dorsal skinfold chamber; install micro-TEWL sensor; colonize with S. aureus-lux; use 4C13R and Pirt-GCaMP lines for immune/neuron readouts. Perform event-triggered 1 mm micro-punch biopsies spanning margin-to-core for scRNA-seq and chromatin profiling, paired with lipidomics and microbial sequencing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9270450/?utm_source=openai))
- Human chip: Full-thickness skin equivalents with iPSC sensory neurons and defined microbiota under ALI. Induce AD-like states with IL-4/IL-13; integrate TEER/optical TEWL and MEA/Ca2+ imaging; execute microfluidic pulses at threshold events; sample for scRNA-seq/snATAC-seq and spatial transcriptomics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8878506/?utm_source=openai))
- Analytics: Event-aligned differential state analysis; RNA velocity and ligand–receptor directionality; constrained trajectory inference that penalizes paths violating lipid mass-balance vs TEWL coupling; evaluation of hysteresis and basin stability after pulses. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43120-6?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and interpretation
- Support for the hypothesis would be: (i) reproducible identification of local TEWL/IL-4/IL-13/neurite/S. aureus down-crossings at lesion edges; (ii) discovery of a conserved keratinocyte “edge-state” program (PPAR/SREBP/AHR-linked differentiation/lipid elongation) that precedes immune quieting; (iii) evidence that micro-dosed, time-locked pulses produce durable local remission with orders-of-magnitude lower drug exposure than chronic therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13297085/?utm_source=openai))
- Refutation would be: absence of discrete crossings; need for chronic suppression; or inability to maintain remission despite combined pulses, implying a non-thresholded, distributed process.

Therapeutic translation
- Protocolize “lock-in windows” using noninvasive proxies: wearable TEWL plus digital scratch and optical lesion metrics to trigger short courses of topical PPAR/AHR formulations, brief neuromodulator gels, and targeted anti-staphylococcal applications in patients. This aligns with continuous barrier monitoring feasibility and kappa-agonist antipruritic efficacy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12528383/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbiome stabilization: After quorum crash, seed commensals (e.g., CoNS producing anti-staphylococcal factors or Roseomonas strains) to maintain the low-virulence niche, cognizant of mixed clinical signals. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8052297/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and feasibility
- Novelty: Event-triggered sampling and intervention at coupled thresholds in AD remission has not been systematically executed; spatially ordered, threshold-oriented causal reconstruction surpasses generic pseudotime. The components are feasible individually (dorsal skinfold chambers; IL-4/IL-13 reporters; S. aureus bioluminescence; sensory-neuron imaging; skin-on-chip with neurons/microbiome), but have not been integrated to target spontaneous remission dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9270450/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- Year 1: Establish triggers and show that TEWL and IL-4/IL-13 down-crossings co-occur with an edge keratinocyte lipid-differentiation signature and pruriceptor Ca2+ decline in mice. Go if ≥70% of events show concordance. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Demonstrate that single, localized, time-locked pulses reduce IL-4/IL-13 reporter area and sustain local TEWL normalization for ≥7 days vs untimed controls. Go if effect size ≥0.5 with ≥50% drug-sparing.
- Year 3: Replicate in human skin-on-chip and derive proxy-to-state maps to schedule interventions using noninvasive signals.

Pathophysiological coverage
- Barrier: TEWL, lipidomics, FLG/LOR/ELOVL/PPAR/AHR dynamics. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29467325/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune: IL-4/IL-13 reporters; scRNA-seq of DC/T cell axes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9437001/?utm_source=openai))
- Neuro-immune: IL-31/TRP-linked pruriceptor imaging and neuromodulator pulses. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13555-023-01081-0?utm_source=openai))
- Microbiome: S. aureus load/quorum proxies and commensal stabilization. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2023.1178650/full?utm_source=openai))

Impact
If remission is governed by brief, coupled threshold crossings at lesion edges, then detecting and locking these events with minimal, well-timed, spatially restricted therapies can reproduce natural healing while reducing systemic exposure and polypharmacy. This reframes AD control from continuous suppression to precision tipping-point management grounded in mechanism.
