Title
Airflow-triggered reinforcement of the nasal epithelial barrier to prevent and treat allergic rhinitis

Background and rationale
- In allergic rhinitis (AR), aeroallergen proteases (e.g., Der p 1) and inflammatory mediators disrupt tight and adherens junctions in the sinonasal epithelium, increasing paracellular permeability, allergen translocation, and epithelial alarmin release (TSLP, IL-33, IL-25). This primes and amplifies type 2 immunity and symptoms; barrier loss begets more inflammation. The apical junctional complex (claudins, occludin, ZO proteins) and E‑cadherin-based adherens junctions are central to barrier integrity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5752131/?utm_source=openai))
- The nasal surface experiences substantial, spatially heterogeneous wall shear stress from oscillatory airflow and pressure gradients during breathing; these mechanical loads can modulate epithelial function and barrier properties. Current barrier sprays (e.g., HPMC or bentonite-based thixotropic films) reduce symptoms by passive interception but do not actively strengthen junctions or respond to mechanical insult. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.01049.2005?utm_source=openai))
- Junction opening is driven in part by perijunctional actomyosin contraction via epithelial myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) signaling; transient increases in intracellular Ca2+ and stretch/shear stimuli can trigger junction disassembly and increased leak. Targeted, local suppression of this mechano‑leak pathway is a rational lever to block the initiating event in AR. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384706/?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis (question-as-hypothesis)
Can we convert the inevitable oscillatory airflow over nasal epithelium into an on‑demand signal that locally reinforces apical junctions—by damping mechanical strain and transiently biasing MLCK-regulated junction mechanics—thereby preventing allergen ingress, alarmin release, and downstream symptoms?

Atomic strategy
Exploit airflow-induced shear as the trigger: engineer a muco-adherent, mechanoresponsive intranasal film that stiffens and releases microdoses of a junction-stabilizing modulator only when and where shear/strain rise, thus reinforcing the barrier at risk windows without continuous drug exposure. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169409X1630299X?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- First event‑triggered barrier therapy for AR: existing intranasal barriers are passive; none couple physiological shear to active junction reinforcement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10064392/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanobiology-guided causality: the device targets the MLCK‑actomyosin leak pathway that executes tight junction opening under stress, rather than downstream inflammatory cascades. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384706/?utm_source=openai))
- Intranasal localization minimizes systemic exposure and dosing burden by releasing only during breathing-induced stress cycles. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169409X1630299X?utm_source=openai))

Proposed therapeutic prototype (M-ReN: Mechano-Responsive Epithelial eNforcer)
- Formulation: a shear-thinning, self-healing hydrogel film (nasal spray) that rapidly re-forms at rest. Under elevated local shear (e.g., high-velocity inspiration, sneezing), reversible cross-links transiently rearrange, increasing apparent modulus and expelling a small, surface-confined payload. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4847551/?utm_source=openai))
- Payload: an intranasally retained MLCK1-pathway modulator (e.g., a surface-anchored analog of the allosteric MLCK1 inhibitor “Divertin” or equivalent) formulated at microdose to bias the perijunctional actomyosin ring against contraction without impairing ciliary function. Comparative arms will test a mechano-triggered release of a TRPV4 antagonist as an alternative mechanotransduction brake, acknowledging tissue- and context-specific TRPV4 roles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7037368/?utm_source=openai))
- Mode of action: (i) mechanical damping of apical strain reduces cytoskeletal tension transmitted to junctions; (ii) brief, shear-triggered microrelease reduces MLCK-driven MLC phosphorylation, stabilizing TJ/AJ continuity during insult; (iii) reduced leak lowers allergen flux and alarmin output, blunting DC priming and type 2 amplification. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384706/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Establish that nasal airflow shear can be harnessed to actuate on-demand delivery and junction reinforcement in vitro.
- 1a. Build a human nasal epithelium “air–liquid interface with airflow” platform: primary human nasal epithelial cells (HNECs) matured at ALI under physiologic oscillatory airflow reproducing regional wall shear profiles. Readouts: TEER, FITC‑dextran flux, ZO‑1/occludin/E‑cadherin continuity, and ciliary beat frequency. ([research.tue.nl](https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/a-nasal-airway-on-chip-model-to-evaluate-airflow-pre-conditioning/?utm_source=openai))
- 1b. Characterize mechano-actuation: quantify M‑ReN shear thresholds and release profiles under tidal (0.1–0.5 Pa) and sneeze-mimetic (≥1 Pa) shear; map film stiffening and recovery kinetics; ensure negligible release at rest. Use fluorescent surrogates and LC–MS of apical washes. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/japplphysiol.01049.2005?utm_source=openai))
- 1c. Demonstrate barrier protection during challenge: expose HNECs to HDM extract/Der p 1 ± oscillatory airflow. Primary endpoints: prevention of TEER loss and paracellular leak; preservation of junctional protein localization; reduced apical alarmins (TSLP/IL‑33/IL‑25). Mechanism endpoints: decreased MLC phosphorylation and cortical actin contraction. Comparators: passive HPMC/bentonite barrier film; non‑triggered constant‑release film; vehicle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC408401/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: M‑ReN + shear achieves ≥50% reduction in HDM‑induced leak versus vehicle and ≥25% superiority over passive barrier, with preserved ciliary function.

Aim 2. Quantify the causal role of MLCK-pathway biasing in the mechano-protective effect.
- 2a. Causality tests: replicate Aim 1 with (i) pharmacologic MLCK inhibition (payload off; soluble control), (ii) CRISPRi/siRNA knockdown of MLCK1 in HNECs, and (iii) nonreleasing “mechanical-only” M‑ReN. Determine the fraction of benefit attributable to payload versus mechanical damping. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16638813/?utm_source=openai))
- 2b. Pathway mapping: measure MLC‑2 phosphorylation, RhoA/ROCK activity, and caveolar occludin endocytosis dynamics under HDM ± shear ± M‑ReN. Outcome: confirm that on-demand MLCK biasing is necessary and sufficient for junction preservation under stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384706/?utm_source=openai))
- 2c. Exploratory comparator: mechano-triggered TRPV4 antagonist release to test whether blocking mechanosensitive Ca2+ influx affords equal or lesser protection; monitor for adverse effects given context-dependent epithelial TRPV4 functions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5430398/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: MLCK-axis dependence demonstrated by loss of protection when MLCK signaling is genetically/pharmacologically disengaged; TRPV4 arm informs future payload selection.

Aim 3. Test efficacy, prevention potential, and dosing convenience in vivo.
- 3a. Prevention in sensitization: in HDM intranasal sensitization models, dose M‑ReN once daily during aeroallergen exposure. Endpoints: nasal symptom surrogates (sneezes/rubs), nasal airway resistance, TEER ex vivo, mucosal allergen penetration, alarmins, Th2 cytokines/eosinophilia, and Der p 1–specific IgE. Comparator: HPMC/bentonite passive barrier. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5535861/?utm_source=openai))
- 3b. Treatment in established AR: in HDM‑sensitized/challenged rodents, apply M‑ReN pre‑challenge (prophylaxis) or post‑challenge (treatment). Endpoints as in 3a plus histology for junctional integrity. Dosing cadence: test once‑daily versus every‑other‑day. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5500700/?utm_source=openai))
- 3c. Safety and local tolerability: olfaction assays, ciliary beat frequency, mucociliary clearance, histopathology, and systemic exposure. Exploratory human‑factor study: simulate user breathing patterns to confirm actuation robustness.

Study design considerations and feasibility
- Mechanically responsive drug delivery under physiologic shear has been demonstrated in multiple hydrogel systems; nasal airflow provides repeatable, benign actuation. Shear-thinning mucoadhesive films are clinically deployed as passive barriers, supporting intranasal film residence and safety. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169409X1630299X?utm_source=openai))
- Epithelial MLCK is a validated regulator of tight junction permeability in response to diverse stressors; its allosteric inhibition restores barrier function without global cytoskeletal paralysis in gut models, motivating localized nasal translation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384706/?utm_source=openai))

Endpoints and statistical plan
- Primary efficacy endpoint (in vivo): reduction in nasal symptom composite score (sneezes, rubs, nasal resistance) and mucosal allergen translocation versus vehicle. Secondary: alarmins (TSLP, IL‑33, IL‑25), tissue eosinophilia, junctional continuity scores, and TEER ex vivo. Power: detect 25–30% superiority over passive barrier with α=0.05, 1–β=0.8.
- Device–biologic coupling: pre‑specify correlation between instantaneous shear (flow plethysmography) and burst release (in situ fluorescence) during challenge.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Risk: over-inhibition of contractility could impair mucociliary function. Mitigation: microdosed, apical-confined payload; ciliary beat monitoring; mechanical-only arm to bound required pharmacology. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169409X1630299X?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: TRPV4 role is context dependent. Mitigation: restrict to exploratory arm; proceed only if barrier benefit without adverse epithelial responses is shown. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-01201-3?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: passive barriers already effective. Differentiation: demonstrate prevention of sensitization (Aim 3a) and reduced alarmin release—outcomes passive barriers do not mechanistically target. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10064392/?utm_source=openai))

Translational path and clinical experiment concept
- Phase 0/1: randomized, crossover human allergen-challenge chamber study comparing M‑ReN to passive HPMC/bentonite barrier. Primary endpoints: TNSS AUC and nasal airflow; mechanistic endpoints: nasal TEER surrogate (acoustic rhinometry), Der p 1 in lavages, TSLP/IL‑33, safety/tolerability; exploratory: breath-by-breath actuation–release coupling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10064392/?utm_source=openai))
- Target product profile: once-daily intranasal spray, event‑triggered, with prevention and treatment labeling, minimal systemic exposure, and compatibility with standard AR pharmacotherapy.

Impact
If successful, this work repositions AR as a mechanically exploitable barrier disease: using breathing itself to harden the epithelial gate and suppress the alarmin “starter pistol.” Such a platform could generalize across aeroallergens and comorbid airway diseases in which junctional failure and shear-sensitive leak initiate pathology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7727704/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Installing keratinocyte tolerance to pathogenic staphylococcal vesicles to preserve differentiation after sequential microbial signaling

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can a brief preconditioning pulse with attenuated Staphylococcus aureus extracellular vesicles (aEV-SA) or Staphylococcus epidermidis EVs (EV-SE) install A20/IRAK-M–mediated tolerance in skin organoid stem/progenitors, thereby reducing S. aureus–driven IL-6–dominated inflammation and preserving differentiation capacity under clinically relevant “pathobiont-first/commensal-later” or “commensal-first/pathobiont-later” schedules?

Rationale (what is known and what is missing)
- Commensal S. epidermidis activates keratinocyte TLR2 and AhR to induce antimicrobial programs and modulate inflammatory tone; these axes intersect with differentiation control. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15349630?utm_source=openai))
- S. aureus secreted factors and EVs drive strong IL-6/TNF responses in keratinocytes and can be cytotoxic; EVs can carry α-hemolysin and PSMs that worsen barrier injury and differentiation defects. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923181113003897?utm_source=openai))
- Keratinocytes possess inducible negative regulators (A20/TNFAIP3, IRAK-M) that brake TLR/NF-κB signaling; commensal exposure and TLR ligands can upregulate these factors, a mechanistic basis for tolerance-like hyporesponsiveness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3214908/?utm_source=openai))
- Gap: It is unknown whether preconditioning with non-cytotoxic staphylococcal vesicle inputs can deliberately install this brake in skin organoids to shape history-dependent plasticity of inflammation and differentiation under sequential S. aureus/S. epidermidis signaling.

Atomic strategy
Prime keratinocyte stem/progenitors with a short, non-cytotoxic vesicle input that engages surface TLR2 (±AhR) but minimizes toxin delivery, to induce A20/IRAK-M before the pathogenic hit. The single design choice—tolerizing before challenging—should globally compress the subsequent inflammatory burst and protect differentiation programs.

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Build attenuated S. aureus EVs (aEV-SA) that preserve TLR2 agonism but reduce pore-former activity; benchmark against EV-SE.
- Aim 2. Test whether a 6–12 h priming pulse with aEV-SA or EV-SE blunts inflammatory amplitude/duration and induces tolerance regulators, then challenge with intact S. aureus EVs (EV-SA).
- Aim 3. Determine whether tolerance preserves differentiation and barrier metrics under sequential, time-differential regimens (pathobiont-first vs commensal-first) with explicit recovery windows.

Experimental design and methods (POC scale; 3 months)
- Vesicle production and attenuation
  - Culture S. aureus (e.g., USA300) and S. epidermidis reference strains in vesicle-permissive conditions; isolate EVs by differential ultracentrifugation and density cushion; NTA and protein quantification.
  - Generate aEV-SA via brief protease (e.g., proteinase K, calibrated) or mild heat treatment to reduce α-hemolysin/PSM activity while retaining lipoprotein/LTA content; confirm by hemolysis assay, α-hemolysin immunoblot, and TLR2 reporter activation (HEK-Blue TLR2 or keratinocyte IL-8). Use intact EV-SA and EV-SE as comparators. Rationale: EV-associated α-hemolysin and PSMs drive cytotoxicity; EV disruption or attenuation reduces delivery of toxic effectors. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24992681/?utm_source=openai))
- Model system
  - Human 3D organotypic epidermal organoids (primary keratinocytes on collagen/fibroblast dermal equivalent) at air–liquid interface. Maintain replicate transwells for TEER and histology.
- Sequential schedules (temporal buffering as variable)
  - Regimen A (pathobiont-first): Prime (aEV-SA or EV-SE; 6–12 h) → 12–24 h recovery → EV-SA long exposure (24–48 h) → 12 h recovery → EV-SE short exposure (6–12 h).
  - Regimen B (commensal-first): Prime (aEV-SA or EV-SE) → 12–24 h recovery → EV-SE long exposure → 12 h recovery → EV-SA short exposure.
  - Include “no prime” controls and “vehicle” controls; include TLR2 blockade (neutralizing Ab) to test mechanism.
- Readouts and decision thresholds
  - Early inflammation: live-cell NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation kinetics, IL-6/IL-8/TNF multiplex; target effect size ≥30% reduction in IL-6 AUC with priming vs no-priming under identical EV-SA challenge. S. aureus secretome/PSMs are known to drive IL-6 that suppresses differentiation; compressing IL-6 should preserve KRT10/FLG. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923181113003897?utm_source=openai))
  - Tolerance regulators: A20/TNFAIP3 and IRAK-M mRNA/protein induction at 6–24 h post-prime and post-challenge; necessity tested by siRNA knockdown rescue of hyperinflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3214908/?utm_source=openai))
  - Cytotoxicity and barrier: LDH release, viability; TEER and FITC-dextran permeability.
  - Differentiation capacity: KRT14→KRT10 switch, involucrin, filaggrin, loricrin by qPCR/IF; histological stratification score.
  - Plasticity metric: sequence-dependence index = (OutcomeA − OutcomeB)/max(|OutcomeA|, |OutcomeB|) for cytokine AUC and differentiation composite score.
- Optional mechanistic add-on (contingency if priming effect is modest)
  - Present EVs via reversible surface tethering to bias sensing compartmentalization: pattern EVs onto a thin, cell-compatible hydrogel film using EV–matrix affinity (e.g., HSPG-binding or CD9/CD63-binding peptides) to prolong surface residency and reduce uptake; pH/salt-triggered release enables fast switching. EV–hydrogel tethering is established for controlled release; TLR2 ligands can signal when surface-presented, supporting feasibility of “anchored” presentation to favor surface TLR2 over endosomal nucleic-acid sensing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8096714/?utm_source=openai))

Controls
- Heat-inactivated whole bacteria (HKSA/HKSE) as a priming comparator; known to modulate keratinocyte susceptibility to viral infection, indicating functional priming capacity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42159017/?utm_source=openai))
- Vehicle and buffer controls for attenuation steps; isotype control for TLR2 blockade.
- Batch controls for EV production temperature because EV cargo and cytotoxicity vary with culture temperature. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34612674/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes
- Priming with aEV-SA or EV-SE induces A20/IRAK-M and compresses EV-SA–elicited NF-κB/IL-6 kinetics without increasing cytotoxicity, preserving TEER and terminal differentiation markers under both sequence schedules; effect partially reversed by TLR2 blockade and A20/IRAK-M knockdown. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3214908/?utm_source=openai))
- Pathobiont-first regimens show the largest benefit from priming (bigger window to preserve differentiation against long EV-SA exposure); commensal-first plus priming yields near-baseline inflammatory tone with maintained differentiation.

Criteria for success (POC)
- ≥30% reduction in IL-6 AUC and ≥20% improvement in TEER recovery at 48 h post-EV-SA challenge with priming vs no-priming.
- Significant induction of A20 and/or IRAK-M (≥2× baseline) post-prime; loss of protection with their knockdown.
- Preservation of KRT10/FLG/LOR expression (≥25% vs no-priming under identical challenge).

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Month 1: EV production/attenuation calibration and reporter validation; establish organoids and baseline EV responses.
- Month 2: Execute priming/challenge matrices for Regimens A/B; collect cytokine, NF-κB, cytotoxicity, TEER.
- Month 3: Differentiation/barrier histology; A20/IRAK-M mechanistic tests; analysis.

Risks and mitigations
- Over-attenuation abolishes TLR2 agonism: dial down protease/heat using TLR2 reporter readouts to bracket activity; if needed, switch to EV-SE priming only (retains TLR2/AhR activation with low cytotoxicity). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15349630?utm_source=openai))
- Batch variability in EV cargo: standardize growth phase and temperature; lock to single donor strains per run. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34612674/?utm_source=openai))
- If priming effect is weak: deploy anchored EV presentation to restrict uptake and bias surface signaling during challenge. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8096714/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is novel and the right test
- Prior work shows S. epidermidis and S. aureus differentially modulate keratinocyte inflammation and that EV-associated toxins drive pathology, but deliberate, short priming with attenuated staphylococcal EVs to install A20/IRAK-M tolerance before a sequential pathogenic EV challenge in skin organoids has not been tested. Anchored EV presentation is available as a mechanistically orthogonal contingency. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923181113003897?utm_source=openai))

Optional extension (time-permitting)
- Deliver identical priming/challenge at two circadian phases after serum-shock entrainment to test whether the skin clock gates tolerance strength and recovery, as circadian networks modulate cutaneous immune programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8515909/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Do stem cells decide before or after entering a niche? Dissecting order- and neighborhood-dependent effects of Staphylococcus aureus versus Staphylococcus epidermidis extracellular vesicles on inflammatory state and differentiation in human skin organoids using spatial “sink” microdomains.

Integrated hypothesis–question
Do migrating basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors commit to inflammatory and differentiation trajectories based on their prior exposure history to bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs) or based on the BEV concentration field of the neighborhood they enter next? Because keratinocytes sense Gram-positive cues primarily via TLR2 to activate NF-κB and downstream programs, and S. aureus products (e.g., LTA, SpA) bias against terminal differentiation while S. epidermidis signals can dampen inflammation via TLR2–TLR3 crosstalk, we ask whether exposure order (pathobiont-first vs commensal-first) interacts with spatial ligand availability to determine fate. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15305820?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Encode neighborhood-level BEV availability without restricting cell movement by embedding spatially addressable glycosaminoglycan (GAG) “competitive binding sinks” that sequester BEVs and BEV-associated proteins, thereby shaping local free-ligand exposure kinetics as cells migrate. Heparinized (sulfated GAG) microgels are established high-affinity depots for vesicles and heparin-binding proteins; deploying them as micro-islands adjacent to inert microgels yields stable, neighboring “low-BEV” and “high-BEV” zones under the same global perfusion. This single perturbation—altering local free BEV through spatial affinity capture—tests whether order memory is cell-intrinsic or niche-instructive. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4437317/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Build and calibrate BEV-availability neighborhoods in skin organoids using heparinized microgels as spatial sinks.
- Aim 2. Test whether order of exposure (S. aureus-first long then S. epidermidis-short; reverse sequence) produces distinct inflammatory and differentiation outcomes when cells subsequently migrate into matched “low-BEV” versus “high-BEV” neighborhoods.
- Aim 3. Determine whether niche-instructive effects can overwrite prior exposure memory, or whether memory persists independent of current BEV availability.

Model system and inputs
- Human skin organoids enriched for basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors (p63+, K14+).
- Purified BEVs from S. aureus (pathobiont) and S. epidermidis (commensal), quantified by NTA and protein content. Gram-positive BEVs and their immunomodulatory cargo are established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7671900/?utm_source=openai))

Neighborhood engineering (selected element: competitive binding sinks)
- Microgel fabrication: Produce 40–80 µm microgels of PEG-heparin (methacrylated heparin copolymerized with PEG-diacrylate) and matched inert PEG-only microgels. Heparin immobilization avoids leaching and preserves high-affinity capture.
- Neighborhood layout: In a collagen I or collagen–GAG hydrogel slab hosting day-7–10 organoids, embed two adjacent bands (∼1–2 mm wide) of microgels: Band A, high-density heparin microgels (sink); Band B, PEG-only microgels (no sink). Bands are contiguous to allow unrestricted cell migration across the interface.
- Calibration with fluorescent BEVs: Pulse organoids with labeled S. aureus or S. epidermidis BEVs and quantify spatial free-BEV profiles (confocal FRAP/steady-state imaging) to confirm sink strength and wash-in/wash-out half-times. Heparin affinity for EV capture and for diverse bacterial and host heparin-binding proteins supports feasibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4437317/?utm_source=openai))

Sequential exposure regimens (3-month POC; two sequences; 2 durations)
- Sequence SA-long→SE-short: 48 h S. aureus BEVs (10–50 µg/mL protein equivalent) followed by 12 h S. epidermidis BEVs.
- Sequence SE-long→SA-short: 48 h S. epidermidis BEVs followed by 12 h S. aureus BEVs.
- Optional cocktail arms: Concurrent 1:1 BEV mixtures at equivalent total dose to benchmark coexistence versus sequence.
- All exposures delivered by gentle perfusion in a laminar chamber to minimize unstirred layers; neighborhood bands remain stationary and continuously functional.

Core readouts and analytics
- Inflammatory state dynamics:
  - Live NF-κB reporter keratinocytes (p65–mNeon translocation or κB–luciferase): quantify pulse frequency/amplitude per cell over time and per neighborhood band.
  - Endpoints: qPCR/RNA-seq of NF-κB/MAPK/IRF target modules; cytokines (e.g., IL6, CXCLs) in supernatant.
  - Mechanistic anchors: Keratinocytes engage TLR2 to activate NF-κB to S. aureus components, and S. aureus LTA/SpA are known drivers; S. epidermidis can reduce injury-triggered cytokines via TLR2–TLR3 crosstalk. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15305820?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation capacity:
  - Immunostaining and image cytometry for K14/K10/IVL/FLG; p63 and Notch1/ICD; colony-forming efficiency after dissociation.
  - Rationale: S. aureus LTA suppresses differentiation via p63/Notch pathway interference; IL-6 signaling also impairs terminal differentiation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593072/?utm_source=openai))
- Behavior-to-fate linkage:
  - Track single cells crossing from Band A→B or B→A after each sequence; correlate per-cell cumulative dwell time in each neighborhood with inflammatory reporter history and fate markers at 72–96 h.

Experimental logic and discriminative tests
- Test 1: Neighborhood-instructive vs memory.
  - After SA-long→SE-short, relocate cells (by migration or microdissection) into the opposite band and continue in BEV-free medium. If outcomes converge by current neighborhood irrespective of history, niche instruction dominates; if differences persist despite matched current availability, cell-intrinsic memory dominates.
- Test 2: Order effect independent of cumulative dose.
  - Equalize total BEV protein exposure across sequences. Compare outcomes within the same band. Divergence implies true order dependence.
- Test 3: Receptor-pathway anchoring.
  - TLR2 blockade (neutralizing antibody or small-molecule inhibitor) during the short second phase only. Loss of order dependence with TLR2 blockade in SE-short or SA-short phase indicates that the second pulse is instructive via TLR2.

Controls
- Vehicle and heat-inactivated BEVs.
- Heparin competition control: pre-saturate heparin microgels with high-salt rinse to reduce affinity and collapse neighborhood contrast.
- Protein specificity: spike with purified S. aureus LTA or SpA at sub-BEV doses to test phenocopy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593072/?utm_source=openai))
- Barrier-only control: PEG-only microgels in both bands to confirm that spatial effects require affinity sinks.

Outcomes and interpretation criteria
- Primary endpoint: statistically significant interaction between exposure order and neighborhood band on NF-κB dynamics and differentiation markers.
  - Neighborhood-instructive signature: Within a given current band, SA-long→SE-short and SE-long→SA-short converge; across bands they differ.
  - Memory signature: Within a band, sequences differ even when current BEV availability is equal.
- Secondary endpoint: Commensal-first sequences reduce IL-6 and preserve differentiation versus pathobiont-first, consistent with prior commensal tolerance. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0923181113003897?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Weeks 1–2: BEV isolation/characterization (S. aureus, S. epidermidis); heparin-microgel synthesis and calibration for EV capture. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29643357/?utm_source=openai))
- Weeks 3–5: Embed organoids with neighborhood bands; validate spatial free-BEV profiles.
- Weeks 6–9: Run sequential exposure experiments and live NF-κB imaging.
- Weeks 10–12: Endpoints (immunostaining, RNA-seq), analysis.

Risk management
- BEV capture inefficiency: Increase heparin density/crosslinking; add charge-tuned sulfated GAG variants. Heparin- and GAG-based capture of EVs and proteins is established; adjust ionic strength to tune binding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4437317/?utm_source=openai))
- Heparin off-target effects: Use covalently immobilized heparin; verify no free heparin in supernatant.
- BEV heterogeneity: Normalize by TLR2-activating equivalents using κB reporter dose–response curves.

Statistical plan
- n≥3 organoid batches; ≥200 tracked cells per condition for live imaging; mixed-effects models with factors sequence, neighborhood, and their interaction; FDR-controlled multi-testing on gene panels.

Deliverable
A decision map linking exposure order and current neighborhood availability to inflammatory state and differentiation competence of human skin stem/progenitors. By altering only the local free-BEV field via heparin “sinks,” this POC distinguishes intrinsic memory from niche instruction in a biologically grounded, migration-permissive organoid context. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11756038/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Does metabolic state, not timing, encode microbial vesicle control of skin stem cell inflammation and differentiation?

Central hypothesis-question
If keratinocyte stem/progenitors are pre-clamped into defined cytosolic redox states, will sequential S. aureus versus S. epidermidis extracellular vesicle (EV) exposures still produce order-dependent differences in inflammatory status and differentiation capacity? Or do sequence effects collapse to the metabolic trajectory alone? Prior data justify that: (i) S. aureus EV lipoproteins potently activate TLR2→NF-κB/MAPK and inflammation; S. epidermidis signals engage distinct defensive/repair pathways (e.g., TLR2- and AhR-linked) in keratinocytes; (ii) butyrate promotes keratinocyte differentiation largely via HDAC inhibition with low FFAR2/3 expression; (iii) lactate/pyruvate ratios and O2 availability set cytosolic NADH:NAD+ and thereby gate redox-sensitive inflammatory checkpoints; (iv) epidermal stem cells store inflammatory epigenetic memory that could confound order tests unless metabolic state is controlled. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat cytosolic redox (NADH:NAD+) as the single integrator of prior metabolic inputs. Use a skin-on-chip to gate exposure: advance to EV delivery only when sensors confirm entry into a target energetic/redox state. Then randomize EV order and duration while recording the metabolic trajectory. If matched trajectories yield different outcomes, timing carries non-metabolic information; if not, sequence reduces to state. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/8/1077?utm_source=openai))

Model system
- Microfluidic skin-on-chip: perfused epidermis–dermis co-culture with integrated O2/metabolite monitoring; optional NADH FLIM readout. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/8/1077?utm_source=openai))
- Treatments: purified EVs from S. aureus (WT and Δlgt as reduced-lipoprotein control) and S. epidermidis; sequential orders with differential durations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))
- Optional metabolic memory actuator: PLGA microparticles releasing butyrate/propionate to impose durable HDAC-mediated differentiation bias before EVs. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927775725015092?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and validate metabolic “gates” that reproducibly set keratinocytes to glycolytic-high NADH versus oxidative-low NADH states before EV exposure.
2) Test whether maintaining identical metabolic trajectories abolishes order effects of S. aureus→S. epidermidis versus S. epidermidis→S. aureus EVs on inflammatory and differentiation readouts.
3) Determine whether SCFA-driven epigenetic preconditioning occludes EV order effects, implicating metabolic/epigenetic memory rather than timing per se.

Key design and methods (POC scale; ≤3 months)
- EV prep and qualification:
  - Culture S. aureus and S. epidermidis; isolate EVs; normalize by protein and TLR2 activity (NF-κB reporter in HEK-TLR2 or keratinocytes). Include S. aureus Δlgt EVs to reduce TLR2 lipoprotein activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolic gating on-chip:
  - Gate A (glycolytic/high NADH): 18 mM glucose, 1% O2 apical, perfusate lactate:pyruvate 10:1 for 2–4 h.
  - Gate B (oxidative/low NADH): 5 mM glucose, 10% O2 apical, perfusate lactate:pyruvate 1:10 for 2–4 h.
  - Advance only when sensor thresholds are reached (stable O2 consumption; lactate flux plateau; optional NADH-FLIM bound:free shift). Rationale: extracellular lactate/pyruvate sets cytosolic NADH:NAD+ via LDH equilibrium; O2 tunes mitochondrial electron flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7983055/?utm_source=openai))
- Sequence regimens (factorial, n=3–4 chips/arm; two donors):
  - Long→short: 24 h EV1 then 6 h EV2.
  - Short→long: 6 h EV1 then 24 h EV2.
  - Orders: S. aureus EVs→S. epidermidis EVs; reverse. Cocktail controls (simultaneous).
  - Redox-trajectory matching: under each order, implement both Gate A and Gate B and enforce that real-time sensor traces overlap (tolerance bands ±10%) before proceeding.
- Optional epigenetic preconditioning:
  - Apical PLGA microparticles (50–200 µm) loaded with butyrate±propionate; two kinetics: burst (≤6 h) and sustained (24–72 h). Confirm release by HPLC; verify HDAC inhibition (global H3/H4 acetylation). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12994588/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts:
  - Inflammatory status: NF-κB nuclear translocation; phospho-JNK/p38; DUSP1 oxidation state; cytokine/chemokine panel (IL1A, IL6, CXCL8, CCL20); AMP genes (DEFB4/3). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2613485/?utm_source=openai))
  - Differentiation capacity: mRNA/protein of FLG, LOR, IVL, TGM1; cornified envelope formation; lipid enzymes (ELOVL6, CERS3). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9385498/?utm_source=openai))
  - Barrier/physiology: TEER or dye penetration; oxygen consumption and lactate flux logs; optional NADH-FLIM lifetime shift. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4804294/?utm_source=openai))
  - Pathway specificity: AhR target genes after S. epidermidis EVs; TLR2 blockade (C29) abrogation; Δlgt EV phenotypes; control with Pam3CSK4. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6738203/?utm_source=openai))
  - Keratinocyte EV cargo: quantify filaggrin in keratinocyte-derived sEVs as a TLR2-responsive output. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37338870/?utm_source=openai))

Planned analyses
- Primary comparison: For each redox-gated trajectory (A or B) whose sensor traces match, compare inflammatory and differentiation outputs between orders. Use two-way ANOVA (order × gate) with donor as random effect; adjust for multiple testing.
- Collapse-to-state criterion: If outputs under matched trajectories do not differ by order (<10% effect size; power 0.8), infer metabolic state sufficiency.
- Hidden-order criterion: If order differences persist under matched trajectories, infer non-metabolic encoding (e.g., receptor desensitization/endosomal routing, AhR–TLR2 crosstalk, epigenetic bookmarking).
- SCFA occlusion test: If sustained SCFA preconditioning diminishes order effects across gates, attribute sequence dependence to metabolic/epigenetic memory; if not, implicate orthogonal signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9932284/?utm_source=openai))

Rigor and controls
- EV identity/activity: TEM/NTA; lipoprotein content; TLR2 activity benchmark; heat-inactivated EV control; Δlgt EVs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))
- Pathway controls: TLR2 inhibitor (C29); AhR antagonist; antioxidants (NAC) for redox sensitivity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20625996/?utm_source=openai))
- State controls: swap lactate/pyruvate without O2 change and vice versa to demonstrate independent levers; confirm NADH-state by FLIM where possible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4804294/?utm_source=openai))
- SCFA controls: blank PLGA; free butyrate bolus to decouple release kinetics from dose. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12994588/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Month 1: Chip setup, sensor calibration, NADH-state gating validation; EV isolation/qualification.
- Month 2: Sequence × gate factorial runs; metabolic trajectory logging; primary inflammatory/differentiation panels.
- Month 3: SCFA preconditioning arms; pathway inhibition controls; data integration.

Decision matrix (outcomes → interpretation)
- Order effects vanish under matched trajectories: timing is epiphenomenal; cytosolic redox/metabolism suffices to encode bacterial EV influence.
- Order effects persist: bacteria convey order-encoded signals beyond metabolism (e.g., S. aureus TLR2 lipoproteins vs S. epidermidis AhR ligands; receptor crosstalk/hysteresis; vesicle routing).
- SCFA preconditioning erases order effects: metabolic/epigenetic memory dominates (HDAC-mediated); if not, prioritize non-metabolic pathways for mechanistic follow-up. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is novel and corrective
- Tests “metabolic state sufficiency” directly by clamping NADH:NAD+ via lactate/pyruvate and O2 in a perfused skin model, rather than assuming sequence inherently matters. Prior work links lactate/pyruvate to cytosolic NADH control, but this has not been used to falsify order effects of microbial EVs in keratinocyte organoids. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7983055/?utm_source=openai))
- Uses SCFA-releasing PLGA microparticles as a time-coded epigenetic actuator to parse metabolic memory from order information in a skin system, repurposing a delivery approach mostly explored outside skin. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927775725015092?utm_source=openai))

Selected references (representative)
- S. aureus EV lipoprotein–TLR2–NF-κB inflammation; PSM-dependent export. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8268867/?utm_source=openai))
- S. epidermidis signals: TLR2- and AhR-linked defense/barrier effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2922455/?utm_source=openai))
- SCFA–keratinocyte differentiation via HDAC inhibition; low FFAR2/3. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9385498/?utm_source=openai))
- Lactate/pyruvate set cytosolic NADH:NAD+. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/7983055/?utm_source=openai))
- Redox gating of inflammatory signaling (NF-κB/DUSP1). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2613485/?utm_source=openai))
- Epidermal stem cell inflammatory memory. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables (POC)
- Dataset linking metabolic trajectories to inflammatory/differentiation outputs across EV orders.
- Evidence supporting or refuting metabolic-state sufficiency for sequence effects.
- A validated, sensor-guided skin-on-chip protocol for order-versus-state discrimination, and an SCFA preconditioning module for future mechanism dissection.

text:
Title: Order versus dominance: phage-timed flips and lipid-gradient succession reveal how skin stem cells decode competing staphylococcal signals

Integrated hypothesis–question
- Do basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors encode a history of microbial dominance shifts (order) beyond their instantaneous exposure state, when exposed to competing S. epidermidis and S. aureus or their vesicle-derived signals? Specifically, does an early commensal-dominant epoch followed by a pathobiont-dominant epoch produce distinct inflammatory priming and differentiation outcomes compared with the reverse sequence, under matched cumulative microbial load?

Atomic strategy
- Use an endogenous skin-lipid gradient (palmitoleic/sapienic acid) embedded in a hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogel to drive autonomous early S. epidermidis bias and late S. aureus resurgence, then enforce a timed dominance flip with an S. aureus–specific lytic phage pulse. This creates controlled sequences of “who dominates when” without re-seeding, allowing separation of order (history) from state (current dominance). Mechanistic basis: skin long-chain unsaturated fatty acids differentially inhibit S. aureus more than S. epidermidis and modulate staphylococcal programs including agr-controlled virulence; agr is density/nutrient responsive and cross-inhibited by S. epidermidis AIPs, while lytic phage provides acute, species-selective S. aureus reduction with transient PAMP release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5263133/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build a lipid-gradient organoid niche that generates reproducible early commensal advantage and late pathobiont encroachment.
2) Superimpose a timed, partial S. aureus–specific phage pulse to invert dominance on demand.
3) Quantify whether keratinocyte stem/progenitors retain exposure-order memory in inflammatory signaling and differentiation capacity, independent of instantaneous dominance at readout.
4) Parallel EV-only sequences (S. epidermidis EVs then S. aureus EVs, or reverse) to test if history effects persist without live competition.

Rationale and mechanistic checkpoints
- Skin fatty acids: Sapienic/palmitoleic acids inhibit S. aureus more strongly than S. epidermidis; both species mount distinct survival programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5263133/?utm_source=openai))
- HA hydrogels can sustain controlled fatty-acid release; recent HA–PEGDA systems release palmitoleic acid with tunable kinetics, supporting feasibility of FA-loaded HA matrices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42461343/?utm_source=openai))
- S. aureus virulence is agr-regulated, density- and nutrient-dependent; S. epidermidis AIPs cross-inhibit S. aureus agr, shaping competitive signaling seen by keratinocytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452892/?utm_source=openai))
- Lytic phages are highly specific, acutely debulk target bacteria, and lysis can transiently increase PAMP burden; organoid-relevant phage–bacteria–epithelium studies demonstrate feasibility of phage-tuned host responses. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40560-024-00759-7?utm_source=openai))
- Keratinocytes integrate staphylococcal cues via TLRs/NF-κB; S. epidermidis can dampen injurious inflammation, while S. aureus toxins/vesicles drive proinflammatory responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4219649/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design (POC, ≤3 months)

System
- Human skin organoids enriched for basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors (KRT14+) embedded in HA hydrogel discs (∼4–6 mm diameter, 1–2 mm thickness).
- HA hydrogel loaded with a radial gradient of palmitoleic acid (surrogate for sapienic for stability/sourcing) via FA-loaded lipid nanocarriers covalently or physically entrapped in HA–PEGDA network; gradient confirmed by LC–MS line scans. Release kinetics targeted to half-life 24–72 h to allow succession. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42461343/?utm_source=openai))
- Live-bacteria arms: co-inoculate with S. epidermidis (commensal isolate) and S. aureus (agr+ clinical isolate) at 1:1 CFU.
- EV-only arms: sequential exposure to purified EVs from each species (dose matched by protein or particle number) without live bacteria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8657977/?utm_source=openai))

Temporal programs
- Program A (Comm→Path): Early commensal advantage driven by FA gradient (days 0–2). On day 2, withdraw a fraction of FA source (by media exchange to promote gradient flattening) allowing S. aureus encroachment (days 2–4). On day 4, deliver S. aureus–specific lytic phage pulse (MOI 1–5) to flip dominance back to commensal for days 4–5. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5263133/?utm_source=openai))
- Program B (Path→Comm): Same as A but apply early phage pulse at 12 h to suppress early S. aureus, then wash out phage at day 2 to permit S. aureus resurgence by day 4.
- Program C (State control): Maintain constant dominance by continuous low FA and no phage (S. aureus–dominant) or high FA and intermittent phage (S. epidermidis–dominant) to test whether readouts track current state only.
- EV sequences: EV-Epi→EV-Aur vs EV-Aur→EV-Epi with identical cumulative EV dose and timing as Programs A/B.

Controls
- Hydrogels without FA; heat-inactivated phage; agr-defective S. aureus; single-species cultures; vehicle EV preps.
- Validate competitive dynamics by qPCR of species markers and CFU plating over time; agr activity by RNAIII qRT-PCR or fluorescent reporter in S. aureus; AIP cross-inhibition inferred by RNAIII suppression in mixed culture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452892/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts (order memory vs state)
- Inflammation: NF-κB activity (luciferase reporter) at prespecified checkpoints: end-epoch sampling immediately before and 6 h after each dominance flip; cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, CXCL8) by ELISA; AMPs (hBD2, LL-37) by qRT-PCR/immunoblot. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4219649/?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation capacity: immunostaining for KRT14 (basal), KRT10/involucrin/filaggrin (suprabasal), EdU incorporation; post-exposure clonogenicity in 2D progenitor outgrowth.
- Vesicle-specific: compare live-bacteria Program A/B to EV A/B to determine whether order effects require live QS/competition or are recapitulated by signal sequence alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8657977/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbial state metrics: species proportions, RNAIII levels, and total biomass to statistically adjust for current state at the time of host sampling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452892/?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and interpretation
- Order memory: If Program A and B yield distinct NF-κB/differentiation outcomes when measured at matched current dominance and biomass, conclude keratinocyte stem/progenitors encode exposure history (e.g., early S. aureus primes persistent hyper-reactivity; early S. epidermidis induces durable tolerance). If differences vanish after controlling for current dominance, state dominates over order.
- Live versus EVs: If EV sequences recapitulate order effects, vesicle cargo timing is sufficient; if not, live competition (agr dynamics, metabolite flux, lysis-derived PAMPs) is necessary. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6452892/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Month 1: Fabricate FA-gradient HA hydrogels; verify FA release; calibrate co-culture growth curves and agr/RNAIII assays; titer S. aureus–specific phage for partial debulking (∼1–2 log). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42461343/?utm_source=openai))
- Month 2: Run Programs A–C (live-bacteria arms), collect time-resolved microbial and host readouts.
- Month 3: Run EV-only sequences; complete differentiation and clonogenic assays; analyze order vs state using generalized linear models adjusting for species proportion and biomass.

Risk and mitigation
- Phage over-clearance of S. aureus: use sublethal MOI and shortened exposure; select phages with characterized host range to avoid off-targets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11680127/?utm_source=openai))
- FA cytotoxicity to organoids: pretest FA ranges; leverage carrier-based loading to smooth peaks.
- Unstable gradients: stage hydrogels in transwells to limit convective mixing; refresh media gently.
- Ambiguous dominance readouts: include RNAIII and CFU/qPCR to triangulate state.

Novelty and plausibility anchors
- FA-loaded HA hydrogel to steer staphylococcal succession and QS-regulated virulence inside a living skin organoid is not standard practice, but HA-based hydrogels can release palmitoleic acid and antimicrobial cargos with defined kinetics, supporting feasibility. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42461343/?utm_source=openai))
- Using an S. aureus–specific lytic phage as a precise, timed switch to interrogate host decoding of dominance (not therapy per se) extends organoid–microbe models where phage modulates epithelial responses. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42243284?utm_source=openai))

Decision rule for success (POC)
- Predefine a ≥30% divergence in NF-κB area-under-curve and a ≥20% shift in basal-to-suprabasal marker ratio between Program A and B, at matched instantaneous dominance, as evidence of order memory. If achieved in live arms and partially in EV arms, proceed to mechanistic dissection of chromatin and receptor-level tolerance pathways in follow-up studies.

text:
Title
Signal-history encoding in skin stem cells: Do sequential S. aureus and S. epidermidis vesicle signals write durable enhancer-density and nuclear-position “memory states” that bias inflammation and differentiation in organoids?

Background and rationale
- Skin epithelial stem cells retain an inflammation-primed state through chromatin accessibility changes that persist beyond the initial stimulus and alter later responses, indicating cell-intrinsic memory. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271))
- NF-κB–driven inflammatory programs recruit acetylation readers such as BRD4 to super-enhancers; these assemblies show density-dependent, acetylation-sensitive condensate behavior that can stabilize transcriptional states beyond transient signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4224636/?utm_source=openai))
- The epidermal differentiation complex (EDC) undergoes regulated repositioning from the nuclear lamina toward the interior during keratinocyte differentiation, linking spatial genome organization to lineage programs. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/58541?utm_source=openai))
- Bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs) from S. aureus elicit TLR2/NOD2-dependent pro-inflammatory programs in keratinocytes, whereas S. epidermidis produces factors that activate TLR2/AhR and induce antimicrobial peptides with distinct immunomodulatory tone. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27910159/?utm_source=openai))
- Collagen-based matrices can bind and sustain release of EVs, shaping exposure kinetics experienced by cells without ongoing microbial presence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7534280/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis-question
Do basal epidermal stem cells encode the amplitude–duration profile of sequential S. aureus and S. epidermidis EV signals into durable enhancer-density and nuclear-position states that (i) persist after stimulus removal, and (ii) bias inflammatory set points and differentiation trajectories when those cells are later assembled into skin organoids without bacteria?

Atomic strategy
Treat the EV exposure sequence itself as the single control knob that writes a discrete “memory state” in stem cells: NF-κB pulse history → stable BRD4/H3K27ac enhancer-density states → reinforced nuclear positioning of inflammatory and EDC loci → altered organoid inflammation/differentiation in the absence of microbes. No added factors; the only variable is the sequential EV signal history. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/am/pii/S0955067422000564?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Determine whether sequential EV signal histories imprint persistent enhancer-density states in stem cells that predict later organoid behavior.
- Aim 2. Test whether these states correlate with repositioning of inflammatory clusters and the EDC within the nucleus.
- Aim 3. Establish whether a collagen-based matrix that differentially retains EVs can implement exposure histories that yield equivalent memory states, separating cell-intrinsic memory from residual ligand confounders.

Experimental overview (POC-level, non-operational)
- Source system: Human epidermal stem/progenitor cells primed at the single-cell stage with purified EVs from S. aureus and S. epidermidis; then washed, expanded, and assembled into standard skin organoids with no microbes or EVs present thereafter.
- Exposure regimens (conceptual arms): 
  1) Long S. aureus EVs → short S. epidermidis EVs; 
  2) Long S. epidermidis EVs → short S. aureus EVs; 
  3) Concurrent cocktail with matched total exposure; 
  4) Vehicle controls. 
  Optional kinetic-encoding arm: Implement the “long” phase via EV preloaded collagen matrix to produce a decaying tail; deliver the “short” phase as a brief input before organoid assembly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7534280/?utm_source=openai))
- Washout/EV absence is verified prior to organoid assembly to ensure any downstream effect reflects stored cellular memory rather than ongoing stimulation.

Primary readouts and endpoints
- Memory-state reporters collected after washout, before organoid formation:
  - Enhancer-density state: low-input chromatin profiling of H3K27ac and BRD4 occupancy at sentinel inflammatory super-enhancers (e.g., IL1/IL6 loci) and key EDC enhancers; quantification focuses on peak density and cluster-level occupancy distributions rather than absolute peak calls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4224636/?utm_source=openai))
  - NF-κB condensate microdomains: imaging-based quantification of nuclear NF-κB/BRD4 foci number/size as a proxy for encoded enhancer activity density. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2643823/?utm_source=openai))
  - Nuclear positioning: DNA-FISH or equivalent spatial genomics assays for the EDC and inflammatory clusters relative to the lamina/interior. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/58541?utm_source=openai))
- Functional outcomes in organoids (no EVs present):
  - Inflammatory set point: basal cytokine/chemokine transcript and secreted profiles characteristic of keratinocyte-intrinsic programs; acute-response kinetics to a standardized non-microbial cue to test “trained” responsiveness. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271))
  - Differentiation capacity: expression patterns across the K14→K10/loricrin/filaggrin axis and structural EDC gene programs; morphological layer organization.

Key comparisons and predicted patterns
- Prediction P1 (pathobiont→commensal): Higher residual BRD4/H3K27ac density at inflammatory super-enhancers; increased NF-κB/BRD4 condensate burden; inflammatory clusters biased away from the lamina; organoids show elevated basal inflammatory tone and delayed/altered terminal differentiation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4224636/?utm_source=openai))
- Prediction P2 (commensal→pathobiont): Reduced inflammatory enhancer density with relative EDC interiorization and more efficient differentiation programs in organoids despite identical total EV input, indicating sequence-dependent coding rather than cumulative dose effects. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/58541?utm_source=openai))
- Prediction P3 (matrix-encoded long-phase): Collagen-retained EVs reproduce the “long” history and converge on the same memory-state signatures and organoid outcomes as direct exposure, confirming that temporal kinetics alone can write the state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7534280/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and feasibility
- Novel substrate of memory: density and spatial genome states, rather than only canonical histone-repressive mark erasure, in epithelial stem cells exposed to bacterial EV sequences. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271))
- Novel lever: using ECM-mediated EV retention to implement signal history without live microbes during organoid development. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7534280/?utm_source=openai))
- POC scale and timeline are met by focusing on sentinel loci, condensed chromatin/spatial assays, and basal functional readouts.

Analysis plan
- Encode each cell population’s memory state as a low-dimensional vector: [inflammatory SE density index, EDC enhancer density index, NF-κB/BRD4 condensate score, EDC and IL cluster radial position scores]. Use these to prospectively predict organoid inflammatory/differentiation outcomes via cross-validated regression/classification. Success criterion: memory-state vectors predict outcomes across exposure sequences and are reproducible with matrix-encoded kinetics.
- Causality probe (non-perturbative at POC level): Pharmacologic displacement of BRD4 during the priming window is not introduced here to avoid confounds; interpretation relies on convergent density and spatial signatures.

Outcomes that would falsify the hypothesis
- No differences in enhancer-density or nuclear-position states across sequences after washout, yet divergent organoid outcomes.
- Robust memory-state differences that fail to predict organoid inflammation/differentiation.
- Matrix-encoded long-phase failing to phenocopy direct long exposure, implicating residual ligand rather than encoded history.

Impact
If confirmed, the work establishes that bacterial EV signal history is written into durable enhancer-density and nuclear-position memories in skin stem cells, which independently bias later tissue behavior. This reframes microbe–epithelium interactions as programmable histories rather than transient cues and opens matrix-based temporal encoding as a controllable, microbe-free lever for shaping organoid development and epithelial disease modeling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271))

text:
Title: Encoding “first colonizer” history in a skin-on-chip to test epithelial memory against sequential Staphylococcus exposures

Integrated hypothesis–question:
Do brief, early S. epidermidis signals, when kinetically buffered by an enzyme‑remodelable PNAG‑rich EPS layer at the epithelial interface, imprint a chromatin–metabolic “memory” in keratinocyte stem/progenitors that durably attenuates subsequent S. aureus–driven inflammatory reprogramming and preserves stemness/differentiation capacity? Prior epithelial inflammatory memory is established in vivo; here the question is whether order and exposure kinetics alone—without immune cells—are sufficient to endow protection. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy:
Program the first wave. Use a PNAG‑based, remodelable EPS preconditioning film as a low‑pass kinetic filter that retains and slowly releases commensal ligands/vesicles during a defined plasticity window, then partially erase it enzymatically before the pathogen pulse. This converts “order” into distinct stimulus waveforms at PRRs, a known lever for durable epithelial memory formation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/microbiology/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2020.00952/full?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims (3‑month POC):
- Aim 1: Build a PDMS skin‑on‑chip with an EPS‑programmed apical interface to deliver sequence‑controlled exposures (S. epidermidis → S. aureus vs reverse) using live bacteria or EVs. Exploit PDMS oxygen permeability to stabilize staphylococcal and epithelial metabolism across multi‑day runs. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2012/lc/c2lc20982a?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Test whether S. epidermidis first exposure imprints attenuated recall to S. aureus: quantify cytokine kinetics, NF‑κB activity, and non‑destructive SERS metabolic fingerprints before and after pathogen challenge and washout. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5395151/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Link recall states to epithelial fate: measure basal stemness (p63, KRT14/15), early differentiation (KRT10, involucrin, loricrin), and colony‑forming efficiency; validate memory persistence post‑wash. Use minimal targeted ATAC‑qPCR or CUT&RUN at sentinel loci as optional stretch. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and feasibility checkpoints:
- Epithelial inflammatory memory is chromatin‑encoded in skin stem cells and alters later responses, providing a measurable ground truth for “memory” after stimulus removal. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))
- S. epidermidis ligands (e.g., lipoteichoic acid) signal via TLR2 to dampen TLR3‑driven keratinocyte cytokines, establishing a plausible protective first wave; EVs from S. epidermidis and S. aureus modulate keratinocyte programs, enabling bacteria‑free signal delivery options. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6386899/?utm_source=openai))
- PNAG is a dominant matrix polysaccharide in staphylococcal biofilms; Dispersin B specifically hydrolyzes PNAG, letting us “edit” the preconditioning layer between waves to test true history dependence. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/microbiology/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2020.00952/full?utm_source=openai))
- PDMS chips provide high O2 permeability to support stratifying keratinocytes and stable microbial secretomes over days; O2 control is a known confounder we explicitly stabilize. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6564678/?utm_source=openai))
- SERS can rapidly, label‑free track extracellular metabolic states and bacterial secreted metabolite signatures in supernatants, enabling time‑resolved state monitoring to gate destructive assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5395151/?utm_source=openai))

Model and platform:
- Chip: Two‑channel PDMS device with an apical exposure channel and a basal perfusion channel separated by a porous hydrogel membrane (collagen I/laminin). Primary human keratinocytes seeded to stratify for 5–7 days before exposures. Maintain 18–21% incubator O2; leverage PDMS diffusion for adequate apical oxygenation and minimize hypoxic variability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6564678/?utm_source=openai))
- EPS preconditioning layer: Spin‑coat or adsorb a thin PNAG‑rich film (with minor proteinaceous components for mechanical robustness) on the apical membrane prior to seeding. After epithelial confluence, perform a brief apical PNAG “activation” (hydration + Ca2+). For sequence switching, apply Dispersin B (5–50 µg/mL, 15–30 min) to partially digest PNAG, then wash to leave a remodeled residue that encodes first‑wave history. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711985/?utm_source=openai))

Exposure design (live or EVs):
- Order and timing:
  - SE→SA: S. epidermidis (10^6–10^7 CFU/mL) or SE‑EVs (5–20 µg/mL protein) for 24–48 h → wash 2× → rest 48–72 h → S. aureus (10^5–10^6 CFU/mL) or SA‑EVs (1–10 µg/mL) for 6–12 h → wash → rest 72 h.
  - SA→SE: reverse sequence with identical total AUCs.
  - Rationale: longer commensal, shorter pathogen pulses to model colonization precedents and acute challenges; rests unmask stimulus‑decoupled persistence (memory). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8657977/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls:
  - Cocktail co‑exposure, single‑species exposures, EPS without Dispersin B editing, Dispersin B vehicle, heat‑inactivated EVs. Include a 3D epidermal mixed‑infection model as a positive control for known commensal–pathogen interactions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8481888/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts and endpoints:
- Inflammation and signaling:
  - NF‑κB p65 nuclear translocation (live reporter if available), qPCR/ELISA for IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, TNF at 0, 6, 12, 24, 72 h post‑challenge; SERS on apical effluents every 6–12 h to track lactate/pyruvate, aromatic and purine bands indicative of metabolite flux and state. Use SERS principal component trajectories to define “persistent” states >48 h post‑wash as operational memory. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5395151/?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation capacity and stemness:
  - Basal markers: p63, KRT14/15; early/late differentiation: KRT10, involucrin, loricrin; colony‑forming efficiency (CFE) post‑challenge. A protective memory is defined by preserved CFE and delayed KRT10/involucrin induction in SE→SA versus SA→SE. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))
- Optional chromatin validation (single‑locus POC):
  - CUT&RUN or ChIP‑qPCR for H3K27ac at NF‑κB/AP‑1 target enhancers identified in prior epithelial memory studies. Persistence of enhancer acetylation in SE→SA after wash supports memory encoding. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34320411/?utm_source=openai))
- Microbial/EV controls:
  - Plate counts during live exposures; nanoparticle tracking and TEM for EV quality. For SERS, subtract known bacterial purine‑dominated spectral contributions using washout baselines and parallel bacteria‑only controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4911336/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes and interpretation:
- SE→SA with EPS preconditioning and partial PNAG editing yields attenuated cytokines, faster NF‑κB shutoff, SERS signatures consistent with lower glycolytic activation and earlier lipid recovery, and preserved CFE relative to SA→SE or no‑EPS conditions. This indicates protective epithelial memory set by first‑wave commensal kinetics and matrix‑encoded history. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature24271?utm_source=openai))
- SA→SE yields heightened cytokines, prolonged inflammatory SERS trajectories, and reduced CFE, signifying maladaptive memory or sensitization.
- If EV‑only sequences recapitulate live‑bacteria order effects, vesicular cargo is sufficient; if not, physical occupancy/metabolite depletion or EPS–ligand interplay is required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8657977/?utm_source=openai))

Falsification criteria:
- No sequence effect after controlling for dose/AUC, despite EPS programming and rests.
- No persistence of state by SERS or fate metrics beyond 48–72 h post‑wash.
- Dispersin B editing has no impact on second‑wave responses versus unedited EPS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711985/?utm_source=openai))

Risk mitigation:
- Oxygen confounding: log chip O2 using established methods; if needed, laminate PDMS with low‑permeability films regionally to clamp O2. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6564678/?utm_source=openai))
- SERS specificity: validate with ELISA/qPCR at SERS‑defined state transitions; include bacteria‑only and EV‑only spectral libraries to regress confounders. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5395151/?utm_source=openai))
- Biofilm overgrowth: cap live exposures to 6–12 h for S. aureus; rely on EVs for longer kinetics; use low‑MOI commensal conditioning.

Experimental plan and timeline (weeks):
- Weeks 1–2: Chip fabrication and EPS coating optimization; Dispersin B titration on PNAG films; keratinocyte seeding/stratification; establish SERS baselines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3711985/?utm_source=openai))
- Weeks 3–6: Sequence runs (live and EVs), with SERS‑gated destructive sampling for cytokines and markers.
- Weeks 7–10: Replication; CFE assays; optional single‑locus chromatin assays; analysis.

Advancement over status quo:
Co‑colonization skin models exist but do not explicitly encode or edit “first‑colonizer” history in an organoid‑compatible interface nor read out label‑free metabolic memory online. This proposal tests whether order and exposure kinetics alone can install protective epithelial memory, separating epithelial programming from immune contributions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8481888/?utm_source=openai))
