text:
Title
Source–sink metamaterial grafts: spatially selective rectification and engineered current sinks to enforce host-driven activation of hPSC-CM patches

Premise
- Human pluripotent stem cell–derived cardiomyocytes (hPSC-CMs) are immature at baseline with reduced IK1, depolarized resting potential, phase-4 depolarization, and Ca2+-clock/NCX–driven automaticity; these properties increase susceptibility to triggered activity and ectopy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3757253/?utm_source=openai))
- Large-animal studies demonstrate successful 1:1 host–graft coupling after transplantation, but also a clinically relevant syndrome of early engraftment ventricular arrhythmias. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4154594/?utm_source=openai))
- Increasing IK1 via dynamic clamp or Kir2.1 overexpression hyperpolarizes RMP, restores NaV availability, and suppresses spontaneous activity; recent work combining KCNJ2 upregulation with reduced depolarizing currents lowered arrhythmia burden in nonhuman primates. These approaches act chiefly at the single-cell level and do not guarantee tissue-level quiescence across adverse post-graft conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618522/?utm_source=openai))
- Non-excitable, coupled cells and their electrical state modulate propagation through resistive/capacitive loading; anisotropy and micro-geometry shape wavefront safety factors and reentry likelihood. These properties can be engineered in vitro. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32273847/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a temporal–spatial filter: at rest and for slow, local perturbations, the graft presents a high sink (strong inward rectification plus engineered current-sink geometry) that dissipates subthreshold fluctuations; for fast, coherent host wavefronts, the same structures are functionally transparent via designated high-coupling “highways,” preserving excitability, conduction velocity, and force.

Hypothesis–Goal (indistinguishable)
A graft designed as a source–sink metamaterial—combining (i) rest-strong, upstroke-transparent inward rectification in hPSC-CMs and (ii) tissue-level geometry that concentrates sink at the perimeter and distributes passive, non-regenerative sinks within the interior—will eliminate graft-origin automaticity and propagation of slow triggers under inflammatory, ischemic, catecholaminergic, and electrolyte stress, while maintaining near-normal host-driven activation times, conduction velocity, and contractile contribution.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and validate rest-strong, upstroke-transparent rectification in hPSC-CMs without compromising excitability.
- Design: Lentiviral or CRISPRa upregulation of KCNJ2 (Kir2.1) with tuning of rectification via Kir2.1/Kir2.3 subunit ratio or pore-block–modulating point mutants to maximize inward rectification at negative Vm and minimize outward current during rapid depolarization. Include a trafficking-optimized Kir2.1 variant to ensure membrane expression at adult-like densities.
- In vitro readouts: Single-cell APs (RMP, dV/dtmax, APD90), spontaneous rate, DAD/EAD incidence under isoproterenol, hypoxia/reoxygenation, hyperK+/hypoK+, and cytokine cocktail; dynamic-clamp IK1 benchmarking. Syncytial monolayer optical mapping for CVlong/CVtrans and capture threshold.
- Success criterion: ≥80% reduction in spontaneous activity and triggered events with ≤10% change in CVlong vs control hPSC-CM syncytia under all stressors; restored RMP ≤ −78 mV; preserved force under 1–3 Hz pacing.
- Rationale: IK1 augmentation stabilizes RMP and increases Na+ channel availability, suppressing automaticity without opposing a steep dV/dt host wavefront; this is well-grounded in hiPSC-CM dynamic clamp and Kir2.1 overexpression studies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618522/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build a perimeter “moat” plus interior “highways” to enforce tissue-level quiescence while preserving host entry and fast propagation.
- Design: Engineer ring-shaped zones at the graft perimeter with high Kir2.1 density and modestly reduced gap junctional coupling (e.g., Cx43 down-tuning to 50–70% via CRISPRi) to raise local sink and slightly increase axial resistance; create 2–4 radial “highways” (tracks) from host–graft interfaces into the graft core with high Cx43 and aligned myofiber anisotropy. Microcontact printing and collagen alignment will set fiber orientation and anisotropy (target CVlong/CVtrans ≈ 2). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17689494/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro readouts: Spatially targeted optogenetic/field stimuli to probe nucleation; measure critical nucleation area for ectopy, perimeter block probability, host-to-core activation latency, and reentry inducibility across pacing protocols. Compare to uniform constructs.
- Stress tests: Repeat under isoproterenol, hypoxia, high/low K+, and TNFα/IL-1β exposure.
- Success criterion: ≥5× increase in critical nucleation area and ≥90% suppression of outward propagation from graft-origin triggers, with ≤5 ms added latency to host-driven activation at graft core and ≤10% reduction in CVlong.
- Rationale: Source–sink mismatch at the perimeter absorbs slow, local depolarizations; coherent host wavefronts delivered via high-coupling highways overcome the moat through higher instantaneous source current and aligned anisotropy. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17689494/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Introduce a sparse lattice of non-excitable, hyperpolarized “sink units” to quench slow fluctuations without penalizing fast drive.
- Design: Engineer hiPSC-derived stromal cells (or neonatal cardiac fibroblasts for prototyping) to express Cx43 and strong IK1 (Kir2.1), while lacking NaV1.5 and CaV1.2 (CRISPR knockout or shRNA), yielding non-regenerative, low-Ra, hyperpolarized sinks. Interleave as a 5–10% areal density lattice within the graft interior.
- In vitro readouts: Optical mapping to quantify effects on τm for slow vs fast perturbations, wavefront curvature, activation delay, and DAD/EAD containment. Use optogenetic tools (e.g., halorhodopsin in sinks) transiently to partition resistive vs capacitive loading components and validate selectivity for slow components. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32273847/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criterion: ≥70% reduction in subthreshold fluctuation amplitude and DAD propagation distance with ≤5% change in host-driven activation time and CVlong at physiologic rates.
- Rationale: Coupled, non-excitable sinks spread local charge perturbations and lower input resistance for slow dynamics, but impose minimal voltage drop to brief, high-current wavefronts; prior myocyte–fibroblast coupling studies define the loading regimes to avoid conduction penalty. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3506117/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Systems-level verification in engineered tissue patches and in vivo
- Computational design loop: Calibrate a bidomain monodomain hybrid with myocyte–sink coupling, perimeter geometry, and anisotropy; optimize moat width, sink density, and highway number/width to maximize suppression of slow triggers while minimizing activation latency. Use interface conductance sweeps to model early post-graft coupling states. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37014103/?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo tests: 
  - Small-animal epicardial patch (rat) with optical mapping windows to quantify ectopy nucleation, capture ratio, and reentry under catecholamine and electrolyte challenges.
  - Large-animal (porcine) intramyocardial grafts with contact mapping and implantable monitors for early engraftment arrhythmia burden vs matched controls (uniform Kir2.1-only grafts).
- Primary endpoints: Arrhythmia burden during weeks 1–4; host-driven 1:1 capture across heart rates; absence of independent rhythm sources; preservation of regional conduction velocity and mechanical contribution.
- Comparator arms: Kir2.1-only graft; geometry-only graft; sink-only graft.

Milestones and criteria for stopping
- Gate 1 (months 0–9): Demonstrate Aim 1 success criteria in vitro.
- Gate 2 (months 6–15): Establish perimeter moat + highways meeting Aim 2 metrics across stressors.
- Gate 3 (months 12–24): Validate sink lattice selectivity (Aim 3) and integrate with Aim 2; finalize optimized design via modeling.
- Gate 4 (months 18–36): Reduce early engraftment arrhythmias ≥80% vs Kir2.1-only control in porcine model without degradation of host-driven CV or contractile indices.

Risk management
- Excessive conduction slowing from sinks or moat: tune sink density (≤10%), Cx43 levels, and moat width; validate safety factor >1.5 by 1D strand assays prior to patch assembly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3506117/?utm_source=openai))
- Incomplete efficacy under hyperkalemia/ischemia: model EK shifts to pre-tune Kir density; perimeter sink designed to fail gracefully (uniformly) without creating sharp gradients that favor unidirectional block. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37014103/?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty cross-check: While IK1 augmentation to suppress automaticity is established and has progressed to large-animal evidence, the tissue-level metamaterial strategy—perimeter sink with designated conduction highways and a sparse, hyperpolarized sink lattice—targets multicellular initiation and propagation thresholds directly and has not been systematically tested in graft engineering. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/Supplement_1/ehaf784.4823/8308522?utm_source=openai))

Validation of mechanistic assumptions
- Low IK1/immature electrophysiology and Ca2+-clock/NCX automaticity in hPSC-CMs: confirmed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3757253/?utm_source=openai))
- Early engraftment arrhythmias despite 1:1 coupling potential: confirmed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4154594/?utm_source=openai))
- IK1 augmentation suppresses automaticity but is not by itself a tissue-level guarantee: supported by single-cell dynamic clamp and overexpression literature and by recent multi-gene editing in NHPs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618522/?utm_source=openai))
- Non-excitable cell loading is bidirectional and tunable; hyperpolarized, coupled sinks can reduce resistive load penalties: supported by optogenetic dissection of RL vs CL. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32273847/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcome and impact
A graft that is electrically quiescent by design at the tissue level—silencing slow, local triggers under diverse stressors—yet fully excitable and force-generating when driven by the host. This satisfies the requirement for immediate and chronic host-driven synchrony without independent rhythmogenesis, addressing a primary translational barrier for hPSC-CM therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6329375/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Guardian-sink composite grafts to enforce host-driven activation of hPSC-CM tissues

Central hypothesis-question
Can a deliberately interdigitated network of non-excitable, gap junction–coupled, IK1-rich “guardian” cells embedded within hPSC-CM grafts convert subthreshold, local depolarizations into harmless shared load while sparing the fast, host-driven wavefront—thereby abolishing engraftment arrhythmias from day 0 without sacrificing conduction velocity or contractile output under catecholaminergic, ischemic, and electrolyte stressors? Engraftment arrhythmias are a major barrier after large-animal hPSC-CM transplantation, with focal ectopy arising at graft sites early post-implantation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature19815?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit source–sink physics at the tissue scale: distribute an inwardly rectifying, resting-range K+ sink through a coupled guardian-cell lattice so that slow, local voltage drifts and DADs are shunted across the network, but a rapid, spatially coherent host wavefront encounters negligible instantaneous load and propagates. IK1-like rectification provides large stabilizing conductance near rest and minimal outward current during the AP upstroke/plateau, preserving excitability and APD. Dynamic-clamp studies and electrotonic IK1 transfer support that augmenting IK1 hyperpolarizes hPSC-CMs, suppresses spontaneous activity, and improves upstroke without harming propagation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25691870/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build guardian-sink composites and quantify single-cell and tissue-level filtering
- Construct guardian cells from hPSC-derived stromal/myofibroblast-like cells engineered to express Cx43 and Kir2.1, but lacking NaV1.5 and Cav1.2 (non-excitable). Co-culture with ventricular-committed hPSC-CMs at graded guardian fractions (0–35%) and controlled interdigitation patterns.
- Readouts in 2D monolayers and 3D strips: spontaneous rate, resting membrane potential, (dV/dt)max, APD, conduction velocity (optical mapping), and contractile stress (traction microscopy). Trigger ectopy with isoproterenol, caffeine, extracellular K+ 5.5–7.5 mM, and pH 6.8.
- Benchmarks: relative to CM-only controls, composites show >90% reduction of spontaneous events, unchanged CV (±10%), preserved APD90 (±10%), and no sustained reentry under provocation.
- Rationale support: IK1 injection stabilizes RMP and increases upstroke in hiPSC-CMs; electrotonically delivered IK1 from Kir2.1-expressing non-cardiac cells suppresses automaticity; heterocellular coupling modulates pacemaking depending on sink size and ionic makeup. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25691870/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer topology to guarantee tissue-level quiescence without conduction penalty
- Use microfabrication to pattern alternating CM tracts and guardian lattices with tunable CM–guardian coupling (Cx43 vs Cx40/45) to bias load away from the rapid upstroke while maximizing spatial averaging of slow drifts. Vary guardian fraction and inter-nodal spacing to set a minimum “consensus area” required for spontaneous activation.
- Derive a quantitative guarantee: probability of ectopic breakthrough as a function of guardian density, coupling, and noise amplitude. Validate with real-time voltage imaging under stochastic current injection and DAD induction.
- Quantify CM–guardian coupling with OptoGap and dual patch to ensure CM–CM coupling remains dominant, preserving safety factor. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-88573-1?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate elimination of engraftment arrhythmias in vivo
- Prepare vascularized epicardial patches containing pre-patterned CM–guardian composites. Transplant onto subacute infarcts in pigs. Continuous telemetry and weekly high-density epicardial mapping for 4–6 weeks.
- Primary endpoint: reduction in ventricular arrhythmia burden and absence of sustained VT/VF versus CM-only grafts; focal arrhythmia origins not co-localizing with graft sites. Secondary endpoints: host-driven activation of graft, CV, graft contractile contribution, and safety labs.
- Context: large-animal studies show functional remuscularization but early, graft-originating arrhythmias; the proposed composite targets this failure mode mechanistically. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.4162?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and key methods
- Guardian engineering: lentiviral Kir2.1 and Cx43; CRISPR knockout of SCN5A and CACNA1C. Confirm IK1 density, rectification, and absence of fast inward currents by patch clamp.
- Composite assembly: photopatterned ECM to set adjacency matrices; define CM–guardian junctional conductance via connexin isoform ratios.
- Electrophysiology: voltage-sensitive dye mapping at 1 kHz sampling; dynamic clamp in sentinel CMs to titrate “virtual guardians” and calibrate the effective GK1 provided by the lattice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618522/?utm_source=openai))
- Stress testing: β-adrenergic drive, acidosis, hyperkalemia; quantify DAD/EAD incidence and breakthrough probability.
- Coupling assays: OptoGap to map functional connectivity and ensure guardian cells are electrically, but not mechanically, integrated. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-88573-1?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria and decision points
- In vitro: composites meet Aim 1 benchmarks across all stressors. If CV falls >10%, reduce guardian fraction or weaken CM–guardian coupling until safety factor and CV normalize.
- In vivo: ≥80% reduction in arrhythmia burden vs CM-only; no sustained VT/VF from day 0–28; activation maps show host-led excitation of graft; contractile benefit non-inferior to CM-only grafts.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Excess APD shortening or conduction load: leverage IK1’s inward rectification to minimize depolarized-phase load; cap guardian fraction; favor CM–CM over CM–guardian coupling by connexin tuning. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25691870/?utm_source=openai))
- Insufficient suppression under catecholamines: increase guardian IK1 density modestly or refine lattice density; perioperative anti-arrhythmic regimen as rescue, which is effective in large animals. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44385-025-00048-4?utm_source=openai))
- Heterogeneous coupling: measure and adjust with OptoGap-guided feedback. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-021-88573-1?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline
- Months 0–6: Guardian construct validation; composite assembly; in vitro filtering metrics established.
- Months 6–12: Topology optimization and guarantee curve; finalize clinical-scale patch fabrication.
- Months 12–24: Pig study with telemetry/mapping; go/no-go on arrhythmia endpoints; dossier for regulatory discussion.

Innovation
This proposal shifts anti-arrhythmia control from single-cell channel edits to a dynamics-aware, tissue-scale source–sink design that selectively damps slow, local perturbations yet passes fast, global drive. It is mechanistically grounded in IK1’s stabilizing effects and heterocellular electrotonic interactions, and targets the specific early, graft-originating arrhythmias documented in large animals. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25691870/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Epicardial microelectrode mesh–shaped extracellular potential control for quiescent, host-capturable hPSC-CM grafts

Central hypothesis–question
Can a conformal, low-impedance epicardial microelectrode mesh that homogenizes and mildly biases the extracellular potential (Ve) of an engineered heart tissue (EHT) enforce tissue-level electrical quiescence of hPSC-CM grafts without degrading excitability or conduction, so that activation is exclusively host-driven from day 0 through chronic remodeling and stress? The mechanistic basis is v_m = v_i − v_e: shaping Ve with a conductive mesh raises the threshold for disorganized, small-source depolarizations while preserving or improving capture by fast, coherent host wavefronts. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bidomain_model?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Manipulate the extracellular domain rather than the myocyte membrane: a conformal Au/Pt microgrid in intimate contact with the graft and border zone acts as a field homogenizer and optional mild anodal bias source. In grounded mode, it shunts and flattens local Ve gradients that would otherwise assist ectopic initiation; in biased mode, a small positive Ve offset hyperpolarizes cells (more negative v_m), increasing NaV availability and source–sink on organized activation. This decouples automaticity from conduction at the tissue scale, immediately upon grafting. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0735109794005588?utm_source=openai))

Background and rationale
- Engraftment arrhythmias after hPSC-CM transplantation are frequent and linked to immature electrophysiology (low IK1, spontaneous automaticity, depolarized diastolic potential) and incomplete coupling in the border zone. Conventional fixes target channels within cells but may not guarantee tissue-scale quiescence, especially early post-graft and under stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10283080/?utm_source=openai))
- Kir2.1 enhancement or dynamic-clamp IK1 abolishes automaticity and deepens resting potential in vitro, but tissue-level ectopy can still arise from source–sink imbalances and heterogeneity; therefore, a complementary, extracellular field solution is warranted. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1161/circresaha.118.311209?utm_source=openai))
- Conformal, stretchable epicardial meshes and bioelectronic patches already achieve high-fidelity sensing and pacing on beating hearts, establishing feasibility of stable, large-area, low-impedance interfacing. Modeling and physical data show that an equipotential conductive patch region reduces local potential gradients under it; recent simulations suggest highly conductive epicardial patches can suppress reentry and conduction block. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4521772/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Demonstrate that a grounded epicardial microelectrode mesh integrated with hPSC-CM EHT enforces tissue-level quiescence without loss of excitability or conduction in vitro.
- Build 3D EHTs (hiPSC-ventricular CMs ± Kir2.1 enhancement for adult-like MDP) on a porous elastomer carrying a 2D Au/Pt serpentine microgrid (line width 5–20 μm; open area >80%). Compare to identical EHTs without mesh and to non-conductive metallic dummy patterns (negative controls). ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1161/circresaha.118.311209?utm_source=openai))
- Metrics: spontaneous ectopy incidence, dV/dt_max, CV, APD, and source–sink (optical mapping + multielectrode recordings). Stressors: isoproterenol, hypokalemia, and hypoxia/reoxygenation. Endpoint: ≥80% reduction in spontaneous ectopy with no decrease in dV/dt_max or CV versus no-mesh EHT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9411865/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Quantify dose–response and safety of mild anodal bias (Ve offset) delivered by the mesh to maintain quiescence under adrenergic, ischemic, and electrolyte stress.
- Deliver low-current, DC-stabilized bias via the mesh to elevate local Ve by +1 to +5 mV (measured with reference microelectrodes). Test whether bias eliminates stress-evoked ectopy while preserving host-capture thresholds and conduction during imposed wavefronts. Monitor electrochemistry (charge density, pH, faradaic products) to remain within safe, platinum-compatible charge injection limits; preferentially operate in grounded mode and reserve bias for closed-loop suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10903405/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism validation: map Ve and v_m fields to show reduced spatial Ve gradients under the grounded mesh and hyperpolarization with bias. Compare to finite-element bidomain simulations incorporating a high-conductivity boundary to recapitulate measured ectopy suppression. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41551-026-01659-x?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test efficacy and host capture in large-animal infarct models.
- Implant mesh-integrated EHTs onto subacute infarcts in pigs. Use high-density epicardial mapping to quantify arrhythmia burden, capture by sinus and paced wavefronts, and wavefront curvature at graft borders, comparing mesh-EHT vs EHT-only vs non-conductive mesh. Closed-loop bias is triggered only upon ectopy detection. Primary endpoints at 1–8 weeks: reduction in graft-originated ectopy, preserved conduction velocity across graft–host interface, and synchronous contraction with host. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-020-00493-6?utm_source=openai))

Study design and methods (key elements)
- Mesh–EHT construct: microfabricate Au/Pt serpentine meshes on soft elastomers with open architecture (3D-MIM design rules) to ensure mechanical compliance and nutrient diffusion; interconnect to percutaneous leads or a subcutaneous header for grounding/bias. Confirm conformal contact and minimal tissue stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4521772/?utm_source=openai))
- Electrophysiology: optical mapping (RH237 or GEVIs) and microelectrode arrays across EHT and border zones; quantify spontaneous activity and conduction. Apply standardized stressors (isoproterenol, low [K+]o, hypoxia). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9411865/?utm_source=openai))
- Modeling: bidomain simulations of an EHT slab on host myocardium with a high-conductivity boundary condition to predict Ve homogenization, threshold elevation for focal sources, and unchanged capture by synchronous wavefronts; calibrate with measured Ve/v_m maps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10903405/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: electrochemical monitoring at the tissue–metal interface; prioritize passive grounded operation. Bias magnitudes limited to subthreshold Ve shifts; no chronic DC when unnecessary. Histology for inflammation/fibrosis at the interface.

Why this satisfies constraints
- Decoupled automaticity vs conduction at design stage: quiescence emerges from Ve control (tissue-level) independent of waiting for maturation; optional Kir2.1 deepens MDP and further increases NaV availability without inducing pacemaking. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1161/circresaha.118.311209?utm_source=openai))
- No compromise of excitability or CV: Ve homogenization reduces destabilizing ephaptic pre-depolarization but leaves dV/dt_max and gap junctional conduction intact; deeper rest via small Ve elevation increases NaV availability and source strength for host-driven waves. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1152%2Fphysrev.00025.2003?utm_source=openai))
- Tissue-level guarantee: a mm–cm scale conductive boundary modifies Ve over the graft and border zone, the spatial scale at which ectopy recruits myocardium. Empirically, conductive patches reduce potential gradients beneath them and modeling predicts suppression of reentry/blocks when patch conductivity is high. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0735109794005588?utm_source=openai))
- Robustness under stress: closed-loop, temporary Ve bias adds safety margin during adrenergic drive, ischemia, and electrolyte perturbations, when ectopy risk peaks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10903405/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1 (months 0–9): In vitro proof that grounded mesh cuts spontaneous ectopy ≥80% under stress with unchanged or improved dV/dt_max and CV. Go if achieved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9411865/?utm_source=openai))
- M2 (months 9–18): Demonstrate safe, reversible suppression with +1 to +5 mV Ve bias; document negligible electrochemical byproducts at interface. Go if ectopy suppressed without conduction slowing.
- M3 (months 18–36): Pig study shows ≥50% reduction in graft-originated arrhythmia burden and consistent host-capture across all conditions versus EHT-only. Proceed to scale-up if met. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-020-00493-6?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- Grounded meshes will create an equipotential “Ve canopy” over the graft, raising the recruitment threshold for small ectopic sources while allowing immediate host capture; mild bias will expand safety margin under stress. Success would establish extracellular field-shaping as a generalizable, orthogonal control axis to ion-channel engineering for nonarrhythmogenic cardiac remuscularization. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0735109794005588?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If any conduction slowing is detected, adjust mesh openness and contact impedance to preserve extracellular resistivity seen by fast wavefronts. If bias proves electrochemically limiting, restrict to grounded mode and rely on mesh conductivity alone, guided by modeling that favors high-conductivity patches for antiarrhythmic effects. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41551-026-01659-x?utm_source=openai))

References (indicative)
- Engraftment arrhythmia/immaturity: ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10283080/?utm_source=openai))
- IK1 strategy and excitability: ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1161/circresaha.118.311209?utm_source=openai))
- Epicardial meshes/bioelectronics feasibility: ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4521772/?utm_source=openai))
- Ve control principles and virtual electrodes: ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bidomain_model?utm_source=openai))
- Conductive patch field effects and antiarrhythmic modeling: ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0735109794005588?utm_source=openai))

Title
Host-border rectifying gap junctions to enforce one‑way activation of hPSC‑CM grafts

Central hypothesis-question
Can we convert the graft–host interface from bidirectional to polarity-gated coupling by programming border-zone host cardiomyocytes to form heterotypic, voltage-rectifying gap junctions that pass host→graft activation with native conduction safety factor while suppressing graft→host ectopy across post-graft inflammation, adrenergic stress, ischemia, and electrolyte perturbation? Engraftment arrhythmias generally emerge after host–graft coupling forms (≈1–3 weeks), whereas very early after transplantation the graft is field-entrained by the host; thus, an interface that becomes direction-selective as soon as coupling appears should decouple conduction competence from graft automaticity and prevent arrhythmia at its mechanistic onset. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cardiovascres/article/121/11/1638/8215798?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Install a “rectifying border ring”: engineer a narrow annulus of host cardiomyocytes at the graft perimeter to express a connexin complement that forms heterotypic, transjunctional voltage (Vj)-dependent rectifying channels with the graft’s Cx43-rich membranes. These channels exhibit high open probability for the Vj polarity corresponding to host‑leading action potentials but close for reverse polarity, thereby allowing anterograde capture while blocking retrograde graft ectopy without depressing forward excitability or conduction velocity. Inspiration comes from invertebrate rectifying electrical synapses built from ShakB innexins; feasibility in mammalian tissue leverages documented Vj‑polarity asymmetry of heterotypic connexin channels (e.g., Cx40–Cx43; Cx43–Cx45) and the dominant role of connexin N‑terminal structures in voltage gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2663713/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and quantify rectification in mammalian heterotypic gap junctions optimized for the host‑border.
- 1.1 Channel design. Prioritize human Cx40 (high unitary conductance; atrial/His-Purkinje isoform) paired heterotypically with graft Cx43 to bias Vj‑dependent gating. Create minimal N‑terminus–guided variants of Cx40 or Cx43 (domain swaps or point substitutions in NT/TM1–CL interface) to tune rectification without lowering forward conductance. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.4161/19336950.2014.949188?utm_source=openai))
- 1.2 Biophysics. Use Xenopus oocytes and N2a/HeLa pairs for dual voltage clamp to obtain steady-state gj–Vj curves, time constants, and rectification ratios (R = gj,forward/gj,reverse at physiological Vj). Map conductance under adrenergic signaling (PKA), PKC activation, Ca2+/CaM elevation, acidosis, hypoxia, high [K+]o to ensure forward-path robustness and reverse-path closure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2716739/?utm_source=openai))
- Go/no‑go criteria: R ≥ 5 at ±40 mV with forward gj ≥ 70% of Cx43–Cx43 controls and <10% reduction under isoproterenol or pH 6.8.

Aim 2. Build a border‑ring tissue model to test one‑way capture, conduction safety, and arrhythmia suppression under stress.
- 2.1 Interface construct. Pattern 1D cables and 2D slabs where “host” human ventricular myocytes (or iPSC‑CMs matured to ventricular phenotype) expressing the selected border connexin variant contact hPSC‑CM graft tissue enriched in Cx43. Use microcontact printing to define a 200–400 µm annulus of modified host cells around the graft core.
- 2.2 Electrophysiology. Optical voltage/Ca2+ mapping with stimulation from host or graft sides to quantify anterograde and retrograde capture thresholds, conduction velocity (CV) across the interface, and unidirectional block. Challenge with isoproterenol, hypoxia (1–2% O2), [K+]o 6–8 mM, and burst pacing to elicit graft ectopy. Outcomes: preserve forward CV within ±10% of host–host controls while reducing retrograde triggers by ≥80%. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cardiovascres/article/121/11/1697/8046285?utm_source=openai))
- 2.3 Early-post-graft relevance. In organotypic human myocardial slices with graft spheroids, assess immediate field entrainment from host and the transition to junctional coupling; verify that once coupling appears, retrograde propagation is selectively suppressed by the border ring. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cardiovascres/article/121/11/1638/8215798?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. In vivo proof-of-concept: arrhythmia prevention without loss of contractile benefit.
- 3.1 Delivery. In a rat MI model, perform “gene painting” of a 1–2 mm annulus at the infarct border with AAV9-cTnT:CX40 (or optimized variant), then deliver an epicardial hPSC‑CM patch. Spatial confinement is ensured by local epicardial application and limited spread of AAV9 in scarred tissue.
- 3.2 Endpoints. Telemetry ECG and programmed stimulation to quantify VT/VF incidence and burden for 6–8 weeks; ex vivo optical mapping of the host–graft interface to assess directionality and CV; echocardiography/MRI for ejection fraction and regional strain. Stress tests: isoproterenol, transient LAD occlusion (ischemia/reperfusion), and electrolyte shifts.
- 3.3 Large‑animal bridge. In swine with transmural infarcts, deliver border‑ring AAV under surgical visualization followed by hPSC‑CM patch; employ panoramic optical mapping and high-density electrograms to assess unidirectional gating and arrhythmia suppression. Background: hPSC‑CM therapies in large animals show transient but serious engraftment arrhythmias; directional gating addresses this failure mode mechanistically. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10901678/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and analyses

1) Channel selection and optimization
- Screen Cx40–Cx43 and Cx43–Cx45 heterotypic pairs; prioritize the pair with higher forward gj and rectification. Use NT swaps guided by ShakB rectification motifs to amplify polarity sensitivity without compromising trafficking. Outcomes include single-channel conductance, gj–Vj asymmetry, and kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2663713/?utm_source=openai))

2) Ensuring tissue-level guarantees
- Source–sink metrics: compute activation thresholds and safety factor across the interface using measured gj and cell geometry; require that only host‑side coherent wavefronts can excite the graft. Perform 2D propagation assays to verify that graft‑initiated wavefronts experience unidirectional block at the interface. 
- Stress robustness: repeat assays under catecholamines, hypoxia, acidosis, and elevated [K+]o to emulate early inflammatory and ischemic environments; the targeted channel design relies on Vj polarity rather than absolute membrane potential, which should maintain selectivity across depolarizing conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2716739/?utm_source=openai))

3) Border‑localized expression without degrading host conduction
- Spatial confinement: deliver AAV9 locally to the border annulus; quantify off‑target expression by RNAscope and immunostaining. Host–host CV within the annulus is benchmarked; Cx40’s high conductance supports preserved CV if expression levels are controlled. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.4161/19336950.2014.949188?utm_source=openai))
- Interface specificity arises naturally because heterotypic Cx40–Cx43 channels form at host–graft contacts (graft is Cx43-dominant), while host–host contacts may be homotypic Cx40 or mixed; we will titrate expression to avoid slowing intrahost CV.

Key readouts and success criteria
- Biophysical: rectification ratio R ≥ 5; forward gj ≥ 0.7× Cx43–Cx43; no significant forward gj loss under isoproterenol or pH 6.8.
- Tissue: forward CV across interface within ±10% of host–host; ≥80% reduction in retrograde captures during ectopic graft pacing; elimination of sustained reentry seeded from graft.
- In vivo: ≥70% reduction in VT/VF incidence and burden versus controls with identical grafts but no border rectifier; preserved or improved regional wall strain relative to graft-only animals.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- If heterotypic rectification is insufficient at physiological Vj, proceed to Cx43 NT-engineered variants to enhance polarity sensitivity, guided by NT/TM1–CL biophysics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3735448/?utm_source=openai))
- If intrahost conduction slows within the annulus, lower expression using weaker promoters or switch to Cx40 variants with higher open probability and minimal slow gating; as a contingency, add a thin, graft‑facing polyelectrolyte hydrogel coating on the patch that modestly increases reverse extracellular resistance (ionic‑diode behavior) without affecting forward fields. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8707621/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and novelty
- Mechanistic correctness: Engraftment arrhythmias correlate with the emergence of bidirectional electrical coupling; early field entrainment precedes this stage. A polarity-gated interface directly targets the causal window. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cardiovascres/article/121/11/1638/8215798?utm_source=openai))
- Biological plausibility: Rectifying electrical synapses are established in vivo (ShakB variants), and mammalian heterotypic connexins display Vj‑dependent asymmetry; connexin NT domains encode voltage gating, enabling rational protein engineering within human isoforms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2663713/?utm_source=openai))
- Unmet need: Prior strategies emphasize graft maturation or global conduction changes; a host‑border rectifier is an interface‑level, tissue‑scale control that decouples conduction competence from automaticity without suppressing contractile contribution.

Milestones and timeline (24–30 months)
- Months 0–6: Channel design and screening; select lead pair/variant meeting Aim 1 criteria.
- Months 6–15: Interface tissue models; demonstrate one‑way capture and stress robustness; refine dosing to preserve forward CV.
- Months 15–24: Rat MI study with telemetry and ex vivo mapping; gate optimization.
- Months 24–30: Swine feasibility (small cohorts) focusing on safety and directional conduction metrics.

Expected outcome
A validated, host‑centric interface that renders hPSC‑CM grafts electrically obedient to the native myocardium from the onset of coupling, preventing graft‑to‑host ectopy while preserving anterograde conduction and contractile benefit across clinically relevant stressors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10901678/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
A one-way host→graft electrical interface for hPSC-CM patches using heterotypic Cx43/Cx45 rectification with source–sink geometry to enforce follower-only activation

Central hypothesis (research goal as a question)
Can a cardiac graft be made intrinsically incapable of initiating beats in the host by programming the host–graft boundary to behave as a tissue-scale electrical diode that: (i) conducts host→graft with high safety factor; (ii) attenuates graft→host below threshold; and (iii) preserves intra-graft excitability and force?

Atomic strategy
Program rectified intercellular current transfer at the host–graft boundary by forming heterotypic Cx43/Cx45 gap junctions that exhibit strong transjunctional-voltage–dependent gating asymmetry favoring host→graft current, and embed the boundary in a micro-funnel geometry that increases source–sink asymmetry for forward versus reverse propagation. This single interface-level change decouples conduction competence from automaticity at the tissue scale without depressing myocyte excitability. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11509355/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale
- hPSC-CM grafts can cause early post-transplant ventricular arrhythmias in large animals, highlighting the need for interface-level solutions that work before full maturation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24776797/?utm_source=openai))
- Heterotypic Cx43/Cx45 channels show direction- and Vj-dependent conductance asymmetry (rectification) and reduced conductance only when biased unfavorably; this can be exploited so that host depolarization opens the interface, while graft-led depolarization closes it. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11509355/?utm_source=openai))
- Source–sink physics predicts that geometrical expansion produces unidirectional block; a boundary composed of many narrow host-facing entries (sources) merging into thicker graft tissue (sink) favors host→graft conduction and attenuates the reverse direction. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00025.2003?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build a rectifying “diode belt” at the host–graft interface using Cx45 in a boundary layer of hPSC-CMs and quantify direction-dependent coupling and excitation transfer.
- Construct: 3D patches whose outermost ~200–300 µm ring expresses Cx45; core expresses Cx43 (native) and lacks ectopic Cx45. Pattern by ring-seeding during assembly; verify by immunostaining and single-cell RNA-seq of boundary vs core.
- Biophysics: Dual patch clamp in heterotypic pairs (host-like Cx43+ ventricular cells vs graft boundary Cx45+) to measure steady-state gj–Vj and instantaneous rectification index; fit with 4-state models parameterized for Cx43/Cx45. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684404/?utm_source=openai))
- Tissue function: Co-culture patterned graft edges with adult ventricular syncytia in microfluidic “two-domain” chips. Optical mapping during pacing from host-side vs graft-side to quantify: conduction probability, delay, CV, and safety factor across the boundary. Controls: homotypic Cx43 boundary; scrambled ring geometry.

Success criterion: ≥95% successful host→graft activation with ≤5 ms added latency; ≤1% graft→host exits during 10^5 premature beats/provocation stimuli at baseline and under β-adrenergic drive. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00025.2003?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer boundary micro-geometry to amplify forward source–sink and dissipate reverse waves; define robustness across stressors.
- Geometry: Photopattern an interface composed of 10–50 “microfingers” (5–15 µm width, 50–200 µm length) projecting from host tissue into the graft ring, merging into thicker graft bundles. Map families of geometries and boundary ring thickness.
- Metrics: Determine forward vs reverse activation thresholds, wavefront curvature, and block probability under: isoproterenol, mild hyperkalemia, partial uncoupling (carbenoxolone), and transient hypoxia. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4201087/?utm_source=openai))
- Modeling: Calibrate 2D monodomain models with measured gj–Vj and geometry to predict minimal ring width and channel density for diode behavior; validate against experiments. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00025.2003?utm_source=openai))

Success criterion: Across stressors, forward conduction probability ≥0.95 and reverse ≤0.01 for at least one geometry–density combination that preserves intra-graft CV within 10% of Cx43-only controls.

Aim 3. Test anti-arrhythmic efficacy in vivo using a pre-formed rectifying boundary.
- Preparation: Matured patches with Cx45 boundary and microfunnelized edge are sutured epicardially onto infarct border in swine; then in a non-human primate cohort as scale-up.
- Endpoints: Continuous telemetry for 4–6 weeks post-implant; programmed stimulation with and without isoproterenol; ultra-high-density epicardial mapping to identify graft→host exits versus host→graft capture; contractile contribution by MRI strain.
- Comparators: Patches with homotypic Cx43 boundary; patches without microgeometry; sham.

Primary outcome: Reduction of spontaneous and provoked graft-originating ventricular arrhythmias versus controls without loss of host capture or intra-graft conduction. Secondary: preserved or improved wall strain relative to controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6329375/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and methods (key elements)
- Gene constructs and patterning: Cx45 expression driven by a doxycycline-off cassette in boundary cells for tunability; ring-seeding to confine expression. Validate absence of Cx45 in core by spatial transcriptomics.
- Electrophysiology: Whole-cell dual patch in heterotypic pairs to obtain gj–Vj and time constants; optical mapping (voltage and calcium) at 1 kHz frame rate; quantify safety factor and wavefront curvature.
- Geometry fabrication: Photolithographic ECM patterns on elastomeric membranes; microcontact printing to define finger arrays. Confirm anisotropy by SHG imaging of fibers.
- Provocation: Isoproterenol, K+ 5.5–6.5 mM, carbenoxolone titration, hypoxia 5% O2.
- Statistics and power: Pre-registered thresholds for forward capture and reverse exit probability; bootstrap CIs for rare-event estimates.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- Risk: Excessive reduction of boundary conductance by Cx43/Cx45 could slow forward activation. Mitigation: increase junctional density at the ring; widen microfingers; titrate Cx45 expression; compare Cx40 as an alternative heterotypic partner with Cx43. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4594514/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Rectification insufficient under extreme catecholaminergic states. Mitigation: strengthen geometric asymmetry; shorten finger width; increase ring thickness to raise forward safety factor. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00025.2003?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Novelty/feasibility: Rectified heterotypic coupling is established in multiple systems (heart Cx43/Cx45; neuronal electrical synapses) and has been exploited in silico for directional control, but not for anti-arrhythmic cardiac graft design—supporting novelty with biological plausibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861779/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Demonstrate rectification at single-junction and boundary tissue levels; define gj–Vj parameters and initial geometry set.
- Year 2: Map robustness across stressors; finalize ring thickness and finger array for diode behavior; preclinical safety (no negative inotropy; preserved CV).
- Year 3–4: Swine efficacy; NHP pilot with continuous telemetry and high-density mapping; go/no-go based on arrhythmia reduction and preserved contractile contribution.

Outcome and impact
If successful, this interface-level “electrical diode” converts an arrhythmia-prone hPSC-CM graft into a follower-only syncytium that conducts and contracts in synchrony with the host while being structurally unable to pace the host, from the first hours post-implant through physiological stress. This directly targets the documented graft-related arrhythmia problem with a mechanism grounded in connexin rectification and source–sink physics rather than global suppression of excitability. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24776797/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Rectifying electrotonic-sink companion cells to enforce tissue-level quiescence of hPSC-CM grafts without impairing host-driven conduction

Hypothesis–goal (merged)
Engineered, non-excitable, high-Cx43 companion cells endowed with strong inward-rectifier K+ current (Kir2.1) will act as a rectifying electrotonic sink that prevents tissue-level automaticity of hPSC-CM grafts under acute and chronic stresses, yet preserves rapid host-driven activation, thereby eliminating engraftment arrhythmias while maintaining conduction velocity and contractile contribution.

Atomic strategy
Impose a multicellular, source–sink gate on excitability: at diastole and for slow, local depolarizations the coupled sink dominates and clamps Vmem; during a fast, spatially coherent host wavefront the sink “turns benign” due to Kir2.1 rectification and high-gap-junction coupling, allowing normal propagation.

Rationale
- hPSC-CMs are immature with low IK1, significant If, and spontaneous activity, which contribute to engraftment arrhythmias in large animals; antiarrhythmic drug regimens (amiodarone+ivabradine) blunt but do not mechanistically eliminate the source. Gene-edited “quiescent-yet-excitable” hPSC-CMs (↓HCN4/CACNA1H/SLC8A1, ↑KCNJ2) reduce arrhythmias, supporting automaticity as a key driver. A tissue-level solution that works immediately post-graft and under stress is still needed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8514851/?utm_source=openai))
- Non-excitable cells electrically coupled to myocytes behave as electrotonic loads that can suppress spontaneous activity and modulate conduction; effects depend on density, coupling, and I–V properties. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4001130/?utm_source=openai))
- Kir2.1 provides strong inward rectification via voltage-dependent polyamine block: high conductance near rest, minimal outward current at depolarized potentials. Thus, a Kir2.1-rich sink strongly stabilizes diastole yet imposes limited dynamic load during the AP upstroke. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4145359/?utm_source=openai))
- Proof-of-principle: Kir2.1-expressing non-cardiac cells, when coupled to spontaneously active myocytes, hyperpolarize and silence their automaticity by electrotonic clamp. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16937189/?utm_source=openai))
- Augmenting Cx43 at graft interfaces enhances electrotonic coupling and can improve conduction across injured myocardium. This supports using high-Cx43 companion cells to create a controllable, distributed sink network. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature06321?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Engineer and characterize rectifying-sink companion cells (rSink) that are non-excitable, high-Cx43, high-Kir2.1, with defined passive properties and zero NaV/ICaL.
2) Determine rSink density and spatial patterning that enforce tissue-level quiescence of hPSC-CM constructs without reducing longitudinal conduction velocity (θ) or dV/dtmax under host-like stimulation.
3) Test efficacy and robustness of rSink+hPSC-CM grafts in ex vivo human myocardial slices and in a large-animal infarct model against engraftment arrhythmias from day 0 through 8 weeks under catecholaminergic, ischemic, and electrolyte stresses.

Methods

Aim 1: Build and verify rSink cells
- Cell chassis: Human ventricular fibroblasts or mesenchymal stromal cells rendered non-excitable (CRISPR ablation of SCN5A/CACNA1C) and overexpressing Cx43 and Kir2.1; validate absence of APs. Quantify I–V and inward rectification, resting potential, input resistance; confirm strong diastolic K+ conductance with reduced outward current during depolarization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4001130/?utm_source=openai))
- Coupling: Dual patch and FRAP to measure junctional conductance to hPSC-CMs; ensure high, stable coupling at 37°C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4001130/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2: In vitro tissue-level quiescence without conduction penalty
- Constructs: 2D monolayers and 3D engineered tissues combining hPSC-CMs (optimized NaV1.5/Cx43 expression) with rSink at varied ratios (0–20%) and spatial patterns: perimeter ring, interpenetrating lattice (below percolation threshold), and random sparse seeding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3013501/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts:
  - Spontaneous activity maps, focal source formation, and wavebreak via high-speed optical mapping (Vmem and Ca2+). 
  - Host-like drive: field or optogenetic pacing to emulate a rapid, coherent wavefront; measure θ, dV/dtmax, capture rate, and safety factor over distances. 
  - Stress testing: isoproterenol, hypoxia/ischemia-reperfusion, K+/Mg2+ shifts. 
- Success criteria: ≥90% reduction in spontaneous focal activations and ectopic runs; unchanged θ (±10%) and dV/dtmax under paced conditions versus hPSC-CM-only control; preserved twitch force at matched rate.
- Mechanistic tests:
  - “Quorum” assay: minimal cluster size of rogue hPSC-CMs needed to initiate propagation with/without rSink. 
  - Rectification necessity: replace Kir2.1 with weak-rectifier variant to test loss of conduction preservation despite quiescence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4145359/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Ex vivo slice and large-animal validation
- Human ventricular slices: Inject hPSC-CM±rSink islands; map conduction and automaticity under catecholamines and hypoxia; quantify ectopy suppression and preserved entrainment by native Purkinje/host inputs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42396870/?utm_source=openai))
- Large-animal MI model (pig or NHP): Co-graft hPSC-CMs with rSink (optimized from Aim 2) into infarct border; continuous telemetry 0–8 weeks; serial EP studies to localize ectopy. Primary endpoint: reduction in engraftment-arrhythmia burden and VT/VF events without bradycardia or conduction block; secondary: graft activation synchrony and regional function. Include an amiodarone+ivabradine control arm to benchmark against current best practice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8514851/?utm_source=openai))

Key design parameters and controls
- rSink density/pattern: sweep to identify subcritical loading that enforces quiescence yet preserves θ; leverage known biphasic loading effects to avoid conduction slowing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16484613/?utm_source=openai))
- Interface management: ensure high Cx43 at rSink–CM junctions; confirm that conduction across graft–host borders is not reduced relative to CM-only grafts. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature06321?utm_source=openai))
- Falsification controls: CM-only; CM+rSink with Kir2.1 blocked (Ba2+); rSink with weak rectification; rSink with low Cx43.

Predicted outcomes
- rSink produces an immediate, tissue-level veto on automaticity that persists under catecholaminergic stimulation, ischemia, and electrolyte perturbations, while host-driven activation propagates with preserved θ and dV/dtmax because Kir2.1 outward current is minimized during rapid depolarizations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4145359/?utm_source=openai))
- rSink reduces engraftment-arrhythmia initiation sites localized to graft regions observed in prior studies, outperforming drug-only regimens by removing the micro-source rather than only rate-controlling it. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39196193/?utm_source=openai))

Risks and mitigations
- Excess load slowing conduction: mitigate by lowering rSink fraction, perimeter-only placement, or tuning Kir2.1 density; verify with conduction mapping. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3013501/?utm_source=openai))
- Heterocellular pacemaking: avoid depolarized rSink phenotypes; enforce non-excitability and hyperpolarized rest; monitor for unintended NaV/ICaL expression. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0025556411000113?utm_source=openai))
- Ischemic remodeling of coupling: periodic assessment of Cx43 localization and function; adjust dosing or spacing as needed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3578694/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go gates
- M1: rSink biophysics validated; strong rectification and high coupling achieved.
- M2: ≥90% suppression of spontaneous activations in vitro with θ within ±10% of control at 2–5% rSink density.
- M3: Ex vivo slice shows elimination of ectopy and preserved entrainment across stressors.
- M4: Large-animal study shows ≥70% reduction in arrhythmia burden versus CM-only and non-inferior conduction and function.

Novelty and impact
This proposal reframes graft safety as a network-level property achieved by a rectifying electrotonic sink, rather than solely by cell-autonomous maturation or pacemaker-current suppression. The approach draws on established biophysics of Kir2.1 rectification and fibroblast–myocyte electrotonic interactions but repurposes them as a designed, graft-coupled, tissue-level “quorum gate” to prevent engraftment arrhythmias while preserving conduction and contractile integration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4145359/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Write–read–recall of stress-hormone exposure in skin-resident mast cells: site-specific microdialysis secretomics linked to mast-cell-intrinsic memory marks

Central hypothesis–question
Does repeated, localized exposure to endogenous stress hormones at defined skin sites reprogram skin-resident mast cells into a trained-immunity-like state that persists after hormone withdrawal and biases the recall secretome, and can this state be causally linked to mast cell–intrinsic memory substrates (repressive H3K27me3 at effector loci and/or stable N-linked glycosylation remodeling)? If so, can a site-resolved in vivo write–read–recall paradigm using dermal microdialysis and stable-isotope hormone pulses quantify this memory and its downstream impact on endothelial and sensory-neuron targets? ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014488604001049?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Write exposure history with brief, site-specific pulses of stable-isotope-labeled stress hormones delivered by dermal microdialysis; read the extracellular secretome kinetically and at recall; and link altered recall outputs to mast-cell-intrinsic H3K27me3 deposition at effector loci. The isotope label separates residual agonist from true memory, and site-resolved microdialysis provides quantitative, longitudinal secretome profiles including histamine and tryptase. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1433982/pdf))

Specific aims
1) Establish a site-resolved in vivo write–washout–recall framework and matched in vitro training to quantify trained-immunity-like mast cell recall responses.
2) Test whether promoter/enhancer H3K27me3 at mast cell effector loci encodes altered recall secretomes after chronic β-adrenergic and/or CRH exposure, and assess causality by EZH2 inhibition during training. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/aps20177?utm_source=openai))
3) Define the functional consequences of trained mast cell secretomes on priority downstream targets: endothelial barrier integrity and sensory-neuron excitability, with attribution to histamine (H1R) and tryptase (PAR-2). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4497677/?utm_source=openai))

Model systems and design
- In vivo (mouse): Two to three cutaneous sites per animal (e.g., ear pinna, dorsal back, paw pad) receive intradermal microdialysis probes (3000 kDa MWCO to recover proteins). Training phase: retrodialysis of [13C/2H]-labeled epinephrine or norepinephrine, [13C]-cortisol, or [13C]-CRH for 10 minutes per day on days 1–3. Washout to day 10. Recall: standardized, unlabeled challenge at each site (anti-DNP/ovalbumin for FcεRI crosslinking or substance P for MRGPRB2), with continuous dialysate collection. Parallel sham sites receive vehicle. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1433982/pdf))
- In vitro (mouse BMMCs; human LAD2 and primary human skin mast cells): Matched pulse–washout–recall with identical agonists and timing. Cells are washed and rested before recall with heterologous or homologous triggers.

Exposure validation and receptor context
- Confirm mast cell expression and functionality of β2-adrenergic and CRH receptors by qPCR/flow and acute cAMP responses. Use receptor-selective antagonists to isolate pathway contributions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1575266/?utm_source=openai))

Primary readouts
- Secretome composition and proportions: Data-independent LC–MS/MS on dialysates and conditioned media; normalize to total protein and report relative mediator proportions across training/recall states.
- Histamine: targeted LC–MS (e.g., benzoyl chloride derivatization) plus ELISA for orthogonal quantification; report absolute concentrations and proportion of total secretome signal. Established skin microdialysis methods and kinetics anchor the assay. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1398-9995.1997.tb02598.x?utm_source=openai))
- Tryptase: immunocapture–LC–MS of signature peptides and ELISA/activity assays; use 3000 kDa MWCO probes and low-adsorption perfusates to maximize recovery from dialysate. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1433982/pdf))
- Isotope tracing: LC–MS/MS quantifies labeled hormones/metabolites to confirm exposure kinetics and absence at recall, distinguishing true memory from residual agonist. Stable-isotope retrodialysis/microdialysis calibration supports this approach. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3656751/?utm_source=openai))

Chromatin memory substrate (Aim 2)
- ChIP–qPCR/ChIP–seq for H3K27me3 at pre-registered mast cell effector loci (e.g., tryptases, Hdc, cytokine/chemokine genes) from: a) trained vs vehicle-treated mast cells isolated from in vivo sites by FACS; b) in vitro–trained mast cells. Use CUT&Tag as low-input alternative. Expect selective H3K27me3 gain at down-tuned loci correlating with altered recall secretion. Causality: include PRC2/EZH2 inhibitor (e.g., GSK126) only during training; prediction is loss of the biased recall secretome and reduced H3K27me3 deposition. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/aps20177?utm_source=openai))

Downstream target engagement (Aim 3)
- Endothelium: Apply dialysates from trained vs control sites to primary mouse/human microvascular endothelial monolayers; measure TEER, dextran/albumin flux, and junctional VE-cadherin imaging. Pharmacology: H1R antagonist to attribute histamine-dependent effects; PAR-2 antagonist or nafamostat to attribute tryptase-dependent effects. Expect site- and training-dependent differential barrier disruption profiles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4497677/?utm_source=openai))
- Sensory neurons: Apply dialysates to cultured DRG neurons; quantify Ca2+ responses and excitability. Include PAR-2 blockade to test tryptase dependence and H1R blockade for histamine signaling.

Criteria for trained-immunity-like state
- Persistence: altered secretome proportions at recall ≥7 days post-training without detectable hormone in dialysate.
- Recallability: change evident upon heterologous triggers (e.g., FcεRI after adrenergic training).
- Cell-intrinsic: reproduced in vitro after matched pulses and washout.
- Mechanistic linkage: training-associated H3K27me3 changes correlate with and are required for biased recall outputs (blocked by EZH2 inhibition during training). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/aps20177?utm_source=openai))

Secondary analyses (optional extension)
- Stable N-linked glycosylation remodeling: intact-glycopeptide LC–MS on FcεRI subunits and secreted granule proteins (e.g., tryptase) from trained vs control mast cells; lectin-binding flow cytometry on surfaces. Test functional impact by enzymatic desialylation/defucosylation and assess secretome recall/responder-cell activation. This explores a non-genomic memory substrate that could persist alongside chromatin changes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8360486/?utm_source=openai))

Controls and confound mitigation
- Vehicle-trained sites and cultures; contralateral skin sites as internal controls.
- Recovery controls: in vivo retrodialysis of a non-endogenous, stable-isotope internal standard to correct for probe recovery drift.
- Verify absence of labeled hormone at recall; exclude sites with residual label.
- Non-mast-cell sources: deplete mast cells (c-Kit mutant or anti–c-Kit) in subset of mice to show dependence; alternatively, use mast cell–deficient mice reconstituted with trained vs naïve mast cells.

Power and statistics
- Primary endpoint: difference in recall secretome composition (centered log-ratio transformed mediator intensities) between trained and control sites/cells.
- N per group based on pilot variance in histamine/tryptase and global proteomics (target power 0.8, alpha 0.05; mixed-effects models for repeated measures and site-level nesting).

Expected outcomes and interpretation
- Site-specific, exposure-history–dependent shifts in mast cell secretome proportions at recall, with orthogonally quantified histamine and tryptase changes driving differential endothelial leak and neuronal excitability. The absence of labeled hormone at recall, plus parallel in vitro reproduction, supports true memory. Concordant H3K27me3 remodeling at effector loci—and its prevention by EZH2 inhibition during training—would identify a mechanistic memory substrate linking stress-hormone signaling to durable mast cell output bias. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4497677/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility notes
- Cutaneous microdialysis robustly quantifies histamine in vivo; large-MWCO probes and low-adsorption perfusates enable protein recovery and have been used in skin and ex vivo human skin. Stable-isotope infusion/retrodialysis is an established strategy for microdialysis calibration and kinetic separation of write vs read phases. β2-adrenergic and CRH receptors are expressed and functional in mast cells, supporting physiological relevance of the training stimuli. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7523474/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- A validated, site-resolved in vivo write–read–recall platform for mast cell trained-immunity-like states.
- An atlas of mast cell recall secretomes (with absolute histamine and tryptase) by stress-hormone training modality and skin site.
- Mechanistic evidence for H3K27me3-encoded memory at mast cell effector loci controlling recall outputs.
- Functional maps linking trained mast cell secretomes to endothelial and sensory-neuron outcomes.

text:
Title
pH-gated normalization of adipocyte lactate microdomains to blunt macrophage IL-1β programming in obesity

Premise and rationale
- In hypertrophic adipose tissue, local hypoxia drives a glycolytic shift in adipocytes with increased lactate production and export via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs), creating lactate/proton-enriched microdomains. This adipocyte-derived signal stabilizes HIF‑1α in neighboring macrophages via PHD2 inhibition, elevating IL‑1β and sustaining depot inflammation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19876643/?utm_source=openai))
- Human and rodent microdialysis studies demonstrate adipose tissue releases lactate in vivo, with altered regulation in obesity/insulin resistance, supporting a relevant extracellular pool amenable to local interception. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8282793/?utm_source=openai))
- Lactate’s effects on immunity are context dependent; in inflamed obese adipose, lactate augments macrophage IL‑1β via myeloid HIF‑1α, indicating that removing the acidic/lactate enabling condition should decompress inflammatory programming without globally suppressing immunity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-32871-3?utm_source=openai))
- pH-responsive polymers and histidine/imidazole‑bearing hydrogels can buffer acidic milieus and are established in other tissues, enabling conditional material formation or drug release at mildly acidic pH. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7730929/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis/question
If we impose pH-gated buffering that forms only within adipocyte-generated acidic microdomains, will normalization of the extracellular lactate/proton condition reduce macrophage HIF‑1α→IL‑1β activation and thereby attenuate adipocyte-driven inflammation without disrupting systemic metabolism?

Atomic strategy
Replace trigger blocking with microenvironment normalization: remove the enabling condition (local extracellular acidosis/lactate accumulation) that allows adipocyte signals to switch macrophages into an IL‑1β‑high state.

Specific aims and experimental plan
Aim 1. Map the coincidence of adipocyte lactate export and extracellular acidosis that predicts macrophage IL‑1β activation.
- Organ-on-a-chip: Co-culture mature adipocytes and primary murine macrophages under normoxia vs hypoxia; quantify extracellular lactate (enzymatic assay) and interstitial pH (ratiometric dyes) across ECM stiffness conditions. Measure macrophage HIF‑1α stabilization and Il1b induction; quantify adipocyte chemokines (Ccl2, Il6). scRNA‑seq of both compartments to resolve lactate/pH‑responsive modules.
- Diet-induced obesity (DIO) mice: Use intradepot microdialysis and pH-sensitive fluorescent probes to validate lactate/pH microdomains; isolate stromal vascular fraction for scRNA‑seq and link macrophage IL‑1β programs to local chemistry.

Aim 2. Engineer a pH-gated buffering microdepot that forms only in acidic adipose interstitium and evaluate its impact on inflammatory programming.
- Material design: An injectable, shear-thinning polymer bearing histidine/imidazole moieties for proton buffering and incorporating acid‑labile crosslinkers (e.g., acetal/imine) to trigger in situ gelation/retention when extracellular pH drops below a preset threshold (target pH 6.6–6.9). Chemistry leverages established pH‑sensitive linkers and histidine-based buffering. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11752822/?utm_source=openai))
- Chip validation: Titrate depot formation versus pH; demonstrate minimal gelation at pH ≥7.2 and robust formation at acidic pH. Endpoints: restoration of interstitial pH, reduction of macrophage HIF‑1α and Il1b, decreased adipocyte NF‑κB targets and chemokines, and reduced macrophage chemotaxis.
- Safety/compatibility: Assess adipocyte viability, lipolysis, and insulin signaling; ensure no intracellular acid stress (the buffer acts extracellularly).

Aim 3. Test therapeutic efficacy and specificity in vivo.
- Intra‑depot microinjection in DIO mice: Image depot formation, track interstitial pH normalization, and quantify local lactate. Endpoints: macrophage HIF‑1α target gene expression and IL‑1β protein; adipose cytokines/chemokines; immune cell composition by flow cytometry and scRNA‑seq; systemic glucose and insulin tolerance. Compare to neutral polymer control and systemic alkalinization control (negative comparator for specificity).

Key readouts and analyses
- Chemistry-to-biology linkage: Spatial coupling of pH normalization to suppression of macrophage IL‑1β programs and secondary reductions in adipocyte inflammatory transcripts.
- Single-cell resolution: Loss of lactate/pH‑responsive modules in macrophages and diminution of proinflammatory adipocyte clusters.
- Depot specificity: Minimal effect in lean depots lacking acidification, demonstrating context-dependent activation.

Success criteria
- Demonstration that pH-gated buffering normalizes interstitial pH in obese depots and reduces macrophage HIF‑1α stabilization and IL‑1β without impairing adipocyte viability or whole-body glucose homeostasis. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-32871-3?utm_source=openai))
- Confirmation that effects are contingent on local acidity (no efficacy in neutral pH environments), establishing therapeutic coincidence with the adipocyte-derived enabling condition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11752822/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and alternatives
- If acidification is insufficiently spatial or persistent to gate the depot, pivot to lactate-absorbing, weak‑base polymers that sequester lactate via reversible ionic pairing while maintaining extracellular pH, or to a dual-trigger design that couples pH‑sensitive crosslinking with lactate‑binding motifs validated in vitro (screened by ITC). Chemistry grounded in the same pH-responsive linker toolbox. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7730929/?utm_source=openai))
- If buffering reduces inflammation but impairs adipose function, titrate buffer capacity and depot density; prioritize partial normalization that preserves adipocyte physiology.

Platforms and feasibility
- Organ-on-a-chip enables controlled creation of hypoxia-driven lactate/pH microdomains and real-time measurement of macrophage responses.
- Transgenic mouse models and DIO paradigms allow intra‑depot delivery and causal testing.
- scRNA‑seq resolves cell-state changes across adipocytes, macrophages, and stromal cells with pathway attribution to lactate/pH signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9445001/?utm_source=openai))

Impact
This work operationalizes adipocyte-derived lactate/proton output as the actionable cause of inflammatory amplification, substituting context-gated microenvironment normalization for pathway blockade. It directly targets the adipocyte mechanism that enables macrophage IL‑1β programming and provides a translationally tractable, locally acting therapy for adipose inflammation in obesity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19876643/?utm_source=openai))
