text:
Title
Auto-titrating pro-resolving adipocytes to invert white adipose tissue inflammatory tone

Central hypothesis–question (inseparable)
Can we convert the very signal that drives adipocyte inflammation (NF-κB activation) into a self-limiting trigger for specialized pro-resolving mediator (SPM; e.g., resolvin D1/D2) biosynthesis within adipocytes, so that hypertrophic, inflamed fat depots autonomously downshift their own NF-κB program and macrophage recruitment and re-stabilize immunometabolic homeostasis? This asks whether adipocyte-intrinsic inflammatory signaling can be repurposed, in situ, as a closed-loop “resolution switch” rather than suppressed exogenously. The question targets the causal adipocyte mechanisms (NF-κB cytokine/chemokine output, monocyte recruitment) that sustain WAT inflammation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30229891/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Embed a metabolite-gated negative feedback: an NF-κB–inducible, adipocyte-confined SPM-biosynthetic cassette that turns on only when adipocyte NF-κB is active and turns itself down as SPMs dampen NF-κB. This inverts the pro-inflammatory driver into a resolution output without requiring continuous external dosing. Feasibility rests on: (i) NF-κB–responsive synthetic promoters validated to control therapeutic genes, and (ii) resolvins that suppress adipose inflammatory tone and macrophage influx. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533793/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build and calibrate an NF-κB–inducible SPM cassette in primary human adipocytes.
- Construct: 5× NF-κB response elements linked to a minimal promoter driving a low-gain SPM module (ALOX15 + ALOX5 + ALOX5AP) with secretion tags; incorporate 3′UTR miRNA-gated specificity by adding target sites to suppress expression outside adipocytes and bias toward inflamed adipocytes (e.g., leverage high miR-155 in inflamed adipocytes to relieve repression via a switch/decoy, while sparing preadipocytes and non-adipocyte stromal cells via sites complementary to their enriched miRNAs). Titrate expression to avoid lipid peroxidation burden.
- Readouts: In 2D human adipocytes, activate NF-κB with TNF-α or LPS; quantify RvD1/RvD2 and 17-HDHA by LC–MS/MS; measure autocrine NF-κB activity (reporter), cytokines/chemokines (TNFα, IL-6, CCL2), and lipolysis markers. Define dose–response and dynamic range; confirm miRNA-gated specificity by qPCR and targeted scRNA-seq of mixed cultures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533793/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test closed-loop resolution on a vascularized human WAT-on-chip under inflammatory stress.
- Platform: Immunocompetent, perfused WAT-on-chip with endothelial barrier and autologous stromovascular cells/macrophages; impose pro-inflammatory stressors (hypoxia/low pO2, TNF-α, saturated FFA) to model obese WAT.
- Interventions: Engineer only the adipocytes within the chip to carry the circuit; supply physiologic DHA/EPA in perfusate to ensure substrate availability.
- Outcomes: Continuous perfusate sampling for SPMs; reductions in NF-κB targets and monocyte transmigration; macrophage polarization shift (↓CD11c^+ M1/MMe, ↑CD206^+ M2) by flow cytometry/imaging; preserved adipocyte endocrine function (adiponectin/leptin, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake). Single-cell RNA-seq to map circuit expression to adipocytes, quantify NF-κB program collapse in adipocyte clusters, and paracrine reprogramming of immune/stromal clusters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Evaluate depot-confined efficacy in obese mice via ex vivo engineered adipocyte implants.
- Method: Differentiate syngeneic preadipocytes ex vivo, transduce with the NF-κB–SPM cassette, and implant into visceral WAT in diet-induced obese mice; feed an EPA/DHA-sufficient diet.
- Readouts (8–12 weeks): WAT metabololipidomics for RvD1/RvD2; local cytokine/chemokine suppression; reduced crown-like structures and M1 macrophage density; improved glucose/insulin tolerance and fasting insulin; confirm target receptor presence (ALX/FPR2, ChemR23) and downstream signaling in WAT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424332/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and methods

Construct design and delivery
- Sensor: Synthetic NF-κB promoter (multimerized κB sites + minimal promoter) to ensure inflammation-gated induction with low basal leak. Circuit validated in prior therapeutic gene-delivery studies; here repurposed to drive pro-resolving lipid mediator biosynthesis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533793/?utm_source=openai))
- Effector: Minimal SPM biosynthesis module enabling conversion of DHA to D-series resolvins (ALOX15, ALOX5, ALOX5AP), codon-optimized, with weak Kozak contexts and insulated 5′/3′ UTRs to keep enzymatic flux sub-homeostatic.
- Specificity: miRNA-gated 3′UTR with binding sites to silence expression in non-adipocytes and a switch responsive to miR-155 to bias activation in inflamed adipocytes (miR-155 is induced by TNF-α in adipocytes and elevated in obese WAT). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4880153/?utm_source=openai))
- Substrate support: Provide DHA/EPA (chip perfusate; dietary in vivo) to ensure sufficient flux toward SPMs known to reduce adipose inflammation and monocyte accumulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424332/?utm_source=openai))

Key assays
- Lipid mediators: Targeted LC–MS/MS panel for RvD1/RvD2 and precursors (17-HDHA).
- Inflammatory outputs: Multiplex cytokines/chemokines; NF-κB reporter dynamics; qPCR of NF-κB targets.
- Immune function: Monocyte transmigration across the endothelium-on-chip; ATM polarization markers; histology of crown-like structures.
- Systems readout: scRNA-seq of chip tissues and WAT depots to resolve cell-type specificity and pathway shifts.

Criteria for success
- Closed loop: NF-κB activation induces SPM output that, in the same cultures, reduces NF-κB activity and adipokine/chemokine secretion with auto-tapering to baseline upon resolution.
- Tissue function: On-chip, reduced monocyte transmigration and M1/MMe signatures with preserved adipocyte metabolic function; in vivo, elevated WAT SPMs with reduced local inflammation and improved systemic insulin sensitivity.

Risk analysis and contingencies
- Substrate limitation or pathway competition: Elevate DHA/EPA supply; test enzyme ratios; consider pushing ALOX15 only if full triene pathway overloads cells.
- Off-target expression: Strengthen miRNA gating; limit vector dose; depot-restricted implantation.
- Excess oxidation by-products: Maintain low-gain expression; monitor lipid peroxidation; if needed, add weak ARE-driven antioxidant support in vitro (not essential to mechanism). 
- Receptor engagement: Verify ALX/FPR2 and ChemR23 expression in WAT and adipocyte/macrophage fractions before in vivo studies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424332/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is mechanistically grounded and distinct
- Mechanism addressed: Directly targets the adipocyte NF-κB axis that drives CCL2/TNF/IL-6 and monocyte recruitment, the core feed-forward loop in obese WAT. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30229891/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinction: Prior work shows exogenous resolvins lower adipose inflammation; here the adipocyte’s own inflammatory state controls on-demand, self-limiting SPM production, implementing depot-autonomous resolution without chronic dosing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424332/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline
- Months 0–9: Construct assembly, calibration in primary human adipocytes; define transfer functions and safety window.
- Months 9–18: WAT-on-chip functional validation and scRNA-seq mapping.
- Months 18–36: Ex vivo–engineered adipocyte implantation in obese mice; depot and systemic readouts.

Validation platforms
- Vascularized, immunocompetent WAT-on-chip for perfused, oxygen-controlled, continuous sampling of mediators and immune trafficking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))
- Transplantation into WAT of obese mice for in vivo depot-confined testing.
- scRNA-seq for cell-type–resolved verification of gating and pathway modulation.

Expected outcome and impact
A depot-confined, auto-titrating “resolution switch” in adipocytes that reduces adipocyte-derived cytokines/chemokines and macrophage recruitment while preserving adipocyte metabolic function, converting excess adipose mass from an inflammation amplifier into a pro-resolving factory. If successful, this establishes a generalizable template for redirecting pathogenic adipocyte signaling into autonomous resolution programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533793/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
MiT/TFE+FOXO coincidence-gated suppression of PRMT5 to flip autophagy from tumor-supportive to tumor-lytic programs in advanced cancers

Hypothesis–Question
In established, autophagy-dependent tumors characterized by AMPK-high/mTORC1-low signaling and nuclear MiT/TFE and FOXO activity, does coincidence-gated suppression of PRMT5 reprogram autophagy transcription and p53 target selectivity to favor cell death, while sparing early-stage or non-stressed tissues in which these inputs do not co-occur? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit an intrinsic AND condition in advanced tumors—concurrent nuclear MiT/TFE (TFEB/TFE3) and FOXO—by building a dual-input promoter that drives PRMT5 knockdown only when both TF programs are active, thereby removing PRMT5-dependent arginine methylation that sustains pro-survival autophagy (e.g., via ULK1 methylation) and biases p53 away from apoptosis. The result should be a stage-selective collapse of autophagy-mediated stress tolerance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale
- Context dependence: Autophagy suppresses early tumorigenesis but supports survival and therapy resistance in established tumors; thus any intervention must read stage/stress context. Nuclear TFEB/TFE3 marks low mTORC1 stress states; FOXO nuclear localization marks AKT-low/energy-stress states. Their coincidence is enriched in hypoxic/nutrient-poor tumor niches. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41580-023-00585-z?utm_source=openai))
- PRMT5 as an epigenetic choke point: PRMT5 symmetrically methylates histones and non-histone substrates (including p53; ULK1; FOXO1), shaping autophagy gene accessibility, autophagy initiation, and p53 target choice. Clinically advanced PRMT5 inhibitors and MTAP/MTA-dependent selectivity de-risk translation and provide orthogonal selectivity layers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7529871/?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolite–epigenetic feedback: Autophagy-derived metabolites (amino acids → one‑carbon flux → SAM; acetate/acetyl‑CoA; NAD+) modulate chromatin enzymes and TF co-regulators, creating potential self-limiting or self-reinforcing loops after PRMT5 suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9775183/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims

Aim 1. Build and verify a MiT/TFE+FOXO AND gate that actuates only under AMPK-high/mTORC1-low stress.
- Construct: A minimal promoter bearing tandem CLEAR elements (MiT/TFE-responsive) and FOXO response elements driving Pol II expression of a microRNA cluster targeting PRMT5 (shPRMT5). Reporter version drives destabilized GFP. Use established logic-gate design in mammalian cells to ensure AND-like behavior and low leak. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms6393?utm_source=openai))
- Manipulations: Toggle inputs with Torin1 (↓mTORC1) or EBSS/starvation (↑AMPK), and MK-2206 (↓AKT → FOXO nuclear). Confirm TFEB/TFE3 and FOXO nuclear translocation by live imaging and TFEBC/N scoring. Validate AND behavior by single vs dual input dosing matrices. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: Gate fidelity (GFP output, PRMT5 protein), pathway state (p-S6K, p-ACC), TF occupancy at the synthetic promoter (ChIP for TFEB/FOXO). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Determine how gated PRMT5 suppression rewires autophagy and p53 programs under stress.
- Autophagy: Monitor flux (LC3-II, p62 turnover ± bafilomycin), autophagosome formation (GFP-LC3 puncta), and ULK1 symmetric dimethyl-arginine (SDMA) to assess loss of PRMT5-dependent ULK1 activation. Test rescue with PRMT5 re-expression or catalytically dead mutants. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37400460/?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin and splicing: Quantify global and locus-specific SDMA (H4R3me2s/H3R8me2s) at CLEAR/FOXO target loci (ChIP–qPCR/ChIP–seq); RNA-seq to identify splicing changes of ATG pathway genes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7529871/?utm_source=openai))
- p53 target selection: Measure shift from survival/cell-cycle arrest targets (e.g., p21, TIGAR) to apoptotic targets (e.g., PUMA/NOXA) after PRMT5 suppression under DNA-damage or metabolic stress; use p53 WT vs mutant isogenic lines as control. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19011621/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Map metabolite–epigenetic feedbacks that stabilize desired outcomes and encode stage selectivity.
- Metabolomics: Targeted quantification of SAM, MTA, acetyl‑CoA, NAD+ post-gated PRMT5 suppression; isotope tracing (U‑13C‑serine/acetate) to link flux to chromatin marks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9775183/?utm_source=openai))
- Epigenetic coupling: Assess histone acetylation dynamics and sirtuin activity (H3K27ac ChIP; acetyl‑FOXO1; SIRT1 activity) to determine whether reduced autophagy lowers acetyl‑CoA and compresses CLEAR/FOXO transcription, yielding self-reinforcement; test reversal upon acetate supplementation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41568-022-00543-5?utm_source=openai))
- Selectivity layer: In MTAP-deleted models with elevated MTA, benchmark the gate against MTA‑cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors (e.g., AMG 193) to evaluate pharmacologic synergy and orthogonal selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11726016/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Demonstrate therapeutic efficacy and stage selectivity in vivo.
- Models: Autophagy-addicted tumors (e.g., KRAS-driven PDAC; TNBC xenografts or PDXs). Stratify by autophagy signatures and MTAP status. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41580-023-00585-z?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: AAV or LNP delivering the AND-gated shPRMT5 cassette; compare to systemic PRMT5 inhibitor (e.g., JNJ‑64619178) with/without autophagy inhibitor to assess window expansion. Endpoints: tumor growth, survival, pharmacodynamic markers (SDMA, ULK1 methylation, TFEB/FOXO nuclear ratios), and systemic toxicity. ([clinicaltrials.gov](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03573310?intr=JNJ-64619178&rank=1&utm_source=openai))

Key controls and falsification criteria
- Controls: Gate with scrambled CLEAR or FOXO elements; non-targeting shRNA; shPRMT5 under constitutive promoter; PRMT5-independent autophagy suppression (ULK1/ATG5 knockdown). 
- Falsification: If dual-input gating does not enrich in advanced tumor contexts (e.g., equal activation in normal proliferating tissues), or if PRMT5 suppression fails to diminish autophagy flux or shift p53 targets under stress, the hypothesis is rejected. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risk management
- Feasibility is supported by: (i) well-defined mTORC1 control of TFEB/TFE3 localization; (ii) FOXO-driven autophagy programs; (iii) logic-gated gene circuits in mammalian cells; (iv) extensive toolkits and clinical compounds for PRMT5; and (v) documented PRMT5 control of ULK1, FOXO1, and p53. Risks include promoter leak, p53 mutation frequency, and compensatory autophagy circuits; we mitigate by promoter optimization, p53-stratified models, and combination with MTA‑cooperative or classical PRMT5 inhibitors in MTAP-deficient tumors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision points (12–24 months)
- Months 0–6: Gate construction, leak minimization, and input–output characterization in cell lines; go/no-go on AND behavior. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms6393?utm_source=openai))
- Months 6–12: Demonstrate autophagy/p53 rewiring and PRMT5 substrate changes under stress; confirm causality via ULK1 methylation assays and rescue. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37400460/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 12–18: Map metabolite–chromatin feedbacks and identify biomarkers predictive of response (TFEBC/N, FOXO nuclear fraction, SDMA levels, SAM/MTA ratios). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10547473/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 18–24: In vivo efficacy and safety; benchmark against systemic PRMT5 inhibition and evaluate MTAP-selective combinations (AMG 193). Downselect indications for follow-up. ([clinicaltrials.gov](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03573310?intr=JNJ-64619178&rank=1&utm_source=openai))

Expected outcome and impact
A stage- and stress-selective epigenetic therapy that converts autophagy from a survival pathway into a liability by harnessing endogenous MiT/TFE and FOXO logic to conditionally suppress PRMT5, thereby reshaping chromatin and p53 outputs toward tumor cell death without broadly compromising the tumor-suppressive functions of autophagy in early lesions or normal tissues. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41580-023-00585-z?utm_source=openai))

label: baseline
text:
Title
Decoupling autophagic clearance from nutrient refeeding in cancer by reprogramming LC3+ vesicles to secretory endpoints

Central research question-hypothesis
Can a tumor-selective, engineered secretory-autophagy receptor that recognizes damaged cargo and biases LC3+ vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane (rather than lysosomes) preserve quality-control clearance while preventing lysosomal nutrient efflux and mTORC1 reactivation, thereby converting autophagy into a stage-independent anticancer mechanism? Autophagy’s dual role derives from selective damage removal versus catabolite recycling; redirecting vesicle trafficking to secretion should keep the former and abrogate the latter. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12003146/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Retarget the endpoint of selective autophagy from degradation/refeeding to secretion/immobilization by installing a synthetic cargo adapter that couples damage recognition and LC3 binding to a secretory-autophagy SNARE interface (SEC22B–SNAP23/29–STX3/4), ensuring expelled waste cannot re-enter cancer metabolism. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5210154/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and feasibility
- Duality to break: Established tumors exploit lysosomal catabolite efflux to reactivate mTORC1 and fuel growth; SLC38A9 is a key lysosomal effluxer and arginine sensor upstream of mTORC1 and is necessary for using protein-derived amino acids as nutrient. Preventing autophagic cargo from reaching lysosomes (or preventing lysosomal hydrolysate access to cytosol) should blunt this loop. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5704964/?utm_source=openai))
- Secretory autophagy exists and is genetically addressable: TRIM16 functions as a selective secretory-autophagy receptor that binds SEC22B, handing cargo to LC3+ membranes that dock/fuse with the plasma membrane via SNAP23/29 and STX3/4. This provides a native wiring diagram to program secretion of defined cargo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5210154/?utm_source=openai))
- TFEB/TFE3–TRPML1 axis can potentiate lysosomal exocytosis without relying strictly on mTORC1 inhibition; calcineurin/TRPML1-driven Ca2+ release promotes TFEB nuclear entry and lysosomal exocytosis, offering compatibility across stress states and integration with MiT/TFE logic. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/199845?utm_source=openai))
- Synthetic cargo adapters are feasible: AUTAC/ATTEC/AUTOTAC and LC3/LIR-based chimeras demonstrate that engineered linkers can recruit LC3 machinery to defined cargo and drive selective autophagy. Here, the same principle is repurposed to bias secretory, not degradative, routing. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1722-1?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build and validate a secretory-autophagy cargo adapter (SACA).
- Design: A single polypeptide with (i) damage-binding module (e.g., oxidized-lipid or ubiquitin-chain reader for damaged mitochondria/proteins), (ii) LC3-interacting region (high-affinity LIR), and (iii) TRIM16-mimetic SEC22B-binding coiled-coil or short peptide that recruits the SEC22B–SNAP23/29–STX3/4 fusion machinery; include an optional extracellular matrix–binding tag to immobilize expelled cargo. Expression placed under FOXO- or p53-responsive minimal promoters to couple to stress/DNA-damage states in tumors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5210154/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: Live-cell TIRF imaging of LC3+ vesicle–plasma membrane fusion; secretion assays for mitochondrial proteins/DAMPs; protease-protection EM to confirm extracellular encapsulation; minimal secretion of non-damaged cargo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486376/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: TRIM16-loss-of-function cells, SNARE knockdowns, LIR-mutant SACA.

Aim 2. Test whether SACA decouples clearance from refeeding and suppresses mTORC1 rebound.
- Assays: Pulse-chase 13C,15N-protein labeling to quantify reincorporation of autophagy-derived amino acids into new biomass; lysosomal metabolomics and cytosolic amino acid pools; p-S6K and p-4EBP1 dynamics after starvation–refeeding; dependency on SLC38A9 function. Prediction: SACA reduces intracellular recovery of labeled amino acids and blunts mTORC1 reactivation despite ongoing selective clearance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5704964/?utm_source=openai))
- Complementation: Overexpress TFEB or activate TRPML1 to enhance exocytosis and test ceiling effects on decoupling; effects should persist in variable mTORC1/AMPK states. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7263086/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Determine therapeutic impact and stage independence in cancer models.
- Models: RAS-driven PDAC and BRAF-driven lung adenocarcinoma lines and organoids; early versus established tumor xenografts. Delivery by AAV or LNP mRNA encoding SACA under stress-responsive promoters.
- Endpoints: Tumor growth under metabolic stress, survival after chemotherapy, clonal evolution under hypoxia; immune profiling of tumor microenvironment for uptake of expelled material by phagocytes and any pro- or anti-tumor secretome changes. Benchmark against ATTEC/AUTAC that increase degradative flux to show distinct metabolic outcomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8850458/?utm_source=openai))

Key experimental workflows
- Trafficking fate mapping: Dual-color mito-Keima and extracellular vesicle proteomics; quantify fraction of damaged mitochondria routed to secretion versus lysosomal degradation.
- Nutrient recycling index: Ratio of labeled amino-acid reincorporation to total autophagic cargo clearance; SLC38A9 loss-of-function and rescue to confirm that reduced efflux, not reduced capture, explains the effect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5704964/?utm_source=openai))
- Transcription-factor integration: qChIP for FOXO/p53 occupancy on SACA promoter; evaluate TFEB/TFE3 nuclear localization and lysosomal exocytosis markers upon SACA expression or TRPML1 activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9345944/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes and interpretation
- If SACA increases export of damaged cargo while lowering intracellular amino-acid rebound and mTORC1 reactivation, this supports the hypothesis that reprogrammed secretory endpoints can preserve tumor-suppressive autophagy while disabling nutrient refeeding. Failure to reduce amino-acid rebound would suggest leakage of catabolites prior to secretion or compensatory uptake pathways, guiding adapter redesign or co-targeting of efflux transporters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5704964/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Pro-tumor secretome risk: Secretory autophagy can release cytokines; restrict SACA to damage-linked cargo and include ECM-anchoring tags to immobilize expelled material; profile secretome and block unintended cytokine secretion via SNARE interface tuning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6735501/?utm_source=openai))
- Inflammation/DAMPs: Titrate expression; evaluate in immunocompetent models; if excessive inflammation occurs, include miRNA target sites for myeloid cells to reduce off-target expression.
- Redundancy with degradative autophagy: Use SNARE dependency and extracellular capture to confirm pathway specificity.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: Demonstrate SACA-driven LC3+ vesicle PM fusion and extracellular accumulation of damaged mitochondrial/protein cargo without increased bulk secretion. (Months 0–9) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486376/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Show ≥50% reduction in labeled amino-acid reincorporation and blunted mTORC1 rebound after starvation versus controls at equal cargo clearance. (Months 6–15) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5704964/?utm_source=openai))
- M3: Demonstrate tumor growth inhibition under metabolic stress and enhanced therapy response in xenografts/organoids without systemic toxicity. (Months 12–24)

Significance
This proposal reframes cancer autophagy control as an endpoint routing problem. Rather than raising or lowering autophagy globally, we install a minimal, stage-agnostic switch that preserves selective damage disposal while denying tumors access to autophagy-derived nutrients that reactivate mTORC1. The approach leverages native secretory-autophagy machinery, integrates with MiT/TFE- and FOXO/p53-driven stress programs, and is testable with existing genetic, chemical, and metabolic tracing tools. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12003146/?utm_source=openai))

label: baseline
text:
Title
A metabolite-sensing chromatin switch to trap autophagy-addicted cancer

Central hypothesis (question and goal are indistinguishable)
Does sustained, stress-induced autophagy in advanced cancers elevate local histone crotonylation at MiT/TFE- and FOXO-driven autophagy/lysosome loci to a threshold that can be exploited by a crotonylation “reader-to-repressor” fusion to flip these loci into a stably repressed state, thereby collapsing autophagy dependence and killing tumor cells while sparing non-addicted tissues? This project will design and test a chromatin switch that converts autophagy-enabled survival into self-termination.

Atomic strategy
Convert an autophagy-driven metabolic/chromatin state (histone Kcr written from crotonyl‑CoA generated by lipophagy-fueled β-oxidation) into recruitment of a YEATS-based repressor that deposits H3K9me3±DNA methylation specifically at MiT/TFE- and FOXO-target autophagy genes, irreversibly silencing the very program the tumor relied on. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/cdd201263?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and mechanistic priors to be stress-tested
- Autophagy control node: mTORC1 phosphorylation retains TFEB/TFE3 in the cytosol; AMPK- and calcineurin-regulated dephosphorylation and phosphorylation events drive nuclear entry and transcriptional activation of autophagy/lysosome genes (CLEAR network). FOXO factors similarly promote autophagy gene expression when AKT is low/AMPK is high. p53’s role is context dependent: nuclear p53 can promote autophagy (e.g., DRAM, SESN) while cytoplasmic p53 represses autophagy. These axes are active in therapy-stressed, advanced tumors that become autophagy-addicted. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-01850-6?utm_source=openai))
- Link to metabolism and chromatin: Lipophagy liberates fatty acids that feed β-oxidation, increasing acyl‑CoA intermediates; crotonyl‑CoA is produced from fatty-acid and amino-acid catabolism and writes histone crotonylation (Kcr), a mark of active chromatin. YEATS domains (AF9/ENL/YEATS2/TAF14) selectively recognize Kcr and couple it to transcriptional activity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/cdd201263?utm_source=openai))
- Operative novelty: No prior system intentionally couples an autophagy-generated Kcr state to a YEATS-gated repressor to silence MiT/TFE- and FOXO-driven autophagy programs in cancer.

Design overview
- Construct: TFEB-DBD(Δactivation)-YEATS-KRAB[±DNMT3A-cat], and FOXO-DBD(Δactivation)-YEATS-KRAB[±DNMT3A-cat]. The TFEB/FOXO DNA-binding modules tether to CLEAR/FOXO motifs at autophagy loci; the YEATS domain requires local Kcr for high-avidity residence; KRAB (via TRIM28/KAP1→SETDB1) seeds H3K9me3; optional DNMT3A deposits CpG methylation for durability. The result is an AND gate: sequence motif AND autophagy-induced Kcr. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRIM28?utm_source=openai))
- Trigger provenance: The same autophagy that sustains the tumor (via AMPK↑/mTORC1↓; TFEB/TFE3/FOXO nuclear) generates β‑oxidation and crotonyl‑CoA that elevates Kcr at these active loci, licensing YEATS-dependent recruitment and subsequent repression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Map the autophagy-to-crotonylation axis at autophagy gene regulatory elements.
- Systems: Autophagy-addicted tumor models (e.g., PDAC, AML, MiT/TFE-high RCC); matched non-addicted controls.
- Perturbations: Starvation, mTORC1 inhibition, AMPK activation; measure flux dependency.
- Readouts:
  - ChIP-seq/ChIP–qPCR for H3K9cr/H3K18cr and H3K27ac at CLEAR and FOXO motifs of canonical autophagy/lysosome genes (e.g., LC3B/MAP1LC3B, ATG7, BECN1, LAMP1; DRAM/SESN where p53 is intact). 
  - LC–MS for crotonyl‑CoA and acetyl‑CoA pools; lipid oxidation rates; TFEB/TFE3 and FOXO occupancy; autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover).
- Decision criterion: Sustained autophagy elevates Kcr specifically at MiT/TFE- and FOXO-controlled loci in addicted cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build and test the crotonylation-sensing silencer and quantify trap dynamics in vitro.
- Constructs: TFEB-DBD(ΔAD)-YEATS(AF9 or YEATS2)-KRAB[±DNMT3A-cat]; parallel FOXO-DBD(ΔAD) variants. Lentiviral, doxycycline-inducible.
- Controls: DBD-only-KRAB; YEATS mutant defective in Kcr binding; KRAB-dead; dCas9-KRAB at the same promoters as a positive control for repression capacity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-34269-7.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Protocol:
  1) Precondition cells with autophagy-inducing stress to build dependence and Kcr at target loci.
  2) Induce the fusion; withdraw stress after defined intervals to test irreversibility.
- Readouts:
  - Time-resolved ChIP for fusion occupancy; H3K9cr→H3K9me3 swap; CpG methylation (bisulfite) if DNMT3A used.
  - RNA-seq for autophagy/lysosome gene network collapse; TFEB/TFE3/FOXO nuclear levels; autophagic flux and lysosomal capacity.
  - Viability/apoptosis/necrosis; rescue by overexpressing autophagy genes lacking target motifs (specificity control).
- Success criterion: Repression and loss of flux occur only after Kcr build-up; YEATS-defective mutants fail to trap, establishing Kcr‑gated causality. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8055951/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test selectivity, durability, and antitumor efficacy in vivo.
- Models: Xenografts or orthotopic models with documented autophagy addiction; inducible expression of the fusion in tumor only.
- Regimens: Single-cycle “induce-dependence then flip” schedule versus continuous stress; evaluate minimal necessary preconditioning.
- Endpoints:
  - Tumor regression, time-to-relapse after stress withdrawal, survival.
  - On-target chromatin editing at CLEAR/FOXO sites (CUT&RUN for H3K9me3; targeted bisulfite).
  - Safety: liver, gut, and hematopoietic tissues (autophagy-active) for off-tumor editing.
- Stopping rule: Proceed if efficacy requires antecedent autophagy activation and spares non-addicted tissues.

Key falsifiable predictions
- If autophagy does not elevate Kcr at autophagy loci, YEATS-gated trapping will not outperform DBD‑KRAB and the strategy fails at Aim 1. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8055951/?utm_source=openai))
- If Kcr rises globally without locus enrichment, YEATS-gated repression causes broad toxicity; restricting with TFEB/FOXO DBDs should rescue specificity; if not, approach is nonviable.

Methods and controls (selected details)
- CLEAR/FOXO motif catalogs from TFEB/TFE3/FOXO ChIP-seq datasets will define targets; motif mutations in luciferase reporters will confirm DBD dependence.
- AMPK/mTOR state verification by TFEB S211 phosphorylation status and nuclear TFEB/TFE3 localization; pharmacologic modulation as orthogonal controls. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-01850-6?utm_source=openai))
- p53 context: In p53WT tumors, DRAM/SESN loci will be included among targets; in p53-mutant tumors with cytoplasmic p53, reliance on TFEB/FOXO will dominate; stratified analyses test generality. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12789782/?utm_source=openai))
- KRAB mechanism confirmation via TRIM28/SETDB1 recruitment and H3K9me3 seeding. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRIM28?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go gates
- M1 (6 months): Kcr enrichment at CLEAR/FOXO sites after autophagy induction in ≥2 autophagy-addicted models; fail → ideation pivot.
- M2 (12 months): YEATS-gated fusions flip ≥50% of sentinel autophagy loci to H3K9me3 with ≥10× selectivity over housekeeping Kcr+ loci; fail → revert to dCas9-KRAB with stress-inducible guide expression.
- M3 (18 months): Single‑cycle trap induces durable loss of autophagy flux and ≥70% loss of viability in vitro that is YEATS- and preconditioning‑dependent.
- M4 (24 months): In vivo tumor control with minimal off‑tumor editing and evidence of locus‑specific H3K9me3/CpG methylation.

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- Support for hypothesis: Autophagy-induced Kcr acts as a context gate that licenses locus‑specific repression only in adapted, high‑flux states, yielding selective collapse of autophagy dependence.
- Refutation: Absence of Kcr gating or inability to achieve durable repression indicates that autophagy-driven metabolic marks do not provide sufficient context information; the autophagy paradox would then require alternate timing devices.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Risk: Global Kcr rise causes off-target repression. Mitigation: AND-gating via TFEB/FOXO DBDs; YEATS mutants titrating affinity; restricting expression window to post‑induction.
- Risk: KRAB alone lacks durability. Mitigation: DNMT3A co-fusion in late-stage tests; confirm CpG methylation and maintenance across cell divisions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3193484/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Autophagy induction reactivates mTORC1 via acetyl‑CoA feedback. Mitigation: Short, pulsed preconditioning; quantify TFEB nuclear occupancy and Kcr accumulation kinetics to time the flip. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8386617/?utm_source=openai))

Validation and success metrics
- Molecular: CLEAR/FOXO occupancy by the fusion scales with Kcr; H3K9cr→H3K9me3 swap; CpG methylation gain at targeted promoters/enhancers.
- Functional: Loss of autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, lysosomal function), sensitivity to metabolic stress, and tumor cell death after the flip, with minimal effects in non-addicted controls.

Impact
This study tests a principled epigenetic trap: it uses the tumor’s own autophagy-driven metabolic output (crotonyl‑CoA→histone Kcr) as a license to shut off autophagy gene programs wired by MiT/TFE/FOXO, addressing the context-dependent duality of autophagy while enabling an experimentally tractable, potentially durable therapeutic modality. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-01850-6?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Autophagy memory as a therapeutic vulnerability: transient AMPK-high/mTORC1-low pulses that seed ACSS2–TFEB enhancer acetylation and BRD4/p300 condensates to drive post-withdrawal collapse in autophagy‑addicted cancers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3070934/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis and goal
A short, well-timed hyperautophagy pulse can be converted into a transient “autophagy memory” at CLEAR enhancers through ACSS2‑mediated local acetyl‑CoA supply and reader–writer feedback (BRD4/p300 condensates), producing sustained autophagy transcription after drug withdrawal. In advanced, autophagy‑addicted tumors, abruptly removing the pulse while allowing mTORC1 to rebound forces a catabolism–anabolism mismatch that selectively kills tumor cells; normal cells, with weaker enhancer locking, recover. We will define scheduling rules and biomarkers for this epigenetically encoded vulnerability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3070934/?utm_source=openai))

Biological rationale
- mTORC1 restrains autophagy by phosphorylating TFEB/TFE3 (e.g., S211) to create 14-3-3 binding and cytosolic retention; stress and lysosomal Ca2+ activate calcineurin, dephosphorylating TFEB/TFE3 to drive nuclear entry and CLEAR-program transcription. AMPK activation concurrently promotes autophagy initiation and stress programs. FOXO and p53 provide additional context-dependent transcriptional inputs to the autophagy network. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10873368/?utm_source=openai))
- In glucose deprivation or hypoxia, AMPK-phosphorylated ACSS2 translocates to the nucleus, binds TFEB at autophagy/lysosome promoters, and regenerates acetyl‑CoA from acetate to maintain H3 acetylation and target-gene expression. This establishes a direct metabolic–epigenetic feed-in to the CLEAR network. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))
- Active enhancers use acetylation-dependent positive feedback: p300/CBP write H3K27ac, recruiting BRD4; BRD4 and Mediator form transcriptional condensates at super‑enhancers that sustain high output and exhibit slow-decay kinetics, providing a mechanistic basis for short‑term “memory” after signal withdrawal. ([pure.mpg.de](https://pure.mpg.de/pubman/item/item_3040689_1/component/file_3040690/Sabari.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Advanced PDAC and other RAS-driven tumors are autophagy‑addicted; perturbing autophagy homeostasis compromises survival. A timed pulse that seeds enhancer memory, followed by withdrawal, should flip this dependence into a liability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3070934/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use a single controllable variable—time-structured AMPK-high/mTORC1-low exposure—to nucleate ACSS2–TFEB–p300/BRD4 enhancer assemblies at CLEAR loci, then remove the exposure to unmask a lethal mismatch between persistent catabolic transcription and recovering mTORC1-driven anabolism specifically in autophagy‑addicted tumor cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define the formation and decay kinetics of “autophagy memory.”
- Model systems: PDAC (KRAS-mutant) lines and organoids versus matched non-transformed pancreatic epithelia; extend to additional autophagy‑addicted lines. 
- Pulse design: 2–8 h exposure to AMPK agonism (e.g., AICAR) ± short‑acting mTORC1 inhibition (e.g., Torin1), +/- glucose restriction; then rapid washout and nutrient repletion to allow mTORC1 rebound. Titrate amplitude and duration. 
- Readouts: time-resolved CUT&Tag for H3K27ac/H3K9ac at canonical CLEAR targets (e.g., LAMP1, ATG5, GABARAPL1), TFEB/BRD4/ACSS2 ChIP‑seq occupancy, nascent RNA (PRO‑seq), live-cell BRD4/Med1 condensate imaging and FRAP, nuclear TFEB dynamics, and targeted metabolomics (acetyl‑CoA, acetate) before/during/after withdrawal to quantify memory half‑life. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))

2) Establish causality of ACSS2 and BRD4/p300 feedback in memory formation and tumor‑selective lethality.
- Interventions: (i) CRISPRi/siRNA or small‑molecule ACSS2 inhibition during the pulse; (ii) acute p300 bromodomain inhibition; (iii) BRD4 perturbation (degron or BET inhibitor) only during the pulse (not after) to test seeding requirement versus maintenance. 
- Endpoints: persistence of enhancer acetylation/BRD4 occupancy after withdrawal; autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover with bafilomycin A1), cell fate (apoptosis, catastrophic ER/energetic stress), and clonogenic survival. Expect that disrupting ACSS2 or BRD4/p300 during the pulse prevents memory and abrogates post‑withdrawal lethality in tumor cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))

3) Map context dependence via mTORC1/AMPK, FOXO, and p53 status to ensure safety and selectivity.
- Stratify lines by TP53 status (WT vs mutant with cytoplasmic accumulation), FOXO3 nuclear competence, and basal AMPK activity. 
- Test whether nuclear p53 (which can promote autophagy genes) enhances memory formation, while cytoplasmic p53 (which restrains autophagy) blunts it. 
- In normal epithelia and low‑autophagy cancers, quantify lower enhancer valency (BRD4/p300 occupancy) and faster memory decay as a basis for therapeutic index. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614182/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and methods
- Pulsing and withdrawal: plate-synchronized cells; induce with AMPK agonist ± Torin1; rapidly washout; refeed with leucine‑replete medium to stimulate mTORC1 and challenge the locked transcriptional state.
- Chromatin/transcription assays: CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for H3K27ac and TFEB/BRD4; ATAC‑seq; Pol II ChIP‑seq; PRO‑seq at 0, 2, 6, 12, 24 h post‑withdrawal to quantify hysteresis loops (ascending vs descending stimulus).
- Condensate biophysics: endogenous BRD4‑Halo/MED1‑mNeonGreen knock‑in; single‑particle tracking/FRAP to measure residence times during pulse and decay constants after withdrawal.
- Metabolic coupling: isotope‑tracing of acetate during pulse to test ACSS2‑dependent local histone acetylation; nuclear/cytosolic acetyl‑CoA compartment measurements.
- Causality tests: timed addition of ACSS2 inhibitor or BRD4 degrader only during the pulse; rescue by ectopic ACSS2-NLS or BRD4 mutants.
- Cell fate assays: Seahorse for OCR/ECAR switching; ER stress reporters; apoptosis/necrosis markers; long‑term clonogenicity.
- In vivo: orthotopic PDAC xenografts; two schedules—(i) Pulse+Withdrawal and (ii) Continuous exposure—matched for AUC. Pharmacodynamics: nuclear TFEB/ACSS2 colocalization and H3K27ac at CLEAR promoters in tumor biopsies; tumor response and tolerability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes and decision points
- Pulse seeds durable H3K27ac and BRD4 occupancy at CLEAR enhancers, with slow post‑withdrawal decay (“autophagy memory”); ACSS2 or BRD4/p300 inhibition during the pulse erases memory. 
- In autophagy‑addicted models, withdrawal triggers selective loss of viability linked to failed metabolic switching despite mTORC1 rebound; normal cells show rapid enhancer de‑acetylation/condensate dissolution and recover. 
- If memory is weak, increase pulse amplitude/duration or combine with transient calcineurin activation to enhance TFEB occupancy; if toxicity emerges in normal cells, shorten pulse or reduce AMPK drive. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3070934/?utm_source=openai))

Biomarkers and patient selection
- Positive selection: high basal autophagy flux; strong TFEB/BRD4 co‑occupancy at CLEAR loci; ACSS2 nuclear translocation capacity; KRAS‑mutant PDAC as initial indication. 
- Pharmacodynamic marker: persistence of H3K27ac and BRD4 at CLEAR targets 6–24 h after drug withdrawal in on‑treatment biopsies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/3070934/?utm_source=openai))

Risks and alternatives
- Risk: BRD4 inhibition during pulse may blunt seeding but also globally perturb transcription. Mitigation: time‑restrict perturbations and use minimal doses; or substitute with p300 modulation to bias local acetylation without global suppression. 
- Risk: AMPK’s context‑dependent effects on autophagy could complicate interpretation. Mitigation: use direct TFEB nuclearization via short lysosomal‑Ca2+/calcineurin activation to cross‑validate. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fphar.2021.794298/full?utm_source=openai))

Impact
This work reframes autophagy modulation from static inhibition to temporal control of enhancer biophysics and nuclear metabolism. By converting a brief autophagy surge into an epigenetic “memory” and then exploiting its decay mismatch with mTORC1 recovery, we propose a tumor‑selective, schedule‑dependent therapy rooted in endogenous ACSS2–TFEB coupling and BRD4/p300 condensate dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5521213/?utm_source=openai))

label: baseline
text:
Title
Reprogramming autophagy capacity in cancer by promoter–enhancer loop rewiring to favor p53/FOXO damage signaling over nutrient signaling

Hypothesis and goal
- Hypothesis: Redirecting enhancer inputs of core autophagy/lysosome genes from nutrient/growth–responsive enhancers to p53/FOXO damage‑responsive enhancers will establish a transcriptional set‑point in which autophagy is preferentially engaged during genotoxic/oncogenic damage (tumor‑suppressive) but not during starvation/metabolic stress (tumor‑promoting). This will reduce survival autophagy in advanced tumors while preserving damage‑clearing functions. Autophagy’s dual role and its control by MiT/TFE, FOXO, p53, and mTORC1/AMPK motivate the strategy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12375893/?utm_source=openai))
- Goal: Build and test a chromatin‑level intervention to convert context‑coupled autophagy into damage‑privileging tumor suppression across stages.

Atomic strategy
- Single insight: Change the wiring, not the knobs. Force physical contact between promoters of sentinel autophagy/lysosome genes (e.g., BECN1, GABARAPL1, ATG5/7, DRAM1, SESN2) and enhancers enriched for p53/FOXO occupancy active under DNA damage/oxidative stress, while disconnecting contacts to nutrient/growth enhancers. Use CRISPR loop‑tethering/insulation to reweight cis‑inputs without globally inhibiting mTORC1/AMPK. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/40856?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Identify damage‑biased enhancers that can drive autophagy‑capacity genes
- Map candidate damage enhancers near MiT/TFE–FOXO–p53 target genes using:
  - Public enhancer–gene atlases (ENCODE‑rE2G) and TF ChIP‑seq/ATAC‑seq under etoposide/H2O2 vs EBSS starvation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10781-4?utm_source=openai))
  - enhancer RNA (eRNA) activity by NET‑CAGE to confirm stimulus‑specific activation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-019-0485-9?utm_source=openai))
- Prioritize enhancers with p53/FOXO motif enrichment and stress‑selective eRNA induction; include DRAM1/SESN1/2‑linked elements due to p53‑autophagy coupling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8443158/?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPRi tiling of prioritized enhancers to quantify their contribution to target gene expression and autophagy flux baselines.

Aim 2. Rewire promoter–enhancer contacts to favor damage inputs and insulate nutrient inputs
- Forced looping: Deploy inducible CRISPR loop‑tethering (CLOuD9 or dCas9–LDB1) to juxtapose damage enhancers with promoters of BECN1, GABARAPL1, ATG5/7, DRAM1, SESN2. Validate loop formation (3C/HiChIP), enhancer activation (H3K27ac), and transcriptional upshift. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5511349/?utm_source=openai))
- Detach/insulate nutrient/growth enhancers: Use dCas9‑KRAB to silence eRNAs/anchors of TEAD/MYC/nutrient‑responsive enhancers contacting the same promoters, minimizing starvation‑only inducibility. Confirm contact loss and reduced pass‑through of mTORC1/AMPK‑linked inputs at the transcriptional level. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11876437/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic checkpoint: Ensure TFEB/TFE3 cooperation with p53 is preserved or enhanced (not blocked), leveraging known TFEB/TFE3 amplification of p53 programs during damage. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/40856?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test whether rewiring converts autophagy into a damage‑privileging tumor‑suppressive program
- Stimulus discrimination assays in isogenic cancer cells (p53WT and p53mut):
  - Inputs: starvation (EBSS), AMPK agonist, rapamycin; DNA damage (etoposide/IR); oxidative stress (H2O2); combined conditions.
  - Readouts: autophagy/lysosome transcription (CLEAR, FOXO/p53 targets), TF nuclear localization, flux (LC3‑II turnover, mCherry‑GFP‑LC3), lysosomal biogenesis, mitophagy (mt‑Keima), apoptosis/senescence (caspase‑3, SA‑β‑gal), clonogenic survival, ΔGI50 with chemo/IR. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8833990/?utm_source=openai))
- Expected discrimination:
  - Post‑rewiring: minimal transcriptional upshift and limited survival benefit under starvation/AMPK activation; robust transcriptional and cell‑fate responses (apoptosis/senescence) under DNA damage with upregulation of DRAM1/SESNs and selective autophagy. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12672-026-05143-5?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic decoupling: Show promoter output becomes less sensitive to mTORC1‑TFEB cytosolic sequestration and more contingent on p53/FOXO occupancy; monitor TFEB/TFE3 activation states given mTORC1/AMPK regulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41420-024-01850-6.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. In vivo efficacy and safety
- Models: Orthotopic and PDX models engineered to carry inducible loop modules; administer etoposide/IR ± metabolic stress.
- Delivery (research‑grade): tumor‑targeted LNPs carrying gRNAs to a constitutively expressed dCas9‑tether in tumor cells; or dual‑AAV for localized delivery.
- Endpoints: tumor growth delay, time to progression under therapy, minimal residual disease; single‑cell RNA/ATAC to verify program stability; off‑target transcriptome and 3D‑genome safety profiling.

Key mechanistic and novelty checkpoints
- Autophagy’s context‑dependent tumor suppression/promotion is established; MiT/TFE master CLEAR regulators are controlled by mTORC1/AMPK and cooperate with p53/FOXO during damage. Our intervention targets this convergence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12375893/?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPR‑based chromatin loop engineering (CLOuD9; dCas9‑LDB1 tethering) can forcibly create or reconfigure promoter–enhancer contacts and alter gene expression, but has not, to our knowledge, been used to convert autophagy’s role in cancer; this represents the novelty vector. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6235177/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones, go/no‑go criteria
- M1: Identify ≥3 damage‑biased enhancers whose CRISPRi reduces target autophagy gene expression >40% under DNA damage but <10% under starvation.
- M2: Demonstrate forced loops increase target transcription >2‑fold and CLEAR output with validated new contacts.
- M3: Show discrimination: under starvation, rewired cells do not gain clonogenic survival; under DNA damage, they exhibit increased apoptosis/senescence and improved chemo/IR response (ΔGI50 or ΔTGI with significance).
- M4: In vivo, demonstrate improved therapeutic efficacy without cachexia/toxicity; maintain limited global enhancer perturbation.

Risk and mitigation
- Off‑target loops/transcription: multiplex high‑specificity gRNAs, RNA‑seq and Hi‑C safety screens.
- p53 deficiency: In p53mut contexts, prioritize FOXO‑biased damage enhancers; stratify by TF dependencies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8833990/?utm_source=openai))
- Compensatory enhancer switching: add minimal insulation at emergent nutrient enhancers identified by eRNA/HiChIP.

Impact
- Provides a cis‑regulatory method to stabilize autophagy in its tumor‑suppressive regime by privileging damage surveillance over nutrient stress, addressing a central obstacle to autophagy‑targeted oncology. If successful, it establishes “wiring therapy” as a generalizable modality for state‑locking stress programs in cancer. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10781-4?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Chromatin deadbolt: sequence-programmed recruitment of endogenous HDAC3 to stress-activated autophagy enhancers to lock tumors out of survival autophagy

Hypothesis and goal
A subset of autophagy/lysosome genes is driven by stress-activated enhancers bound by MiT/TFE (TFEB/TFE3), FOXO, and context-dependent p53 when AMPK is high and mTORC1 is low. If we tether an endogenous histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3)–activating peptide directly at these enhancers, we can prevent stimulus-dependent acetylation, transcription factor occupancy, and induction of survival autophagy while sparing basal housekeeping autophagy. This will convert autophagy from a tumor-aiding stress response in established cancers into a fixed, tumor-suppressive background flux compatible with therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single causal lever: locus-specific deacetylation at stress-activated autophagy enhancers. Deploy a programmable pyrrole–imidazole (Py–Im) polyamide that recognizes CLEAR/E-box–centered DNA segments at these enhancers and carries the minimal SMRT/NCoR deacetylase-activation domain (DAD) peptide to nucleate catalytically active endogenous HDAC3 in situ, thereby maintaining a closed, hypoacetylated enhancer state during AMPK activation or mTORC1 inhibition. This directly breaks the AMPK/mTORC1 → MiT/TFE/FOXO/p53 → transcription coupling at the chromatin switch without altering upstream signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1087922/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale (mechanistic grounding)
- Stress gating: AMPK-dependent phosphorylation activates TFEB/TFE3 and promotes their nuclear translocation; mTORC1 phosphorylation/14-3-3 retains TFEB in the cytosol. Under stress, MiT/TFE and FOXO occupy CLEAR/E-box and FOXO motifs to induce autophagy and lysosomal genes. Nuclear p53 can cooperate in this program; cytoplasmic p53 opposes it. These axes define a stimulus-responsive enhancer set. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin as the operational switch: activation requires local H3K27ac and chromatin opening; enforcing local deacetylation is expected to prevent factor binding and enhancer function. HDAC3 enzymatic activity is uniquely dependent on DAD peptides from SMRT/NCoR, enabling small-peptide–mediated catalytic activation at defined loci. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3565028/?utm_source=openai))
- Deliverability and locus selectivity: Py–Im polyamides enter nuclei, bind minor-groove sequences with high specificity, and have shown in vivo antitumor activity when programmed to transcription factor motifs. Prior work attached HDAC inhibitors (e.g., SAHA) to Py–Im polyamides to activate genes; here, we invert the logic by recruiting endogenous HDAC3 for repression—an unreported but mechanistically grounded variant. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4646452/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define stress-activated autophagy/lysosome enhancer targets in tumor models and verify their TF dependencies.
- Induce stress (EBSS starvation; phenformin for AMPK activation; rapalogs for mTORC1 inhibition) in PDAC and melanoma cell lines/xenografts. Map open chromatin and active enhancers (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac CUT&RUN) at baseline vs stress; map TF occupancy (TFEB, TFE3, FOXO3, p53 CUT&RUN). Prioritize enhancers co-gaining H3K27ac and TF occupancy only under stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))
- Validate transcriptional outputs and autophagic flux coupling (RNA-seq; LC3-II turnover with lysosomal blockade; p62 degradation). Separate housekeeping loci (constitutive expression) from stress-only enhancers for selective targeting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10244319/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and test CLEAR-targeted Py–Im polyamide–DAD conjugates as locus-specific autophagy enhancer repressors.
- Design: select 12–16 bp windows spanning CLEAR/E-box–centered sequences within Aim 1 enhancers; synthesize hairpin Py–Im polyamides to those sites. Conjugate the minimal human SMRT/NCoR DAD peptide via a flexible linker using established Py–Im–peptide ligation chemistry. Controls: unconjugated Py–Im; scrambled-binding Py–Im–DAD; Py–Im–SAHA (activation-biased) as orthogonal control. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/16/6/12631?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism tests under stress: measure HDAC3 recruitment (ChIP/CUT&RUN), local histone acetylation (H3K27ac/H3K9ac), TF occupancy loss (TFEB/TFE3/FOXO/p53 CUT&RUN), enhancer RNA suppression, and target gene mRNA. Test dose–response and reversibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3565028/?utm_source=openai))
- Function: quantify autophagy flux and cell fate with and without chemo/targeted therapy (e.g., gemcitabine in PDAC; BRAF/MEK inhibitors in BRAF-mutant melanoma). Expect reduced survival autophagy and increased therapy sensitivity only under stress, with basal flux preserved at baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10244319/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity profiling: genome-wide binding by COSMIC-seq for the conjugates; RNA-seq to assess off-target transcriptional effects. Benchmark against published binding specificity of Py–Im scaffolds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7755219/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Therapeutic evaluation and context dependence in vivo.
- Pharmacology: assess tumor uptake and nuclear localization (fluorophore-labeled conjugates) and plasma/tissue exposure. Prior Py–Im studies support tumor penetration and in vivo efficacy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3651785/?utm_source=openai))
- Efficacy: in xenografts and patient-derived organoids, compare therapy ± Py–Im–DAD under nutrient/hypoxia stress. Endpoints: tumor growth delay, apoptosis markers, and autophagy flux. Evaluate normal tissues for basal autophagy markers and proteostasis to confirm sparing of housekeeping autophagy.
- Stage sensitivity: test early vs established tumor models; predict greatest benefit in established, stress-adapted tumors. Monitor p53 status to stratify contexts where p53 augments stress-autophagy transcription. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-026-02688-3?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and readouts
- Target discovery: ATAC-seq, H3K27ac CUT&RUN, and TF CUT&RUN ± stress; overlap with CLEAR/FOXO/p53 motif calls to nominate sites.
- Conjugate synthesis and validation: HPLC/MS for purity; electromobility shift/surface plasmon resonance for sequence binding; cell-based occupancy by COSMIC-seq. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7755219/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic validation: ChIP/CUT&RUN for HDAC3 and histone acetyl marks; locus-specific qPCR for enhancer RNAs; TF occupancy displacement assays; MNase accessibility at target enhancers.
- Functional outcomes: LC3-II and p62 turnover; lysosomal activity assays; clonogenic survival ± therapy; synergy analysis.

Risk assessment and contingency
- Risk 1: Enhancer redundancy blunts repression. Contingency: multiplex Py–Im–DAD mixes to target clusters within a gene program; or switch to an alternative repressor peptide (mSin3 SID) to recruit HDAC1/2-containing complexes if HDAC3-centric repression is insufficient. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC133736/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk 2: Insufficient recruitment of active HDAC3. Contingency: optimize DAD length/stoichiometry; confirm catalytic activation by HDAC3 activity assays at chromatin; include inositol phosphate supplementation strategies known to stabilize active complexes in cells if needed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4505066/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk 3: Off-target repression of housekeeping autophagy. Contingency: restrict target selection to enhancers that only gain H3K27ac under stress; monitor basal autophagy and proteostasis in non-stressed normal cells; titrate dosing to stress windows.

Milestones
- Year 1: Map stress-only enhancers and validate TF dependence in two tumor types; select 6–10 high-value targets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Synthesize Py–Im–DAD panel; demonstrate locus-specific HDAC3 recruitment, loss of acetylation, and TF displacement; achieve ≥70% suppression of stress-induced target transcripts and flux reduction in vitro.
- Year 3: Demonstrate enhanced therapy response and preserved basal autophagy in vivo; complete off-target and safety profiling; nominate a lead conjugate for translational development.

Innovation
- Converts autophagy control from upstream signaling modulation to a locus-specific chromatin intervention that is engaged only where and when tumors activate survival autophagy.
- Introduces, to our knowledge, the first use of a Py–Im polyamide to recruit and catalytically activate endogenous HDAC3 via DAD at defined enhancers; contrasts with prior SAHA–polyamide activators that globally inhibit HDACs to open chromatin. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5167308/?utm_source=openai))

Why this respects autophagy’s dual role
- By targeting enhancers that are silent at baseline and open only under AMPK-high/mTORC1-low stress, repression is preferentially engaged during the survival-autophagy state of established tumors, leaving early tumor-suppressive housekeeping autophagy largely intact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8726606/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
A single, programmable “deadbolt” at stress-activated autophagy enhancers should disable a common resistance axis across cancers while avoiding systemic autophagy shutdown. The approach generalizes to other stress programs driven by TFEB/TFE3/FOXO/p53 and can be iterated by retargeting the DNA code without re-engineering signaling interventions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10244319/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Time-gated rewriting of autophagy-addiction memory by TFEB-timed KDM6B modulation to sensitize advanced cancers to autophagy blockade

Premise and question-as-hypothesis
Autophagy-addicted tumors maintain high flux through stress-driven TFEB/TFE3 activity and permissive chromatin states at CLEAR/autophagy loci. TFEB nuclear localization is set by nutrient/Ca2+ signals via mTORC1 and calcineurin and displays reproducible dynamics after transient stress. We hypothesize that these TFEB-bound loci pass through short-lived, labile chromatin states during TFEB entry/exit; if the H3K27 writer/eraser balance is briefly biased toward deposition (EZH2>demethylase) exactly as TFEB disengages, autophagy-gene promoters can be reprogrammed to a stably repressed state, decoupling autophagy induction from upstream stress and unmasking vulnerability to autophagy inhibitors in advanced cancers. This strategy must be gated to advanced, autophagy‑addicted settings to respect autophagy’s tumor‑suppressive role earlier in oncogenesis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22692423/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use TFEB nuclear shuttling as a live “timer” to deliver a short, precisely phased decrease in KDM6 demethylase activity at autophagy loci, allowing PRC2 to re‑establish H3K27me3 and close the positive feedback that sustains high autophagy flux in addicted cells; then apply autophagy blockade. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40089585/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 1. Map TFEB‑defined plasticity windows at autophagy loci in autophagy‑addicted cancers
- Models: MiT/TFE‑high renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic cancer lines/organoids with documented high basal autophagy; isogenic p53 WT/mutant panels.
- Readouts: Generate TFEB-mNeonGreen knock‑in reporters; perform starvation→refeeding or Torin1→washout pulses while imaging TFEB nuclear shuttling to extract entry/exit dwell-time distributions (microfluidics for timing precision). Parallel CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN time series for TFEB, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, H3K4me3 at CLEAR loci; ATAC‑seq for accessibility dynamics. Include USF2 ChIP and NuRD components to capture TFEB–USF2 promoter competition that gates acetylation at these genes. Outcome: define cell‑type–specific “labile” intervals surrounding TFEB exit when marks are most rewritable. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40089585/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 2. Test whether brief, TFEB‑phased KDM6B suppression rewrites autophagy‑gene memory
- Intervention: Build inducible, rapid KDM6B off‑switch (dTAG/AID degron) and, in parallel, short‑pulse pharmacology with GSK‑J4 (dual KDM6A/B inhibitor) delivered only during the labile window identified in Aim 1. As a mechanistic control, pulse EZH2 activity (CRISPRa‑EZH2 or transient EED agonist if available) without changing components outside the window to test stoichiometric dominance of writers over erasers.
- Readouts: Locus‑specific H3K27me3 gain and H3K27ac loss at ULK1, BECN1, WIPI1, LC3B, RAB7A promoters/enhancers; sustained reduction of TFEB/TFE3 occupancy upon re‑pulsing; blunted transcriptional induction after repeated starvation; decreased LC3‑II flux and autolysosome formation at baseline and under stress. Outcome: demonstrate durable, promoter‑localized repression of autophagy genes after a single timed KDM6 perturbation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7010817/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 3. Convert rewritten chromatin states into therapeutic vulnerability with autophagy blockade
- Strategy: After confirmation of stable H3K27me3 re‑establishment, administer autophagy inhibitors (ULK1 or VPS34 inhibitors; or late‑stage lysosomal inhibitors) and measure viability/apoptosis/ferroptosis in vitro and in vivo (xenografts and patient‑derived organoids).
- Context gating and safety: Restrict to models showing (i) robust TFEB pulses and high basal flux, (ii) survival advantage from autophagy under nutrient/drug stress, and (iii) advanced‑disease transcriptional signatures. In p53‑WT settings, exploit SESN–AMPK to standardize TFEB pulsing; in p53‑mutant settings, control pulsing via mTORC1/AMPK modulators without relying on p53. Primary epithelial controls assess preservation of homeostatic/early tumor‑suppressive autophagy. Success criterion: selective loss of viability in addicted models after the two‑step “rewrite→block” regimen. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18762019/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic rationale (concise)
- TFEB/TFE3 activate CLEAR network genes when dephosphorylated (mTORC1 off) and return to cytosol as mTORC1 resumes; calcineurin–MCOLN1 Ca2+ signaling provides a rapid dephosphorylation arm, generating characteristic nuclear pulses that define reproducible timing windows. These windows coincide with increased promoter accessibility and dynamic histone acetylation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22692423/?utm_source=openai))
- H3K27me3 at autophagy loci is actively opposed by KDM6 demethylases; hepatic and dental‑pulp systems show KDM6B‑dependent demethylation and upregulation of autophagy genes, supporting feasibility of flipping these marks by transiently biasing the writer/eraser balance. TFE3 complexes with KDM6A at autophagy loci in RCC, indicating MiT/TFE factors physically interface with H3K27 demethylases. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7010817/?utm_source=openai))
- USF2‑NuRD competes with TFEB at CLEAR promoters to suppress H3K27ac in fed state; transitioning through TFEB exit likely re‑exposes these loci to repressive complexes, providing a natural timing cue for writer dominance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12087643/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design details
- Timing control: Use on‑chip microfluidics to deliver 10–60 min pulses of starvation/Torin1 followed by rapid refeeding/washout; synchronize degron‑mediated KDM6B depletion to TFEB exit (e.g., 15–45 min post‑washout per Aim 1 kinetics).
- Locus targeting (optional refinement): dCas9‑EED (to seed H3K27me3) or dCas9‑KDM6B (to erase) tethered to CLEAR‑adjacent sgRNAs, each delivered only within labile windows to test causality and reduce genome‑wide off‑target chromatin effects.
- Multi‑omic endpoints: CUT&Tag for H3K27me3/H3K27ac/H3K4me3 at 0/15/45/120 min and 24/72 h; nascent RNA‑seq (4sU‑seq) for immediate transcriptional effects; LC3 flux assays ± bafilomycin; lysosomal pH and proteolysis assays; viability and clonogenic survival after autophagy blockade.

Milestones and go/no‑go criteria
- M1: Identify a labile window with ≥2‑fold change in H3K27ac and TFEB occupancy decay at ≥30% of CLEAR loci.
- M2: A single KDM6B “off” pulse during the window increases H3K27me3 ≥1.5‑fold at ≥30% of target loci and depresses autophagy‑gene induction ≥40% upon re‑challenge.
- M3: The rewrite→block sequence reduces viability ≥50% vs. block‑only in addicted models, with ≤15% effect in non‑addicted controls.

Contingencies
- If KDM6B is dispensable in a tumor type, pivot to KDM6A (supported TFE3–KDM6A interaction) or enhance PRC2 occupancy (EED agonism or transient CRISPRa‑EZH2) during the same window. If TFEB dynamics are weak, use TFE3 as timer or exploit circadian coupling to TFEB/TFE3 to pre‑schedule windows. If repression increases cytoprotective pathways, invert the polarity: time a brief KDM6B “on” pulse to overshoot autophagy gene expression, then apply late‑stage lysosomal blockade to trigger lethal accumulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10141522/?utm_source=openai))

Therapeutic endgame
Demonstrate that epigenetic reprogramming of autophagy dependence is achievable by modulating existing chromatin machinery in time rather than by adding new components, converting resistance (autophagy addiction) into a treatable weakness when combined with autophagy inhibitors, and respecting context by gating to advanced disease with documented TFEB pulsing and high autophagy flux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214848/?utm_source=openai))
