text:
Title
Peripheral nociceptor output as a systemic metabolic command: partitioning endocrine neuropeptide versus autonomic reflex pathways in diabetic glucose control

Hypothesis–Question
Does sustained hyperactivity of small-diameter DRG nociceptors function as a distributed catabolic command that worsens hyperglycemia in diabetes, and is its primary mechanism acute sympathetic reflex–driven hepatic glucose production or endocrine/paracrine neuropeptide (CGRP/substance P) action that impairs islet function and vascular insulin delivery? If route-specific, can targeted interruption of the dominant pathway improve glycemic control without inducing further nerve injury? ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00005.2023?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Evoke or suppress nociceptor secretory output in vivo while orthogonally blocking either autonomic ganglionic transmission or CGRP/NK1R signaling, then read out whole-body glucose fluxes within minutes. Mirror the endocrine arm in a DRG–islet organ-on-chip lacking reflex circuits to establish sufficiency.

Model systems and genetic/viral tools
- Nav1.8-CreERT2 mice for inducible nociceptor-restricted manipulations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2992507/?utm_source=openai))
- Peripheral neuron–tropic AAV (e.g., AAV-PHP.S or AAV9) carrying Cre-dependent hM3Dq (Gq) and hM4Di (Gi/o) for bidirectional control of DRG neuron excitability and dense-core vesicle release; intrathecal or systemic delivery optimized for DRG transduction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/pmid/28671695/?utm_source=openai))
- Chemogenetic ligands (e.g., DCZ/CNO) to acutely dial nociceptor internal state; hM3Dq depolarizes via PLC and can elevate terminal Ca2+ to trigger neuropeptide release. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00009.2017?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 1: Partition acute routes from nociceptor output to glycemic control in vivo
Design
- Cohort: adult male and female Nav1.8-CreERT2 mice injected with AAV-PHP.S–DIO-hM3Dq or –DIO-hM4Di; tamoxifen-induced recombination completed ≥3 weeks pre-test.
- Interventions (Latin-square, crossover):
  1) Vehicle.
  2) DRG activation (hM3Dq ligand).
  3) DRG activation + autonomic ganglionic blockade (hexamethonium; blocks both sympathetic and parasympathetic efferents).
  4) DRG activation + CGRP receptor antagonist (e.g., rimegepant or anti-CGRPα mAb) ± NK1R antagonist (aprepitant).
  5) DRG activation + both blockades.
  6) DRG silencing (hM4Di ligand) in diabetic models (DIO or db/db) as comparator.
- Primary readouts: tracer-based endogenous glucose production (EGP) during basal and hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp; plasma catecholamines; plasma CGRP and SP; hepatic cAMP/PKA substrate phosphorylation; liver glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis indices. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5777172/?utm_source=openai))
- Predictions discriminating routes:
  - Autonomic reflex–dominant model: DRG activation increases catecholamines and EGP; hexamethonium abolishes these effects, whereas CGRP/NK1R blockade has little impact. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00005.2023?utm_source=openai))
  - Endocrine neuropeptide–dominant model: DRG activation suppresses glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) and raises glycemia with minimal catecholamine signature; CGRP/NK1R blockade normalizes GSIS and glycemia even with intact ganglia. Anti-CGRPα improves glycemia in diabetic mice. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/endo/article/119/2/865/2540543?utm_source=openai))
Controls and validation
- Direct CGRP infusion to match plasma levels observed in (2) with concurrent ganglionic blockade tests endocrine sufficiency for glycemic effects (concentration–response, acknowledging reported dual, dose-dependent insulin effects of CGRP). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/016701159090213G?utm_source=openai))
- Sensory denervation precedent for metabolic benefit (capsaicin/RTX) establishes construct validity of the nerve-to-metabolism axis. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpendo.00356.2004?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 2: Establish endocrine sufficiency without reflex circuits using DRG–islet–endothelium organ-on-chip
Design
- Tri-compartment microfluidic chip: hM3Dq-expressing DRG neurons; primary islets; microvascular endothelium. Activate DRG with ligand while recording islet Ca2+ dynamics and GSIS under controlled glucose ramps. Introduce CGRP and SP alone or in combination to quantify dose–effect on GSIS; apply CGRP receptor and NK1R antagonists to rescue. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK476117/?utm_source=openai))
- Endpoints: GSIS amplitude/kinetics; endothelial insulin transcytosis markers; islet gene expression of cAMP/PKA targets after peptide exposure.

Specific Aim 3: Test therapeutic directionality by toggling nociceptor internal state in diabetic mice
Design
- Chronic silencing: In DIO and db/db mice, hM4Di activation daily for 4 weeks; outcomes: CGM-based glycemic profiles, HbA1c, clamps, hepatic PKA readouts, adipose lipolysis markers, islet GSIS ex vivo; compare to anti-CGRPα treatment. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33089134/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic profiling: scRNA-seq of DRG neurons and liver–islet vascular/immune compartments to map ligand–receptor engagement (CALCRL/RAMP1, NK1R) and downstream pathway activation states after interventions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5777172/?utm_source=openai))

Key methodological considerations and risk mitigation
- Decoupling evidence base: Peripheral terminals can release CGRP/SP via GPCR/TRP-dependent Ca2+ signals even when spike conduction is altered; local anesthetics themselves evoke TRPV1-dependent CGRP release, underscoring that terminal exocytosis can be driven independently of long-range signaling. Thus, reflex blockade at autonomic ganglia isolates endocrine effects without suppressing peripheral secretion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2157564/?utm_source=openai))
- Viral targeting: AAV-PHP.S/AAV9 reliably transduce DRG after systemic or intrathecal delivery; restrict expression using Cre-dependent cassettes in Nav1.8-CreERT2 mice. Titer and promoter choice minimize off-target expression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/pmid/28671695/?utm_source=openai))
- Chemogenetics: hM3Dq/hM4Di provide rapid, reversible state control suitable for separating fast (minutes) metabolic outcomes from slower structural adaptations. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00009.2017?utm_source=openai))
- Pharmacology: Hexamethonium blocks autonomic ganglionic transmission, removing sympathetic efferent drive to liver; CGRP antagonists and NK1R blockers isolate peptide-mediated endocrine effects. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganglionic_blocker?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and decision points
- If hexamethonium eliminates DRG activation–induced increases in EGP while CGRP/NK1R blockade does not, autonomic reflexes are the primary route; prioritize neuromodulatory strategies targeting sensory–autonomic coupling. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00005.2023?utm_source=openai))
- If CGRP/NK1R blockade normalizes GSIS/glycemia during DRG activation with little change from hexamethonium, prioritize anti-CGRP–like therapeutics for neuropathy-associated dysglycemia; supportive prior data show anti-CGRPα lowers hyperglycemia and adiposity in T2D mouse models. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33089134/?utm_source=openai))
- If both contribute, quantify relative effect sizes to guide combination strategies and patient stratification.

Milestones
- Month 6: Validate DRG transduction and chemogenetic control; establish clamp platform and peptide assays.
- Month 12: Complete Aim 1 acute partitioning with effect-size estimates for each route.
- Month 18: Complete organ-on-chip endocrine sufficiency tests and antagonism rescues (Aim 2).
- Month 24: Complete chronic silencing/anti-CGRPα interventions in diabetic models with scRNA-seq mechanistic maps (Aim 3).

Impact
This proposal tests whether neuropathy-like nociceptor activity is not merely a symptom but an upstream systemic driver of diabetic dysregulation, and it identifies the dominant mechanistic route—autonomic reflex or endocrine neuropeptide—controlling hepatic glucose production and islet output. Route-resolved outcomes translate directly to therapeutic levers: neuromodulation of sensory–autonomic coupling versus CGRP/NK1R antagonism, both with existing toolchains for rapid preclinical to clinical iteration. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00005.2023?utm_source=openai))

Title
Sensor-gated ketone switching to install a resilient metabolic state in DRG neurons under diabetic stress

Unified hypothesis–goal
A subset of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons naturally enters a transient, metabolically resilient state that preserves energy charge and limits redox/ionic derailment during hyperglycemia. We hypothesize that pre-emptive activation of endogenous redox sentinels in DRG neurons to a lower set-point, coupled to on-demand delivery of β‑hydroxybutyrate (BHB) as an alternate oxidative substrate and signaling metabolite, will reproduce this resilient state across the DRG population and prevent progression of diabetic neuropathy. The goal is to define, induce, and lock-in this resilient state in DRG neurons, with minimal systemic perturbation. DRG are chosen because they express ketolytic machinery (BDH1/OXCT1) and monocarboxylate transporters for ketone uptake, and because Nrf2 signaling in DRG mitigates diabetic nociception and stress responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12940000/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Lower the activation threshold of the DRG redox sentinel (Nrf2) so that small redox/ionic deviations trigger anticipatory stabilization, and gate brief BHB microdoses to these sentinel events to (i) maintain ATP supply independent of glycolysis/PDH and (ii) reinforce pro-resilience transcription via BHB’s HDAC-inhibitory and HCAR2–immunomodulatory actions. This single, closed-loop intervention aims to shift the timing of protective responses rather than increase their magnitude. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2021.783659/full?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and novelty
- DRG-targeted Nrf2 activation reduces methylglyoxal-induced nociception and stress signaling; we leverage this as an early-warning node to pre-empt collapse. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12015141/?utm_source=openai))
- BHB supports neuronal oxidation and directly enters mitochondria-derived acetyl‑CoA pools without requiring glycolysis/PDH, while also functioning as an HDAC inhibitor and an HCAR2 agonist that reprograms innate immunity toward neuroprotection. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2021.783659/full?utm_source=openai))
- Ketogenic interventions reduce allodynia and restore intraepidermal nerve fiber density in diabetic mice, but have not been engineered as DRG-sentinel–gated, microdosed fuel switches; we test this timing-centric reframing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34252910/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 1. Map resilient DRG states and define sentinel-triggered “entry criteria” on an innervated microvasculature-on-chip
- Platform: A microfluidic DRG–endothelial–macrophage “innervated vasculature-on-chip” that recapitulates neurovascular crosstalk; impose diabetic-mimetic media (high glucose, fatty acids, methylglyoxal). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10152403/?utm_source=openai))
- Perturbations: Pulsatile low-dose MMF/DRF to tune KEAP1–Nrf2 threshold; nanomolar-to-millimolar BHB microdoses delivered only when predefined optic reporters cross set-points (e.g., NADPH/NADP+ and ATP/ADP drops, ROS spikes).
- Readouts: Time-resolved axonal transport, calcium stability, mitochondrial potential; cytokine flux from endothelium/immune cells; scRNA-seq/ATAC-seq to identify “resilient-entry” signatures across DRG neuronal subtypes.
- Success criteria: Identification of a minimal sentinel signature that predicts survival and axon maintenance; demonstration that sentinel-gated BHB outperforms constant BHB or sentinel activation alone in preserving energy charge and axon integrity.

Specific Aim 2. Test whether sensor-gated BHB installs a durable resilient state via combined metabolic and epigenetic programs
- Mechanistic assays:
  - Metabolism: 13C‑BHB tracing to confirm neuronal ketolysis; metabolic flexibility tests (glucose→BHB switching) and PDH-bypass benefit under glycolytic restriction. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2021.783659/full?utm_source=openai))
  - Epigenetics and signaling: Quantify histone acetylation/kbhb marks and transcription of antioxidant/stress-resilience genes after BHB pulses; evaluate HCAR2-dependent reprogramming of co-cultured macrophages and endothelial activation states. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23223453/?utm_source=openai))
  - Inflammation: Test BHB-mediated NLRP3 suppression (IL‑1β/IL‑18) in the on-chip immune compartment. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25686106/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Sentinel-gated BHB establishes a stable DRG transcriptional-metabolic attractor that confers superior recovery after metabolic stress withdrawal versus controls.

Specific Aim 3. Validate DRG-targeted sentinel–fuel coupling in diabetic mice
- Genetics: Use Advillin-Cre or Avil‑CreERT2 for DRG neuron-specific manipulations (e.g., modest KEAP1 knockdown or Nrf2 stabilization; BDH1/OXCT1 or MCT2 enhancement to bias ketone utilization). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3185264/?utm_source=openai))
- Interventions: Deliver oral ketone ester or BHB via micro-osmotic pumps; include a cohort with timed, low-dose fumarate to adjust sentinel thresholds.
- Outcomes: Pain behavior (von Frey, Hargreaves), nerve conduction, intraepidermal nerve fiber density, DRG single-nucleus RNA-seq to confirm installation of the resilient-state signature. Benchmark against ad lib ketogenic diet as a positive control. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34252910/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: DRG-targeted sentinel–fuel coupling outperforms diet alone on function, structure, and transcriptomic resilience with lower systemic burden.

Key measurements and analytics
- Antioxidant reserve turnover: Dynamic GSH/GSSG and Trx redox cycling rates under repeated repair challenges.
- Early-warning efficacy: Latency from sentinel deviation to restoration of ATP/redox homeostasis.
- State classification: scRNA-seq–derived probabilistic “resilience score” predicting structural recovery; causal mediation to attribute benefit to sentinel timing versus fuel identity.

Milestones
M1 (6 months): On-chip resilient signature defined; sentinel thresholds calibrated. M2 (12 months): Demonstrate superiority of sentinel-gated BHB over constant dosing on-chip. M3 (24 months): In vivo proof that DRG-targeted sentinel–fuel coupling improves neuropathy endpoints over ketogenic diet or fumarate alone.

Risk mitigation
- If fumarate-based tuning causes off-target effects, switch to DRG-restricted KEAP1 RNAi or Nrf2 degron modulation to maintain sentinel specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12015141/?utm_source=openai))
- If BHB immunomodulation via HCAR2 is insufficient, add selective HCAR2 agonism to the immune/endothelial compartments in-chip to reinforce the neuroprotective macrophage phenotype before advancing in vivo. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms4944?utm_source=openai))

Impact
This work reframes therapy from repairing downstream mitochondrial injury to controlling timing and fuel choice: a sensor-gated, DRG-specific switch that reproduces the naturally occurring resilient state and prevents diabetic neuropathy progression with minimal systemic trade-offs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12940000/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Stress-gated reinforcement of ER–mitochondria contacts via PDZD8 to restore Ca2+ microdomains and bioenergetics in diabetic DRG neurons

Rationale and novelty check
- In sensory neurons, PDZD8 is a neuronal ER membrane protein that tethers ER to mitochondria and sharpens ER→mitochondria Ca2+ microdomains required for mitochondrial dehydrogenase activation; PDZD8 loss blunts synaptically evoked mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake. This establishes PDZD8 as a neuron-relevant MERC organizer. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5818999/?utm_source=openai))
- PDZD8 also functions as an ER–endolysosome tether with SMP-domain lipid-transfer activity, indicating modular tethering and lipid-handling capacity that can be repurposed; its MERC role in peripheral neurons under metabolic stress has not been therapeutically targeted. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6842579/?utm_source=openai))
- Diabetic neuropathy features DRG neuron mitochondrial dysfunction, altered Ca2+ homeostasis, and nociceptor hyperexcitability; direct MERC defects are well documented in metabolic tissues and hypothesized in DRG, but causal tests in DRG are lacking—creating a tractable gap. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8720329/?utm_source=openai))
- Acute, synthetic ER–mitochondria tethers (rapamycin-inducible FKBP–FRB) can increase contacts and Ca2+ transfer, providing a causal assay to test whether contact restoration normalizes microdomains before committing to genetic therapies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3178184/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use the pathological signal itself—excess local Ca2+ at failing microdomains—to gate a modest, reversible increase in PDZD8-mediated ER–mitochondria contact only where and when coupling is insufficient, thereby restoring Ca2+ microdomains and mitochondrial ATP production without global over-tethering.

Hypothesis–question (indistinguishable)
Can a Ca2+-thresholded PDZD8 tether that assembles only at hyperactive, energetically failing ER–mitochondria microdomains in diabetic DRG neurons restore beat-to-beat ER→mitochondria Ca2+ transfer and ATP production, thereby reversing nociceptor hyperexcitability and neuropathy phenotypes, while avoiding mitochondrial Ca2+ overload? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5818999/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define MERC structural–functional failure in diabetic DRG neurons.
- Question: Do db/db and STZ models show reduced MERC area/optimized spacing and impaired fast ER→mitochondria Ca2+ coupling in DRG nociceptors?
- Approach: DRG-on-a-chip to segregate axons/somas; EM/TEM stereology for MERC area and spacing; contact reporters; ER- and mito-targeted Ca2+ GECIs during physiological firing; mito-ATP and ROS reporters; pairwise correlation of MERC metrics with Ca2+ microdomain fidelity and ATP transients. Controls: MCU inhibition to define Ca2+ coupling ceiling; acute rapalog-induced FKBP–FRB tethering to test causality that restoring contacts improves coupling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3178184/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and validate a Ca2+-gated PDZD8 “autopatch” that restores MERCs only at pathological microdomains.
- Design: Two-component, Ca2+-dependent inter-organelle bridge:
  - ER membrane: PDZD8 minimal tethering scaffold fused to an M13 peptide.
  - OMM: TOM20-anchored calmodulin (CaM).
  - High local Ca2+ (pathological microdomains) drives CaM–M13 binding, transiently bridging ER and OMM and enriching endogenous PDZD8 at the interface; as Ca2+ normalizes, the bridge disengages. Linker lengths are pre-calibrated to target physiologic MERC spacing (10–30 nm) to avoid mitochondrial Ca2+ overload. Safety: low-expression promoters and degrons to cap maximal tether density; MCU-inhibition rescue as fail-safe.
- Benchmarks: In diabetic DRG-on-chip, quantify restoration of ER→mitochondria Ca2+ transfer gain, ATP transients, and reduction of ROS bursts; verify reversibility and absence of sustained mito-Ca2+ elevation/mPTP opening. Compare to constitutive PDZD8 overexpression to show superiority of stress-gated control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5818999/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test therapeutic efficacy and transcriptomic safety in vivo.
- Delivery: AAV9/Php.S with sensory-neuron–biased promoters to L4–L6 DRG in db/db and STZ mice.
- Endpoints: Mechanical and thermal nociception, nerve conduction, intraepidermal nerve fiber density; DRG EM for MERC metrics; ex vivo neuronal Ca2+ and ATP imaging; single-nucleus RNA-seq for UPR, inflammatory, and cell-death signatures to detect over-tethering or ER stress.
- Comparators: Vehicle, rapalog-tether positive control, and non-gated PDZD8. Criteria for success: improved sensory behavior and conduction with normalized microdomain metrics and no adverse transcriptomic signatures.

Key design justifications
- Neuron relevance: PDZD8 organizes neuronal MERCs that couple synaptic ER release to mitochondrial uptake; leveraging this native machinery is more physiologic than non-native tethers alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5818999/?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility: Drug-inducible tethers validate causality between contact density and Ca2+ transfer; Ca2+-gated CaM–M13 pairs provide reversible, thresholded assembly compatible with 10–30 nm MERC geometry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3178184/?utm_source=openai))
- Disease linkage: Diabetic DRG neurons exhibit Ca2+ dysregulation and mitochondrial dysfunction that are mechanistically rescued by improving Ca2+ microdomain fidelity; targeting the microdomain should correct both signaling and energetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8720329/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental details and readouts
- MERC structure: Transmission EM; quantification of ER–mitochondria apposition length per mitochondrion and intermembrane distance distributions.
- Microdomain function: ER-GCaMP and mito-GCaMP or cepia under physiological burst firing; deconvolution to compute transfer gain and delay; mito-PercevalHR/ATeam for ATP; roGFP-Orp1/HyPer for ROS.
- Safety: Rhod-2/mitoRCaMP plateau levels; mPTP opening assay; cell viability and electrophysiology.
- sc/snRNA-seq: Differential expression of UPR (BiP/Grp78, Xbp1s), apoptosis (Bax/Bcl2), oxidative stress, and pain transduction genes.

Milestones
- M1 (months 0–9): Establish microdomain failure in diabetic DRG and rescue with rapalog tether; predefine overload thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3178184/?utm_source=openai))
- M2 (months 10–18): Optimize Ca2+-gated PDZD8 spacing and expression; demonstrate reversible, local rescue on-chip with no overload.
- M3 (months 19–30): In vivo efficacy and safety; prespecified success if ≥30% improvement in mechanical allodynia and ≥20% increase in nerve conduction with normalized microdomain metrics and no adverse snRNA-seq signatures.

Risks and alternatives
- If PDZD8 localization or function at MERCs in DRG is insufficient, use the validated rapalog tether for proof-of-concept efficacy and then translate to a minimalist, non-PDZD8 synthetic coiled-coil MERC bridge with the same Ca2+ gate.
- If Ca2+ gating is too permissive, raise thresholds via lower-affinity CaM mutants or local Ca2+ buffering domains.
- If MERC strengthening causes overload in a subset, combine with partial MCU inhibition titrated to preserve microdomain coupling without sustained matrix Ca2+. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8720329/?utm_source=openai))

Impact
This work converts a pathological Ca2+ signal into a self-limiting structural correction at ER–mitochondria interfaces in DRG neurons. It directly tests whether restoring microdomain coupling resolves the coupled energy and calcium failures that drive diabetic neuropathy, using a neuron-native tether (PDZD8) and stress-gated control absent from current therapies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5818999/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Extracellular vesicle microRNAs encode and sustain “pain memory” in diabetic neuropathy by reprogramming DRG neuron–satellite glia circuits

Hypothesis/goal (merged)
A transient hyperglycemic episode imprints a pro-nociceptive state in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and satellite glial cells (SGCs) that persists after normoglycemia (“metabolic/pain memory”). This imprint is written and maintained by extracellular vesicle (EV) microRNAs released primarily from vascular endothelium and DRG-infiltrating macrophages and taken up by DRG neurons/SGCs. Blocking EV-miRNA export or uptake after glycemic normalization will erase established pain, and a brief blockade during an early diabetic window will prevent chronic pain even if hyperglycemia continues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460341/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat EV-miRNA transfer as the minimal, transferable memory unit between non-neuronal compartments and DRG cells. Identify the specific EV-miRNA→mRNA network modules that show hysteresis after a glucose pulse and interrupt that single communication channel either at export, uptake, or the top 2–3 miRNA species.

Rationale and prior evidence
- Diabetic complications show persistent, epigenetically mediated “metabolic memory” after glycemic control, supporting the plausibility of a decoupled, self-sustaining state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460341/?utm_source=openai))
- EV-miRNAs modulate neuropathic pain and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) in preclinical models, and keratinocyte-derived exosomes are altered in painful DPN, consistent with skin-to-sensory neuron communication via EV cargo. However, whether EV-miRNAs sustain pain after normoglycemia has not been explicitly tested. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42095965/?utm_source=openai))
- DRG-origin EVs can drive pain phenotypes via miRNA cargo, and nerve injury increases EV-miRNA release from DRG cells, demonstrating both sufficiency and activity dependence of this channel in nociceptive circuits. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38750549/?utm_source=openai))
- DRG macrophages contribute to initiation and persistence of neuropathic pain, nominating them as a source of EVs that could reinforce a sensitized state locally. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6959328/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define EV-miRNA modules that convert transient hyperglycemia into stable pro-nociceptive states in DRG neurons/SGCs.
- Platform: A 4-compartment organ-on-a-chip linking mouse (or human iPSC-derived) vascular endothelium and macrophages to intact DRG neuron–SGC units with microfluidic EV-permeable barriers. Apply glucose pulses (e.g., 48 h at 25–30 mM) followed by normoglycemic media.
- Measurements:
  - Time-resolved EV quantification and small-RNA sequencing from the endothelial and macrophage compartments.
  - Parallel single-cell RNA-seq of DRG neurons and SGCs at baseline, pulse end, and post-normoglycemia (24 h, 7 d). Integrate EV-miRNA and target mRNA changes to build miRNA→mRNA regulatory maps.
  - Electrophysiology (rheobase, spontaneous firing) in small-diameter nociceptors and Ca2+ imaging to quantify excitability.
- Analysis:
  - Compute a decoupling index for each gene module and excitability metric: post-normoglycemia level divided by peak level during hyperglycemia. Prioritize miRNA–target modules with high decoupling indices and strong network centrality in nociceptors or SGCs.

Aim 2. Test necessity and reversibility: block EV-miRNA traffic after normoglycemia in diabetic mice.
- Model and normalization:
  - STZ-induced type 1 diabetes (or db/db type 2). At week 6, normalize glycemia to euglycemic ranges for 2–3 weeks via subcutaneous insulin pumps or SGLT2 inhibitor, while pain behaviors persist.
- Interventions (DRG-focused, non-Schwann):
  - Export blockade: inducible, cell type–specific Rab27a/b knockdown in vascular endothelium (Cdh5-CreERT2) and LysM-CreERT2 macrophages; or transient GW4869 delivery restricted to these compartments.
  - Uptake blockade: intrathecal phosphatidylserine masking with Annexin V–decorated nanoparticles designed to remain perisomatic around DRG neuronal somata; or short pulses of dynamin-dependent endocytosis inhibitors delivered intrathecally with pharmacokinetic profiling to limit exposure.
  - Cargo neutralization: DRG/SGC-targeted AAV9 expressing sponges/antimiRs for the 2–3 highest-priority EV-miRNAs identified in Aim 1 (e.g., let-7/miR-23 families if nominated by chip data).
- Outcomes:
  - Behavioral: von Frey, Hargreaves, cold plate before/after interventions.
  - Molecular: small-RNA-seq of DRG to confirm knockdown of target miRNAs; scRNA-seq to test collapse of the high-decoupling gene modules; histology for DRG macrophage burden.
  - Electrophysiology: reversal of hyperexcitability in nociceptors.
- Interpretation:
  - Rapid behavioral and molecular reversion after post-normoglycemia EV interruption indicates that EV-miRNAs are necessary to maintain the pain memory.

Aim 3. Test sufficiency and early-window prevention.
- Sufficiency:
  - Isolate EVs from hyperglycemia-exposed endothelial/macrophage cultures and inject intrathecally into naive mice; assess acute and persistent changes in DRG neuron/SGC states and pain behaviors. Deliver synthetic EVs carrying the top miRNAs to recapitulate effects.
- Early-window prevention (without normalizing glucose):
  - In new diabetic cohorts, apply transient (2–3 weeks) EV export blockade (endothelium/macrophage) or DRG uptake blockade restricted to the initial diabetic period. Maintain hyperglycemia otherwise. Assess whether chronic pain fails to develop, and whether “memory-indexed” modules remain low.
- Decision rule:
  - Prevention of chronic pain by early, time-limited EV intervention demonstrates a commitment window for EV-mediated pain memory formation.

Experimental details and controls
- Compartment specificity: Validate that interventions do not suppress Schwann cell EVs to honor the constraint; focus on vascular and immune compartments and on DRG neuron/SGC uptake.
- EV tracing: Use fluorescent barcoded EVs to quantify delivery to DRG neuronal somata and SGCs in vivo and on-chip.
- Off-target controls: Use scrambled anti-miRs, vehicle nanoparticles, and AAVs lacking sponges. Confirm normal motor function and general behavior to exclude nonspecific effects.
- Macrophage confounds: Distinguish EV effects from cytokine spillover by using EV-depleted conditioned media controls and protease treatment to remove surface-bound cytokines.

Primary endpoints and success criteria
- Aim 1: Identification of 2–3 EV-miRNAs whose targets show high decoupling indices in DRG neurons/SGCs and whose modulation shifts nociceptor excitability on-chip.
- Aim 2: Post-normoglycemia interventions reduce mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity by at least 50% versus control and collapse the nominated DRG gene modules toward baseline within 7–14 days.
- Aim 3: EVs from hyperglycemic sources reproduce pain phenotypes in naive mice, and transient early-window EV blockade prevents chronic pain development under sustained hyperglycemia.

Mechanistic falsification tests
- If EV export/uptake blockade fails to reverse pain post-normoglycemia, but cargo neutralization succeeds, the sustaining signal is likely miRNA-specific rather than EV quantity–dependent.
- If neither EV nor miRNA interventions alter the decoupling modules, the memory resides in cell-intrinsic chromatin states independent of ongoing intercellular transfer; re-scope to direct epigenetic erasure mechanisms.

Why this matters
- It reframes diabetic neuropathy as a communication-driven memory problem. The testable claim is that a minimal set of EV-miRNAs maintains a sensitized DRG neuron–SGC attractor after glucose normalizes, aligning with clinical observations that pain can persist despite euglycemia. This creates a finite, time-bounded therapeutic window for prevention and a tractable, molecularly precise erasure strategy for established pain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460341/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation relative to prior art
- Prior work implicates EV-miRNAs in neuropathic pain and DPN but has not explicitly tested post-normoglycemia maintenance or early-window prevention in neuron–SGC circuits, nor integrated small-RNA-seq with single-cell state hysteresis mapping to nominate causal miRNA→mRNA modules. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42095965/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risks
- EV manipulations and AAV-based sponges are established in pain models; organ-on-chip enables controlled, pulse–washout paradigms. Redundancy among miRNAs is a risk; mitigate by targeting convergent families and validating network-level collapse rather than single-node changes. DRG-intrinsic O-GlcNAc pathways will be monitored but not perturbed given essential roles in sensory neuron survival. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnmol.2025.1625943/full?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Redox-gated ketone delivery to dorsal root ganglia to prevent diabetic neuropathy without lowering glycemia

Rationale framed as inseparable question-hypothesis
Does hyperglycemia-driven redox stress in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and their endoneurial microvessels provide a selective chemical handle to uncage ketone fuel in situ, forcing substrate switching away from glycolysis and protecting axons despite persistent high blood glucose? DRG mitochondria exhibit redox overload and ROS generation in diabetes; endoneurial microvessels develop barrier dysfunction and hypoxic stress, amplifying neuronal oxidative injury. If a therapy uses the very redox stress to gate local β‑hydroxybutyrate (BHB) release, then mass action plus intact ketolysis in DRG should stabilize ATP supply, reduce ROS, and halt neuropathy progression without changing glycemia. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13162866/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit the pathological ROS/peroxynitrite excess in the DRG neurovascular unit as the trigger to uncage a BHB prodrug only where and when redox stress is high, thereby enforcing ketone utilization and relieving glycolytic/PDH pressure in diabetic nerves. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer and validate ROS-activated BHB prodrugs.
- Design: BHB masked by arylboronate or thioketal linkers that cleave in response to H2O2/peroxynitrite or mixed ROS, yielding free BHB and benign fragments. Synthesize two chemotypes (boronate–self‑immolative carbonate; thioketal–carbonate) with tunable oxidation thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro chemistry: Determine second-order rate constants for uncaging with H2O2 and peroxynitrite; quantify BHB release by LC–MS. Establish stability in plasma and CSF mimics.
- Cell assays: In primary mouse DRG neurons and human iPSC-derived sensory neurons exposed to high glucose (25–30 mM), quantify uncaging using ROS reporters and extracellular BHB sensors; readouts: mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX), NADH/NAD+ (Peredox), ATP (ATeam), oxygen consumption/RCR (Seahorse). Compare prodrug vs equimolar BHB or non-ROS–cleavable analog. Expect preferential BHB liberation and reduced ROS at matched ATP versus free BHB, owing to higher local concentration near stressed mitochondria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7422494/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Recreate the DRG neurovascular microenvironment on-chip and test redox-gated ketone delivery.
- Model: A compartmentalized DRG–endoneurial microvessel organ-on-a-chip consisting of mouse or human DRG neurons plus primary human endoneurial endothelial cells forming a perfused barrier that models the blood–nerve barrier (BNB). Induce “diabetic” conditions (hyperglycemia ± cytokines) to reproduce endothelial dysfunction and redox stress. Endpoints: barrier permeability (dextran flux), endothelial ROS, and neuronal excitability/axon integrity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20010300/?utm_source=openai))
- Intervention: Perfuse prodrugs luminally. Map uncaging and BHB gradients across endothelium into the ganglionic compartment; assess neuronal metabolic switching (decreased glycolytic flux proxies, increased ketolytic flux), axonal preservation, and firing thresholds. Expect selective uncaging under redox stress with improved neuronal bioenergetics and structure without altering perfusate glucose. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6339909/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test efficacy in diabetic mice without altering glycemia.
- Models: STZ (type 1–like) and db/db (type 2–like). Maintain hyperglycemia; deliver prodrug intrathecally or perineurally to lumbar DRGs at doses achieving sub-millimolar local BHB after uncaging. Outcomes: mechanical and thermal thresholds, nerve conduction velocity, intraepidermal nerve fiber density, DRG mitochondrial function (complex I/IV activity, mtDNA copy), and oxidative adducts. Monitor plasma glucose/ketones to verify glycemia-independent protection. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/ilarjournal/article/54/3/259/687329?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism confirmation: DRG metabolomics and scRNA-seq for ketolytic genes; inhibition studies with MCT blocker (control for transport). Given that DRG neurons broadly express OXCT1/SCOT and that MCT1 is present in DRG, protection should depend on intact ketone transport/ketolysis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9882096/?utm_source=openai))

Design choices justified by biology
- Target tissue: DRG is outside the BBB with fenestrated capillaries, enabling small-molecule access; in diabetes, endoneurial microvessels show basement membrane thickening, pericyte loss, and reduced luminal area, contributing to hypoxia and ROS—ideal for redox-triggered release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6598622/?utm_source=openai))
- Fuel pathway capacity: Single‑cell and bulk data show near-ubiquitous OXCT1 in DRG neurons, supporting ketolysis; thus, local BHB availability—not absence of pathway—is the limiting step under high glucose. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9882096/?utm_source=openai))
- Energetics: BHB oxidation can support neuronal ATP while decreasing net ROS generation relative to high glycolytic/PDH flux, improving redox poise. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27826689/?utm_source=openai))
- Trigger chemistry: Arylboronates and thioketals enable selective, bioorthogonal uncaging by pathological ROS/peroxynitrite; these motifs have been validated across neuro and vascular delivery contexts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))

Key experiments and readouts
- Uncaging specificity window: Determine minimal ROS needed for half‑maximal release and compare to ROS measured in diabetic DRG and endothelium on-chip. Target release at pathological but not physiological ROS.
- Metabolic rerouting: In neurons, show reduced PDH flux proxy (PDH‑E1 phosphorylation), increased TCA acetyl‑CoA labeling from [U‑13C]BHB, and stable ATP/Δψm with lower MitoSOX.
- Neuroprotection: Preservation of IENF and conduction velocity with unchanged HbA1c; histology for axonal swellings and DRG neuronal soma size; behavioral improvement without systemic ketosis.

Falsification and decision thresholds
- Falsify if prodrug fails to uncage selectively under diabetic redox conditions on-chip, or if neuronal ROS and injury markers are not reduced relative to equimolar free BHB at matched glycemia. Stop if in vivo efficacy correlates with systemic ketosis (plasma BHB ≥1 mM), indicating loss of selectivity.

Risk mitigation
- If endogenous ketolysis proves insufficient in late disease, a contingency sub‑study will add DRG-targeted AAV to modestly boost BDH1/OXCT1 under a sensory neuron promoter (Advillin) without affecting Schwann cells; this preserves the same redox‑gated substrate supply as the primary lever. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5459312/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target release: Use higher-oxidation‑threshold linkers and pegylation to reduce background uncaging; perform biodistribution and hematology panels.

Milestones
- Year 1: Synthesize/benchmark prodrugs; demonstrate selective uncaging and metabolic benefit in DRG neurons in high glucose.
- Year 2: Validate efficacy and mechanism in DRG–BNB chip; finalize PK/PD and dosing.
- Year 3: Demonstrate glycemia‑independent neuroprotection in STZ and db/db mice; complete safety pharmacology.

Anticipated impact
This work reframes hyperglycemic redox stress from a liability into a targeting signal, enforcing local ketone use where injury originates. It complements dietary ketosis by delivering fuel only to stressed DRG neurovascular units, aiming for disease modification without systemic fasting mimetics or glycemic change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10067134/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Demand-gated, adenosine-sensing immunoreprogramming at the metabolic–epidermal interface to treat obesity-associated psoriasis

Central hypothesis and integrated research question
Excess extracellular adenosine generated by hypoxia/metabolic stress in obese tissue and inflamed skin can be repurposed as an endogenous gate to localize and self-limit delivery of keratinocyte-targeted immunoreprogramming agents. Does an intradermally placed, adenosine-aptamer–gated hydrogel that releases an A2B receptor antagonist only when adenosine is pathologically elevated reprogram keratinocyte–immune signaling and attenuate psoriasiform inflammation preferentially in obese/high-adenosine skin? Extracellular adenosine accumulates under metabolic stress and hypoxia typical of obese adipose and inflamed tissues, and keratinocytes prominently signal via A2B receptors that drive IL-6 and proinflammatory programs; therefore, adenosine is both a disease-coupled cue and a mechanistic lever for site- and state-specific intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert metabolite overload into a brake: use adenosine itself as the gating signal for a depot that (i) opens to release an A2B antagonist when adenosine is high and (ii) passively re-sequesters adenosine as levels fall, closing release. This single control principle directly ties therapeutic flux to a core metabolic abnormality without continuous external control. Adenosine-aptamer hydrogels and phenylboronic-acid (PBA) materials already demonstrate adenosine-responsive dissolution/release and in vivo adenosine binding, enabling rapid translation to skin. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and calibrate an intradermal, adenosine-gated depot that self-limits payload release.
- Construct PEG-based microgels crosslinked with adenosine aptamer duplexes that dissociate upon adenosine binding to increase mesh size and release small-molecule payload; co-display PBA moieties to reversibly bind cis-diols on adenosine, providing sequestration and hysteresis so that release closes as adenosine normalizes. Tune aptamer sequence density and PBA:aptamer ratios to set opening thresholds within 1–100 μM adenosine, a pathophysiological range. Readouts: adenosine-titrated swelling, diffusion coefficients, and release kinetics for model fluorophores and the drug. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))
- Select payload: a selective A2B antagonist (e.g., MRS1754 or PSB-603) to blunt adenosine–A2B–EGFR–IL-6 signaling in keratinocytes. Validate target engagement in HaCaT and primary human keratinocytes by measuring IL-6 after adenosine challenge ± antagonist. ([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpbreports/4/2/4_64/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 1):
- Microgel synthesis and characterization; thresholded release profile established; antagonist retains activity post-encapsulation.

Aim 2. Demonstrate keratinocyte and epidermal–immune reprogramming under obese-mimetic metabolic stress in vitro.
- Culture keratinocytes under hypoxia (1–3% O2) and with adipocyte-conditioned media to model obese microenvironments; quantify extracellular adenosine. Assess whether gated release reduces IL-6, CXCL8, CCL20, and dampens NF-κB/EGFR transactivation compared to ungated delivery at equal total dose. Co-culture with human PBMCs or IL-17–competent T cells to test reduction in Th17-skewing cues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- System-level validation on-chip: couple a human WAT-on-chip that recapitulates immune-competent adipose to a keratinocyte/fibroblast skin-on-chip via microfluidic perfusion. Induce adipose hypoxia/inflammation to elevate adenosine in the shared medium; test whether intraluminally placed microgels gate payload delivery and normalize keratinocyte cytokines and barrier readouts (TEER, stratification markers) only under high-adenosine flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 2):
- Dose–response curves demonstrating adenosine-thresholded suppression of keratinocyte IL-6; reduced Th17-skewing in co-culture; on-chip demonstration of state-specific gating.

Aim 3. Establish efficacy and selectivity in vivo with metabolic context.
- Use imiquimod-induced psoriasiform dermatitis in high-fat diet (HFD) mice versus lean controls to generate differential interstitial adenosine. Administer aptamer–PBA microgels by shallow intradermal microinjection within lesional skin. Endpoints (day 5–7): epidermal thickness, Munro microabscesses, Ly6G+ neutrophils, and lesional transcripts (Il6, Cxcl1/Cxcl2, Il17a, Il23a). Compare gated microgels, scrambled-aptamer microgels, and free antagonist. Expect stronger efficacy and lower off-target suppression in HFD mice due to higher adenosine-driven gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism control: topical/intradermal adenosine challenge to force gate opening in lean mice; blockade reversal with an A2B agonist to confirm pathway positioning. Keratinocyte-favored readouts supported by known A2B expression and function. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (month 3):
- Significant improvement of psoriasiform endpoints in HFD mice with gated depot versus controls; pharmacodynamic evidence of localized A2B pathway modulation.

Experimental details and feasibility
- Materials: Adenosine aptamer sequences and hydrogel chemistries are published; adenosine-responsive dissolution and release have been shown; PBA scaffolds sequester adenosine in vivo. Synthesis and tuning can be completed rapidly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))
- Biology: Keratinocyte A2B signaling drives IL-6; extracellular adenosine rises with hypoxia/metabolic stress in obese tissue; these provide both mechanism and disease-coupled cue. ([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/bpbreports/4/2/4_64/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai))
- Platforms: Immunocompetent WAT-on-chip and skin-on-chip systems support adipose–epidermis crosstalk modeling and compound testing within the project window. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9218765/?utm_source=openai))

Primary outcomes and decision points
- Outcome 1: Steep, programmable release versus adenosine concentration with built-in hysteresis (aptamer opening, PBA rebinding). Go if release ratio (pathological:physiological adenosine) ≥5 and payload remains potent.
- Outcome 2: Suppression of keratinocyte IL-6 and Th17-skewing only under high adenosine; proceed to in vivo if ≥50% reduction versus scrambled/ungated controls at equal total drug.
- Outcome 3: In vivo efficacy in HFD mice exceeding lean mice for the same total dose indicates successful demand-gating; if not, retune aptamer density or switch payload to an A2A positive allosteric modulator to bias toward immunoregulation while maintaining adenosine-gated delivery. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and contingencies
- If adenosine levels in lesional skin are insufficient for robust gating, pre-enrich local adenosine transiently using low-dose ecto-5′-nucleotidase substrate pulses in a small area to test principle, or increase aptamer affinity via multimerization. Evidence supports adenosine surges with tissue stress, but thresholds must be empirically mapped. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11892559/?utm_source=openai))
- If A2B antagonism alone is inadequate, swap or add a low-dose A2A agonist payload within the same gate to reinforce anti-inflammatory cAMP/PKA signaling in keratinocytes and resident immune cells. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022202X15356773?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and impact
This proposal re-architects control at the metabolic–epidermal interface by making a pathologic metabolite the real-time governor of immunoreprogramming, rather than merely a target to block. Prior art demonstrates adenosine-responsive hydrogels and in vivo adenosine-binding biomaterials, but they have not been applied to obesity-associated psoriatic inflammation or to enforce state-specific A2B pathway reprogramming in keratinocytes. If successful, this establishes a generalizable, demand-gated therapeutic paradigm for metabolically amplified skin inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757630/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Skin-first neuromodulation to normalize systemic metabolism in obesity-associated psoriasis

Integrated hypothesis–question
Does selectively collapsing nociceptor–CGRP output from psoriatic skin lower the exported signal burden that surpasses systemic disruption thresholds, thereby normalizing insulin action and lipid homeostasis in obese hosts? If yes, can we map the minimal cutaneous “setpoint” of exported factors required to restore whole-body metabolic tone? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
A single lever at the metabolic–epidermal interface: skin-restricted suppression of sensory neuron CGRP signaling at psoriatic plaques reduces IL-23/Th17 drive and collapses outbound endocrine traffic (cytokines and EV-miRNAs) below a causal threshold for systemic insulin resistance. We quantify and enforce this threshold using gradient-inversion microphysiology to define directionality and minimal effective cutaneous suppression before translation to mice. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))

Background and gap
- Psoriatic skin inflammation—especially when induced by TLR7 activation—can provoke systemic glucose intolerance and a pre-diabetic phenotype via endocrine actions of the skin secretome. Treating skin can improve metabolic readouts in some settings, but precise, skin-initiated causal levers and thresholds are undefined. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- TRPV1+ cutaneous nociceptors drive IL-23 production from dermal dendritic cells and amplify IL-23/IL-17 signaling; neuromodulation (including RTX-mediated neuron ablation) reduces this axis in the imiquimod model. Whether skin-local CGRP pathway suppression alone can restore systemic insulin action in obesity-associated psoriasis has not been directly tested. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))
- CGRP influences adipose metabolism and whole-body insulin sensitivity in obesity, yet prior work focuses on global or adipose-centric actions, not plaque-local cutaneous modulation as a metabolic therapy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13256775/?utm_source=openai))
- Keratinocyte-derived EV miRNAs (including miR-21/miR-155) are altered in psoriasis and circulate as potential effectors; their role as exported metabolic disruptors remains underexplored compared with adipose/liver EVs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define the outbound skin-to-metabolic organ signal threshold and dependence on CGRP using a gradient-inversion skin–adipose/liver microphysiological system.
Aim 2. Test whether plaque-restricted CGRP pathway suppression rescues systemic insulin sensitivity and lipid homeostasis in obese psoriasiform mice.
Exploratory Aim 3. Determine whether plaque therapy secondarily rewires circulating EV-miRNA cargo (miR-21/miR-155/miR-146a) and whether epidermal anti–miR delivery adds benefit.

Models
- Human skin–metabolic organ-on-a-chip (psoriatic equivalent ± TLR7 activation) linked to human adipocyte and hepatocyte microtissues (primary or iPSC-derived).
- Diet-induced obese (DIO) C57BL/6 mice with imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform dermatitis (back/ear). This model exhibits systemic metabolic disruption attributable to the skin secretome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 1. Gradient-inversion mapping of actionable exported signals and setpoints
Rationale: If cutaneous outputs causally drive systemic insulin resistance, then during disease they form a directional gradient from skin→receiver tissues that collapses when the driver (skin CGRP) is suppressed. Establishing the minimal “skin-output setpoint” that restores downstream insulin signaling derisks translation.

Design
- Build a tri-compartment chip: (i) human psoriatic skin equivalent (keratinocytes + dermal fibroblasts + myeloid cells ± TRPV1+ sensory neurite co-culture); (ii) adipocyte or hepatocyte chamber; (iii) microfluidic channel with switchable flow.
- Induce psoriasiform state by topical IMQ or IL-23/IL-17A; record baseline exported factors with flow skin→metabolic organ, then invert to metabolic organ→skin.
- Intervene at the skin side with: (a) CGRP pathway suppression—CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) or CGRP-neutralizing antibody applied only to the skin chamber; (b) vehicle control.
- Readouts:
  - Directional flux: CGRP/SP, IL-6, IL-17A, IL-23 in effluents; EV counts (CD63+), EV-miRNA cargo (miR-21/miR-155/miR-146a).
  - Receiver function: insulin-stimulated pAKT in adipocytes; hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3 and insulin signaling; NF-κB reporters in macrophage co-cultures.
  - Thresholding: titrate skin-side neuromodulation intensity to define minimal reduction in exported signals that restores receiver insulin signaling ≥80% of control.
Success criteria: Demonstration that (i) disease-state export is directional (skin→receiver) and (ii) skin-side CGRP suppression collapses one or more exported factors below a quantifiable threshold that normalizes insulin signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Skin-restricted CGRP pathway suppression normalizes systemic metabolism in obese psoriasiform mice
Rationale: IMQ-induced psoriatic skin disrupts glucose homeostasis; TRPV1+ nociceptors and CGRP drive lesional IL-23/Th17. We test whether local CGRP suppression at plaques in DIO mice improves whole-body insulin sensitivity and lipid handling without systemic immunosuppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Design
- Cohorts: Male and female DIO mice (16–20 weeks on HFD). Randomize to IMQ or vehicle on shaved back skin for 5–7 days to induce psoriasiform dermatitis and metabolic stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- Interventions (plaque-restricted, contralateral vehicle control):
  1) Resiniferatoxin (RTX) microinjection into plaques (TRPV1+ nociceptor desensitization), schedule day 0 and day 3. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7583491/?utm_source=openai))
  2) CGRP receptor antagonist formulated for intradermal delivery (gepant hydrogel), daily topical/ID at plaques for 5–7 days; pharmacodynamic confirmation by lesional microdialysate CGRP reduction.
- Primary systemic endpoints (days 5–10):
  - Glucose tolerance test (GTT), insulin tolerance test (ITT); fasting insulin and HOMA-IR; hepatic triglycerides; serum triglycerides/HDL/LDL.
  - Tissue signaling: insulin-stimulated pAKT in epididymal fat and liver; hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15845623/?utm_source=openai))
- Skin and circulating endpoints:
  - Lesional IL-23/IL-17A and dendritic-cell activation; microdialysate CGRP/SP; EV abundance and EV-miRNA (miR-21/155/146a) in plasma.
Expected outcome: Local CGRP pathway suppression reduces lesional IL-23/Th17, collapses exported cytokine/EV gradients, and improves GTT/ITT and hepatic insulin signaling in DIO+IMQ mice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory Aim 3. Epidermal EV-miRNA editing as a downstream amplifier
Rationale: Psoriatic keratinocytes contribute to circulating EV-miRNAs, with miR-21/miR-155 upregulated; exosomal miRNAs can remodel insulin action in distal tissues in metabolic disease. If plaque neuromodulation only partially normalizes EV cargo, add epidermal anti–miR-21/miR-155 (LNA) via microneedles to test incremental systemic benefit. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Design
- Apply anti–miR-21/miR-155 locally to plaques (± neuromodulation). Quantify plasma EV-miRNA shifts and systemic insulin signaling as in Aim 2.
- Expected readout: Additional decrease in plasma EV miR-21/155 and increased miR-146a, correlating with improved insulin action.

Key controls and analyses
- Side-by-side lesional vs non-lesional skin treatment within the same animal to prove site specificity.
- Non-IMQ DIO controls to ensure effects require active psoriatic inflammation.
- Power calculations: n≥10 per group for 80% power to detect 20% change in AUC-GTT (alpha 0.05).
- Statistics: Mixed-effects models for repeated measures; ANCOVA for tissue signaling with lesion severity as covariate.

Milestones and 12-week timeline
- Weeks 0–3: Build/validate gradient-inversion chip; calibrate assays; complete Aim 1 threshold maps and identify minimal CGRP suppression needed.
- Weeks 3–10: Execute DIO+IMQ cohorts with RTX and gepant-ID arms; complete metabolic tests and tissue signaling.
- Weeks 8–12: Exploratory anti–miR add-on; integrate EV-miRNA analytics; finalize data synthesis.

Readouts anchoring causality
- Directionality and threshold: outbound factor gradients that invert/flatten with skin therapy (Aim 1).
- Necessity and sufficiency: local CGRP suppression reduces lesional IL-23/Th17 and rescues systemic insulin signaling (Aim 2). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24759321/?utm_source=openai))
- Generalizability: improvement observed with two distinct skin-restricted neuromodulatory modalities (RTX vs gepant).

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Risk: Gepant dermal delivery insufficient. Mitigation: prioritize RTX intervention (established in IMQ), and/or use CGRP-neutralizing antibody intradermally. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7583491/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: IL-6/STAT3 hepatic responses can be context dependent. Mitigation: prespecify hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3 and insulin-stimulated pAKT as orthogonal endpoints; incorporate adipose insulin signaling and macrophage polarization to avoid overreliance on a single hepatic pathway. ([journal-of-hepatology.eu](https://www.journal-of-hepatology.eu/article/s0168-8278%2816%2900083-0/fulltext?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: EV-miRNA shifts are modest. Mitigation: treat EV-miRNA as mechanistic secondary; focus success criteria on metabolic and signaling endpoints.

Innovation
- Skin-first neuromodulation as metabolic therapy: leverages a local neuroimmune circuit (CGRP→IL-23/Th17) to reprogram systemic insulin action in obesity-associated psoriasis. Prior CGRP–metabolism links exist, but not via plaque-restricted intervention to treat systemic metabolism. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13256775/?utm_source=openai))
- Gradient-inversion mapping to define causal, exported skin effectors and actionable thresholds before in vivo testing, reducing complexity and failure modes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- EV-miRNA reprogramming as a downstream amplifier tied to observed circulating changes in psoriasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Decision points and success criteria
- Aim 1 Go/No-Go: Demonstrate a directional export of at least one factor (CGRP/IL-6/EV-miRNA) that, when reduced by skin-side CGRP suppression, restores insulin signaling in receiver tissues on-chip by ≥80%.
- Aim 2 Success: In DIO+IMQ mice, plaque-limited CGRP suppression improves AUC-GTT and ITT by ≥20%, increases insulin-stimulated pAKT in adipose and liver by ≥30%, and reduces hepatic pSTAT3/SOCS3, with concordant decreases in lesional IL-23/IL-17A and microdialysate CGRP/SP. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))
- Exploratory success: Plasma EV miR-21/155 decrease correlates with improved systemic insulin signaling; local anti–miR adds incremental benefit over neuromodulation alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11140073/?utm_source=openai))

Impact
Validating a skin-origin metabolic setpoint and demonstrating that plaque-restricted neuromodulation normalizes systemic insulin action would establish a bidirectional skin–metabolic organ axis that is therapeutically targetable without systemic immunosuppression. This reorients psoriasis comorbidity management from “treat body to fix skin” toward “treat skin to fix body,” with immediate translational paths via local neuromodulators and topical nucleic-acid therapeutics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7452265/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Phage-RBP-patterned GelMA/alginate hydrogel on titanium to selectively seed Lactobacillus and prevent early Staphylococcus biofilm formation: a 3‑month proof-of-concept

Hypothesis-question
Can a titanium coating composed of an antifouling GelMA/alginate hydrogel that presents immobilized receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) from Lactobacillus phages selectively capture and stabilize viable Lactobacillus at first contact strongly enough to (i) outcompete S. aureus/S. epidermidis for surface real estate and (ii) suppress their transition to PNAG/PIA-dependent biofilms? The premise is that RBPs evolved to bind strain-specific cell-wall glycopolymers (e.g., wall/lipoteichoic acid or CWPS) with high avidity; immobilizing them in a soft hydrogel should raise the on-rate and lower the off-rate for the intended probiotic while the hydrogel’s PEG-like hydration layer keeps staphylococci in the reversible-adhesion regime. If this early kinetic bias holds, established Lactobacillus metabolism (organic acids, H2O2, bacteriocins) will further depress staphylococcal attachment and biofilm maturation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4033162/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use host-range-defined phage RBPs as non-lytic, species-specific adhesion ligands to convert an antifouling hydrogel-coated titanium surface from “generically repellent” into a “Lactobacillus-selective capture” interface at the very first attachment step. This single substitution (RBP arrays in place of generic binders) is the minimal, system-level perturbation that can flip the early adhesion kinetics without making the surface attractive to staphylococci. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11732128/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims (3 months, benchtop PoC)
- Aim 1. Build and validate RBP-patterned antifouling hydrogels on titanium.
- Aim 2. Quantify selective capture and viability of Lactobacillus versus S. aureus/S. epidermidis.
- Aim 3. Test whether pre-seeded Lactobacillus suppresses staphylococcal attachment and early biofilm formation on the coated titanium.

Materials and design
- Substrate and antifouling backbone: Titanium discs (orthopedic grade). Prime with polydopamine (PDA) to anchor polymer; cast a thin GelMA/alginate hydrogel (photocrosslinked GelMA; Ca2+ crosslinked alginate). Blend a PEGylated/zwitterionic fraction to minimize nonspecific protein/bacterial fouling. Rationale: PDA provides robust adhesion to Ti; PEG/zwitterions on Ti reduce fibrinogen/fibronectin adsorption and S. aureus attachment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533074/?utm_source=openai))
- Capture ligands: Recombinant distal carbohydrate-binding modules from Lactobacillus phage RBPs (e.g., J‑1 Dit/RBP modules) engineered with AviTag/His-tag for oriented immobilization and optional trimerization to increase avidity; site-specifically biotinylated and attached via streptavidin embedded in the hydrogel. Mechanistic basis: LAB phage RBPs recognize strain-specific cell-wall saccharides/teichoic acids; multivalent presentation on soft hydrogels increases effective affinity and preserves cell viability, as shown for other phage RBPs/tail fibers used to capture live bacteria. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28196397/?utm_source=openai))
- Bacteria: Target probiotic, Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and/or Lactobacillus plantarum; pathogen controls, S. aureus (including MRSA lab strain) and S. epidermidis. Note: Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium can form biofilms on abiotic surfaces under laboratory conditions, enabling in vitro assessment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8304991/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty statement (checked)
Phage RBPs have been immobilized to capture and detect pathogens (e.g., Salmonella, Listeria) and whole phages have been oriented on sensors, but we find no reports using RBPs to selectively seed beneficial probiotics on titanium implant-relevant hydrogels to preempt staphylococcal biofilms. This proposal repurposes RBPs from diagnostic capture elements into probiotic colonization ligands on antifouling orthopedic coatings. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5452813/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1. Coating fabrication and surface analytics (Weeks 1–3)
- Titanium prep: Solvent clean, oxygen plasma, PDA deposition (10 mM Tris, pH 8.5), rinse/dry. Cast 20–50 μm GelMA/alginate layer (e.g., 5–10% GelMA with LAP photoinitiator; 1–2% alginate; brief CaCl2 exposure). Incorporate 2–5% w/w PEG-methacrylate or zwitterionic comonomer to strengthen antifouling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10217943/?utm_source=openai))
- Ligand immobilization: Embed streptavidin (or biotin-binding protein) during gelation; then couple biotinylated RBPs. Quantify ligand density by fluorimetric calibration using labeled RBPs.
- Characterization: Contact angle, XPS/FTIR, gel thickness (ellipsometry/profilometry), swelling ratio, QCM-D to confirm low fibrinogen adsorption versus Ti and Ti+hydrogel controls; bacterial nonspecific adhesion screens with S. aureus under static exposure to confirm antifouling baseline. Success criteria: ≥80% reduction of fibrinogen adsorption and S. aureus attachment versus bare Ti. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3777270/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Selective capture and viability (Weeks 3–6)
- Static and flow adhesion assays: Expose coated discs to L. rhamnosus GG at 10^6–10^8 CFU/mL in PBS+0.5% MRS under gentle shear (parallel plate flow, 1–10 dyn/cm^2) for 10–30 min; wash; enumerate adherent cells by CFU (sonication recovery) and confocal imaging. Controls: (i) hydrogel without RBP, (ii) hydrogel with noncognate RBP (e.g., Salmonella S16 LTF), (iii) hydrogel with streptavidin only. Expectation: ≥10× capture enrichment on RBP surfaces vs controls with retained viability of captured cells, consistent with prior RBP-based capture systems. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5452813/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity panel: Challenge RBP surfaces with S. aureus and S. epidermidis at 10^7 CFU/mL in PBS; quantify binding. Acceptance: ≤10% of Lactobacillus capture signal for either staphylococcal species, consistent with disparate wall glycopolymers not recognized by Lactobacillus phage RBPs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4033162/?utm_source=openai))
- Live/dead and retention: Track captured Lactobacillus for 24–48 h in diluted MRS at 37°C; measure lactate accumulation and local pH near-surface; verify growth/viability and lack of cytotoxic effect from the coating. Background: Lactobacillus secreted acids/H2O2/bacteriocins are expected as they proliferate on abiotic surfaces in vitro. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10139968/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Competitive colonization and early staphylococcal biofilm suppression (Weeks 6–12)
- Head-to-head attachment: In a flow cell, introduce a 1:1 or 10:1 mixture of Lactobacillus:S. aureus (or S. epidermidis) over (i) RBP-hydrogel and (ii) antifouling-hydrogel without RBP; quantify adherent fractions at 30–60 min and 4 h by species-specific qPCR and microscopy. Success: RBP-hydrogel shows ≥80% Lactobacillus occupancy with ≥75% reduction in staphylococcal counts versus non-RBP hydrogel at matched conditions. Mechanistic comparator: On ordinary Ti, staphylococci exploit adsorbed host proteins via MSCRAMMs; antifouling blocks this, but without a selective capture, probiotics lack a kinetic edge. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3777270/?utm_source=openai))
- Biofilm challenge after probiotic seeding: Pre-seed RBP-hydrogel with Lactobacillus for 6–24 h; then challenge with S. aureus/S. epidermidis in TSB under low shear for 24–48 h. Quantify staphylococcal biomass (crystal violet), PNAG/PIA staining, CFU, and CLSM thickness. Acceptance: ≥1–2 log reduction in staphylococcal CFU and ≥70% reduction in PNAG-positive matrix relative to (a) unseeded RBP-hydrogel and (b) PEG-only antifouling hydrogel. Rationale: Once established, Lactobacillus antimicrobial outputs and niche occupation are expected to inhibit staphylococcal adhesion and matrix elaboration. ([spj.science.org](https://spj.science.org/doi/10.1016/j.csbj.2020.10.027?utm_source=openai))

Controls and comparators
- Surface controls: Bare Ti; PDA-only; hydrogel-only; hydrogel+streptavidin without RBP; hydrogel+noncognate RBP.
- Biological controls: Heat-killed Lactobacillus (tests requirement for viability); pre-neutralized spent medium from Lactobacillus (separates contact-dependent from diffusible effects).
- Optional comparator: A mucin-binding protein (MUB) fragment surface to benchmark capture efficiency versus RBP; not required for the hypothesis.

Readouts and statistics
- Surface analytics: Protein adsorption by QCM-D; contact angle; XPS elemental ratios.
- Microbiology: CFU recovery; species-specific qPCR; confocal microscopy with dual stains; PNAG immunostaining.
- Metrics: Capture yield (CFU/cm^2), selectivity index (Lactobacillus:Staphylococcus adhesion ratio), retained viability (% live cells at 24 h), staphylococcal biomass/PNAG area fraction.
- Statistics: n≥3 discs/condition; two-sided tests with correction for multiple comparisons.

Risks and mitigations
- RBP–host mismatch: Screen 2–3 Lactobacillus RBPs targeting different glycan epitopes; if capture is weak, increase ligand density or switch to trimerized formats; as fallback, test a MUB-derived ligand to establish upper-bound capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4033162/?utm_source=openai))
- Loss of antifouling due to ligand crowding: Titrate RBP surface density; maintain PEG/zwitterion fraction to preserve low nonspecific adsorption demonstrated on Ti. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8988846/?utm_source=openai))
- Viability on surface: Prior bead-based RBP capture kept cells viable; confirm minimal shear and nutrient access in flow assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5452813/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (by Week)
- 1–2: Clone/express/biotinylate RBPs; fabricate PDA–GelMA/alginate–PEG coatings; baseline antifouling confirmed.
- 3–4: Achieve ≥10× Lactobacillus capture over controls with ≥80% viability at 24 h.
- 5–8: Demonstrate ≤10% staphylococcal nonspecific binding to RBP surfaces; complete competition assays showing ≥75% reduction of staphylococcal occupancy versus non-RBP hydrogel.
- 9–12: Probiotic pre-seeding yields ≥1–2 log reduction in staphylococcal CFU and PNAG area; deliver full dataset.

Why this should work now
- Early adhesion bottleneck: Staphylococci rapidly exploit host-protein conditioning via MSCRAMMs; antifouling PEG layers can blunt this, but then no microbe has an advantage. RBPs add an evolved, saccharide-specific capture layer for Lactobacillus, biasing first contact. LAB phage RBPs recognize teichoic/CWPS motifs with high specificity; when immobilized, RBPs and tail fibers capture live hosts across pH/salt ranges while preserving viability. Lactobacillus metabolism then imposes colonization resistance via acids/H2O2/bacteriocins, suppressing PNAG/PIA biofilm maturation. Each component is independently evidenced; their combination on titanium hydrogels has not been reported. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23564165/?utm_source=openai))

Regulatory and biosafety
BSL‑2 handling for staphylococci; standard chemical safety for PDA, photoinitiators, and crosslinkers. No in vivo work in this PoC.

References (representative)
- Staphylococcal adhesion/biofilm: MSCRAMMs, PNAG/PIA and icaADBC; antifouling PEG on Ti. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23564165/?utm_source=openai))
- LAB antimicrobial outputs and anti-biofilm effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13362303/?utm_source=openai))
- Phage RBPs recognize LAB glycopolymers; immobilized RBPs/tail fibers capture viable bacteria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4033162/?utm_source=openai))
- PDA anchoring and hydrogel/Ti coatings for antifouling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6533074/?utm_source=openai))
