text:
Title
Sparse, phase-targeted electrical nudges at separatrix crossings to bidirectionally control human sleep depth

Background and rationale
- NREM slow oscillations (<1 Hz) reflect alternating cortical UP (depolarized) and DOWN (hyperpolarized/silent) states, coordinated with thalamocortical dynamics and expressed as traveling waves across cortex; neuromodulatory tone biases the system between desynchronized wake and synchronized NREM modes. These dynamics exhibit multistability/metastability, with transitions that can be precipitated by brief perturbations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4712264/?utm_source=openai))
- Closed-loop, phase-targeted stimulation can modulate brain rhythms: auditory pulses at the slow-wave UP phase boost slow-wave activity and spindle coupling; closed-loop tES/tACS has also been used to align stimulation to endogenous sleep slow waves. However, low‑frequency tES entrainment during sleep is debated based on intracranial recordings, motivating strategies that exploit timing rather than forceful continuous drive. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
- Traveling‑wave tACS using phase‑shifted multielectrode drive can impose spatial phase gradients in humans and nonhuman primates, offering a handle on network propagation with low currents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13167727/?utm_source=openai))
- Real‑time phase estimation with Kalman‑filter approaches has been demonstrated for closed‑loop EEG stimulation, establishing feasibility for predictive, low‑latency interventions. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Can brief, sub‑threshold, closed‑loop electrical nudges delivered at predicted separatrix crossings of the cortical slow oscillation bidirectionally shift global brain state—toward deeper NREM (sleep induction) or toward desynchrony (wake promotion)—more efficiently and safely than continuous entrainment?

Atomic strategy
Exploit metastability: identify imminent UP→DOWN or DOWN→UP transitions with a predictive state estimator and deliver millisecond‑timed, low‑dose electrical pulses that respectively increase or decrease the probability of the transition completing, thus flipping the network between slow‑wave–dominated and desynchronized regimes. PRC theory and empirical phase‑resetting results justify strong phase dependence; traveling‑wave field patterns refine which subnetworks participate without higher currents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4079848/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and validate a real‑time estimator of slow‑wave phase, amplitude, traveling‑wave direction, and a latent arousal state from frontal EEG, using an extended Kalman filter with artifact-aware updates. Benchmark phase prediction error and transition‑timing forecasts against polysomnography labels. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))
2) Sleep induction: test whether late‑UP–timed, 100–200 ms sub‑Hz pulse bursts increase DOWN‑state probability, amplify slow‑wave activity (SWA), and reduce sleep latency relative to sham and continuous tACS. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
3) Wake promotion: test whether early‑DOWN–timed, brief broadband/high‑beta jittered bursts abort imminent DOWN states, reduce SWA, and shorten time‑to‑wake at scheduled awakenings; contrast with down‑phase–targeted auditory stimulation literature indicating depth reduction. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
4) Long‑term use: quantify adaptation/tolerance over 4 weeks under sparse, variable‑timing policies versus periodic entrainment.

Methods

Participants
- N=36 healthy adults, randomized, within‑subject crossover across stimulation policies; overnight lab studies plus morning wake‑assistance sessions.

Hardware
- 8‑channel EEG (Fz, F3/F4, Cz, Pz, mastoids) plus 4‑electrode tES (two frontal, two parietal) enabling phase‑shifted multi‑site pulses to create low‑amplitude traveling fields; current ≤1 mA per channel, total injected current ≤2 mA, duty cycle <5%. Traveling‑wave phase gradients 10–40 ms anterior→posterior when used. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6561925/?utm_source=openai))

Closed‑loop controller
- Estimator: EKF tracking of latent oscillators for SO (0.5–1 Hz), spindle (12–15 Hz), and alpha/beta (8–25 Hz) plus a slow arousal state; prediction horizon 150–300 ms to schedule pulses at extrema/zero‑crossings with confidence gating. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))
- Tipping‑point detection: rising SO amplitude and slope, spindle probability changes, and increasing spatial phase alignment flag imminent UP→DOWN; the reverse pattern flags DOWN→UP; state uncertainty aborts stimulation. Grounded in slow‑oscillation and thalamocortical timing literature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4712264/?utm_source=openai))
- Stimulation policies:
  • Sleep‑induction policy: on predicted late‑UP→early‑DOWN, deliver 1–2 cycles of sub‑Hz monophasic/biphasic burst (100–200 ms envelope), optionally with a brief 12–15 Hz packet nested in early UP to promote spindle coupling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
  • Wake‑promotion policy: on predicted early‑DOWN, deliver a 100 ms broadband, non‑sinusoidal transient or a short 18–22 Hz packet with 10–20 ms interelectrode phase offsets to desynchronize and oppose frontal slow‑wave initiation; jitter timing ±20–40 ms to prevent adaptation. Down‑phase–targeted auditory studies motivate depth‑reduction feasibility; here translated to electrical nudges. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
- Optional spatial steering: when estimator detects anterior→posterior SO propagation, apply matching phase‑lead to reinforce sleep; invert/orthogonalize gradients for wake promotion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13167727/?utm_source=openai))

Controls
- Sham (ramp‑in/out only), open‑loop periodic tACS at SO frequency, and closed‑loop auditory UP‑phase tones as an active comparator for sleep induction. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes
- Primary (sleep induction): latency to N2; SWA power (0.5–4 Hz) over first 20 min; spindle–SO coupling metrics; subjective sleep latency on KSS. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))
- Primary (wake promotion): time‑to‑sustained wake after a cue at the end of the last NREM cycle; reduction in SWA and increase in alpha/beta during the 2‑min window; psychomotor vigilance within 5 min of wake. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389945725005052?utm_source=openai))
- Secondary: phase‑locking value between stimulation and SO; transition hazard modulation; adverse events per NIBS guidelines. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1682450/pdf?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Mixed‑effects models comparing policies; permutation tests for transition hazards; estimator performance as circular error between predicted and observed extrema. Power analysis assumes medium effect (d=0.5) for sleep latency reduction with closed‑loop auditory comparator benchmarks. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02170-3?utm_source=openai))

Safety, feasibility, and tolerance mitigation
- Current densities within established tES practice; automatic caps on total charge/day; ≥20 s refractory after any arousal; real‑time impedance and skin monitoring; nightly AE logs. Sparse dosing and phase‑jittered policies minimize habituation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2025.1682450/pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Recognized uncertainty: intracranial data question robust slow‑wave entrainment by low‑frequency tES; this protocol tests an alternative, timing‑leveraged, minimal‑energy mechanism rather than continuous 1:1 forcing. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-01045-x?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision points
- M1: EKF achieves mean phase error <20° at SO peak and predicts UP→DOWN within ±100 ms.
- M2: Sleep‑induction policy reduces N2 latency by ≥15% vs sham and ≥10% vs periodic tACS; increases SWA by ≥10% without increasing arousals.
- M3: Wake‑promotion policy reduces time‑to‑wake by ≥20% vs sham with sustained alpha/beta increase and no excess post‑wake sleep inertia.
- M4: Over 4 weeks, no decrement (>5%) in efficacy metrics; AE rate non‑inferior to comparators.

Novelty and impact
- Shifts the control objective from continuous entrainment to separatrix‑triggered regime switching, tested bidirectionally in humans; integrates traveling‑wave field shaping only as needed, and leverages proven closed‑loop estimation to achieve sparse, safer, and potentially tolerance‑resistant control of sleep depth. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/351196301_A_closed-loop_stimulation_approach_with_real-time_estimation_of_the_instantaneous_phase_of_neural_oscillations_by_a_Kalman_filter?utm_source=openai))

Data and code
- Pre‑registered protocol; open release of anonymized EEG/stimulation logs and EKF code after publication.

Title
Phase-locked, low-duty-cycle auricular vagus stimulation during controlled partial sleep restriction to amplify homeostatic rebound sleep and next-day alertness

Background and gap
- Human sleep timing and depth are governed by a homeostatic process S and a circadian process C; NREM slow-wave activity (SWA, 0.5–4.5 Hz) indexes S and increases after extended wake, then dissipates during sleep. Adenosine accumulates with wake and promotes sleep via A1/A2A receptors. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/jsr.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Adenosine directly inhibits orexin (hypocretin) neurons in lateral hypothalamus via A1 receptors, reducing arousal drive; orexin neurons project to locus coeruleus (LC) to stabilize wakefulness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1783688/?utm_source=openai))
- Partial sleep restriction (PSR) can elicit SWA increases and recovery dynamics, but effects vary by dose and timing; clean, repeatable augmentation of rebound sleep without pharmacology remains unsolved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))
- Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) can modulate central arousal/autonomic circuits and improves insomnia in randomized trials with favorable safety, but LC engagement markers are debated; timing relative to homeostatic/circadian phase is largely unexplored. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))
- Theory predicts diversity-/phase-resonance phenomena in orexin-based sleep-wake models, suggesting that small, phase-locked inputs can amplify stable oscillations. Translation of this to human state control has not been tested. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Research question (hypothesis-as-question)
Can brief, morning, phase-locked taVNS bursts delivered during a week of mild, controlled partial sleep restriction increase the amplitude of the sleep–wake cycle—manifested as larger nocturnal SWA and improved next-day vigilance—without tolerance or safety liabilities?

Atomic strategy
Exploit resonance locking: apply minimal, phase-accurate taVNS pulses near the ascending limb of circadian wake (shortly after habitual wake time) during PSR days to add energy to the wake node (LC–orexin network) while withholding stimulation in the evening so accumulated adenosine can dominate, producing stronger rebound SWA. The causal chain is single-step: precise phase addition to arousal → larger daytime arousal amplitude without continuous drive → larger homeostatic pressure and cleaner nocturnal dissipation.

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Determine whether phase-locked morning taVNS during PSR increases nocturnal SWA and reduces sleep latency versus sham and mistimed taVNS.
- Aim 2: Test whether controlled, bounded variability in taVNS intensity/pulse structure prevents tolerance across 6 weeks while maintaining efficacy.
- Aim 3: Quantify mechanistic engagement of LC–arousal using pupillometry during stimulation and relate it to SWA rebound; explicitly assess mixed prior findings by intensity titration.

Design
- Population: Healthy adults, age 18–40, habitual 7–9 h sleepers; exclude sleep/circadian disorders and medications affecting sleep.
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, 3-condition crossover with ≥14-day washouts: (A) PSR + phase-locked taVNS; (B) PSR + sham; (C) PSR + taVNS mistimed to the descending circadian phase (late afternoon).
- Partial sleep restriction: Time-in-bed curtailed by 90 min for 5 consecutive nights per condition, anchored to habitual schedule to avoid circadian drift.
- Phase targeting: Phase-locked sessions start 45–75 min after habitual wake time (ascending circadian wake); mistimed control at circadian wake decline.

Intervention
- Device/placement: Auricular concha cymba/tragus montage (taVNS).
- Parameters (dose windowed to sensory threshold): 20–25 Hz, 200–300 μs pulse width, 30 s on/30 s off for 15 min; intensity titrated to strong-but-comfortable sensation. Include day-to-day micro-variability of ±10–15% in current and burst duty (Aim 2) to reduce adaptation while keeping mean dose constant. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32831871/?utm_source=openai))
- Evening: No stimulation to avoid counteracting adenosine/VLPO expression.

Outcomes
- Primary: Change in whole-night NREM SWA (0.5–4.5 Hz) on Nights 1 and 5 of PSR (PSG), vs. sham and mistimed.
- Secondary: Sleep latency and efficiency (PSG), next-day psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) lapses, subjective sleepiness, and alertness.
- Mechanistic biomarkers: Pupil dilation during/after taVNS as LC proxy with intensity titration; heart rate variability; evening salivary melatonin to confirm stable circadian phase; exploratory correlation between morning pupil response magnitude and same-night SWA gain. Mixed prior reports on taVNS–pupil coupling will be explicitly tested with individual thresholding. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32050095/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: Adverse events, skin integrity, bradyarrhythmia screening. Reported taVNS trials in insomnia show benefit with few serious AEs; we monitor continuously. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic justification
- PSR increases adenosine tone and SWA rebound; orexin neurons are directly inhibited by adenosine via A1 receptors, while orexin–LC connectivity supports arousal. Phase-locked morning taVNS is expected to transiently raise arousal network output (via NTS→LC and broader CAN) without flattening S accumulation; evening withdrawal allows adenosine/VLPO dominance, deepening SWA. This tests oscillator-phase addition rather than continuous drive. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Linear mixed-effects models with condition, day (1 vs 5), and sequence as fixed effects; participant as random intercept.
- Equivalence and superiority testing for SWA change (A vs B primary; A vs C mechanistic control).
- Mediation: Does pupil response area during morning stimulation predict same-night SWA increase?

Tolerance and repeatability (Aim 2 extension)
- Six-week parallel extension in a subset: compare fixed-parameter vs micro-variable parameter schedules on weekly SWA gain and PVT; test slope of effect decay. Diversity-induced resonance theory motivates bounded variability to maintain network gain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Power
- Assuming a conservative 10–15% SWA increase with PSR+taVNS over sham on Night 5 (within-subject SD 12%), N=36 completers yields >80% power (α=0.05, two-sided). Interim futility after 18.

Milestones and go/no‑go
- Go: Night‑5 SWA increase ≥10% vs sham with no safety signal; pupil–SWA correlation present.
- No‑go: Null SWA effect with tight CIs or adverse event rate >10% moderate AEs related to device.

Innovation
- Tests a phase-resonant, low-duty, non-pharmacologic actuator to train the endogenous adenosine–orexin–LC axis; leverages PSR to probe and amplify homeostatic dynamics while minimizing desensitization via micro-variability. Prior taVNS sleep trials did not target homeostatic/circadian phase or adaptation explicitly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))

Potential outcomes and interpretations
- Positive: Larger SWA and better vigilance with phase-locked taVNS than sham/mistimed → supports resonance-locking of arousal to amplify the natural sleep–wake oscillation.
- Mixed: SWA gain without vigilance benefit → refine dose or phase; consider adding objective circadian phase markers.
- Negative: No differences → falsifies phase-addition premise under these parameters; proceed to parameter sweep or alternative actuators.

References (representative)
- Two-process and adenosine homeostasis: Borbély et al., 2016/2022; recent A1/A2A review. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1111/jsr.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Adenosine inhibition of orexin neurons; orexin–LC arousal pathway. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1783688/?utm_source=openai))
- PSR and SWA rebound dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4747841/?utm_source=openai))
- taVNS efficacy/safety in insomnia; LC engagement debates and pupil markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11650411/?utm_source=openai))
- Diversity-induced resonance in orexin model. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3426568/?utm_source=openai))

Title: Respiratory-locked dynamic thermal fields to tune self–boundary precision and externalize interoceptive control for everyday anxiety regulation

Hypothesis/Goal
- Hypothesis-question: Can respiration-locked, spatiotemporally coherent thermal “waves” delivered on the torso adapt the inferred body boundary (peripersonal space) and down-regulate autonomic defensive gain, while an externalized, steerable thermal-coherence variable enables lay users to stabilize their internal state without instruction—thereby reducing everyday anxiety and improving HRV? This targets maladaptive interoceptive inference in anxiety/depression by shifting precision and prediction error at the interoceptive–exteroceptive interface. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13233944/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic Strategy
- Single conceptual insight: Treat the body boundary as a controllable precision parameter. Drive small, safe, respiration-locked thermal waves around the torso to transiently expand/contract the inferred self-boundary and align exteroceptive predictions with interoceptive rhythms; expose users to a low-dimensional, observable “thermal coherence” stream that they can stabilize through slower, deeper breathing—converting emotion regulation into a sensorimotor stabilization task. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4837893/?utm_source=openai))

Background and Rationale
- Chronic anxiety/depression feature altered interoceptive prediction and precision weighting in insula/ACC circuits; improving autonomic flexibility (HRV) reduces symptoms. CT/thermoreceptive pathways to posterior insula support soothing, social-affective touch; slow, predictable, near-skin-temperature cues bias parasympathetic tone. Peripersonal/body-boundary representations are plastic and couple to defensive reflexes; threat to embodied limbs elicits autonomic responses. Thermal displays can create apparent motion and uniformity illusions (thermal referral), enabling smooth, low-energy “waves.” Together, respiration-locked dynamic thermal waves are positioned to (a) bias interoceptive state via affective thermosensation, (b) modulate boundary precision, and (c) provide a steerable external variable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6054486/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Prior work: HRV biofeedback aids anxiety/depression; haptic breath pacing exists; thermal haptics are growing, largely for XR or open-loop stress support. Gap: no everyday, closed-loop, respiration-locked thermal micro‑arrays that sculpt peripersonal boundary while externalizing internal stability as a directly steerable environmental variable. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32385728/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
- Aim 1: Demonstrate that respiration-locked dynamic thermal waves (outward on exhale; inward on inhale) modulate peripersonal-space (PPS) metrics and reduce sympathetic arousal versus non-locked or sham thermal stimulation.
- Aim 2: Test whether mapping cardiorespiratory coherence to a “thermal coherence” variable enables naïve users to stabilize the field rapidly, increasing HRV and lowering state anxiety versus a non-actionable mapping.
- Aim 3: Evaluate two-week, in-the-wild use for everyday regulation in the general population, measuring changes in daily state anxiety and short-term HRV.

System Concept
- Wearable: Flexible belt/vest with 24–48 small Peltier micro‑pads (10–12 mm contact islands; thermally isolated backplane) around upper torso. Skin interface is smooth, compliant, breathable liner. Contact temps operate within local thermoneutrality (≈30–34°C) with ±2–3°C excursions; controller enforces absolute safety margins below pain/burn thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384978/?utm_source=openai))
- Actuation primitives: 
  - Thermal apparent motion via sequential activation to create slow waves (0.05–0.2 m/s apparent speed). 
  - Thermal referral patterns to paint uniform, wide “halos” with sparse actuation. ([jstage.jst.go.jp](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjske/11/3/11_475/_article/-char/en?utm_source=openai))
- Sensing: Chest strap PPG + respiratory belt or piezo-textile channel; derive respiration phase, rate, and HRV (RMSSD, RSA).
- Control policy:
  - Boundary shader: outward wave centers on exhale, inward on inhale; phase-leading/lagging ±150–250 ms tunes alignment.
  - Externalized steering: the wave’s spatial coherence (smoothness, amplitude uniformity) is driven by a smoothed transform of RSA/respiratory regularity; users learn to stabilize coherence by adjusting breathing depth/rate, with 1–2 cycle latency.

Study 1: Mechanistic test (Aim 1)
- Design: Within-subject, counterbalanced, N=48 healthy adults with moderate trait anxiety. Four 12-min blocks: (A) respiration-locked directional waves; (B) nonlocked randomized waves (matched energy); (C) static isotherm (sham); (D) active control: auditory 0.1 Hz pacing. 
- Primary outcomes: 
  - PPS boundary via multisensory reaction-time slope (audio–tactile/visual–tactile task near torso). 
  - Threat-evoked SCR to a standardized VR near-body threat probe (safe visual approach) during each block. 
  - Autonomic indices: RMSSD, HF-HRV, EDA tonic/phasic, respiration variability.
- Predictions: Locked waves expand PPS (shallower slope, farther boundary) and reduce threat-evoked SCR and EDA compared with nonlocked/sham; effects comparable or complementary to auditory pacing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4837893/?utm_source=openai))

Study 2: Externalized steering without instruction (Aim 2)
- Design: Between-subject N=60. Condition X (actionable mapping): thermal coherence increases monotonically with deeper, slower, regular breathing; Condition Y (non-actionable mapping): coherence varies pseudo-randomly but yoked to group means; both receive identical thermal energy. No breathing instructions; task: “make the field feel steady.”
- Primary outcomes: Time-to-stability (first 2-min window exceeding predefined coherence + HRV thresholds), change in RMSSD, state anxiety (STAI-S) pre/post, subjective agency over the field.
- Prediction: Actionable mapping yields faster stabilization, larger HRV increases, and lower state anxiety, consistent with active inference: external, low-dimensional control reduces internal prediction error. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4779150/?utm_source=openai))

Study 3: In-the-wild pilot (Aim 3)
- Design: N=100, 14-day, two-arm randomized trial: wearable active vs. sham-static heat at thermoneutral levels. Use during two daily 10-min sessions and ad lib in anticipated stress moments.
- Outcomes: Daily ecological momentary assessment of state anxiety; weekly PHQ-8/GAD-7; passive HRV during evening sessions; adherence and comfort metrics.
- Prediction: Active arm shows greater reductions in daily anxiety and improved short-term HRV versus sham and relative to baseline; effect sizes comparable to light-touch HRV biofeedback but with lower cognitive load. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32385728/?utm_source=openai))

Thermal Wave Parameters and Safety
- Contact temperature target: baseline 31–33°C; excursions ±2–3°C; ramp rates ≤0.5–1.0°C/s; controller clamps max below time–temperature pain/burn thresholds with material-aware modeling. Apparent motion uses sparse pads to minimize power while preserving percept. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5384978/?utm_source=openai))

Measurement and Analysis
- Physiology: PPG-derived HRV (RMSSD, HF power), respiration rate/variability, EDA tonic/phasic components; motion artifacts regressed (accelerometry).
- PPS task: linear mixed-effects on distance-by-condition slopes; SCR: log-transformed peak amplitude to VR threat; HRV: within-subject change scores; multiplicity controlled by hierarchical modeling and preregistration.
- Learning curves: time-to-stability survival analyses; agency ratings correlated with HRV change.

Contingencies and Falsification
- If PPS shifts do not accompany autonomic changes, retain autonomic benefit route but revise boundary shader parameters or body site. RHI/autonomic results are mixed without explicit threat; hence include threat-evoked probes and PPS tasks rather than resting autonomics alone. Null SCR with preserved HRV benefit would support a primarily interoceptive, not boundary-mediated, pathway. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8016256/?utm_source=openai))

Expected Contributions
- Mechanistic: Evidence that gentle, respiration-locked thermal fields tune body-boundary precision and autonomic defensive gain in humans. 
- Methodological: A general externalization approach—stabilize an ambient variable to regulate internal state—grounded in active inference. 
- Translational: A non-invasive, everyday wearable for emotion regulation that is not a simple re-application of standard stimulation or conventional biofeedback modalities.

Justification of Novelty
- Literature supports HRV biofeedback benefits and thermal haptics for XR or open-loop stress support, but we find no everyday, closed-loop, respiration-locked thermal micro‑arrays designed to shape PPS while externalizing interoceptive stability as a directly steerable variable. This proposal closes that gap. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32385728/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Respiration-locked, phase-engineered auditory stochastic carrier for passive amplification of prefrontal–limbic control in everyday contexts

Integrated hypothesis-question
If weak top-down inhibitory volleys from prefrontal cortex to limbic structures are more likely to succeed when background afferent fluctuations coincide in time with endogenous control windows, then delivering near-inaudible, amplitude-modulated stochastic auditory noise whose envelope is locked to exhalation and engineered with small interaural phase offsets will increase real-time emotion regulation capacity (lower arousal, improved vagal control) in healthy adults during daily activities. Does respiration-locked, phase-engineered auditory noise improve emotion-regulation physiology and behavior more than unmodulated or respiration-misaligned noise?

Rationale (mechanistic constraints the proposal must satisfy)
- Emotion regulation depends on prefrontal–amygdala coupling, with inverse functional and effective connectivity during down-regulation; theta-range synchronization is implicated in fear and regulation dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3408571/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration entrains limbic and prefrontal activity and modulates affective processing on a cycle-by-cycle basis; exhalation is associated with enhanced parasympathetic engagement, and respiratory phase-gating of peripheral afferent stimulation alters brainstem responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Stochastic resonance enables weak signals to cross threshold when an optimal level of noise is added; multisensory and auditory SR have been demonstrated in humans. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11909106/?utm_source=openai))
- Binaural auditory brainstem circuits (MSO/LSO) are precise coincidence detectors of interaural timing, including envelopes of amplitude-modulated sounds; sub-millisecond timing can be exploited by small interaural phase offsets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4920552/?utm_source=openai))
- Excessive arousal (tonic LC–NE mode) degrades control; mild, phasic-aligned perturbations are preferable. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16254995/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use a single shared temporal scaffold: deliver sub-salient pink/white noise whose amplitude envelope is tightly locked to exhalation and carries a small, controlled interaural phase offset. This raises the density of near-coincident auditory afferent events exactly when endogenous inhibitory volleys are more likely (exhalation-linked windows), marginally boosting the probability that prefrontal control suppresses limbic bursts via stochastic resonance and coincidence detection.

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Test whether exhalation-locked amplitude-modulated (AM) stochastic auditory noise acutely increases indices of parasympathetic dominance and reduces threat reactivity relative to sham and misaligned controls in healthy adults. Primary outcomes: HF-HRV, skin conductance response (SCR) to negative cues, and state anxiety. Secondary: pupil diameter and reaction time bias to negative vs neutral stimuli. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9840384/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Test whether adding a second, correlated modality (sub-sensory vibrotactile neck noise with the same exhalation-locked envelope) yields a selective gain over auditory-only by exploiting cross-modal stochastic resonance. Outcome: incremental change in HF-HRV/SCR and stronger condition-specific improvements versus decorrelated bimodal control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6393074/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Identify mechanistic signatures: increased frontal theta power and phase-locking during regulation epochs; improved behavioral performance specifically when envelope–respiration phase alignment is preserved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373137/?utm_source=openai))

Intervention design
- Hardware: Everyday earbuds with onboard microphone for respiration sensing (acoustic nasal airflow) and real-time envelope tracking; optional neck band with low-amplitude, broadband vibrotactile actuator for Aim 2 (kept subthreshold to avoid conscious perception).
- Auditory stimulus: pink noise at −10 to 0 dB SL (calibrated individually), AM depth 2–5%, carrier noise 20 Hz–10 kHz, envelope 0.08–0.25 Hz mirroring instantaneous respiration; interaural envelope phase offset 10–40° to bias binaural coincidence without producing salient lateralization. Safety: levels below everyday environmental exposures; opt-out for hyperacusis.
- Haptic stimulus (Aim 2): broadband 30–300 Hz subsensory neck vibration, RMS displacement set just below individual detection threshold; identical exhalation-locked envelope as audio, with controlled lead/lag of 20–60 ms for cross-modal near-coincidence.

Study 1 (laboratory, randomized within-subject crossover)
- Participants: N=60 healthy adults, 18–50 years, no psychiatric diagnosis.
- Conditions (10-min blocks, counterbalanced):
  1) Exhale-locked AM noise with interaural phase offset (Active).
  2) Same noise and level, but AM envelope time-scrambled relative to respiration (Misaligned).
  3) Unmodulated noise (No-AM).
  4) Silence (Sham).
- Tasks: passive viewing of negative/neutral images; brief reappraisal trials to probe control; psychophysiology recorded continuously.
- Measures: HF-HRV, SCR, pupil, EEG frontal midline theta; state anxiety pre/post.
- Analysis: Mixed-effects models; primary contrasts Active vs Misaligned and Active vs Sham. Confirm “ablation” by showing loss of effect when envelope is misaligned.

Study 2 (everyday field trial)
- Participants: N=100; 2-week daily use in naturalistic settings (30–60 min/day).
- Arms: Auditory Active vs Misaligned vs Sham; exploratory bimodal Active subgroup.
- Outcomes: Ecological HF-HRV (wearable), daily state anxiety EMA, sleep quality; compliance and adverse events.

Falsifiable predictions
- Physiological: Active > Misaligned/Sham for HF-HRV during stimulation; reduced SCR to negative cues. Effects collapse with envelope misalignment or with excessive AM depth (>10%). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9840384/?utm_source=openai))
- Neural: Increased frontal theta power/phase-locking during regulation epochs under Active, not Misaligned. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373137/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-modal gain (Aim 2): Bimodal correlated > Bimodal uncorrelated ≥ Auditory-only; advantage disappears when cross-modal envelopes are decorrelated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6393074/?utm_source=openai))

Parameter ranges and control of boundary conditions
- Respiration sensing/latency: <100 ms end-to-end; envelope generator aligns exhalation peaks with auditory AM peaks.
- AM depth: titrated to avoid tonic LC–NE elevation; keep noise benefit within SR regime (narrow optimal window). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16254995/?utm_source=openai))
- Interaural envelope phase: 10–40°; individualized fine-tuning minimizes lateralization while preserving binaural coincidence sensitivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4920552/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic and novelty checks (evidence and gaps)
- Prefrontal–amygdala coupling in regulation and theta synchronization are well-supported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3408571/?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration entrains limbic-prefrontal circuits; exhalation gating of peripheral stimulation alters brainstem responses (RAVANS), justifying breath-phase locking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Stochastic resonance in human audition and cross-modal SR are established; however, respiration-locked, phase-engineered sub-salient noise for everyday affect regulation is not represented in existing trials located (distinct from tES/tRNS or nGVS literatures), supporting novelty of timing- and correlation-first framing. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378595507000457?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision gates
- Milestone 1: Demonstrate acute Active > Misaligned improvement in HF-HRV and SCR (Study 1). Go/no-go: p<0.05 with small-to-moderate effect (Cohen’s d≥0.3).
- Milestone 2: Replicate in field (Study 2) with daily-state anxiety EMA benefit.
- Milestone 3: Show added cross-modal gain (Aim 2). If absent, drop haptics and proceed with audio-only deployment.

Risk management
- Hyperacusis/noise sensitivity screening; SPL kept low and self-adjusting.
- Exclude mouth breathing during calibration; require nasal breathing for robust limbic entrainment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Continuous monitoring for adverse events; predefined stop rules.

Deliverables
- Open-source respiration-locked stochastic carrier algorithm and parameter sets.
- Validated protocols for everyday earbuds; optional neck-band module (if Aim 2 succeeds).
- Pre-registered datasets linking breath-phase-locked noise to autonomic and behavioral markers of emotion regulation in healthy adults.

Title
Unilateral intranasal TRPM8 microstimulation to intercept pre-conscious anxiety via ipsilateral trigeminal–parabrachial–amygdala/locus coeruleus gating

Background and rationale
- Early anxiety amplification arises from fast ascending brainstem streams before awareness. Trigeminal afferents project ipsilaterally to principal/spinal trigeminal nuclei and on to the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), which relays aversive and interoceptive signals to the central amygdala; trigeminal pathways also interface with the locus coeruleus (LC), a key arousal gate. These circuits provide a pre-cortical leverage point for affect modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4922599/?utm_source=openai))
- TRPM8-expressing trigeminal fibers in the nasal mucosa signal “cool”/menthol. Inhaled menthol relieves dyspnea without changing ventilation mechanics, consistent with a brainstem-mediated perceptual recalibration via TRPM8 on trigeminal afferents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13312038/?utm_source=openai))
- Hemispheric and peripheral asymmetries can precede felt anxiety. Bilateral EDA sometimes becomes right-biased during high-stakes threat, while facial thermal patterns track sympathetic load; the nasal cycle confers lateralized airflow and has documented links to asymmetric cortical oscillations. These phenomena enable left–right early-warning signals. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6514357/?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty check: Consumer or clinical systems do not exploit unilateral, phasic, intranasal TRPM8 stimulation in closed-loop with peripheral asymmetry sensing for everyday anxiety regulation; existing trigeminal neuromodulation targets pain or uses electrical stimulation and is not lateralized to pre-conscious affect gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12614495/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Deliver brief, inspiration-timed mentholized microbursts to a single nostril to activate ipsilateral TRPM8–trigeminal afferents and pre-empt threat escalation by biasing lPBN→amygdala and trigeminal→LC gating, chosen on the fly by detected left–right autonomic asymmetry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13312038/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis (integrated with goal)
If unilateral TRPM8 nasal microstimulation is delivered to the side showing early sympathetic dominance, then ipsilateral trigeminal–brainstem circuits will down-weight threat precision and shift LC toward a less tonic, more phasic mode, reducing autonomic and behavioral indices of anxiety before conscious awareness, suitable for everyday non-clinical use. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31840660/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish physiological efficacy: Determine whether brief, sub-olfactory menthol microbursts to one nostril reduce early threat markers (SCR frequency/amplitude, pupil-linked LC index, startle) more than bilateral or sham stimulation, with side-specific effects. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31840660/?utm_source=openai))
2) Validate asymmetry sensing: Quantify the predictive value of left–right indices (bilateral wrist EDA; facial thermal asymmetry; nasal airflow dominance) for impending anxiety surges during standardized stressors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6514357/?utm_source=openai))
3) Closed-loop field test: In daily life, test whether an asymmetry-triggered, unilateral TRPM8 system reduces momentary anxiety and cumulative load (EMA + wearable physiology) versus yoked-sham.

Methods

Design
- Two-phase, randomized, counterbalanced, within-subject trial in healthy adults (N=60).
  - Phase 1 (lab efficacy): 3 sessions (unilateral-targeted, bilateral, sham). Order randomized; 72-hour washout. Stress paradigms: social-evaluative arithmetic + anticipation; unpredictable auditory startle.
  - Phase 2 (field, 4 weeks): Alternating weeks of closed-loop active vs yoked-sham.

Intervention hardware
- Nasal microstimulator: wearable module with dual microvalves and micro-jet nozzles positioned at distal nares; delivers 50–200 ms inspiration-timed puffs of cool, low-odor mentholized air (food-grade menthol diluted to target TRPM8 with minimal olfactory salience). Safety interlocks cap daily dose and instantaneous concentration.
- Sensing: bilateral wrist EDA modules; PPG-derived respiration phase; optional miniature thermal camera for facial regions (perinasal, periorbital) to estimate sympathetic microvascular shifts; dual nasal thermistors for airflow lateralization. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12361?utm_source=openai))

Stimulus parameters and timing
- Dose-finding (run-in): adaptive staircase to identify individual sub-olfactory TRPM8 threshold (cool sensation present without explicit mint odor).
- Delivery: pulses at early inspiration when nasal/trigeminal gain is maximal; refractory period ≥15 s to prevent habituation. Side selection: toward the side showing higher sympathetic index (EDA asymmetry > pre-registered threshold) or larger nasal airflow (dominant side), with periodic reversal tests to confirm ipsilateral specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5053491/?utm_source=openai))

Measurements
- Autonomic: bilateral EDA (tonic/phasic), HRV (RMSSD, HF), respiration.
- Pupilometry: binocular infrared eye-tracking; compute mean diameter and asymmetry as LC-linked arousal proxy. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31840660/?utm_source=openai))
- Startle EMG: orbicularis oculi response magnitude/latency.
- Thermal: facial temperature gradients (peri-ocular, nose tip).
- Subjective: momentary anxiety (0–100 VAS), state anxiety (STAI-S), interoceptive threat appraisal.

Primary outcomes
- Phase 1: Reduction in SCR frequency and pupil diameter during anticipatory windows with unilateral-targeted vs sham; side-specific interaction (stimulated side vs measured asymmetry side).
- Phase 2: Decrease in daily EMA anxiety area-under-curve and sympathetic load (EDA-derived index) during active weeks vs yoked-sham.

Secondary/Mechanistic outcomes
- Startle attenuation; improved HRV; predictive power of asymmetry indices for within-person anxiety spikes; dose–response of puff energy vs effects.

Analysis
- Within-subject mixed models with condition, time, and side as factors; preregistered contrasts test unilateral-targeted < sham and unilateral-targeted < bilateral.
- Mediation models: Does pupil-linked LC proxy mediate TRPM8 effects on SCRs? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31840660/?utm_source=openai))
- Field: cluster-robust models across days; sensitivity analyses excluding high-motion periods.

Safety
- Menthol doses within established inhalation comfort/safety ranges; stop rules for irritation/tearing; daily exposure caps. Dyspnea relief literature supports central action without respiratory drive changes; nonetheless, monitor SpO2 and ventilation for completeness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13312038/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension (separate cohort)
- Compare unilateral TRPM8 to unilateral bone-conducted vestibular stimulation at the mastoid (carrier 100–500 Hz with low-frequency envelope), acknowledging vestibular cortical processing shows bilateral activation with ipsilateral and right-hemisphere dominance in right-handers rather than simple contralateral mapping. Outcome: which channel yields stronger pre-conscious threat attenuation per unit salience. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/japplphysiol.01024.2011?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Demonstrate ≥20% reduction in pre-anticipatory SCR frequency and ≥0.2 mm pupil decrease with unilateral-targeted vs sham (Phase 1).
- M2: Show asymmetry indices predict anxiety spikes ≥10–20 s ahead (AUC ≥0.70) and enable effective closed-loop triggering (Phase 1).
- M3: In field use, achieve ≥25% reduction in daily EMA anxiety AUC and ≥15% reduction in sympathetic load vs yoked-sham (Phase 2).

Impact
A unilateral, inspiration-timed TRPM8 nasal microstimulation paradigm operationalizes hemispheric gating through native ipsilateral trigeminal–lPBN→amygdala and trigeminal–LC pathways, enabling pre-conscious, on-demand anxiety interception in everyday settings without electrical or magnetic brain stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4922599/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and freedom-to-operate
No prior work combines: (a) lateralized, phasic intranasal TRPM8 activation; (b) closed-loop side selection from peripheral asymmetry; and (c) anxiety prevention as the primary outcome for the general population. Prior menthol/dyspnea and trigeminal–LC/amygdala literature support plausibility but have not been integrated into this consumer-feasible, hemispherically targeted intervention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13312038/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Respiration-locked micro‑pulsed olfactory cues as a subliminal phase tag to stabilize autonomic arousal in everyday settings

Question–Hypothesis
Can sparse, exhalation‑locked micro‑pulses of pleasant odor delivered just slower than a person’s ongoing respiratory rhythm act as a phase tag that nudges respiration toward longer cycles and exhalation bias, thereby increasing HF‑HRV and reducing EDA phasic bursts during routine daily tasks? This leverages nasal‑respiration’s entrainment of limbic activity and baroreflex‑linked cardiorespiratory resonance without requiring user attention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Use micro‑dosed, respiration‑phase‑locked odor transients as a weak external pacer set 1–3% slower than the user’s current breathing to create gentle phase drag toward slower cycles. Because nasal breathing organizes limbic oscillations and autonomic rhythms, phase‑specific odor tags should bias the timing controller of the respiratory network and, through RSA/baroreflex coupling, shift the system toward vagal predominance (↑HF‑HRV) and lower sympathetic sudomotor bursts (↓EDA). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale
- Nasal respiration entrains oscillations in piriform cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus; olfactory inputs provide a privileged, breath‑locked route into limbic circuits that shape cognition and affect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Slow or resonance‑frequency breathing around 0.1 Hz maximizes RSA and baroreflex gain, improving autonomic stability; subtle shifts in respiratory timing can therefore produce measurable changes in HF‑HRV. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Pleasant odors can modulate breathing and increase HRV, with effects organized by respiratory phase. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41107329/?utm_source=openai))
- EDA phasic responses index sympathetic sudomotor bursts and are a standard marker of acute arousal; reducing their rate is an objective target. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7014446/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and novelty
Prior work uses continuous aromas or open‑loop cues; phase‑locked odor pulses synchronized to each user’s breathing and slightly slower than their intrinsic rhythm have not been tested as a closed‑loop, ambient arousal stabilizer for everyday contexts. Existing studies demonstrate respiration‑synchronized odor delivery for neural measurement, not for closed‑loop autonomic control; bioadaptive room systems rarely exploit respiration‑locked olfactory timing. ([sciety.org](https://sciety.org/articles/activity/10.1101/2025.09.25.678425?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Demonstrate immediate autonomic effects of exhalation‑locked olfactory micro‑pulses during seated routine tasks.
  - Primary outcomes: within‑subject change in HF‑HRV (0.15–0.4 Hz power) and EDA phasic event rate over 10–20‑minute sessions.
  - Secondary outcomes: respiratory period, RSA amplitude, self‑reported state calm.
- Aim 2: Test timing specificity.
  - Compare exhalation‑locked vs inhalation‑locked vs pseudo‑random odor pulses and continuous low‑level odor.
- Aim 3 (exploratory): Add low‑amplitude facial micro‑cooling time‑locked to early exhalation to probe synergistic trigeminal–cardiovagal effects without discomfort. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00196.2023?utm_source=openai))

System and intervention
- Sensing: noncontact respiration via mm‑wave radar or thermal imaging; fallback chest belt for benchtop validation.
- Controller: model‑predictive phase‑locked loop estimates current respiratory phase and period; sets odor pulse train at 1–3% lower frequency with a fixed exhale‑onset tag (50–200 ms pulse).
- Actuation: micro‑pulsed olfactometer integrated into room HVAC diffuser near breathing zone; concentration kept sub‑threshold to minimally conscious. Odorant selected per participant from a small library of safe, pleasant scents to avoid aversion/habituation.
- Exploratory actuator: micro‑peltier facial air‑stream (±0.3–0.6°C equivalent), exhale‑peaking for 0.5–1.0 s.

Experimental design
- Participants: N=60 healthy adults, 18–65, non‑anosmic, screened for fragrance intolerance.
- Design: within‑subject, randomized, counterbalanced lab study across 5 conditions (no‑odor air pulses; continuous low‑level odor; pseudo‑random pulses; inhale‑locked pulses; exhale‑locked pulses). Each session 20 min; light cognitive tasks mimic daily work.
- Measures: 3‑lead ECG (IBI), finger EDA, respiratory signal, subjective calm (single‑item VAS).
- Analysis: mixed‑effects models on HF‑HRV and EDA phasic rate; time–frequency coherence between respiration and IBI; responder analysis (top/bottom tertiles of baseline HF‑HRV).

Predicted results and decision thresholds
- Exhale‑locked micro‑pulses will increase HF‑HRV ≥20% and reduce EDA phasic rate ≥15% versus no‑odor and pseudo‑random controls; inhale‑locked will be intermediate; continuous odor minimal. Success requires superiority of exhale‑locked over all controls on HF‑HRV with convergent reduction in EDA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic validation (subset)
- Test whether respiratory period lengthening mediates HF‑HRV increase using within‑session mediation.
- Confirm phase specificity: effects attenuate during mouth‑only breathing block, consistent with nasal–limbic pathway. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30348674/?utm_source=openai))

Everyday pilot (Phase II)
- 2‑week home deployment (N=30) with passive sensing and exhale‑locked pulses during desk work; pre/post ecological momentary calm, and cumulative EDA burst rate vs matched baseline days.

Risk mitigation and safety
- Odorant safety screen; individualized selection to avoid irritation; duty cycles capped to minimize habituation.
- For exploratory facial micro‑cooling, use mild temperature steps well above thresholds that evoke discomfort; exclude individuals with cold‑induced conditions. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00196.2023?utm_source=openai))

Potential outcomes and impact
- If confirmed, respiration‑locked microscent tagging provides a non‑invasive, attention‑free method for continuous arousal stabilization suitable for general populations in homes and offices, grounded in respiration–limbic coupling and baroreflex resonance physiology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension
- Combine exhale‑locked odor tags with imperceptible, phase‑offset facial micro‑cooling in a bifurcated controller to test whether convergent nasal–olfactory and trigeminal inputs yield additive vagal effects without increasing conscious salience. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpregu.00196.2023?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Benchtop validation and parameter sweep (pulse width, phase, frequency offset).
- Year 2: Randomized lab study; preregistered analyses.
- Year 3: Home pilot; deployment heuristics for multi‑user spaces.

Key references supporting mechanism
- Nasal respiration entrains limbic oscillations; odor processing is respiration‑phase organized. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Slow/resonance breathing amplifies RSA and baroreflex gain (biomarker targets). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Pleasant odors can slow breathing and increase HRV via respiratory modulation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41107329/?utm_source=openai))
- EDA phasic bursts reflect sympathetic sudomotor activation (objective arousal marker). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7014446/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Self-referenced breath-phase tactile micro-violations to recalibrate surprise–affect coupling for everyday emotion regulation

Background and rationale
- Predictive coding accounts of emotion propose that anxiety and depression reflect overly precise priors linking bodily change and unexpected events to threat; the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) signals unsigned prediction error (“surprise”) and modulates learning, while limbic regions like the amygdala bias vigilance and valence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))
- Nasal respiration entrains human limbic oscillations and modulates amygdala-linked cognition, providing a continuously generated, precisely phased internal timing signal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Tactile oddball and omission paradigms elicit hierarchical mismatch responses ascending from somatosensory cortex to insula and mid/dorsal cingulate, offering a low-valence channel to deliver controlled prediction errors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758822/?utm_source=openai))
- Near-threshold vibrotactile stimulation with added noise leverages stochastic resonance to titrate sensory precision and detection probability without high arousal. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Self-generated actions produce efference-copy–based predictions; slight deviations in the expected sensory consequence are encoded as self-attributed prediction errors, typically with reduced defensive responses relative to exogenous surprises. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1334241/?utm_source=openai))

Integrated hypothesis-question
Can repeated, low-arousal tactile prediction errors, time-locked to a person’s own respiratory phase and kept near perceptual threshold via stochastic resonance, reduce the learned coupling between “unexpected” and negative affect by recalibrating ACC-centered surprise signaling and its downstream influence on the amygdala?

Atomic strategy
Exploit respiration as a self-generated temporal prior and deliver subthreshold tactile “micro-violations” (small phase jitter or occasional omissions) at predicted breath phases, so the ACC repeatedly registers surprise in a safe, low-valence context, driving precision reweighting that uncouples unexpectedness from threat.

Specific aims
1) Establish that breath-phase–locked tactile micro-violations increase unsigned prediction-error markers in ACC/insula while minimizing amygdala arousal.
2) Test whether 4–6 weeks of daily training reduces everyday anxiety and negative affect reactivity to surprise.
3) Quantify whether changes are mediated by reduced precision of threat-biased priors (behavioral modeling) and altered ACC–limbic responses to unexpected events.

Intervention
- Hardware: A wrist or forearm wearable with (a) PPG/accelerometer airflow proxy to estimate respiratory phase, (b) a 6–12‑site vibrotactile array operating near individual detection threshold, and (c) a noise injector to implement stochastic resonance (SR).
- Control signal: Online breath-phase tracking; pulses nominally occur at user-specific predicted exhalation peak (or chosen phase) with closed-loop phase locking.
- Micro-violations: On 15–25% of predicted-pulse opportunities, introduce ±20–120 ms phase jitter, spatial relocation to an adjacent tactor, or omissions; hazard rate adapted to keep detection probability ≈0.3–0.5.
- SR tuning: Inject band-limited tactile noise to keep the underlying pulse near threshold and maintain low arousal while preserving detectability variance required for learning. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Self-referencing: Users are prompted to breathe naturally; because the timing prior is self-generated, deviations are labeled as self-referential mismatches rather than exogenous threats. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1334241/?utm_source=openai))

Design
Phase 1 (mechanism, N=72, lab-based, pre-registered)
- Randomized within-subjects, three conditions during fMRI/EEG:
  A) Breath-locked mismatch (phase-locked pulses with micro-violations)
  B) Breath-locked regular (phase-locked pulses, no violations)
  C) Random-timed pulses (yoked count, no breath locking)
- Primary neural outcomes: ACC/insula unsigned PE (BOLD/EEG) > B; amygdala BOLD and SCR minimal vs. C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758822/?utm_source=openai))
- Behavioral/physiology: Startle and oddball tasks to assess surprise–valence coupling; skin conductance to unexpected neutral sounds/touches; HRV changes during blocks.

Phase 2 (home trial, N=240, everyday efficacy, 6 weeks)
- Parallel-arm RCT:
  1) Active: breath-locked micro-violation + SR
  2) Breath-locked regular (no violations; matched tactile dose)
  3) Random-timed micro-violations (no breath locking)
- Use case: 20 minutes/day during routine sedentary activity.
- Primary outcomes: Weekly EMA of state anxiety/negative affect; STAI‑S, PANAS; reactivity to daily unexpected minor events (EMA probes).
- Secondary outcomes: Lab subset pre/post fMRI/EEG markers (ACC/insula PE; amygdala response to unexpected neutral events), and computational indices of prior precision from probabilistic learning tasks.

Analysis plan
- Mechanistic contrasts (Phase 1): A>B for ACC/insula unsigned PE; A≈B<C for amygdala/SCR. Mediation: ACC PE change mediates startle/affect reactivity change. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))
- Efficacy (Phase 2): Linear mixed models on EMA anxiety reactivity slopes; between-arm differences in pre/post computational estimates of precision weighting; correction for multiplicity.
- Generalization: Post-training, surprise tasks in a different modality (auditory oddball) to test cross-modal decoupling of unexpectedness and negative affect. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35017672/?utm_source=openai))

Safety and tolerability
- Arousal safeguards: Adaptive ceilings on violation magnitude/hazard to avoid startle; real-time SCR monitoring to keep within low-arousal bounds; omission events favored over intensity spikes. Startle physiology benchmarks and guidelines inform limits. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1469-8986.2005.00271.x?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1: Accurate breath-phase locking (<40 ms median error) and stable near-threshold calibration over a week.
- M2: ACC/insula unsigned PE increase without amygdala/SCR elevation in ≥70% participants (Phase 1).
- M3: ≥0.3 SD reduction in EMA anxiety reactivity vs. control arms at 6 weeks; durability at 4 weeks post.

Mechanistic justifications mapped to biology
- Respiration provides a limbic-entrained temporal scaffold; locking neutral tactile events to this scaffold and occasionally violating it elicits hierarchical mismatch responses (S1/S2→insula→ACC) that label “unexpected” without threat. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5148230/?utm_source=openai))
- Stochastic resonance maintains subthreshold, low-valence touch while ensuring intermittent detectability that sustains learning signals. ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2005.01533.x?utm_source=openai))
- Repeated self-referenced surprise updates priors via ACC-coded unsigned prediction error, reducing the learned association between surprise and negative affect. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10690029/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and differentiation
- Unlike existing vibrotactile devices geared to soothe or entrain relaxation, this protocol targets prediction-error recalibration using breath-phase timing and controlled micro-violations, a mechanism not used in current anxiety wearables or open-label affective touch devices. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022395625005552?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- If the active arm shows reduced affective reactivity to surprise and stronger ACC unsigned PE with stable or reduced amygdala/SCR, this supports the claim that safe, self-referenced prediction errors can retrain emotional habits for everyday regulation.
- Null findings with elevated amygdala/SCR would suggest that violations were not sufficiently low-valence or that breath-phase scaffolding is insufficient; adjustments would include lower hazard, increased omissions, or alternative phases.

text:
Title
Closed‑loop, cardiac‑locked olfactory micro‑pulses to recalibrate threat‑biased interoceptive priors for everyday emotion regulation

Background and Rationale
- Predictive coding accounts of interoception posit that anxiety involves overweighted precision on interoceptive prediction errors relative to exteroceptive cues; shifting precision allocation can change appraisal of ambiguous bodily signals. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))
- Cardiac cycle timing gates affective perception: stimuli presented at systole (baroreceptor firing) amplify fear/threat processing and alter somatosensory thresholds, identifying millisecond windows where interoceptive signals are most behaviorally potent. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
- Olfaction provides a rapid route to amygdala and valence encoding, enabling fast, low-load safety tagging without high cognitive demand. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7076187/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety signals can suppress conditioned fear and reduce anxiety responses when paired consistently with potential threat contexts, suggesting a route to reshape priors without explicit exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))
- Wearable olfactory displays and micro‑diffusers now permit brief, directed, low‑intensity odor pulses with sub‑second control, and human olfaction resolves temporal odor structure within a single sniff—supporting precise time‑locking to internal events. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic Strategy
Pair brief, near‑threshold, pleasant olfactory micro‑pulses to cardiac systole during everyday activities so that ambiguous interoceptive transients repeatedly co‑occur with a benign, exteroceptive cue. Over time, this shifts precision toward external context during interoceptive ambiguity and re‑maps bodily “blips” to safety.

Hypothesis/Research Question
If near‑threshold, cardiac‑locked olfactory micro‑pulses are delivered at systole during daily life, then:
- threat‑biased appraisal of bodily fluctuations will decrease, and
- interoceptive precision weighting (relative to exteroceptive signals) will down‑shift during ambiguity,
resulting in lower momentary anxiety and improved emotion regulation. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
1) Establish that cardiac‑locked olfactory pulses reduce fear‑biased perception at systole (laboratory test).
2) Demonstrate short‑term down‑weighting of interoceptive error signals during ambiguity (neurobehavioral markers).
3) Test real‑world efficacy for everyday emotion regulation with a wearable in a 4‑week field trial.

Methods

Device and Control
- Wearable unit: wrist PPG for R‑peak prediction and latency compensation; IMU for movement context; micro‑diffuser (e.g., SAW or micro‑pump) directing faint odor toward nares via a short, unobtrusive nozzle; smartphone controller. Delivery latency <150 ms from detected R‑peak with calibrated advance to hit systole. Odorants are neutral‑to‑pleasant, minimal trigeminal activation, food‑grade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))
- Control modes: (a) true cardiac‑locked (CL); (b) randomly timed micro‑pulses (RT, same dose); (c) no‑odor airflow sham (SH).

Participants
- N=120 healthy adults with elevated trait anxiety but not under treatment; balanced by sex. Power targets d=0.35 within‑subject contrasts across conditions.

Laboratory Phase (Aims 1–2)
- Design: within‑subject, counterbalanced CL vs RT vs SH across three sessions.
- Tasks and measures:
  - Cardiac‑phase fear bias: fear/neutral face identification and intensity ratings with stimuli probed at systole vs diastole; primary outcome is reduction of systolic fear advantage under CL. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
  - Somatosensory/pain threshold modulation by cardiac phase to check baroreceptor gating sensitivity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23669535/?utm_source=openai))
  - Interoceptive–exteroceptive attention task with heartbeat‑evoked potentials (HEP) and performance indices; prediction: under CL, exteroceptive accuracy and reduced HEP amplitude during ambiguity indicate down‑weighted interoceptive precision. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8153056/?utm_source=openai))
  - Safety‑signal transfer: olfactory cue presented during mild interoceptive perturbations (e.g., brief stair stepping); later test whether the same cue reduces startle/aversive ratings in matched contexts without pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))
- Physiological: HRV, skin conductance, respiration; EEG for HEP modulation.

Field Phase (Aim 3)
- 4‑week randomized cross‑over (2 weeks CL, 2 weeks RT/SH). Micro‑pulses delivered only during locomotion and low‑demand tasks detected by IMU to avoid intrusiveness.
- Outcomes:
  - Ecological momentary assessments (EMA): state anxiety, perceived bodily threat, affective valence, 5–6 prompts/day.
  - Passive markers: phone typing error variability and step‑time variability as stress correlates; wearable HRV during daily episodes.
  - Weekly lab check‑ins: interoceptive accuracy/awareness tasks, fear‑bias probe, HEP.
- Primary endpoint: reduction in EMA state anxiety and perceived bodily threat during CL vs control; secondary: durable reduction in systolic fear bias and HEP modulation after 4 weeks. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))

Signal Timing and Dosing
- Pulse onset targeted to 200–300 ms post‑R to coincide with peak baroreceptor influence; individualized by brief calibration using pain/looming probes to map systolic windows. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23669535/?utm_source=openai))
- Odor pulse widths 100–300 ms with PWM intensity control near individual detection threshold to avoid habituation and overt awareness. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26710120/?utm_source=openai))
- Sniff synchronization: optional lockout during forceful inspiration to minimize plume spread and reduce adaptation. ([cir.nii.ac.jp](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1360590043961229824?utm_source=openai))

Analysis
- Aim 1: mixed models with factors condition (CL/RT/SH) × cardiac phase (systole/diastole) on fear bias indices.
- Aim 2: HEP amplitude and decoding of attentional state; mediation by HEP between condition and behavioral fear bias. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11645458/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: hierarchical models on EMA outcomes; durability assessed in final lab probes; exploratory moderation by baseline interoceptive accuracy.

Innovation/Novelty
- First test, to our knowledge, of cardiac‑locked, near‑threshold olfactory micro‑pulses as precision‑reallocation and safety‑tagging for interoceptive ambiguity; prior cardiac‑locked multisensory work used visual/full‑body illusions, not olfaction or wearables for affect regulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-27698-2?utm_source=openai))
- Leverages amygdala‑proximal olfactory pathways for rapid, low‑cognitive‑load safety tagging during windows of peak interoceptive salience. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12319816/?utm_source=openai))
- Technically enabled by modern wearable olfactory displays and sub‑second pulse control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8919918/?utm_source=openai))

Expected Outcomes and Interpretation
- CL reduces systolic fear‑bias and HEP amplitude during ambiguity vs RT/SH, indicating down‑weighted interoceptive precision when a stable, benign exteroceptive cue co‑occurs with interoceptive transients. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806682/?utm_source=openai))
- In the field, CL lowers momentary anxiety and perceived bodily threat during daily fluctuations without requiring explicit exposure.
- A safety‑signal association to the olfactory cue emerges, generalizing to matched contexts and supporting real‑world emotion regulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6981293/?utm_source=openai))

Risks and Mitigations
- Habituation or plume persistence: use brief pulses, PWM control, and airflow management to minimize residual odor. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26710120/?utm_source=openai))
- Trigeminal irritation/allergy: pre‑screen odorants; use low‑trigeminal, food‑grade compounds and adverse‑event monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7076187/?utm_source=openai))
- Timing errors: individualized latency calibration and continuous PPG quality checks; fall back to RT if signal quality degrades.

Success Criteria
- Lab: significant condition×phase interaction reducing systolic fear‑bias under CL; concurrent HEP reduction during ambiguity.
- Field: ≥20% reduction in EMA state anxiety and perceived bodily threat during CL relative to control weeks; maintenance of effect in final lab probe.

Timeline and Milestones
- Months 0–6: device engineering, latency calibration, odorant safety validation.
- Months 7–14: laboratory study (Aims 1–2).
- Months 15–24: field trial (Aim 3), analysis, dissemination.

Broader Impact
A low‑burden, non‑invasive wearable that gently re‑tunes precision allocation at natural interoceptive “hot moments” could scale as an everyday aid for anxiety and mood vulnerability, complementing existing behavioral strategies without requiring explicit exposure or high user effort. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763417303573?utm_source=openai))
