Title: Electricalizing leptin to restore symmetric adiposity defense: a leptin-gated synthetic GPCR-channel for set‑pointed control of appetite, thermogenesis, and nutrient partitioning

Background and significance
- Adiposity-to-brain feedback is mediated largely by leptin acting on arcuate nucleus (ARC) POMC and AgRP neurons, relayed to paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), dorsomedial and ventromedial hypothalamus (DMH/VMH), and brainstem to govern feeding, sympathetic outflow, and endocrine tone. In obesity, central leptin resistance (SOCS3/PTP1B and related mechanisms) blunts the “high-fat brake,” while the “low-fat brake” (starvation defense) remains robust, creating asymmetry that favors weight gain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12212007/?utm_source=openai))
- ARC melanocortin circuitry suppresses intake and can drive sympathetic activation of brown adipose tissue (BAT) and related thermogenic programs; PVH/VMH/DMH circuits link hypothalamic activity to energy expenditure and substrate utilization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))
- Chemogenetic and electrophysiological studies show that directly changing membrane potential of LepR-expressing hypothalamic neurons rapidly alters firing and autonomic outputs (including heart rate and thermogenesis), underscoring that “electrical” control is the native lever for multi-axis metabolic effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4259491/?utm_source=openai))
- Synthetic receptor platforms (e.g., MESA, synNotch, PAGER) and ion channel–coupled receptors (ICCRs) demonstrate that extracellular ligand binding can be rewired to programmable intracellular actions, including direct modulation of ion channels. However, an endogenous leptin-gated electrophysiological receptor has not been reported. This gap motivates converting elevated leptin into immediate voltage changes in defined neurons to impose a programmable anti-weight-gain response. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12380174/?utm_source=openai))

Integrated hypothesis-question
- If we convert high adiposity (high leptin) into a thresholded, bidirectional electrophysiological command in ARC/PVH circuits, can we re-establish a symmetric homeostatic defense that automatically reduces intake, increases thermogenesis, and diverts nutrients away from fat storage above a programmable adiposity set point? What leptin concentration–to–firing transfer function best normalizes body fat without impairing defenses against weight loss? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12212007/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
- Electricalize leptin: Build a single synthetic receptor that senses circulating leptin and, upon exceeding a tuned threshold, directly modulates membrane potential (excite POMC-lineage satiety/thermogenic nodes; inhibit AgRP orexigenic nodes) via tight coupling to endogenous ion channels, bypassing JAK/STAT nodes prone to SOCS3/PTP1B desensitization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11108307/?utm_source=openai))

Proposed system: Leptin-Gated Electrophysiology Receptor (Leptin-GER)
- Input: Serum leptin (proxy for fat mass).
- Core device: A synthetic GPCR-based receptor (using a PAGER-like chassis) bearing a high-affinity leptin-binding domain, whose ligand-induced conformational change engages native G-protein signaling to gate ion channels (e.g., GIRK via Gβγ for inhibition; TRPC/Cav via Gq/Ca2+ for excitation). We will generate two versions with mirrored outputs:
  1) Leptin-GERExcite (Gq-biased) for POMC/VMH/DMH neurons to depolarize and increase SNS thermogenic drive.
  2) Leptin-GERInhibit (Gi/o-biased) for AgRP neurons to hyperpolarize via GIRK activation.
  Tuning: A bivalent binding interface (two non-overlapping leptin binders on receptor dimers) creates cooperative activation so signaling sharply turns on above a leptin concentration corresponding to the desired adiposity set point. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08282-3?utm_source=openai))
- Output axes embedded in circuit anatomy:
  - Appetite: ↑POMC firing, ↓AgRP firing → reduced intake. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/mend/article/30/1/3/2526351?utm_source=openai))
  - Energy expenditure: PVH/VMH/DMH premotor engagement → increased SNS outflow to BAT/white adipose tissue (WAT) and muscle thermogenesis/oxidation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))
  - Nutrient partitioning: SNS tone shifts adipose toward lipolysis/browning and muscle/liver toward oxidation, lowering hepatic DNL/VLDL output and fat re-esterification. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Receptor engineering and biophysical calibration
- Construct leptin-binding GPCR sensors by grafting anti-leptin binders or leptin-binding domains onto a PAGER-like GPCR scaffold; build Gq-biased and Gi/o-biased variants. Engineer two non-overlapping leptin binders (e.g., distinct epitopes) on separate protomers to enforce dimeric/cooperative activation and set-point tunability via affinity mutations. Validate coupling to endogenous channels (TRPC/HCN/Cav for Gq; GIRK for Gi/o) in HEK293 and primary hypothalamic cultures using patch clamp and Ca2+/cAMP reporters. Map activation curves against physiological leptin ranges to select constructs with Hill slopes >2 and EC50 values corresponding to target set points. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08282-3?utm_source=openai))

2) Cell-type–specific in vivo electrophysiology and acute function
- AAV delivery of Leptin-GERExcite under Pomc- or Sf1-promoters; Leptin-GERInhibit under Agrp-promoter in diet-induced obese (DIO) mice. Use in vivo fiber photometry and optotagged single-unit recordings to quantify firing versus endogenous leptin fluctuations and controlled leptin infusions. Assess immediate behaviors (meal size/number), SNS readouts (BAT iBAT temperature by thermal imaging), and heart rate/energy expenditure (indirect calorimetry). Establish that responses are silent below set point and switch on above set point. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9076616/?utm_source=openai))

3) Whole-body homeostasis, set-point programming, and nutrient partitioning
- Longitudinal studies compare programmable set points (different binder affinities) versus controls. Endpoints: defended fat mass, rebound feeding after weight loss, and resistance to diet-induced weight gain. Partitioning readouts: respiratory quotient, tracer-based lipid oxidation, BAT Ucp1 expression, hepatic DNL and VLDL-TG secretion, WAT browning markers. Evaluate whether defended adiposity converges near the programmed leptin threshold without impairing normal hypoleptinemic (weight-loss defense) physiology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))

4) Safety, reversibility, and translational path
- Off-switches: Competitive decoy (systemic anti-idiotype Fab) to block leptin binding; small-molecule allosteric blocker of the PAGER-like scaffold if available. Restrict expression to target nuclei with cell-type promoters and microRNA target sequences to avoid off-target autonomic effects. Benchmark against leptin pathway desensitization markers (SOCS3/PTP1B) to confirm bypass of canonical negative feedback. Explore NHP delivery feasibility with clinically used AAV serotypes to peri-hypothalamic regions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11108307/?utm_source=openai))

Key design choices and justifications
- Direct voltage control matches the native computational currency of ARC/PVH neurons and yields immediate, multi-axis outputs, unlike transcription-only synthetic receptors. By using a synthetic GPCR chassis that directly gates endogenous ion channels, we avoid saturating kinase cascades implicated in leptin resistance. Cooperative, bivalent leptin sensing enforces a sharp “exceeded set point” switch using the body’s own adiposity signal, minimizing interference below threshold. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08282-3?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan highlights
- In vitro: Quantify receptor-channel coupling efficiency (I–V curves), G-protein bias, EC50/Hill coefficients across human leptin concentrations spanning lean to obese ranges.
- In vivo acute: Titrate plasma leptin by infusion to map firing and behavioral/sympathetic responses across thresholds; confirm bi-directionality (POMC excitation; AgRP inhibition). ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/mend/article/30/1/3/2526351?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo chronic: Pair-fed and ad lib protocols under high-fat diet; evaluate defended fat mass versus programmed set point; assess BAT thermogenesis and substrate use. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: Telemetry for BP/HR; histology for gliosis; neuroendocrine profiling (thyroid/adrenal axes) to exclude off-target catabolic stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4259491/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: Leptin-GER variants with EC50 5–20 ng/mL and Hill ≥2; ≥50 pA GIRK activation (Gi/o) and ≥20% ΔF/F Ca2+ rise (Gq) in vitro. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5286527/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: In vivo, >30% reduction in 24 h food intake at endogenous leptin above threshold; >1.0°C iBAT rise within 30–60 min without hypotension. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))
- M3: Chronic, ≥15% reduction in fat mass with stable lean mass and RQ shift toward oxidation; normalization of defended adiposity near programmed set point. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4630288/?utm_source=openai))
- No-go: Tonic activation below threshold, autonomic instability, or blunted hypoleptinemic defense (e.g., impaired refeeding after fast).

Translational considerations
- Human set-point programming via binder affinity selection (using human leptin levels as calibrators), with intra-parenchymal AAV delivery to hypothalamic targets in severe obesity refractory to pharmacotherapy. Device modularity enables swapping the leptin-binding domain if human neutralizing antibodies arise. Synthetic GPCR scaffolds and ICCR precedents support feasibility of ligand-to-ion-flux transduction in mammalian cells, while central leptin resistance nodes are skirted by avoiding JAK/STAT dependence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08282-3?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- First use, to our knowledge, of a leptin-gated synthetic GPCR-channel to impose a programmable, thresholded electrophysiological response in hypothalamic control nodes, coupling a native adiposity signal to immediate, multi-axis metabolic outputs. It operationalizes a symmetric homeostatic defense against weight gain by design. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08282-3?utm_source=openai))

Title
AdipoSET: An adipocyte-intrinsic fatty‑acid–occupancy switch that latches thermogenesis and endocrine outputs to normalize energy balance once adiposity chronically exceeds a set point

Hypothesis and integrated research question
A cell-autonomous sensor that reads sustained intracellular long-chain fatty acid (LCFA) occupancy in adipocytes can be engineered to trip a latch that 1) converts white adipocytes to a beige/thermogenic state, 2) secretes a low, steady anorexigenic cue, and 3) biases systemic nutrient fluxes away from fat storage. Will a single, adiposity‑dependent “occupancy-to-latch” axis be sufficient to restore homeostatic control when fat mass chronically exceeds a preset threshold? This reframes obesity treatment from chasing fluctuating hormones to decoding a persistent intracellular feature of overfilled fat cells—the conformational state of fatty‑acid binding proteins (FABPs). FABPs undergo ligand-dependent structural changes and nuclear shuttling and are positioned to report LCFA load and quality inside adipocytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2032018/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit ligand‑dependent conformational switching of FABPs as a direct, genetically encoded reporter of adipocyte LCFA occupancy; couple it to a slow, duration‑dependent latch (hysteretic memory) that only engages when LCFA occupancy remains above threshold for Tcrit, thereby distinguishing chronic overfill from transient feeding. Once latched, the circuit co‑drives beiging and controlled secretion of an anorexigenic peptide plus adiponectin to re-divert nutrients and lower defended adiposity. Prior mammalian circuits establish that hysteresis/latching is feasible and durable in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1172236/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 1. Build and tune an adipocyte-intrinsic LCFA‑occupancy sensor based on FABP conformational dynamics
Rationale and design
- Mechanism: FABP family proteins bind LCFAs within a β‑barrel; ligand binding induces portal/helix movements, alters backbone mobility, and exposes motifs that regulate nuclear access and protein–protein interactions. We will harness these ligand‑dependent conformational shifts to control reconstitution of a split transcription factor (TF). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2032018/?utm_source=openai))
- Construct: Fuse FABP4 or FABP1 variants to complementary split‑TF halves (e.g., Gal4DBD–FABP and VP64–FABP). LCFA binding stabilizes a docking interface that reconstitutes the TF and drives a minimal UAS promoter. Chain‑length/saturation discrimination will be achieved by mutating portal residues known to tune ligand access and stability. Readout is transcriptional, enabling compact downstream wiring. Feasibility is supported by engineered split‑TFs in mammalian cells and by genetically encoded FA reporters based on nuclear receptor LBDs; using FABP as the allosteric transducer is the novel step. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43484-9?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro characterization (human primary adipocytes): Map input–output curves versus intracellular LCFA load using controlled lipolysis and FA supplementation; quantify sensitivity (EC50), dynamic range, and specificity to saturated vs unsaturated FAs. Validate that nuclear translocation of FABP-linked halves tracks activation. Confirm no activation by confounders (ketones, bile acids) using NR-LBD reporters as controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4315049/?utm_source=openai))
Go/no‑go and novelty check
- If FABP-driven complementation is weak, pivot to a chimeric design in which FABP ligand binding recruits a coactivator peptide (e.g., SRC‑1 RID) to a pre-bound DBD (one-hybrid), an approach validated for ligand‑sensing with PPAR LBDs but not yet with FABPs (preserves novelty). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8147873/?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aim 2. Convert sustained sensor positivity into a latching “on” state that resets only after prolonged leanness
Rationale and design
- Implement a duration-above-threshold (Tcrit) integrator that drives a recombinase flip (e.g., Bxb1/Cre‑FLEx) only when the FABP‑sensor output persists, thereby creating hysteresis (on-threshold high, off-threshold lower). Mammalian gene networks with positive feedback and recombinases have demonstrated robust hysteresis and memory suitable for therapeutic control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1172236/?utm_source=openai))
- Architecture: FABP‑TF → slow integrator (protease‑activated recombinase or recombinase expressed with an unstable degron) → FLExed promoter controlling effectors. A decay path (repressor expressed under a lean‑state promoter) provides time‑below‑threshold (Toff) reset. Benchmarks: Tcrit spanning 1–4 weeks to discriminate chronic overfill from meal/noise; Toff spanning 2–8 weeks to prevent yo‑yo. 

Readouts in vitro and in vivo
- In adipocyte cultures: time‑stamped reporters quantify the minimal continuous exposure needed for flipping and the hysteresis gap.
- In DIO mice: measure fraction of adipocytes flipped vs depot FA load to derive operational Tcrit and hysteresis in tissue.

Specific Aim 3. Program the three effector axes under the latched promoter and assess whole‑organism homeostasis
- Energy expenditure: Induce beige transition with PRDM16±PGC‑1α and UCP1. Prior AAV/CRISPRa activation of PRDM16/UCP1 in human adipocytes and mouse fat pads increases thermogenic gene expression and oxidative flux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10081280/?utm_source=openai))
- Appetite: Express a low, steady anorexigenic cue from adipose once latched. We prioritize GLP‑1–based transgenes owing to established central appetite suppression and clinical safety; dosing burden is mitigated because expression is depot‑restricted and conditionally engaged. As an alternate or second‑line module, a tuned GDF15 transgene can be evaluated, given its validated GFRAL‑mediated appetite suppression and additional energy‑expenditure effects; nausea liabilities will be dose‑titrated. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39892489/?utm_source=openai))
- Nutrient partitioning: Upregulate adiponectin to enhance peripheral fatty‑acid oxidation and insulin sensitivity, improving partitioning away from WAT storage; monitor lipids to avoid hypertriglyceridemia that can arise with strong LPL inhibition. ([kjim.org](https://www.kjim.org/upload/kjim-2019-109.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Delivery and targeting plan
- Vector: AAV8/9 with adiponectin or mini‑adiponectin promoter plus liver‑detargeting miR‑122 target sites; these cassettes restrict expression to adipose in mice and sustain depot‑level transduction. Local pad injection for first‑in‑mouse studies; systemic dosing for large‑animal work once biodistribution is verified. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4281237/?utm_source=openai))
- Manufacturability: The sensor, latch, and effectors fit within dual‑AAV or compact single‑AAV with minimized promoters; effectors can be split across vectors with cross‑activation after latching.

Experimental plan and milestones
Phase I: Sensor construction and validation (months 0–12)
- Engineer FABP‑split‑TF libraries (FABP1/4/5; portal mutants). Screen in 3D human adipocyte cultures for ratiometric selectivity to SFA‑rich versus MUFA/PUFA loads. Success criteria: ≥10‑fold induction at physiologically relevant LCFA levels; negligible activation in lean‑state mimic. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1367305/?utm_source=openai))
Phase II: Latch tuning and safety (months 12–24)
- Build integrator→recombinase flip; quantify Tcrit/Toff in vitro with pulsatile FA exposures. In DIO mice, define adiposity set point window that engages the latch and the time to reset after weight normalization; leverage established mammalian hysteretic circuits for parameter bounds. Success: depot‑level latching with minimal off‑target flipping, demonstrable hysteresis gap. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1172236/?utm_source=openai))
Phase III: Systems-level efficacy (months 18–36)
- AAV delivery to DIO mice; endpoints: food intake, indirect calorimetry (EE, RER), thermography of depots, body composition (MRI), plasma GLP‑1/GDF15/adiponectin, hepatic/muscle lipid content, and insulin sensitivity. Histology and single‑nucleus RNA‑seq confirm beiging and endocrine outputs in latched adipocytes. Success: ≥15% fat‑mass reduction with sustained EE increase and reduced intake while latched; reversal to baseline expression after Toff with weight stabilization rather than rebound.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Sensor specificity: If FABP complementation is insufficient, switch to one‑hybrid recruitment using FABP‑ligand‑dependent coactivator docking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8147873/?utm_source=openai))
- Appetite module tolerability: Start with low‑expression GLP‑1 transgene; escalate only if needed. Evaluate GDF15 only with stringent behavioral monitoring due to aversive pathways. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7923658/?utm_source=openai))
- Off‑target AAV expression: Combine adiponectin promoter with miR‑122 detargeting; verify by qPCR and reporter imaging across organs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7566077/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is novel and clinically oriented
- Novel sensing axis: Prior fat‑state control relies on endocrine concentrations (e.g., leptin) or exogenous drugs. Here, adipocyte LCFA occupancy is the primary state variable, transduced by FABP conformational switching into transcription—a modality not reported for metabolic set‑point control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2032018/?utm_source=openai))
- Single‑knob control: One intracellular variable (sustained LCFA occupancy) drives a latch that coherently modulates appetite, thermogenesis, and partitioning; hysteresis matches the slow dynamics of fat gain/loss and avoids meal‑by‑meal oscillation. Feasibility of latching in mammalian cells is established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1172236/?utm_source=openai))
- Translational pathway: Adipose‑targeted AAV and adipocyte secretion of therapeutic peptides are tractable; PRDM16/UCP1 beiging and GLP‑1/GDF15/adiponectin mechanisms are human‑validated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4281237/?utm_source=openai))

Key outcomes
- A deployable, adipocyte‑autonomous, occupancy‑to‑latch circuit that activates only when adiposity chronically exceeds a preset threshold and remits after sustained normalization, addressing the asymmetric defense of weight. Success establishes a general template for using intracellular physical‑chemistry states as master integrators for metabolic homeostasis.

Title
Raising the SUCNR1 activation threshold to intercept systemic metabolic remodeling

Hypothesis (integrated with research goal)
A discrete extracellular succinate threshold gates SUCNR1 activation across multiple tissues. Crossing this threshold converts reversible metabolic stress into a self-sustaining remodeling program (inflammation, angiogenesis, fibrogenesis). Temporarily elevating the SUCNR1 activation set-point—by buffering extracellular succinate excursions in interstitial and portal compartments or by receptor antagonism—prevents commitment and enables disease interception. Extracellular succinate routinely reaches SUCNR1 EC50–maximal activation ranges (≈30–200 μM) during pathophysiologic surges, whereas basal plasma levels are typically lower, defining a tractable window for threshold control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7778787/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Decouple intracellular TCA overflow from intercellular remodeling by raising the effective concentration threshold for SUCNR1 activation in vivo.

Rationale (load-bearing facts)
- SUCNR1 (GPR91) is a GPCR for extracellular succinate with EC50 ~28–56 μM; local succinate can reach 60–200 μM during surges, sufficient to fully activate SUCNR1. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3355999/?utm_source=openai))
- SUCNR1 engagement promotes HIF-1α signaling and proinflammatory/profibrotic programs in immune, endothelial, renal tubular, and hepatic stellate cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10342291/?utm_source=openai))
- Hepatic stellate cells express SUCNR1 and are activated by extracellular succinate; SUCNR1 loss or blockade reduces fibrotic programs in preclinical models. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1986575/?utm_source=openai))
- Elevated circulating and tissue succinate associates with metabolic disease and microbiome composition, implying gut–liver contributions to portal succinate exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7575719/?utm_source=openai))
- Potent, selective SUCNR1 antagonists and structural insights exist, supporting druggability. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1663-8?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Quantify organism-level succinate thresholds that precede early remodeling.
- 1.1 Map dynamic succinate exposure. Use microdialysis and rapid sampling to quantify extracellular succinate in liver (periportal and pericentral zones), visceral adipose, and kidney cortex during standardized metabolic challenges (mixed-meal tolerance, cold exposure, exercise bout, LPS microdose). Compare to SUCNR1 EC50/efficacy curves to define tissue-specific activation margins. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7778787/?utm_source=openai))
- 1.2 Link threshold crossing to early remodeling signals. In the same tissues, measure SUCNR1 pathway activation (G protein signaling markers), HIF-1α target induction, inflammasome priming, and fibroblast/myofibroblast markers. Include single-cell RNA-seq and phospho-proteomics to define the earliest switch-like transitions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10342291/?utm_source=openai))
- 1.3 Define portal contribution. Concurrent portal and systemic venous sampling in diet-induced disease models to resolve gut-derived succinate loads and their temporal relation to hepatic SUCNR1 activation in stellate and Kupffer cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7575719/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Elevate the SUCNR1 activation set-point using two complementary, druggable modalities.
- 2.1 Systemic succinate buffering via a soluble SUCNR1 ectodomain–Fc decoy. Engineer high-affinity SUCNR1 ectodomains (guided by recent SUCNR1 structures) fused to Fc for long half-life; optimize affinity and off-rate to clamp 30–200 μM succinate spikes without perturbing basal micromolar levels. Evaluate binding kinetics versus endogenous succinate and selectivity against dicarboxylates. Assess biodistribution and stoichiometric buffering capacity in vivo. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1663-8?utm_source=openai))
- 2.2 Pharmacologic threshold shift via small-molecule SUCNR1 antagonists. Use known chemotypes (e.g., NF-56-EJ40 class) as tool compounds to test whether partial/biased antagonism can raise the activation threshold while preserving any beneficial low-level signaling. Establish concentration–effect relationships that prevent pathway activation at surge concentrations with minimal baseline impact. ([public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org](https://public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1404441/pdf?utm_source=openai))
- 2.3 Portal-focused succinate depletion. Develop gut-restricted succinate sinks: (i) non-absorbed polymeric resins with engineered dicarboxylate affinity; (ii) engineered probiotic strains with inducible succinate utilization modules to consume luminal succinate and blunt portal spikes. Quantify portal succinate reduction and first-pass hepatic SUCNR1 signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7575719/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test disease interception across organs by timed threshold control.
- 3.1 Interception in liver. In MASLD/NASH models, deliver decoy or antagonist during windows identified in Aim 1 (post-prandial, stress, nocturnal lipolysis). Primary endpoints: stellate cell activation (α-SMA, collagen I), inflammatory gene networks, and early biomechanical remodeling (MR/elasto-imaging; crosslink ratio assays). Secondary endpoints: hepatic insulin sensitivity, lipid handling. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X18301219?utm_source=openai))
- 3.2 Interception in kidney and adipose. In CKD and diet-induced obesity models, assess tubular injury/fibrosis markers and adipose macrophage polarization after threshold elevation. Include renal function, albuminuria, and adipose cytokine profiles. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/ajpcell.00327.2022?utm_source=openai))
- 3.3 Cross-tissue generalization. Test whether preventing succinate threshold crossing in one compartment (portal) reduces remodeling markers in distant tissues, establishing tissue-agnostic checkpoint behavior.

Key methods and experimental design
- Quantitative succinate physiology: validate mass-spec assays for 1–500 μM range; microdialysis calibration; rapid blood micro-sampling.
- SUCNR1 pathway readouts: mini-G protein BRET reporters ex vivo; phospho-ERK/PLCβ/Ca2+ imaging; HIF-1α stabilization assays; scRNA-seq to detect discrete state transitions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10556696/?utm_source=openai))
- Structural-guided decoy design: use SUCNR1 extracellular pocket structures to engineer high-affinity ectodomains; surface plasmon resonance to measure succinate binding; in vivo PK/PD modeling to size dose required to buffer predicted spikes. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1663-8?utm_source=openai))
- Antagonist pharmacology: compare chemotypes (including NF-56-EJ40-like) across human/mouse SUCNR1; assess bias by β-arrestin vs G protein signaling; model partial antagonism to preferentially suppress surge responses. ([public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org](https://public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2024.1404441/pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Portal succinate sinks: screen polymer libraries for succinate partition coefficients and selectivity; engineer probiotics with succinate dehydrogenase overexpression and inducible uptake; confirm gut restriction and portal depletion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7575719/?utm_source=openai))
- Early remodeling endpoints: elastography and crosslink profiling; fibroblast/myofibroblast state mapping; quantify whether interventions avert YAP/TAZ-positive feedback initiation secondary to reduced SUCNR1-driven inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6192510/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes and decision criteria
- If succinate excursions above ~30–60 μM correlate with abrupt induction of SUCNR1-HIF/inflammatory modules and early fibrogenic markers, and if decoy/antagonist or portal sinks prevent these transitions without perturbing basal metabolism, the checkpoint model is supported. Conversely, absence of threshold effects or inability to prevent early transitions would falsify the checkpoint framing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3355999/?utm_source=openai))
- Go/no-go: proceed to IND-enabling studies if timed threshold elevation reduces early remodeling metrics by ≥40% across at least two tissues without impairing acute host responses.

Safety/risk management
- SUCNR1 participates in DC migration, renal sensing, and vascular biology. Use timed, surge-synchronized dosing and portal-restricted strategies to minimize chronic pathway suppression. Track infection susceptibility and hemodynamic endpoints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6030209/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty relative to prior art
- Prior work implicates succinate/SUCNR1 in specific pathologies and documents antagonist chemistry and receptor structure. This proposal formalizes and tests SUCNR1 activation as a quantitative, tissue-agnostic metabolic checkpoint defined by extracellular succinate dynamics, and introduces threshold-raising via stoichiometric succinate buffering and timed partial antagonism as an interception strategy before irreversible remodeling. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006291X18301219?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Tissue succinate atlases; SUCNR1 activation curves in vivo; decoy prototype with sub-100 nM succinate KD. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1663-8?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Proof-of-interception in MASLD and CKD models with timed dosing; portal sink validation reducing portal succinate AUC by ≥50%. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7575719/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Cross-tissue generalization; safety pharmacology; biomarker panel (dynamic plasma succinate, SUCNR1 occupancy, early remodeling indices) for first-in-human design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7778787/?utm_source=openai))

Translational path
- Patient selection by succinate stress test (standardized mixed-meal or exercise challenge with serial plasma succinate) to identify low-threshold individuals.
- FIH: short-acting SUCNR1 antagonist or decoy with post-prandial dosing; primary endpoints are safety and blockade of succinate-induced SUCNR1 signaling biomarkers; secondary endpoints are suppression of early remodeling signatures in liver/adipose/kidney. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3355999/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Erasing inflammasome “seeds” to intercept metabolic disease: polymer‑selective clearance of ASC prionoid assemblies as a metabolic checkpoint therapy

Central hypothesis/question
Do polymerized ASC “specks” function as a binary metabolic checkpoint that locks tissues into a chronic, trained inflammatory–glycolytic state after transient nutrient stress, and can transient, polymer‑selective clearance of ASC specks reset this state and halt progression to irreversible metabolic disease? ASC specks exhibit prion‑like, self‑templating polymerization and intercellular propagation; they are detectable in human biofluids and amplify inflammation. If their abundance crosses a nucleation threshold, commitment to pathology ensues. Reversing speck load below the percolation threshold should erase the memory and restore homeostasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4116676/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat ASC speck mass—not NLRP3 enzymology—as the causal, switch‑like substrate of metabolic memory. A brief, polymer‑selective autophagy tether (ATTEC/AUTOTAC‑class degrader) reduces intracellular and extracellular speck burden below the propagation threshold, allowing inflammatory tone, innate epigenetic marks, and metabolic flux to relax to a pre‑scar state. This intervenes upstream of tissue remodeling and independently of cell type. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31690177/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale
- ASC specks are prionoid assemblies that seed further inflammasome activation and can propagate between cells; they are measurable in human serum/CSF. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4116676/?utm_source=openai))
- Chronic metabolic disorders (obesity/T2D/NAFLD) are driven in part by NLRP3–ASC inflammasome activity and IL‑1 family cytokines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7826517/?utm_source=openai))
- Innate immune “trained immunity” explains durable, diet‑induced inflammatory memory via epigenetic/metabolic reprogramming; erasing the seeding substrate should permit memory decay. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41577-020-0285-6?utm_source=openai))
- Prion‑like adaptors such as MAVS illustrate how organellar signalosomes use nucleation‑propagation logic; this supports a generalizable “seed erasure” paradigm. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21782231/?utm_source=openai))
- Polymer‑tethering degraders (ATTEC/AUTOTAC) can selectively eliminate large aggregates and organelle‑associated cargos through autophagy, enabling polymer‑biased targeting of ASC. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31690177/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define ASC specks as a thresholded metabolic checkpoint after transient nutrient stress.
- Model: Pulsed Western‑diet or lipotoxic challenge in mice (and human primary myeloid–adipocyte co‑cultures), followed by recovery.
- Readouts: Quantify intracellular/pericellular ASC polymers (native‑state single‑molecule pull‑down, flow‑FACS for extracellular specks), seeded polymerization assays, and hysteresis under second‑hit challenges; correlate with IL‑1β/IL‑18 output, glycolytic flux, and trained‑immunity chromatin marks (H3K4me3/H3K27ac at inflammatory–glycolytic loci). Establish a per‑tissue speck percolation threshold that predicts failure to revert after stress withdrawal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9163349/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer polymer‑selective “Speck‑ATTECs” that tether ASC polymers to autophagy for clearance without broad immunosuppression.
- Design: Identify conformer‑selective ligands (peptides/peptidomimetics/aptamers) for polymeric ASC PYD/CARD interfaces; couple to LC3‑ or p62‑recruiting ATTEC/AUTOTAC warheads. Favor binders with poor affinity for monomeric ASC to preserve acute inflammasome competence.
- Assays: In LPS+palmitate‑primed macrophages and adipocyte co‑cultures, quantify target engagement, autophagic flux, speck load, cytokine output, and glycolytic reprogramming. Benchmark against anti‑ASC biologics (e.g., polymer‑preferring antibodies) to validate targetability. Assess antiviral RIG‑I/MAVS responses to ensure innate defense remains intact. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31690177/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test checkpoint interception in vivo by transient speck erasure before irreversible remodeling.
- Intervention: Single or short‑pulse Speck‑ATTEC dosing in early disease windows during or immediately after nutrient‑stress pulses.
- Endpoints: Durability of speck reduction; decay of inflammatory transcripts and trained‑immunity marks in tissue myeloid cells; systemic insulin sensitivity, glucose tolerance; prevention of transition to fibrosis/beta‑cell failure under imposed second hits.
- Biomarker strategy: Serum ASC specks as a real‑time pharmacodynamic and patient‑selection marker. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-53547-0?utm_source=openai))

Key methods and analyses
- Conformer‑selective binder discovery: display libraries and negative selection against recombinant monomeric ASC.
- Polymer bias quantification: BLI/SPR with polymeric ASC filaments; EM imaging; cellular speck FRET biosensors.
- ATTEC/AUTOTAC optimization: ternary‑complex modeling; live‑cell LC3 recruitment; autophagosome flux (mCherry‑GFP‑LC3); dose “hook effect” profiling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7870735/?utm_source=openai))
- Systems readouts: single‑cell RNA‑seq/ATAC‑seq; Seahorse assays; cytokine multiplex; in situ IL‑1β imaging; metabolic phenotyping.
- Safety: Acute host‑defense assays (viral mimetics), wound‑healing models, hematology, and liver/cardiac panels.

Milestones and go/no‑go criteria
- M1: Demonstrate speck hysteresis and a quantifiable percolation threshold that predicts non‑reversion after stress withdrawal (≥3 independent models).
- M2: Achieve ≥70% intracellular speck reduction with ≥50% preservation of acute inflammasome response to canonical pathogens in vitro.
- M3: In vivo, a single pulse normalizes serum ASC specks and improves HOMA‑IR and GTT by ≥30% for ≥4 weeks without increased infection susceptibility.
- No‑go: Failure to show thresholded behavior in Aim 1 or inability to achieve polymer selectivity.

Therapeutic concept and development path
- Lead modality: Small‑molecule/peptidomimetic Speck‑ATTECs with polymer selectivity; subcutaneous or liver/adipose‑targeted nanoparticle delivery for short pulses.
- Companion diagnostic: Serum ASC speck assay for enrichment and PD. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-53547-0?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation: Contrasts with NLRP3 enzyme inhibitors by erasing the physical memory substrate (ASC polymers) and preserving acute host defense.
- Expansion: Apply “seed erasure” to other prion‑like signalosomes (e.g., MAVS filaments) that may underpin metabolic–inflammatory memory at mitochondria. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21782231/?utm_source=openai))

Expected impact
If successful, transient, polymer‑selective erasure of ASC specks will validate a druggable, tissue‑agnostic metabolic checkpoint that converts a chronic inflammatory attractor back to a reversible state, enabling true disease interception before fibrosis, beta‑cell exhaustion, or cardiovascular remodeling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7826517/?utm_source=openai))

Title
R as a Metabolic Checkpoint: Intercepting Disease by Maintaining the Reactive Carbonyl Load-to-Detox Capacity Ratio Below a Tissue-Specific Threshold

Central hypothesis and goal
Crossing a tissue-specific threshold in the ratio R = reactive carbonyl species (RCS) load to detoxification capacity commits metabolic tissues to an irreversible, self-reinforcing path characterized by covalent adduct accumulation (AGEs/ALEs), altered mechanics, and proinflammatory signaling. Keeping R below its threshold (R*) prevents lock-in and enables disease interception across organs. We will define R*, build minimally invasive readouts for R in vivo, and test closed-loop interventions that maintain R < R*. The work reframes interception around a single intensive variable rather than pathway-specific nodes.

Rationale
- Methylglyoxal (MGO) is detoxified primarily by the glutathione-dependent glyoxalase pathway (GLO1/GLO2), a saturable system; when flux exceeds capacity, “dicarbonyl stress” drives widespread protein/lipid/DNA modification implicated in metabolic complications. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- 4‑hydroxynonenal (4‑HNE), a lipid peroxidation product, forms Michael adducts with proteins and is cleared by GSH conjugation (GSTs) and aldehyde dehydrogenases; detox capacity limits are linked to cytotoxicity and organ injury. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5643026/?utm_source=openai))
- AGE/ALE accrual and RAGE engagement amplify inflammation and fibrosis, providing a systems-level feed-forward mechanism once adduct density passes a tipping point. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))
- Real-time readouts of detox reserve exist: genetically encoded NADPH sensors (iNap family) and GSH redox reporters (Grx1-roGFP variants) quantify antioxidant/phase‑II cofactor availability in living systems. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5555402/?utm_source=openai))
- Live-cell and in vivo fluorescent probes for MGO are available and can report RCS load with organelle or tissue targeting, enabling numerator measurements for R. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11629108/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Treat R (RCS load/detox capacity) as a checkpoint variable. Detect imminent threshold crossing and actuate short, precisely timed pulses that reduce RCS load and/or transiently raise detox capacity, preventing commitment to the high‑adduct, profibrotic state.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Quantify R* (the commitment threshold) in metabolic tissues and establish its predictive value.
- Build an R-meter combining:
  - Numerator: fast near-infrared or two‑photon MGO probes validated in cells and diabetic mouse tissues; parallel targeted LC‑MS for 4‑HNE adduct burden. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11629108/?utm_source=openai))
  - Denominator: cytosolic and mitochondrial detox reserve via iNap NADPH sensors and Grx1‑roGFP2 reporters in sentinel cells implanted subcutaneously or delivered via adeno‑associated vectors to target tissues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5555402/?utm_source=openai))
- Models and outputs:
  - Diet‑induced obesity/NASH, β‑cell stress, and pressure‑overload heart models. Track when R surpasses R* and whether this predicts (weeks later) persistent increases in AGE/ALE density and RAGE pathway activation, independent of transient glycemia or lipidemia. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))
- Definition of R*: the minimal sustained R that yields (i) irreversible elevation of proteome carbonylation and (ii) failure to normalize stiffness/inflammatory signaling after acute stress withdrawal.

Aim 2. Engineer and validate an event-triggered, closed-loop actuator that maintains R < R* in vivo.
- Actuation palette grounded in mechanism:
  - Reduce numerator (RCS load): microdosed MGO scavenger pulses (e.g., carnosine derivatives) and 4‑HNE lowering via ALDH2 activation (Alda‑1) during threshold‑crossing events. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41897532/?utm_source=openai))
  - Increase denominator (detox capacity): brief, sensor‑gated boosts that elevate NADPH/GSH availability (e.g., transient Nrf2/Keap1 axis activation or PPP bias) to raise GLO1/GST/ALDH activity windows without chronic exposure. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/physrev.00023.2017?utm_source=openai))
- Control architecture:
  - Implement an event detector that computes R in real time from the two channels and triggers actuation when R approaches R* (predictive threshold with hysteresis to avoid oscillation).
  - Delivery routes: subcutaneous micropump for small-molecule pulses; oral Alda‑1 for ALDH2 activation. Time constants target minutes to hours, matching probe kinetics and detox enzyme response.
- Endpoints:
  - Immediate: prevention of R crossing (area under R above R* minimized).
  - Delayed: blunted accrual of AGE/ALE adducts and reduced RAGE target gene induction compared with yoked, open-loop dosing. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test disease interception across tissues by maintaining R below R*.
- Hypothesis: sustaining R < R* prevents transition to persistent profibrotic signaling and mechanical lock-in.
- Readouts:
  - Proteome carbonylation and ECM crosslink density (AGE/ALE assays); functional outcomes (insulin sensitivity, liver stiffness, ventricular stiffness).
  - In fibroblast-rich organs, verify that long-term R control limits YAP/TAZ nuclear localization and matricellular gene programs indicative of fibrosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4329470/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design highlights
- Sensor development and calibration:
  - Validate iNap and Grx1‑roGFP2 dynamics under metabolic and oxidative challenges; quantify sensor lag and dynamic range in target tissues to constrain controller timing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5555402/?utm_source=openai))
  - Select and calibrate MGO probes with documented in vivo performance; pair with orthogonal LC‑MS quantification for 4‑HNE adducts to cover both glycolytic and lipoperoxidation branches. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S2041652023055931?utm_source=openai))
- Threshold mapping:
  - Systematically vary R via substrate load (glycolytic push or lipid peroxidation stimuli) and partial inhibition/activation of detox nodes (GLO1, ALDH2) to observe bifurcation behavior and define R*. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00001.2019?utm_source=openai))
- Closed-loop trials:
  - Compare event-triggered pulses vs matched open-loop dosing for equal total drug exposure. Primary metric: fraction of time above R* and cumulative adduct formation. Secondary: organ-level function and early fibrosis markers. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- If R* exists and is conserved across tissues with context-specific values, it will function as a quantitative metabolic checkpoint. Demonstrating that short, sensor‑gated pulses keep R < R* while reducing long‑term adduct accrual and fibrotic signaling would validate interception at the commitment point rather than downstream symptoms. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and alternatives
- Probe kinetics: if fluorescence probes are too slow for real-time control in a tissue, use periodic sampling with microdialysis and rapid ex vivo readout, or focus on tissues where validated probes perform well. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13261436/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target Nrf2 activation: prioritize denominator-raising via substrate supply (PPP fueling) or enzyme activators; keep Nrf2 pulses brief and event-triggered. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/abs/10.1152/physrev.00023.2017?utm_source=openai))
- HNE specificity: if systemic Alda‑1 leads to confounds, use tissue-targeted ALDH2 delivery or GST induction strategies with pharmacodynamic monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6054945/?utm_source=openai))

Significance and innovation
- Introduces R as a tissue-agnostic, druggable metabolic checkpoint distinct from canonical signaling nodes; embeds it in an actionable, closed-loop interception framework.
- Leverages existing, validated sensing modalities for detox reserve (iNap, Grx1‑roGFP2) and RCS load (in vivo MGO probes), minimizing de novo biology while enabling real-time decision-making. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5555402/?utm_source=openai))
- Aligns therapy with threshold physics of covalent damage formation and inflammation amplification (AGE/ALE → RAGE), aiming to halt progression before fibrosis and organ remodeling. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-med-041316-085215?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Build and calibrate R-meter in two tissues; estimate R*; demonstrate predictive value for adduct accrual.
- Year 2: Implement closed-loop control; show reduction in time above R* and early molecular endpoints.
- Year 3: Demonstrate disease interception in two organ systems with functional benefit and reduced fibrosis markers relative to open-loop dosing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4329470/?utm_source=openai))

Therapeutic translation path
- The controlled variable R is measurable with minimally invasive imaging/sampling and modulated with small molecules (MGO scavengers, ALDH2 activators) already supported by mechanistic and preclinical evidence, positioning the approach for rapid translation once R* is defined. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2856486/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title: Restoring the mitochondrial free‑CoA threshold to reset cellular metabolism

Hypothesis/Goal
A discrete tipping point in the mitochondrial free‑CoA:acyl‑CoA ratio converts reversible metabolic stress into a self‑reinforcing disease program by (i) driving nonenzymatic protein acylation of metabolic enzymes and (ii) suppressing pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH)–dependent carbohydrate oxidation. Elevating free CoA above this threshold—without chronically pushing upstream signaling—will reset metabolic flux and proteostasis, intercepting disease progression. The research will identify this mitochondrial CoA threshold across tissues and develop small‑molecule positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of mitochondrial acyl‑CoA thioesterases (ACOTs) that engage only under low‑CoA/high‑acyl‑CoA conditions to produce a self‑limited “pause‑and‑purge” reset.

Rationale
- Mitochondrial protein acylation is largely nonenzymatic and proportional to acyl‑CoA abundance in the alkaline matrix; proteome‑wide hyper‑acylation accompanies elevations of specific acyl‑CoAs and impairs enzyme function. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6498146/?utm_source=openai))
- PDH flux is inhibited by its product acetyl‑CoA and by PDK activation downstream of high acetyl‑CoA/NADH; free CoA is a required PDH co‑substrate. Thus, low free CoA and high acyl‑CoA together suppress carbohydrate oxidation and reinforce lipid reliance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9871338/?utm_source=openai))
- The mitochondrial CoA pool is limited; acyl‑CoA accumulation limits free CoA and can force export as acylcarnitines, a systemic signal of incomplete β‑oxidation seen in insulin resistance. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1432-1033.2003.03947.x?utm_source=openai))
- Multiple mitochondrial ACOTs (e.g., ACOT2/9/13) hydrolyze acyl‑CoAs to fatty acid + CoA and are inhibited by CoA—an intrinsic negative feedback implying activity increases as CoA falls, creating natural threshold behavior that a PAM can sharpen without driving activity in healthy states. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31676684/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit the endogenous CoA‑inhibited regulation of mitochondrial ACOTs by discovering PAMs that preferentially stabilize the ACOT–acyl‑CoA active conformation under low‑CoA/high‑acyl‑CoA conditions, thereby restoring free CoA above the tipping point. As free CoA normalizes, PAM effect becomes self‑limiting, avoiding chronic pathway forcing. This single perturbation simultaneously (i) reduces nonenzymatic acylation pressure and (ii) relieves PDH inhibition, resetting flux and proteostasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6498146/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define the mitochondrial free‑CoA:acyl‑CoA tipping point that commits cells to maladaptive metabolism.
2) Discover and optimize mitochondria‑localized ACOT PAMs that are conditionally active when CoA is low.
3) Demonstrate disease interception in vivo by pulsed restoration of free CoA above the threshold.

Aim 1: Map the mitochondrial CoA threshold
- Systems: Primary hepatocytes, myotubes, adipocytes, and β‑cells; high‑fat–exposed mice prior to fibrosis.
- Protocols:
  - Titrate fatty‑acid supply and respiratory constraints to produce graded acyl‑CoA stress; quantify free CoA and chain‑resolved acyl‑CoAs by LC‑MS (including recent pan‑chain methods) and acylcarnitines in media/plasma. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-025-01358-y?utm_source=openai))
  - Readouts: (i) mitochondrial acetyl/succinyl/glutaryl‑proteomes (DIA‑MS); (ii) PDH flux (stable‑isotope tracers); (iii) respiration and substrate switching; (iv) ISR/UPR markers.
  - Analysis: Identify inflection points and hysteresis in the relationships between free CoA, acyl‑CoA load, proteome acylation, PDH flux, and respiration to define a bistable boundary.
- Success criteria: A reproducible free‑CoA:acyl‑CoA ratio at which proteome acylation and PDH suppression accelerate nonlinearly across cell types. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11601992/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2: Discover conditional ACOT activators
- Target selection: Mitochondrial ACOT2/9/13 (substrate breadth and matrix localization). CoA acts as a feedback inhibitor; activators should increase kcat/Km for long‑ and short‑chain acyl‑CoAs while preserving CoA feedback to ensure self‑limitation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31676684/?utm_source=openai))
- Assay design:
  - Primary biochemical screens under matrix‑like pH with variable free CoA to enrich for modulators showing greater activation at low CoA. Develop FRET/thermal‑shift reporters that distinguish apo, CoA‑bound, and acyl‑CoA‑bound ACOT conformers. 
  - Secondary cellular assays in permeabilized mitochondria measuring real‑time liberation of CoA and fall in acyl‑CoA pools by targeted LC‑MS; prioritize hits whose activity drops as free CoA rises (preserved feedback).
  - Mitochondrial delivery: Triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) or peptide‑based carriers; medicinal chemistry to avoid detergent‑like effects. 
- Benchmarking comparators:
  - Negative control: previously reported ACOT11 (Them1) inhibitors (demonstrate orthogonality; we seek activators, not inhibitors). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663673/?utm_source=openai))
  - Orthogonal reset: short pulse of 4′‑phosphopantetheine prodrug to transiently increase CoA, as a pharmacological positive control. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13352496/?utm_source=openai))
- Off‑target triage: Whole‑proteome reactivity screens; lack of covalent adducts; no inhibition of CPT1/2, PDH complex, or respiratory complexes.

Aim 3: Interception testing in vivo
- Models: Diet‑induced metabolic dysfunction in mice, intervening before fibrosis or β‑cell failure; acute lipid‑infusion challenge to stress acyl‑CoA pools.
- Dosing paradigm: Intermittent PAM pulses (e.g., weekly) timed to periods of high metabolic load; adjust to restore free‑CoA ratio without altering basal metabolism.
- Endpoints:
  - Primary: Restoration of mitochondrial free‑CoA:acyl‑CoA in liver/muscle/adipose; reduction in acylcarnitines; reversal of mitochondrial protein hyper‑acylation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4285541/?utm_source=openai))
  - Secondary: Improved PDH flux; enhanced metabolic flexibility; reduced ISR/UPR and inflammatory cytokines; histology showing absence of fibrosis/β‑cell loss.
  - Safety: Lipidomic profile to exclude excess FA release; no hepatic steatosis worsening; cardiac energetics unchanged.

Key experiments and decision points
- Hysteresis test: Drive cells across the acyl‑CoA load up‑sweep and down‑sweep with/without PAM; a true checkpoint will show steep transition and PAM‑induced left‑shift of the boundary.
- Mechanistic confirmation: PAM lowers mitochondrial acyl‑CoA pools and protein acylation, and increases PDH flux, at constant nutrient input—i.e., action is via CoA chemistry, not AMPK/mTOR signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6498146/?utm_source=openai))
- Go/No‑Go (end of year 1): (i) defined tipping ratio in ≥2 cell types; (ii) ≥2 PAM chemotypes with >2‑fold activation at low‑CoA and <1.2‑fold at high‑CoA; (iii) on‑target mitochondrial localization.
- Go/No‑Go (end of year 2): In vivo restoration of free‑CoA ratio with reduction of acylcarnitines and proteome acylation, without adverse lipid accumulation.

Contingencies
- If ACOT activation is limited, deploy a mitochondria‑targeted, short‑lived acyl‑thioester scavenger that reacts preferentially with acyl‑CoAs over CoA and is unmasked by redox cues enriched in high‑debt mitochondria; or use brief pulses of 4′‑phosphopantetheine prodrug to validate the reset principle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13352496/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Frames a metabolic checkpoint as a small‑molecule‑tunable chemical pool threshold rather than a kinase or GPCR.
- Leverages an intrinsic, CoA‑dependent negative feedback of mitochondrial ACOTs to build ultrasensitivity and self‑termination into the therapy. No existing therapy intentionally sharpens this endogenous threshold; published efforts focus on ACOT inhibition (Them1) or global CoA augmentation in rare diseases. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663673/?utm_source=openai))

Outputs and metrics
- A quantitative atlas of mitochondrial free‑CoA:acyl‑CoA tipping points across tissues.
- First‑in‑class ACOT PAMs with conditional activity windows defined by CoA.
- Preclinical proof that pulsed restoration of free CoA erases recent “metabolic debt” (reduced acyl‑proteome, normalized PDH flux) and intercepts progression before fibrosis/β‑cell exhaustion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11601992/?utm_source=openai))

Potential risks and how they are addressed
- Risk: Excess hydrolysis of acyl‑CoAs could raise free fatty acids. Mitigation: Mitochondria‑targeted PAMs with preserved CoA feedback ensure activity falls as free CoA rises; monitor FA re‑esterification and β‑oxidation coupling. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31676684/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Off‑target effects on cytosolic acyl‑CoAs. Mitigation: Matrix targeting; verify cytosolic acyl‑CoA pools by compartment‑resolved profiling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-025-01358-y?utm_source=openai))

Timeline
- Year 1: Define tipping points; build assays; identify hit PAMs.
- Year 2: Optimize leads; demonstrate in vivo interception with pharmacodynamic biomarker panel.
- Year 3: IND‑enabling safety pharmacology focused on lipid handling and cardiac energetics.

Significance
Demonstrating that transient, conditional restoration of mitochondrial free CoA is sufficient to flip a bistable metabolic circuit back to health would establish a new class of “chemical‑pool checkpoint” therapeutics that reset flux and proteostasis without chronically engaging canonical signaling pathways. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6498146/?utm_source=openai))

Title
The lactate–histone lactylation gate as a human metabolic checkpoint for disease interception

Central hypothesis–question
Do short-lived, sub-threshold pulses of histone lysine lactylation (Kla) in circulating and tissue-homing myeloid cells mark resilient “recovery” after transient metabolic stress, whereas supra-threshold, long-dwell Kla commits the organism to progressive insulin resistance and fibrotic remodeling—and can early, local control of proton-coupled lactate entry and/or Kla erasure prevent that commitment in real humans? ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1678-1?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Clamp the Kla pulse. Prevent crossing of the Kla initiation/maintenance threshold during transient metabolic stress by briefly limiting proton-coupled lactate influx and/or accelerating Kla removal in myeloid cells, without suppressing physiological lactate shuttling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7062045/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define the human Kla checkpoint and its threshold.
- Cohort: 300 adults enriched for “transiently unhealthy” phenotypes (episodic hyperglycemia after illness/overfeeding) plus matched controls; 12-month follow-up for conversion to durable metabolic impairment (composite: ≥2 visits with HOMA-IR >2.5 or HbA1c ≥5.7% or NAFLD progression by CAP).
- Provocation experiments: two standardized challenges per subject at baseline and 6 months:
  1) Mixed-meal (75 g carbohydrate, 25 g fat), 4 h sampling.
  2) 15-min moderate-intensity exercise bout, 2 h sampling.
- Readouts:
  - Plasma lactate kinetics and venous pH.
  - Single-cell profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells at 0, 60, 180, 240 min: multi-omic cytometry for pan-Kla and H3K18la, plus targeted CUT&Tag for H3K18la in CD14+ monocytes; paired scRNA-seq for resolution/repair vs inflammatory programs.
  - Stool metagenomics and targeted metabolomics for confounders (e.g., imidazole propionate, SCFAs). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1678-1?utm_source=openai))
- Analysis: estimate individual Kla pulse amplitude, dwell time, and area-above-baseline; fit change-point/bistability models to define a Kla threshold (T) that best separates “recoverers” from “progressors” at 12 months; preregister T from baseline data and test at 6 months (primary endpoint: AUC-ROC for conversion).

Aim 2. Establish causality and druggability ex vivo.
- Cells: freshly isolated human CD14+ monocytes from 60 cohort participants spanning the Kla spectrum.
- Perturbations (1–3 h):
  - Proton-coupled lactate entry: titrate extracellular lactate and pH to physiological ranges; ± selective MCT1 blockade (AZD3965, research-grade) to quantify right-shift of Kla initiation curve; rescue with excess lactate to verify transport specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7062045/?utm_source=openai))
  - pH-sensing: agonize/antagonize GPR65/68 to test acid-signal gating of inflammatory vs resolution programs and Kla dwell time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11431078/?utm_source=openai))
  - Erasers: increase class I HDAC activity window (HDAC1/3 complexes) using targeted recruitment peptides or NAD+-independent cofactor modulation; measure Kla half-life and transcriptional relaxation; orthogonal validation with HDAC1/3 knockdown. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8769552/?utm_source=openai))
- Outputs: lactate–pH–Kla transfer functions, erasure kinetics, and identification of minimal intervention that keeps Kla below T while preserving acute cytokine competence.

Aim 3. Pilot interception trial: clamp the Kla pulse in vivo.
- Design: randomized, double-blind, 3-period crossover (n=60 Kla-high subjects from Aim 1).
- Interventions timed to meal challenge:
  A) Micro-alkali clamp: oral sodium bicarbonate microdose (0.1 g/kg) 30 min pre-meal to blunt extracellular acidification peaks; placebo control. 
  B) Gut-restricted MCT1 modulation: low-dose, non-absorbed MCT flux modulator formulation targeting intestinal immune cell exposure (exploratory, safety-first).
- Primary endpoint: reduction in monocyte H3K18la AUC and dwell time vs placebo; Secondary: preservation of lactate disposal kinetics, improvement in Matsuda index, and dampening of pro-fibrotic transcriptional modules at 3–4 h.
- Safety: serial electrolytes/CO2, GI tolerance; DSMB stopping rules.

Key measurements and assays
- Targeted mass spectrometry for lactate; venous blood gas for pH.
- Flow/mass cytometry panel including pan-Kla and H3K18la antibodies validated to spike-in controls.
- CUT&Tag for H3K18la with UMIs; scRNA-seq for paired state calling.
- Stool metagenomics (HUMAnN3) to quantify UrdA abundance; plasma imidazole propionate by LC–MS/MS as covariate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11872695/?utm_source=openai))

Major outcomes and decision gates
- A pre-specified Kla threshold (T) that prospectively predicts conversion with AUC ≥0.75.
- Ex vivo demonstration that modest reduction of proton-coupled lactate influx or accelerated delactylation prevents surpassing T without broad immunosuppression.
- In vivo demonstration that meal-timed micro-alkali reduces Kla dwell time ≥30% and improves acute insulin signaling proxies, supporting a disease interception window.

Why this fulfills the checkpoint brief
- Switch-like biology: lactate-driven Kla directly couples metabolic flux to chromatin, with known writers/erasers and delayed, program-level effects suitable for commitment gating. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1678-1?utm_source=openai))
- Druggable levers at the gate: proton-coupled transport (MCT1/4), extracellular pH signaling (GPR65/68), and HDAC1/3-mediated Kla erasure offer orthogonal, titratable interventions before irreversible tissue remodeling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7062045/?utm_source=openai))
- Human-first discovery: threshold inference in real exposures identifies the interception window; interventions are brief and peri-stressor, aligning with disease interception rather than chronic suppression.

Exploratory extension (covariate gate)
- Model overlap of the Kla gate with microbiome-derived imidazole propionate spikes that impair insulin signaling via p38γ–p62–mTORC1 and inhibit AMPK via Ser485/491, to test whether coincident ImP and Kla elevations increase commit probability; enables a parallel microbial–metabolite interception arm in subsequent trials. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30401435/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline
- Year 1: assay validation; first 150 subjects; threshold discovery.
- Year 2: full enrollment; ex vivo causality maps; finalize T.
- Year 3: crossover pilot; go/no-go for a targeted Kla-clamp therapeutic (transport/pH/eraser) for prevention in high-risk, pre-fibrotic individuals.

Title
A binary extracellular crosslink checkpoint in metabolic disease: defining and dismantling ε-(γ-glutamyl)lysine “locks” to reopen reversibility

Rationale
- Transglutaminase‑2 (TG2) catalyzes ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine isopeptide bonds that stiffen extracellular matrix (ECM), promote TGF‑β activation, and drive fibrosis across organs. Crosslink accumulation reduces ECM turnover and commits cells to profibrotic, metabolically inflexible programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8307792/?utm_source=openai))
- Stiffness‑dependent YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction sustains fibroblast activation and exhibits mechanical memory, a hysteretic state that persists even after softening—consistent with a thresholded, switch‑like commitment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4329470/?utm_source=openai))
- ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine linkages are chemically stable; their catabolism in mammals is attributed to γ‑glutamylamine cyclotransferase (GGACT), which cleaves γ‑glutamyl‑ε‑lysine motifs to lysine and 5‑oxoproline—but characterized activity is mainly on isodipeptides generated after proteolysis, implying limited capacity to reverse intact ECM crosslinks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2843214/?utm_source=openai))
- Current antifibrotic strategies inhibit crosslink formation (TG2/LOX inhibitors) but do not remove existing locks; a TG2 inhibitor has reached the clinic in celiac disease, validating druggability but not reversal. ([nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2032441?utm_source=openai))
- Independent of TG2, accumulation of reactive carbonyls (e.g., methylglyoxal) displays detox capacity thresholds (Glo1 balance), supporting a kinetic saturation framework for binary transitions to damage accrual. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5297820/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis and Research Goal
Hypothesis: A tissue‑agnostic checkpoint exists when ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine crosslink density surpasses the combined Vmax of ECM proteolysis and γ‑glutamylamine catabolism, producing a thermodynamic/mechanical trap that locks YAP/TAZ‑driven profibrotic and metabolic dysfunction. Direct enzymatic cleavage of a minimal fraction of ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine bonds in situ will cross a reversal threshold, reduce stiffness‑dependent signaling, and restore repair capacity before irreversible organ remodeling.

Goal: Discover the crosslink‑density threshold (C*εγ) that commits tissues to disease and invent a druggable, conditionally activated “isopeptidase” that dismantles ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine locks in the ECM to intercept progression.

Atomic Strategy
Leverage allosteric unmasking to create a GGACT‑based, ECM‑targeted enzyme that is catalytically latent in normal tissue and switches ON only upon multivalent engagement of ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine motifs, thereby providing localized, thresholded cleavage of TG2 crosslinks.

Specific Aims

Aim 1. Define the ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine crosslink checkpoint (C*εγ) and its coupling to mechanotransduction.
- Build quantitative maps of ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine density, ECM stiffness, and YAP/TAZ nuclear localization across liver, lung, kidney, and adipose in diet‑induced and toxin‑induced models from early injury to fibrosis.
- Methods: targeted LC‑MS/MS for ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine after standardized pepsin/trypsin digestion; AFM and Brillouin microscopy for micromechanics; immunofluorescence and nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation for YAP/TAZ. Statistical breakpoint and hysteresis analyses to estimate C*εγ and irreversibility windows.
- Decision criterion: identify a slope change in YAP/TAZ nuclear ratio vs ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine density indicating a thresholded commit point.

Aim 2. Evolve an ECM‑active ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine isopeptidase using GGACT as a scaffold and allosteric unmasking for threshold gating.
- Design: (i) extend GGACT’s substrate tunnel and binding pocket via focused libraries to accept peptide‑embedded ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine; (ii) fuse an autoinhibitory pro‑segment occluding the catalytic base, tethered to a crosslink‑binding reader (single‑domain binder for ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine) that disengages only upon bivalent occupancy in crosslink‑dense ECM (avidity‑dependent switch).
- Selection: yeast/bacterial display with peptide‑crosslinked hydrogels presenting defined densities of ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine; FACS‑based activity readouts using self‑immolative fluorogenic ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine substrates embedded in gels.
- Engineering goals: kcat/KM ≥ native GGACT on isodipeptides; >100‑fold activity increase between low‑ and high‑density crosslink gels (digital response).
- Delivery: AAV or LNP‑mRNA encoding a secreted, ECM‑affinity‑tagged enzyme; biodistribution tuned by tissue‑specific peptides.

Aim 3. Test whether dismantling ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine locks reopens metabolic reversibility in vivo.
- Models: early‑to‑mid stage fibrosis in lung (bleomycin), NASH‑like liver injury, kidney UUO; dosing before established collagen crosslink plateaus.
- Endpoints: reduction of ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine by LC‑MS/MS; decreased stiffness; cytoplasmic re‑localization of YAP/TAZ; downregulation of profibrotic transcripts; improved insulin sensitivity or organ‑specific metabolic readouts; safety (no excess ECM fragility).
- Controls: TG2 inhibition (formation block) without cleavage; catalytically dead enzyme; constitutively active enzyme to evaluate off‑target risk.

Aim 4. Define translational biomarkers and the therapeutic window.
- Fluid biomarkers: circulating ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine isodipeptide fragments (post‑proteolysis) as a proxy for crosslink turnover; 5‑oxoproline increases as on‑target pharmacodynamic readout of cyclotransferase activity.
- Imaging: MRI elastography to gate patient selection at or just beyond C*εγ; ratiometric YAP/TAZ target gene panels from accessible biopsies/cells.

Key Tests That Falsify the Hypothesis
- If crosslink reduction fails to shift YAP/TAZ localization or profibrotic programs despite substantial ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine bond cleavage, the crosslink checkpoint is not causal.
- If constitutive cleavage causes ECM failure at sub‑threshold densities, the approach lacks a therapeutic window and the allosteric gate is inadequate.

Innovation
- Reframes fibrosis/metabolic progression as a binary extracellular crosslink checkpoint and targets bond cleavage—not merely formation inhibition—to exit the locked state. Existing work links TG2‑mediated crosslinking to fibrosis and validates TG2 as a target but does not address in situ reversal; GGACT provides a natural catalytic chemistry to build upon. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8307792/?utm_source=openai))
- Uses avidity‑driven allosteric unmasking so catalysis occurs only above crosslink density thresholds, satisfying disease interception requirements and limiting off‑target ECM weakening.

Feasibility and Mechanistic Soundness
- TG2 crosslinks are abundant and profibrotic; YAP/TAZ confer stiffness‑dependent commitment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8307792/?utm_source=openai))
- GGACT cleaves γ‑glutamyl‑ε‑lysine chemistry to lysine and 5‑oxoproline; engineering for peptidyl substrates is a tractable catalytic extension, testable in directed evolution with crosslinked peptide substrates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2843214/?utm_source=openai))
- Binary response is enforced by multivalent binding and local crosslink density, consistent with threshold behavior in other detox/repair systems (e.g., Glo1‑MGO). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5297820/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and Go/No‑Go
- Year 1: establish C*εγ across two organs; demonstrate ≥10‑fold on/off switch in engineered enzyme on synthetic gels.
- Year 2: reduce ε‑(γ‑glutamyl)lysine by ≥30% in vivo with concurrent YAP/TAZ cytoplasmic shift and stiffness drop ≥15%.
- Year 3: demonstrate functional rescue (organ performance/metabolic endpoints) without ECM rupture; finalize PD biomarkers.

Risk Mitigation
- If direct cleavage within intact ECM is inefficient, deploy a two‑step strategy: (i) mild proteolysis to expose isodipeptides followed by GGACT‑mediated cleavage; (ii) bias endogenous TG2 toward isopeptidase/transamidase activity using sacrificial amine donors to transfer γ‑glutamyl groups to soluble acceptors, then clear with GGACT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8307792/?utm_source=openai))

Expected Outcome
A validated, druggable extracellular “unlocking” enzyme that converts a crosslink‑defined metabolic/fibrotic checkpoint from committed to reversible, creating a general interception modality across organs before fibrosis, β‑cell exhaustion, or cardiovascular remodeling become irreversible. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8307792/?utm_source=openai))
