Title
Dynamic-noise fingerprinting for rapid, quantitative deconvolution of two-source exosome mixtures using high-speed SERS power spectra

Background and novelty check
- Label-free SERS differentiates exosomes by biochemical fingerprints but is typically analyzed via static spectra or machine learning classifiers; mixture quantification remains challenging. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532067/?utm_source=openai))
- Temporal SERS fluctuations at plasmonic hotspots encode nanoscale dynamics and have been resolved at microsecond-to-millisecond timescales, but this dynamic information has not been exploited to unmix exosome mixtures. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-019-0535-6?utm_source=openai))
- Tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS) work uses power spectral density (PSD) primarily to mitigate environmental noise rather than as a composition fingerprint, indicating an opportunity to repurpose PSD as an analytic signal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10237153/?utm_source=openai))
- As an optional identifiability aid, brief cholesterol extraction by methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) perturbs vesicle membranes; EVs and related particles are cholesterol-rich, and MβCD rapidly depletes cholesterol, supporting a controlled differential response step if needed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9227390/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis and goal
Hypothesis: The power spectral density of high-speed SERS intensity fluctuations generated by exosome–plasmonic interfaces is source-specific and mixes linearly across populations; therefore, deconvolving the measured PSD of a blended sample against reference PSDs from pure sources yields an accurate and rapid estimate of mixture ratios. Goal: Build a reference-calibrated, inline-capable platform to quantify two-source exosome mixture fractions over 20:80–80:20 within minutes.

Atomic strategy
Treat temporal “noise” (PSD of SERS intensity fluctuations) as the primary compositional signal. Use convex PSD unmixing against library PSDs from each pure source to estimate mixture coefficients; add a short, calibrated cholesterol-depletion pulse only when conditioning is poor to create a second independent equation.

Specific aims
1) Establish dynamic-noise reference libraries: Generate source-specific PSD signatures for pure exosomes under fixed optics and flow conditions. 
2) Develop convex PSD unmixing: Implement fast deconvolution of mixed-sample PSDs to estimate mixture fractions with confidence intervals.
3) Validate accuracy and speed across wide ratios: Benchmark against orthogonal quantification; define limits of detection and robustness to matrix effects.
4) Scale to inline QC: Integrate a flow-through plasmonic cartridge and streaming analysis suitable for manufacturing.

Rationale
- SERS time traces fluctuate due to nanoscale motion of membranes, adsorbates, and near-field gap dynamics; sources with distinct lipid/protein compositions generate distinct fluctuation spectra even when mean spectra overlap. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-019-0535-6?utm_source=openai))
- In a mixture, independent emitter populations contribute additively to the measured PSD under stationarity and linear response, enabling convex decomposition.
- SERS provides rapid, label-free readouts and has been demonstrated on exosomes and plasmonic capture platforms compatible with flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532067/?utm_source=openai))

Research plan

Aim 1: Reference PSD libraries
- Materials: Two cell-type sources (A, B) cultured under standardized conditions; EVs isolated by SEC/UC with particle counts normalized by NTA; optional proteo-/lipidomic profiling for characterization.
- Plasmonic flow cell: Silver or gold nanobowl/metasurface cartridge optimized for stable hotspot distributions and low drift; validated for exosome SERS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11781986/?utm_source=openai))
- Acquisition: Continuous-flow capture at fixed shear; 532–785 nm excitation; 100–500 kHz photodetector sampling of total SERS intensity in a fixed spectral window around dominant bands. For each pure source, record ≥200 independent 0.5–2 s traces.
- Feature extraction: Compute PSDs (Welch method), Allan variance, and intermittency metrics; retain frequency bands with minimal instrument noise and maximal between-source divergence (cross-validated by day and cartridge).

Milestones and success criteria:
- Day-to-day PSD stability within ±10% across key bands for each source.
- Cross-validated classifier AUC ≥0.95 distinguishing A vs B using PSD features alone.

Aim 2: Convex PSD unmixing
- Model: M(f) ≈ α·PA(f) + (1−α)·PB(f) + ε(f), where PA, PB are reference PSDs and α is the fraction of source A by particle count within the probed ensemble.
- Estimation: Nonnegative least squares on log-PSD within selected bands; bootstrap over time windows to yield α̂ and uncertainty. Include a multiplicative scale parameter to accommodate total intensity variations.
- Calibration: Verify linearity by measuring defined binary mixes (10:90…90:10). Assess bias vs. particle count vs. mass-normalized definitions; report both if size distributions differ.

Milestones:
- Mean absolute error (MAE) ≤5% across 20:80–80:20; ≤8% at 10:90 and 90:10.
- Throughput ≥12 mixtures/hour in bench format; algorithm runtime <1 s/sample.

Aim 3: Validation against orthogonal quantification
- Comparator 1: Targeted bead immunoassay of shared tetraspanins (e.g., CD9, CD63, CD81); exploit relative expression trends that are preserved across batches to compute ratio-based mixture estimates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8508895/?utm_source=openai))
- Comparator 2: TRPS particle counts and size profiles to ensure no gross selection bias during SERS capture; use TRPS primarily for QC. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))
- Comparator 3: Label-free static SERS classification baseline to demonstrate added value of dynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6532067/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones:
- Concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) ≥0.9 between PSD-unmixed α̂ and comparator estimates across all mixes and matrices (buffer, 10% serum).

Aim 4: Inline and perturbation module
- Flow integration: Install the plasmonic cartridge inline with a sampling loop; continuous PSD streaming and rolling-window α̂ outputs every 30–60 s.
- Optional identifiability pulse: For samples with high PSD similarity (condition number > threshold), inject a brief MβCD pulse (≤0.1–0.5 mM, ≤60 s) then quench. Pre-calibrate fractional PSD shifts (εA, εB) using pure sources and solve the two-equation system from pre/post states to refine α̂. Cholesterol depletion in extracellular particles and membranes supports a measurable, reversible perturbation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9227390/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones:
- Inline operation ≥2 h with drift-corrected α̂ stability (CV ≤5% on constant mixes).
- In ill-conditioned cases, perturbation reduces α̂ uncertainty by ≥2× without altering particle integrity metrics.

Data analysis and QC
- Internal standard: Spike a small fraction of synthetic liposomes with fixed PSD to normalize instrument drift.
- Blind tests: 30 blinded mixtures spanning ratios and matrices; preregister accuracy targets.

Risk, alternatives, and stopping rules
- Risk: PSD drift due to substrate variability. Mitigation: cartridge QC using a standard liposome PSD; discard runs exceeding drift thresholds.
- Risk: Sources with near-identical PSDs. Mitigation: deploy optional MβCD pulse; if still ill-conditioned, fall back to ratio-invariant immunoassay for that pair.
- Stop if PSD stability cannot reach ±10% across days or if MAE >8% persists after mitigation.

Expected outcomes and impact
- A fast, label-free, and scalable approach that quantifies two-source exosome mixtures by repurposing temporal SERS “noise” as the compositional signal, validated against orthogonal assays and integrated for inline QC. This reframes a nuisance (fluctuations) into a robust fingerprint, enabling rapid mixture quantification without particle sorting. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-019-0535-6?utm_source=openai))

Title
Counterflow electrokinetic stall-manifold sorting with inline nanopore counting for rapid, label-free quantification of mixed exosome populations

Fused hypothesis–question
Can we tune a microchannel so that the net axial velocity equals zero for one exosome population but not the other—by co-adjusting pressure-driven flow, electroosmotic flow, and electrophoretic mobility—thereby creating a stable “stall manifold” that diverts one population into a capture lane while the other passes through; and can inline resistive‑pulse nanopores count each fraction fast enough to return accurate mixing ratios across 20:80–80:20 blends? This rests on documented variability in EV surface charge (zeta potential) and mechanics by origin, dominance of negative surface charge under physiological conditions, and the existence of electrokinetic zero‑velocity conditions in microchannels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7364712/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Engineer an iso‑velocity landscape: set the local balance vnet = vpressure + vEO(wall) + vEP(particle) to zero along a short constricted zone for population A (given its electrophoretic mobility and deformation‑dependent hydrodynamic slip) while keeping vnet ≠ 0 for population B. Side collectors placed at the zero‑velocity manifold bleed off A; the through‑lane collects B. Quantify both outlets by inline tunable resistive‑pulse nanopores that provide single‑particle counts and pulse‑shape parameters sensitive to deformation, enabling rapid ratio estimation and an orthogonal cross‑check on stiffness. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Map electrokinetic contrast between the two exosome sources. Measure ζ‑potential distributions and electrophoretic mobilities in the intended buffer; confirm that distributions are separable enough to position a stall manifold. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7364712/?utm_source=openai))
2) Build and validate a counterflow electrokinetic sorter with a designed stall manifold. Demonstrate diversion of one population into a capture lane while the other transits, at >10^6 particles/min per chip via channel parallelization. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
3) Integrate resistive‑pulse nanopores at each outlet for absolute counting and deformation‑aware signatures; validate linearity of ratio readout from 20:80 to 80:20 and beyond. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and novelty relative to prior art
- Electrokinetic deterministic lateral displacement (eDLD) and related schemes have fractionated EVs using post arrays and applied fields. Here, separation is not by DLD critical size or post interactions but by creating a local zero‑velocity manifold via EP–EO–pressure balance in a smooth constricted segment, i.e., a stall‑and‑bleed geometry. This exploits property‑dependent net velocity rather than obstacle‑mediated trajectories. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2022/lc/d2lc00583b?utm_source=openai))
- Zero‑net‑velocity trapping/focusing in microfluidics is known in electrokinetics, but has not been coupled to exosome fractionation with inline nanopore counting to return absolute mixing ratios in continuous flow. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2009/lc/b819054b?utm_source=openai))
- Resistive‑pulse sensing for EVs is established for size/concentration; leveraging pulse dynamics and voltage‑dependent electrodeformation to extract stiffness for vesicles provides an orthogonal confirmation channel on subtype identity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Device architecture
- Materials: Glass/SiO2 or COC microchannels with thin-film Ag/AgCl electrodes. 2‑cm main channel, 50–200 µm wide, with a 1–2 mm long constricted segment (depth 1–2 µm; width 2–5 µm) flanked by shallow side collectors (0.5–1 µm deep). Constriction amplifies local E to enhance EP/EO contrast while increasing lubrication sensitivity to vesicle deformation. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
- Surface chemistry: Wall ζ tuned with silane or polyelectrolyte multilayers to set EO mobility independently of particle EP. PEGylation reduces adhesion. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2009/lc/b819054b?utm_source=openai))
- Actuation: Superposed pressure drop (ΔP) and axial electric field (E). Adjust ionic strength (1–10 mM) to increase Debye length and EP contrast while limiting Joule heating. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2009/lc/b819054b?utm_source=openai))

Operating principle and tuning
- Determine ζ‑mobility distributions of each exosome source via capillary electrophoresis or multi‑pore transit times; choose E and ΔP such that μEP,A·E + μEO·E + μP(ΔP, geometry, deformationA) ≈ 0 at the constriction for population A, while the same sum remains >0 (or <0) for B. This creates a spatially confined stall band for A; shear‑aligned collectors continuously withdraw stalled vesicles. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
- Validation: Inject pure A and pure B to confirm, respectively, near‑unity recovery in the side lane and through lane; then test mixtures. Record residence time distributions around the constriction to confirm selective stalling only for the targeted mobility band. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))

Inline quantification
- At each outlet, integrate one to tens of resistive‑pulse nanopores (polymer or solid‑state) in parallel microchannels. Each event yields ΔI (size proxy) and τ (dwell time) features; multi‑bias acquisition leverages electrodeformation to add stiffness sensitivity for vesicles. Solid‑state and nanopipette studies demonstrate deformation‑dependent pulse shapes for soft nanoparticles and liposomes, supporting stiffness inference. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))
- Throughput and scaling: Current solid‑state microfluidic integrations demonstrate tens of pores per chip; scale by duplicating channels across the wafer rather than pushing pore count per node. Use real‑time “data sieving” for multichannel acquisition. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13394?utm_source=openai))

Calibration and analytics
- Build a forward model linking E, ΔP, buffer, and wall ζ to the stall manifold location and capture fraction for a given mobility distribution; fit parameters using pure‑source runs. Use this model to convert paired outlet counts into mixture ratios. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
- Orthogonal validation: Compare outlet‑specific pulse‑shape distributions (stiffness proxy) to ensure the manifold targeted the intended population; confirm with AFM or bulk ζ‑potential as needed. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2016/nr/c6nr03371g?utm_source=openai))

Performance targets and metrics
- Distinguishability: Receiver‑operating characteristic AUC ≥0.9 for two exosome sources differing by ≥5–10 mV in modal ζ or by clear stiffness signatures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7364712/?utm_source=openai))
- Quantitative accuracy: Absolute ratio error ≤5% across 20:80–80:20; linear regression slope within 0.95–1.05; R^2 ≥0.98. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))
- Throughput: ≥10^6 vesicles/min/chip via 50–100 parallel lanes with single nanopore per lane; sample‑to‑answer <10 min. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13394?utm_source=openai))

Controls and confounders
- Buffer dependence: Because EV ζ depends on medium, all calibrations use the assay buffer; report ionic strength and pH explicitly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9563386/?utm_source=openai))
- Heterogeneity: If ζ distributions overlap, shift selectivity by adjusting wall ζ (thus EO) and constriction geometry to re‑center the stall manifold; verify that shifts do not rupture vesicles by monitoring pulse statistics and recovery. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
- Electrolysis/thermal management: Use salt bridges/agarose‑embedded electrodes and pulsed fields to limit gas formation and heating. Monitor conductivity to ensure stability of EO/EP balance. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- M1: Mobility mapping and buffer standardization for two cell‑type exosome sources; establish separable ζ distributions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7364712/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Demonstrate selective stalling and diversion with ≥80% recovery and ≤10% cross‑over in continuous flow for pure sources. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c01303?utm_source=openai))
- M3: Integrate nanopore counters; achieve linear, absolute ratio quantification on 20:80–80:20 mixtures within ±5% error. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335984/?utm_source=openai))
- M4: Wafer‑level parallelization to ≥50 lanes with per‑lane nanopore; validate stability over 8‑hour operation with controls. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.13394?utm_source=openai))

Impact
This work converts intrinsic electrokinetic and mechanical heterogeneity of exosomes into a deterministic spatial separation without labels, then counts both fractions at single‑particle resolution. It avoids DLD/post arrays and immunocapture while remaining compatible with planar, parallel microfabrication for scale‑out. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2022/lc/d2lc00583b?utm_source=openai))

Title
ROS-activated, HS-mimetic glyco-coatings on extracellular vesicles to target damage-state lectin networks via avidity thresholds

Unified hypothesis–question
Can exogenously glycoengineered EVs, bearing short highly sulfated glycan mimetics that are chemically masked until exposed to pathological ROS, achieve selective adhesion and uptake only at sites where damage-state lectin networks (RAGE oligomers, scavenger receptors, and selectins/chemokine depots) are dense and the endothelial glycocalyx is degraded?

Atomic strategy
Exploit two convergent pathophysiologic filters to gate binding: (i) inflammation-driven receptor clustering and dependence on sulfated glycan co-receptors (especially RAGE oligomerization on HS motifs; scavenger receptors’ preference for polyanions; selectin/chemokine engagement by sulfated GAGs), and (ii) local ROS bursts. Engineer EVs post-isolation with short heparan-sulfate–like (HS-mimetic) sulfated oligomers as polyvalent, low-affinity ligands, then install a ROS-cleavable stealth cap that prevents off-target binding until it is removed by pathological ROS. Binding arises only where receptor density and ROS jointly surpass thresholds. This targets the damage state, not cell identity. (RAGE–HS dependence and oligomerization; selectin/chemokine–heparin interactions; scavenger receptor polyanion recognition; endothelial glycocalyx loss in inflammation; ROS-cleavable linkers on EVs/nanocarriers.) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build and characterize ROS-unmaskable HS-mimetic displays on EVs post-isolation.
Aim 2. Establish damage-state selectivity in vitro by thresholded avidity: receptor-density and ROS co-dependence.
Aim 3. Demonstrate selective in vivo homing and uptake in acute vascular-injury models, benchmarked against control EVs and non-ROS-responsive coatings.

Rationale and novelty
- Damage/inflammation remodels endothelium: glycocalyx degradation (heparanase, MMPs, hyaluronidases) exposes receptors; RAGE and scavenger receptors engage sulfated or polyanionic ligands; selectins and immobilized chemokines are presented on inflamed luminal surfaces. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8668992/?utm_source=openai))
- RAGE signaling requires HS-mediated oligomerization (hexamers stabilized by HS oligos), creating a density-sensitive binding platform for sulfated motifs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))
- Class A scavenger receptors and LOX-1 preferentially bind polyanionic/oxidation-associated ligands and are upregulated in vascular injury and atherosclerotic inflammation. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/31549?utm_source=openai))
- Heparin/HS oligos bind selectins and many chemokines; short, highly sulfated fragments retain binding with tunable anticoagulation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7694675/?utm_source=openai))
- EV deglycosylation increases nonspecific uptake; here, instead of broad unmasking, we use a ROS-gated cap to minimize off-target capture, exposing HS-mimetics only at diseased foci. ROS-labile linkers have been used on exosomes and nanoparticles to de-shield or release cargos selectively in inflamed tissues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7006786/?utm_source=openai))
- Prior EV work has installed dextran sulfate tags via producer-cell metabolic glycoengineering; our approach is exogenous, post-isolation, and adds a ROS gate to enforce state specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13045864/?utm_source=openai))

Research plan

Aim 1. Synthesize and validate ROS-unmaskable HS-mimetic EVs
1.1 Ligand selection and synthesis
- Two HS-mimetic panels:
  - Short heparin/HS oligos (dp8–dp12) with minimized anticoagulant activity (favor 6-O/N-sulfation with limited 2-O-sulfation). Alternative: low-anticoagulant heparins (ODSH). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30061484/?utm_source=openai))
  - Dextran-sulfate or styrenesulfonate oligomers (defined DP, high sulfation) as SR-A/RAGE-interacting mimetics. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/31549?utm_source=openai))
- Conjugate each to a membrane anchor (DSPE-PEG(2–5k)-N3 or -maleimide). Prepare a ROS-cleavable stealth cap: a short PEG shell linked via aryl boronate or thioketal to the ligand anchor, such that cleavage sheds PEG and unveils the sulfated chain. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5689534/?utm_source=openai))

1.2 Post-isolation EV functionalization
- Purify parental EVs (size exclusion/ultrafiltration). Graft anchors by post-insertion (DSPE) or mild surface amine coupling (sulfo-NHS–DBCO), followed by strain-promoted click to ligands and ROS-cleavable PEG cap. Confirm colloidal integrity and marker retention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12905755/?utm_source=openai))

1.3 Physicochemical and biochemical QC
- Size/ζ-potential (NTA/DLS), TEM/cryogenic TEM, grafting density by fluorophore-tagged ligands, sulfate quantification, PEG cap density.
- ROS responsiveness: kinetics of cap cleavage at 50–500 μM H2O2/ONOO−; negligible cleavage at ≤10 μM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13220273/?utm_source=openai))
- Binding surrogates: surface plasmon resonance with immobilized RAGE ectodomain ± HS oligos; selectin-Ig binding; SR-A ectodomain binding; inhibition by soluble heparin or poly I (SR-A competitor). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria, Aim 1
- Stable EVs with tunable ligand densities; ROS cap half-life 5–30 min at ≥100 μM H2O2; <10% cleavage at ≤10 μM over 2 h.
- On-cap EVs show minimal binding to RAGE/selectins/SR-A; de-capped EVs show >10× increase.

Aim 2. Demonstrate receptor-density and ROS co-thresholding in vitro
2.1 Cell models under flow
- Human endothelial cells: resting vs TNFα/IL-1β–activated (E-/P-selectin, ICAM-1 up; RAGE up), with enzymatic glycocalyx modulation (heparinase to mimic shedding). Include macrophage-like cells (M1/M2) for SR pathways. Quantify receptor density by flow cytometry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7237145/?utm_source=openai))
- Microfluidic flow assays (1–20 dyn/cm2) comparing: unmodified EVs, HS-mimetic EVs (no cap), capped HS-mimetic EVs ± ROS pulse.

2.2 Causality tests
- Blockers: anti-RAGE, heparinase pretreatment (disrupt RAGE–HS coreceptoring), selectin antagonists, and SR-A blockade (poly I or dextran sulfate competition). Evaluate adhesion, rolling-to-firm arrest, and internalization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))
- Thresholding: vary ligand density on EVs and receptor density on cells; fit multivalent binding models to identify avidity cutoff. Benchmark against deglycosylated EVs to show the necessity of HS-mimetic ligands and ROS gating for state selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7006786/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria, Aim 2
- Minimal binding of capped EVs to resting endothelium; robust adhesion/uptake only when both: ROS pre-exposure and receptor density exceed predefined thresholds.
- Blockade profiles consistent with RAGE/SR/selectin co-engagement: >60% reduction with combined anti-RAGE + poly I; sensitivity to heparinase on the cell surface. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Validate in vivo targeting to damage-state tissues
3.1 Models
- Acute lung inflammation (intratracheal or systemic LPS) and hepatic ischemia–reperfusion injury; both feature glycocalyx shedding, elevated RAGE/lectins, and ROS bursts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8668992/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: naïve mice, ROS-scavenger pre-treatment cohorts.

3.2 Dosing and readouts
- Systemic administration of fluorescently labeled EVs: capped HS-mimetic vs uncapped vs unmodified.
- Biodistribution (IVIS), organ EV load by flow cytometry/histology, endothelial co-localization, and pharmacodynamics (e.g., reduction in neutrophil infiltration if therapeutic cargo is included).
- Specificity tests: heparinase in situ (local), RAGE-blocking mAb pre-dose, poly I pre-dose.

3.3 Safety
- Coagulation panel to ensure no anticoagulant effects from short heparin oligos/ODSH; cytokines; complement activation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30061484/?utm_source=openai))
- RES capture assessment; confirm masking reduces liver/spleen uptake compared to uncapped HS-mimetic EVs. Use SR-A blockade to dissect mechanism. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378517306007010?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria, Aim 3
- ≥3-fold higher lesion-to-healthy tissue EV ratio for capped HS-mimetic EVs vs controls; significant loss of targeting with RAGE or SR-A blockade; reduced off-target RES uptake relative to uncapped condition.

Methods overview
- EV source: human MSC- or HEK-derived sEVs; SEC purification; endotoxin-free.
- Chemistry: DSPE-PEG anchors; maleimide-thiol or SPAAC click for ligand/cap attachment; aryl boronate or thioketal linkers for ROS lability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5689534/?utm_source=openai))
- Analytics: NTA, ζ-potential, TEM; proteomics; glycan profiling; ligand density calibration; ROS-cleavage kinetics.
- In vitro flow: microfluidic endothelium-on-a-chip; rolling/adhesion quantification. Receptor density modulation by cytokine dose/time.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: RES clearance via scavenger receptors. Mitigation: ROS cap in circulation; tune ligand density and chain length; use short HS oligos/ODSH to reduce nonspecific interactions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30061484/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Anticoagulation by heparin fragments. Mitigation: choose dp8–dp12 with low 3-O-/2-O-sulfation; verify thrombin time; consider non-heparin sulfated mimetics (dextran sulfate, PSS). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30061484/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Excessive general stickiness. Mitigation: maintain low per-site affinity and rely on multivalency and receptor clustering; demonstrate blockade specificity (RAGE/selectins/SR-A). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: ROS heterogeneity across tissues. Mitigation: adjust linker kinetics; test both aryl boronate (fast) and thioketal (moderate) caps; include dual-trigger caps (ROS + pH) in future work. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5689534/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision gates (12–18 months)
M1 (Month 4): Stable, capped HS-mimetic EVs with validated ROS-decap kinetics and negligible basal receptor binding. Go/No-Go: If cap cannot prevent basal binding, switch to higher-MW PEG or denser capping.
M2 (Month 8): In vitro demonstration of dual-threshold gating (receptor density + ROS) with >10× on/off binding ratio; defined blockade signatures. Go/No-Go: If selectivity <5×, re-optimize ligand density/spacing and cap kinetics.
M3 (Month 14): In vivo lesion-to-healthy accumulation ≥3×; blocked by anti-RAGE/poly I; safety panel clean. Go/No-Go: If not achieved, pivot to alternative sulfation patterns or combine with mild EV desialylation plus ROS cap to raise avidity only after activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7006786/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
This work reframes natural inflammatory barriers and chemistry as gates rather than obstacles. By combining HS-mimetic polyvalent ligands with ROS-activated exposure, EVs read the damage-state code—RAGE–HS oligomers, scavenger receptor clusters, and selectin/chemokine depots revealed by glycocalyx loss—yielding delivery that is conditional on pathology, not lineage. The exogenous workflow avoids producer-cell engineering and is broadly compatible with clinical EV sources. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3806902/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Pan-cancer organotropism prediction by glycohydrodynamic compatibility on a glycobiomimetic multi‑organ adhesion chip

Central hypothesis–question
Do tumor cells and extracellular vesicles (EVs) preferentially tether and roll under physiologic shear on vascular interfaces whose glycocalyx charge/hydration barrier and glycan-binding landscapes match their surface glycan motifs, and can this functional “glycohydrodynamic compatibility index” (GCI) serve as a pan‑cancer predictor of organ‑specific metastasis? This rests on two established observations: (i) endothelial and tumor glycocalyces impose electro‑steric and electrostatic barriers that gate receptor–ligand engagement and leukocyte/tumor adhesion; their degradation or reduced sialylation increases adhesion, indicating barrier control of capture under flow; and (ii) tumor and EV glycans (high‑mannose, core fucose, sialylation) modulate rolling, uptake, and organ‑biased biodistribution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214841/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Recast organotropism as a glycohydrodynamic matching problem: destination is predicted not by motif lists alone but by the joint fit between (a) motif‑specific adhesion kinetics and (b) the opposing organ endothelial glycocalyx’s electro‑steric (charge/hydration/thickness) barrier under the relevant shear regime. Quantify this fit as an organ‑lane GCI and use the GCI vector as a pan‑cancer organ‑destination classifier. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7136287/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and calibrate a glycobiomimetic multi‑organ adhesion chip that parameterizes the endothelial glycocalyx barrier.
2) Embed glycan‑templated molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) microdomains to provide stable, valency‑tunable surrogates of organ lectin landscapes and to extract motif‑specific kinetic parameters.
3) Derive per‑sample GCI vectors from functional adhesion readouts of tumor cells and EVs across cancers; train and validate a multi‑organ organotropism classifier against clinical/metastatic outcomes.

Aim 1. Glycobiomimetic multi‑organ adhesion chip
- Design: Parallel microchannels (“lanes”) represent target organs (brain, lung, liver, bone, lymph node). Each lane presents a polymer‑brush glycocalyx with independently tunable grafting density, thickness, and fixed charge to emulate organ endothelium barriers. Tuning uses polyelectrolyte/hydrophilic brushes to set hydration and Donnan potentials within the Debye length relevant to receptor engagement. Validation criteria: barrier thickness, zeta potential, and antiadhesive function. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7136287/?utm_source=openai))
- Physiologic shear: Operate each lane at microvascular shear relevant to the organ. Readouts under flow include capture probability, rolling velocity distribution, pause frequency, transition to firm arrest, and detachment under step‑shear. These metrics map to effective kon/koff and barrier‑height terms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))
- Biological validation: Demonstrate that neuraminidase‑mediated reduction of endothelial sialic acid increases tumor‑cell capture at fixed ligand density (positive control for barrier gating). Show restoration of antiadhesive behavior with re‑sialylation or increased brush hydration/charge. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6668365/?utm_source=openai))
- Context with field: Multi‑organ chips probing organotropism exist but largely rely on living organ‑specific cell layers; here the advance is explicit parameterization of glycocalyx barrier physics per organ lane, independent of cell‑line idiosyncrasies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12158725/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. MIP‑defined glycan microdomains as receptor surrogates and calibrants
- Rationale: Natural lectin landscapes vary by density, clustering, and microenvironment; MIPs provide water‑stable “digital lectins” templated to N‑glycan motifs with tunable affinity and multivalency, enabling standardized surfaces across lanes and runs. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))
- Implementation:
  - Synthesize MIPs templated to high‑mannose, core‑fucosylated, and defined α2,3/α2,6‑sialylated N‑glycan epitopes; embed as patterned microdomains within each lane’s brush to emulate organ‑relevant glycan‑binding repertoires while decoupling chemistry (motif identity) from physics (barrier properties). ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))
  - Kinetic calibration: Use model glycoproteins/lectins to extract kon/koff per motif on the chip and verify retention of specificity under flow. Use competitive binding with fluorescent MIPs spiked into samples to estimate effective motif abundance/avidity on cells/EVs. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))
- Justification: Glycan‑imprinted nanoparticles and surfaces selectively bind complex glycans and glycoproteins in water and have been used for imaging/capture; no prior work deploys them to parameterize organ‑specific adhesion under shear. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Derive GCI vectors and train a pan‑cancer organotropism classifier
- Inputs: Panels of human cancer cell lines and PDX‑derived cells across primary sites; matched plasma EVs from retrospective cohorts with documented first‑site metastasis; prospectively, EVs from newly diagnosed patients with longitudinal outcome capture. EV glycosylation features (high‑mannose, α2,6‑sialylation) and sialylation‑dependent uptake provide orthogonal priors and mechanistic anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7827205/?utm_source=openai))
- Assay: For each sample, run cell and EV modes separately across lanes. Compute lane‑wise GCI from adhesion kinetics adjusted for barrier parameters and motif‑specific kinetics derived in Aim 2. The GCI vector is the feature for a multi‑label classifier predicting organ probabilities. Concordance between EV‑GCI and cell‑GCI supports robust organotropism; discordance flags pre‑metastatic niche conditioning without efficient extravasation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks: Compare performance to baselines from lectin microarrays or label‑free biosensors on EVs alone and to organ‑on‑chip models without explicit barrier parameterization. Expect improvement because destination depends on both bond kinetics and the opposing barrier. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10540341/?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
- Chip fabrication: Microfluidic lanes with surface‑initiated brush grafting to set thickness/charge; patterned MIP microdomains for motif‑specific binding; configurable shear per lane. Barrier parameters are measured via AFM force‑distance, QCM‑D hydration mass, and streaming potential. Adhesion assays are imaged at high speed to extract rolling/tethering events and pause lifetimes. Polymer‑brush theory provides the barrier term entering a probabilistic capture model. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7136287/?utm_source=openai))
- Samples: Size‑selected EVs by SEC/density gradient; optional lectin‑depletion/enrichment subsets to stress‑test motif dependency. Desialylation or glycosylation‑editing controls on cells/EVs perturb charge and ligand exposure to verify expected shifts in GCI across lanes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6687741/?utm_source=openai))
- Statistics and learning: Train on retrospective cohorts with nested cross‑validation; evaluate AUROC/AUPRC per organ and calibration of probability outputs. Prospective validation in PDX metastasis models and clinical follow‑up assesses time‑to‑site concordance.

Milestones and decision gates
- M6: Reproducible tuning of barrier thickness/charge and demonstration that barrier modulation alone shifts capture of a standard tumor line as predicted. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6668365/?utm_source=openai))
- M12: MIP microdomains yield distinct motif‑specific rolling kinetics under identical barrier settings; competitive binding with soluble MIPs recapitulates expected rank‑order avidity. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))
- M18: Classifier trained on EV‑GCI and cell‑GCI achieves >0.75 AUROC for top‑1 organ prediction in retrospective data; ablation shows barrier terms materially improve performance over motif‑only features. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10540341/?utm_source=openai))
- M24+: Prospective validation reaches predefined accuracy thresholds; blinded testing on external cohort.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Risk: Organ endothelium involves more than glycans. Mitigation: Include minimal protein cues common across organs (e.g., E‑selectin) at controlled density to avoid overfitting to non‑glycan signals; demonstrate that barrier changes modulate adhesion even at fixed protein levels. ([jci.org](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/116928?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: EV heterogeneity. Mitigation: Fractionate EVs by glycan class using lectin monoliths and analyze subfractions separately to increase signal‑to‑noise. ([sj.jst.go.jp](https://sj.jst.go.jp/news/202303/n0315-01k.html?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Prior multi‑organ chips model organotropism but without explicit glycocalyx parameterization. Our advance is orthogonal and testable by side‑by‑side comparison under matched flows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12158725/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
- A functional GCI fingerprint that mechanistically encodes the combined effects of glycan motifs and endothelial glycocalyx barriers under flow, enabling pan‑cancer prediction of organ destination from either cells or EVs.
- Mechanistic insight into when sialylation/charge acts as anti‑adhesive barrier versus as part of high‑affinity ligands, resolving context dependencies seen in EV uptake and tumor rolling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7827205/?utm_source=openai))
- A standardized, cell‑agnostic platform for organotropism that complements cell‑based organ‑on‑chip models and leverages stable synthetic glycan receptors (MIPs) to enhance reproducibility. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.0c01305?utm_source=openai))

Novelty statement
No prior study has built a multi‑organ adhesion platform that (i) explicitly tunes and measures the endothelial‑mimetic glycocalyx barrier per organ lane and (ii) combines this with synthetic glycan‑binding microdomains to derive a quantitative compatibility index for organ‑destination prediction across cancers; existing organotropism chips are primarily cell‑based without explicit barrier parameterization, and glycan‑imprinted materials have not been used to mechanistically predict metastatic destination. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12158725/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Organ-first glycan filter metrics for predicting organotropism across cancers

One-sentence hypothesis-question
Do organ-specific endothelial glycocalyces function as competitive filters whose shear-dependent displacement signatures against a calibrated glycan/lectin ladder provide sufficient information to predict where a given tumor will seed metastases across organs? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Recast organotropism as a surface thermodynamics problem: quantify how a tumor’s native multivalent glycome displaces reference ligands from intact organ glycocalyx under physiologic flow, and use that competition profile (not partner identification) as the compatibility score predicting organ-specific arrest/extravasation. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925400509002585?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build and validate an organ glycocalyx competitive displacement assay under physiologic flow to compute an organ Filter Compatibility Index (oFCI)
- Rationale: Initial arrest and extravasation depend on weak, multivalent, flow-modulated glycan–lectin interactions on the luminal glycocalyx that differ by organ. A competition assay directly reports relative free energies and avidities experienced by a tumor glycome on each organ surface without enumerating all binding partners. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))
- Assay construction:
  - Source luminal surfaces via: (i) ex vivo perfused microvessel segments (lung microvasculature, liver sinusoids, bone marrow sinusoids) decellularized minimally to preserve brush ultrastructure; or (ii) detergent-free glycocalyx-enriched vesiculated extracts immobilized on low-fouling supports while retaining charge density and sulfation/sialylation features. Validate by lectin panel staining and AFM brush-height; quantify organ-dependent porosity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41575-018-0020-y?utm_source=openai))
  - Reference ladder: A barcoded set of soluble competitors spanning affinity/valency classes (e.g., sLeX/a mimetics for selectins, LacNAc oligos for galectins, HS sulfation-defined fragments for HSPG/chemokine hubs), each with known ΔG°, kon/koff. Pre-equilibrate surfaces with the ladder to defined occupancy. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK453057/?utm_source=openai))
  - Tumor probes: intact CTCs, membrane blebs, or vesicle-enriched glycoconjugate fractions from diverse cancer types (pan-cancer panel). Perfuse under organ-matched shear (lung 10–20 dyn/cm2 arteriolar entry; liver/bone sinusoid 0.1–1 dyn/cm2) and ionic conditions. Record real-time ladder displacement by multiplexed fluorescence or electrochemical readouts across flow ramps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4592324/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts and analysis:
  - For each reference species i, fit displacement kinetics to obtain ΔGeff,i and avidity class weights under each shear. Aggregate into oFCIorgan = Σi wi ΔGeff,i normalized to organ surface site density. Shear-dependent oFCI curves are the primary predictors. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925400509002585?utm_source=openai))
  - Glycan-dependency controls: neuraminidase and heparinase challenge should collapse organ-rank separations in oFCI consistent with loss of sialic acid or HS contributions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28524373/?utm_source=openai))
- Milestones:
  - M1: Reproducible oFCI ranking across lung, liver, bone surfaces for a calibration set of organotropic cell lines (e.g., breast-to-bone, colon-to-liver, melanoma-to-lung). Ground truth: early vascular arrest patterns in mouse flow-chamber organs or intravital microscopy. Success criterion: AUROC ≥0.80 for destination identification across ≥3 organs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5663538/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Flow-gated proximity-barcoded lectin sequencing (PBL-seq) to map each organ’s accessible multivalency grammar and improve calibration
- Rationale: Multivalent co-display within tens of nanometers drives avidity and catch-bond stabilization; maps must reflect flow-limited accessibility, not bulk composition. DNA-barcoded lectin sequencing exists, and lectin/antibody proximity-ligation has been demonstrated; here it is adapted for lectin–lectin co-binding under physiologic perfusion on intact organ microvessels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))
- Method:
  - Perfuse a pool of lectins each tagged with unique DNA oligos plus proximity-ligation adaptors; apply under organ-appropriate shear, then fix. Ligation occurs only when distinct lectins co-bind within a nanoscale radius on the luminal face. Sequence ligated barcodes to yield pairwise/higher-order co-binding frequencies and derive co-localization graphs per organ. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))
- Use: Convert co-binding networks into accessibility/avidity priors (e.g., HS–Galectin hubs in liver sinusoids; sLeX–E-selectin clusters in lung microvasculature) and incorporate as covariates that rescale oFCI. Success criterion: PBL-informed models reduce calibration error (Brier score) versus oFCI alone. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41575-018-0020-y?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Physics-informed glyco-compatibility model constrained by oFCI and PBL-seq for pan-cancer organotropism prediction
- Rationale: ML models exist for organotropism from transcriptomes or clinical trajectories, but not from glycan–lectin thermodynamics or organ-first accessibility. We integrate measured oFCI constraints with lectin–glycan binding priors to produce interpretable organ-specific probabilities. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8611885/?utm_source=openai))
- Model specification:
  - Construct bipartite organ–tumor graphs where organ nodes carry motif/lectin densities and co-localization weights (from PBL-seq), tumor nodes carry glycan motif propensities inferred from glycomics or glyco-gene expression, and edges carry ΔG°, kon/koff from literature/arrays. Incorporate flow-dependent catch-bond modifiers for selectins. Train to predict observed metastatic destinations with penalties for violating measured oFCI orderings. ([advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/advs.202103807?utm_source=openai))
- Validation:
  - Retrospective: apply to TCGA/CPTAC tumors with known first-met site annotations; prospective: orthotopic xenografts with longitudinal organ bioluminescence. Primary metric: top-1 organ hit-rate and calibration across tumor types.

Experimental design and controls
- Organ surfaces: compare intact microvessels vs extracted glycocalyx coatings to quantify loss-of-context penalties; include non-glycan blocking (integrin/ICAM inhibitors) to show glycan-dominant phase of initial capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))
- Flow dependence: sweep shear to reveal catch vs slip regimes; predictions must invert appropriately across organs with distinct shear profiles (lung vs liver/bone). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4592324/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity: metastasis-paired isogenic lines differing in glycosyltransferase expression; enzymatic editing of tumor glycomes to shift oFCI and organ choice in vivo.

Data products
- Organ oFCI atlases (per shear and ionic condition), PBL-seq co-binding networks, and a constrained prediction model with code and trained weights.

Go/no-go gates
- Gate 1 (month 9): oFCI reproducibility CV <15% across runs; displacement curves capture expected enzyme sensitivities.
- Gate 2 (month 15): oFCI ranks correlate with early arrest across ≥3 tumor types (Spearman ρ ≥0.5).
- Gate 3 (month 24): Integrated model improves organ destination AUROC by ≥0.1 over transcript-only baselines on held-out cohorts.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: Loss of native ultrastructure in glycocalyx extracts. Mitigation: preferential use of ex vivo perfused segments; cross-validate with endothelial organ-on-chip that develops organ-typic brushes. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/tr/content/articlelanding/2024/lc/d3lc00889d?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Proximity ligation background. Mitigation: shear-on/shear-off gating with time-controlled ligation; require dual lectin co-occurrence over negative controls; spike-in standards. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Overfitting in ML. Mitigation: physics priors, oFCI order constraints, and multi-cohort external validation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8611885/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables and impact
- A validated, glycobiology-first, organ-specific metastasis predictor that operates via a measurable, surface thermodynamics compatibility index rather than enumerating all ligands; a standardized assay and open dataset enabling pan-cancer destination risk stratification and therapeutic design targeting organ-specific glycan–lectin hubs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Inverse organ-lectin fingerprinting from settled metastases to predict pan-cancer organotropism

Central hypothesis-question
Do settled metastases encode a measurable, organ-conditioned lectin/avidity “demand vector” that, when inverted with biophysically and pathway-constrained glycome models and informed by differential glycan turnover, yields generalizable, organ-specific metastasis predictions across cancer types? If yes, can this inversion outperform forward predictors trained solely on primary tumor features? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Read the organ’s lectin constraints directly from metastatic sites with multivalency- and spacing-controlled glycan “polymer-brush” probes, then invert those constraints—under glycosylation-network feasibility and glycochronology priors—into minimal glycosyltransferase activity programs that confer colonization fitness for specific organs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6824935/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and mechanistic soundness
- Vascular arrest/extravasation depends on selectin–sialyl Lewis interactions, which are organ-contextual (e.g., bone marrow endothelium constitutively expresses E-selectin). Multivalency and shear-dependent avidity dominate capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
- Immune dampening in metastatic niches is mediated by tumor hypersialylation engaging inhibitory Siglecs on macrophages/NK cells; Siglec profiles vary among tissue-resident macrophages. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13010965/?utm_source=openai))
- Stromal anchoring and receptor retention are regulated by galectin lattices binding branched N-glycans (MGAT5), which reduce endocytosis and tune signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2811491/?utm_source=openai))
- Differential kinetics: terminal sialylation can be rapidly removed/readded during endocytic recycling, whereas lattice-stabilized branched N-glycans modulate receptor residency; isotope-labeling shows glycan-type-specific incorporation and turnover. These enable “glycochronology” priors. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK20729/?utm_source=openai))

Prior art and novelty check (brief)
- Multivalency-sensitive glycan arrays and polymer-brush microarrays exist; DNA barcoded soluble or bead-like carriers (e.g., LiGA) exist. None target capture of organ-derived lectins from metastatic tissues to derive an “organ demand vector,” nor link density/spacing-resolved capture to an inverse organotropism predictor. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6824935/?utm_source=openai))
- Lectin-based deconvolution of glycan structures from binding data and pathway models for glycosylation have appeared, but no thermodynamics- and stoichiometry-constrained inversion has been reported to predict organ-specific metastasis from settled lesions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10274649/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build a barcoded glycan–polymer-brush bead library to quantify metastatic-site “organ lectin demand vectors.”
- Bead design: silica or polystyrene microspheres functionalized with surface-initiated glycopolymer brushes. Parameters independently tunable per bead barcode: grafting density, chain length, spacer flexibility, and net charge. Ligand panels include sLea/x (selectins), α2,3- vs α2,6-sialylated LacNAc series (Siglecs), poly-LacNAc length variants (galectins), and sulfated GAG mimetics. DNA barcodes are internal to each bead identity; readout by NGS after assay. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3458438/?utm_source=openai))
- Assay modes:
  1) Lectin-capture: incubate beads with clarified lysates and interstitial fluids from freshly resected human metastases (liver, lung, bone, brain). Proteomics of bead-bound proteins yields identities/abundances of organ- and niche-derived lectins (E-/P-selectin, galectins, Siglecs, etc.). Density/spacing-response curves across brush variants quantify avidity/geometry preferences, forming the organ’s demand vector. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
  2) Vesicle-binding: capture extracellular vesicles from the same metastases; binding versus brush parameters reports effective display valency/spacing of the tumor’s outermost glycocalyx. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3458438/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: isotype/CRD-mutant lectins, nonspecific brushes, enzymatic pre-treatments (sialidases, fucosidases) to confirm motif and linkage dependence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3458438/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criterion: reproducible, organ-clustered demand vectors across cancer types, with significant density- and spacing-dependence reflecting known in vivo multivalency effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6824935/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Quantify metastatic glycochronology to constrain inversion.
- Ex vivo pulse labeling of freshly resected metastases with 13C-glucose or ManNAz for 2–8 h; isolate cell-surface glycans; apply linkage-specific sialidases (α2,3 vs α2,6) and perform quantitative glycomics to estimate incorporation into terminal sialylation versus core branching states. Compute Δstate between fast-updating terminal caps and lattice-stabilized receptor residency. Use Δstate as temporal priors on feasible enzyme activity changes. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2019/sc/c9sc01653h?utm_source=openai))
- Success criterion: Δstate features reduce degeneracy of inferred enzyme programs versus terminal-motif-only fits.

Aim 3. Develop a thermodynamics- and pathway-constrained inverse glycome model to predict organotropism.
- Inputs: (i) organ demand vectors (lectin identities, densities, spacing sensitivities); (ii) vesicle-binding fingerprints; (iii) Δstate priors; (iv) bounds on tumor glycosyltransferase expression/flux from multi-omics where available. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10274649/?utm_source=openai))
- Biophysics: compute effective free energies of adhesion/signaling under shear and at the cell surface for selectins, Siglecs, and galectins as functions of ligand valency/spacing and receptor density; include cooperative galectin lattice formation and Siglec signaling thresholds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
- Pathway constraints: enforce glycosylation-network stoichiometry/topology (e.g., branching prerequisites for poly-LacNAc extension), donor sugar budgets, and enzyme competition. Penalize solutions that violate Δstate kinetics. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01725?utm_source=openai))
- Outputs: (a) minimal glycosyltransferase edit sets that map a typical primary glycome to the organ-compatible metastatic state; (b) organ fitness scores for candidate primary tumors; (c) ranked organotropism predictions.
- Validation: retrospective testing on annotated cohorts with known metastatic destinations; prospective validation in patient-derived xenograft models with longitudinal sampling of circulating tumor cells and emergent metastases. Benchmark against genomic organotropism predictors. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-27017-w?utm_source=openai))

Study design and analyses
- Cohorts: n≥30 metastases per organ site across multiple primaries (lung, breast, colorectal, melanoma, pancreas). Power analyses target detection of organ-clustered demand vectors (multivariate effect size f2≥0.15) and AUC improvements ≥0.1 over genomic baselines.
- Statistics: mixed-effects models for inter-patient variability; manifold learning to visualize demand-vector clustering; cross-validated inversion to avoid overfitting; calibration/Brier scores for organ probability outputs.

Milestones
- Year 1: Bead library fabrication; assay optimization; pilot with 10 metastases/site; initial organ demand vectors.
- Year 2: Glycochronology priors established; first inversion model; retrospective validation in two cancer types.
- Year 3: Pan-cancer expansion; prospective PDX validation; preclinical clinical-decision prototype.

Potential outcomes and interpretation
- Outcome A: Organ demand vectors cluster by destination across primaries; inversion yields accurate organotropism predictions. Interpretation: organ-conditioned lectin fields are dominant constraints on colonization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
- Outcome B: Weak clustering or poor inversion. Interpretation: additional, non-glycan determinants dominate in some organs; revise ligand panels to include organ-specific sulfation/charge or integrate chemokine axes.

Deliverables
- An open-source inverse-glycome software with curated multivalent affinity matrices and pathway constraints.
- A validated, barcoded glycan–polymer-brush bead kit for metastatic-site profiling.
- A pan-cancer organotropism risk report for clinical studies.

Feasibility checks against biology
- Selectin/Siglec/galectin mechanisms and tissue distributions are established; bone marrow E-selectin exemplifies organ-constitutive vascular lectin expression relevant to organotropism. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
- Multivalency and spacing control are known to shift lectin binding by orders of magnitude; polymer-brush and density-variant arrays capture these effects. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6824935/?utm_source=openai))
- Differential glycan turnover and lattice-stabilized receptor residency justify temporal priors. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK20729/?utm_source=openai))

Risk and mitigation
- Low lectin abundance in lysates: enrich with CRD-focused pulldowns; increase tissue area; orthogonal confirmation by targeted MS. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3458438/?utm_source=openai))
- Heterogeneity across metastases: use mixed-effects modeling and bootstrap ensemble inversion.
- Confounding inflammation: parallel profiling of matched non-tumor organ tissue to subtract baseline organ lectin fields.

Novelty statement
- Prior tools profile glycans or display multivalent ligands; DNA-barcoded glycan carriers exist, but capturing native organ lectins from metastatic sites and using density/spacing-resolved capture as an inverse constraint to predict organotropism has not been reported to our knowledge. The proposed thermodynamics- and pathway-constrained inversion extends beyond existing lectin-to-glycan deconvolution or glycosylation-pathway forward models. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8380037/?utm_source=openai))

Criteria for success
- Reproducible, organ-specific demand vectors and Δstate priors that reduce inversion degeneracy.
- External validation demonstrating improved accuracy of organ-destination prediction versus genomic baselines in at least three cancer types. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-27017-w?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Reading endothelial glyco–zip codes with binding-gated DNA nanobarcodes to predict organ-specific metastasis across cancers

Hypothesis-question
Do conserved, organ-intrinsic endothelial glycan/lectin neighborhoods that support prolonged multivalent adhesion under physiological shear define where circulating tumor cells can stably arrest and extravasate, and can these “zip codes” be read functionally by binding-gated DNA nanobarcode reporters and matched to a patient tumor glycome to predict organotropism across cancers? Endothelial lectins and glycosaminoglycans (e.g., L-SIGN/CLEC4M, LSECtin/CLEC4G, galectins; organ-distinct heparan sulfate phenotypes) exhibit tissue-programmed patterns, and tumor arrest/extravasation involves selectin/galectin/HS-mediated adhesion steps under flow. These observations motivate a functional readout of organ-intrinsic glycobiology rather than tumor-derived preconditioning. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7396565/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert only those endothelial engagements that cross an avidity-and-dwell-time threshold (the same regime required for productive arrest/extravasation) into a countable DNA signal using multivalent, glycan-presenting DNA-origami reporters that release unique DNA barcodes via binding-induced strand displacement only when ≥k binding arms are simultaneously engaged for ≥t seconds under shear. This translates “functionally relevant adhesion” into “sequencing counts,” creating an organ zip-code atlas agnostic to tumor variability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8283757/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and workplan

Aim 1. Engineer and calibrate binding-gated glyco–DNA nanobarcode reporters that register functional endothelial adhesion under flow.
- Reporter design: 30–50 nm DNA-origami scaffolds (rod and icosahedral variants) displaying defined multivalent glycan ligands (modules: sLeX clusters for selectins; LacNAc repeats for galectin-3; oligomannose for L-SIGN/LSECtin; sulfated HS-mimetic glycooligomers to probe HS-binding sites) at tuned interligand spacings (4–12 nm) and valencies (16–64). Each reporter carries a latent barcode locked by a toehold circuit that requires formation of a multi-arm DNA three-way junction upon ≥k concurrent receptor–ligand bonds to trigger strand displacement and barcode release; unproductive collisions cannot trigger release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8283757/?utm_source=openai))
- Flow calibration: In parallel-plate flow chambers seeded with primary human organ-specific microvascular endothelium, measure barcode release as a function of wall shear stress (0.5–8 dyn/cm2), ligand valency/spacing, and binding time gates (t = 1–60 s). Blockade controls: soluble glycans, heparinase III (HS removal), anti-lectin antibodies. Endpoints: threshold shear and dwell producing barcode release; specificity by competitive inhibition; dependence on HS integrity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13115945/?utm_source=openai))
- Analytical readout: Sequencing-based quantification of released barcodes in perfusate; on-chip controls include barcodes from nonbinding scaffolds and UV-releasable “spike-ins” to normalize recovery. Decision rule: retain only reporter–condition pairs exhibiting ≥10-fold signal over nonbinding controls and complete abrogation by cognate blockade.

Aim 2. Build an organ-resolved endothelial glyco–zip code atlas in ex vivo–perfused human organs.
- Platforms: Normothermic ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) and ex vivo human liver perfusion circuits using transplant-discard organs; optionally brain microvasculature explants with controlled perfusion. Perfuse multiplexed reporter pools (n≈64 designs) for 30–60 minutes; collect venous effluent for barcode sequencing. Tissue samples are taken post-run for lectin/antibody histology and HS disaccharide profiling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6237445/?utm_source=openai))
- Stability filters: Repeat across donors and across basal versus cytokine-activated states; retain only motifs with low intra-organ coefficient of variation and preserved accessibility under native shear. Sensitivity tests: enzymatic HS editing (heparinase), competitive mannan (L-SIGN), and lactose (galectin). Outcome: an “organ zip vector” (normalized barcode intensities across reporter motifs) for each organ. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7396565/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-validation with static technologies: Compare atlas features with (i) DNA-barcoded lectin sequencing on tissue sections and (ii) proximity-ligation glycan assays to confirm motif co-localization on endothelium; require concordant motif presence but prioritize functional signals under flow for atlas inclusion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Derive and validate a pan-cancer organotropism predictor by matching tumor glycomes to the organ atlas.
- Tumor glycome vectors: Profile patient tumor biopsies and/or circulating tumor cells using DNA-barcoded lectins (Glycan-seq/scGR-seq) to quantify surface glycan motifs (e.g., sialylation/fucosylation patterns, LacNAc repeats). Output is a normalized tumor glycan vector per sample. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))
- Match function: Learn a supervised ranking model that maps tumor glycan vectors to organ zip vectors to yield a metastasis destination probability distribution. Training labels: (i) experimental organ colonization in murine metastasis models across diverse human cancer lines; (ii) retrospective clinical cohorts with first-site metastasis annotations. Primary performance metric: top-1 organ prediction accuracy and calibrated risk scores. Biological interpretability: dominant glycan–organ motif pairs that drive predictions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8930623/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic validation: Under flow, test predicted high-match tumor cells on organ-specific endothelium; measure rolling velocity, arrest frequency, and transendothelial migration; abrogate with glycan or lectin blockade (e.g., anti-E-selectin, lactose for galectin-3, mannan for L-SIGN, heparinase for HS) and show loss of function and loss of barcode release concordantly. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/64/15/5261/511528/Rolling-of-Human-Bone-Metastatic-Prostate-Tumor?utm_source=openai))

Key methods and controls
- Multivalency/spacing design is grounded in DNA-origami control of nanoscale ligand geometry and its known impact on receptor binding and complement/lectin pathway activation; we exploit it to tune avidity and catch-bond regimes relevant to adhesion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8283757/?utm_source=openai))
- Binding-gated strand displacement converts receptor engagement into DNA release with low background; binding-induced DNA circuits and three-way-junction motifs are established for live-cell sensing and are adapted here to multivalent gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3580983/?utm_source=openai))
- Organ perfusion platforms preserve native endothelial architecture and shear, enabling functional mapping of luminal glycocalyx accessibility at scale. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6237445/?utm_source=openai))
- Orthogonal confirmation of endothelial glycofeatures includes proximity-ligation glycan assays and DNA-barcoded lectin sequencing, ensuring cross-technique coherence while keeping the atlas defined by flow-competent binding. ([2bscientific.com](https://www.2bscientific.com/getmedia/9d6c9101-9344-4220-ba19-33a9076f955d/Glysite-Explorer-user-guide.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes
- A quantitative atlas of organ-specific endothelial glyco–zip codes defined by functional, shear-resilient ligand neighborhoods (e.g., LacNAc–galectin and oligomannose–L-SIGN signatures in liver; selectin-binding motifs in lung/activated endothelium; HS-dependent motifs with organ-distinct sensitivity to heparinase). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7396565/?utm_source=openai))
- A pan-cancer predictor that ranks likely metastatic destinations by computing tumor–organ glycan complementarity; predictions are mechanistically anchored and testable by targeted blockade under flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8930623/?utm_source=openai))
- A modular diagnostic substrate: the same reporters can be repurposed to monitor disease- or therapy-induced remodeling of endothelial glyco–zip codes in perfused organs or organ-on-chip systems.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1 (Months 0–9): Reporters exhibit ≥10:1 signal-to-background at ≥2 dyn/cm2 with complete inhibition by cognate blocking ligands/enzymes in flow chambers. Go/No-Go: shear- and ligand-specific gating demonstrated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13115945/?utm_source=openai))
- M2 (Months 10–18): Reproducible organ zip vectors from ≥5 human livers and ≥5 lungs with intra-organ CV <25% and preservation across donors; atlas entries show expected sensitivity patterns (e.g., mannan- and lactose-sensitive signals in liver). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6237445/?utm_source=openai))
- M3 (Months 19–30): Predictor achieves ≥60% top-1 first-site accuracy across diverse cancer lines in mouse models and validates on retrospective human cohorts; predicted high-match pairs show increased arrest and TEM in flow assays, reversible by targeted glycan/lectin blockade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3874033/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and feasibility
- DNA-barcoded nanoparticles have been used to quantify biodistribution, and DNA-barcoded lectins have been used to sequence glycans; however, leveraging multivalent glycan-presenting DNA nanostructures that convert shear-competent, dwell-time–gated endothelial adhesion into releasable DNA barcodes to build an organ endothelial glyco–zip atlas has not been reported. This proposal fuses these threads into a functional, organ-intrinsic readout aligned with the physics of metastasis seeding. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28167778/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management
- Inflammatory plasticity of endothelium: We explicitly map basal and cytokine-activated states and filter for motifs with low variance; the atlas is defined by functional accessibility under physiologic shear, mitigating confounding by transient epitopes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6337777/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target nanoparticle clearance: Ex vivo human organ perfusion minimizes reticuloendothelial confounds while preserving luminal architecture; in vitro flow calibration ensures interpretability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6237445/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- The Organ Endothelial Glyco–Zip Atlas (open resource): motif-by-organ vectors with associated inhibition profiles, validated under shear.
- A sequencing-ready diagnostic kit: multiplexed reporters and a matching algorithm that takes a patient tumor glycan vector and outputs an organotropism risk distribution, with mechanistic interpretability and actionable blockade candidates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8349903/?utm_source=openai))
