text:
Title
GlycoPreference: Predicting organ-specific metastasis by kinetic adhesion profiling of patient CTCs on organ‑coded boronic glycomesh under flow

Background and significance
- Intravascular arrest of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is governed by a multistep adhesion cascade: weak, force-dependent tethers and rolling transitions to firm arrest, with kinetics dictated by ligand density, multivalency, and shear. Reconstituted flow systems recapitulate selectin-mediated rolling and show that rolling-to-arrest transitions can be engineered and quantified. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))
- The endothelial glycocalyx varies by organ in thickness, charge and glycosaminoglycan sulfation patterns, shaping adhesion and permeability; thus organ beds present distinct adhesion filters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10551284/?utm_source=openai))
- Boronic acids form reversible covalent esters with cis-diols and recognize terminal sialic acids abundant on many cancer cell surface glycoconjugates. Boronic-acid–based micro/nanostructured substrates and chips have captured CTCs across cancer types via sialyl-glycan binding and allow gentle release—establishing pan-cancer, label-free feasibility. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15838860/?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis–question
Can a microfluidic array of organ-coded, boronic‑acid glycopolymer brushes—tuned for glycan multivalency, chemistry (pKa), and mechanics—convert CTC surface glycan architecture into distinctive rolling/arrest kinetic fingerprints that predict a patient’s organotropism?

Atomic strategy
Exploit reversible boronate–diol binding as a universal, label-free transducer of CTC surface sialyl/fucosyl glycan topology; encode organ specificity by globally tuning brush density/height, boronic-acid pKa, and substrate compliance to match organ glycocalyx regimes, and read out preference as the channel with maximal rolling-to-arrest transition probability under physiological shear. This converts organ selection physics into a measurable kinetic signature without enumerating molecular markers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15838860/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build and calibrate “organ-coded” glycomesh lanes.
- Fabrication: Surface-initiated RAFT to grow boronic‑acid glycopolymer brushes on glass/PDMS in four parallel lanes. Use benzoboroxole- and phenylboronic-acid derivatives spanning pKa 6.5–8.5; independently tune brush height (50–500 nm) and grafting density to modulate multivalency and mechanical compliance.
- Organ coding: Parameter sets approximate lung (thin/low-density), liver (fenestrated/medium-density), bone marrow (dense, high on-rate), brain (thick/soft brush). Calibrate diol-binding equilibria and on/off-rates by QCM-D, SPR, and FRAP of fluorescent diol probes; adjust to achieve matched capture forces at 0.5–2 dyn/cm2.
- Glycan specificity controls: Competitive fructose/mannitol elution, neuraminidase and fucosidase pretreatments on cells; quantify losses in adhesion. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15838860/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Establish kinetic organ-preference metrics with organotropic model lines.
- Models: Use well-characterized organotropic variants (lung-, liver-, brain-, bone-seeking) and heterogeneous parental lines.
- Assay: Perfuse cells (and spiked whole blood) through the four-lane chip at stepped shear (0.5→4 dyn/cm2). Record trajectories to extract rolling velocity distributions, pause frequency, arrest probability, and detachment under ramped shear.
- Preference index: For each lane, compute a composite Kinetic Preference Score KPS = P(arrest) × τpause/(vroll CV); define organotropism as argmax(KPS).
- Expected result: Each organotropic line maximizes KPS in its cognate lane; neuraminidase/fucosidase abolish differential KPS. Benchmark against E-selectin/HA rolling standards to ensure physiologic kinetic ranges. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Clinical feasibility with patient CTCs and blinded correlation to first-site metastasis.
- Input: Immunomagnetically depleted whole blood enriched for rare cells; no positive selection.
- Run: Acquire kinetic fingerprints across lanes; compute patient-level preference vector.
- Outcomes: Primary—concordance of top-ranked lane with first radiographic site within 6–12 months. Secondary—time-to-event stratification by KPS margin (ΔKPS1−2).
- Orthogonal biology checks: Release viable CTCs by sorbitol or mild pH shift for single-cell RNA/glycoproteomics; test whether high-KPS cells express glycan biosynthesis programs consistent with their predicted niche. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6946854/?utm_source=openai))

Research plan and methods (concise)
- Chemistry: Synthesize boronic-acid methacrylate monomers (phenylboronic acid, benzoboroxole analogs) with spacers to reduce steric hindrance; copolymerize with hydrophilic comonomers to tune brush hydration.
- Patterning: Photomask to create sub-millimeter organ-coded domains per lane for internal standards; profilometry/ellipsometry to confirm thickness; streaming ζ-potential to match charge regimes.
- Flow assay: Straight channels with ridged near-wall features to enhance margination without introducing non-glycan binding; syringe pump with feedback to impose precise shear ramps.
- Imaging/analysis: High-speed video, automated trajectory segmentation; Bayesian hierarchical models for KPS estimation with uncertainty.
- Validation of glycan dependence: Enzymatic stripping, metabolic glycoengineering (Ac4ManNAz) to up/down-modulate sialylation; check KPS shifts accordingly.

Innovation
- Reframes organotropism prediction from molecular enumeration to a functional glycan-physics readout using a single reversible chemistry that is pan-cancer and label-free. Prior boronic‑acid platforms capture CTCs but do not map organ-specific preference or kinetic fingerprints; prior rolling chips use immobilized adhesion proteins but not organ-coded glycocalyx-mimetic landscapes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6946854/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and interpretation
- If KPS vectors consistently align with known/observed first metastasis sites, it supports that organ-coded glycocalyx physics plus CTC glycan topology is sufficient to predict destination.
- Divergence between KPS and outcomes will guide re-coding (brush density/pKa/compliance) for specific cancers, or indicate dominant non-glycan determinants in those contexts.

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1: Lanes achieve targeted binding kinetics for diol probes at 0.5–2 dyn/cm2 and reversible release (>90% viable). Go if CV<15% across chips.
- M2: ≥75% correct organ assignment in blinded organotropic lines; effect abolished by neuraminidase. Go if AUC>0.8.
- M3: Prospective pilot (n=40): ≥65% concordance with first-site metastasis within 6–12 months; hazard ratio>2 for ΔKPS margin.

Risk mitigation
- Leukocyte interference: Differentiate by kinetics (shorter pauses, higher vroll); leukocyte depletion if needed. Benchmark with leukocyte controls from healthy donors.
- pH/ionic sensitivity of boronate binding: Use benzoboroxoles (lower pKa) and buffered media; confirm stability at pH 7.4. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7340346/?utm_source=openai))
- Overfitting of organ codes: Constrain codes by organ glycocalyx literature (thickness/charge) and tune with independent diol probes before using cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10551284/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- An open, standardized four-lane GlycoPreference chip and analysis pipeline producing a patient-specific organotropism vector.
- A validated dataset linking CTC kinetic fingerprints to metastatic destinations across cancers.

Impact
Provides a clinically adaptable, pan-cancer functional assay that lets CTCs “choose” organ-mimetic glycocalyx environments under flow, translating native adhesion physics into an actionable prediction of metastatic destination. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5636711/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Force-calibrated glycan adhesion mechanoprints for pan-cancer prediction of organ-specific metastasis

Hypothesis–Question
Does a patient’s circulating tumor cells (CTCs) encode a force-dependent, glycan-mediated adhesion “mechanoprint” that matches specific organ microvascular glyco-lectin environments—and can this mechanoprint predict first metastatic destination across cancers? This rests on the established biology that early vascular capture in metastasis is governed by shear-modulated lectin–glycan interactions (notably selectins) that mediate tethering/rolling and transition to firm arrest, with organ-specific endothelial heterogeneity and shear profiles biasing successful capture. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Isolate the single global gate of organotropism—force-dependent multivalent glycan adhesion under physiologic shear—and read it out directly. First, let organotypic endothelium “teach” which glycan presentations form catch-like, force-stable adhesions in each organ (discovery). Then, phenotype patient CTCs on a force-calibrated, organ-specific glycan flow array to generate an individual mechanoprint vector that predicts metastatic destination (diagnostic).

Specific Aims

Aim 1. Discover organ-specific, force-stabilized glycan presentations by shear-selection against organotypic endothelium.
- Rationale: Selectin/lectin–glycan bonds display catch-to-slip behavior and govern first contact and rolling; organ microvessels differ in both lectin display and shear, e.g., lung capillaries ~5 dyn/cm2, bone marrow sinusoids ~1–3 dyn/cm2, liver sinusoids ~0.1–0.5 dyn/cm2. Enriching for glycan presentations that remain adherent or slow-rolling under organ-matched shear yields a causal “glycan homing lexicon.” ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))
- Library: A barcoded, surface-display glycan library using glycoengineered mammalian cell sublibraries (HEK293/CHO panels spanning sialylation/fucosylation/branching; inclusion of GAGOme GAG variants), augmented by synthetic insertion of defined glycopolymers/glycolipids to tune valency and nanoscale presentation. Each clone’s glycome is genetically specified and barcoded. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6660356/?utm_source=openai))
- Selection substrate: Primary or iPSC-derived organotypic microvascular endothelium (lung, liver, bone, brain) cultured in microchannels. Apply organ-matched steady/pulsatile shear ramps; collect adherent and slow-rolling fractions across shear steps; deep-sequence barcodes to quantify enrichment. Include competitive inhibition with lectin blockers (e.g., anti-E-/P-selectin) to confirm glycan dependence. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.1052192/full?utm_source=openai))
- Output: For each organ, a minimal panel of glycan motifs and presentation parameters (terminal structures, sulfation, scaffold, tether compliance, density) that maximize force-stable adhesion.

Go/No-Go for Aim 1: >10-fold enrichment over input for ≥5 distinct motif–presentation combinations per organ and reproducible enrichment profiles across donors.

Aim 2. Build a high-throughput, organ-mimetic flow glycan array to phenotype patient CTC mechanoprints.
- Rationale: Static glycan slides poorly support intact cell interrogation; adding controlled shear and compliant tethers converts arrays into dynamic adhesion phenotypers. Prior fluidic glycan arrays have profiled microbes; here we engineer force-calibrated organ lanes for human CTCs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13016201/?utm_source=openai))
- Device (Glyco-Mechanoprint Cytometer, GMC): Parallel microchannels; each lane presents an organ-specific mixture of Aim 1 motifs immobilized via PEG tethers of tuned lengths/densities, optionally co-presenting recombinant E-/P-selectin and ICAM/VCAM ectodomains to capture cooperative rolling-to-arrest transitions. Lanes run at organ-matched shear (lung ~5 dyn/cm2; bone marrow ~2 dyn/cm2; liver ~0.3 dyn/cm2). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))
- Assay: Enrich CTCs from whole blood by label-free, negative selection; perfuse in autologous plasma with hematocrit control to approximate margination. Quantify per-lane metrics: rolling velocity distributions, pause frequency, firm-arrest fraction, and critical detachment shear. Include on-chip perturbations (sialidase/fucosidase lanes; selectin blockade) as internal controls of glycan dependence. ([rsc.org](https://www.rsc.org/images/loc/2011/pdfs/papers/178_0961.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Output: Patient-specific organotropism mechanoprint vector M = [mv_lung, mv_liver, mv_bone, …], where each element aggregates calibrated force-dependent adhesion features.

Go/No-Go for Aim 2: Signal-to-noise >5 for firm-arrest fraction versus scrambled-glycan control lanes; loss of signal (>70%) with sialidase or selectin blockade for at least one organ lane in >80% of samples.

Aim 3. Train and validate a pan-cancer predictor of metastatic destination using mechanoprints.
- Design: Prospective, multi-institutional cohort (n≈180; breast, colorectal, lung, prostate, pancreatic, melanoma; 30 each), sampled at diagnosis of stage II–III or de novo stage IV without known metastatic site. Baseline GMC assay to generate M. Follow for 18 months or until first radiologically confirmed distant metastasis; metastasis site is the label. Existing multi-organ metastasis-on-chip models demonstrate organotropism feasibility but rely on complex co-cultures; our readout isolates the vascular glycan adhesion gate. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40510151/?utm_source=openai))
- Analysis: Multiclass classifier (e.g., regularized multinomial model) trained on 2/3 of cohort, validated on 1/3; primary endpoint: top-1 accuracy of predicted first site vs. observed. Secondary endpoints: time-to-metastasis stratification by mechanoprint intensity; calibration across cancer types.
- Benchmarks and novelty: Flow- and selectin-based rolling cytometry exists; intact-cell glycan arrays exist but are limited; no validated platform predicts organ-specific destination from CTC adhesion to organ-matched glycan presentations under physiologic shear. ([pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2014/lc/c3lc50923k?utm_source=openai))

Methods in detail

Organ shear calibration
- Program per-lane wall shear based on physiologic ranges: lung capillary ~5 dyn/cm2; bone marrow sinusoid ~1–3 dyn/cm2; liver sinusoid ~0.1–0.5 dyn/cm2. Verify by micro-PIV and CFD; validate endothelial alignment markers in parallel endothelialized mimics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8616606/?utm_source=openai))

Motif presentation engineering
- Tether mechanics: Use PEG linkers (1–20 kDa) to modulate nanoscale compliance; calibrate molecular density by fluorescence standards to match endothelial presentations inferred from Aim 1 enrichment.
- Cooperative adhesion: Include recombinant E-/P-selectin ectodomains where Aim 1 implicates selectins; tune co-ligand ratios to reproduce catch–slip transition shear windows measured in Aim 1. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11003720/?utm_source=openai))

Assay controls
- Specificity: Competitive inhibition with soluble lectins; enzyme edits (sialidase, fucosidase) on CTCs pre-perfusion; loss of signal confirms glycan causality. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK593921/?report=reader&utm_source=openai))
- Hemodynamics: Repeat assays at ±50% shear to test robustness of rank-order across organ lanes.

Linking mechanoprints to outcomes
- Primary analysis: For each patient, compute normalized adhesion energy per organ (area under shear–adhesion curve). Predict top destination as argmax across organs.
- Cross-cancer generalization: Train with stratified folds by cancer type; test on held-out types to verify pan-cancer behavior.

Mechanistic cross-validation
- Compare GMC mechanoprints to adhesion on organotypic endothelial monolayers under matched shear; expect correlated rank order if vascular capture is the bottleneck. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.1052192/full?utm_source=openai))
- For a subset (n=30), test in a multi-organ endothelium-based chip to cross-validate organ preference; use this as an orthogonal system-level comparator. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40510151/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: Intact-cell binding to 2D glycan arrays may be weak. Mitigation: Use compliant tethers, multivalent presentation, and organ-matched shear that favors catch-bond stabilization; prior fluidic arrays and rolling cytometers support feasibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2755068/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Non-glycan adhesions dominate. Mitigation: Enzymatic edits and lectin blockade as internal controls; exclude samples without glycan sensitivity from predictive training. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK593921/?report=reader&utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Confounding by RBCs/plasma proteins. Mitigation: Use autologous plasma with controlled hematocrit; sensitivity analyses in buffer vs plasma; leverage literature on whole-blood effects in microfluidic adhesion. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.02752?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and deliverables (24 months)
- M6: Aim 1 enrichment maps for ≥3 organs; shortlist 6–10 motifs/presentations per organ.
- M12: GMC v1 with calibrated organ lanes; analytical validation (repeatability CV<15%).
- M18: Interim analysis of first 90 patients; blinded prediction of first metastasis site in validation subset.
- M24: Final classifier and locked assay protocol; dataset and reference panel of organ-specific glycan motifs.

Significance and innovation
- Mechanistic parsimony: Reads the proximal, force-dependent glycan adhesion gate that initiates extravasation—a conserved, pan-cancer step—rather than downstream, cancer-type–specific programs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21301059/?utm_source=openai))
- Novel diagnostic modality: A force-calibrated, organ-mimetic glycan flow array built from shear-selected motifs; to our knowledge, no validated platform uses such mechanoprints to forecast organotropism from patient CTCs across cancers. Contemporary organ-on-chip models demonstrate organotropism but are not glycobiology-first diagnostics; static glycan arrays struggle with intact cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40510151/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension (post hoc)
- Extend lanes to brain and adrenal motifs; incorporate EVs to test whether vesicle adhesion mechanoprints also predict organotropism; compare to multimodal CTC features reported for organotropism forecasting. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42462627/?utm_source=openai))

Ethics and feasibility
- Peripheral blood draws under IRB-approved protocol with broad consent; CTC enrichment by negative selection; de-identified data linked to clinical follow-up.

Outcome
A validated, pan-cancer glycan adhesion mechanoprint assay that predicts first metastatic destination with actionable lead time, grounded in the physics and chemistry of vascular capture under physiological shear.

Title
Shear-conditioned heparan-sulfate mimetic decoder for blood-based prediction of organotropism across solid cancers

Background and rationale
- Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) arrest in microvessels through a multistep adhesion cascade that includes carbohydrate-mediated tethering/rolling and subsequent firm adhesion; hemodynamic shear critically shapes which bonds persist in vivo. E- and P-selectin–ligand catch-bonds exemplify this shear dependence and help explain early vascular capture of CTCs. ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/130/19/2101/36703/Selectin-catch-bonds-mechanotransduce-integrin?utm_source=openai))
- The endothelial glycocalyx is dominated by heparan sulfate (HS) proteoglycans; HS sulfation patterns (N-, 2‑O-, 6‑O-, 3‑O‑) regulate binding/presentation of chemokines, growth factors, and adhesion effectors. Critically, HS structure and sulfation vary by vascular bed and organ, creating organ-distinct “glycocalyx phenotypes.” ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK54123/?utm_source=openai))
- HS microarrays and sequence-defined HS glycomimetics exist and demonstrate sulfation-dependent binding to diverse proteins, but have not been used to functionally decode live CTC adhesion fingerprints under flow to forecast organ-specific metastasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8022954/?utm_source=openai))
- Tumor–endothelium interactions involve HS and HS-binding ligands; HS proteoglycans and heparanase modulate adhesion, extravasation, and metastasis across cancers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3296185/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis-question
Can a minimal, synthetic basis set of HS sulfation motifs, interrogated under organ-relevant shear, serve as a functional decoder that projects each patient’s CTC adhesion fingerprint onto an organ-resolved endothelial HS “codebook,” thereby predicting organ-specific metastasis across cancers?

Atomic strategy
Use a shear-conditioned HS-mimetic polymer microarray as an intermediate decoder: the many-to-many complexity of CTC glycoconjugates is reduced to a small combinatorial basis of HS sulfation motifs whose adhesion outputs, measured under flow, are matched to an atlas of organ-resolved endothelial HS signatures and shear spectra.

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Build a sequence- and sulfation-defined HS-mimetic decoder array operable under controlled shear to read live CTC adhesion fingerprints.
- Aim 2: Construct an organ-resolved endothelial HS codebook and shear taxonomy, then learn the mapping from CTC decoder fingerprints to organotropism.
- Aim 3: Validate prognostic performance in retrospective and prospective cohorts; probe mechanism with targeted perturbations.

Research plan

Aim 1. HS-mimetic decoder array under flow
- Library design: Synthesize or source HS-mimetic oligomers/polymers varying N-, 2‑O-, 6‑O-, and rare 3‑O‑sulfation; modulate chain length (dp4–dp18), iduronic acid content proxies, and valency via surface grafting density. Immobilize on inert hydrogels to preserve accessibility; include controls (non-sulfated, fully sulfated, chondroitin-sulfate spots). HS microarray feasibility and sulfation-dependent binding are established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8022954/?utm_source=openai))
- Flow interrogation: Integrate the array in a microfluidic chamber with programmable shear ramps (0.2–20 dyn/cm2) spanning capillary-to-venular ranges. Record single-cell rolling velocity distributions, pause frequencies, detachment under shear spikes, and firm-adhesion fractions on each HS motif. Shear-dependent adhesion metrics capture functional stability of multivalent interactions and align with in vivo selection by hemodynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3103268/?utm_source=openai))
- Samples: Enrich CTCs (antigen-agnostic size/deformability plus negative leukocyte depletion to maximize pan-cancer applicability). Run in autologous plasma to preserve opsonins/chemokines that can co-organize on HS. HS-binding chemokines co-presented in solution are allowed since HS presents such ligands in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6152867/?utm_source=openai))

Output of Aim 1: A per-patient, shear-conditioned adhesion vector A over the HS basis (A = f[sulfation motif, valency]).

Aim 2. Organ HS codebook and classifier
- Endothelial HS signatures: Assemble an atlas of organ-resolved HS from primary/immortalized human endothelial cells representing lung, liver, bone marrow, brain microvessels, and kidney; perform HS disaccharide profiling and domain mapping to quantify N-, 2‑O-, 6‑O-, 3‑O‑sulfation and domain clustering. Prior reports support organ/vessel-specific HS differences (e.g., bone marrow vs. HUVEC; lung heterogeneity; Sulf1/2-dependent organ specificity). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11438211/?utm_source=openai))
- Functional alignment: On organ endothelial monolayers, measure chemokine binding/presentation and CTC adhesion under organ-typical shear. Link these readouts to HS profiling via regression to derive an organ HS interaction vector Horgan. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6152867/?utm_source=openai))
- Shear taxonomy: Compile organ-specific shear spectra from literature and microfluidic surrogates to weight decoder features by the shear bands most relevant to each organ (e.g., lung capillaries vs. hepatic sinusoids). Shear influences early adhesion stability in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3103268/?utm_source=openai))
- Classifier: Train a probabilistic model P(organ | A) using retrospective cohorts with adjudicated first-metastasis site. Include calibration with conformal prediction to provide abstain options when uncertainty is high.

Output of Aim 2: A calibrated predictor producing a per-organ probability vector for each patient.

Aim 3. Validation and mechanism
- Retrospective multi-cancer cohort: n≈200 patients (breast, colorectal, lung, melanoma, prostate, pancreas, ovarian). Endpoint: first metastatic organ within 12–24 months. Metrics: per-organ AUROC/AUPRC, top-1/top-2 accuracy, Brier score, decision-curve analysis versus clinical baselines (e.g., sLeX levels, imaging-only). Selectin-mediated rolling assays on E-/P-selectin surfaces under identical flow serve as orthogonal comparators. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7443332/?utm_source=openai))
- Prospective pilot: n≈60 high-risk patients; blinded predictions with pre-specified thresholds to trigger targeted surveillance (e.g., bone scan vs. liver MRI). Safety endpoint: false reassurance avoided via abstain policy.
- Perturbations: Heparinase or soluble HS competitors reduce decoder signals if HS-dependent; heparanase-high CTCs shift adhesion vectors; E-/P-selectin blockade distinguishes selectin versus HS contributions. Prior data link HSPGs/heparanase to metastasis modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3296185/?utm_source=openai))

Key controls and falsification tests
- Non-sulfated and fully sulfated controls test non-specific electrostatics vs. motif selectivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5588662/?utm_source=openai))
- Swapping plasma across samples tests dependence on soluble HS-binding cofactors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6152867/?utm_source=openai))
- Endothelial HS editing (siRNA/CRISPR of HS6ST/NDST/Sulf1/2) should shift Horgan in predicted directions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3308746/?utm_source=openai))
- Shear-dependence: If predictions degrade when measured only at static/no-flow, it supports the necessity of flow conditioning, consistent with in vivo mechanics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3103268/?utm_source=openai))

Clinical and biological outputs
- A standardized microfluidic HS-decoder assay and trained classifier yielding per-organ risk distributions from a single blood draw.
- A first-in-kind, organ-resolved endothelial HS atlas aligned to functional adhesion metrics, enabling mechanistic interpretation of organotropism.

Novelty statement
- While HS microarrays and HS glycomimetics are established for protein-binding studies, and organ/vessel-specific endothelial HS differences are documented, there is no prior report of using a synthetic HS-sulfation-pattern microarray as an intermediate decoder to map live CTC adhesion under shear to an organ-resolved endothelial HS codebook for metastasis forecasting. This research directly operationalizes “glycocalyx address codes” into a predictive, pan-cancer blood test. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8022954/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risk
- Chemistry and microarray methods are available; endothelial HS heterogeneity is supported; CTC–glycan/selectin adhesion under flow is well documented. Risks include confounding by non-HS adhesins; mitigated via perturbations and orthogonal selectin assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8022954/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Build HS-decoder, establish shear protocols, pilot reproducibility.
- Year 2: Generate organ HS codebook, train classifier on retrospective data.
- Year 3: Prospective pilot, lock algorithm, plan multicenter validation.

Deliverable form
- An IVD-ready microfluidic cartridge and analytical software that report per-organ metastasis probabilities and confidence intervals from 7–10 mL of blood, with an accompanying endothelial HS reference dataset and mechanistic audit trail.

text:
Title: GlycoFlux: A functional, glycocalyx-guided CTC assay to predict organ-specific metastasis via multivalent lectin–glycan compatibility under physiologic flow

Central hypothesis-question:
Do organ-specific endothelial lectin landscapes and hemodynamics define a minimal functional compatibility test such that a circulating tumor cell’s rolling/tethering kinetics across a calibrated panel of endothelial glycan receptors predict its metastatic destination across cancers? If so, can we read this “compatibility” directly from patient CTCs using organ-mimetic flow lanes, and is the readout causally governed by defined sialylated/fucosylated glycan determinants? E-/P-selectin–mediated initial arrest is a conserved gateway for extravasation, bone marrow expresses E-selectin constitutively, and liver sinusoidal endothelium uniquely presents C-type lectins (CLEC4G/LSECtin; CLEC4M/LSIGN) that modulate liver metastasis; brain microvessels possess a thicker glycocalyx that generally suppresses adhesion. These features motivate an organ-resolved, glycobiology-first functional test. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selectin?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8167702/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8489908/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy:
Predict organotropism by measuring how individual CTCs roll, pause, and adhere across parallel, organ-mimetic microchannels presenting defined endothelial lectins (E-/P-selectin; CLEC4G/LSIGN) and glycocalyx contexts under organ-appropriate shear. Calibrate the assay’s sensitivity to glycan valency/spacing using glycan-patterned DNA nanocalibrators displaying sLeX variants at controlled nanometer spacing. The single-cell kinetic barcode across lanes is the destination predictor; small, targeted glycome edits on CTCs test causality.

Specific aims:

Aim 1. Build an organ-mimetic endothelial lectin array under flow (GlycoFlux) and calibrate multivalency sensitivity.
- Lanes and receptor sets:
  - Liver: E-selectin + CLEC4G (LSECtin) ± CLEC4M (LSIGN); sinusoid-like low shear (1–10 s−1). LSEC lectins promote colon cancer liver metastasis; genetic or ligand perturbation alters hepatic seeding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8167702/?utm_source=openai))
  - Lung: E- and P-selectin; moderate shear; cytokine-inducible E-selectin facilitates tumor cell endothelial activation and extravasation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27488527/?utm_source=openai))
  - Bone marrow: Constitutive E-selectin on sinusoidal endothelium; low-to-moderate shear. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai))
  - Brain (exploratory): Thick, highly anionic glycocalyx coating; low basal selectins; use glycocalyx-rich coatings to assess adhesion suppression as a negative-control signature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8489908/?utm_source=openai))
- Fabrication: Glass/PDMS microchannels with receptor ectodomain immobilization at defined surface densities; overlay organ-typical hemodynamics. Record trajectories at ≥500 fps to extract rolling velocity distributions, pause frequency, and detachment forces; validate with standard selectin rolling assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2546510/?utm_source=openai))
- Calibration with glycan-patterned DNA nanocalibrators: Flow sLeX/sLea/6-sulfo-sLeX DNA-based multivalent scaffolds with tunable interligand spacing (5–50 nm) to map each lane’s capture sensitivity to glycan valency/spacing and to benchmark catch-bond regimes. Prior DNA-scaffolded glycan displays show spacing-dependent lectin recognition (including L-selectin and sLeX) and multivalency effects. Use these as traceable standards to convert kinetic readouts into inferred ligand topology on cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4462854/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones for Aim 1:
- Receptor density–response curves per lane; CV <15% across chips.
- Calibrated response surfaces linking glycan valency/spacing to rolling velocity and pause statistics for each receptor set.

Aim 2. Derive a CTC adhesion kinetic barcode (AKB) that predicts organotropism and validate across cancers.
- Cohorts: Banked plasma from patients with colorectal, breast, pancreatic, and lung cancers with longitudinal imaging defining first metastatic site(s). Isolate CTCs, run within 6 h to preserve native glycocalyx.
- Readout: For each CTC, compute AKB = [Vroll, fpause, τpause, Fdetach] across lanes. Aggregate per patient to yield an organotropism vector.
- Model: Train a probabilistic classifier mapping AKB to first-site metastasis labels; evaluate AUC and calibration. Use time-to-event models to assess lead-time advantage over standard biomarkers.
- External validation: Patient-derived xenografts (PDX) with known destination bias; sample CTCs prior to endpoint metastasis and test blinded prediction vs necropsy distribution. Selectin-dependent arrest correlates with metastatic capacity in microfluidic enrichment and in vivo lung seeding, supporting construct validity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7657380/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones for Aim 2:
- Retrospective AUC ≥0.80 for liver vs lung vs bone marrow first-site prediction; prospective PDX accuracy ≥75%.
- Decision thresholds with positive likelihood ratio ≥4 for top-destination call.

Aim 3. Establish glycan causality by minimal glycome perturbations on CTCs and observe predictable AKB shifts.
- Perturbations (ex vivo, ≤6 h):
  - Reduce sLeX: feed 5-thiofucose to inhibit fucosyltransferases; expect decreased E-/P-selectin rolling and reduced liver/lung lane adhesion. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021925820622955?utm_source=openai))
  - Increase sLeX: N-propanoyl-ManNAc to elevate sLeX; expect enhanced E-/P-selectin-mediated rolling. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0014482704000461?utm_source=openai))
  - Modulate sialic acid acetylation state (e.g., de-O-acetylation genetics/enzymes where feasible) and test predicted increase in selectin binding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11663943/?utm_source=openai))
- Re-run perturbed CTCs through GlycoFlux; quantify directional AKB shifts. Prior metabolic glycoengineering alters selectin-mediated adhesion without necessarily changing ligand abundance, consistent with chemistry-driven affinity and catch-bond modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2911014/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones for Aim 3:
- Directionally correct AKB shifts in ≥70% of perturbed samples vs autologous controls.
- Perturbation-response mapping that links specific glycan edits to organ-lane adhesion changes.

Experimental considerations and controls:
- Shear profiles: Set organ-typical wall shear rates; verify with micro-PIV.
- Specificity: Blockade controls with soluble E-selectin-Fc or antibodies; confirm abrogation of rolling. E-/P-selectin dependence of tumor cell arrest is well documented. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selectin?utm_source=openai))
- Liver lectins: Include CLEC4G/LSIGN lanes; test loss-of-function with anti-CLEC4G and compare to selectin lanes; hepatic metastasis is enhanced by LSECtin in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8167702/?utm_source=openai))
- Glycocalyx context: Incorporate heparan sulfate coatings to present chemokines and modulate rolling-to-adhesion transitions where relevant; HS sulfation controls chemokine immobilization and L-selectin rolling in microvessels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2996097/?utm_source=openai))
- Brain lane: Use thick anionic glycocalyx mimetics (sialylated glycosaminoglycans) to establish low-adhesion baseline consistent with BBB; test whether brain-tropic CTCs display distinct non-selectin kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8489908/?utm_source=openai))

Endpoints and analytics:
- Primary endpoint: Accuracy of first-destination prediction within 12 months of sampling.
- Secondary endpoints: Time-to-metastasis stratification by top-destination score; concordance with imaging.
- Mechanistic inference: From nanocalibrator-informed models, infer minimal glycan ligand topology (epitope, valency, spacing) that best explains observed AKB per patient.

Deliverable:
A CLIA-ready assay reporting a per-patient organotropism vector (liver/lung/bone marrow/brain probabilities) derived from CTC AKBs on GlycoFlux, grounded in lectin–glycan physics and calibrated with glycan-patterned DNA nanocalibrators.

Novelty:
- Functional, destination-specific phenotyping of patient CTCs across organ-matched lectin/glycocalyx contexts under flow, rather than static glycan staining or primary tumor profiling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7657380/?utm_source=openai))
- Use of DNA-scaffolded glycan nanocalibrators to parameterize multivalency/spacing effects that govern selectin/C-type lectin capture, enabling inverse inference of CTC glycan topology from kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4462854/?utm_source=openai))
- Integration of minimal metabolic glycoengineering to demonstrate causality between defined glycan chemistry and organ-lane adhesion shifts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2911014/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risk:
- Receptor sourcing and stability under flow are established for selectins; C-type lectin immobilization will be optimized with oriented capture. Selectin rolling assays are robust; liver LSEC lectins are implicated in metastasis biology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2546510/?utm_source=openai))
- Heterogeneous CTC viability is mitigated by rapid processing and low-temperature handling to preserve the native glycocalyx.
- Brain predictions are exploratory in Phase I; expansion will incorporate additional BBB-relevant lectins as evidence accumulates.

Success criteria (24 months):
- Technically: Reproducible lane responses (intra/inter-chip CV <15%), validated nanocalibrator maps.
- Biologically: Demonstrated selectin/CLEC4G dependence of AKB features with blocking and perturbation.
- Clinical signal: Retrospective AUC ≥0.80 and prospective PDX confirmation of destination calls.

Key supporting biology:
- Selectins mediate initial tumor cell tethering/rolling via sLeX-bearing ligands (e.g., PSGL-1, CD44); catch-bond kinetics govern rolling under shear. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26124272/?utm_source=openai))
- Bone marrow endothelium constitutively expresses E-selectin; lung and liver upregulate E-selectin with inflammatory cues; hepatic LSEC lectins (CLEC4G/LSIGN) modulate liver metastasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1861610/?page=1&utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/8167702/?utm_source=openai))
- Glycocalyx architecture varies by organ and shapes adhesion; BBB glycocalyx is thicker and suppresses nonspecific arrest. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8489908/?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolic glycoengineering predictably remodels sialylation/fucosylation to modulate selectin adhesion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2911014/?utm_source=openai))

Outcome:
A mechanistically grounded, pan-cancer, glycobiology-first diagnostic that reads the functional “entry pass” CTCs use to arrest in organ-specific vascular beds, converting real-time adhesion physics into an organotropism prediction that can guide surveillance and therapy.

Title: Fragment-and-Force AND-gated engagement of injury-remodeled endothelial glycocalyx to enhance therapeutic cell homing and transendothelial migration

Central hypothesis-question
- Can a single, logical-AND molecular gate that requires simultaneous detection of hyaluronan (HA) degradation fragments and a specific tensile loading regime—conditions that co-occur only where the endothelial glycocalyx is thinned and compositionally altered—unlock local presentation of adhesion/chemokine cues to selectively promote homing and diapedesis of endogenous stem cells or administered cell therapeutics? This question presumes: (i) injury increases HS/CS/HA shedding and generates soluble HA/HS fragments at the luminal interface; (ii) glycocalyx loss increases endothelial access and alters force transmission; and (iii) HA fragments function as short-lived DAMPs. These premises are well supported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
- Couple compositional readout (HA-fragment cofactor) to a calibrated force switch so that productive adhesion signaling occurs only when “injury chemistry” and “injury mechanics” co-exist. The gate unlocks integrin/chemokine instructions for extravasation exclusively at injured endothelium.

Rationale and novelty
- Injury-remodeled glycocalyx: Protease/glycosidase activity (MMPs, heparanase, hyaluronidases) sheds HS/CS/HA and releases GAG fragments, thinning the barrier and re-patterning ligand access. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))
- HA fragments act as DAMPs that engage CD44/TLRs at the vascular interface; their presence is both spatially restricted and temporally transient after injury. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
- The glycocalyx modulates shear mechanotransduction and nanoparticle/endothelium interactions; its degradation increases endothelial accessibility and changes the local force landscape felt by surface ligands. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214841/?utm_source=openai))
- DNA hairpin/duplex mechanoswitches and synthetic catch bonds provide pN-resolved, force-gated activation compatible with living systems. Prior work used these to sense/quantify cell forces, not to gate endothelial engagement for cell homing; leveraging injury-remodeled glycocalyx mechanics as the “force input” is, to our knowledge, unexplored. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710701/?utm_source=openai))

Proposed system: F2T (Fragment-and-Force Tether)
- Composition (modular, minimal):
  1) Weak endothelial docking: a low-affinity HS-recognizing peptide/aptamer (nM–µM KD) to permit transient tethering without strong adhesion on intact glycocalyx. (Any HS-binding module is acceptable; the gate provides specificity.) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214841/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Fragment cofactor latch: a binding pocket (aptamer or peptide) selective for short HA oligos (e.g., 6–20-mers). Pocket engagement is necessary but not sufficient for activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
  3) Force switch: a DNA hairpin or duplex with calibrated opening/shear threshold (≈5–15 pN) arranged so that only under reduced damping at an injured glycocalyx does hydrodynamic loading across the tether open the switch. Opening unmasks a payload that activates rolling-to-arrest (e.g., a CXCL12/SDF-1α mimetic or integrin-activating ligand) to promote diapedesis of therapeutic cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710701/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted behavior
- Healthy endothelium: low/no HA oligos; intact glycocalyx dissipates force; HS-docking is reversible; force switch remains closed; no payload exposure; normal barrier preserved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214841/?utm_source=openai))
- Injury site: HA fragments present; barrier thinned, higher force transmission; both inputs satisfied; switch opens; localized chemokine/adhesion presentation increases capture and transmigration of circulating therapeutic cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Quantify injury-state inputs and force transfer.
  - 1a. Define HA-oligo abundance and lifetime at endothelial surfaces after enzyme (heparanase, hyaluronidase, MMP) challenge and in microinjury models under flow; resolve fragment sizes by fluorophore-assisted carbohydrate electrophoresis and LC-MS. Confirm DAMP-like signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))
  - 1b. Map force transmission across the luminal interface as a function of glycocalyx thickness/porosity under physiological shear (1–20 dyn/cm2) using surface-immobilized DNA hairpin/TGT probes and endothelialized microfluidic channels before/after controlled glycocalyx degradation. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.6b06812?utm_source=openai))
  - Go/no-go: Detection of a force window (≥5–10 pN) that is rare on intact endothelium but frequent after glycocalyx thinning; quantifiable HA-oligo elevations at injury interfaces.

- Aim 2. Build and calibrate F2T.
  - 2a. Engineer an HA-oligo latch (aptamer or peptide) with dissociation constants tuned to HA8–HA20; validate selectivity vs HMW-HA and HS/CS by BLI/SPR and competition assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
  - 2b. Integrate a DNA hairpin/duplex mechanoswitch (opening at 5–15 pN) in series with the latch so that fragment binding primes the switch but does not expose payload without mechanical opening. Calibrate thresholds with single-molecule force spectroscopy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710701/?utm_source=openai))
  - 2c. Couple the switch to a minimal pro-extravasation payload (e.g., CXCL12 mimetic or ICAM-1–binding peptide) on a PEGylated nanoscale scaffold that remains stealthy until gate opening; verify that payload exposure requires both HA-oligo binding and force. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.6b06812?utm_source=openai))

- Aim 3. Demonstrate selective promotion of homing and TEM.
  - 3a. Endothelial injury-on-chip: Human microvascular endothelial monolayers with intact vs enzyme-thinned glycocalyx; perfuse therapeutic cells (e.g., MSCs or CD34+ HSPCs) with or without F2T-coated “docking pads” pre-applied to endothelium; measure rolling velocity, arrest frequency, and transendothelial migration by live imaging. Controls: remove HA fragments (hyaluronidase inhibitors), block CD44/TLR4, or use force-inert F2T mutants. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
  - 3b. In vivo microinjury: Localized endothelial glycocalyx injury (e.g., ischemia-reperfusion segment or focal photochemical injury) with systemic infusion of therapeutic cells ± F2T “docking pads.” Quantify site-selective homing and extravasation; assess off-target capture in healthy tissues by intravital microscopy and biodistribution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))

Key design parameters and validation
- Force threshold: start at 7–12 pN to match regimes known to be sampled by integrin–ligand linkages during early adhesion and below the ~40 pN peak integrin tension measured for RGD-binding integrins, ensuring switchability at injury-modified interfaces under flow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710701/?utm_source=openai))
- Fragment selectivity: favor HA8–HA20 where DAMP activity is documented; include negative selection against HMW-HA to avoid activation on healthy endothelium. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
- Docking valency: fix low valency to maintain reversible pre-contacts and avoid adhesion on intact glycocalyx; validate minimal binding in intact-state microchannels. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.6b06812?utm_source=openai))

Readouts and success criteria
- Chemistry: HA-fragment dependent priming of F2T latch; no priming by HMW-HA/HS/CS.
- Mechanics: Force-dependent unmasking only above calibrated threshold; no unmasking under low shear or intact glycocalyx.
- Function: ≥3× increase in firm arrest and ≥2× increase in TEM of therapeutic cells at injury sites with ≤10% off-target adhesion in non-injured vascular beds.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: HA-oligo latch cross-reacts with HMW-HA. Mitigation: size-selective aptamer evolution and competitive blockers; confirm by mass-resolved fragment binding. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Force threshold too high/low for vascular conditions. Mitigation: tune hairpin GC content/geometry to shift opening force; benchmark with TGT panels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9973368/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Endothelial activation by HA fragments. Mitigation: gate requires both inputs; payload exposure zone is limited; include TLR4/CD44 pathway monitoring; dose-titrate to avoid exacerbating inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2196009/?utm_source=openai))

Why this meets constraints
- Tissue-specific glycocalyx differences are read via relative injury-state chemistry (HA fragments) and mechanics (reduced damping), not a single marker; the gate is inherently combinatorial. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214841/?utm_source=openai))
- Effect is confined: no HA fragments or insufficient tensile loading → no activation; intact endothelium remains unperturbed. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.6b06812?utm_source=openai))
- Disease-agnostic: HA/HS shedding and fragment generation occur across sepsis, trauma, ischemia-reperfusion, diabetes, viral injury; the gate keys off generic injury hallmarks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))
- Target of modulation: only homing/extravasation cues are locally presented; no systemic barrier disruption or global enzyme manipulation.

Milestones
- Month 0–9: Quantify inputs; calibrate force landscapes; evolve HA-oligo latch.
- Month 9–18: Assemble F2T; complete in vitro logic validation; select payload.
- Month 18–30: Endothelium-on-chip homing/TEM; optimize thresholds/valency.
- Month 30–42: In vivo validation of selective homing/extravasation; safety and biodistribution.

Deliverable
- A validated, fragment-and-force AND-gated endothelial interface that converts injury-specific glycocalyx remodeling into localized adhesion/chemokine presentation, thereby increasing therapeutic cell capture and diapedesis with high spatial fidelity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9304628/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Myofiber-targeted HAS2 gene augmentation to establish a protective pericellular hyaluronan brush that reduces contraction-induced membrane injury and downstream degeneration in Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Rationale and novelty
- In DMD, loss of dystrophin destabilizes the sarcolemma. During lengthening contractions, focal membrane defects allow extracellular Ca2+ to enter, triggering calpains, mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS, necrosis, inflammation, and fibrosis; this positive-feedback loop drives progressive weakness. Mechanical stabilization and reduced leak duration upstream of calcium overload ameliorate pathology in preclinical models, validating the interface as a therapeutic control point. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8729700/?utm_source=openai))
- The pericellular hyaluronan (HA) layer behaves as a hydrated polymer brush that modifies near-membrane mechanics and shear transmission and participates in mechanosensing; high–molecular weight HA (HMW-HA) generally biases toward anti-inflammatory signaling, whereas fragmented HA can be pro-inflammatory. TSG-6–mediated crosslinking can further stabilize HA networks and modulate cell–matrix signaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2174428/?utm_source=openai))
- In DMD muscle, fibrosis includes altered glycosaminoglycans, with increased HA reported early in fibrotic remodeling; however, targeted, myofiber-restricted enhancement of an organized HMW-HA brush has not been pursued as a gene therapy to reduce stress concentration and membrane failure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3631802/?utm_source=openai))
- Prior membrane-stabilizing small molecules (for example, poloxamer 188) can attenuate contraction-induced injury in dystrophic muscle, supporting the concept that modifying interfacial mechanics reduces damage, but they are not durable and are not gene therapies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2493563/?utm_source=openai))
- AAV vectors can express HAS2 in vivo and have precedent across tissues; we did not identify preclinical or clinical studies applying AAV-HAS2 to DMD as of August 11, 2026, supporting novelty while indicating feasibility. ([patentimages.storage.googleapis.com](https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/a0/04/e2/3d6e11b6937006/US20170198263A1.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Unifying hypothesis
Augmenting HAS2 specifically in skeletal (and secondarily cardiac) myofibers will thicken and organize a localized, high–molecular weight pericellular HA brush that reduces peak mechanical stress transfer to the sarcolemma and shortens the dwell time of microdefects, thereby lowering Ca2+ leak, protease/ROS activation, and inflammatory signaling; this will slow degeneration and preserve function without restoring dystrophin.

Atomic strategy
Change the boundary condition rather than the broken scaffold: install a tunable, HA-based pericellular cushion at the myofiber surface by myofiber-targeted HAS2 gene augmentation to mechanically and chemically bias the interface away from rupture and inflammation.

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Engineer and validate a myofiber-targeted HAS2 gene therapy cassette that yields a stable, surface-localized HMW-HA brush without ectopic accumulation.
  - Design principle: skeletal muscle–restricted promoter and untranslated region architecture with microRNA de-targeting to minimize liver expression; optional inclusion of an extracellular HA-binding/tethering domain to bias HA retention at the sarcolemma. Benchmarks: increased pericellular HA around myofibers; minimal systemic HA change; no edema or interference with neuromuscular transmission. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11640742/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2. Test whether the HA brush reduces mechanical injury and calcium dysregulation in dystrophin-deficient muscle.
  - Primary endpoints: reduced contraction-induced membrane permeability and Ca2+-overload signatures; improved resistance to lengthening-contraction force loss; decreased markers of calpain activation and oxidative damage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8537421/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3. Determine effects on inflammation, fibrosis, and function over time.
  - Endpoints: reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine signatures and macrophage infiltration; decreased profibrotic signaling and collagen deposition; preserved muscle performance and ambulation metrics. Mechanistic correlates: maintenance of HMW-HA predominance and increased TSG-6/HC–HA complexes consistent with anti-inflammatory matrix remodeling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6376563/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 4. Translation readiness.
  - Evaluate biodistribution, immunogenicity, and reversibility controls; define dose–response and safety margins that avoid viscosity-related diffusion penalties or ectopic HA effects. Guidance informed by gene therapy regulatory expectations. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/science-research-biologics/immunogenicity-gene-therapy-products?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic justification
- Mechanical: A dense, surface-tethered HMW-HA brush increases interfacial slip length and distributes shear, lowering focal stress at costameric discontinuities and raising the strain threshold for membrane failure—conceptually analogous to the partial benefit observed with membrane stabilizers, but encoded durably and locally by gene expression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2174428/?utm_source=openai))
- Ionic/injury cascade: By reducing the frequency and dwell time of microtears, the HA brush decreases Ca2+ entry events that initiate calpain activation and mitochondrial dysfunction, mitigating downstream necrosis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8729700/?utm_source=openai))
- Inflammation/fibrosis: HMW-HA biases anti-inflammatory signaling; TSG-6–facilitated crosslinking and heavy-chain transfer onto HA further stabilizes an inflammation-dampening matrix, countering the chronic profibrotic milieu of DMD muscle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6376563/?utm_source=openai))

Study design overview
- Vector and expression
  - AAV serotype with strong skeletal muscle tropism paired with a compact muscle-specific promoter; inclusion of microRNA target sites to de-target liver and optionally heart depending on cardiomyopathy goals. Manufacturing follows contemporary AAV practices with release testing for genome integrity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11640742/?utm_source=openai))
- Proof-of-concept models
  - Dystrophin-deficient mouse models for dose-ranging, biodistribution, and mechanistic readouts; subsequent large-animal feasibility for scaling transduction and functional endpoints.
- Readouts
  - Interface mechanics: quantitative assays of membrane integrity under controlled contractions; imaging of pericellular HA distribution and organization.
  - Calcium and injury: optical and biochemical markers of Ca2+ dysregulation and protease/ROS activation; histology for myonecrosis and regeneration.
  - Inflammation/fibrosis: transcriptomic and histological assessment of inflammatory and fibrotic pathways; quantification of HA size distribution and TSG-6/HC–HA complexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3138277/?utm_source=openai))
  - Function: standardized muscle performance metrics and cardiopulmonary assessments aligned with DMD preclinical norms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10330733/?utm_source=openai))

Safety and risk management
- HA fragmentation risk: incorporate design features that favor HMW-HA (enzyme choice, expression level control); monitor HA size distribution; define mitigation criteria if low–molecular weight HA predominates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6376563/?utm_source=openai))
- Edema or diffusion barriers: titrate expression toward activity-proportional levels; incorporate reversible control elements to attenuate expression if adverse biomechanics emerge.
- Off-target expression: use muscle-restricted regulatory elements and microRNA de-targeting to minimize hepatic or synovial expression; predefine stopping rules for unintended biodistribution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11640742/?utm_source=openai))
- Immunogenicity: follow current guidance for AAV product immunogenicity risk assessment and monitoring. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/science-research-biologics/immunogenicity-gene-therapy-products?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go milestones
- Go: demonstration of sustained, myofiber-localized HMW-HA brush; significant reduction in contraction-induced membrane permeability and Ca2+ overload with acceptable safety signals.
- No-go or pivot: persistent LMW-HA predominance, edema, or functional impairment attributable to the HA layer; lack of effect on primary mechanical/ionic endpoints.

Translation plan
- Indication scope: ambulatory boys with DMD irrespective of genotype, as an adjunct to standard care and potentially combinable with dystrophin-restoring modalities due to pathway orthogonality.
- Clinical path: begin with localized administration to a single muscle group for safety and biomarker validation, progressing to systemic delivery if safety and efficacy thresholds are met; incorporate noninvasive biomarkers of membrane injury and matrix remodeling to guide dose selection.
- Differentiation: dystrophin-independent, mechanism-upstream intervention with durable, activity-agnostic protection at the sarcolemma–ECM boundary; compatible with existing and emerging DMD therapies.

Expected impact
If successful, myofiber-targeted HAS2 gene augmentation will recondition the myofiber’s immediate extracellular boundary to be more forgiving under load, reducing the initiating events of the DMD damage cascade. This single-axis, boundary-layer intervention is designed to slow disease progression without engaging or replacing dystrophin biology, meeting the goal of a dystrophin-independent gene therapy for DMD. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7074327/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Cortex-tether augmentation for DMD: AAV delivery of a minimal EPB41 FERM–SAB construct to reduce mechanoporation and Ca2+-driven pathology without dystrophin

Central hypothesis–question
If sarcolemmal failure in DMD originates from insufficient membrane–cortex coupling, will increasing the density and avidity of spectrin–actin–membrane tethers using a muscle-tuned, minimal EPB41 (protein 4.1) FERM–SAB construct reduce contraction-induced mechanoporation and Ca2+ influx enough to attenuate calpain activation, necrosis, and fibrosis, thereby improving muscle function without targeting dystrophin? This reframes DMD as a correctable cortex-insufficiency problem. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00037.2014?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Install additional mechanical load paths by gene-encoding compact EPB41 tethers that bind inner-leaflet lipids (FERM) and strengthen spectrin–actin connections (SAB), thereby raising the local rupture threshold and lowering pore nucleation probability per contraction cycle. One encoded tether family; no reliance on dystrophin or DGC reconstitution. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10887211/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and validate minimal EPB41 tethers that increase membrane–cortex coupling in myofibers.
- Design: Construct a 1.2–1.6 kb cDNA encoding EPB41 FERM + SAB with the exon‑16 21-aa motif critical for spectrin–actin affinity; truncate nonessential regions (FA/CTD) to fit AAV while preserving high-affinity binding. Add flexible linkers; optional low-affinity basic patch to modestly enhance PIP2/PS binding if needed. Benchmarks: soluble expression; no aggregation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10887211/?utm_source=openai))
- Cell validation (human iPSC-derived and primary myotubes): quantify cortical mechanics by optical tweezer tether-pulls and AFM; measure FRAP-based residency at sarcolemma; co-IP with β-spectrin/actin; super-resolution mapping of costameric enrichment. Success metric: ≥20% increase in effective cortical shear modulus without impairing sarcolemmal trafficking.
- Safety/physiology screens: patch-clamp assays for stretch-activated currents (Piezo/TRPC) and resting membrane properties; Ca2+ imaging during cyclic stretch; RNA-seq for channel/transporter expression shifts. Stop rule: any ≥20% rise in resting [Ca2+]i or arrhythmic Ca2+ events triggers construct re-tuning. Rationale: EPB41 family proteins influence ion channel complexes; we avoid maladaptive coupling by domain minimization. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1079979609000412?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Test whether EPB41 tethering lowers mechanoporation, Ca2+ load, and proteolysis in dystrophic muscle.
- Models: mdx4cv and D2‑mdx mice; ex vivo single-fiber assays; in vivo injury and exercise challenges.
- Readouts of membrane failure: FM1‑43/fura-2 influx during lengthening contractions; Evans Blue uptake; laser-wound resealing kinetics (time to half-closure). Target: ≥40% reduction in dye influx AUC and ≥30% faster resealing versus AAV-GFP. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00037.2014?utm_source=openai))
- Downstream cascade: calpain activation (spectrin breakdown products), mitochondrial membrane potential under load, serum CK/LDH, macrophage infiltration and fibrosis (Picrosirius). Target: ≥30% reduction in calpain biomarkers and fibrosis area at 12 weeks. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00037.2014?utm_source=openai))
- Function: in situ EDL and soleus force after eccentric protocols; diaphragm specific force. Target: ≥20% improvement in torque–angle hysteresis and post-injury force retention.

Aim 3. Optimize delivery and translational parameters for clinical plausibility.
- Vector and expression control: compare AAV9 and MyoAAV variants for potency at reduced dose; drive with tMCK/CK8 muscle-specific promoters; include a degradation (PEST) tag to avoid over-stiffening; consider microRNA target sites to suppress expression in off-target tissues. Go/no‑go: achieve target Aim 2 efficacy at ≤3×10^13 vg/kg with no overt toxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9344975/?utm_source=openai))
- Biodistribution and safety: vector genomes in major organs; hematology for elliptocytosis; blood smear morphology (mitigates concern given erythrocyte non-permissiveness to AAV and muscle-restricted promoters); ECG/echo for cardiac conduction homeostasis.
- Manufacturability: single-gene payload within AAV capacity; standard producer lines; release testing per current chemistry, manufacturing, and controls practices for muscle gene therapy. Benchmarking against contemporary muscle-tropic AAV performance. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9059/13/8/1994?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Mechanistic novelty: directly strengthens the membrane–cortex lattice using EPB41 tethers rather than restoring DGC or overexpressing known repair proteins; focuses on rupture prevention instead of emergency repair. To our knowledge, EPB41-based gene augmentation has not been evaluated as a therapeutic strategy in DMD models. Foundational evidence supports EPB41’s FERM/SAB roles in lipid association and spectrin–actin stabilization, and muscle expresses 4.1R isoforms with muscle-specific splicing—together enabling a muscle-tuned tether design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10887211/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design details

Construct set
- M1: FERM–SAB minimal (human EPB41; SAB includes exon 16 motif).
- M2: FERM–SAB with modest membrane-affinity enhancement (polybasic loop swap).
- M3: SAB-only control (tests necessity of FERM–lipid binding).
- Safety control: kinase-dead-like FERM mutant that reduces lipid binding but preserves folding.

In vitro assays
- Mechanics: AFM indentation and tether-pull assays under tonic and cyclic stretch.
- Localization/partners: STED imaging for colocalization with β-spectrin/costameres; co-IP/mass spectrometry to verify preserved interactome.

In vivo protocol
- Systemic AAV at 6 weeks (mdx4cv, D2‑mdx); 12-week follow-up.
- Functional tests: grip strength; treadmill downhill running; in situ torque frequency curves; susceptibility to lengthening contraction injury.

Readouts and statistics
- Pre-specified endpoints per aim; blinded analyses; power from pilot variance on dye influx and force deficit; mixed-effects models across muscles.

Risk mitigation
- Over-stiffening: tune promoter strength; add degron; terminate if endocytic flux or membrane capacitance deviates >15% from baseline.
- Channel perturbation: screen currents; if altered, reduce SAB affinity by fine-tuning exon‑16-adjacent residues.
- Immunogenicity: human sequence reduces risk; monitor T-cell responses; if needed, transient tacrolimus or rapamycin per standard AAV practice.

Translational path and criteria for advancement
- Success: Aim 2 efficacy thresholds met with favorable safety, plus dose linearity and durability ≥6 months.
- Next steps: large-animal feasibility with MyoAAV at reduced dose; GLP tox in two species; IND-enabling CMC; early-phase trial in ambulatory adolescents with exon‑skipping-ineligible genotypes, measuring creatine kinase, microperforation biomarkers, and MRI T2 mapping.

Rationale anchors
- DMD pathology features Ca2+-triggered proteolysis following membrane injury; reducing mechanoporation and shortening lesion lifetime is causal for benefit. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00037.2014?utm_source=openai))
- EPB41 family architecture: FERM for membrane association; SAB (exon‑16 motif) for spectrin–actin stabilization; 4.1R isoforms and muscle-specific splicing documented in skeletal muscle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10887211/?utm_source=openai))
- SAB-driven integration strengthens spectrin–actin networks and increases elastic resilience in model systems, supporting the load-distribution premise. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2199952/?utm_source=openai))
- Potent, next-generation muscle-targeted AAV capsids and validated muscle promoters improve feasibility at clinically acceptable doses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9344975/?utm_source=openai))

Outcome
A single encoded, human-derived tether system that upgrades the sarcolemmal cortex to operate safely in a dystrophin-free regime, reducing Ca2+-driven degeneration and improving force without touching the dystrophin locus.
