text:
Title
Driving cerebrospinal–interstitial fluid dynamics during wake to restore multi‑axis homeostasis under time‑restricted sleep

Rationale
- Sleep restriction impairs neurocognitive performance, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory control, and autonomic balance. A substantial fraction of sleep’s restorative work depends on slow, large‑scale physiological oscillations (0.1–1 Hz) that expand perivascular spaces and couple vascular/respiratory pulsations to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)–interstitial fluid exchange. NREM slow waves show alternating waves of blood volume and CSF flow; lowering noradrenergic tone during natural sleep supports this clearance regime. Lateral body posture increases glymphatic transport in rodents. These observations suggest a mechanical control handle on clearance that could be engaged during wakefulness. ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Respiration is a dominant, tunable driver of CSF flow. In humans, paced or deep breathing shifts CSF velocities and stroke volumes (cervical/foramen magnum), while also engaging the baroreflex and increasing heart‑rate variability (HRV) at ~0.1 Hz. This offers a single actuator with concurrent effects on clearance physics and autonomic recalibration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))
- Non‑contrast MRI methods (RT‑PC MRI; diffusion tensor imaging along perivascular spaces, DTI‑ALPS) provide feasible human surrogates of CSF/ISF transport suitable for interventional testing, though ALPS requires cautious interpretation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Integrated hypothesis‑question
Can brief, fully awake “clearance blocks” that combine lateral decubitus posture with 0.1 Hz paced diaphragmatic breathing increase CSF/ISF transport and, as a consequence, partially normalize neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic endpoints after multi‑day sleep restriction—approximating a recovery state without extending sleep time? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26245965/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit respiration‑driven pressure swings at 0.1 Hz in a lateral posture to amplify cranio‑spinal CSF pulsatility and perivascular advective flow during wake, thereby substituting part of sleep‑dependent waste‑clearance/autonomic recalibration with a controllable mechanical input. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1 (Mechanism): Determine whether 0.1 Hz paced breathing in lateral decubitus acutely increases CSF flow metrics versus sham during wakefulness.
- Aim 2 (Systems outcomes): Test whether thrice‑daily “clearance blocks” blunt multi‑axis impairments induced by time‑restricted sleep.
- Aim 3 (Dose–response and timing): Map the minimal effective duration and optimal timing (relative to learning and circadian phase) for maximal multi‑axis benefit.

Design
- Participants: 36 healthy adults (18–40), randomized, within‑subject, counterbalanced, three 4‑day laboratory conditions separated by ≥14 days.
  1) Sleep restriction (4.5 h time‑in‑bed, 00:30–05:00) + clearance blocks (active).
  2) Sleep restriction + sham blocks (supine, 12–14 breaths/min audio; attention control).
  3) Ad libitum sleep (7.5–8.5 h) no blocks (physiological reference).
- Clearance block (active): 15 min, lateral decubitus, head‑neutral alignment, paced diaphragmatic breathing at individualized resonance (~6 breaths/min) with capnography feedback to maintain normocapnia; guided by metronome and respiratory belt; eyes closed, awake. Three sessions/day at 10:00, 14:00, 18:00. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Sham block: 15 min, supine, 12–14 breaths/min, identical monitoring and instructions without resonance pacing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Primary mechanistic endpoints
- Real‑time phase‑contrast MRI (RT‑PC MRI) at foramen magnum and upper cervical levels immediately pre/post the first daily block on Days 2 and 3: CSF stroke volume, peak‑to‑peak velocity, respiratory‑to‑cardiac power ratio. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28152239/?utm_source=openai))
- Whole‑brain diffusion MRI for DTI‑ALPS index at baseline and morning Day 4 as a surrogate of interstitial transport efficiency (sensitivity analyses acknowledge ALPS limitations). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805491/?utm_source=openai))

Multi‑axis secondary endpoints
- Neurocognitive: psychomotor vigilance task; n‑back working memory; delayed word‑pair recall (evening training, morning test). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-39178-2?utm_source=openai))
- Metabolic: oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) incremental AUC; HOMA‑IR; continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) variability (Days 1–4). 
- Immune: plasma IL‑6, TNF‑α, hs‑CRP morning draws; salivary cytokines exploratory.
- Autonomic: 24‑h HRV (time/frequency, non‑linear); baroreflex sensitivity via sequence method; pupillometry (sympathetic index). Paced‑breathing sessions also yield intra‑session HRV coherence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5709795/?utm_source=openai))
- Sleep architecture check (polysomnography) to confirm restricted sleep protocol and quantify NREM SWS density per minute slept; exploratory coupling with SWS‑dependent clearance signatures. ([websites.ucy.ac.cy](https://websites.ucy.ac.cy/neurology/documents/brain_oscillations_and_sleep_Fultz_et_al_2019.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Procedures and analyses
- Sleep restriction verification by PSG/actigraphy; caffeine/alcohol controlled.
- MRI: RT‑PC MRI acquired during free breathing and during the paced‑breathing block; spectral decomposition isolates respiratory versus cardiac components. Primary contrast: Δ (post–pre) in respiratory‑band CSF stroke volume, active vs sham. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))
- DTI‑ALPS processed with standardized pipelines; report ALPS index and free‑water–adjusted metrics. Pre‑registered plan treats ALPS as surrogate with validation sensitivity tests. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/12362905/?utm_source=openai))
- Systems outcomes: mixed‑effects models with condition and day as fixed effects; composite “homeostatic recovery” z‑score across the four axes.

Power and effect benchmarking
- RT‑PC MRI studies indicate detectable breathing‑mode effects on CSF flow with n<20; crossover design increases power. HRV resonance breathing effects on baroreflex/HRV are medium‑to‑large. We power for d=0.5 on primary mechanistic endpoint (α=0.05, 1−β=0.9) requiring 30 completers; recruit 36 to allow attrition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and feasibility
- Maintain normocapnia with capnography to avoid hypocapnic vasoconstriction; lateral posture avoids head‑down tilt. Motion‑minimized breathing cues compatible with MRI acquisitions. ALPS limitations are acknowledged a priori with mechanistic primacy placed on RT‑PC MRI measures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/12362905/?utm_source=openai))

Predicted outcomes
- Active blocks will increase respiratory‑band CSF stroke volume and velocity and raise the respiratory‑to‑cardiac power ratio relative to sham; Day‑4 ALPS index will be higher in active vs sham. Multi‑axis deficits under sleep restriction will be attenuated: faster reaction times and improved working memory; smaller OGTT iAUC; lower IL‑6/TNF‑α/CRP; higher daytime HRV and baroreflex sensitivity. Together these approximate a recovery state without increasing sleep time. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Exploratory extension (optional)
- Test whether adding nocturnal gentle rocking at ~0.25 Hz within the fixed 4.5‑h sleep window further compresses SWS density per minute (SWS‑per‑time), synergizing with daytime clearance blocks. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982218316622?utm_source=openai))

Criteria for success
- Mechanistic: Significant active>sham increase in respiratory‑band CSF stroke volume/velocity and improved ALPS index.
- Systems: Significant active>sham improvement in the pre‑specified four‑axis composite and in at least three individual axes.
- Constraint adherence: No increase in total sleep time; effects achieved during wake or within the fixed window.

Impact
If successful, respiration‑posture clearance blocks would establish a single‑lever, physiologically grounded method to partially replace sleep‑gated clearance and autonomic recalibration during wakefulness, offering a practical countermeasure to neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic impairments under time‑restricted sleep. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9749305/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop temporal-interference neuromodulation to selectively damp stress-evoked sympathetic vasoconstriction in the uterus without systemic sympatholysis

Background and rationale
- Pelvic sympathetic efferents relevant to the uterus descend via the hypogastric nerves into the inferior hypogastric (uterovaginal) plexus, distributing along uterine vessels; this localization enables field targeting from the lower abdomen/sacrum. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567711/?utm_source=openai))
- Norepinephrine contracts human uterine artery predominantly via post-junctional α1-adrenoceptors, so reducing burst-wise adrenergic release at this plexus should acutely relax uterine resistance vessels and restore perfusion. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2324242/?utm_source=openai))
- Human sympathetic outflow is organized into cardiac-synchronous bursts that increase in frequency and within-burst spike count during stress; high-frequency trains increase axonal vulnerability to conduction failure through Na+ channel use-dependent inactivation and extracellular K+ accumulation. This creates an intrinsic “burst-selective” weakness to subthreshold perturbations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3273724/?utm_source=openai))
- Temporal-interference stimulation (TI) uses multiple kHz carriers to form a low-frequency envelope at depth with better tolerability in superficial tissue. TI has reached early human use and has also been demonstrated for peripheral nerves, supporting feasibility of extrapelvic actuation of autonomic fibers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Uterine artery resistance/pulsatility indices are standard transabdominal Doppler endpoints; emerging wearable ultrasound patches can continuously track deep-vessel flow, enabling closed-loop, organ-specific control. ([obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.12371?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis (question = goal)
Can a uterus-focused, closed-loop TI montage that remains quiescent at baseline but scales envelope amplitude only during Doppler-detected uterine vasoconstrictive episodes suppress stress-evoked sympathetic bursts in the uterovaginal plexus, thereby normalizing uterine vascular resistance without altering systemic sympathetic markers?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the burst-specific drop in axonal safety factor during sympathoexcitation: apply a deep-focused, subthreshold TI envelope over the uterovaginal plexus that slightly increases membrane polarization/accommodation only when bursts occur (detected via real-time rise in uterine artery PI/RI). This selectively increases conduction failure probability for closely spaced spikes, clipping pathological bursts while sparing basal discharge. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00048.2009?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1: Field targeting and safety. Use individualized finite‑element models from pelvic MRI to design 3–4 electrode montages (bilateral lower abdomen, sacral triangle) with 3–6 kHz carriers and Δf 30–60 Hz that maximize the envelope along the uterovaginal plexus and uterine artery pedicles while minimizing fields in bladder/rectum and somatic nerves; verify skin current densities within established tES/TI safety limits and assess comfort in healthy volunteers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Physiology in humans (nonpregnant). Establish a standardized laboratory stressor (e.g., mental arithmetic with cold pressor). Primary endpoint: attenuation of stress-evoked rise in uterine artery PI/RI by active TI versus sham, measured transabdominally. Co-primary: no significant change in systemic sympathetic readouts (HR/BP, skin conductance) relative to sham. Exploratory: finger PPG amplitude and spectral HRV indices. ([obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Closed-loop control. Integrate a belt-mounted ultrasound patch positioned over the uterine artery origin. Real-time PI/RI drives proportional TI envelope A(t)=k·max(0,PI(t)−PI0). Compare closed-loop to open-loop (same mean dose) for efficacy and off-target effects; quantify duty cycle reduction and baseline quiescence. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42191988/?utm_source=openai))

Methods overview
- TI hardware: Two or three independent current sources deliver kHz carriers (e.g., 3.2/3.24 kHz; optional third pair for steering). Initial current intensities set by modeling; envelope adjusted by controller. Stimulation blocks limited to ≤20 min, with thermal/sensation monitoring each minute. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Target verification: Field maps co-registered to pelvic vasculature; montage tweaks guided by maximizing envelope overlap with the uterine artery/plexus corridor identified anatomically. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9321487/?utm_source=openai))
- Sensing: Transabdominal Doppler in Aims 1–2; wearable patch for Aim 3 provides continuous PI/RI with quality metrics and auto-site guidance. ([obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.12371?utm_source=openai))
- Participants: Healthy, nonpregnant adults with regular menses; exclude implanted electronics, dermatologic issues at electrode sites, or pelvic neuropathies.
- Outcomes and statistics: Aim 2 primary analysis compares ΔPI during stress across active vs sham (mixed models, within-subject crossover; n estimated to detect 20–25% reduction in stress-evoked ΔPI with 80% power). Aim 3 compares closed- vs open-loop ΔPI and off-target symptom scores; report effect sizes and Bayes factors.

Mechanistic readouts (substudies)
- Cutaneous comfort/somatic recruitment thresholds during TI vs matched tACS to confirm superficial sparing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Optional microneurography of peroneal MSNA in a subset to confirm no reduction in systemic burst frequency/incidence during active TI versus sham. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6146303/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and ethical safeguards
- TI parameters remain within consensus safety guidance; continuous monitoring for heating and dysesthesia; immediate abort criteria predefined. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Pregnancy excluded in early studies; separate obstetric safety pathway required before antenatal trials.

Success criteria
- Technical: Stable focusing of TI envelope to the targeted pelvic corridor with acceptable comfort.
- Physiological: Significant attenuation of stress-evoked rise in uterine artery PI/RI with preserved systemic sympathetic indices.
- Control: Closed-loop outperforms open-loop with lower duty cycle and zero baseline stimulation.

Why this meets constraints
- Non-invasive, uterus-targeted actuation via TI; no systemic drugs.
- Selectivity for excessive activation emerges from coupling actuation to uterine hemodynamic deviations and exploiting burst-state conduction vulnerability; basal tone is preserved.
- Novelty: No prior reports of TI directed at uterine or inferior hypogastric/uterovaginal plexuses; leverages established uterine α1-mediated vasoconstriction and validated Doppler endpoints with emerging wearable ultrasound for clinical translation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2324242/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated failure modes and contingencies
- Insufficient focusing/depth: adopt multi-pair steering and individualized montage optimization; if necessary, reduce Δf to shift focal maximum without raising superficial fields. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12162641/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target somatic activation: increase carrier frequency, reduce envelope depth of modulation, or move to asymmetric carrier amplitudes to cancel superficial fields. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40112352/?utm_source=openai))
- Weak Doppler signal (obesity, anatomy): guided placement with B-mode landmarks; if needed, switch to transvaginal probe for calibration sessions only, with subsequent patch operation matched to transabdominal targets. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4418013/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables and milestones (24 months)
- M6: Validated FEM-based montage library for three body habitus classes; safety/comfort dataset in 20 volunteers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- M12: Crossover pilot (n=24) demonstrating attenuation of stress-evoked ΔPI/RI with active TI vs sham.
- M18: Closed-loop prototype integrating ultrasound patch; controller validated on bench and in 10 participants. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42191988/?utm_source=openai))
- M24: Powered trial (n≈40) comparing closed- vs open-loop efficacy and off-target effects; dossier for IDE/IRB expansion.

References (selected)
- Inferior hypogastric/uterovaginal plexus anatomy and relation to uterine artery: StatPearls; pelvic dissections. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567711/?utm_source=openai))
- α1-mediated contraction of human uterine artery; NE sensitivity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2324242/?utm_source=openai))
- Sympathetic burst physiology and stress modulation in humans. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3273724/?utm_source=openai))
- Frequency-dependent conduction failure mechanisms in axons. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/physrev.00048.2009?utm_source=openai))
- TI mechanisms, safety, and human/peripheral demonstrations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11806287/?utm_source=openai))
- Uterine artery Doppler endpoints; wearable deep-vessel ultrasound patches. ([obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/uog.12371?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop, state-gated, low-intensity focused ultrasound to evoke endothelial nitric oxide and locally suppress excessive uterine sympathetic drive

Integrated hypothesis–question
Can a uterus-targeted, rate-of-rise–gated, low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) stimulus that mechanically activates uterine/periuterine endothelium to release nitric oxide (NO) reduce excessive, sympathetically driven myometrial hypercontractility, while preserving basal uterine tone and systemic sympathetic functions? ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpcell.1998.275.6.C1668?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit ultrasound mechano-transduction of vascular endothelium to produce a brief, spatially confined NO surge at the uterine wall/arterioles only when contraction kinetics exceed a pathological slope (high dε/dt). Local NO directly relaxes myometrium and presynaptically damps norepinephrine (NE) release at uterine neurovascular junctions, curbing excessive sympathetic activity without altering basal tone or non-uterine targets. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpcell.1998.275.6.C1668?utm_source=openai))

Background and significance
- Uterine sympathetic outflow (via hypogastric pathways) and α-adrenergic signaling promote myometrial contraction and vasoconstriction; excessive adrenergic drive contributes to hypercontractility and ischemic pain. ([anatomy.ttuhscep.edu](https://anatomy.ttuhscep.edu/modules/pelvic_autonomic_module/pelvic_page11.html?utm_source=openai))
- NO potently relaxes human myometrium and contributes to uterine quiescence; notably, NO’s tocolysis in human tissue can be partly cGMP-independent, expanding mechanistic latitude. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpcell.1998.275.6.C1668?utm_source=openai))
- Endothelium is ultrasound-mechanosensitive: low-intensity pulsed ultrasound increases eNOS expression/activity, intracellular Ca2+, and NO generation, producing vasodilatory effects without thermal injury. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783622157338?utm_source=openai))
- NO can inhibit sympathetic neurotransmission presynaptically (reduced NE release or signaling) in peripheral neuroeffector junctions, offering a local, non-systemic path to sympatholysis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3139802/?utm_source=openai))
- Ultrasound can modulate peripheral mechanosensitive channels (e.g., Piezo/TRAAK) and peripheral afferents, supporting feasibility of mechano-biased neuromodulation in end organs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9173751/?utm_source=openai))
- Pathological uterine activity is identifiable noninvasively; electrohysterography (EHG) and ultrasound strain analysis provide reliable contraction timing and permit estimation of dynamic features (e.g., slope). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649034/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety windows for diagnostic-range ultrasound and widely used LIPUS parameters (1.5 MHz, 200 μs, 1 kHz, ~30 mW/cm2 SATA) are well established and clinically translatable. ([aium.org](https://www.aium.org/resources/official-statements/view/prudent-use-and-safety-of-diagnostic-ultrasound-in-pregnancy?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Determine ultrasound parameter envelopes that maximize endothelial NO release in uterine-relevant endothelium while remaining within diagnostic safety indices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39306482/?utm_source=openai))
2) Develop and validate a closed-loop controller that triggers sonications only when contraction rate-of-rise (dε/dt or dP/dt surrogate) exceeds an adaptive threshold. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649034/?utm_source=openai))
3) Test whether gated uterine-focused LIFU reduces hypercontractile episodes and pain without altering basal uterine activity or systemic autonomic indices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31303075/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and methods

Stage I: Mechanistic calibration (in vitro/ex vivo)
- Models: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and, where available, human uterine artery endothelial cells (ex vivo). Outcome: NO (DAF-FM), eNOS phosphorylation, KLF2 expression; rule out thermal rise with needle thermistors. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26279754/?utm_source=openai))
- Ultrasound paradigms: Start with LIPUS canonical parameters (1.5 MHz, 200 μs, 1 kHz, Ispta ≈ 30 mW/cm2), vary pulse-burst envelopes (50–500 ms packet lengths, 0.5–2 Hz packet rate) to map NO dose–response; keep MI/TI within AIUM guidance. ([nice.org.uk](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg481/chapter/2-The-condition-current-treatments-and-procedure?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism controls: Pharmacologic eNOS inhibition (L-NAME), Piezo1 siRNA in endothelial cultures, to test mechano-initiated NO. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0753332220309896?utm_source=openai))

Stage II: Proof-of-concept (rodent, nonpregnant)
- Preparation: Anesthetized rat; measure uterine contractility (serosal strain via high-frame-rate B-mode speckle tracking) and intrauterine pressure; place abdominal EHG electrodes. Induce sympathetic overdrive with systemic NE or α1-agonist microdose to create hypercontractile phenotype. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35389865/?utm_source=openai))
- Intervention: Transabdominal focused sonications targeted to uterine wall/perivascular regions using small-aperture 1–2 MHz array. Controller triggers a 200–400 ms LIPUS packet when dε/dt exceeds threshold; hysteresis to prevent chattering. Maintain MI ≤ 1.5 and TI within diagnostic bounds; log acoustic indices in real time. ([aium.org](https://www.aium.org/resources/official-statements/view/prudent-use-and-safety-of-diagnostic-ultrasound-in-pregnancy?utm_source=openai))
- Endpoints: Change in contraction slope, peak amplitude, and duty time; uterine artery Doppler resistive index; tissue NO (electrochemical NO sensor where feasible). Mechanism confirmation: repeat with L-NAME to test NO dependence. Off-target check: HR, BP, HRV LF/HF unchanged at rest. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783622157338?utm_source=openai))

Stage III: First-in-human feasibility (nonpregnant, primary dysmenorrhea)
- Design: Single-blind, sham-controlled, crossover in clinic. Inclusion: severe cramp episodes; exclusion: pregnancy, coagulopathy, implanted stimulators. Monitoring: EHG for timing and slope estimation; optional B-mode strain tracking for calibration. Sonications delivered only on excessive slope detections. Safety: MI/TI within diagnostic guidelines; exposure time capped by ALARA. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649034/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary outcome: Area-under-curve of hypercontractile events per hour. Secondary: Pain VAS, uterine artery Doppler indices, lack of change in resting HRV LF/HF and blood pressure (systemic sympatholysis screen). ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK532927/?utm_source=openai))

Controller and sensing
- Sensing: Abdominal EHG array provides robust contraction onset and slope estimation superior to external toco; optional ultrasound speckle-tracking estimates strain rate for calibration. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649034/?utm_source=openai))
- State gating: Trigger only when dε/dt exceeds an adaptive percentile relative to subject’s baseline, ensuring dormancy during normal activity and avoiding basal tone suppression. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169260726002142?utm_source=openai))
- Patterned sonication: Short burst packets (200–400 ms) at 1 kHz PRF, SATA ≈ 30 mW/cm2; slight inter-packet jitter to limit adaptation; parameters kept within nonthermal ranges. ([nice.org.uk](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg481/chapter/2-The-condition-current-treatments-and-procedure?utm_source=openai))

Safety and risk management
- Acoustic indices monitored and enforced (MI, TI) per AIUM/FDA guidance; exposures minimized (ALARA). Avoid cavitation regimes; duty cycles and intensities in diagnostic/LIPUS range. Adverse event surveillance: skin/soft-tissue effects, menstrual pattern changes, vasovagal symptoms. ([aium.org](https://www.aium.org/resources/official-statements/view/prudent-use-and-safety-of-diagnostic-ultrasound-in-pregnancy?utm_source=openai))

Effectiveness tests and success criteria
- Stage II success: ≥30% reduction in pathological contraction slope and duty time versus sham; effect abolished by L-NAME. No change in resting HRV LF/HF. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3139802/?utm_source=openai))
- Stage III success: Within-subject reduction in hypercontractile AUC and pain VAS versus sham without changes in basal uterine activity between episodes or systemic autonomic indices. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31303075/?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Uses local, state-triggered endothelial mechano-NO as the actuator to downregulate sympathetic drive in a single organ, rather than systemic sympatholysis. To our knowledge, uterus-targeted, closed-loop, NO-centered, LIFU control of hypercontractility has not been clinically explored; existing pelvic neuromodulation is electrical or ablative, and prior ultrasound work emphasizes imaging, ablation, or non-specific physiotherapy. ([ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK567751/?utm_source=openai))

Clinical translation
- Hardware leverages diagnostic ultrasound platforms and adhesive EHG patches. Regulatory pathway aligns with non-significant risk device studies under existing acoustic output standards, enabling rapid iteration and controlled clinical testing. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf17/K172056.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If endothelial NO activation alone is insufficient, parameter sweeps will incorporate modest modulation targeting mechanosensitive ion channels in local afferents to augment inhibitory gating while keeping organ specificity and safety. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9173751/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables and milestones (24 months)
- Months 0–6: Endothelial NO parameter map; thermomechanical safety characterization. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39306482/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 6–12: Rodent closed-loop efficacy and NO dependence. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1538783622157338?utm_source=openai))
- Months 12–24: Human feasibility (n≈20) with sham control; go/no-go for pivotal based on predefined success criteria. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28649034/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Closed-loop, uterus-derived-signal–gated low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) to suppress excessive sympathetic drive at the uterovaginal plexus while preserving basal tone

Rationale
- Convergent autonomic control. Sympathetic fibers via the hypogastric pathway and parasympathetic fibers via pelvic splanchnics converge in the inferior hypogastric/uterovaginal plexus before distributing to the uterus and its vasculature. This anatomical convergence creates a local control point for autonomic balance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500855/?utm_source=openai))
- Pathophysiology. Acute psychological or physiological stress elevates uterine vascular resistance and reduces blood flow via α1-adrenergic vasoconstriction; animal and human data link stress and catecholamines to higher uterine artery resistance indices (RI/PI). ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10253890.2016.1203417?utm_source=openai))
- Biomarkers. Uterine artery Doppler RI/PI and related waveform features are standard, noninvasive readouts of uterine vascular tone and can be trended continuously. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7409544/?utm_source=openai))
- Modality. Low-intensity focused ultrasound can modulate peripheral nerve excitability, with multiple reports showing reversible inhibition of nerve activity and mechanosensitive channel involvement, at acoustic exposures within diagnostic safety envelopes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8828880/?utm_source=openai))
- Unmet need and novelty. No noninvasive, uterus-specific neuromodulation exists that suppresses only pathologic sympathetic surges without systemic sympatholysis. Focused ultrasound has not been clinically applied to modulate the uterovaginal plexus for autonomic rebalance; prior uterine ultrasound applications are ablative (fibroids), and pelvic TENS/IFC trials address pain without closed-loop, organ-specific autonomic control. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43586-024-00368-6?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis (research goal as question)
Can on-demand, low-intensity focused ultrasound directed to the uterovaginal plexus, gated by real-time uterine artery hemodynamic signatures of sympathetic overactivity, reduce excessive sympathetic vasoconstriction and myometrial hyperexcitability while preserving basal sympathetic tone and avoiding systemic sympatholysis?

Atomic strategy
Exploit activity-dependent susceptibility of sympathetic efferents at the plexus: deliver short LIFU pulse trains only during detected surges in uterine vascular resistance, biasing presynaptic and axonal mechanosensitive processes that disproportionately damp high-frequency, high-amplitude sympathetic output; remain inert at baseline.

Specific aims
1) Define uterine-local “excess sympathetic” signatures and thresholds
- Map individualized baselines and stress-evoked ranges of uterine artery RI/PI and waveform dynamics across menstrual phases in nonpregnant participants.
- Establish criteria for “excess” as deviations beyond personalized tolerance bands (e.g., RI percentile thresholds, rapid upslopes, diastolic notch re-emergence). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7409544/?utm_source=openai))

2) Establish a safe, selective LIFU parameter space for plexus-targeted suppression
- Using transabdominal or transperineal sonication geometry guided by B-mode imaging, focus within the known anatomic corridor of the uterovaginal plexus lateral to the cervix/uterine artery crossing.
- Parameterize frequency (0.5–1.5 MHz), pulse duration (0.2–5 ms), PRF, duty cycle, and intensity below diagnostic limits to maximize reduction of stress-evoked RI elevations while maintaining baseline RI within subject-specific corridors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500855/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary selectivity test: compare effects on uterine RI/PI during standardized sympatho-excitation (mental arithmetic, cold pressor) vs resting baseline; verify minimal change in systemic markers (heart rate variability, finger PPG amplitude) to exclude systemic sympatholysis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9888905/?utm_source=openai))

3) Implement and evaluate a closed-loop controller (“uterus-gated LIFU”)
- Sensing: continuous pulsed-wave Doppler of one uterine artery with beat-to-beat RI/PI estimation; optional redundancy with deep pelvic electrical impedance or optical perfusion.
- Control: state estimator computes real-time deviation from baseline; when excess sympathetic likelihood crosses threshold, trigger a brief LIFU burst; cease when RI returns to band.
- Outcomes: time-above-threshold RI, area under excess-RI curve, and variance reduction during stress tasks; maintenance of baseline RI and absence of systemic sympatholysis.

Study design
- Phase 0/feasibility, randomized, sham-controlled, crossover.
- Participants: healthy, nonpregnant women (18–40), regular cycles; exclude pelvic pathology and anticoagulation.
- Sessions: two visits in mid-luteal phase. Each visit includes baseline resting, two stress epochs, and recovery. Within each visit, deliver either closed-loop LIFU or sham according to randomization; cross over at second visit.
- Targeting: transabdominal ultrasound localizes cervix/uterine arteries; sonication focus positioned 5–10 mm lateral to cervix at the uterovaginal plexus region. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500855/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety: acoustic outputs within FDA diagnostic limits; monitor skin, bladder, rectal symptoms; serial urinalysis; pregnancy test pre-session. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43586-024-00368-6?utm_source=openai))

Primary endpoint
- Percent reduction in excess sympathetic burden: AUC of RI above individualized threshold during stress with closed-loop LIFU vs sham.

Secondary endpoints
- Baseline preservation: mean RI at rest unchanged (noninferiority margin ≤2%).
- Systemic specificity: no significant change in HRV LF/HF ratio or finger PPG amplitude vs sham during stress. 
- Myometrial excitability proxy: change in pelvic impedance oscillation power in vasomotor band during stress.
- Safety and tolerability.

Mechanistic checks and falsification tests
- If LIFU reduces RI at rest, re-tune duty cycle/PRF to enforce baseline preservation; if impossible, ideation fails the constraint.
- If systemic markers change with uterine RI, include a “off-target focus” control 2–3 cm lateral to plexus; effect disappearance supports local mechanism.
- If responders cluster by cycle phase, incorporate phase as a stratification factor and explore hormone-level covariates.

Technical specifications
- Transducer: 0.75–1.0 MHz, f-number 1–1.5, focal spot ~5–8 mm; SPPA/Ispta below diagnostic limits; real-time beam steering within ±10 mm.
- Sensing: 3–5 MHz linear/curvilinear probe co-registered to sonication; Doppler processing at ≥100 Hz sample of envelope for beat-to-beat RI/PI.
- Controller: adaptive thresholding using rolling baselines; refractory windows to prevent over-delivery; safety interlocks on temperature rise estimated by acoustic modeling.

Validation pathway
- Bench-top phantom to validate co-registration accuracy and Doppler-driven triggering latency.
- Preclinical large-animal pilot (nonpregnant ewe) to relate sonication to uterine artery flow and catecholamine challenges. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10253890.2016.1203417?utm_source=openai))
- First-in-human feasibility as above; expansion to dysmenorrhea cohort if uterine hypertonicity and vasoconstriction signatures are demonstrated.

Clinical translation and risk
- Device integrates widely used diagnostic ultrasound hardware with a low-intensity neuromodulation module, facilitating regulatory path as a software-controlled therapeutic mode of an imaging platform.
- Known gaps: exact cellular mechanism of peripheral ultrasound neuromodulation remains under study; nonetheless, multiple studies show safe, reversible inhibition of peripheral nerves, justifying parameter exploration under strict safety monitoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8828880/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- Demonstrate ≥30% reduction in excess-RI AUC during stress without rest RI change and without systemic sympatholysis in ≥60% of participants under closed-loop LIFU vs sham.
- Reproducible targeting and safety across visits.

References (selected)
- Pelvic autonomic convergence and uterovaginal plexus anatomy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500855/?utm_source=openai))
- Stress and catecholamine-linked uterine vasoconstriction, α1 mediation. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10253890.2016.1203417?utm_source=openai))
- Uterine artery Doppler as vascular tone readout. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7409544/?utm_source=openai))
- Low-intensity focused ultrasound neuromodulation and safety. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43586-024-00368-6?utm_source=openai))
- Prior electrotherapy for dysmenorrhea lacks closed-loop autonomic targeting (context for novelty). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11262556/?utm_source=openai))

Title
H2O2-gated augmentation of the uterine Gαq “off-switch” to selectively damp stress-evoked adrenergic bursts without systemic sympatholysis

Central question/hypothesis
Can local, non-invasive delivery of a hydrogen peroxide–activatable RGS2 regulator restore the uterus’s endogenous Gαq brake only when adrenergic drive is excessive, thereby reducing pathological myometrial contractions while preserving basal sympathetic tone elsewhere? The hypothesis rests on three established facts: (i) α1-adrenergic/Gq signaling contracts human myometrium; (ii) RGS2 is an endogenous GAP that shortens Gαq signaling and is linked to uterine quiescence; and (iii) monoamine oxidase (MAO) catabolism of norepinephrine generates H2O2 near active sympathetic terminals. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Tie brake strength to a chemical signature of excess catechol turnover: use MAO-derived H2O2 as the trigger to unmask an intracellular RGS2 Gαq-GAP, so inhibition appears only when and where adrenergic bursts occur, not at baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12267328/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish that sympathetic burst activity elevates perineuroeffector H2O2 and intensifies α1/Gq-driven myometrial contractions.
2) Engineer and validate an H2O2-activatable, cell-penetrating RGS2 reagent that accelerates Gαq deactivation only under high-ROS conditions.
3) Achieve uterine-first-pass, non-invasive delivery via a mucoadhesive intravaginal hydrogel and demonstrate selective dampening of stress-evoked contractions in vivo, without systemic sympatholysis.

Rationale and innovation
- Biology: α1-ARs in human myometrium couple to Gq/PLCβ→IP3/Ca2+→MLCK to drive contraction; β2-ARs oppose via cAMP. RGS2 is a selective GAP for Gαq, upregulated in quiescent states and downregulated toward labor, positioning it as an intrinsic brake. MAO-mediated oxidative deamination of catecholamines generates H2O2 at sympathetic terminals. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: Vaginal administration can enrich drug in the uterus via the uterine first-pass effect, minimizing plasma exposure and systemic impact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Control logic: Arylboronate/borinic triggers enable H2O2-activated self-immolative cleavage to switch “on” a masked bioactive only where ROS rises; borinic acids increase reaction rates, improving biological responsiveness. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty: No reported uterine therapy uses MAO-H2O2 to gate an RGS2-based, Gαq-targeted intracellular brake; this reframes tocolysis from receptor blockade to state- and byproduct-gated restoration of endogenous termination.

Approach

Aim 1: Map ROS–adrenergic–contractility coupling in myometrium
- Ex vivo human myometrium strips (nonpregnant hysterectomy tissue, IRB-approved). Electrical field stimulation of sympathetic varicosities and phenylephrine boluses to produce graded α1-adrenergic bursts; record force and Ca2+ transients. Measure local H2O2 with boronate-based fluorescent probes and polymeric ratiometric nanoprobes; control with catalase/peroxidase. Quantify threshold relation between H2O2 rise and suprabasal contractile gain. Expected: μM-scale phenylephrine or burst trains elevate perijunctional H2O2 and steepen α1/Gq gain; catalase blunts both readouts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3935537/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2: Engineer an H2O2-activatable RGS2-GAP that is quiescent at baseline
- Construct: Minimal RGS2 RH domain (e.g., residues ~72–203) fused to a cell-penetrating peptide (CPP). Block CPP uptake and/or RGS2–Gαq interface using an arylboronate self-immolative cage that cleaves with H2O2; evaluate faster borinic triggers to meet biological kinetics. Add an N-terminal membrane-targeting motif to enrich at the sarcolemma where Gαq operates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro biophysics: Measure GTPase acceleration on purified Gαq and off-rate on Gαq·GTP versus Gαq·GDP. Define “activity threshold” by comparing GAP activity at 0–10 μM H2O2; benchmark against uncaged RH domain. Confirm minimal activity at ≤100 nM H2O2. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Cell assays: Human myometrial smooth muscle cells. Readouts: PLCβ activity, IP3/Ca2+ spikes, and ERK under α1 stimulation. Compare basal versus burst-like agonist paradigms. Confirm that catalase suppresses activation of the construct, and that an RGS-insensitive Gαq mutant rescues signaling, verifying on-target action. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety chemistry: Quantify byproducts (phenol/boric species) and show no cytotoxicity at exposure levels; this is consistent with prior boronate prodrug literature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Non-invasive uterine delivery and in vivo selectivity
- Formulation: Mucoadhesive, pH-tolerant intravaginal hydrogel embedding the prodrugged RGS2 construct. Optimize residence and uterine exposure using fluorescein-tagged constructs in rodents; quantify uterine/plasma ratios to confirm first-pass uterine enrichment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Models and endpoints:
  - Stress-evoked adrenergic surges: In awake rodents, use restraint/cold stress or systemic tyramine to elicit sympathetic NE release; monitor intrauterine pressure via telemetric balloons and electromyography. Test that the hydrogel reduces peak amplitude/frequency during surges but leaves basal tone unchanged. Include phenylephrine-challenge arm to standardize α1 input. Off-target guardrails: heart rate, blood pressure, pupil size to exclude systemic sympatholysis. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6311865/?utm_source=openai))
  - Mechanism confirmation: Co-administer catalase-mimetic to suppress H2O2 and abrogate efficacy; deliver an RGS2-inactive mutant control. Tissue assays for Gαq·GTP lifetime and PLCβ activity.
- Translational safety: Local irritation scores, vaginal microbiome profiles, reproductive hormone levels. Pharmacokinetics to ensure negligible systemic CPP–RGS2 in plasma.

Milestones and success criteria
- Aim 1: Demonstrate a monotonic relation between burst intensity and H2O2 with a clear threshold where contractile gain steepens; catalase flattens this slope. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24123627/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: Show ≥10-fold increase in Gαq-GAP activity after H2O2 activation with ≤5% baseline activity at 0–100 nM H2O2; in myocytes, suppress burst-evoked Ca2+ peaks by ≥40% while altering basal Ca2+ <5%. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Achieve uterine:plasma exposure ratio ≥5 after intravaginal dosing; reduce stress-evoked intrauterine pressure AUC by ≥30% with no change in resting tone and no change in systemic cardiovascular indices. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated limitations and design adaptations
- H2O2 reaction kinetics: If arylboronate cleavage is too slow at physiological H2O2, switch to borinic acid triggers or co-localize peroxidase-mimetic nanozymes within the hydrogel to raise local effective rate. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8685692/?utm_source=openai))
- Variability in uterine first-pass: If uterine enrichment is suboptimal in some anatomies, restrict molecular size/charge or add uterine-tropic motifs to enhance retention. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Species differences in adrenergic control: Use human tissue ex vivo for primary validation and select a second species with robust myometrial α1 biology before clinical translation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9937490/?utm_source=openai))

Clinical path (Phase 0/1 concept)
- Indication: Nonpregnant individuals with stress-exacerbated primary dysmenorrhea or uterine hyperreactivity.
- Design: Crossover, intravaginal hydrogel vs placebo. Primary endpoint: reduction in stress-provoked uterine EMG/intrauterine pressure peaks during standardized mental stress; secondary: pain scores, absence of changes in resting uterine tone and systemic sympathetic markers.

Why this meets constraints
- Non-invasive intravaginal delivery with uterine first-pass avoids systemic sympatholysis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))
- Excess-only damping: ROS gating confines activation to adrenergic surge microdomains; basal low-ROS conditions leave signaling intact. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786010/?utm_source=openai))
- Endogenous brake amplification: Uses RGS2’s native role to shorten Gαq signaling, not receptor blockade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3638996/?utm_source=openai))
- Clinically translatable: Peptide/CPP cargos, mucoadhesive hydrogels, and boronate/borinic triggers have precedent in biomedical applications. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8871440/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop sacral-dermatomal afferent stimulation to attenuate bursty uterine sympathetic drive without systemic sympatholysis

Premise and rationale
- The uterus receives mixed autonomic innervation: sympathetic fibers via hypogastric pathways (predominantly T10–L1) and parasympathetic fibers via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) coursing through the inferior hypogastric plexus. Cervical and uterovaginal afferents project to lumbosacral dorsal horn segments, enabling somato-visceral reflex interactions at the spinal level. Excess adrenergic signaling increases myometrial excitability via α-adrenergic mechanisms, whereas β-adrenergic signaling tends to relax myometrium; the balance varies with hormonal state. Segmental somatic afferent input can modulate sympathetic preganglionic neuron (SPN) activity through inhibitory interneurons and presynaptic mechanisms within the spinal cord. Noninvasive TENS reduces dysmenorrhea pain, but typical open-loop protocols have not shown consistent changes in intrauterine pressure, indicating a gap between analgesia and direct modulation of uterine efferent bursts. Cervical stretch can excite myometrial activity via the Ferguson reflex; therefore, targeting external sacral dermatomes avoids mechanically exciting cervicovaginal pathways while still engaging lumbosacral circuitry. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1472029919301134?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question (atomic strategy embedded)
Can high-pass, closed-loop activation of low-threshold sacral dermatomal afferents (S2–S4) be used as a tunable, on-demand inhibitory gain on lumbosacral sympathetic outflow to the uterus—attenuating only supra-physiological, bursty uterine activity while sparing tonic uterine and systemic sympathetic tone? The atomic strategy is to use thresholded, phasic Aβ-dominant cutaneous input as a spinal “inhibitory gain” that engages fast interneuronal and presynaptic inhibitory processes only when uterine EMG features indicate excessive adrenergic-driven activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075457/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Establish that closed-loop, burst-gated sacral-dermatomal TENS (S2–S4) reduces high-frequency, high-slope components of uterine EMG during dysmenorrheic episodes without altering baseline EMG. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))
2) Demonstrate segmental specificity: show no concurrent systemic sympatholysis via heart-rate variability (HRV) indices and palmar skin conductance during stimulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10049654/?utm_source=openai))
3) Compare closed-loop versus time-matched open-loop TENS to determine the necessity of high-pass, error-triggered engagement for selective suppression. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8296814/?utm_source=openai))

Design and methods
- Population: Nonpregnant adults with primary dysmenorrhea (PD), regular cycles, no hormonal therapy changes in prior 3 months; exclude secondary causes. Two-site, randomized, double-crossover study across three menses: (A) closed-loop sacral-dermatomal TENS; (B) open-loop TENS; (C) sham. Each participant serves as own control. Safety: avoid pregnancy to preclude interference with labor-associated reflexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12975252/?utm_source=openai))
- Sensing: Adhesive abdominal uterine EMG patch (FDA-classified uterine EMG monitor) sampling ≥500 Hz. Derived features: EMG envelope slope, phasic band power (e.g., 0.2–1 Hz), and a composite burst index via adaptive percentile thresholds calibrated during quiescent baseline on day −1. Secondary sensors: ECG-derived HRV and palmar skin conductance. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))
- Actuation (intervention): Sacral-dermatomal TENS over S2–S4 (paravertebral/posterior sacral foramina region) with large gel pads to bias Aβ recruitment (e.g., 100–200 μs pulse width; carrier 80–120 Hz; amplitude individualized to strong but comfortable sensation, below nociceptor thresholds). Stimulation is delivered in brief bursts (e.g., 1–3 s trains with fast on/off ramps), locked to detected EMG bursts with a refractory lockout (≥30 s) to prevent tonic suppression. Open-loop uses identical parameters at matched duty cycle but decoupled from EMG. Sham uses identical hardware with imperceptible subthreshold output. Safety monitoring includes skin integrity checks and adverse event logs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078521/?utm_source=openai))
- Control logic (closed-loop): High-pass controller triggers only when the composite burst index exceeds an individualized threshold, scaling stimulus amplitude by error magnitude (proportional) with anti-windup and short decay to avoid baseline bias. No integral accumulation across minutes. This implements inhibitory “gain” only during supra-physiological events. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-neuro-112723-042229?utm_source=openai))
- Outcomes:
  • Primary: Change in burst index area-under-curve (AUC) per hour versus baseline and versus open-loop/sham. 
  • Co-primary: No change in tonic EMG (median baseline power) across conditions.
  • Secondary: Pain VAS, uterine artery Doppler resistive index in a subset, HRV LF/HF and palmar skin conductance changes ≤ prespecified margins (noninferiority bounds) to confirm absence of systemic sympatholysis; rescue analgesic use. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3892726/?utm_source=openai))
- Statistics: Within-subject mixed models with condition and time as fixed effects; hierarchical false-discovery control across outcomes. Powering assumes moderate effect (Cohen’s d 0.5) on burst-AUC reduction, α=0.05, 1−β=0.8, requiring ~34 completers; inflate to 45 to allow attrition.

Mechanistic validation substudies
- Segmental mapping: Vary electrode positions rostral-caudal (L5–S1 vs S2–S4) to test segmental dependence of effects on EMG bursts. Prediction: maximal effect with S2–S4 placement. ([anatomy.ttuhscep.edu](https://anatomy.ttuhscep.edu/modules/pelvic_autonomic_module/pelvic_page11.html?utm_source=openai))
- Parameter titration: Compare Aβ-favoring settings to higher pulse widths that recruit nociceptors; prediction: nociceptor recruitment degrades selectivity and may increase sympathetic markers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2075457/?utm_source=openai))

Risk management and constraints compliance
- Noninvasive only: surface EMG and TENS; no intracavitary stimulation or drugs. Device parameters adhere to TENS safety norms; prior dysmenorrhea TENS trials show favorable safety. Avoid direct cervicovaginal mechanical stimulation to prevent Ferguson reflex activation. ([cochrane.org](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013331_tens-electrical-nerve-stimulation-through-skin-effective-treatment-period-pain-and-does-it-cause?utm_source=openai))
- Preserve basal and systemic sympathetic function: High-pass gating, short bursts, and refractory intervals aim to confine inhibition to phasic events; systemic markers provide stopping rules if deviations exceed bounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10049654/?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and differentiators
- Prior TENS studies in PD were analgesic-focused and open-loop, with no consistent impact on intrauterine pressure; here, uterine EMG-driven, burst-gated control explicitly targets autonomic efferent dynamics rather than pain alone. Emerging closed-loop TENS wearables for PD focus on symptom relief, not physiological suppression of uterine sympathetic bursts with segmental specificity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8296814/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and translation
- All components are available: FDA-recognized uterine EMG monitors, programmable TENS, and wearable controllers for real-time closed-loop neuromodulation. Success criteria: ≥25% reduction in EMG burst-AUC versus open-loop without change in tonic EMG and without systemic sympatholysis; reproducibility across cycles. Positive results justify a pivotal trial and potential 510(k) pathway as a new intended use for TENS with closed-loop uterine EMG control. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpcd/classification.cfm?id=OSP&utm_source=openai))

Contingency
- If external sacral-dermatomal stimulation fails to achieve selectivity, pivot to optimizing segmental recruitment (electrode size/vectoring) within S2–S4 or refine burst detection features; abort criterion is failure to separate burst suppression from tonic suppression across two cycles in >60% of participants.

text:
Title
Closed-loop, phase-targeted low-intensity focused ultrasound to desynchronize uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor bursts while preserving basal tone

Premise and significance
- The uterus receives sympathetic efferents via the hypogastric nerves and the inferior hypogastric (uterovaginal) plexus; sympathetic fibers accompany uterine vessels and regulate vasomotor tone and smooth muscle targets. Disruption here influences uterine vascular resistance and myometrial excitability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9321487/?utm_source=openai))
- Near term, adrenergic pharmacology shifts: β-agonists classically relax myometrium and have been used as tocolytics; conversely, uterine arteries exhibit enhanced α1-mediated constriction with reduced β-mediated relaxation, increasing susceptibility of uteroplacental perfusion to sympathetic bursts. This implies that selectively attenuating high-rate vasoconstrictor drive—without global sympatholysis—could improve uteroplacental flow without abolishing basal tone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3892726/?utm_source=openai))
- Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) can noninvasively modulate peripheral autonomic pathways with reversible inhibition at intermediate intensities; neuromod effects have been demonstrated in vagus and other peripheral targets. Safety frameworks from diagnostic ultrasound (ALARA; FDA/WFUMB indices) guide exposure, especially in pregnancy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8188893/?utm_source=openai))
- Noninvasive uterine/placental sensing—surface electrohysterography (EHG) for uterine activation, uterine artery Doppler for flow, and diffuse optical/NIRS for placental oxygenation—provides real-time, local biomarkers to detect self-reinforcing sympathetic–vascular episodes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3090039/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–question
Can locally sensed, quasi-periodic uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor bursts be identified in real time from transabdominal EHG–perfusion signatures and desynchronized on-demand by delivering brief, phase-targeted LIFU pulses to the uterovaginal branch region of the inferior hypogastric plexus, thereby reducing pathologic uterine vascular resistance while preserving basal sympathetic tone and avoiding systemic sympatholysis? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit dynamics-selectivity rather than amplitude-selectivity: detect local, coherent high-rate sympathetic burst structure (regularity, phase-locking across EHG–perfusion channels) and deliver minimally dosed, phase-shifted LIFU microbursts timed to extend refractoriness/induce spike timing jitter in the most excitable vasoconstrictor fibers, breaking synchrony (“resonance-based cancellation”) while leaving aperiodic, low-rate basal signaling and non-target pelvic sympathetic functions unaffected. Mechanistic precedent for phase-targeted cancellation and collision-based spike suppression exists in closed-loop neurostimulation and peripheral axon physiology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Define a local “burst-likeness” signature of uterine sympathetic vasoconstrictor episodes.
- Combine features: EHG narrowband power/coherence (0.3–1.0 Hz), uterine artery Doppler pulsatility index surges, and placental NIRS/DOS desaturations indicating transient uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Build an online metric that rises only when these channels synchronize in a quasi-periodic pattern. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/15/4669?utm_source=openai))
2) Engineer a transabdominal, phase-targeted LIFU system for uterovaginal plexus region.
- Parametric LIFU pulses (frequency 0.5–3 MHz; short pulse trains with low duty cycle) are time-locked anti-phase to the detected burst fundamental, targeting parametrium adjacent to the uterine artery where sympathetic fibers concentrate. Exposures constrained under obstetric safety guidance (monitor TI/MI; ALARA). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
3) Test selectivity: suppress pathologic bursts while preserving basal tone and systemic sympathetic function.
- Primary outcomes: (i) reduction in episodic uterine artery resistance (Doppler PI), (ii) attenuation of placental desaturation events (NIRS/DOS), (iii) minimal change in basal perfusion indices and maternal systemic autonomic markers (HRV, skin microvascular LDI outside uterine field). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9944515/?utm_source=openai))

Study design and methods
- Population and models
  - Preclinical: pregnant ewe model (uterine size and wall thickness approximating human) to validate targeting and dosing; simultaneous intra-arterial flow probes, EHG, and DOS over placentomes.
  - First-in-human feasibility: hospitalized patients with threatened preterm labor (24–34 weeks) under standard monitoring; single-session, on-demand LIFU with real-time safety gating.
- Sensing and detection
  - 8–16 channel abdominal EHG grid; uterine artery Doppler (transabdominal) for beat-to-beat PI; placental NIRS/DOS patch over placental bed for StO2; optional uterine magnetomyography (if available) to validate synchrony maps. Online phase-locked loop extracts the dominant burst phase only when EHG–perfusion coherence exceeds threshold; otherwise the system remains idle. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3090039/?utm_source=openai))
- Targeting
  - Sonographic targeting to the uterovaginal plexus region: lateral parametrium along the uterine artery course where sympathetic fibers are concentrated at the media–adventitial border. Steering minimizes fetal insonation and confines the focus to the maternal uterine wall/parametrium. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
- Stimulation protocol
  - Phase-targeted pulses: brief LIFU microbursts delivered at a phase that maximally disrupts the detected cycle (determined during a 30–60 s calibration sweep). Closed-loop controller disengages within 1–3 cycles after coherence collapses. Exposure caps enforced by MI/TI watchdogs, with total sonication time per hour constrained below diagnostic practice norms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls
  - Sham sonication (no output) with identical targeting and timing; open-loop, non-phase-timed LIFU with matched dose to isolate the contribution of phase locking.
- Endpoints
  - Primary mechanistic: reduction in burst-likeness index; drop in uterine artery PI and concurrent recovery of placental StO2 during detected episodes versus sham/open-loop. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9944515/?utm_source=openai))
  - Physiologic selectivity: no significant change in basal uterine artery PI, placental StO2 outside episodes, maternal HR/BP, or distal skin microvascular flow.
  - Obstetric safety: no fetal heart rate abnormalities, no increase in contraction frequency/intensity on EHG, adherence to ALARA and ITRUSST thermal/MI bounds. ([acog.org](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2017/10/guidelines-for-diagnostic-imaging-during-pregnancy-and-lactation?utm_source=openai))
- Statistics and design features
  - Within-subject randomized cross-over (phase-targeted vs sham/open-loop) across multiple naturally occurring or oxytocin-provoked sympathetic–vascular episodes; mixed-effects models quantify treatment effect on PI and StO2 trajectories aligned to detection onset.
  - Powering based on paired reduction in episode-integrated placental desaturation AUC.

Mechanistic justifications
- Dynamics-selectivity: Pathologic bursts are coherent and quasi-periodic; phase-targeted perturbations preferentially disrupt synchronized activity without suppressing irregular basal firing, paralleling successful phase-cancellation paradigms in movement disorders. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3629558/?utm_source=openai))
- Locality: Actuation focus is confined to uterine parametrium; sensing derives from uterus/placental bed. Systemic sympathetic outflow is not directly engaged, satisfying the no-systemic-sympatholysis constraint. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10932059/?utm_source=openai))
- Biological plausibility: Peripheral ultrasound neuromodulation can inhibit nerve conduction/non-neuronal mechanoelectrical signaling at safe intensities; late-gestation uterine arteries are particularly sensitive to α1-mediated constriction—making pathologic vasoconstrictor bursts a rational and organ-specific target. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8188893/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and translational path
- Year 1: Define and validate burst-likeness metric and safe parameter space in pregnant ewe; demonstrate on-demand reversal of induced uterine artery vasoconstriction and placental desaturations.
- Year 2: Feasibility in 20 patients with threatened preterm labor; demonstrate ≥30% reduction in episode PI peaks and ≥30% reduction in desaturation AUC versus sham without affecting basal indices.
- Year 3: Early efficacy signal—reduced progression from threatened to active preterm labor over 48–72 h adjunctive window—while monitoring obstetric safety.
- Regulatory/safety: Operate within obstetric ultrasound safety frameworks (ALARA, MI/TI monitoring) and emerging neuromodulation exposure consensus; noninvasive hardware leverages clinical ultrasound platforms with software-only closed-loop extensions. ([acog.org](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2017/10/guidelines-for-diagnostic-imaging-during-pregnancy-and-lactation?utm_source=openai))

Novelty
- No prior reports of closed-loop, phase-targeted neuromodulation of the uterine sympathetic plexus to specifically desynchronize vasoconstrictor bursts; pelvic magnetic chairs target pudendal/sacral somatic pathways for incontinence, not uterine autonomic control or frequency/phase-selective suppression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/9145499/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
A dynamics-selective, organ-local, noninvasive neuromodulation that blunts episodic uterine sympathetic vasoconstriction without flattening basal tone offers a path to stabilize uteroplacental perfusion in high-risk pregnancies while avoiding systemic sympatholysis—meeting safety and translational constraints and opening a controllable, on-demand window for standard obstetric care. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8485361/?utm_source=openai))
