text:
Title: AND-gated demolition of the KSR1 scaffold complex to test whether architectural disruption produces signaling outputs unattainable by single-enzyme inhibition

Hypothesis–Question (intentionally fused):
Does degrading the KSR1 scaffold only when it is actively assembled with MEK1/2 (architecture-sensing AND gate) rewire ERK-pathway dynamics and cell-fate decisions in ways that cannot be phenocopied by inhibiting or degrading any single enzymatic component (RAF, MEK, or ERK) alone?

Atomic strategy:
Exploit avidity and geometry to implement a true intracellular AND gate: a bivalent, protein-based degrader binds weakly to KSR1 and weakly to MEK1, but binds avidly only when KSR1:MEK1 are co-assembled in their native orientation; only then does the degrader present an E3-recruitment surface at a productive distance/angle to ubiquitinate KSR1 and collapse the scaffolded complex.

Rationale (evidence anchors):
- KSR1 is a core scaffold for the RAF–MEK–ERK module; it pre-assembles MEK and coordinates Ras-dependent membrane translocation and Raf activation. Its localization and assembly are regulated by PP2A and 14-3-3, and it binds MEK via defined surfaces; KSR1 itself is difficult to drug with small molecules. Architectural control, not a single catalytic site, is the control variable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5490495/?utm_source=openai))
- Ubiquitination efficiency depends on precise multi-site engagement and geometry; the canonical CRL3–Keap1:Nrf2 system requires two degrons bound in a defined “hinge-and-latch” arrangement to correctly present lysines for E2~Ub transfer, underscoring that productive ubiquitination is a geometric problem, not merely co-localization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2169061/?utm_source=openai))
- Logic-gated degraders exist (e.g., small-molecule DAO‑PROTACs that require two orthogonal stimuli; sortase-assembled LASER bioPROTACs), but they are triggered by exogenous cues or enzymatic switches—not by sensing a specific native protein–protein assembly state. The proposed complex-sensing, three-body AND gate remains underexplored. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12949432/?utm_source=openai))
- Protein-based degraders (bioPROTACs/AdPROMs/ubiquibodies) are feasible, modular ways to redirect endogenous UPS machinery using intracellular binders fused to E3 adaptors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10362593/?utm_source=openai))

Design overview (construct: ARCH-AND-KSR)
- One-chain protein degrader comprising:
  1) KSR1-binder module: a designed monobody/DARPin recognizing a solvent-exposed, MEK-proximal surface on KSR1 (moderate affinity, KD ~1–5 µM).
  2) MEK1-binder module: a designed monobody/DARPin recognizing the KSR1-contacting face of MEK1 (KD ~1–5 µM).
  3) Rigid, length-defined spacer between binders: 20–30 nm alpha-helical rod (ER/K repeats or de novo helical repeat) tuned so the two binders achieve high avidity only when KSR1:MEK1 are in their native complex geometry; mis-assembled or isolated proteins cannot satisfy both reach and orientation.
  4) E3 engagement module: VHL adaptor (for CRL2) fused via a short, semi-rigid linker positioned to present the E2~Ub near lysines on KSR1 that are solvent-exposed in the KSR1:MEK complex; in silico docking and lysine accessibility guide the spacer length/attachment site to maximize ubiquitin transfer probability only in the AND-gated state.
- Safety/containment features:
  - No activity on free KSR1 or free MEK1 due to weak monovalent affinities and geometric mismatch.
  - No global proteostasis stimulation; UPS is engaged only upon productive ternary assembly (KSR1:MEK1:ARCH-AND-KSR).

Model system and readouts
- Cell models: HEK293T (tractable ERK signaling), KRAS-dependent cancer lines (e.g., HCT116) for disease relevance.
- Readouts: pERK dynamics (time-resolved), ERK activity reporters, immediate-early gene expression profiles, proliferation/apoptosis, and phospho-proteomics of MAPK nodes.

Specific Aim 1. Establish the complex-sensing AND gate and geometric safety lock in cells
- 1A. Binder generation and calibration:
  - Select monobody/DARPin scaffolds against KSR1 and MEK1 surfaces known to participate in their interface; screen phage- or yeast-display libraries for moderate-affinity clones to avoid monovalent “always-on” binding.
  - Map epitope locations by competition with KSR1:MEK complex and crosslinking-MS; prioritize clones that bind only when the partner is present to amplify avidity effects.
- 1B. Spacer and orientation optimization:
  - Build a panel of constructs varying rod length (e.g., 100–250 Å) and junction angles; use live-cell BiFC or NanoBRET to quantify ternary complex formation only in the presence of both targets.
  - Use a degronless VHL (E3-dead) control to decouple sensing from degradation while optimizing geometry.
- 1C. AND-gate validation:
  - Quantify degrader recruitment to KSR1 in cells lacking MEK1 (CRISPR KO) or expressing a MEK1 interface mutant; expect loss of binding/ubiquitination.
  - Conversely, disrupt KSR1:MEK binding (mutant KSR1 or MEK1) and verify loss of degrader activity.
  - Compare to monovalent controls (KSR1-only binder–VHL or MEK1-only binder–VHL): expect high off-target binding and poor selectivity; our construct should show minimal activity without the complex.

Milestone/Go–No-Go for Aim 1:
- ≥80% reduction in KSR1 levels only in wild-type KSR1:MEK1 cells; <20% reduction in KSR1 when MEK1 is absent or KSR1:MEK1 interface is disrupted; negligible degradation of MEK1 itself.

Specific Aim 2. Test whether architecture-specific demolition yields unique ERK-pathway behaviors
- 2A. Compare against single-enzyme perturbations:
  - Benchmark against MEK inhibition (trametinib), RAF inhibition (vemurafenib in BRAF-mutant cells), and CRISPRi or bioPROTAC-mediated degradation of MEK1 alone.
  - Metrics: ERK activation amplitude and duration, pulse frequency, feedback signatures (DUSP/SPRouty induction), and gene-expression programs.
- 2B. Deterministic vs ultrasensitive control:
  - Use live-cell ERK KTR to quantify digital vs graded responses to EGF dose ramps; test whether scaffold demolition converts graded responses to all-or-none or vice versa.
- 2C. Network rewiring:
  - Phospho-proteomics to assess compensatory re-routing (e.g., PI3K/AKT crosstalk); assess whether KSR1 demolition prevents known bypass routes that persist under MEK inhibitors.

Milestone for Aim 2:
- Identify at least one quantitative behavior (e.g., ERK pulse duration distribution, response ultrasensitivity, adaptation kinetics) that cannot be replicated by any single-enzyme inhibition or degradation, indicating a unique architectural effect.

Specific Aim 3. Generalize the AND-gated scaffold demolition concept
- 3A. Swap binder modules to other scaffolds (e.g., IQGAP1:ERK or MP1:MEK1) while retaining the same VHL module and spacer logic; measure portability of the design rules.
- 3B. Alternate E3s and geometry:
  - Replace VHL with SPOP-based CRL3 adaptor to test whether BTB-dimer geometry enhances ubiquitination when spacing is matched, drawing on the mechanistic precedent that two-site engagement improves lysine presentation in CRLs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2169061/?utm_source=openai))

Key controls and falsification tests
- Proteasome and neddylation inhibitors to confirm UPS dependence.
- Ternary complex biophysics (CETSA shifts, co-IP stoichiometry) to correlate geometry and degradation.
- Rescue with degrader-resistant KSR1 (epitope-silent) to prove on-target effects.
- Rule out E3 sequestration toxicity by measuring HIF1α stabilization (VHL pathway) and general proteostasis markers.

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- If architecture-sensing degradation of KSR1 alters ERK dynamics in ways not matched by RAF/MEK/ERK perturbations, this supports that scaffold architecture is a unique control knob.
- Failure modes that would refute the hypothesis:
  - No measurable difference from MEK inhibition across dynamics and transcriptomics.
  - Construct degrades KSR1 regardless of MEK1 presence (gate failure).

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Off-target binding: keep monovalent affinities weak, rely on avidity; map interactomes by IP–MS to confirm selectivity.
- Global pathway perturbation via VHL engagement: use low-expression promoters and inducible systems; monitor HIF targets.
- Kinetic lag: because KSR1 pre-assembles complexes, degradation may show delays; tune degrader expression and use proteasome flux reporters.

Feasibility notes
- KSR1–MEK1 physical interactions and 14-3-3/PP2A regulation are well established, providing known epitopes and structural constraints for binder design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5490495/?utm_source=openai))
- The necessity of correct spacing/orientation for efficient ubiquitination is a validated principle in CRL systems, informing our geometric safety lock design. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2169061/?utm_source=openai))
- AND-gated degraders have been achieved with exogenous triggers (small-molecule or enzyme responsive), but complex-sensing AND gating remains a gap this work addresses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12949432/?utm_source=openai))
- Protein-based degraders are supported by multiple platforms (AdPROM, bioPROTACs), de-risking the UPS recruitment module. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10362593/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- A context-gated degrader that selectively eliminates KSR1 only when scaffolded with MEK1, and yields at least one non-phenocopiable network-level behavior relative to enzyme-centric perturbations.

Potential impact
- Establishes “architecture-sensing TPD” as a distinct intracellular therapeutic modality, enabling targeted demolition of undruggable scaffolds when—and only when—they are functionally engaged, to reprogram signaling dynamics without broad proteostasis disruption. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5490495/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title: OFF-by-ATP: a de novo ATP-clamped scaffold that turns ON under energy stress to rewire intracellular fate in cancer cells

Premise and question
Healthy cells maintain high millimolar ATP that suppresses spontaneous biomolecular condensation and aberrant multivalency; ATP dissolution of condensates is a well-established physical constraint. When cells become energy-stressed (hypoxia, nutrient limitation), ATP falls locally, favoring condensate formation. Can a de novo protein exploit ATP as a native “safety ligand” to remain OFF in healthy cytosol and turn ON only where ATP is pathologically low, thereby performing an intracellular function (e.g., selective degradation of oncogenic clients) that is hard for small molecules and antibodies to achieve? The hypothesis and question are identical: Does an ATP-bound conformational latch that occludes a multivalent oligomerization seam provide sufficient thresholding to nucleate functional condensates only in low-ATP microenvironments and thereby enable targeted intracellular action? References support ATP’s hydrotropic suppression of phase separation, ATP-depletion–driven condensates, the feasibility of de novo allosteric switches, de novo ATP binding pockets, and therapeutic condensate functions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28522535/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit ATP as an allosteric OFF-ligand. Engineer an ATP-occupiable clamp in a de novo helical scaffold so that ATP binding stabilizes a closed, monomeric state that buries a multivalent “sticker”/oligomerization seam. When ATP falls below a tunable threshold, the clamp opens, the seam is exposed, and multivalency drives a mesoscale condensate that carries a prewired intracellular function (here, targeted degradation of a specified client). This single design choice—ATP as the negative allosteric safety cue—provides global, physiology-anchored selectivity without hunting mutable disease markers. ATP’s role in suppressing condensation and stress-dependent reversal underpins the gating. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28522535/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Design and in vitro validate an ATP-Clamped Oligomerization Module (ACOM).
- Construct a de novo six-helix bundle with a buried P-loop/Walker-A–like pocket that binds ATP nonproductively and stabilizes a lid helix over the oligomerization seam. ATP-bound state is monomeric; ATP-depleted state exposes the seam for oligomerization.
- Calibrate ATP affinity (target apparent Kd 2–4 mM with Mg2+) to be below healthy cytosolic ATP and above stressed intracellular ATP, informed by the hydrotrope literature indicating ATP dissolves condensates near the 8–10 mM regime. Validate by ITC, DSF, and oligomerization assays ±ATP/ADP/AMP-PNP; use K/A mutation of the Walker-Lys as a control to disrupt clamping. Precedent for de novo allosteric scaffolds and de novo ATP-binding folds justifies feasibility. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1425-7?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build an ATP-gated condensate that recruits endogenous degradation machinery to a specified intracellular target.
- Fuse ACOM to: (i) a low-complexity sticker domain optimized for reversible condensates; (ii) a compact E3-adaptor–recruiting motif (e.g., SPOP- or CHIP-interacting helix); and (iii) a weak monomeric binder for a client (e.g., mutant KRAS or nuclear MYC), designed/selected to be minimally active unless multivalently concentrated in the ON condensate. This leverages recent demonstrations that engineered condensates can act as intracellular degradation hubs while introducing ATP-gated selectivity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-022-01203-3?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate cell-state–specific function and safety.
- In live cells, co-express ACOM constructs with a genetically encoded ATP sensor and modulate ATP with respiratory inhibitors to map the activation curve and spatial thresholds. Quantify condensate nucleation, client recruitment, ubiquitination, and degradation kinetics. Assess proteostasis safety by global ubiquitylome profiling and stress reporters; benchmark against a constitutively oligomerizing positive control. Use nuclear vs cytosolic targeting to test compartment-specific outcomes.

Research plan and key methods
1) Computational design
- Use Rosetta/AlphaFold2-guided design to place a P-loop–like pocket (GxxxxGKT[S/T] motif) in a de novo helical bundle so that phosphate binding stabilizes a lid helix packing across the oligomerization seam. Enforce noncatalytic geometry (no Walker-B/Arg finger) to eliminate hydrolysis and emphasize binding-driven allostery, informed by recent blueprint designs of ATP-binding P-loop folds. Sequence and interface energies tuned to yield two near-degenerate states separated by ATP binding energy, following de novo switch design principles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12075096/?utm_source=openai))
2) Biophysical validation
- Purify ACOM variants; measure ATP/ADP/AMP-PNP binding (ITC), seam exposure (limited proteolysis/H-D exchange), and oligomerization (AUC, SEC-MALS) ±ATP. Determine phase diagrams for ACOM-sticker fusions with controlled ATP titrations to confirm ATP-locked dissolution and ATP-depletion–driven condensation, consistent with ATP’s hydrotropic behavior. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28522535/?utm_source=openai))
3) Cellular characterization
- Express ACOM-fusions in human cell lines; quantify activation thresholds using a cytosolic ATP sensor and pharmacology (oligomycin, 2-DG). Track condensates and client dynamics by live-cell imaging and FRAP. Compare WT clamp to Lys→Ala mutant (constitutively ON) and pocket-disrupting mutants (constitutively OFF).
- Function: For KRASG12V or MYC clients, use validated binders or mini-domains; monitor endogenous protein levels, pathway readouts, and proliferation. Probe dependency on proteasome with MG132. Benchmark against a non-gated condensate degrader to quantify selectivity gain.
4) Safety engineering
- Add a built-in OFF-restore timer: expose a degron only in the assembled polymer (protease-sensitive loop) so that when ATP normalizes and assembly dissolves, residual monomers turn over. Limit sticker valency to avoid global sequestration; tune nuclear/cytosolic targeting to avoid compartmental hazards suggested by p62-condensate studies.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: ACOM binds ATP with target Kd and shows ATP-dependent seam occlusion and oligomerization in vitro.
- M2: In cells, condensates form only below a defined ATP threshold and dissolve upon ATP restoration; ON/OFF dynamic range >10-fold by microscopy and biochemical fractionation.
- M3: Client degradation occurs only in ON conditions, reducing client abundance by >70% without elevating global ubiquitination or proteotoxic stress markers above baseline.
- No-go: If ATP thresholds required for gating overlap tightly with normal physiology across compartments, pivot to suborganelle targeting (e.g., mitochondrial matrix) where ATP gradients are larger.

Why this modality and where it beats existing tools
- Selectivity emerges from a universal healthy cue (ATP abundance) rather than mutable oncogenic markers; condensation is the effector, not an artifact. Unlike small molecules or antibodies, the de novo scaffold unifies sensing, spatial multivalency, and proximity-driven degradation in one programmable macromolecule. Prior art shows de novo switches are buildable and engineered condensates can drive intracellular degradation; what is new is inverting ATP from “fuel” into a safety ligand that keeps the therapeutic OFF in healthy cells and ON only when ATP safety fails. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1425-7?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and risk
- Feasibility: Multiple labs have designed de novo allosteric switches; ATP’s hydrotropic role and its millimolar action on condensates give a robust physical handle; de novo P-loop ATP binders have been built, supporting an ATP-occupiable pocket without catalysis. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1425-7?utm_source=openai))
- Risks and mitigations: Off-target condensation is mitigated by ATP threshold tuning, modest sticker valency, and self-limiting degrons; proteasome overload is mitigated by client-specific weak binders that require ON-state avidity; immune activation risk is minimized by intracellular expression.

Deliverables
- An ATP-clamped, state-selective intracellular degrader scaffold with tunable thresholds, mechanistically grounded in endogenous biophysics and distinct from extracellular receptor agonism/antagonism; a platform generalizable to other functions (e.g., organelle triage) where the same ATP-gated assembly could scaffold repair or clearance depending on co-fused effectors. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-022-01203-3?utm_source=openai))

Title
Proximity-and-strain–enabled endogenous protease switching (PSEEPS) for irreversible, domain‑specific inactivation of rogue intracellular proteins

Central hypothesis-question
Can a single de novo intrabody that (i) binds an allosterically coupled surface on a pathological intracellular protein, (ii) mechanically exposes a latent, calpain‑susceptible loop, and (iii) conditionally docks endogenous calpain via non‑inhibitory calpastatin exosites, drive one‑cut, irreversible loss of function in living cells without globally elevating protease activity? The bet is that accessibility and nanoscale geometry—rather than protease abundance—are the bottlenecks for productive, limited proteolysis of many disease drivers. If true, “mechanics plus proximity” becomes a general intracellular safety‑switch modality orthogonal to degraders and receptor agonism/antagonism. Calpains are chosen because they perform physiological limited proteolysis and can inactivate signaling hubs when a correct site is presented; calpastatin’s modular exosites offer endogenous, tunable docking without overactivating the enzyme. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single causal lever: raise the effective rate of a specific endogenous, inactivating calpain cut at a cryptic site by simultaneously increasing (a) site accessibility via piconewton‑scale strain and (b) local calpain effective molarity and orientation via a short, non‑inhibitory calpastatin‑derived docking motif that is unveiled only upon target engagement. This mirrors natural force‑assisted proteolysis (e.g., ADAMTS13 on VWF) but is repurposed intracellularly for targeted inactivation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3179391/?utm_source=openai))

Aims and work plan

Aim 1. Identify inactivating, cryptic calpain sites on hard intracellular targets.
- Targets: β‑catenin (oncogenic Wnt effector) and YAP/TAZ (Hippo co‑activators) as exemplar undruggables where limited cleavage can rewire transcriptional programs. Prior work shows calpain can clip β‑catenin and modulate Yki/YAP ortholog stability; however, usable “off‑switch” bonds must be mapped precisely. Combine:
  - Sequence‑level prediction of calpain cuts (DeepCalpain/CalCleaveMKL/GPS‑CCD) to nominate P2/P1‑favored motifs within disordered loops that, if severed, disrupt TCF/TEAD binding or nuclear localization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
  - Limited proteolysis‑mass spectrometry (LiP‑MS) with purified calpain on recombinant targets ± mild denaturants to reveal latent scissile bonds; validate in cell lysates with Ca2+‑titrated calpain. Use N‑terminomics to confirm single‑cut products and map neo‑N‑termini. Evidence that calpain can generate loss‑of‑function fragments for β‑catenin and cleave regulatory hubs motivates feasibility. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/64/20/7237/511898/Cleavage-of-Catenin-by-Calpain-in-Prostate-and?utm_source=openai))
  - Structural modeling (AlphaFold2/MD) to choose leverable epitopes whose mechanical perturbation would expose the nominated bond without global unfolding.
Go/no‑go: identification of at least one bond per target where a single in vitro calpain cut abrogates DNA‑binding or co‑activator function.

Aim 2. Build PSEEPS: a de novo intrabody that couples strain to conditional calpain recruitment.
- Construct: a rigid repeat‑protein or helical bundle “lever” bearing (i) a high‑affinity binder to a mechanically coupled epitope remote from the scissile loop; (ii) a short “tether arm” contacting a loop flanking the nominated bond to apply torsion/bending; and (iii) a calpastatin‑derived A/C exosite micropeptide (no B‑subdomain) as a low‑nM, non‑catalytic calpain docking tag. A de novo allosteric mask (LOCKR‑like) occludes the docking tag and only opens when the primary binder engages the target, implementing an AND gate for safety. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Rationale: calpastatin A/C bind calpain PEF domains away from the catalytic cleft (B mediates active‑site occlusion), enabling recruitment without inhibition; gating prevents off‑target docking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Optimization: vary lever length (2–6 nm), hinge stiffness, and docking‑tag affinity (μM→nM) to tune effective molarity/orientation. Readouts: (a) site‑specific cleavage by N‑term proteomics; (b) absence of bystander cleavage proteome‑wide; (c) loss of target function (TOPFlash for β‑catenin; 8xGTIIC for YAP/TAZ) with preserved cell viability at baseline Ca2+. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate intracellular, irreversible pathway rewiring with safety margins.
- Acute tests: transient expression in human cells; measure time‑resolved appearance of the exact neo‑N‑terminus, loss of target‑driven transcription, and lack of global calpain hyperactivation (spectrin breakdown product as sentinel). Compare to degrader controls to show distinct modality (single‑bond inactivation vs wholesale degradation). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6588652/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity: rescue with cleavage‑resistant target mutants (±single P1/P2 substitutions) and with PSEEPS lacking the docking tag or with docking tag locked; require geometric coincidence of lever and site.
- Safety: verify no activation of apoptotic caspases and no global proteostasis stress. Calpains are physiological limited proteases; recruitment without active‑site engagement and without Ca2+ elevation minimizes systemic risk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Generalization and disease‑proximal models.
- Extend mapping to additional proteins where limited proteolysis is known to inactivate activity (e.g., EGFR kinase domain, MET juxtamembrane) to demonstrate portability across folds and compartments. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8055914/?utm_source=openai))
- In 3D tumor spheroids with constitutive Wnt/YAP signaling, quantify durable suppression after transient PSEEPS pulse; track clonal escape via sequencing of the targeted loop.

Key design controls and exclusion criteria
- Exclude targets where reported calpain cuts generate constitutively active fragments (e.g., PKC→PKM); pre‑filter with literature and in vitro mapping. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7607311/?utm_source=openai))
- Disallow constructs that increase global calpain activity or sequester calpain broadly; docking tag Kd and expression kept low; mask enforces binding‑dependent exposure.
- No recruitment of apoptotic caspases or lysosomal cathepsins.

Milestones
- M1 (Month 6): For at least one target, validated inactivating calpain bond and intrabody epitope pair; cleavage confirmed by LC‑MS neo‑N‑termini. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26796116/?utm_source=openai))
- M2 (Month 12): First‑gen PSEEPS drives >70% site‑specific clipping and >80% loss of reporter activity without spectrin breakdown at baseline. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
- M3 (Month 18): Proteome‑wide off‑target cleavage <0.5% of quantified proteins (TAILS/ChaFRADIC); durable pathway rewiring in spheroids.

Why this fulfills the goal
- Defined intracellular consequence: single‑bond, irreversible switch‑off of a rogue function (e.g., TCF/TEAD co‑activation), distinct from receptor agonism/antagonism and from wholesale degradation.
- Solves an inadequacy of small molecules/antibodies: uses protein‑scale mechanics and geometry to expose and align a buried bond that occupancy inhibitors cannot access and antibodies cannot reach intracellularly.
- Feasibility and novelty: leverages native limited proteolysis and calpastatin exosites; to our knowledge, endogenously recruiting calpain via non‑inhibitory calpastatin fragments to inactivate unmodified intracellular proteins has not been demonstrated. Related induced‑proximity modalities focus on E3 ligases (PROTACs); our approach is protease‑centric and cleavage‑site specific. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsptsci.5c00730?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and decision points
- Success supports a new intracellular therapeutic class: “site‑specific protease switches.” Failure modes (no productive cut; activation fragments) trigger target re‑selection or switch to a different inactivating bond guided by N‑terminomics.

Selected references (supporting mechanistic premises)
- Calpains perform limited proteolysis that modulates signaling; predictors and assays exist. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10507866/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanical force exposes cryptic scissile bonds in natural systems, motivating strain‑assisted accessibility. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3179391/?utm_source=openai))
- Calpastatin A/C exosites bind calpain PEF domains; B mediates inhibition—enabling non‑inhibitory recruitment designs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847431/?utm_source=openai))
- Calpain can inactivate key signaling proteins when the correct site is presented (e.g., β‑catenin; EGFR kinase domain). ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/64/20/7237/511898/Cleavage-of-Catenin-by-Calpain-in-Prostate-and?utm_source=openai))
- De novo allosteric masks (LOCKR) implement binding‑dependent motif unveiling for safety. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6733528/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverable
A minimal, genetically encodable protein “safety switch” that co‑opts endogenous proteolytic flux to permanently switch off disease‑causing intracellular proteins by one precise cut, with encoded geometric specificity and built‑in safety gating.

Title
A membrane-mechanics triage switch for organelle quality control: repurposing a HAMP transmembrane register to choose repair (p97/ESCRT) before clearance (LC3)

Rationale, question-as-hypothesis
Cells repair mildly damaged mitochondria and ER via local proteostasis and membrane repair (e.g., p97/VCP-driven extraction; ESCRT sealing; mitochondria-derived vesicles, MDVs). If stress persists or overwhelms capacity, selective autophagy removes organelle fragments or whole organelles via LC3-interacting receptors (LIR-containing mitophagy/ER‑phagy receptors). We ask whether a single de novo, organelle-embedded protein can sense membrane-state perturbations associated with damage, compute local repair capacity through occupancy, and then execute a binary choice: recruit repair machinery when salvageable; expose autophagy motifs when not. This aims to reduce unnecessary organelle loss while accelerating removal of irreparable segments. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a bacterial HAMP-domain transmembrane register switch as an allosteric, reversible translator of bilayer physical state into alternative cytosolic interfaces. In the low‑damage state, the output surface presents short p97/ESCRT‑recruiting motifs; when local bilayer stress surpasses a threshold and/or repair capacity is saturated, the conformational register flips to expose tandem LIRs (± UBD) to commit that membrane patch to selective autophagy. HAMP domains natively convert small TM piston/rotation changes into large helical‑bundle reorientations; membrane lipid peroxidation and curvature/thickness changes provide the physical input. To our knowledge, HAMP has not been used in mammalian cells to control organelle‑autophagy decisions; current mammalian synthetic receptors rely on other architectures (synNotch, MESA, GEMS). ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.micro.112408.134215?utm_source=openai))

Design overview (construct: TRIAGE-HAMP)
- Localization/topology: Single C‑terminal tail anchor targets the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) or ER; cytosolic N‑terminus carries the HAMP bundle followed by a short output coiled‑coil. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))
- Repair-first face (default): Surface displays one or more short p97-binding SLiMs (SHP box; VIM; VBM) and, for ER deployment, a minimal ALIX-binding LYPX(n)L to seed ESCRT when needed. These motifs enhance local extraction/sealing without global proteostasis activation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Clearance face (switched): Surface exposes a tandem LC3/GABARAP‑binding LIR array (optionally a compact UBD such as UBAN/UBA) to nucleate selective autophagy microdomains only when revealed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7615515/?utm_source=openai))
- Steric exclusion gate: The repair-motif docking surface overlaps the autophagy‑motif surface so that bound repair factors physically occlude LIR/UBD exposure; only when local repair occupancy falls (capacity exceeded) does the autophagy face become available. This converts endogenous factor saturation into a decision point (no added signaling species).

Specific Aims

Aim 1. Calibrate a HAMP-based membrane-state sensor on the OMM/ER
Question/hypothesis: Does local bilayer perturbation characteristic of oxidative/morphological organelle damage drive a HAMP register change in situ?
- Engineering: Use Af1503/Tsr-derived HAMP with output coiled‑coil; create state‑locked mutants from literature models to define ONrepair and ONclearance references; fuse FRET reporters across the HAMP output to quantify state. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2892831/?utm_source=openai))
- Perturbations: Induce graded lipid peroxidation (photosensitizers or iron-mediated Fenton chemistry), curvature/thickness shifts, and Δψm loss; measure sensor response independent of ubiquitin signaling. Use established biophysical links between peroxidation and altered packing/thickness/viscoelasticity as the physical basis. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42004-022-00809-x?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Monotonic FRET shift with peroxidation dose and curvature stress; no shift with unrelated cytosolic stresses; correct topology and membrane targeting.

Aim 2. Implement “repair-first, capacity-gated” output logic
Question/hypothesis: Can repair-factor occupancy enforce default repair and delay autophagy until capacity is exceeded?
- Design: Position SHP/VIM/VBM motifs to recruit endogenous p97 at the sensor site; for ER, include LYPX(n)L to access ALIX/ESCRT when needed. Place tandem LIRs on the alternative face; map steric overlap via structure-guided spacing and flexible linkers to ensure mutual occlusion. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Assays: Live-cell recruitment (endogenous p97/ALIX/LC3 via knock‑in tags), proteomics of proximal interactors, and single-organelle readouts (mitoKeima or mito‑QC; ER‑phagy reporters). Titrate repair capacity by acute p97 inhibition or partial knockdown to reveal the autophagy face; quantify the switching boundary. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4313695/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: Under mild stress, increased local p97/ESCRT without LC3 recruitment; as repair is titrated down or stress escalates, sharp transition to LC3 recruitment and autophagic capture at the same membrane patch.

Aim 3. Demonstrate functional triage: rescue when salvageable, removal when not
Question/hypothesis: Does TRIAGE‑HAMP reduce unnecessary mitophagy/ER‑phagy while accelerating removal of irreparable segments?
- Paradigms: Pulsed oxidative or proteotoxic insults that normally trigger MDVs/ERAD before organellophagy; and sustained insults that drive PINK1/Parkin mitophagy or ER‑phagy. Track MDV flux, OMMAD/ERAD throughput, and autophagic capture kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9189329/?utm_source=openai))
- Metrics: (i) Faster recovery of membrane potential/protein import after transient stress; (ii) increased MDV/ERAD throughput with reduced whole-organelle mitophagy/ER-phagy; (iii) under high damage, accelerated LC3 engagement and cargo delivery versus controls. Safety: no global proteostasis collapse (p97 activity assays; UPS markers), no chronic LC3 flux elevation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9189329/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility and controls
- Minimal parts: All domains/motifs are short and genetically encodable; p97-binding SLiMs (SHP/VIM/VBM) are established; LIRs are modular and their spacing/adjacency tune LC3 vs GABARAP selectivity. Include state‑locked HAMP controls and motif‑dead mutants to isolate sensing vs effector functions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18208387/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinction from existing modalities: The switch acts at organelle membranes, reading bilayer mechanics unavailable to small molecules/antibodies, and computing capacity via occupancy—functions that demand protein‑scale interfaces and conformational switching. Reviews of mammalian synthetic receptors list no HAMP‑based, autophagy‑directing systems, supporting novelty. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41392-023-01680-5?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: HAMP is unresponsive in eukaryotic membranes. Mitigation: Use state‑locked variants to validate effector logic; screen alternative TMs with different hydrophobic lengths/tilt propensities to couple to HAMP rotation/piston; if needed, deploy on ER where curvature/thickness shifts are pronounced during stress and ESCRT repair is well documented. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9229795/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: p97 sequestration causes off‑target effects. Mitigation: Use low‑affinity SLiMs, decreased motif valency, and organelle‑restricted expression; verify no change in global UPS flux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5559722/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Premature autophagy. Mitigation: Enforce steric occlusion geometry; tune LIR affinity and spacing; optionally incorporate a short multisite‑phospho IDR immediately downstream of HAMP as a temporal integrator to further delay LIR exposure under transient stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3001445/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Sensor calibration and topology validation; state‑locked references; peroxidation/curvature response curves established. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42004-022-00809-x?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Functional triage outputs demonstrated; occupancy‑dependent occlusion confirmed; quantitative switching boundary mapped versus repair capacity.
- Year 3: Efficacy and safety in disease-relevant cells (e.g., neurons or cardiomyocytes): improved recovery after transient stress; accelerated clearance under catastrophic stress; no global proteostasis or UPR activation.

Outcomes and significance
This work introduces a compact, programmable, membrane‑embedded protein that computes organelle health from bilayer mechanics and local capacity, executing repair-first triage before selective autophagy. It advances de novo intracellular therapeutic proteins beyond binding or receptor agonism by actively rewiring quality‑control pathways at their point of action. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/abs/10.1146/annurev.micro.112408.134215?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title: Valency-programmed condensate switches to triage intracellular damage: rescuing salvageable cells while clearing unsalvageable ones

Rationale (succinct prior art and gap)
- Protein triage in cells toggles between refolding/repair and degradation, with Hsp70–CHIP/HOP modules acting as key nodes; stress PTMs can bias the choice, but an engineered, context-aware switch that commits to repair first and degradation only upon persistent damage is missing. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27863257/?utm_source=openai))
- Ubiquitin signaling and condensates are tightly coupled: polyubiquitin chain architecture controls phase behavior and client fate, yet natural UBQLN2/p62 hubs can either protect or clear substrates depending on valency and residence time—a controllable design lever. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- Engineered ankyrin/DARPin scaffolds enable rigid, multispecific, geometry-controlled assemblies suitable for implementing multi-input logic and presenting mutually exclusive effector surfaces in cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593856/?utm_source=openai))

Unified hypothesis–goal–question
- Can a single, genetically encoded scaffold that senses local “damage valency” (exposed misfolded surfaces and accumulating K48/K63 polyubiquitin) undergo a reversible material-state transition that first enriches refolding/repair factors, but upon sustained high valency switches to recruit clearance machinery—thereby restoring function in salvageable cells while eliminating terminally damaged ones within the same tissue? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
- Encode a time-integrated threshold in a designer condensate: below a polyubiquitin/misfolding valency threshold, the scaffold forms dynamic, Hsp70/Hsp40-accessible microcondensates that accelerate client repair; above a sustained threshold, the same scaffold increases crosslinking and flips its client-interaction surface to reveal E3/adaptor docking sites, committing clients to proteasomal/autophagic clearance. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Design concept: ViDA (Valency-integrated Damage Assessor)
- Chassis: consensus ankyrin repeat scaffold (8–10 repeats) with two modular client-sensing rows:
  - Misfolding sensors: two repeats grafted with binders to generic exposed hydrophobic motifs (engineered to low µM affinity to avoid off-target binding when folded clients are scarce).
  - Ubiquitin valency sensors: a tandem array of engineered ubiquitin-binding modules with defined spacing/affinity tuned to preferentially bind ≥K48-Ub4 and/or K63-Ub3+ chains; spacing set to maximize cooperative partitioning as chain length and local density increase. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- State control via sticker–spacer grammar:
  - Repair state (R): low-valency engagement yields small, dynamic droplets; ankyrin N-terminus presents Hsp70/Hsp40/HOP docking grooves; C-terminus masks E3/adaptor motifs.
  - Clearance state (C): sustained high valency (misfolds + polyUb) increases multivalent crosslinks, rotates terminal repeats to occlude chaperone grooves and expose E3/adaptor motifs (e.g., short VHL/SOCS-box or LC3-interacting regions for autophagy routing), biasing K48-ubiquitination or aggrephagy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Spatial variants: mitochondrial outer membrane-targeted ViDA (mito-ViDA) and cytosolic ViDA to evaluate organelle-specific salvage-versus-clearance without global proteostasis perturbation.

Specific aims
1) Build and calibrate ViDA’s two-state phase behavior and effector selectivity in living cells.
2) Demonstrate intracellular triage on mixed client populations: rescue refoldable clients while clearing irreparable ones in the same culture.
3) Test organelle-targeted ViDA for mitochondrial proteostasis: restore function where Δψm is recoverable and remove collapsed organelles via mitophagy.

Aim 1: Build and calibrate ViDA
- Constructs
  - ViDA-RC: full switchable scaffold.
  - R-locked and C-locked controls: terminal-repeat mutations that fix terminal geometry to permanently present chaperone grooves (R) or E3/adaptor motifs (C). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8229355/?utm_source=openai))
  - ΔUBD and Δmisfold modules to dissect inputs.
- Assays
  - Live-cell FRAP and partitioning: quantify droplet dynamics and client partition coefficients across graded proteotoxic stress; tune UBD spacing/affinity for desired threshold using Ub chain standards expressed in cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
  - Effector composition: proximity labeling mass spectrometry (TurboID fused to ViDA) to profile R vs C condensate proteomes; expectation: Hsp70/Hsp40/HOP enrich in R; E3s/proteasome (or LC3/SQSTM1) enrich in C. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
  - Switching hysteresis: stress-pulse protocols to confirm time-integration (residence time) and avoid oscillation.
- Success criteria
  - Bistable state occupancy with tunable threshold; mutually exclusive enrichment of repair vs clearance effectors.

Aim 2: Mixed-client triage in the same cell population
- System
  - Co-express two fluorescent clients: (i) repairable temperature-sensitive folding mutant (rescues at permissive chaperone levels), and (ii) irreparable truncation/misfold designed to accumulate K48-Ub chains.
- Readouts
  - Client fate mapping by single-cell imaging: track refolding kinetics and proteasomal degradation rates ± proteasome or autophagy inhibitors to validate pathway choice. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
  - Function-first metrics: restoration of client enzymatic activity for the salvageable mutant vs elimination of irreparable client; cell viability and stress markers.
  - Comparative baselines: R-locked, C-locked, and Δmodules.
- Success criteria
  - Significant increase in functional rescue of repairable clients with no increase in their degradation; accelerated clearance of irreparable clients; net improvement in growth/viability under stress relative to controls.

Aim 3: Organelle-targeted triage (mito-ViDA)
- Design
  - Add outer-membrane targeting to ViDA; restrict to mitochondrial surface or intermembrane space as needed.
- Assays
  - Mixed-stress regime: transient Δψm drops (CCCP pulses) plus ROS bursts to generate salvageable vs terminally damaged mitochondria.
  - Outcomes: recovery of Δψm and respiratory capacity where salvageable; selective mitophagy (Parkin-independent) of collapsed mitochondria with C-state engagement; minimal impact on proteasome/autophagy flux outside mitochondria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria
  - Improved mitochondrial network function and removal of collapsed fragments without global proteostasis disruption.

Key experimental choices and justifications
- Why condensate switching: Condensates are natural time-averaging integrators; chain-type/length-dependent Ub signaling alters valency, providing a physically grounded “timer” that distinguishes transient from persistent damage. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))
- Why ankyrin repeats: repeat scaffolds allow rigid, multispecific geometry and mechanically coupled terminal reorientation with minimal parts, enabling mutual exclusivity between repair and clearance interfaces. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5593856/?utm_source=openai))
- Why not simply recruit E3s: in UBQLN2-like hubs, E3 recruitment can paradoxically protect from degradation; ViDA explicitly changes material state and interface geometry to permit proteasomal access or route to autophagy only after sustained high valency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10980000/?utm_source=openai))

Bench plan and controls
- Tuning thresholds: vary UBD stoichiometry and spacing; use Ub-chain mimetics with defined linkages to program switching points; calibrate with cycloheximide-chase and proteostasis stressors.
- Orthogonality and safety: restrict expression with tissue-specific promoters; incorporate degron kill-switch on ViDA itself (small-molecule-controlled) to stop activity if off-target effects emerge; verify that global Hsp70 pools and proteasome capacity metrics are unchanged at baseline. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism falsification tests:
  - If R→C switching occurs without UBD occupancy, redesign misfold sensors to reduce avidity; if switching never occurs despite high K48-Ub, increase UBD affinity or add modest crosslinkers.
  - If E3 recruitment in R-state is detected, mutate masked motifs to confirm geometry-based occlusion.

Milestones
- M6: R/C-lock validation; FRAP-defined dynamics and effector proteomes distinct.
- M12: Mixed-client triage with functional rescue and clearance within one culture.
- M18: Mito-ViDA demonstrates selective mitophagy of terminal mitochondria with improved respiratory capacity.

Potential pitfalls and mitigations
- Over-sequestration of clients in R-state: engineer faster exchange by shortening stickers; reduce IDR content.
- Proteasome exclusion from C-state: bias C-state toward autophagy via LC3-interacting motifs; or lower crosslink density to admit proteasome. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11805624/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target condensates: add localization domains (e.g., TOM/TIM tags) and reduce cytosolic LLPS propensity.

Validation of therapeutic relevance (cell and ex vivo)
- Neuronal or cardiomyocyte stress models with mixed salvageability; endpoints include contractility or synaptic activity recovery in salvageable fractions plus reduction of aggregate burden in terminal fractions. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and impact
- Converts polyubiquitin chain architecture and misfold density—ubiquitin’s native “grammar”—into a programmable, two-state, intracellular decision that preferentially repairs first, then clears only when damage persists. This differs from extracellular receptor agonism/antagonism and from single-function degraders by delivering pathway rewiring and condensate modulation with built-in safety thresholds. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37824531/?utm_source=openai))

Feasibility summary
- Grounded in: (i) established Hsp70–CHIP/HOP triage biology; (ii) well-documented coupling between ubiquitin chains and condensate valency; and (iii) clinically advanced, modular ankyrin/DARPin scaffolds for multispecific, geometry-controlled designs. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27863257/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go criteria
- Proceed to animal models only if ViDA increases functional recovery of salvageable cells ≥30% and accelerates clearance of irreparable clients ≥2× without elevating global proteotoxic stress markers at baseline and without reducing viability of unstressed cells. ([febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://febs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/1873-3468.70371?utm_source=openai))

Title
Membrane-Oriented Site-Selective Artificial Inactivation Catalysts (MOSAIC): catalytic juxtamembrane “clip-and-silence” of native membrane proteins

Hypothesis–Question
Can a ligand-guided, bilayer-embedded organometallic catalyst positioned within nanometers of a juxtamembrane loop catalyze backbone scission or irreversible side-chain oxidation that functionally inactivates the target membrane protein in living systems, without invoking proteasomal, lysosomal, or autophagic degradation?

Atomic strategy
Exploit membrane confinement and proximity to convert weak, generally unselective metal-mediated peptide modifications into a potent, site-biased reaction at a single juxtamembrane segment: anchor a catalytic center in the lipid bilayer and orient it by a target-binding headgroup so that catalysis occurs only when the complex “docks” at the chosen epitope; the resulting micro-confined chemistry yields cleavage or irreversible micro-damage that breaks signal transmission across the membrane.

Rationale and novelty
- Transition‑metal complexes can cleave or oxidize peptide backbones at defined residues in vitro and even in biorelevant matrices, but lack selectivity and cell‑compatible localization when used freely in solution. Membrane anchoring of catalysts is now feasible and increases local reactivity while confining byproducts to the bilayer. Combining these two lines—membrane-anchored catalysis and residue‑biased artificial proteases—has not been systematized for targeted inactivation of native membrane proteins. MOSAIC formalizes this combination as a therapeutic modality orthogonal to proteasome/lysosome/autophagy. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja952162e?utm_source=openai))
- Prior ligand-directed cleavage on cell surfaces demonstrates biochemical plausibility of affinity-biased scission, but without bilayer-embedded catalysis or juxtamembrane focus. MOSAIC supplies the orientation, confinement, and turnover needed for selective functional silencing in cells and in vivo. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39818953/?utm_source=openai))

Target scope
Single-pass receptors (Notch, EGFR family), mechanosensitive/ligand-gated channels with extracellular loops (Piezo1 ectodomain, ENaC), and adhesion receptors (integrins) whose activity depends on intact juxtamembrane linkers for force or conformational transmission. These classes are historically resistant to orthosteric inhibition and not consistently served by UPS- or lysosome-hijacking modalities.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build MOSAIC scaffolds and validate catalysis geometry on membranes.
- Construct amphiphiles comprising: (i) a bilayer anchor (cholesterol or C18–C24 aryl–alkyl); (ii) a semirigid tether (2–4 nm) enforcing catalyst depth at the inner leaflet of the ectodomain–membrane interface; (iii) a high-affinity binder to a proximal extracellular epitope (e.g., DARPin/peptide/small-molecule for EGFR or Notch negative regulatory region); and (iv) a metal center tuned for residue‑biased reactions: PdII aqua complexes for His‑adjacent amide hydrolysis; CuII/NiII for His/Met‑assisted cleavage; CeIV‑POM or Ru‑arene for Tyr/Trp oxidation to fragmentation. Include “dead‑metal” controls and binder‑scramble controls. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja952162e?utm_source=openai))
- Optimize membrane loading and leaflet orientation using liposome fusion or catalyst‑decorated lipids (MAC‑LiFT). Map catalyst depth/orientation by fluorescence quenchers and molecular dynamics; quantify on‑membrane turnover against peptide-loop mimetics embedded in nanodiscs/liposomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10171822/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: LC–MS mapping of cleavage on loop peptides; catalysis kinetics versus distance/orientation. Success criteria: kcat/KM ≥ 10^2 M^-1 s^-1 on membrane-mimetic substrates; ≥10‑fold drop when the epitope–catalyst distance exceeds 2–3 nm (geometric gating).

Aim 2. Demonstrate functional inactivation of native receptors/channels in live cells via juxtamembrane scission/oxidation.
- Cell systems: EGFR‑overexpressing A431 (ligand‑induced phosphorylation), Notch1 reporter cells (CSL‑luciferase), Piezo1‑expressing HEK293 (patch‑clamp, Ca2+ imaging).
- Dosing: low‑nM to low‑µM MOSAIC; co-substrates limited to O2/ascorbate; no external triggers.
- Molecular endpoints: cell-surface biotinylation followed by Western blot to detect ectodomain fragments; N‑terminomics to map scission sites; proteomics for off‑target mapping.
- Functional endpoints: loss of EGF‑stimulated pERK/pAKT; abrogation of Notch S2/S3 signaling; for Piezo1, irreversible loss of inactivation or current amplitude consistent with ectodomain damage, distinguishing from transient mechanosensitization. Persistence of effect after washout establishes functional irreversibility without reliance on degradation pathways. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms12939?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: free catalyst without anchor; membrane‑anchored catalyst lacking binder; binder‑only. Success criteria: ≥80% reduction in signaling/current with confirmed juxtamembrane scission, ≤10% proteome‑wide off‑target scission at equi-effective concentrations.

Aim 3. Translate to in vivo–compatible delivery and safety.
- Formulate MOSAIC in PEGylated liposomes or lipidated prodrugs for intratumoral or local delivery; quantify biodistribution and membrane loading.
- Off‑target risk management: exploit membrane confinement to restrict reactive species and reduce systemic exposure; compare anchored versus soluble catalysts for ROS leakage and hemolysis; benchmark against known organometallic bioorthogonal systems that operate in living cells and in/on membranes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5954130/?utm_source=openai))
- Efficacy model: EGFR‑driven xenograft; measure acute pathway shutdown and durable tumor growth delay after a limited‑dose regimen. Toxicology: liver enzymes, cytokines, histology.

Design and methods (condensed)

1) Scaffold chemistry and metal selection
- PdII aqua complexes with chelating diamines favor His‑adjacent cleavage under mild conditions; tune ligand lability to enable turnover yet minimize off‑target coordination. CuII/NiII complexes exploit imidazole/thioether assistance for hydrolysis near His/Met; CeIV‑POM can act as redox/hydrolytic artificial proteases and can be tethered via ionic/hydrophobic handles; Ru‑arene platforms support oxidative modifications at Tyr/Trp. Selection is target‑loop dependent (sequence/solvent exposure) determined from structural models and proteomics. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja952162e?utm_source=openai))
- Membrane embedding and orientation by MAC‑LiFT‑like lipid conjugates or cholesterol anchors place the metal center at the leaflet plane; anchor length adjusts depth to juxtapose the catalyst with the flexible juxtamembrane loop. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10171822/?utm_source=openai))
- Proximity enforcement by epitope binders (KD ≤ 10 nM) ensures nanometer-scale positioning; linker rigidity limits “swing,” sharpening the distance–reactivity relationship (effective molarity gating).

2) Catalysis mapping and control
- Reconstituted targets in nanodiscs/liposomes with native juxtamembrane segments allow systematic geometry scans. Stop‑flow MS tracks initial scission; isotopic oxygen labeling distinguishes hydrolysis from radical pathways.
- In cells, clickable capture of oxidized residues pinpoints redox footprints; quantitative proteomics (TMT) profiles system‑wide modifications to deconvolute true on‑target events.

3) Function–structure coupling
- EGFR: inactivation by severing the stalk/CR1‑CR2 junction should block ligand‑induced dimerization; measure dimer interface FRET and phosphorylation. Notch: scission/oxidation in the Negative Regulatory Region decouples ligand pulling from S2 cleavage; measure CSL reporter. Piezo1: ectodomain micro-damage reduces mechanotransduction; assess current–pressure relationships and irreversibility post‑washout. For channels/receptors, lack of intracellular chaperones in the extracellular space makes refolding unlikely, supporting durable inactivation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28921106/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- Month 6: MOSAIC library with measured membrane loading/orientation; catalytic activity on embedded loop mimetics with ≥10‑fold proximity enhancement.
- Month 12: On‑cell scission of EGFR or Notch juxtamembrane loops with mapped sites; ≥70% pathway suppression sustained ≥24 h after washout.
- Month 18: In vivo local dosing shows acute pathway shutdown and tumor growth delay with acceptable safety margins (no >2× ALT/AST; cytokines within reference).

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Slow catalysis: prioritize His/Met‑biased systems (PdII/CuII) where rate enhancements by proximity are documented; increase on‑target residence via higher‑affinity binders, or deploy multivalent low‑valency presentations on the same anchor lipid to raise effective molarity without clustering receptors. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja952162e?utm_source=openai))
- Off‑target oxidation: prefer hydrolytic over radical pathways where possible; for redox routes, use short‑lived oxidants generated at the membrane interface and verify minimal diffusion by reporter assays; exploit membrane confinement shown to amplify local catalysis while reducing systemic exposure. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42388817/?utm_source=openai))
- Membrane perturbation: screen anchor hydrophobicity and loading to avoid bilayer disruption; validate by giant unilamellar vesicle leakage and cell viability.
- Selectivity of epitope engagement: benchmark binders rigorously; use orthogonal binders to distinct epitopes to confirm epitope‑dependence of catalysis.

Why this meets the brief
- Mechanistic orthogonality: chemical scission/irreversible oxidative locking at juxtamembrane segments disables function without UPS/lysosome/autophagy. 
- Addresses “undruggables”: large, conformationally dynamic membrane proteins with shallow pockets.
- Tractable chemistry and in vivo plausibility: small, modular amphiphiles; catalytic turnover reduces dose; membrane anchoring and established bioorthogonal catalysis in/on membranes support operation in living systems. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5954130/?utm_source=openai))

Broader impact and extensions
- A generalizable “catalytic silencers” class for membrane proteins; multiplexing different metals/ligands on the same anchor allows logic‑gated control of inactivation. As a secondary axis, the platform can interface with existing induced‑proximity chemistries for mislocalization when catalytic inactivation is undesirable, building on emerging small‑molecule relocalization precedents. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13170557/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Geometry-gated SUMO seeding to recruit RNF4 and proteasomes for selective clearance of nuclear protein aggregates

Rationale and state-of-field cross-check
- Nuclear proteostasis relies on the ubiquitin–proteasome system (UPS), SUMOylation, and STUbLs such as RNF4; PML bodies and clastosomes organize SUMO/Ub/proteasome activities in the nucleus. Canonical macroautophagy is primarily cytoplasmic; mammalian nucleophagy exists but its direct contribution to intranuclear aggregate turnover is limited and context dependent. These points are established. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-biochem-062917-012730?utm_source=openai))
- Misfolded/aggregated nuclear proteins (e.g., polyQ-expanded ataxins) become SUMOylated; poly-SUMO recruits RNF4, which dimerizes to catalyze K48/K11-linked ubiquitin on SUMOylated substrates, routing them to nuclear proteasomes. This pathway reduces nuclear polyQ burden and toxicity in cell models. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))
- Amyloid-like assemblies display periodic cross-β architecture with conserved interstrand and intersheet spacings (~4.7–4.8 Å and ~10–11 Å) that generate repeated epitope geometry absent on monomers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7617691/?utm_source=openai))
- Protein-based degraders using SPOP or RNF4 fusions can deplete nuclear targets, but they act on any bound species and do not intrinsically distinguish aggregates from monomers. No report demonstrates a geometry-gated, aggregate-selective nuclear degrader that amplifies SUMO/Ub only on aggregates. This is the novelty gap this proposal addresses. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26373678/?utm_source=openai))

Central hypothesis-question
Can a geometry-gated SUMO “seed-and-amplify” module, which only activates on repeating aggregate architecture, drive RNF4-dependent, proteasome-mediated clearance of nuclear aggregates while sparing native monomers?

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Exploit aggregate-only periodic geometry to allosterically expose and nucleate SUMO2/3 chain formation directly on the aggregate surface; endogenous RNF4 then binds poly-SUMO and installs degradative ubiquitin chains. Because monomers cannot support the conformational switch nor sustain SUMO-chain amplification, they are preserved. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build a geometry-gated SUMO writer that activates only on repetitive aggregate surfaces.
2) Demonstrate self-reinforcing SUMO→RNF4→Ub “painting” and proteasomal clearance of nuclear aggregates with pathological-species selectivity.
3) Test generality across nuclear proteinopathy models and benchmark against SPOP- or RNF4-bioPROTACs that lack geometry gating.

Design and methods

Aim 1: Geometry-gated SUMO writer
- Sensor design: Create a low-affinity, multivalent repeat sensor (G-SENS) comprising 6–10 short β-adhesive motifs arrayed on a semi-rigid scaffold (e.g., ankyrin or HEAT-like repeats) whose folding and avidity require matching multiple epitopes spaced by the intersheet/interstrand periodicities found on cross-β surfaces. Off-target monomers lack sufficient periodicity/valency, so G-SENS remains disordered. Structural constraint: periodic recognition targets 2–5 ridges simultaneously, not single 4.7 Å spacings, ensuring realistic protein dimensions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7617691/?utm_source=openai))
- Gating payload: Fuse G-SENS to a masked SUMO seeding cassette (SUMO-SEED), comprising:
  - a short Ubc9-recruiting motif or minimal PIAS E3 fragment,
  - a SIM2–SIM4 array to capture nascent SUMO chains and stabilize engagement,
  - NLS and degron-silencing elements to prevent orphan activity.
  The Ubc9/PIAS segment is sterically occluded by G-SENS in the unbound state and exposed only when G-SENS aligns/folds on a repetitive surface. Outcome: aggregate-bound G-SENS–SUMO-SEED seeds SUMO2/3 on accessible lysines of aggregate-associated clients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7708061/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: In HEK293T nuclei expressing model nuclear aggregates (Htt exon1-97Q-NLS, Atxn1-82Q, FUS-NLS mutants), measure target-bound folding by FRET reporters on G-SENS; quantify local SUMO2/3 accumulation (anti-SUMO2/3), SIM-dependence (mutated SIMs), and requirement for the Ubc9/PIAS motif.

Aim 2: RNF4-dependent amplification and proteasome routing
- Mechanism: Poly-SUMO chains emerging from SUMO-SEED recruit endogenous RNF4 via its SIMs; RNF4 dimerization activates ubiquitin transfer, generating K48/K11 chains on SUMOylated substrates; nuclear proteasomes then degrade tagged species. Test dependence on RNF4 by siRNA/CRISPR ablation and rescue with dimerization-deficient RNF4 RING mutants. Proteasome dependence is tested with MG132 and nuclear-restricted proteasome inhibition. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))
- Positive feedback: SIM array in G-SENS stabilizes residence on growing poly-SUMO, increasing local Ubc9 flux. Quantify threshold behavior by live-cell single-particle tracking and FRAP to show ultrasensitive recruitment only above aggregate-size/valency thresholds; no accumulation on monomers or diffuse clients.
- Execution readouts: K48/K11-ubiquitin staining on aggregates, disassembly kinetics, and reduction in detergent-insoluble nuclear fractions; nuclear proteasome co-recruitment or clastosome engagement by immuno-EM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2064165/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Generality, selectivity, and benchmarking
- Disease targets: polyQ (Atxn1/7), FUS/TDP-43 nuclear assemblies, and intranuclear tau species if present. Quantify clearance, cell viability, and transcriptional rescue.
- Selectivity tests: Proteomics to assess preservation of native monomer pools and nuclear complexes (e.g., PCNA, Pol II, spliceosomal proteins). Challenge with SPOP- or RNF4-bioPROTACs targeting the same client epitopes; expect our module to spare monomers better because they cannot gate SUMO-SEED exposure, whereas bioPROTACs ubiquitinate any bound species. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26373678/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro reconstitution: Purified fibrils/oligomers vs monomers with recombinant G-SENS–SUMO-SEED, Ubc9/PIAS, RNF4, E1/E2, ubiquitin, SUMO2/3. Measure SUMO and ubiquitin deposition only on aggregated substrates; confirm RNF4 requirement for Ub deposition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3104014/?utm_source=openai))

Model systems and delivery
- Cell models: Human neurons derived from iPSCs expressing nuclear-aggregating disease proteins; U2OS/HEK293T for mechanistic imaging in nuclei.
- In vivo: Drosophila SCA1/HD models (nuclear aggregates) and a knock-in mouse line with nuclear polyQ pathology.
- Delivery: AAV-PHP.eB or AAV9 expressing NLS-tagged G-SENS–SUMO-SEED under neuron-specific promoters for CNS nuclei; inducible expression to control dose. Benchmark to SPOP- and RNF4-bioPROTACs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12549912/?utm_source=openai))

Key controls and falsification criteria
- Geometry necessity: scramble repeat spacing or reduce repeat number to abolish folding on aggregates; loss of SUMO seeding and clearance indicates geometry gating is required.
- SUMO pathway dependence: mutate SIM array or Ubc9/PIAS motif; loss of RNF4 recruitment and Ub deposition falsifies the cascade model. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target risk: survey PML bodies/other nuclear condensates; ensure no SUMO painting or client loss without aggregates; use SUMO E2/E3 dead variants as safety brakes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4615786/?utm_source=openai))
- Proteasome routing: MG132 or nuclear-restricted proteasome blockade must prevent aggregate loss and elevate SUMO/Ub-decorated species. ([journals.biologists.com](https://journals.biologists.com/jcs/article/119/10/1977/28967/The-nuclear-ubiquitin-proteasome-system?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- A digital-like threshold in SUMO/Ub deposition and aggregate clearance as aggregate size/valency crosses the gating requirement. Monomers and low-valency native complexes remain unmodified, meeting the pathological-species selectivity constraint.
- RNF4 loss or RING dimerization defects abolish ubiquitination and clearance, confirming STUbL dependence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3104014/?utm_source=openai))

Potential risks and mitigations
- Risk: SUMOylation toxicity if off-target condensates meet the geometry threshold. Mitigation: tune repeat valency/spacing and require dual conditions (geometry + local SUMO enrichment via SIMs) to raise the activation threshold; weaken Ubc9/PIAS affinity to keep SUMO flux low unless multivalency is achieved. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7708061/?utm_source=openai))
- Risk: Proteasomes cannot engage densely packed aggregates. Mitigation: SUMO/Ub interleaving plus RNF4 activity at aggregate peripheries promotes “edge peeling”; combine with nuclear Hsp70/Hsp110 to enhance disaggregation if needed. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24401655/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria and milestones (18–30 months)
- M6: G-SENS–SUMO-SEED shows aggregate-only folding (FRET) and SUMO2/3 seeding in nuclei.
- M12: RNF4-dependent ubiquitination and proteasome-dependent clearance with >70% reduction in nuclear aggregate burden; no significant loss of monomeric target by quantitative proteomics.
- M18: Generalization across at least two nuclear proteinopathy models with neuronal rescue phenotypes; superiority over non-gated SPOP/RNF4-bioPROTACs in preserving monomer pools. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26373678/?utm_source=openai))

Why this fits real biology and advances the field
- Leverages established nuclear PQC logic (SUMO→RNF4→Ub→proteasome) and the conserved geometry of amyloid-like assemblies to enforce aggregate-only activation. It avoids cytoplasmic autophagy dependency and operates entirely within the nucleus, aligning with known nuclear UPS and STUbL mechanisms. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))

References (representative)
- Nuclear PQC and SUMO/RNF4 axis: Guo et al., Mol Cell 2014; reviews on nuclear PQC and PML/RNF4. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24882209/?utm_source=openai))
- RNF4 RING dimerization requirement: Plechanovová et al., 2011. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3104014/?utm_source=openai))
- Cross-β periodicity: Knowles/Dobson reviews and FEBS Letters on 4.7/10–11 Å spacings. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7617691/?utm_source=openai))
- Nuclear proteasome compartments (clastosomes/PML bodies): Lallemand‑Breitenbach/de Thé; Lafarga et al.; recent clastosome reviews. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2064165/?utm_source=openai))
- SPOP/RNF4 bioPROTACs for nuclear targets (benchmarking context): Caussinus/deGradFP derivatives; Partridge PCNA-SPOP; YAP–RNF4 bioPROTAC. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26373678/?utm_source=openai))

End deliverable
A first-in-class, geometry-gated, SUMO-seeding nuclear degrader that enforces pathological-species selectivity by design and harnesses endogenous RNF4 and proteasomes for clearance of intranuclear aggregates.
