Title
Force-gated CTCF to selectively dissolve low-tension enhancer–promoter loops while preserving architectural genome topology

Integrated hypothesis–question
Can embedding a tunable mechanosensitive linker within CTCF convert local chromatin tension into a kinetic discriminator that shortens lifetimes of weak, pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops while preserving high-tension, CTCF-anchored architectural contacts, thereby correcting 3D wiring without sequence edits? This rests on two grounded premises: (i) cohesin-driven loop extrusion operates in the piconewton force regime and stalls at CTCF barriers; (ii) CTCF barrier activity is DNA-tension dependent, implying that anchor lifetimes can be modulated by force-sensitive off-rates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Mechanically gate CTCF off-rate. Engineer a CTCF variant (FG-CTCF) whose DNA-binding lifetime increases under higher chromatin tension and decreases under low tension. This converts local mechanical load—high at stable, convergent CTCF boundaries; low at aberrant E–P tethers—into a self-selecting filter on loop persistence, without predefining disease-specific sequences. Force-dependent off-rate control is a well-established physical principle for protein–ligand and protein–DNA bonds. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19491034.2020.1782024?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
- Aim 1. Engineer FG-CTCF variants with tunable force-dependent off-rates and validate barrier behavior under defined DNA tensions in vitro.
- Aim 2. Replace endogenous CTCF with FG-CTCF in cells and test whether weak, pathological E–P loops are selectively destabilized while TAD boundaries and canonical CTCF loops are preserved.
- Aim 3. Escalation path (if needed): co-express a low-potency RAD21 ring-destabilizing variant to bias cohesin unloading at weak anchors, preserving robust barriers stabilized by STAG–CTCF interactions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))

Design and rationale

1) Protein design: FG-CTCF
- Scaffold: Human CTCF with intact 11 zinc fingers (ZF1–ZF11).
- Mechanosensitive linker insertion: Introduce an elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) segment between central ZF clusters (e.g., between ZF5–ZF6) to create a compliant hinge that exhibits extensible mechanics under pN forces. ELP linkers are genetically encodable, mechanically well-characterized, and tunable in contour length and stiffness. The design goal is a slip-to-stabilized response: at low force (weak loops), the hinge geometry penalizes multizinc-finger engagement (higher off-rate); at elevated force (extrusion stall at strong anchors), extension aligns ZFs to lower the off-rate. A panel of ELP lengths/compositions will be screened to set thresholds within the 0.1–1 pN regime relevant for SMC extrusion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

- Barrier function under load: Test whether FG-CTCF increases cohesin stall probability and dwell under higher DNA tension, consistent with CTCF’s tension-dependent barrier behavior, and allows rapid dissociation at low tension. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05961-5.pdf?utm_source=openai))

2) Optional synergy: RAD21 ring-destabilizing variant (low-potency)
- Rationale: Cohesin release occurs via opening of the SMC3–RAD21 exit gate, promoted by WAPL/PDS5. A mild reduction in RAD21 interface stability should preferentially increase unloading where anchors are not reinforced (weak E–P), leaving high-tension, STAG/CTCF-stabilized barriers largely unaffected. This creates an orthogonal kinetic filter on weak loops. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1. Biophysical engineering and validation
- A1.1 Construct panel: Generate 12 FG-CTCF variants with ELP linkers (varying repeats and guest residues) inserted between ZF5–ZF6 (and two alternatives: ZF4–ZF5, ZF6–ZF7). Purify proteins.
- A1.2 Single-molecule DNA–protein kinetics under force: Use magnetic/optical tweezers with DNA tethers harboring high-affinity CTCF motifs; measure koff(F) for WT- and FG-CTCF at 0.05–1.0 pN. Target behavior: FG-CTCF koff reduced relative to WT at ≥0.3–0.6 pN and increased at ≤0.1–0.2 pN, consistent with load-sensitive barrier formation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
- A1.3 Reconstituted extrusion barrier assay: With human cohesin and NIPBL, quantify loop-extrusion stall frequency and dwell at CTCF sites under controlled tension in DNA curtains/tweezers. Benchmark against WT-CTCF. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))
- Success metric: A variant exhibiting ≥2-fold off-rate decrease at ≥0.3 pN and ≥2-fold increase at ≤0.1 pN vs WT; corresponding ≥1.5-fold increase in cohesin stall probability under high tension.

Aim 2. Cellular selectivity and topology preservation
- A2.1 Controlled replacement: Deliver a single vector encoding FG-CTCF and an shRNA that knocks down endogenous CTCF; include an auxin- or dTAG-degron on endogenous CTCF if a degron line is available. Inducible expression to gate timing.
- A2.2 Assay weak vs strong loops: Identify E–P loops with lower CTCF occupancy/valency (e.g., nonconvergent sites, suboptimal motifs) versus canonical convergent boundary loops. Use Hi-C/HiChIP for CTCF/cohesin to quantify loop strength, aggregate peak analysis, and insulation scores pre/post FG-CTCF induction. Preserve: boundary insulation and convergent CTCF loops; Reduce: low-occupancy E–P loops and hijacked enhancer connections.
- A2.3 Functional outcomes: RNA-seq to test normalization of misexpressed genes linked to weak E–P contacts; ChIP-seq CUT&RUN for CTCF, STAG1/2, RAD21 to confirm anchor-specific occupancy changes. STAG–CTCF interaction is expected to reinforce high-tension sites. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))
- A2.4 Off-target topology guardrails: Quantify global TAD insulation and compartment strength; criterion for preservation: median boundary insulation change <10% and compartment eigenvector correlation >0.9 relative to WT.

Aim 3. Escalation with RAD21 variant (only if Aim 2 shows residual pathological loops)
- A3.1 Co-deliver a bicistronic vector encoding a mild RAD21 variant with reduced stability at the SMC3–RAD21 exit interface (tuned in vitro to increase WAPL-facilitated unloading ≤1.5× WT). Validate no global loss of cohesin at strong CTCF/STAG-enriched barriers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- A3.2 Reassess loop selectivity as in Aim 2; proceed only if boundary insulation remains within preservation criteria.

Mechanistic falsification and decision gates
- F1. If FG-CTCF fails to show force-dependent koff in Aim 1 despite ELP tuning, reject the atomic strategy (“ideation failed”) and do not proceed in cells.
- F2. If FG-CTCF reduces insulation at strong CTCF boundaries by >15% in Hi-C or broadly reduces cohesin occupancy at STAG-enriched barriers, terminate and revert to WT-CTCF controls. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))
- F3. If adding RAD21 variant causes widespread cohesin loss (HiChIP RAD21 reduction across boundaries) or global gene-expression drift (RNA-seq PC1 shift), discontinue Aim 3. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-70484-2?utm_source=openai))

Readouts, statistics, and controls
- Single-molecule: Fit koff(F) to Bell–Evans models; compare FG-CTCF vs WT via ANCOVA on log(koff) vs F. Include control ELP insertions at noncritical CTCF loops (e.g., N-terminus) to rule out generic destabilization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7007008/?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin topology: Perform 3 biological replicates per condition; use insulation score delta distributions and aggregate peak analysis for loop classes; FDR control for RNA-seq differential expression.
- Functional controls: WT-CTCF rescue; catalytically neutral cohesin ATPase mutant to verify extrusion dependence; STAG2 knockdown to test predicted reinforcement role at strong barriers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947815/?utm_source=openai))

Delivery plan (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Single vector expressing FG-CTCF (inducible) plus CTCF shRNA and fluorescent reporter.
- Event 2 (only if Aim 3 triggered): Bicistronic vector for low-potency RAD21 variant (inducible).
- Event 3: Not used; kept in reserve for safety degron or reporter swap if required.

Safety and non-permanence
- No DNA sequence modification of genomic anchors. All interventions are protein-level and reversible via induction/degradation. Cohesin unloading leverages the native WAPL exit gate mechanics without genome edits. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
- A validated FG-CTCF that stabilizes high-tension, convergent CTCF boundaries while preferentially destabilizing weak, pathological E–P loops, restoring normal enhancer wiring without requiring locus catalogs. This exploits established physics of loop extrusion forces and force-dependent barrier activity, translated into a selective, self-tuning 3D genome editor. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If ELP linkers perturb DNA specificity, shift insertion site among ZF interdomains or modulate ELP composition to tune mechanical response.
- If force thresholds mismatch physiological ranges, calibrate via in situ tension reporters or adjust ELP length to match 0.1–1 pN regime measured for SMC complexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7387118/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- M1 (Months 0–6): Identify at least one FG-CTCF with desired koff(F) profile in vitro.
- M2 (Months 6–12): Demonstrate selective weakening of weak E–P loops with preserved boundary insulation in cells.
- M3 (Months 12–18): Optional RAD21 co-tuning achieves further reduction of residual weak loops without boundary loss. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-70484-2?utm_source=openai))

Title: KineLoop — Kinetic biasing of 3D genome reassembly to extinguish pathological enhancer–promoter loops

Hypothesis/Goal
Reversible, global collapse of architectural loops followed by controlled, temporal re-entry of loop-forming machinery will bias a limited pool of cohesin/Mediator toward bona fide enhancer–promoter (E–P) anchors, allowing normal 3D topology to self-reconstitute while deprioritizing re-formation of pathological E–P loops. The atomic strategy is time-ordering: seed early nucleation only at legitimate anchors before bulk reassembly, exploiting factor limitation and nonequilibrium assembly of loop extrusion and transcriptional bridging. This operates without DNA sequence mutation and primarily manipulates structural proteins; it can be reinforced locally by transient, site-specific torsional fences at pathological loci during the reassembly window. Cohesin/CTCF/Mediator underpin TADs and E–P proximity through loop extrusion and bridging; WAPL and NIPBL tune residence and loading; DNA torsion modulates cohesin engagement and extrusion efficiency. ([biorxiv.org](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.08.14.667581v2.full?utm_source=openai))

Innovation
- Converts 3D genome “editing” into kinetic control of reassembly order after a reversible global reset, rather than sequence alteration or forced tethering of loci. Prior methods engineer static loops (CLOuD9, LADL/OptoLoop) or delete/flip CTCF sites; none intentionally bias genome-wide reassembly kinetics to select against pathological loops. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))
- Uses transient, anchor-first nucleation and optional locus-specific torsional barriers to reshape the energy landscape that loop extrusion and Mediator/BRD4 bridging explore during recovery, leveraging known sensitivities of cohesin loading, residence time, and DNA supercoiling. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

Specific Aims
Aim 1. Build anchor-first nucleation seeds to front-load cohesin/Mediator at bona fide E–P anchors prior to bulk reassembly.
- Design: A catalytically inactive dCas9 “seed” targeted to validated normal anchors (convergent CTCF/promoter sites) fused to minimal NIPBL segments that stimulate cohesin ATPase/loading (MINI-NIPBL) and/or a Mediator tail peptide that increases Mediator clustering. Seeds are expressed 2–4 h before global restoration of architectural proteins after acute depletion. Rationale: NIPBL/Mediator accumulate near promoters/enhancers and facilitate cohesin loading/activation; early nucleation at high-affinity native anchors should capture limiting cohesin and establish long-residence loops if WAPL release is temporarily dampened at those sites. Metrics: on-rate and residence of RAD21 at seeded anchors (ChIP-seq/FRAP), early loop re-appearance (Micro-C/Hi-C). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Implement sequential kinetic gating of the global reassembly program in degron-enabled cell systems and quantify topology/selectivity.
- System: Human cells with auxin/dTAG-degradable RAD21 (cohesin), CTCF, and a Mediator subunit to acutely erase loops, then rescue by timed washout/re-expression. Rationale: Eliminating CTCF/cohesin erases loops; reintroduction restores them with characteristic kinetics that can be biased by prior anchor nucleation and transiently reduced WAPL activity. Assays: time-resolved Micro-C/Hi-C, cohesin/CTCF/Mediator CUT&Tag, and allele-resolved HiChIP at disease loci (e.g., enhancer hijacks). Outcome: selective restoration of normal E–P loops and suppression of pathological contacts, with preserved TADs/compartments. Controls: seeds at scrambled sites; reassembly without seeds; WAPL modulation off. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867417305317?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3 (optional reinforcement). Apply transient, locus-specific torsional fences at pathological enhancers/promoters during reassembly, then remove.
- Design: A dCas9 topological clamp (dual gRNAs spanning 100–300 bp) plus recruitment of a Topo1-activity dampening peptide or steric swiveling constraint for 6–12 h post-rescue to accumulate local positive supercoils and reduce cohesin loading/extrusion efficiency at the pathological site; fence is removed after normal anchors are stabilized. Rationale: Cohesin extrusion and loop length are sensitive to torsion; Topo1 inhibition or impaired relaxation shortens loops in cells; modulating supercoiling locally should raise the energy barrier for re-forming the pathological loop without altering sequence. Metrics: reduced cohesin/Mediator residence and contact frequency at the pathological pair during the window, with recovery after fence removal. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124725006278?utm_source=openai))

Experimental Design and Methods
1) Model loci and pathologies
- Select two validated enhancer-hijack models (e.g., oncogenic super-enhancer miswiring) with known pathological E–P loops and normal counterpart contacts for benchmarking; design seed gRNAs to legitimate anchors and clamp gRNAs to pathological anchors.

2) Global disruption and staged rescue
- Deplete RAD21 and CTCF (± Mediator subunit) using AID/dTAG for 4–8 h to remove TAD loops, confirmed by Micro-C and loss of CTCF/Cohesin peaks. Reintroduce seed constructs first; 2–4 h later, washout degron ligands to allow bulk cohesin/CTCF/Mediator return; optionally reduce WAPL activity transiently (chemical degron or RNAi) for 6–12 h to extend residence of early-formed loops. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0092867417305317?utm_source=openai))

3) Readouts
- Structure: time series Micro-C/Hi-C at 0, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48 h post-rescue; loop callers quantify E–P contacts and insulation scores.
- Protein dynamics: RAD21/CTCF/Mediator CUT&Tag and live-cell single-molecule tracking to derive on/off rates and residence.
- Transcription: PRO-seq and nascent RNA at target genes to test restoration of physiological expression.
- Supercoiling state (optional Aim 3): topo-sensitive psoralen-seq or supercoil-trap assays at targeted loci.

4) Selectivity criteria
- Pathological E–P loop frequency reduced ≥50% relative to no-seed rescue while normal E–P loops return to ≥80% of baseline; TAD insulation and A/B compartments comparable to pre-disruption state.

5) Delivery constraints (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Transduce seed/clamp constructs (single vector with multiplexed gRNAs) and optional WAPL-tuner.
- Event 2: Small-molecule degron treatment to deplete, then scheduled washout to rescue structural proteins.
- Event 3: Induce seed/clamp clearance (degron/antisense) after topology stabilizes.

Risk Assessment and Alternatives
- Risk: Seeds mis-target or nucleate at low-affinity/non-native sites. Mitigation: require convergent CTCF motif proximity and promoter histone marks for gRNA design; include seed variants that require TF co-binding domains to limit off-target anchoring.
- Risk: Global disruption harms viability. Mitigation: use short pulses and partial depletion; focus on loci-specific readouts; verify recovery of compartments.
- Risk: Torsional fences perturb local transcription excessively. Mitigation: limit window; measure recovery; deploy only if Aim 1–2 insufficient. The mechanistic link between torsion and extrusion justifies a transient fence as a physical barrier. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124725006278?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and Success Criteria
- M1: Demonstrate that anchor-first seeding advances the timing of cohesin/Mediator accumulation at legitimate anchors by ≥2 h versus bulk rescue alone and increases residence time locally. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Show selective suppression of pathological E–P loops with restoration of normal loops and TAD insulation within 24–48 h post-rescue.
- M3 (optional): Show that a 6–12 h torsional fence further decreases pathological loop re-formation without long-term transcriptional penalty.

Why it will work
Loop extrusion is sensitive to loading sites (NIPBL), residence time (WAPL), CTCF orientation/barriers, and DNA torsion; all are kinetically and mechanically tunable. Early capture at legitimate anchors consumes limited cohesin and sets long-lived loops, while temporary torsional penalties at pathological sites raise their assembly barrier during the critical window. Together, this reweights reassembly trajectories toward physiological topology without altering sequence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36900-7?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Mechanosensitive unloading of diseased enhancer–promoter loops via conformation-selective intrabodies that recruit WAPL/PDS5

Background and novelty assessment
- Mechanistic ground truth: Mammalian chromatin architecture emerges from cohesin-driven loop extrusion constrained by CTCF orientation; residence time and anchor composition modulate enhancer–promoter (E–P) contact frequency and duration. WAPL–PDS5 catalyzes cohesin unloading by opening the Smc3–RAD21 gate, thereby limiting loop extension and enforcing directionality rules. Mediator/BRD4-enriched enhancers can stall cohesin and stabilize contacts. These points are consistently supported by recent syntheses and primary studies. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-024-00795-x?utm_source=openai))
- Disease relevance: Structural variants, boundary erosion, and enhancer hijacking pathologically rewire E–P pairing, often yielding longer-lived contacts and aberrant anchor usage; this is established across genetic disorders and cancers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25959774/?utm_source=openai))
- Gap: Available 3D-genome engineering tools can force loops (e.g., CLOuD9, LADL) or globally alter cohesin dynamics (WAPL depletion) but do not selectively dismantle only aberrant loops based on their physical state. No reports were found of conformation- or tension-state–selective intrabodies against cohesin/CTCF that locally recruit WAPL/PDS5, nor geometry-gated small molecules used as inter-anchor “distance readers” in nuclei. PROTAC selectivity via linker geometry is known, but has not been applied to sense 3D chromatin anchor spacing; targeted WAPL tethering to individual anchors was not identified. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility cues: Cohesin exhibits ATPase-coupled conformational states and interface plasticity (including Smc3–RAD21 and kleisin–STAG surfaces) that plausibly expose strain-dependent epitopes; computational and display-based discovery of epitope-specific nanobodies is tractable. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–goal (deliberately inseparable)
Abnormally stabilized E–P loops impose a distinct mechanical/conformational state on CTCF–cohesin–cofactors at their anchors (greater dwell time, altered interface angles, and stalled extrusion). A conformation-selective intrabody that recognizes a tension-exposed cohesin/CTCF neo-epitope and recruits a minimal WAPL/PDS5 unloading module will preferentially disassemble these pathological loops while sparing normal contacts and preserving global topology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit disease-imposed mechanics as the actuator: bind only to a mechanically strained conformer at E–P anchors and, upon binding, locally bias cohesin’s release reaction via WAPL/PDS5—self-terminating as soon as the aberrant loop opens (epitope relaxes).

Operational design (conceptual; non-procedural)
- Effector architecture: A low-affinity, conformation-specific intrabody (“ms-iBody”) fused to a minimal WAPL/PDS5-interacting peptide. Binding requires a strain-exposed epitope on cohesin/CTCF observed at long-lived, misassembled anchors; in relaxed/healthy states, affinity is insufficient to engage. Primary mechanism: structural protein manipulation of the cohesin cycle; no DNA sequence alteration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Selectivity guards:
  - Force-state gating: epitope exposed only under stalled extrusion/anchor torque. Cohesin state plasticity supports this assumption. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
  - Context gating: an auxiliary weak binder to a Mediator/BRD4 surface increases avidity only at hyperacetylated, condensate-like enhancers known to stall cohesin, sharpening specificity for disease super-enhancers. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00018-024-05559-8?utm_source=openai))
  - Self-limitation: after unloading, the strained conformation dissipates and ms-iBody disengages.

Model systems and mapping of discriminants (Aim 1)
- Define “pathologic anchor” signatures at exemplar loci with enhancer hijacking or boundary erosion (e.g., PDGFRA boundary loss in IDH-mutant glioma; oncogenic super-enhancer–MYC modules). Readouts: local cohesin/CTCF/Mediator occupancy, contact dwell-time proxies, and extrusion stall patterns; ensure normal E–P pairs in the same cells serve as internal controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4880504/?utm_source=openai))
- Outcome: a panel of loci with quantifiable differences in residence/geometry that will be used to benchmark selectivity.

Binder discovery and validation (Aim 2)
- Identify strain- or state-specific epitopes on cohesin/CTCF interfaces implicated in unloading control (e.g., Smc3–RAD21/kleisin–STAG regions). Combine structure-guided in silico designs with display selections against state-biased antigens; screen for intrabodies that bind strongly to the “stalled” conformer and weakly to the “relaxed” conformer. Reference states derive from structural and biochemical knowledge of cohesin’s ATPase cycle and gate opening by WAPL–PDS5. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks: (i) state selectivity in cell-free binding; (ii) negligible binding at fast-turnover/healthy anchors; (iii) loss of binding upon global relaxation of cohesin dynamics.

Mechanism-of-action build (Aim 3)
- Fuse ms-iBody to a minimal WAPL/PDS5-recruitment cassette; confirm that ms-iBody engagement raises local cohesin unloading probability without globally altering TAD organization or anchor usage. Global loop extrusion roles of WAPL/PDS5 and their impact on loop networks provide quantitative expectations for “what not to see” system-wide. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5730888/?utm_source=openai))
- Optional transient chromatin “friction”: a weak, reversible writer/reader (e.g., short-lived deacetylase recruitment) appended to ms-iBody reduces immediate re-stabilization at hyperacetylated enhancers; include washout designs to ensure reversibility and avoid persistent marks. Mediator/BRD4-rich super-enhancers correlate with high contact propensity but are not strictly required for looping, supporting a nudge-only role. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9659172/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts and success criteria
- Topology: restoration of local contact maps toward healthy baselines at target loci with minimal perturbation of non-targeted neighborhoods and global TAD structure. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-024-00795-x?utm_source=openai))
- Kinetics: reduced contact dwell time specifically at pathological E–P pairs; normal short-lived E–P “kisses” retained. Recent live-imaging and synthesis pieces estimate loop lifetimes on the order of minutes, providing quantitative priors. ([annualreviews.org](https://www.annualreviews.org/docserver/fulltext/cellbio/41/1/annurev-cellbio-111822-122324.pdf?accname=guest&checksum=A59DC90DF46E50983E408271E0A524F1&expires=1781441214&id=id&utm_source=openai))
- Transcription: normalization of misexpressed target genes without widespread transcriptional collapse characteristic of global cohesin or BET perturbation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-targets: genome-wide assessment shows low-rate incidental unloading at healthy anchors; no emergence of ectopic long loops or loop networks linked to WAPL loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Comparative arm (orthogonal validation)
- A proximity-activated split-WAPL recruiter (half-modules targeted to enhancer vs promoter anchors via modest-affinity readers) used as an AND-gate control for dwell/orientation dependence. Reconstitution should require prolonged, disease-like proximity; normal fleeting contacts fail to assemble. This tests the necessity and sufficiency of pathological dwell/orientation independent of force-state epitopes. (Background supports the logic that looped proximity increases E–P contact probability but is often transient in healthy cells.) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))

Delivery and deployment
- One delivery event: a single vector expressing ms-iBody–WAPL/PDS5-recruiter (bicistronic inclusion of the optional BRD4/Mediator microbinder permissible within the same event). No DNA sequence editing; effects remain at the level of structural cycling of cohesin.

Key risks and falsification tests
- Risk: disease anchors might not expose unique epitopes. Falsification: if binders cannot discriminate stalled vs relaxed states in vitro and in cells despite adequate search space, the atomic strategy fails.
- Risk: unloading at diseased anchors could trigger compensatory rewiring. Counter-readout: emergence of alternative pathogenic loops in the same domain indicates a need to couple unloading to a transient anti-stabilization nudge at the enhancer surface; the optional module directly tests this.
- Alternative outcome: if mechanics are insufficiently distinct, the split-recruiter AND-gate should still selectively act on long-dwell contacts, providing an independent route to selectivity.

Why this will not collapse global topology
- The trigger is a local conformer plus context avidity (stalled/mechanically strained anchor within a Mediator/BRD4-rich enhancer). WAPL/PDS5 recruitment is transient and spatially constrained; global extrusion remains intact, consistent with known consequences of localized vs global WAPL modulation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Year 1: Map discriminants at chosen disease loci; identify state-biased epitopes and initial ms-iBody hits. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124724010076?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Build ms-iBody–WAPL/PDS5 prototypes; demonstrate selective loop relaxation and transcriptional correction at ≥2 pathological loci with preserved global topology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5422210/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Generalize to additional pathologies (SV-driven enhancer hijacking and methylation-driven boundary erosion) and benchmark safety/selectivity windows. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959437X24000480?utm_source=openai))

Decision rule
If ms-iBody–mediated unloading normalizes pathogenic contact topology and expression at target loci while leaving healthy E–P contacts and TAD structure statistically unchanged, the hypothesis stands; if not, the mechanics-as-trigger premise is rejected in favor of dwell/orientation–gated proximity approaches.

Title
Magneto-mechanical CRISPR-origami nanosprings as a reversible locus-specific chromatin loop switch in mouse embryonic stem cells

Hypothesis/goal/question (merged)
If a mechanically reconfigurable, CRISPR-anchored DNA-origami nanospring bearing anisotropic magnetic nanoactuators is installed across a defined enhancer–promoter pair in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), then a single external, low-frequency rotating magnetic field will reversibly shorten/lengthen their spatial separation and thereby switch loop contact probability and transcriptional output, providing a general, non-dimerizer mechanism to control chromatin loops. Does such magneto-mechanical distance control suffice to toggle gene expression at the Sox2 SCR–promoter pair, given the ongoing debate over the necessity of proximity for Sox2 transcription in ESCs? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4259346/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert loop probability into a single mechanical degree of freedom: a CRISPR-placed nanospring whose end-to-end length is toggled by magnetic torque on attached single-domain nanocubes under a rotating field, changing enhancer–promoter encounter rate and dwell time without any light-activated protein dimerization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9494703/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and novelty
- Mechanistic sufficiency: Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies and loop lifetimes are governed by cohesin-driven loop extrusion and local polymer mechanics; biasing 3D distance at a preselected locus should shift contact probability and transcription. The proposal acts upstream of biochemical recruitment by altering polymer geometry directly. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinct from optogenetic dimerizers: Unlike CRY2/CIBN- or CRY2–CRY2-based OptoLoop systems that stabilize contacts via light-induced protein oligomerization, this design uses a DNA-origami mechanical transducer and magnetic torque; no inducible protein–protein dimerization is used. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12952762/?utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility primitives exist: DNA-origami nanosprings exert and report pN-scale forces and are actuated magnetically; magnetic torque on anisotropic nanomagnets is well established; and dCas9 can be covalently tethered to defined ssDNA handles via HUH-tags for deterministic protein–DNA assembly. Nuclear delivery of functionalized DNA origami is increasingly tractable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5159853/?utm_source=openai))

Model system and target locus
- Cell type: mESCs (rapid chromatin dynamics; strong Sox2 enhancer biology; robust genomics toolkits).
- Locus: Sox2 promoter and the distal Sox2 Control Region (SCR; ~100 kb). The SCR–Sox2 loop is functionally linked to expression but reports disagree about strict proximity requirements, making it a rigorous testbed for mechanical sufficiency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4265674/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build a CRISPR-anchored magnetic nanospring bridge across the Sox2 SCR and promoter and verify reversible, field-driven end-to-end length switching in nuclei.
2) Quantify loop formation/dissolution kinetics and transcriptional consequences under on/off magnetic field cycles.
3) Map the control surface: how nanospring geometry (rest length, stiffness) and handle multiplicity set loop dwell time and transcriptional gain, benchmarking against light-driven dimerizer systems.

Device design
- Scaffold: Coiled DNA-origami nanospring with programmable spring constant and calibrated extension under pN forces; two terminal “landing pads” each bearing N (4–8) orthogonal ssDNA handles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5159853/?utm_source=openai))
- Magnetic actuator: Arrays of single-domain iron-oxide nanocubes (or nanorods) rigidly mounted on defined origami domains to produce net magnetic anisotropy; a 5–50 Hz rotating magnetic field imposes torque that snaps the nanospring between extended and contracted conformations with millisecond–second response, validated in vitro. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9494703/?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPR anchoring: Express dCas9 fused to a small HUH endonuclease tag. The origami terminal pads display the cognate 9-nt HUH ssDNA substrates, enabling sequence-directed, covalent tethering of each dCas9 to the nanospring pad prior to or after nuclear delivery. Guide RNAs target dCas9–HUH at each pad to (i) Sox2 promoter and (ii) SCR (multiple high-occupancy protospacers to increase residence time). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5517037/?utm_source=openai))
- Nuclear delivery: Electroporation or cell squeezing of origami–protein complexes; recent methods demonstrate nuclear import of functional DNA origami, enabling intracellular tracking and activity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41001623/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan

Aim 1: Assembly, delivery, and in-nucleus actuation
- In vitro calibration: Measure nanospring extension vs. field angle using TIRF and magnetic rotation stages; determine torque–extension curve and bistability thresholds. Validate reversibility for ≥10^4 cycles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9494703/?utm_source=openai))
- Complex assembly: Mix purified dCas9–HUH with nanosprings presenting cognate ssDNA tags to form covalent complexes; add sgRNAs for SCR and promoter targeting; confirm stoichiometry by native PAGE and AFM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5517037/?utm_source=openai))
- mESC delivery: Transfect complexes; confirm nuclear localization and locus binding by live-cell CRISPR imaging (fluorescently labeled sgRNAs) and ChIP for dCas9.
- In-nucleus mechanics: Under a rotating magnetic field (uniform, 5–50 Hz, ≤10 mT), quantify nanospring end-to-end distance and locus–locus distance using dual-color CRISPR imaging. Establish field-on contraction and field-off relaxation amplitudes and kinetics.

Aim 2: Looping and transcriptional consequences
- Contact assays: Perform Capture-C/Micro-C at Sox2 to quantify SCR–promoter contact frequency across field states and cycles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))
- Live RNA readout: Introduce MS2-tagged Sox2 reporter allele; monitor nascent transcription bursts versus field on/off; compute changes in burst frequency and burst duration.
- Population assays: RT-qPCR and nascent RNA-seq under defined duty cycles to assess expression gain and reversibility; washout experiments to confirm return to baseline.

Aim 3: Design rules and benchmarking
- Geometry sweep: Build nanosprings with rest lengths 60–200 nm and spring constants spanning 0.1–5 pN/nm; vary handle multiplicity (N=2–8). Map parameter space to: (i) mean locus distance shift, (ii) contact time, (iii) transcriptional gain.
- Cohesin/CTCF dependency: acutely degrade cohesin (AID–RAD21) or invert CTCF motifs near the locus to test whether mechanical proximity alone suffices or requires extrusion arrest, informing mechanism. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmark: Compare against an OptoLoop implementation at Sox2 under identical imaging and transcript assays; quantify switching contrast, kinetics, and off-target contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12952762/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts and success criteria
- Mechanical switching: ≥20% reversible change in inter-locus distance at the single-cell level with sub-second latency.
- Topology: ≥2-fold change in SCR–promoter contact frequency by Capture-C/Micro-C on field-on vs. field-off samples. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))
- Transcription: Significant and reversible modulation of Sox2 burst frequency or output correlated with mechanical state; hysteresis quantified across cycles.
- Specificity: No global compaction detectable by Hi-C compartment scores; minimal perturbation at non-targeted loci.

Controls
- Non-targeting nanospring (scrambled gRNAs).
- Origami without magnetic nanocubes (field insensitive).
- dCas9 lacking HUH tag (no anchoring to origami).
- Field exposure with no nanocubes (field-only control).
- OptoLoop positive control (blue-light inducible CRY2–CRY2 clustering at same sites). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12952762/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Insufficient torque in vivo: Pre-validate torque transfer on chromatinized DNA curtains; increase actuator anisotropy by using nanorod/nanocube trimers and rigid origami mounting; increase the number of CRISPR handles per pad to distribute load. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9494703/?utm_source=openai))
- Nuclear delivery limits: Employ nucleus-directed delivery methods for DNA origami and validate structural integrity post-import. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41001623/?utm_source=openai))
- Binding kinetics bottleneck: Use multiple high-affinity sgRNAs per region to reduce search times; consider dCas9 variants with longer residence time.
- Interpretation at Sox2: Because proximity–transcription coupling at Sox2 is debated, include a second locus with clearer proximity dependence (e.g., Nanog super-enhancers) as a replication target. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5111363/?utm_source=openai))

Why this meets the brief
- Single stimulus: one rotating magnetic field drives switching.
- Reversibility: elastic nanospring states toggle repeatedly with no covalent remodeling.
- Locus specificity: CRISPR targeting defines the loop anchors.
- Non-dimerizer novelty: no light-gated or chemically gated dimerization; the actuator is a physical transducer, mechanistically distinct from CRY2/CIBN systems. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12952762/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline (12–18 months)
- Months 0–4: In vitro device calibration; torque–extension characterization; HUH–dCas9 conjugation optimization. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5517037/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 5–9: Nuclear delivery and single-cell mechanical switching in mESCs; establish imaging and field parameters.
- Months 10–14: Capture-C/Micro-C and live transcription assays; parameter sweep for geometry and handle multiplicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11190842/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 15–18: Cohesin/CTCF dependency tests; benchmarking versus OptoLoop; replication at Nanog.

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- A clear on/off loop switch at Sox2 will indicate that mechanical distance control is sufficient to modulate loop probability and, in at least some contexts, transcription, clarifying the role of proximity in mESC enhancer function.
- A weaker transcriptional response despite robust distance changes would support models in which enhancer activity is dominated by chromatin state or factor availability rather than mere proximity at Sox2, while still validating a generally applicable, reversible, and non-dimerizer loop control technology. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-022-01294-7?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Reversible, light-driven polymer actuators to force enhancer–promoter proximity in human neurons without optogenetic dimerizers

Core question-hypothesis
Can a single near-infrared (NIR) light input that triggers a reversible phase transition in a nanoscale polymer actuator, tethered to two CRISPR-addressed genomic sites, be sufficient to increase enhancer–promoter contact probability and modulate transcription of activity-regulated genes in human neurons? If yes, loop probability and transcriptional burst parameters should scale with the actuator’s on/off duty cycle.

Atomic strategy
Translate photons into a reversible piconewton-scale, submicron mechanical shortening between two dCas9-anchored loci using a PNIPAM brush polymer grafted to a gold nanorod (GNR). A brief NIR pulse creates local photothermal heating above the polymer’s LCST, collapsing the polymer and pulling targeted chromatin segments together; cooling re-extends the polymer and releases the loop. No light-induced protein dimerization is used.

Prior art and novelty check
- Existing loop-forcing systems rely on light- or chemical-induced protein dimerization (e.g., CRY2–CIBN LADL/OptoLoop; ABA-based CLOuD9) to bridge dCas9-targeted loci or reorganize genome positioning (CRISPR-GO). The proposed actuator replaces protein dimerizers with a reversible polymer phase transition mechanically coupled to chromatin, addressing the same function with a distinct mechanism. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))
- Photothermal control of thermoresponsive polymers and elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs) by GNRs is established and reversible; PNIPAM- or ELP-coated gold nanostructures undergo light-controlled collapse/coalescence near physiological temperatures. Nuclear targeting of gold nanostructures is feasible. These data support feasibility of an intranuclear photothermal actuator. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21543835/?utm_source=openai))
- dCas9 can be chemically functionalized (e.g., HaloTag) to recruit synthetic ligands/oligonucleotides, and sgRNAs can display aptamers/adaptors (CRISPR-Display), enabling locus-specific attachment of DNA handles that dock the actuator. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5278450/?utm_source=openai))
- Activity-dependent enhancer–promoter contacts at neuronal IEGs (e.g., BDNF promoter IV, FOS, ARC) are well documented, providing relevant readouts to test loop causality. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neural-circuits/articles/10.3389/fncir.2022.911023/full?utm_source=openai))

Model system
Human iPSC-derived excitatory cortical neurons in 2D culture. Target loci: BDNF promoter IV enhancer–promoter pair (primary), FOS and ARC pairs (secondary). These loci show stimulus-dependent looping with rapid transcriptional responses. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neural-circuits/articles/10.3389/fncir.2022.911023/full?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build and validate a CRISPR-tethered, NIR-switchable PNIPAM–GNR chromatin loop actuator in neuronal nuclei.
2) Quantify how actuator duty cycle sets enhancer–promoter contact probability and transcriptional burst parameters at BDNF promoter IV.
3) Benchmark against CRY2–CIBN LADL/OptoLoop to establish mechanistic differentiation and performance envelopes.

Design and methods
A. Actuator and targeting architecture
- Two genomic anchors: dCas9-HaloTag targeted by sgRNAs to enhancer and promoter. Each anchor is labeled in situ with a chloroalkane-modified ssDNA adaptor (A or B). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5278450/?utm_source=openai))
- Bridging actuator: a single GNR (~10×40 nm) coated with PNIPAM brush bearing two short ssDNA handles A′ and B′ (complementary to A and B). PNIPAM LCST tuned to 39–42°C via copolymer composition. In the dark (37°C), PNIPAM is extended (open state). Under NIR (e.g., 808 or 1064 nm), localized heating above LCST collapses PNIPAM, shortening the end-to-end distance and pulling enhancer and promoter together; removal of light restores the open state. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21543835/?utm_source=openai))
- Nuclear delivery: GNRs functionalized with NLS-bearing peptides for intranuclear accumulation without cytotoxic aggregation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28447447/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: (i) non-complementary handles; (ii) GNR without PNIPAM; (iii) PNIPAM actuator lacking one handle; (iv) NIR only; (v) dCas9–CRY2/CIBN LADL or OptoLoop as positive control for protein-dimerizer bridging. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

B. Photothermal drive and safety characterization
- Stimulation: rastered or widefield NIR at power densities empirically set to raise the local actuator shell to LCST while keeping bulk nuclear temperature ≤39.5°C (measure with fluorescent thermometry; calibrate on fixed cells first). Photothermal reversibility and kinetics measured by actuator FRET reporters or scattering changes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6467806/?utm_source=openai))
- Safety readouts: viability, γH2AX, HSP70 induction, and transcriptional profiles to exclude heat-shock confounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7035993/?utm_source=openai))

C. Locus placement and imaging
- Guide placement 0.5–2 kb from key TF motifs to avoid occlusion. Use orthogonal dCas9 labeling (e.g., dCas9-MS2/PP7 live tagging or fluorescent dCas9 orthologs) to visualize loci and actuator colocalization dynamics at diffraction-limited scales; complement with 3C/HiChIP to quantify contact frequency. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-018-0107-y?utm_source=openai))

D. Transcriptional readouts
- Primary transcripts by intronic RT-qPCR and smFISH; nascent RNA dynamics by MS2 knock-in reporter at BDNF if feasible; PRO-seq for genome-wide off-target effects. Looping measured by Capture-C/HiChIP anchored at promoter/enhancer. ([genome.cshlp.org](https://genome.cshlp.org/content/35/6/1277?utm_source=openai))

E. Benchmarking
- Replicate loop formation and expression changes with LADL/OptoLoop (blue-light CRY2–CIBN) at the same loci to compare magnitude, latency, reversibility, and phototoxicity. Expect similar or faster mechanical on-rates with NIR PNIPAM collapse but reduced pathway cross-talk relative to protein oligomerization. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- Aim 1: Intranuclear PNIPAM–GNR shows ≥80% reversible collapse cycles with NIR on/off; no rise in global HSP70 or γH2AX; specific recruitment to both anchors (>5:1 on-target enrichment over control). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21543835/?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 2: At BDNF IV, NIR “on” increases enhancer–promoter contact frequency ≥2-fold and primary transcript abundance ≥1.5–3-fold within 10–30 min; effects reverse within 30–60 min “off.” Contact and expression magnitude scale monotonically with duty cycle. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neural-circuits/articles/10.3389/fncir.2022.911023/full?utm_source=openai))
- Aim 3: Compared to LADL/OptoLoop, PNIPAM–GNR achieves comparable contact induction with lower light dose and reduced off-target chromatin clustering; maintains function under red/NIR wavelengths that minimize phototoxicity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic predictions and discriminating tests
- Prediction 1: In the presence of cohesin inhibition, actuator-driven contacts still occur but transcriptional gains diminish if cohesin normally stabilizes contacts; this dissociates “contact formation” from “contact stabilization.” Test with acute RAD21 degradation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2151-x?utm_source=openai))
- Prediction 2: If enhancer–promoter dwell time is the primary determinant of burst size, then increasing on-time at fixed peak proximity increases burst amplitude more than burst frequency; resolve with MS2 traces and Hidden Markov modeling. ([genome.cshlp.org](https://genome.cshlp.org/content/35/6/1277?utm_source=openai))
- Prediction 3: For distal noncognate pairings, forcing proximity without compatible regulatory grammar yields contact without transcriptional gain, providing internal negative controls.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- Nuclear delivery inefficiency of actuators: incorporate dual NLS and optimize size/charge; if needed, preassemble actuator–adaptor complexes in permeabilized nuclei for calibration. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28447447/?utm_source=openai))
- Overheating risk: shift LCST downward with copolymer chemistry to minimize ΔT; use 1064 nm to reduce absorption by cellular chromophores; apply pulsed low-duty cycles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6467806/?utm_source=openai))
- If polymer mechanics are insufficient to bias contacts at very long genomic distances, retarget to enhancer–promoter pairs within the same TAD and <200 kb separation where contact probability is more responsive. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2151-x?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- A protein-dimerizer–free, CRISPR-addressable, NIR-reversible chromatin loop actuator with quantitative protocols for setting loop probability and transcriptional output.
- Comparative datasets versus blue-light CRY2–CIBN tools that isolate the role of mechanical proximity from protein oligomerization/condensation effects. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Why this matters
By decoupling loop formation from light-induced protein interactions, this approach tests the sufficiency of pure mechanical juxtaposition to modulate neuronal gene expression and provides a remote, orthogonal “remodeler” for the 3D genome that operates in red/NIR regimes compatible with neurons. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neural-circuits/articles/10.3389/fncir.2022.911023/full?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Acousti-Loop: An ultrasound-gated, CRISPR-targeted mechanoswitch that writes self-sustaining enhancer–promoter loops in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes

Background and motivation
- Existing looping tools force proximity via light- or chemically induced dimerization (CLOuD9, LADL/OptoLoop), but require continued actuator occupancy and do not directly test whether chromatin modifications can convert a transient cue into maintained 3D architecture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5511349/?utm_source=openai))
- Titin Ig domains unfold under modest piconewton-to-tens-of-piconewton tension and can expose cryptic interaction sites, establishing a precedent for mechanically gated ligand recruitment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1299741/?utm_source=openai))
- Ultrasound is a single, deep-tissue stimulus modality that can deliver mechanical energy in cells and has been used to control biomolecular functions via mechano- and thermo-sonogenetic actuators. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13271625/?utm_source=openai))
- Positive-feedback, read–write chromatin systems can convert transient recruitment into sustained chromatin states (e.g., PRC2–H3K27me3; BRD4–p300 acetylation feed-forward), offering a route to “write once, read many” loop stabilization without continuous external input. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6672058/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–research question
A CRISPR-targeted, ultrasound-gated titin-Ig mechanoswitch can reversibly expose short peptide motifs that (i) acutely recruit loop-stabilizing adaptors and a writer of acetylation at targeted enhancer–promoter pairs and (ii) seed a local acetylation feed-forward that sustains enhancer–promoter contact after ultrasound withdrawal; a distinct ultrasound regime can expose an eraser-recruiting motif to dissolve loops. Do mechanically seeded, mark-driven loops persist in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, and what ultrasound dose–history defines on/off hysteresis? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2670939/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Convert acoustic energy into an intramolecular conformational gate on a dCas9-fused titin Ig cassette so that ultrasound toggles exposure of cryptic recruitment motifs: “write” (BRD4/p300- and Mediator-biased adaptors) versus “erase” (HDAC-biased adaptors). The mark itself then scaffolds its own maintenance via acetylation-dependent reader recruitment, extending loop lifetime beyond the stimulus window. ([knowledge.uchicago.edu](https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/record/5344/files/Structural-insights-into-p300-regulation-and-acetylation-dependent-genome-organisation.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Engineer and calibrate an ultrasound-gated dCas9–titin-Ig mechanoswitch that exposes loop- and acetylation-writer recruitment motifs upon acoustic actuation.
2) Test whether brief ultrasound pulses at selected enhancer–promoter pairs in cardiomyocytes convert into persistent, acetylation-dependent looping and gene activation; quantify reversibility by ultrasound-gated eraser exposure.
3) Map the dose–history dependence (intensity, pulse duration, duty cycle) that separates transient versus self-sustained loops and define limits of reversibility.

Design and methods
- Constructs
  - dCas9-IgSwitch-Write: Streptococcus pyogenes dCas9 fused N-terminally to a tandem of two mechanically labile titin I-band Ig domains (I27 variants) whose unfolding threshold spans the targeted ultrasound regime. A cryptic BRD4/p300-recruiting peptide (ET-domain-binding motif derived from NSD3 or NUT minimal segment) and a Mediator-biased adaptor peptide are buried within the folded cassette and become solvent-exposed when Ig domains unfold. A C-terminal flexible, low-modulus tether (elastin-like polypeptide, ELP) increases hydrodynamic drag to couple acoustic microstreaming to domain tension. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6937205/?utm_source=openai))
  - dCas9-IgSwitch-Erase: Identical architecture but with a cryptic HDAC3/NCoR-recruiting peptide masked in the folded state and designed to unfold at a slightly higher mechanical threshold (achieved by domain selection/linker orientation).
  - sgRNAs target the enhancer and promoter anchor sites of a selected cardiomyocyte stress-response gene (e.g., NPPA/NPPB or fetal-program enhancers).
- Cell model
  - Human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) cultured on elastic substrates to preserve mechanotransduction fidelity and nuclear–cytoskeletal coupling.
- Ultrasound actuation
  - Focused 1–3 MHz transducer; peak negative pressures 0.3–0.7 MPa; pulse trains 10–50% duty cycle; no cavitation (passive cavitation detection). “Write” regimen selects lower-threshold unfolding; “erase” regimen uses slightly higher peak pressures or longer bursts to unfold the Erase cassette while minimizing thermal rise (<1.5 °C). Parameters are guided by sonomechanogenetics literature. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13271625/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls
  - dCas9 without IgSwitch; IgSwitch with scrambled motifs; non-targeting sgRNA; optical LADL/OptoLoop positive control to benchmark on-target looping amplitude; acoustic sham. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary readouts
  - Acute mechanogating: intramolecular FRET sensor embedded across the Ig domains to report unfolding during ultrasound, calibrated in single cells.
  - Looping: targeted 3C/HiChIP-MED1; Micro-C for local structure; live split-NanoLuc dCas9 loop biosensor at the same anchors for single-cell kinetics. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41335466/?utm_source=openai))
  - Chromatin marks and factors: CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN for H3K27ac, BRD4, p300, MED1 near anchors; time-resolved after ultrasound.
  - Transcription: nascent RNA-seq (PRO-seq) and qRT–PCR for target genes; burst kinetics by MS2 reporters at the promoter.
  - Reversibility: apply “erase” ultrasound regimen; assay loss of H3K27ac/BRD4, loop strength, and transcription return to baseline.
- Locus selection and targeting
  - Start with a well-characterized enhancer–promoter pair in CMs showing inducible looping and acetylation gain under stress; design sgRNAs flanking CTCF sites to avoid blocking cohesin flow; include off-target assessment by ATAC–seq footprinting and ChIP-qPCR at predicted off-targets.
- Safety and biophysics checks
  - Viability, ROS, temperature mapping by fluorescence thermometry; nuclear morphology and DNA damage (γH2AX) after ultrasound; ensure parameters remain within reported sonogenetic safety envelopes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13271625/?utm_source=openai))

Planned experimental flow
- Aim 1
  - Build dCas9-IgSwitch-Write and -Erase; validate nuclear localization and DNA binding.
  - Calibrate acoustic thresholds: correlate ultrasound pulse features with FRET-detected unfolding and on-demand exposure of an epitope tag engineered within the cryptic peptide (assayed by nanobody recruitment).
  - Demonstrate ultrasound-gated recruitment of BRD4/p300 or HDAC3 by proximity labeling (TurboID) targeted to the motifs.
- Aim 2
  - Deliver paired sgRNAs to enhancer and promoter in hiPSC-CMs; apply “write” pulses; quantify changes in looping (3C/HiChIP), H3K27ac/BRD4/p300 occupancy, and transcription over 0–72 h.
  - Test mark dependence: apply JQ1 or p300 inhibitor A-485 post-write to see if maintenance collapses, distinguishing mark-dependent self-sustainment from continued tethering.
  - Define minimal pulse train that yields sustained effects without loss of viability.
- Aim 3
  - Apply “erase” pulses to the same cells; measure loss of acetylation, BRD4 occupancy, loop strength, and transcription; map hysteresis (on/off thresholds, dwell times).
  - Generalize to a second locus; test scalability by multiplexed sgRNAs.

Decision criteria
- Mechanogating: ultrasound produces ≥2-fold FRET change and ≥3× enrichment of motif-binding factors within minutes, reverting within minutes off-ultrasound.
- Looping: ≥1.5–2× increase in enhancer–promoter contact frequency that persists ≥12–48 h post-write without further ultrasound, with concomitant H3K27ac/BRD4 gain at anchors.
- Reversibility: erase regimen reduces contact frequency and H3K27ac/BRD4 to ≤1.2× baseline within 12–24 h, with transcription returning to baseline, reproducible over ≥3 cycles.

Differentiation from dimerizer-based looping
- Intramolecular mechanogate vs. inter-molecular proximity: no light-gated heterodimerization or polymerization; ultrasound toggles a conformational exposure of recruitment motifs on a single CRISPR-bound protein. This removes continued actuator occupancy as the primary maintenance mechanism and directly tests whether a self-templating acetylation circuit can sustain looping. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated outcomes and interpretation
- If transient ultrasound pulses yield durable enhancer–promoter contact, H3K27ac/BRD4 accumulation, and sustained transcription that can be erased by a distinct ultrasound regimen, this supports a mark-driven, self-sustaining loop mechanism with single-modality, reversible control.
- Failure modes and tests:
  - No persistence after write: maintenance likely requires stronger feed-forward; increase BRD4/p300 motif valency or switch to PRC2 read–write module to test repressive memory. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6672058/?utm_source=openai))
  - Irreversibility after repeated writes: indicates runaway positive feedback; mitigate with weaker motifs or shorter pulses; demonstrate erasure by HDAC recruitment or pharmacology (A-485/JQ1) to confirm mark dependence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4899182/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and feasibility checks (12 months)
- Months 0–3: Build and validate constructs; establish ultrasound dosimetry and FRET mechanogating in HEK293 cells.
- Months 4–6: Port to hiPSC-CMs; demonstrate on-demand recruitment and acute looping increases at one locus.
- Months 7–9: Establish write-induced persistence and quantify acetylation dependence; initial erase toggling.
- Months 10–12: Map hysteresis and cycle stability; second locus; benchmarking vs. LADL/OptoLoop.

Key prior art anchoring feasibility
- Programmable chromatin looping via CRISPR dimerizers (CLOuD9; LADL/OptoLoop). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5511349/?utm_source=openai))
- Ultrasound as a molecular control input in cells (sonogenetics/sono-mechanogenetics). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13271625/?utm_source=openai))
- Titin Ig domains as mechanically labile, cryptic-site-bearing cassettes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2670939/?utm_source=openai))
- Positive-feedback chromatin systems enabling mark maintenance (PRC2; BRD4–p300). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5935545/?utm_source=openai))

Significance
This work establishes a single-modality, reversible, non-dimerizer mechanism for on/off control of endogenous enhancer–promoter loops and tests whether biochemical memory can maintain 3D genome architecture in a mechanically relevant human cell type. It directly addresses whether brief mechanical cues can be “written” into chromatin topology and transcriptional state, with potential applications in cardiac stress-memory biology and beyond.

Title
US-LoopReset: Ultrasound-triggered, locus-anchored, reversible “melt-and-rebuild” of chromatin loops to control gene expression and cell identity

Hypothesis/Goal
A transient, locus-anchored, ultrasound-triggered change in the local solvation and electrostatic environment can reversibly disrupt CTCF/cohesin-mediated loop anchors (“melt”), permitting enhancer–promoter re-sampling; upon cessation of stimulus, endogenous loop-extrusion dynamics rebuild steady-state contacts. This reversible reset, implemented without synthetic bridging, will yield different transcriptional memory and differentiation outcomes than systems that forcibly impose loops. We will test this during directed differentiation of human iPSCs into motor neurons. The single external stimulus is focused ultrasound (FUS). Loop control must be reversible, locus-specific, CRISPR-addressable, and mechanistically distinct from light-driven dimerizer tethers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37852951/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit an ultrasound-to-thermophysical transduction: brief, mild FUS hyperthermia (≈39–41.5°C) actuates a thermoresponsive, sequence-tuned, elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) fused to dCas9 at selected CTCF boundary elements. Crossing the ELP’s transition temperature (Tt) induces local, reversible coacervation at the targeted DNA, altering hydration, dielectric, and excluded-volume properties to transiently reduce boundary occupancy and stabilize fewer contacts; cooling dissolves the coacervate and restores native rebinding and loop re-formation. This is an energy-to-solvation/electrostatics gate at a single locus—no enforced inter-locus tethering.

Specific Aims
1) Engineer and validate dCas9-ELP “thermo-gates” that coacervate only under mild FUS hyperthermia and only when concentrated at a targeted locus.
2) Demonstrate reversible dissolution and re-formation of specific chromatin loops at CTCF/cohesin boundaries in hiPSCs; quantify effects on transcriptional bursting and enhancer–promoter contact selection.
3) Test whether pulsed, locus-specific reset improves fidelity and efficiency of motor neuron differentiation versus forced-loop controls, and map transcriptional/epigenetic memory after reset cycles.

Rationale and novelty
- Ultrasound provides noninvasive, deep, temporally precise deposition of mild heat; image-guided FUS platforms reproducibly create 39–43°C windows with sub-2°C control, within accepted safety envelopes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41356202/?utm_source=openai))
- ELPs exhibit sharp, reversible LCST transitions with <3°C shifts, tunable by sequence, length, and fusion partner; intracellular coacervation and resolubilization are rapid and programmable. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8375696/?utm_source=openai))
- Prior locus-targeted condensation used light-driven oligomerization (CasDrop, LAMPS) or opto-looping (CRY2/CIB), which impose oligomeric scaffolds or forced bridges; our design transiently perturbs local physicochemistry at native anchors without dimerizers, then relinquishes control to endogenous extrusion. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6724728/?utm_source=openai))

Design and Methods

Constructs and targeting
- Thermo-gate: dCas9-NLS fused C-terminally to an ELP variant with Tt = 39.5–40.5°C at nuclear ionic strength; include minimal acidic patches within the ELP flanks to bias client composition toward repelling basic, compaction-prone factors when condensed. A non-coacervating control (scrambled, hydrophilic ELP) and a high-Tt control (Tt ≈ 45°C) are included. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23565607/?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPR addressing: multiplexed sgRNAs tile a 3–5 kb window around selected, convergently oriented CTCF motifs at lineage-relevant loci (e.g., boundaries flanking HOXA subclusters active in neurogenesis). sgRNAs are arrayed to raise local valency so coacervation nucleates only where dCas9-ELP density is high, avoiding global phase transition. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkab1242?utm_source=openai))

Ultrasound actuation
- In-plate FUS (1–3 MHz) with real-time thermometry; pulses (30–180 s) to reach 39.5–41.5°C (≤2°C over baseline), then passive cool to 37°C. Dose mapping adheres to ITRUSST thermal safety criteria. Include water-bath hyperthermia matched to the same thermal dose as a control for non-acoustic confounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12632700/?utm_source=openai))

Cell model and timing
- Human iPSCs with stable dCas9-ELP and sgRNA expression. Apply FUS pulses during early fate-commitment windows (days 1–3 of motor neuron differentiation) to reset local 3D search before enhancer selection stabilizes. Ultrasound-driven gene control in iPSCs via mild hyperthermia has been demonstrated, supporting cell-type feasibility. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40836509/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts
- Loop architecture: Micro-C/Hi-C and CTCF/SMC1 HiChIP before FUS, immediately post-FUS (melt), and at 1–6 h recovery (rebuild) to quantify boundary insulation scores, loop strength, and re-formation kinetics.
- Factor dynamics: CTCF and RAD21 CUT&Tag occupancy and residence-time proxies; FRAP on fluorescent CTCF knock-in lines to assess on-/off-rates during melt vs rebuild.
- Transcription: nascent RNA-seq/PRO-seq to capture burst frequency/amplitude changes at target genes; single-cell RNA-seq across differentiation to assess lineage commitment, heterogeneity, and hysteresis.
- Local condensation: fluorescence recovery and single-cell Tt mapping of dCas9-ELP; condensate formation only at targeted foci confirms locus anchoring. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8375696/?utm_source=openai))

Benchmarks and controls
- Forced-loop positive control: CLOuD9 or OptoLoop at the same loci to compare imposed bridging vs reset mode; quantify differential outcomes in loop topology, expression memory, and differentiation metrics. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))
- Heat-only controls: mock cells lacking dCas9-ELP exposed to the same FUS profile; HSP reporter quantifies global heat-shock engagement to ensure effects require the thermo-gate and not generic stress. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2633569/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity: off-target sgRNA sets; high-Tt ELP nonresponsive control; titration of sgRNA valency to demonstrate thresholding of nucleation.

Success criteria
- Aim 1: FUS induces rapid, reversible dCas9-ELP condensation at targeted foci with no global nuclear phase change; high-Tt/scrambled controls show no foci.
- Aim 2: Significant, reversible reduction of selected CTCF/cohesin loops immediately after FUS, with recovery to baseline upon cooling (half-time quantified); corresponding, transient changes in burst kinetics without permanent loop rewiring.
- Aim 3: During iPSC→motor neuron differentiation, reset mode yields improved acquisition of lineage-appropriate enhancer–promoter contacts and reduced off-lineage transcriptional memory relative to forced-loop controls and no-stimulus conditions.

Potential risks and mitigations
- Global heat-shock confounds: keep ΔT ≤2°C, duty-cycles short; verify minimal HSP induction and match with water-bath controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12632700/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target condensation: enforce locus nucleation via sgRNA tiling; confirm absence of untargeted nuclear droplets.
- Insufficient boundary perturbation: increase local valency or add short acidic patches to enhance compaction-factor exclusion; iterate ELP length/composition to sharpen Tt and condensate density. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10540133/?utm_source=openai))
- Reversibility: predefine cooling intervals; show full restoration of insulation and loop strength in high-Tt and no-ELP controls to set bounds.

Mechanistic differentiation from opto-dimerizer systems
This design does not recruit or bridge distal loci. It actuates a single-chain, CRISPR-anchored, thermophysical gate that transiently alters local solvation/electrostatics to relax native loop-anchoring, then relinquishes control for endogenous cohesin/CTCF dynamics to re-establish architecture. In contrast, CRY2/CIB or similar systems create synthetic oligomers/bridges to impose contacts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12952762/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and timeline (12–18 months)
- Months 0–3: ELP library with Tt tuning; single-cell Tt quantification; stable hiPSC lines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8375696/?utm_source=openai))
- Months 3–6: FUS platform calibration; Aim 1 completion (locus-anchored condensation on/off).
- Months 6–12: Aim 2 completion (loop melt/rebuild kinetics, factor occupancy and transcriptional bursting).
- Months 12–18: Aim 3 differentiation experiments; benchmark against CLOuD9/OptoLoop controls and compile scRNA-seq/Hi-C integration. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15993?utm_source=openai))

Impact
If successful, US-LoopReset establishes a mechanistically orthogonal, reversible, single-stimulus modality for locus-specific 3D genome control, enabling causal tests of whether transiently relaxing, rather than forcing, chromatin geometry improves fate specification and reduces aberrant memory during differentiation.
