Title
Optical, locus-anchored inhibition of the CTCF–cohesin interface to reversibly unlock native chromatin loops and switch hepatocyte metabolic genes

One-sentence hypothesis/question
Can reversible, locus-specific optical inhibition of the native CTCF–cohesin interface de-insulate pre-formed chromatin loops and thereby provide on/off control of endogenous hepatocyte gene expression without creating artificial bridges?

Atomic strategy
Localize a photoisomerizable inhibitory peptide to chosen CTCF loop anchors via dCas9-Halo. Light toggles the peptide’s affinity for the SA2–SCC1 cohesin subcomplex, acutely gating cohesin stalling at that anchor. When affinity is high, cohesin fails to stabilize at the site and the loop dissolves (gene on); when affinity is low, cohesin re-stalls and the loop reforms (gene off). This intervenes at a mechanistically defined native interface, distinct from dimerizer-based looping that forges synthetic contacts. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1910-z?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer a red-shifted azobenzene-stapled peptide that optically gates binding to SA2–SCC1.
- Design: Start from the solved human SA2–SCC1:CTCF interface and the required CTCF N-terminal SA-recognition motif (YxF-like), and build competitive, SA2–SCC1-binding peptides. Introduce tetra-ortho-halogenated azobenzene or arylazopyrazole staples to yield two optical states with >10-fold affinity contrast and visible-light addressability. Benchmark variants for wavelength, photostationary ratios, and thermal stability to permit repeated toggling with green/red light. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1910-z?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro characterization: Measure KD(cis) and KD(trans) for SA2–SCC1 by SPR/ITC; validate selectivity against SA1; assess off-target binding using protein microarrays. Confirm fast photoisomerization and fatigue resistance over ≥100 cycles. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29867216/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Build a CRISPR-tethered delivery to CTCF loop anchors and validate optical de-insulation.
- Locus targeting: Express dCas9-Halo in human primary hepatocytes or iPSC-derived hepatocyte-like cells. Use paired sgRNAs to position dCas9-Halo within ±30 bp of outward-oriented CTCF motifs at both anchors flanking pre-specified insulated neighborhoods that contain nutrient/hormone-responsive metabolic genes (candidate selection from hepatocyte CTCF ChIP-seq and Micro-C). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5986275/?utm_source=openai))
- Chemical localization: Conjugate the photoswitchable peptide to a chloroalkane HaloTag ligand via a PEG linker optimized for reach and minimal steric hindrance. Load cells with the conjugate to covalently decorate dCas9-Halo at the chosen anchors, following precedents for chemically decorating dCas9-Halo with small molecules at genomic loci. Validate anchor occupancy by ChIP–qPCR (anti-Halo) and CUT&RUN. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67074-z?utm_source=openai))
- Optical control/readouts: Illuminate with the activating wavelength to increase peptide affinity for SA2–SCC1 and measure (i) reduced cohesin stalling at the addressed anchors by ChIP-seq of RAD21/SA2 and acute CUT&RUN time courses; (ii) weakened loop strength by Micro-C/Capture-C; (iii) increased enhancer–promoter contact probability by 3D DNA FISH; and (iv) nascent transcription by smFISH/PRO-seq. Switch to the deactivating wavelength and quantify re-stalling/reformation kinetics. Expected timescales: minutes for loop relaxation/reformation, consistent with dynamic loop residence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate functional gene control and reversibility at metabolic loci in hepatocytes.
- Locus choices and assays: Prioritize insulated neighborhoods where insulation limits enhancer access to key metabolic genes (e.g., gluconeogenic or lipid-metabolic control points). Evaluate mRNA bursts (MS2 reporters where feasible), protein levels, and metabolic flux assays (e.g., glucose output). Cycle light ON/OFF repeatedly to establish multi-round reversibility and quantify hysteresis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5125522/?utm_source=openai))
- Causality controls: Use (a) non-targeting sgRNAs, (b) anchors targeted with an inactive peptide isomer locked by light-insensitive staple, (c) peptides mutated at the SA2-contact residues, and (d) comparison to LADL/OptoLoop at the same loci to demonstrate that native-lock removal (not synthetic bridging) drives activation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 4. Define specificity, safety, and generality.
- Specificity: Map genome-wide cohesin (RAD21/SA2) and CTCF occupancy pre/post light to ensure locus-biased effects; quantify off-target chromatin changes by Micro-C at non-targeted boundaries. Titrate tethered-peptide density by limiting Halo ligand dose. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9442299/?utm_source=openai))
- Phototoxicity/photochemistry: Use red-shifted azobenzenes to minimize blue-light exposure; record cell viability and stress responses; confirm intracellular photostationary states with live-cell spectroscopy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10763561/?utm_source=openai))
- Generality: Retarget anchors at additional hepatocyte neighborhoods and at non-hepatic boundaries to test portability across boundary widths and CTCF site clustering architectures. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40063813/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental plan and metrics

1) Molecule build and validation
- Synthesize 6–8 peptide variants; choose two with KD(cis)/KD(trans) ≥10 and visible-light actuation. Record action spectra and thermal half-lives at 37°C. Downselect for minimal aggregation and serum stability. Success metric: optical affinity ratio ≥10; photofatigue <10% over 100 cycles. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30675988/?utm_source=openai))

2) Cellular localization and anchor occupancy
- Generate hepatocyte lines stably expressing dCas9-Halo. Transfect paired sgRNAs to anchors; treat with Halo–peptide; verify co-occupancy by anti-Halo CUT&RUN at both anchors; exclude enrichment at bystander CTCF sites. Success metric: >5-fold enrichment at targeted anchors vs flanking 10 kb windows. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/gpb/article/17/2/119/7231186?utm_source=openai))

3) Loop de-insulation dynamics
- Time-resolved CUT&RUN/ChIP after 1–30 min light to quantify SA2/RAD21 loss at anchors; Capture-C/Micro-C at 15–60 min for loop weakening; DNA FISH for distance increases. Reverse with deactivating light; fit on/off kinetics with single-exponential models; compute half-times. Success metric: ≥30% decrease in loop corner-peak strength upon activation, reversal ≥80% on deactivation; RAD21/SA2 anchor signal follows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))

4) Gene activation and functional output
- Quantify nascent RNA bursts and steady-state mRNA; correlate with enhancer–promoter contact changes. For gluconeogenic targets, measure glucose output under hormone-clamped conditions. Reversibility over ≥5 light cycles. Success metric: ≥2-fold transcriptional activation tightly time-locked to optical switching; return to baseline upon re-formation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5125522/?utm_source=openai))

5) Distinguishing from optogenetic dimerizers
- Deploy LADL/OptoLoop at the same loci to force bridging; compare contact maps, enhancer-promoter specificity, and transcriptional outcomes. Expect our method to increase native enhancer contacts without introducing ectopic loops between non-native pairs. Success metric: Our approach shows contact gain limited to endogenous partners and lower ectopic contact burden than dimerizer tools. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Risk analysis and alternatives
- Binding site degeneracy: If SA2–SCC1 surface plasticity limits inhibitor potency, pivot to a RAD21–STAG interface-mimicking peptide guided by available RAD21–STAG1/2 structural data. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7266993/?utm_source=openai))
- Anchor microenvironment: If steric occlusion near certain CTCF sites reduces access, retarget sgRNAs to adjacent CBSs within clustered boundaries while maintaining motif orientation. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40063813/?utm_source=openai))
- Phototoxicity: If visible-light dose remains limiting, select more red-shifted azo staples or reduce duty cycle using higher extinction-coefficient switches. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10763561/?utm_source=openai))

Key differentiators vs. existing methods
- Mechanistic perturbation of a native stop signal for cohesin at CTCF via a light-gated competitive inhibitor; no synthetic bridging or forced oligomerization. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1910-z?utm_source=openai))
- Locus anchoring of a small-molecule/peptidic effector via dCas9-Halo, building on established chemical recruitment to DNA-bound HaloTag fusions. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-67074-z?utm_source=openai))
- Single-modality, reversible control with minute-scale dynamics aligned to cohesin loop residence, enabling repeated on/off transcription cycles. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: Achieve ≥10-fold optical affinity switching for SA2–SCC1 (go). ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1910-z?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Demonstrate light-tunable RAD21/SA2 occupancy changes at targeted anchors with reversal (go/no-go ≥25% change). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))
- M3: Show corresponding Micro-C/Capture-C loop weakening/strengthening and matched changes in enhancer–promoter contact probability (go/no-go ≥25% effect with reversibility). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6338517/?utm_source=openai))
- M4: Establish on/off regulation of at least one hepatocyte metabolic gene with functional metabolic output changes and return to baseline after deactivation (go). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5986275/?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
A simple, atomic intervention—optically gating cohesin stalling at chosen CTCF anchors—should be sufficient to toggle pre-existing loops and native gene programs in hepatocytes. This delivers reversible, locus-specific, single-modality control of gene expression by removing and restoring native architectural “locks,” offering a mechanistically orthogonal alternative to dimerizer-based loop building and a template to probe loop-function causality across cell types. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1910-z?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Reversible, CRISPR-tethered intranuclear magnetomechanics to break and re-form specific chromatin loops and time transcriptional ON/OFF kinetics in developing human neural progenitors.

Central hypothesis (inseparable from the research question)
A brief, reversible mechanical increase in enhancer–promoter separation beyond the permissive interaction radius, produced by magnetic torque on CRISPR-tethered intranuclear nanorods at loop anchors, acutely shuts down transcription faster than cohesin/CTCF-mediated loop formation can turn it back on; thus, loop destruction, not loop creation, is the rate-limiting step controlling gene-state transitions during neural lineage commitment. Cohesin-driven loop extrusion and CTCF boundary halting define looped neighborhoods that gate enhancer–promoter contact probability and bursting; modest displacements on the 100–300 nm scale should be sufficient to escape the permissive radius and depress k_on without altering sequence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single external magnetic field to apply torque to iron-oxide nanorods tethered by dCas9 to CTCF-flanked anchors of a defined enhancer–promoter loop; the torque elastically displaces the locus just enough to reduce contact probability below the range that sustains bursting, then passively releases when the field stops so extrusion and CTCF rebinding re-establish the loop. This is a dimerization-free, mechanical separation switch at a single, CRISPR-addressed locus. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3192970/?utm_source=openai))

Why this is mechanistically novel versus opto-dimerizer looping
Existing systems (e.g., LADL, OptoLoop) increase proximity by inducible dimerization/oligomerization to build loops. Here, we never bridge loci; we instead deliver calibrated, reversible, locus-bound mechanical work to break the loop and let native extrusion rebuild it, enabling a fair timing comparison of break versus build. Single stimulus = magnetic field; no light, no exogenous dimerizer chemistry. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Target cell type and locus
- Human iPSC-derived cortical neural progenitors (hNPCs), where SOX2 is controlled by a developmentally regulated, CTCF-associated distal enhancer loop. This provides a clean, endogenous setting to test whether acute loop breakage immediately suppresses SOX2 bursting and whether recovery lags after release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822576/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build a CRISPR-tethered intranuclear magnetomechanical actuator at the SOX2 loop.
- Express dCas9-HaloTag-NLS and guide RNAs targeting convergent CTCF motifs flanking the SOX2 enhancer–promoter loop (two to four sgRNAs per anchor for occupancy).
- Introduce nucleus-penetrant iron-oxide nanorods (∼100–200 nm) bearing HaloTag ligands via microinjection or optimized transfection; validate single-rod binding at target foci by live-cell imaging. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3192970/?utm_source=openai))

2) Quantify real-time mechanical de-looping, transcriptional shutoff, and recovery.
- Apply rotating/oscillating magnetic fields (10–50 mT; 0.5–10 Hz) to impose torque τ = m×B on tethered rods, tracked in 3D to estimate local chromatin displacement.
- Measure enhancer–promoter separation with dual-color CRISPR locus tags and transcriptional bursting with a SOX2 MS2 reporter or intronic smFISH; extract τ_off (time-to-bursting-suppression after field ON) and τ_on (time-to-bursting-recovery after field OFF). Predict τ_off < τ_on if loop destruction is kinetically dominant. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.0c00959?utm_source=openai))

3) Map the mechanical threshold for loop breakage and its dependence on anchor context.
- Sweep field amplitude/frequency to derive the minimal displacement/torque causing sustained reduction in bursting and increased E–P distances beyond the permissive radius.
- Compare targeting to CTCF anchors versus nearby non-CTCF control sequences to test whether extrusion-stalled loops are preferentially breakable at low forces (<1 pN scale), consistent with cohesin stall forces. Include controls: nonmagnetic particles, scrambled sgRNAs, and constant-field sham. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8890386/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and methods
- Cell model and locus validation
  - Differentiate hESCs to hNPCs (established protocols). Confirm SOX2 enhancer activation and loop presence by H3K27ac ChIP–seq and Micro-C/HiChIP; confirm CTCF occupancy/orientation at anchors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12822576/?utm_source=openai))
- Actuator construction
  - Synthesize superparamagnetic iron-oxide nanorods with elastomeric polymer grafts to provide a compliant, reversible mechanical coupling. Functionalize with chloroalkane HaloTag ligands for covalent capture by dCas9-HaloTag at targeted DNA.
  - Deliver rods and dCas9-HaloTag; quantify intranuclear localization and single-particle binding kinetics (FRAP/SMT).
- Magnetic stimulation and calibration
  - Use a coil system to generate homogeneous rotating fields; calibrate rod magnetization and torque ex vivo; validate in-cell rotational dynamics by high-speed imaging.
  - Convert rod angle/displacement to estimated chromatin segment displacement using a viscoelastic nucleus model, ensuring displacements are within 100–400 nm to test permissive-radius escape without bond rupture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3192970/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts
  - 3D distances: label the enhancer and promoter with orthogonal dCas9 fluorescent tags; track E–P distance trajectories during field pulses.
  - Transcription: SOX2-MS2 knock-in or intronic smFISH to quantify burst frequency/size; align with E–P distance time series to determine causal ordering of de-looping and transcriptional suppression. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04570-y?utm_source=openai))
- Controls and safety
  - Off-target nuclear stress: γH2AX, nuclear envelope integrity; viability assays.
  - Reversibility: repeated ON/OFF cycles (minutes) to demonstrate restoration of loop contact frequency and bursting after each release.
  - Distinguish magnetic field effects from generic ultrasound/light effects (not used).

Key predictions and success criteria
- A single, brief magnetic pulse increases E–P distance beyond the permissive radius and reduces bursting frequency within tens of seconds; turning the field OFF restores contact probability and bursting on a slower timescale governed by extrusion/CTCF rebinding. Success = τ_off < τ_on with ≥2-fold reciprocal changes in burst frequency across at least five ON/OFF cycles without DNA damage accumulation. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))
- Force/displacement thresholds are lower at CTCF loop anchors than at non-CTCF controls, consistent with cohesin’s low stall forces; a steep sigmoidal relationship between displacement and bursting suppression reveals the effective interaction radius in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8890386/?utm_source=openai))

Differentiation and benchmarking against builder systems
- Side-by-side comparison with a light-driven builder (LADL or OptoLoop) targeted to the same loci will show that dimerizer systems modulate transcription by enforced proximity (build), whereas this actuator gates by mechanical separation (break). Temporal resolution will reveal asymmetric kinetics inaccessible to builder-only tools. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and alternatives
- If rod coupling is too stiff (risking bond rupture), increase linker compliance or reduce duty cycle to favor elastic displacement over detachment.
- If SOX2 shows enhancer redundancy, pivot to another validated neural loop (e.g., FOXG1/POU3F3 loops in neural development) or to cardiomyocyte MYH6/MYH7 loops where enhancer–promoter contacts have been mapped. Ultrasound-based, dCas9-tethered gas vesicles remain a mechanical, single-stimulus fallback if magnetic actuation fails to achieve sufficient displacement. ([med.upenn.edu](https://www.med.upenn.edu/minglab/assets/user-content/documents/MolCell_Jun2020.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Outcomes and impact
This dimerization-free, single-stimulus, CRISPR-addressable mechanical switch directly times gene shutdown upon loop breakage versus reactivation upon loop re-formation in a developmentally relevant human lineage. It will provide quantitative thresholds (displacement, torque, time) linking cohesin/CTCF loop mechanics to transcriptional bursting kinetics and settle whether destroying loops is the true bottleneck for switching gene states during neural development. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-022-00530-4?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Ultrasound-tunable endogenous loop barriers via dCas9-anchored piezoelectric nanotransducers

Central question and hypothesis
Can transient, locus-confined electromechanical perturbations produced by ultrasound-activated piezoelectric nanotransducers, positioned at selected CTCF sites with dCas9, reversibly shift CTCF occupancy and thereby toggle cohesin-defined chromatin loops and gene expression without creating artificial protein tethers? Cohesin extrudes chromatin until it encounters occupied, directionally oriented CTCF barriers; barrier occupancy and DNA tension govern loop frequency and stability on minute time scales. If ultrasound locally increases the effective dissociation rate (koff) or decreases the association rate (kon) of CTCF at a chosen site, the probability of barrier occupancy will drop only during stimulation, permitting loop bypass; upon cessation, occupancy and loop architecture will relax back. This should provide reversible, on/off control of endogenous enhancer–promoter contacts. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05961-5?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Install a piezoelectric-polymer nanotransducer at a single, CRISPR-addressed CTCF motif to modulate the local free-energy landscape of the CTCF–DNA interface with ultrasound, shifting roadblock occupancy without engineered dimerization or synthetic bridges. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.1c03087?utm_source=openai))

Innovation relative to prior art
Current chromatin loop engineering relies on chemically induced proximity or optogenetic dimerizers (e.g., dCas9–CIBN/CRY2) that create non-native tethers. Here, loop control arises from modulating native barrier occupancy using a single physical stimulus (ultrasound) and electromechanical transduction at the DNA–protein interface. No heterodimerization modules are used; specificity is genomic (dCas9), not proteomic. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Target cell model
Human K562 erythroleukemia cells. Rationale: (i) robust division permits nuclear access of nanoparticles during mitosis; (ii) well-characterized, CTCF-delimited enhancer–promoter loops at the β-globin locus enable quantitative loop and expression readouts; (iii) prior CRISPR-based loop engineering in this system provides benchmarks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6235177/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build and validate a dCas9-anchored, ultrasound-responsive piezoelectric nanotransducer at defined CTCF sites.
- Construct: Streptococcus pyogenes dCas9-HaloTag-3×NLS expressed from a single lentivector; guide RNAs target one boundary CTCF motif flanking the β-globin LCR–HBB domain (convergent orientation maintained). Conjugate poled P(VDF–TrFE) nanoparticles (30–80 nm) with a chloroalkane ligand for covalent HaloTag capture and with a short, flexible PEG linker to minimize steric hindrance. Deliver nanoparticles and select clones with robust nuclear accumulation after mitosis. Controls: non-piezoelectric fluoropolymer NPs, off-target gRNA, mutated CTCF motif. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsnano.1c03087?utm_source=openai))
- Physical characterization in cells: quantify piezoelectric response under 1–3 MHz, I_SPPA 0.2–0.6 W cm⁻² focused ultrasound using voltage-sensitive dyes and finite-element modeling of local fields/strains; verify negligible bulk heating. Benchmark against literature values for US-stimulated piezoelectrics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13231556/?utm_source=openai))
- Biochemical validation: CUT&RUN or ChIP–qPCR for CTCF at the targeted motif with and without ultrasound (pulse trains; see Timing below). Expect a reversible decrease in CTCF occupancy during sonication only. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/25776?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible modulation of loop architecture and transcription using ultrasound pulse trains.
- Loop-level readouts: targeted Micro-C or HiChIP (CTCF or cohesin) in four conditions: baseline, ultrasound ON, 5–10 min post-ON, ultrasound OFF (≥30 min). Expect reduced contact frequency across the targeted boundary during ON, with recovery OFF. Complement with CRISPR live-cell imaging of the LCR and HBB anchors to measure inter-locus distances on single cells during stimulation cycles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7566886/?utm_source=openai))
- Transcriptional readouts: RT-qPCR and nascent RNA (4sU-seq) for HBB and flanking genes whose enhancer access depends on the targeted boundary. Expect increases consistent with transient boundary permeability during ON and relaxation OFF. Include non-target loop controls.

Aim 3. Map the stimulus–response transfer function and establish causality at the protein–DNA interface.
- Ultrasound parameter sweep (frequency, duty cycle, burst length, I_SPPA) to build occupancy and loop dose–response curves; identify thresholds and reversibility windows.
- Single-molecule CTCF dynamics: Halo-CTCF tracking in edited cells to quantify residence times (τbound) at/near the targeted site with and without ultrasound. Expect τbound decreases consistent with a reversible increase in koff during stimulation; global CTCF dynamics should remain unchanged. ([elifesciences.org](https://elifesciences.org/articles/25776?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic controls: (i) invert CTCF motif orientation at the targeted site to test direction-dependent loop effects; (ii) target a non-CTCF TF motif to test specificity; (iii) deliver non-piezoelectric NPs to exclude purely acoustic effects.

Mechanistic rationale
- CTCF acts as a direction- and DNA-tension-dependent barrier to cohesin; occupancy and local forces determine extrusion halting. Ultrasound-driven deformation of poled P(VDF–TrFE) nanoparticles at the dCas9-tethered locus produces nanoscale strains and local electric fields that perturb electrostatics and hydration at the protein–DNA interface, raising the effective free energy of the bound state; while the field/strain persists, the equilibrium shifts toward dissociation. Removing ultrasound returns the interface to its native energetics, restoring occupancy. The minute-scale native binding dynamics of CTCF ensure that loop organization can equilibrate between ON and OFF states within experimental windows. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05961-5?utm_source=openai))

Ultrasound actuation protocol
- Transducer: 1–3 MHz focused single-element or phased array; I_SPPA 0.2–0.6 W cm⁻²; 10% duty cycle; 1 s bursts every 10 s for 5–10 min to enter steady state; repeatable across cycles with ≥30 min OFF intervals to re-establish baseline. Parameters drawn from piezoelectric neuromodulation benchmarks while avoiding thermal confounds. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13231556/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- Ultrasound-dependent, reversible decrease in CTCF occupancy at the targeted motif; no effect at control motifs or with non-piezo NPs.
- Concordant, reversible reduction of boundary contacts by Micro-C/HiChIP and increased enhancer–promoter proximity during ON; return to baseline OFF.
- Predictable, reversible changes in gene expression aligned with loop toggling, with no global stress response activation.

Differentiation from dimerizer-based loop engineering
- No heterodimerization or synthetic bridging; a single stimulus (ultrasound) modulates a native barrier at one site, leveraging endogenous cohesin dynamics. Prior systems such as LADL and OptoLoop rely on light-gated CRY2–CIBN interactions to force contacts between two loci. Our intervention leaves chromatin untethered and instead transiently alters barrier permeability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Risk mitigation and alternatives
- Nuclear access of nanoparticles: use dividing K562 cells so nanoparticles present in the cytoplasm enter the nucleus during open mitosis; confirm nuclear localization post-cytokinesis. If delivery limits sensitivity, microinjection of NPs into nuclei of synchronized cells is a fallback.
- If electromechanical transduction proves insufficient to shift CTCF kinetics, an orthogonal actuator will be evaluated in parallel: a dCas9-tethered, genetically encoded gas vesicle as an ultrasound-driven mechanical “pull-off” element to transiently exceed the unbinding force of a DNA-bound roadblock. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-021-00971-8?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and readouts
- Month 3–6: NP synthesis/poling, dCas9 targeting, nuclear delivery, in-cell piezoelectric characterization.
- Month 6–9: CTCF occupancy toggling with ultrasound; parameter mapping.
- Month 9–12: Loop architecture assays (Micro-C/HiChIP) and live distance imaging across ON/OFF cycles; transcriptional validation.
- Month 12–15: Specificity, reversibility, off-target and stress-response profiling; finalize transfer function.

Impact
This work establishes a reversible, dimerizer-free, single-stimulus method to tune native loop barriers at single loci, enabling causal tests of enhancer–promoter control and offering a therapeutic design space distinct from heat- or calcium-based sonogenetic control and from optogenetic loop tethers. It directly leverages the physics of ultrasound–piezoelectric coupling and the biology of cohesin–CTCF loop extrusion to modulate genome topology with temporal precision. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11349879/?utm_source=openai))

label: baseline
text:
Title
Light-gated surface-property toggling to nucleate locus-specific transcriptional condensates and reversible chromatin looping

Central hypothesis/question
At a defined genomic locus, does a single intramolecular light switch that exposes multivalent “sticker” motifs on a CRISPR-tethered scaffold suffice to (i) cross the local phase-separation threshold, (ii) assemble a transient coactivator-rich condensate that increases enhancer–promoter contact frequency, and (iii) dissolve upon light withdrawal to reverse looping and gene activation—without using binary optogenetic dimerizers or oligomerization domains? Prior optogenetic systems formed loops by forced heterodimerization (e.g., dCas9–CIBN/CRY2) or induced condensation via multicomponent clustering (CasDrop, LAMPS); here the control variable is the locus’s local chemical potential governed by sticker exposure, not enforced tethering or global oligomerization. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Rewire the locus into a nucleation seed whose phase behavior is switched by an intramolecular light cue: embed arrays of short, tyrosine/arginine-rich sticker motifs within the AsLOV2 Jα helix so they are sterically/entropically masked in the dark and exposed only under blue light. This toggles net interaction strength and solvent quality for the scaffold, shifting the local saturation concentration (csat) only at the targeted DNA site. When lit, csat is transiently undercut; an LLPS droplet forms, recruiting endogenous Mediator/BRD4/Pol II and “wetting” nearby chromatin, thereby capturing the cognate enhancer and increasing loop frequency. When dark, Jα refolds, stickers are recaged, the condensate dissolves, and looping relaxes. The key intervention is stimulus-gated surface energetics at a single DNA-anchored scaffold—no binary dimerizers, no enforced oligomerization. Evidence base: transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers recruit Mediator/BRD4 and can be controlled optically via sticker valency; LOV2 enables reversible peptide caging. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))

Innovation and differentiation
- From loop-by-tethering (LADL): replaces CRY2–CIBN bridging with a locus-confined phase threshold switch; loops emerge as a consequence of condensate wetting, not forced juxtaposition. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))
- From oligomerization-gated condensates (CasDrop, LAMPS): uses an intramolecular surface-property toggle to set interaction strength, eliminating global oligomerization cores and reducing off-locus nucleation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6724728/?utm_source=openai))
- Conceptual primitive: tune csat at one chromatin address using a single light input; the cell supplies the effectors.

Target cell type and locus
Human erythroid progenitors (HUDEP-2) targeting the β-globin LCR–HBB module. Rationale: a classic, well-mapped enhancer–promoter pair whose activation depends on coactivator concentration and looping; strong assays exist (HiChIP/3C, nascent RNA, chromatin accessibility). This context directly tests whether condensate-mediated wetting outperforms forced tethers for productive transcription.

System design
- DNA anchor: dCas9 (nuclear) with gRNA tiles to the HBB promoter (P) and the LCR core enhancer (E) (two channels allow testing P-only, E-only, and P+E seeding).
- Phase-switchable seed: dCas9 fused to an AsLOV2-masked multivalent sticker array (LOV2[dark]-mask | [sticker]n), where each sticker is a 10–20 aa tyrosine/arginine-rich low-complexity segment engineered for π–π/cation–π “sticker” behavior. In the dark, Jα cages stickers; under blue light, Jα undocks to expose them and increase intermolecular attraction. LOV2 peptide-caging is established; sticker-driven LLPS and its sensitivity to aromatic/charged content are well-supported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3334866/?utm_source=openai))
- Endogenous recruitment interface: stickers are kept minimal to bias recruitment toward endogenous coactivators (Mediator/BRD4/Pol II) rather than direct effector fusion, preserving the test of the condensate mechanism. Coactivator enrichment within transcriptional condensates is well documented. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- Single stimulus: blue light; no binary partners or oligomerization domains.

Specific aims and methods
Aim 1. Calibrate the light-gated phase boundary and reversibility at safe expression.
- Build a tunable sticker library (vary n, Tyr/Arg content, charge patterning) inside LOV2 caging geometry; include dark-locked and lit-locked LOV2 mutants for bounds. Validate caging by in vitro peptide exposure assays and in-cell FRET reporters.
- Express in HEK293T to map LLPS onset vs. light dose; quantify condensate formation kinetics, FRAP, and dissolution upon dark recovery. Use MED1/BRD4/Pol II immunostaining to verify endogenous cofactor enrichment. OptoIDR and super-enhancer condensate work guide assay design; success is light-on droplet nucleation and dark-off dissolution at sub-oligomerizing expression. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28041848/?utm_source=openai))
Controls: sticker-scrambled variants; AsLOV2 without stickers; constitutively exposed stickers (no LOV2). Additional orthogonal control: light-driven recruitment of a solubility tag to demonstrate predicted dissolution, validating interaction-energetic control. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50858-0?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible enhancer–promoter looping and transcriptional control at HBB.
- Deliver dCas9–LOV2–[sticker]n and gRNA tiles to HUDEP-2; apply pulsed blue light (≤0.5 mW/cm², duty-cycled) to minimize phototoxicity.
- Quantify: (i) E–P proximity by targeted HiChIP/3C before, during, and after light; (ii) nascent HBB transcription (EU-seq/PRO-seq) and steady-state RNA; (iii) cofactor occupancy (CUT&RUN for BRD4/MED1). Expect light-on increases in cofactor density and E–P contact frequency with concordant HBB upregulation; dark-off reversal.
Benchmarking: head-to-head with LADL loop-by-tethering and with a CRY2–IDR optoDroplet targeted to the same sites, both known modalities, to test whether condensate wetting yields higher transcriptional gain per unit proximity. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Off-target, scalability, and kinetics.
- Genome-wide: ATAC-seq and Hi-C to assess chromatin accessibility and distal contact changes; RNA-seq for off-target transcription.
- Kinetics/thresholds: measure on/off half-times across light doses and sticker strengths; fit a nucleation/dissolution model to derive csat and ΔGsticker estimates.
- Portability: retarget to a second system with a defined super-enhancer (e.g., MYC in K562) to test generality.

Expected outcomes and interpretation
- Outcome consistent with hypothesis: light induces local condensate assembly at P and/or E with rapid coactivator enrichment, increased E–P contact probability, and HBB activation; dark reverses all three with minimal genome-wide perturbation. This aligns with evidence that transcriptional condensates form via weak multivalency and can be optically modulated; it extends prior dCas9-based LLPS tools by making the switch intramolecular and locus-confined. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- If droplets form but transcription does not increase: suggests insufficient biochemical specificity; iterate sticker composition or add short noncovalent reader motifs (e.g., bromodomain-binding acidic patches) while avoiding direct effector fusions.
- If leakage occurs in the dark: strengthen caging (cpLOV2 geometry; deeper Jα embedding) or reduce sticker valency until condensates require light. LOV2 caging principles support these mitigations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3334866/?utm_source=openai))
- If droplets nucleate off-locus: limit expression, add nuclear export in dark (LEXY motif) so nuclear concentration only rises when lit. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12277013/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: In-cell calibration of reversible LLPS with coactivator enrichment (FRAP recovery >60%, dark-off t1/2 <5 min). Go if achievable at ≤1 µM expression.
- M2: At HBB, ≥2-fold increase in E–P contact probability and ≥2-fold increase in nascent transcription within 10 min of light; full reversal within 30–60 min of dark. Go if both are met.
- M3: Off-target RNA-seq changes limited to <1% of genes at FDR <0.05; Hi-C shows no global compartment shifts.

Risk, alternatives, and ethics
- Phototoxicity: use low-intensity, duty-cycled blue light; if needed, switch to red-shifted LOV variants once the principle is shown.
- If sticker-based recruitment is too generic, minimal MED1-IDR tiles can be substituted as stickers while retaining the intramolecular caging mechanism (distinct from CRY2-based optoDroplets). ([doi.org](https://doi.org/doi%3A10.1126/science.aar3958?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery to HUDEP-2 via lentivirus; include kill-switch and antibiotic selection; standard BSL-2 practice.

Impact
This project reframes gene control from forced molecular proximity to local thermodynamic control: an intramolecularly caged multivalency switch at a defined locus. It tests whether tuning csat—rather than tethering—better couples chromatin architecture to productive transcription, addressing limitations seen with dimerizer-based looping and oligomerization tools. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Prior art and novelty check (concise)
- LADL: light-driven CRY2–CIBN heterodimerization to force loops. Our system avoids binary dimerizers and does not enforce E–P tethering. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))
- CasDrop: dCas9–iLID plus recruited IDRs to induce condensation via light-gated oligomerization. Our control is intramolecular exposure of stickers, not multicomponent clustering. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6724728/?utm_source=openai))
- LAMPS: dCas9-based optogenetic condensation at loci; demonstrated transcription and interaction reconfiguration. We retain locus-specific condensation but replace oligomerization logic with an AsLOV2 caging switch to toggle surface energetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10065442/?utm_source=openai))
- LOV2 peptide caging and sticker-dependence of LLPS are established, supporting feasibility of a single-component light switch that sets local phase behavior. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3334866/?utm_source=openai))

Single external stimulus
Blue light (AsLOV2), reversible on/off, no partner proteins required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3334866/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- A validated dCas9–LOV2–sticker scaffold and gRNA set.
- Quantitative on/off maps linking light dose to csat crossing and loop probability.
- Comparative data versus LADL and CRY2–IDR optoDroplets at the same locus, establishing mechanistic advantages of phase-threshold control. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Locus-specific optogenetic unloading of cohesin to reversibly dissolve chromatin loops in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons

Background and Rationale
- Loop extrusion by cohesin organizes chromatin into loops that are typically halted at convergently oriented CTCF sites; anchor occupancy of CTCF and cohesin determines contact frequency and transcriptional outcomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6065110/?utm_source=openai))
- WAPL, in complex with PDS5 and SA/STAG, promotes opening of the Smc3–Rad21 kleisin gate to release cohesin from DNA; modulating WAPL/PDS5–cohesin interfaces alters cohesin residence and loop stability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))
- In neurons, cohesin and CTCF contribute to activity-related gene programs and loop plasticity; perturbing cohesin turnover reconfigures enhancer–promoter interactions around immediate-early genes (IEGs) such as Fos and Arc. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106336/?utm_source=openai))
- Existing optogenetic systems (CLOuD9, LADL, OptoLoop) induce de novo chromatin contacts via light-driven dimerization or oligomerization; they build bridges rather than dissolving native anchors. A locus-specific, light-gated “unloader” that increases off-rate of anchor components has not been reported. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13005720/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis and Question
A photoswitchable, dCas9-tethered WAPL-mimetic peptide that is sterically caged in the dark and transiently exposed by blue light will locally bias cohesin toward the open/unloading state at pre-existing CTCF loop anchors, reversibly decreasing contact probability and downregulating loop-dependent transcription at targeted neuronal loci. Is increasing the local cohesin off-rate at a single anchor sufficient to impose an on/off gene-expression switch in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons without forming synthetic bridges?

Atomic Strategy
Exploit WAPL’s natural function—promotion of Smc3–Rad21 gate opening—by delivering a minimal WAPL/PDS5-interacting motif in a light-gated, high local concentration precisely at a chosen CTCF anchor via dCas9. The single causal intervention is transiently increasing cohesin koff at one anchor; loop dissolution and transcriptional attenuation follow from reduced enhancer–promoter contact frequency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

System Design (“Opto-WAPL-Local Unloader”, OWL)
- Targeting module: SpCas9(dCas9)-NLS with one or two sgRNAs positioned 20–80 bp from the CTCF motif at an anchor of interest (e.g., Fos or Arc domains in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons). Positioning avoids steric occlusion of Cas9 with CTCF yet ensures proximity to cohesin/CTCF complex. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106336/?utm_source=openai))
- Photoswitch and effector: AsLOV2-Jα caging domain fused to a WAPL-derived peptide that binds the PDS5/SA–Scc1 interface (e.g., YSR-containing PDS5-binding segment or WAPL1–33/PDS5-interacting motif), appended to dCas9 via a flexible linker. In the dark, Jα masks the peptide; blue light (488 nm) undocks Jα, exposing the peptide for local engagement with cohesin to favor exit-gate opening. Dark-state recovery re-cages the peptide (t1/2 ≈ 40–60 s), restoring cohesin reloading and loop re-formation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5107339/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinction from dimerizers: No exogenous bridging partners or oligomerization domains are recruited; the tool does not tether two loci. It operates by locally accelerating cohesin release at a native anchor.

Key Experimental Aims and Methods
Aim 1. Engineer and validate minimal light-gated WAPL mimics
- Construct panel: dCas9-AsLOV2-(linker)-[WAPL1–33], dCas9-AsLOV2-[WAPL YSR-core], and control mutants (YSR→ASA). Include a dark-locked LOV2 mutant and a light-locked LOV2 mutant to bound activity. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1097276516001775?utm_source=openai))
- Cell model: HEK293T for initial kinetics, then human iPSC-derived cortical neurons (glutamatergic) for functional tests. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211124716317089?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts:
  - Light-gated binding: In situ BiFC or split luciferase between the exposed peptide and PDS5B fragment; blue-light pulse trains quantify on/off kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5560056/?utm_source=openai))
  - Cohesin turnover: FRAP of endogenously tagged RAD21-Halo near targeted loci (CRISPR-view with dCas9-mScarlet) under light vs dark. Expect faster local RAD21 recovery under light. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4989898/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible loop dissolution at defined neuronal anchors
- Target selection: CTCF-anchored loops flanking activity-regulated loci (FOS, ARC) with documented activity-dependent chromatin reconfiguration. sgRNAs tiled around CTCF motifs at these anchors. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32451484/?utm_source=openai))
- Chromatin conformation assays:
  - Capture-C/5C or Micro-C in neurons expressing OWL ± blue light. Expect decreased anchor–anchor contact frequency during light, recovery in dark. Time-resolve dissolution/re-formation kinetics (minutes to tens of minutes). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32451484/?utm_source=openai))
  - RAD21 ChIP–seq/ChIP–qPCR at targeted anchors shows reduced cohesin occupancy only under light. Genome-wide Hi-C confirms minimal off-target architectural change. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42258543/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls: Non-targeting sgRNA; CTCF-distal sgRNA at same locus; WAPL-peptide mutant; LOV2 dark-locked variant; LADL/OptoLoop positive controls for loop building to benchmark opposite phenotype. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6599567/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Establish on/off transcriptional control and reversibility
- Nascent transcription: 4sU-seq or PRO-seq and smFISH for FOS/ARC upon KCl or BDNF stimulation with interleaved light pulses. Prediction: Light-triggered unloading reduces enhancer–promoter contacts and dampens IEG transcription; signal rebounds after light-off. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9106336/?utm_source=openai))
- Specificity: RNA-seq to assess global expression; expect confined effects around targeted domains relative to CTCF/AID or cohesin depletion controls that alter genome-wide insulation. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.3390/cells15010051?utm_source=openai))
- Kinetic tuning: Vary light duty cycle to set occupancy of the uncaged peptide, mapping dose–response curves linking unloading fraction to transcriptional output.

Aim 4. Mechanistic dissection and boundary conditions
- PDS5/WAPL dependency: Knockdown PDS5A/B or pharmacologically alter SMC3 acetylation to test whether OWL efficacy requires the canonical releasing axis. Prediction: Loss of PDS5 reduces OWL potency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4989898/?utm_source=openai))
- Anchor asymmetry: Target only one of two convergent anchors to test whether unilateral unloading suffices to collapse the loop. Expect strong contact loss when the higher-occupancy anchor is targeted. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6065110/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and Success Criteria
- M1: Light-gated exposure of WAPL-mimetic peptide with ≥5–10× on/off binding contrast to PDS5 fragment in cells; LOV2 recovery t1/2 within 1 min. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10941968/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: At neuronal CTCF anchors, light reduces local RAD21 ChIP signal by ≥30% with no significant global Hi-C reorganization.
- M3: Capture-C/Micro-C shows ≥30–50% reduction in targeted loop contact frequency during illumination, with full recovery within ≤30–60 min after light-off.
- M4: IEG transcription decreased ≥30% under light with restored expression after dark; negligible change at non-targeted IEGs.

Risk Assessment and Mitigations
- Insufficient peptide potency: Screen multiple WAPL/PDS5-binding segments and linker geometries; incorporate cpLOV2 variants to optimize caging dynamics and dynamic range. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41589-021-00792-9?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target nuclear diffusion: The peptide remains covalently tethered to dCas9; add an auxiliary weak intramolecular coiled-coil to bias rebinding to LOV2 in dark, minimizing free-peptide exposure.
- Anchor inaccessibility: Tile sgRNAs around motifs to find sterically permissive placements; use orthologous dCas9 (Sa-dCas9) if PAM constraints limit positioning.
- Neuronal phototoxicity: Use brief, low-duty-cycle 488-nm pulses; validate two-photon blue-shifted excitation regimes for thick cultures.

Differentiation from prior art
OWL dissolves endogenous loops by locally accelerating cohesin release at native anchors using a single, light-gated inhibitor tethered by dCas9. It does not dimerize effectors, oligomerize chromatin, or create synthetic bridges as in CLOuD9/LADL/OptoLoop; the causal mechanism is increased cohesin off-rate at a defined anchor. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13005720/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- Validated OWL constructs and sgRNA designs for human iPSC-derived cortical neurons.
- Quantified kinetics of light-gated cohesin unloading at targeted anchors.
- Reversible control of loop contact frequency and transcription at IEG loci.
- Open protocols for adapting OWL to other cell types and anchors.

Interpretation
If OWL produces reversible loop dissolution and on/off transcriptional control with minimal global perturbation, it demonstrates that anchor-local modulation of cohesin residence is sufficient to gate gene expression, establishing a mechanistically distinct, locus-specific “loop eraser” complementary to existing loop-forming optogenetic tools. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/4701713/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Torque-gated chromatin de-insulation: a magnetic clutch to reversibly dissolve CTCF/cohesin loops and switch transcription in human iPSCs

Summary
Genome insulation by cohesin-driven loop extrusion halted at CTCF sites reduces enhancer–promoter contact probabilities and modulates transcriptional bursting. We propose a single-modality magnetic system that transiently de-insulates chosen loop boundaries to turn genes on, then restores insulation to turn them off. Superparamagnetic iron-oxide nanorods (SPIONRs) coated with a thermoresponsive PNIPAM copolymer bear a buried HaloTag ligand that is exposed only when locally heated by an alternating magnetic field (AMF). HaloTag-fused dCas9, targeted adjacent to a chosen CTCF/cohesin boundary, acts as a one-molecule mechanical clutch: AMF engagement switches the tether from slack to load-bearing; a superimposed low-frequency rotating field applies torque at the boundary, biasing loop opening and allowing enhancers to contact promoters. Removing the field disengages the clutch and permits boundary re-formation, restoring repression. This mechanism differs fundamentally from optogenetic dimerizer systems (e.g., LADL/CRY2–CIBN) that assemble synthetic chromatin bridges; here, we mechanically relieve native repression at endogenous anchors using a single magnetic input. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–Question
Can a magnetothermally gated, torque-transmitting tether at a specific CTCF/cohesin boundary reversibly modulate enhancer–promoter contact probability and transcriptional bursting in human iPSCs, without introducing synthetic DNA–DNA bridges?

Atomic strategy
Use one field to do two jobs at the same locus: (i) AMF raises the nanoparticle’s local temperature by a few degrees to collapse a PNIPAM shell and present a chloroalkane HaloTag ligand (engage the clutch to make a stiff, load-bearing tether between SPIONR and dCas9–Halo); (ii) the same magnetic modality, now driven in a low-frequency rotating regimen, delivers angular torque that is converted by the nucleoprotein hinge geometry at the boundary into a small extension/twist along the loop axis, transiently lowering CTCF/cohesin boundary stability and increasing enhancer–promoter encounter frequency; field removal disengages the clutch and restores boundary function. Feasibility rests on: dynamic CTCF (~1–4 min) and cohesin (~10–25 min) residence times at loops; in-nucleus magnetic torque actuation; and PNIPAM LCST tunability to 39–41°C for in-cell gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))

Model system and target loci
- Cell type: human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), where developmental control genes are buffered by CTCF/cohesin boundaries and enhancer clusters. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3411781/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary loci: Sox2 distal super-enhancer boundary and NANOG insulated neighborhood boundaries; both show CTCF-dependent insulation and measurable transcriptional outputs upon perturbation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8853952/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build and calibrate a PNIPAM-gated, HaloTag-engageable SPIONR clutch targeted to CTCF/cohesin boundaries.
Aim 2. Test whether field-gated torque at the boundary dissolves loops and acutely increases transcription at Sox2 and NANOG in hiPSCs.
Aim 3. Demonstrate reversibility, locus specificity, and differentiation from optogenetic dimerizer-based looping.

Research plan

Aim 1. Engineering and calibration
- Constructs: Express NLS-dCas9–HaloTag in hiPSCs with sgRNAs that bind 10–40 bp from a boundary CTCF motif to avoid direct steric occlusion yet remain mechanically coupled to the anchor. Use dual-sgRNA tiling around the boundary to map optimal leverage.
- Nanoparticles: Synthesize iron-oxide nanorods (length 150–300 nm; diameter 30–60 nm) with shape anisotropy for efficient magnetic torque. Coat with a PNIPAM-based copolymer whose LCST is tuned to 39–41°C (e.g., co-monomers: N-isopropylmethacrylamide or acrylamide). Graft a short chloroalkane HaloTag ligand on end-tethered linkers that are sterically buried below LCST and exposed above LCST (brush collapse). Validate temperature-dependent ligand presentation by solution labeling kinetics against purified HaloTag and by live-cell pulse labeling of HaloTag–H2B fusions. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.5b05459?utm_source=openai))
- Field regimens and local temperature calibration: Use an AMF (100–400 kHz, H0 ≤ 15 kA/m) to induce magnetothermal heating and engage the clutch; monitor nanoparticle-proximal temperature via a thermoresponsive polymer fluorophore reporter on the shell. Superimpose a low-frequency (0.1–5 Hz) rotating magnetic field (few mT) to apply torque while engaged. Quantify in-nuclear torque/force using bead/rod tracking and magnetic calibration. ([hero.epa.gov](https://hero.epa.gov/reference/7005890/?utm_source=openai))
- Engagement metric: FRAP-like “mechanical FRAP.” In disengaged state (below LCST), rotating field induces rod reorientation with minimal chromatin displacement near the target; in engaged state (above LCST), the same field yields locus displacement/twist and reduced rod reorientation free angle, indicating load transfer.

Milestones for Aim 1
- PNIPAM shell LCST verified at 39–41°C with reversible coil–globule transition and ligand exposure contrast ≥5-fold.
- Robust HaloTag labeling only under AMF on, not off.
- Calibrated in-nucleus torque/force delivery in the pN·nm to pN range at the dCas9-addressed site. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12686234/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Boundary opening, contact remodeling, and transcriptional outputs
- Loop boundary readouts:
  - Rapid: live-cell DNA FISH (Oligopaints) between enhancer and promoter at Sox2/NANOG before, during, and after 2–10 min field application; measure E–P distance distributions and fraction within 100 nm.
  - Population: Capture-C/HiChIP (CTCF, H3K27ac) ± field to quantify loss of boundary corner peaks and increased intra-domain E–P contacts.
  - Locus mechanics: replicate Keizer et al.’s locus micromanipulation controls to benchmark viscoelastic response and confirm that observed remodeling exceeds passive chromatin flow. ([institut-curie.org](https://institut-curie.org/publications/live-cell-micromanipulation-genomic-locus-reveals-interphase-chromatin-mechanics))
- Transcriptional outputs:
  - Acute: MS2/MCP tagging of nascent transcripts at Sox2/NANOG; quantify burst frequency and size during torque-on windows vs off.
  - Population: PRO-seq and smFISH within 5–30 min of field gating; reversibility on repeated on/off cycles (3–5 cycles).
- Causality controls:
  - dCas9 binding without PNIPAM-gated SPIONRs (no torque) and SPIONRs with scrambled sgRNA.
  - AMF only (engage clutch, no rotation) vs rotation only (no AMF; slack), to separate clutch engagement from torque.
  - CTCF-motif mutants at the boundary (base editing) to test dependence on an intact boundary.

Success criteria for Aim 2
- Field-on windows show (i) reduced boundary insulation/contact corner intensity, (ii) increased E–P proximity, and (iii) higher burst frequency, all reversing within one CTCF/cohesin turnover after field-off (≤30 min). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Reversibility, specificity, and distinction from optogenetic dimerizers
- Reversibility: Demonstrate ≥5 on/off cycles with minimal drift in baseline expression and contact maps.
- Locus specificity: Multiplex sgRNAs to engage a second boundary in the same nucleus and show independent control with spatially restricted magnetic gradients (micro-pole pieces) versus global field; quantify off-target transcription and contact changes genome-wide. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1305265/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanistic differentiation from LADL/OptoLoop: Side-by-side in hiPSCs using published light-induced dimerizer constructs to form loops; show that magnetic clutch increases E–P encounters by boundary de-insulation without assembling new bridges, whereas LADL increases proximity by synthetic bridging. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-019-0436-5?utm_source=openai))

Key technical details and justifications
- Endogenous dynamics create an exploitable window: CTCF (~1–4 min) and cohesin (~10–25 min) residence times imply that modest, periodic torque should bias boundary unbinding within minutes, enabling reversible switching on experimental timescales. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))
- In-nucleus magnetic actuation: Rotating fields rotate anisotropic nanorods within nuclei and deform the nuclear interior, establishing that torques of the required scale are deliverable with negligible phototoxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3192970/?utm_source=openai))
- Single stimulus, two functions: AMF magnetothermal engagement and low-frequency rotation are both magnetic-field operations delivered by the same coil set; the modality is strictly magnetic.
- PNIPAM gate tuning: Raising LCST into the 39–41°C range by copolymerization (e.g., with N-isopropylmethacrylamide or acrylamide) ensures engagement occurs only under AMF, avoiding constitutive tethering at 37°C. ([cir.nii.ac.jp](https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1870865117788073088?utm_source=openai))
- CRISPR-based addressability and Halo chemistry: dCas9–Halo fusions enable covalent, stoichiometric capture by chloroalkane ligands at defined genomic coordinates; dCas9–Halo has been used for live genomic labeling, supporting intracellular access and kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6620262/?utm_source=openai))

Readouts, analyses, and statistics
- Imaging: High-throughput single-cell measurements of E–P distances and nascent transcription; hidden Markov modeling of burst kinetics with within-cell paired on/off comparisons.
- 3D genomics: Capture-C/HiChIP differential contact analysis at targeted TADs; quantify insulation scores and corner dot strength changes.
- Mechanobiology: Track SPIONR orientation and locus displacement to estimate load transfer; correlate per-cell mechanical engagement with transcriptional response.

Potential risks and mitigations
- Insufficient local heating to engage PNIPAM: Increase SPIONR core size within biocompatible limits; use higher-loss iron-oxide compositions; optimize AMF duty cycle while monitoring local temperature with polymer thermometers. ([hero.epa.gov](https://hero.epa.gov/reference/7005890/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-axis perturbations: Use anisotropic rods or Janus particles to maximize torque along the loop axis and incorporate flexible linkers to absorb off-axis motion.
- dCas9 occlusion of CTCF binding: Tile sgRNAs ±20–60 bp from the CTCF motif and verify unperturbed CTCF ChIP when field is off.

Milestones and outcomes
- Year 1: Synthesize/calibrate PNIPAM-gated SPIONRs; establish dCas9–Halo targeting and field regimens; demonstrate clutch engagement/disengagement in nuclei.
- Year 2: Show field-on de-insulation and transcriptional activation at Sox2/NANOG with reversibility; complete multi-cycle switching and off-target profiling; benchmark against LADL.

Impact and novelty
This system delivers reversible, locus-specific gene control by selectively relieving native repressive loops with a single magnetic modality, orthogonal to light-gated dimerizer strategies that create synthetic bridges. It leverages endogenous CTCF/cohesin dynamics, established in-nucleus torque delivery, tunable PNIPAM gating, and CRISPR-based addressability to implement a mechanical on/off switch for chromatin insulation. It further generalizes to testing causality of specific boundaries in development and disease, and to multi-locus mechanical logic. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5446243/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Turning the mitochondrial proton motive force into a PYCR1/2 redox trap: a mitochondria‑accumulating, mechanism‑based P5C analog that inactivates PYCR and drains matrix NAD(H) to neutralize PYCR dependency despite extracellular proline.

Background and rationale
- PYCR1 and PYCR2 catalyze the NAD(P)H‑dependent reduction of Δ1‑pyrroline‑5‑carboxylate (P5C) to proline in the mitochondrial matrix; PYCR3 is cytosolic. PYCR1/2 are upregulated in many tumors, and their knockdown impairs growth and stress tolerance. PYCR1 and PYCR2 have highly conserved active sites, enabling cross‑compensation. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/218/1/iyab048/6178002?utm_source=openai))
- The mitochondrial nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT) couples proton motive force (Δp) to reversible hydride exchange between NAD(H) and NADP(H). Perturbations in one pool can be buffered by the other as long as Δp persists. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))
- Exogenous proline does not invariably rescue growth when proline biosynthesis is perturbed, indicating that the biosynthetic flux and its redox coupling (rather than proline abundance per se) can be rate‑limiting. PRODH oxidizes proline at the inner membrane, feeding electrons to the ETC and tying the P5C↔proline cycle to mitochondrial redox. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12523316/?utm_source=openai))
- Lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cations accumulate 100–1000× in mitochondria driven by Δψ; MitoQ exemplifies a TPP‑conjugated quinone that concentrates in the matrix and participates in intramitochondrial redox cycling. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))
- Current PYCR inhibitors include fragment‑like active‑site binders and emerging allosteric or isoform‑selective agents, but none simultaneously: (i) act within the mitochondrial matrix, (ii) disable both PYCR1 and PYCR2 by mechanism‑based capture, and (iii) collapse matrix NAD(H) buffering that otherwise enables cofactor compensation. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960894X19305037?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–question
Can a mitochondria‑accumulating, mechanism‑based P5C analog that binds and inactivates PYCR1/2 while its tethered redox‑active quinone rapidly oxidizes enzyme‑bound/matrix NADH convert the organelle’s own Δψ and NNT into a self‑reinforcing “reducing‑equivalent trap,” thereby neutralizing PYCR dependency even in the presence of extracellular proline? ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit Δψ to concentrate a TPP+‑conjugated P5C analog inside mitochondria; once bound in the conserved PYCR active site, a proximal quinone moiety outcompetes native hydride transfer and oxidizes NADH; repeated redox cycling drains NADH and forces NNT‑mediated NADPH drawdown, while mechanism‑based chemistry locks PYCR1/2 in long‑lived inactive complexes. The same matrix‑localized operation prevents extracellular proline from restoring PYCR‑dependent flux. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12406333/?utm_source=openai))

Proposed agent
Mito‑P5C‑Q: a triphenylphosphonium‑conjugated, mechanism‑based P5C analog bearing a benzo/naphtho‑quinone positioned to accept hydride from NADH within the PYCR active site. Quinone choice is guided by aqueous NADH oxidation kinetics; smaller benzo/naphthoquinones oxidize NADH efficiently without photoactivation. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Validate mitochondrial accumulation and target engagement of Mito‑P5C‑Q.
- Assays: Δψ dependence of uptake (compare ±CCCP); subcellular LC‑MS quantification; CETSA/thermal shift and activity‑based pulldown for PYCR1/2 adducts; in‑organello PYCR activity. Rationale: TPP+ ensures matrix accumulation; conserved PYCR1/2 active sites support dual targeting. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))

2) Test whether Mito‑P5C‑Q drains matrix NADH and collapses NADH↔NADPH buffering via NNT.
- Assays: mito‑SoNar and iNap sensors, matrix‑targeted; redox ratios (NADH/NAD+, NADPH/NADP+); NNT dependency (siRNA or NNT−/− background); oxygen consumption partitioning; effect of Δp perturbation (oligomycin, FCCP). Prediction: rapid fall in NADH/NAD+, followed by NADPH/NADP+ decrease that is attenuated in NNT‑deficient cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))

3) Determine whether extracellular proline fails to rescue PYCR‑dependent functions under Mito‑P5C‑Q.
- Assays: proliferation/colony formation ±proline add‑back; fluxomics of P5C↔proline; PRODH‑dependent P5C accumulation and ROS; compare to cytosolic PYCR3 context. Prediction: add‑back proline does not restore growth or proline biosynthetic flux; PRODH‑driven P5C/ROS rise under oxidized matrix conditions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12523316/?utm_source=openai))

4) Benchmark against existing PYCR inhibitors to establish novelty of mechanism and phenotype.
- Comparators: pargyline‑like PYCR1 binder; PYCR2‑selective covalent (Cys‑targeting) inhibitor; recent allosteric site ligands. Endpoints: mitochondrial vs cytosolic redox impact; isoform compensation; rescue by proline; on‑target adduct verification. Expectation: only Mito‑P5C‑Q produces coupled PYCR inactivation and matrix cofactor drain that resists proline rescue. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960894X19305037?utm_source=openai))

Key design and methods
- Chemistry and structural guidance:
  - Use PYCR1 holo structures (e.g., 5UAV with NADPH/THFA) and active‑site conservation to place the P5C‑mimetic anchor and position a benzo/naphthoquinone within hydride‑transfer distance of the nicotinamide C4. Vary linker length/rigidity to favor preorganization. ([rcsb.org](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5UAV?utm_source=openai))
  - Mechanism‑based inactivation: incorporate a latent electrophile unmasked upon initial binding/attempted hydride transfer (e.g., ring‑opened iminium that forms a stable imine/Schiff base with nearby lysine or captures the reduced nicotinamide in a ternary complex), yielding long‑lived PYCR–NAD(P)H–inhibitor complexes. Justification: PYCR catalysis proceeds via direct hydride transfer to a P5C iminium; substrate‑like anchoring plus timed electrophilicity supports enzyme‑activated capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8599497/?utm_source=openai))
  - Quinone selection: bench‑screen benzo/naphthoquinones spanning E0 to maximize aqueous NADH oxidation without reliance on photoactivation; prioritize scaffolds with favorable NADH oxidation rate constants at pH 7.0. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0009261405012613?utm_source=openai))
- Mitochondrial delivery and accumulation:
  - TPP+ vector; confirm Δψ‑driven uptake and matrix localization; ensure low nonspecific membrane binding by tuning linker hydrophobicity. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))
- Redox and NNT analysis:
  - Quantify sequential NADH then NADPH declines; test NNT reversibility by comparing wild‑type vs NNT‑deficient or pharmacologically inhibited cells. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))
- Functional rescue testing:
  - Proline add‑back (0.2–2 mM) and P5C add‑back under normoxia/hypoxia; monitor proliferation, collagen synthesis (in CAF models), and ROS. Prior work indicates biosynthetic flux—not extracellular proline per se—can be limiting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12523316/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and falsification criteria
- Milestone 1: Matrix enrichment (>100× over cytosol) and PYCR1/2 adduct formation with loss of activity in cell lysates. Fail if uptake is Δψ‑independent or PYCR activity remains intact. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))
- Milestone 2: In live cells, sustained matrix NADH oxidation and secondary NADPH drawdown that is blunted in NNT‑loss backgrounds. Fail if redox effects are purely cytosolic or independent of NNT. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))
- Milestone 3: Extracellular proline fails to restore PYCR flux and growth; instead, PRODH‑linked P5C/ROS rise. Fail if proline add‑back fully rescues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7243120/?utm_source=openai))
- Milestone 4: Compared to existing PYCR inhibitors, only Mito‑P5C‑Q shows isoform‑independent inactivation with built‑in matrix redox drain. Fail if benchmark inhibitors produce indistinguishable phenotypes. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960894X19305037?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcomes and impact
- Mechanistic readout: PYCR1/2 are trapped in long‑lived inactive complexes inside mitochondria; matrix NADH is catalytically siphoned by the tethered quinone and NNT reversibly drains NADPH, collapsing nicotinamide cofactor buffering in the same compartment where PYCR operates. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34155914/?utm_source=openai))
- System‑level consequence: the organelle’s own Δψ and NNT become the engine of an irreversible “reducing‑equivalent sink,” neutralizing PYCR dependency and rendering extracellular proline insufficient to restore the targeted matrix reaction. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00042?utm_source=openai))
- Novelty relative to field: integrates mitochondria‑accumulation (TPP+), mechanism‑based dual‑isoform PYCR capture, and local quinone‑catalyzed NADH oxidation; prior PYCR inhibitors lack this combined, matrix‑confined, cofactor‑collapsing design. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960894X19305037?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and alternatives
- If quinone‑mediated NADH oxidation is insufficient in situ, swap to higher‑potential benzoquinones or incorporate a second‑sphere H‑bond network to accelerate hydride transfer; as an orthogonal control, express mito‑LbNOX to validate that selective matrix NADH oxidation reproduces the cofactor‑drain phenotype without the inhibitor, de‑risking the redox premise. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4850741/?utm_source=openai))
- If mechanism‑based adduct lifetimes are short, optimize electrophile timing or explore adjacent allosteric cavity occupation while retaining quinone proximity. Existing allosteric grooves provide structural precedent. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41569420/?utm_source=openai))

Success criteria
- A mitochondria‑accumulating PYCR‑directed agent that (i) disables both PYCR1 and PYCR2, (ii) drains matrix NADH and, via NNT, matrix NADPH, and (iii) prevents extracellular proline from restoring PYCR‑dependent flux and growth in PYCR‑dependent models. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/218/1/iyab048/6178002?utm_source=openai))
