Title
Disease-gated ASIC3 inhibition to couple pain relief with structural protection in knee osteoarthritis

Hypothesis–Question
Does selectively inhibiting acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) only where extracellular pH is pathologically low in osteoarthritic joints simultaneously (i) normalize nociceptor hyperexcitability to reduce pain and (ii) suppress acid-evoked catabolic programs in joint stromal cells to slow cartilage loss—and can responders be prospectively enriched by imaging or biochemical markers of joint acidosis? ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))

Causal pathway (pre-specified)
Cartilage microdamage and hypoxia → lactate/H+ accumulation in cartilage/synovium (tissue pHe drops despite near-neutral bulk synovial fluid) → activation of shared acid sensors (ASIC3 on joint-innervating DRG afferents and on synoviocytes/chondrocytes) → (a) nociceptor firing → neuropeptide release → neurogenic inflammation; (b) direct acid-evoked catabolic signaling in joint cells → MMP/ADAMTS induction → further matrix loss → sustained peripheral input maintains central sensitization. A pH-gated ASIC3 inhibitor reduces acid-evoked neuronal and stromal activation within acidic niches, decreasing nociceptive drive and catabolism in lockstep. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12563613/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Exploit convergence on ASIC3 as a shared, disease-gated sensor: create a peripherally restricted, state-dependent ASIC3 inhibitor that engages only under acidic pHe (<~7.0) to normalize sensitization and re-balance joint cell programs while preserving baseline nociception in normophysiologic tissues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12563613/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Human relevance and gating window
- Map tissue-level acidosis and ASIC3 axis in human knee OA.
- Methods:
  - AcidoCEST-UTE MRI to quantify cartilage/synovial pHe and define an acidosis threshold predictive of symptoms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))
  - RNA/protein profiling of ASIC3 in arthroscopy-obtained cartilage/synovium; align with pain scores and acidoCEST pHe. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3476728/?utm_source=openai))
  - Ex vivo acid challenge (pH 7.4→6.6) of patient-derived synoviocytes/chondrocytes with and without ASIC3 blockade; readouts: MMP13/ADAMTS5, COX-2, SOX9, neuropeptide-stimulated responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12563613/?utm_source=openai))
- Success criteria: ASIC3 expression in OA joint cells; acidoCEST-UTE pHe correlates with pain/function; ASIC3 inhibition reduces acid-evoked catabolic transcripts ex vivo.

2) Pharmacology: engineer and validate a peripherally restricted, pH-activated ASIC3 inhibitor
- Medicinal chemistry:
  - Start from ASIC3 tool pharmacophores; incorporate acid-labile or protonatable motifs that confer higher affinity to open/protonated ASIC3 states and limit CNS penetration (polar surface area >90 Å²; P-gp substrates). State dependence provides joint selectivity because target is active only at low pHe. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3520115/?utm_source=openai))
- In vitro assays:
  - Whole-cell patch clamp on recombinant human ASIC3: determine IC50 at pH 6.5 vs 7.4; measure use/state dependence.
  - Off-target panel (Nav, Kv, hERG, TRPV1) to minimize homeostatic disruption.
  - Primary human chondrocyte/synoviocyte assays under acid stress ± IL-1β: quantify effects on MMP13/ADAMTS, COX-2/PGE2, and anabolic markers.
- PK/PD:
  - Rodent PK with brain:plasma ratios; in vivo target engagement by inhibiting acid-evoked currents in ex vivo DRG neurons from dosed animals.

3) Mechanistic efficacy in vivo (systemic dosing)
- Models: DMM (surgical) and MIA (chemical) knee OA in rats/mice.
- Dosing: oral or SC systemic administration; no intra-articular dosing (constraint).
- Endpoints:
  - Pain: weight-bearing asymmetry, incapacitance, von Frey/pressure thresholds, movement-evoked pain.
  - Structure: OARSI histopathology, cartilage thickness by MRI, subchondral bone by micro-CT.
  - Mechanism: joint/tissue pHe by acidoCEST-UTE MRI; synovial/neural biomarkers (SP/CGRP levels, DRG pERK), chondrocyte MMP13/ADAMTS5 vs SOX9. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))
  - Sensitization normalization: dorsal horn c-Fos and wind-up decline tracking peripheral input reduction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9949992/?utm_source=openai))
- Comparator arms: vehicle; non–pH-gated ASIC3 blocker (to test necessity of disease gating).
- Success criteria: concurrent improvement in pain and histology in acidic-joint animals; mechanistic biomarker shifts consistent with reduced peripheral drive and catabolism.

4) Precision-enriched first-in-human trial design
- Target population: KL2–3 knee OA with acidoCEST-defined acidic joints (pre-specified pHe threshold), evidence of peripheral sensitization on QST, and/or elevated synovial lactate where arthrocentesis is clinically indicated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))
- Design: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, adaptive Phase 1b/2a.
  - Dosing: oral/SC peripherally restricted ASIC3 inhibitor, 12–16 weeks.
  - Primary endpoints: pain (WOMAC pain; movement-evoked pain) and MRI-based structural progression proxies (T2/T1ρ; cartilage thickness subregion change). 
  - Key secondary/PD: acidoCEST-UTE pHe shift; serum/synovial PGE2; circulating neuropeptides; QST normalization; physical activity–adjusted digital pain scores to reduce placebo susceptibility.
- Effect-size strategy: enrichment by acidosis and sensitization phenotypes; objective imaging PD (pHe shift) to confirm on-target biology; hierarchical testing to control multiplicity and mitigate high OA placebo response.

Mechanistic justifications and constraint alignment
- Joint specificity without local injection: pharmacology is engaged only in acidic microenvironments mapped by acidoCEST-UTE MRI; healthy tissues at neutral pH are pharmacologically silent. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))
- Sensitization normalization vs nociception block: ASIC3 inhibition reduces abnormal acid-evoked firing while sparing baseline protective sensation at physiologic pH; lowering peripheral drive allows central sensitization to decay. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12563613/?utm_source=openai))
- Structural–pain coupling: ASIC3 is present on joint afferents and on synoviocytes/chondrocytes; its blockade reduces both neurogenic input and acid-evoked catabolic gene expression, aligning pain relief with slowed matrix loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3520115/?utm_source=openai))
- Homeostasis avoidance: ASIC3’s pathologic activation requires low pHe; peripherally restricted design reduces CNS exposure, minimizing interference with essential central functions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12563613/?utm_source=openai))
- Excluded crowded areas respected: no IL-1 pathway targeting, no broad MMP inhibition, no NGF blockade, no intra-articular administration.

Exploratory extensions (contingent)
- If ASIC3 stromal effects are modest, evaluate proton-sensing GPCR GPR68 modulation as a complementary shared sensor; human DRG peptidergic neurons and OA chondrocytes express GPR68, and emerging data link GPR68 to acid-evoked nociception and OA cartilage programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10286344/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go criteria
- Go to IND-enabling: demonstration of pH-dependent ASIC3 inhibition in vitro; systemic efficacy on both pain and structure with acidoCEST-confirmed engagement; clean safety/PK with peripheral restriction.
- No-go: absent ASIC3 expression in human joint cells; lack of pH dependence; analgesia without structural benefit in acidic-joint animals; unacceptable off-target ion-channel liabilities.

Milestones and timeline
- Year 1: Human acidoCEST-UTE atlas of OA knees; ex vivo acid-challenge pharmacology completed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 2: Lead optimization and in vivo PK/PD; proof-of-concept efficacy in two OA models with mechanistic biomarker reversal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3520115/?utm_source=openai))
- Year 3: Phase 1 SAD/MAD with peripheral restriction; Phase 1b/2a initiation in acidosis-enriched knee OA.

Anticipated impact
By intervening at a disease-gated, shared acid-sensing node, this program is designed to exceed placebo by prospectively enriching for an “acidic OA” endotype, to mechanistically link pain relief with slower structural degeneration, and to do so without disrupting normal tissue homeostasis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9027981/?utm_source=openai))

Title: Closed-loop, lesion-tuned focused ultrasound to de-acidify the osteochondral interface and normalize nociception in knee osteoarthritis

Hypothesis/research goal:
Can closed-loop, load‑contingent focused ultrasound (FUS) that induces advection-dominated transport in the osteochondral microenvironment reverse the acid-driven coupling between subchondral bone remodeling and nociceptor sensitization, thereby reducing bone marrow lesion (BML) burden and pain in knee OA? The central question is whether targeting the physical choke points that confine protons at osteoclast resorption sites can causally lower ASIC3-mediated afferent drive and, secondarily, central sensitization—without systemic pharmacology or intra‑articular injection. This aligns with evidence that BMLs track pain/progression and that osteoclast lacunae are strongly acidic and promote aberrant sensory ingrowth. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy:
Convert diffusion‑limited acid confinement at osteoclast resorptive lacunae into advection‑dominated transport during injurious load cycles via precisely timed, low‑intensity FUS that generates microscale streaming and radiation‑force‑driven interstitial flow in synovial and osteochondral porous spaces. This reduces proton dwell time at nociceptor terminals, downshifts ASIC3 activation probability, and transiently destabilizes the osteoclast sealing zone in harmful moments—normalizing afferent gain without blocking basal mechanotransduction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10319495/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale (brief):
- Structure→pain linkage: BMLs mark focal remodeling, predict pain and progression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))
- Source of nociceptive drive: osteoclasts acidify resorption lacunae to ~pH 3–6 (≈4.5 typical), activating ASIC3/TRPV1 on joint afferents; osteoclast-derived netrin‑1 promotes sensory sprouting in subchondral bone. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00009.2022?rfr_dat=cr_pub++0pubmed&rfr_id=ori%3Arid%3Acrossref.org&url_ver=Z39.88-2003&utm_source=openai))
- Feasibility of the physical intervention: FUS and therapeutic ultrasound can generate acoustic streaming and interstitial fluid flow that enhance solute transport in cartilage and deep tissue. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6828772/?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanogating rather than blockade: oscillatory mechanical inputs and low‑magnitude, high‑frequency stimuli modulate osteoclastogenesis and osteocyte signaling, supporting reversible load‑dependent control over resorption. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3491440/?utm_source=openai))

Study design overview:
A. Device and control logic
- Wearable + FUS unit: a thigh/calf band with triaxial load/IMU sensors and knee acoustical emission (KAE) microphones maps gait-phase load spikes and joint vibroacoustic signatures. A 0.5–1.5 MHz phased FUS applicator targets subchondral regions identified by baseline MRI BML maps and on-body acoustic “listening.” Energy is delivered in 50–200 ms bursts only when a calibrated load or KAE threshold is exceeded (harmful cycles). Joint selectivity is achieved by spatial focusing plus frequency tuning to lesion-specific resonance/damping differences. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11539188/?utm_source=openai))
- Dosimetry: spatial‑peak temporal‑average intensity 0.2–0.6 W/cm²; duty cycle ≤20%; pulse trains synchronized to mid‑stance/heel‑strike transients. Parameters are chosen to maximize streaming and radiation‑force–driven interstitial flow while remaining non-ablative. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6289639/?utm_source=openai))

B. Mechanism validation (preclinical)
Aim 1: Demonstrate FUS‑induced de‑acidification at the osteochondral interface and reduced ASIC3 drive.
- Ex vivo porcine osteochondral plugs with osteoclasts differentiated on bone slices. Use pH‑sensitive fluorophores and confocal line scans to measure proton boundary‑layer thickness and dwell time at resorption sites with/without FUS bursts. Quantify nociceptor activation by co-culturing DRG neurons expressing ASIC3 and recording firing probability during controlled acid pulses ± FUS. Expected outcome: shorter proton residence, higher effective buffer exchange, reduced ASIC3‑dependent spiking. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/10.1152/physrev.00009.2022?rfr_dat=cr_pub++0pubmed&rfr_id=ori%3Arid%3Acrossref.org&url_ver=Z39.88-2003&utm_source=openai))

Aim 2: Show reversible disruption of resorptive sealing and reduced resorptive flux during injurious transients.
- Live-cell TIRF/SEM imaging of osteoclast podosome belts/sealing zones during brief, FUS‑mimetic shear/radiation‑force inputs; quantify actin ring integrity and pit formation. Expected outcome: transient destabilization of sealing zone only during supra‑threshold bursts, with recovery at physiologic loads. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5979552/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Quantify FUS‑driven advection in cartilage and marrow‑like porous media.
- Particle‑tracking micro‑PIV in cartilage explants and hydrogel phantoms reproducing marrow porosity; measure streaming velocities vs intensity, burst length, and frequency. Expected outcome: controllable streaming that increases Peclet number into advection‑dominated regime near the osteochondral boundary. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6828772/?utm_source=openai))

C. First-in-human mechanistic RCT (device, no pharmacologic payload)
Design: Double‑blind, sham‑controlled, 1:1 randomized study, n=120, duration 24 weeks.
Population: KL 2–3 symptomatic knee OA; index knee with MRI‑defined BML ≥1.0 cm³; serum CTX‑I or NTX above age/sex‑adjusted median; optional synovial pH surrogate via microdialysis in a subcohort. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))
Intervention: Active vs sham FUS; both arms wear identical sensing modules and follow identical daily walking tasks. Active arm receives load‑contingent bursts during harmful cycles; sham produces identical audio/haptics without ultrasound output.
Co‑primary endpoints:
- Structural: change in total BML volume by quantitative MRI (baseline, 12, 24 weeks). ([pubs.rsna.org](https://pubs.rsna.org/doi/10.1148/radiol.240470?utm_source=openai))
- Pain: change in load‑synchronous pain composite (EMA eDiary linked to gait events + evoked pain during standardized sit‑to‑stand/step‑down). Secondary endpoints: WOMAC pain; serum CTX‑I/NTX; quantitative sensory testing (temporal summation); KAE spectral entropy and impulsive event rate; rescue‑analgesic use. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8486814/?utm_source=openai))
Mechanistic readouts: wearable‑derived harmful‑cycle fraction; model‑based estimates of delivered streaming dose; in subcohort, microdialysis pH shift post‑session.
Responder enrichment a priori: larger baseline BML, higher CTX‑I/NTX, abnormal KAE features. Joint specificity derives from geometric focusing and resonance‑based coupling to softened, fluid‑rich BML tissue. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))
Powering and effect size: Assumes −20% BML volume vs −5% sham and −1.0 vs −0.4 WOMAC pain change at 24 weeks; alpha 0.05, 90% power with n=100 evaluable. Placebo risk is mitigated by objective structure-first endpoints, load‑locked dosing, and biomarker‑anchored selection.

Safety/ethics:
- Non‑ablative intensities with low duty cycle; continuous temperature monitoring at skin; exclusion for total joint arthroplasty hardware over the beam path. Adverse events captured by standard device AE reporting and MRI review. Cochrane and guideline reviews indicate mixed efficacy for generic therapeutic ultrasound in OA, reinforcing the need for lesion‑specific, closed‑loop dosing rather than continuous untargeted insonation. ([cochrane.org](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003132_therapeutic-ultrasound-osteoarthritis?utm_source=openai))

Causal pathway to be tested:
Focal overload → BML/osteoclast activation → acidified microdomains (lacunar pH ~4.5) → ASIC3‑mediated afferent hyperexcitability ± netrin‑1–driven sprouting → central sensitization and cartilage catabolism.
Intervention interrupts at two coupled, physical nodes only during harmful cycles:
- Node 1 (chemophysical): FUS‑induced interstitial streaming increases proton clearance and buffer exchange, reducing ASIC3 activation probability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10319495/?utm_source=openai))
- Node 2 (cellular mechanics): brief bursts mechanically gate resorption by destabilizing sealing zones, lowering acid generation at source without tonic anti‑resorptive drug exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5979552/?utm_source=openai))
Predicted downstream: reduced peripheral nociceptive input → reversal of central gain over weeks; improved load distribution from stabilized subchondral plate → BML shrinkage and slowed cartilage loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))

Prospective biomarkers and selection:
- Structural: baseline BML volume and resonance/vibroacoustic abnormality map (wearable KAE); guides targeting and predicts coupling efficiency. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11539188/?utm_source=openai))
- Biochemical: elevated CTX‑I/NTX indicating active resorption; optional synovial/interstitial pH surrogate. Joint‑level specificity is inherent to lesion mechanics plus FUS focusing; normal tissue homeostasis maintained by sparse, event‑triggered dosing.

Milestones and go/no‑go:
- Preclinical: demonstrate ≥30% reduction in proton dwell time at resorption sites and ≥25% reduction in ASIC3‑dependent DRG firing during acid pulses with event‑triggered FUS; reversible sealing‑zone disruption confined to burst windows.
- Clinical: at 12 weeks, interim futility boundary if ΔBML volume <10% vs sham and no signal in load‑synchronous pain; proceed if both are met.

Contingencies:
- If advection is insufficient at permitted intensities, adjust frequency to exploit resonance/damping in BML tissue or shorten focal length; if still inadequate, add circulating, acoustically passive microbubbles in a sub‑study to amplify microstreaming without IA injection. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010482513003077?utm_source=openai))

Impact:
A successful result would establish a non‑pharmacologic, joint‑selective, mechanism‑anchored OA therapy that simultaneously modifies structure and pain by normalizing the acid‑nociceptor axis and osteoclast mechanics, with prospective patient selection and objective, biomarker‑anchored endpoints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6578476/?utm_source=openai))

Title
RESOLVER-KOA: State-dependent amplification of the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex with an oral α7 nicotinic receptor positive allosteric modulator (α7-PAM) to co-improve synovitis-driven structural progression and pain in knee osteoarthritis

Pivoted research question as hypothesis
In knee osteoarthritis (KOA) patients with macrophage-dominant synovitis and preserved cholinergic tone, does systemic, state-dependent potentiation of α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) signaling reduce synovial macrophage activity, normalize peripheral/central sensitization, and slow cartilage loss while improving pain, compared with placebo?

Atomic strategy
Exploit an endogenous, activity-gated resolution circuit—the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway—by using an α7-PAM to selectively amplify acetylcholine/choline-evoked α7 signaling on activated synovial macrophages (and spinal microglia) only where/when the reflex is engaged, thereby coupling anti-inflammatory resolution and analgesia without blocking nociception or disturbing basal homeostasis. Evidence base: α7 on macrophages inhibits NF-κB and activates JAK2–STAT3 to suppress cytokines; α7 is expressed in human RA/OA synovium; α7-PAMs reduce inflammatory pain in rodents; TSPO-PET quantifies synovial macrophage activity in KOA; vagus-nerve–driven anti-inflammatory signaling improves inflammatory arthritis and shows preliminary benefit in OA, supporting pathway druggability and patient enrichment via autonomic tone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4546521/?utm_source=openai))

Causal pathway (pre-specified)
Structural insult/ongoing joint load → synovitis with activated macrophages/endothelium → mediator‑driven nociceptor sensitization and afferent barrage → central sensitization → pain; synovitis also accelerates cartilage degeneration. α7-PAM + endogenous cholinergic input → enhanced α7 signaling on synovial macrophages/endothelium and microglia → reduced TNF/IL‑6/proteases, improved efferocytosis/barrier, damped peripheral sensitization → reduced afferent drive → microglial quiescence → analgesia; lowered synovitis burden slows cartilage loss. Synovitis–progression and synovitis–sensitization links are established. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3496084/?utm_source=openai))

Modality and investigational agent
- Modality: Oral α7-PAM with CNS penetration but activity dependence (e.g., AVL‑3288 class compound; type I PAM) to minimize off-target activation and spare basal immune/neural function. First-in-human and patient studies indicate acceptable safety and CNS target engagement for AVL‑3288-class PAMs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11012235/?utm_source=openai))
- Rationale for PAM over agonist: PAMs potentiate signaling only in the presence of endogenous agonist (ACh/choline), enabling state- and site-selectivity; α7 agonists desensitize rapidly and have had limited clinical success. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3162128/?utm_source=openai))

Population and prospective responder selection
- Disease: Symptomatic medial tibiofemoral KOA (Kellgren–Lawrence 2–3).
- Enrichment for macrophage-dominant synovitis:
  - TSPO PET/MRI (e.g., [18F]FEPPA) SUVratio above predefined threshold in index knee, indicating high synovial macrophage activity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42238373/?utm_source=openai))
  - Synovial fluid or plasma sCD163 and sCD14 above cohort-derived cutoffs; both reflect activated joint macrophages and predict pain/progression. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4441094/?utm_source=openai))
- Autonomic capacity: Resting HRV (RMSSD or HF power) above age/sex-adjusted 25th percentile to ensure adequate endogenous cholinergic tone.
- Exclusions: Inflammatory arthritides; recent nicotine use or cholinesterase inhibitors; unstable cardiovascular disease; seizure history (class precaution).

Joint specificity narrative under systemic dosing
- Activated synovium expresses α7 (on FLS and macrophage‑like cells) and provides the dominant afferent inflammatory drive recruiting the cholinergic reflex; α7-PAMs amplify signaling preferentially where cholinergic input and receptor density/activation coexist (inflamed joint and pain pathways), minimizing effects in quiescent tissues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4476299/?utm_source=openai))

Study design
- Phase 2, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, biomarker-enriched trial.
- N ≈ 160 randomized 1:1 α7-PAM vs placebo; 52-week treatment.
- Two-stage adaptive enrichment:
  - Stage A (first 80 participants): confirm biomarker cutoffs and futility/GO criteria on interim mechanistic endpoints (TSPO PET reduction and QST change).
  - Stage B: continue with locked cutoffs for confirmatory co-primaries.

Intervention and dosing
- α7-PAM: oral, BID dosing titrated to well‑tolerated target (e.g., 10→30 mg AVL‑3288‑class).
- Background analgesics allowed at stable doses; no IA injections during study.

Endpoints (explicit structural and pain pathways)
- Co-primary endpoints:
  1) Structural: qMRI cartilage thickness change in medial femorotibial compartment at 52 weeks (3D DESS-based segmentation), with supportive compositional MRI (T2/T1ρ) to capture early matrix improvement. Synovitis reduction is expected to mediate slower cartilage loss. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3496084/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Pain/sensitization: Hierarchical composite at 16 and 24 weeks—(a) ≥30% WOMAC Pain reduction and (b) improvement in QST composite (pressure pain threshold at knee and remote site + temporal summation), capturing normalization of peripheral/central sensitization linked to inflammation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4827020/?utm_source=openai))
- Key secondary endpoints:
  - TSPO PET/MRI: % change in synovial SUVratio at 12 weeks (target engagement). ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42238373/?utm_source=openai))
  - Synovial fluid biomarkers: ΔTNF/IL‑6, ΔsCD14/ΔsCD163. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4441094/?utm_source=openai))
  - Autonomic readouts: HRV change; exploratory correlation with outcomes.
  - Function: WOMAC Function, KOOS-PS.
  - Rescue and opioid-sparing.
- Placebo control planning: High placebo response in OA addressed via biomarker enrichment, objective imaging co-primary, and early mechanistic endpoints. ([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2797073?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic/target engagement assays
- Ex vivo whole-blood assay: LPS-stimulated TNF production ± physiologic choline to quantify α7‑dependent suppression; expectation is greater choline‑dependent inhibition on‑treatment versus baseline.
- PBMC signaling: ACh-evoked pSTAT3 induction augmented by drug exposure ex vivo; reversibility with α7 antagonist confirms specificity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4546521/?utm_source=openai))
- CSF optional substudy in a subset: neuroinflammatory cytokines and microglial markers.

Statistical analysis (overview)
- Co-primary testing with alpha-split and hierarchical gate (pain composite at 24 weeks then 52-week cartilage thickness).
- Mediation analyses: Test whether early TSPO PET and biomarker reductions mediate pain improvement and cartilage preservation.
- Enrichment validated by interaction terms (baseline TSPO/SF sCD14/sCD163 and HRV with treatment effect).

Safety monitoring
- Adverse events with attention to cholinergic symptoms and CNS effects; periodic ECG, cognitive screening.
- Stopping rules: predefined boundaries for seizure, bradyarrhythmia, or unexpected inflammatory/infectious signal.

Why this works systemically without disrupting homeostasis
- PAMs require endogenous agonist for potentiation, conferring state dependence; α7 agonists desensitize, whereas PAMs maintain signaling within physiologic windows. This reduces risk of broad immunosuppression while allowing robust effects in inflamed, cholinergically engaged tissues. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3162128/?utm_source=openai))

Prospective biomarker assay plan (CLIA-ready where possible)
- TSPO PET/MRI (FEPPA) standardized SUVratio maps of synovium. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42238373/?utm_source=openai))
- SF/plasma sCD14 and sCD163 (ELISA) for screening and pharmacodynamics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4441094/?utm_source=openai))
- HRV (RMSSD/HF power) via 5‑min ECG with standardized posture/breathing.
- Optional synovial fluid α7nAChR expression on CD68+ cells (flow cytometry) in a mechanistic subset. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1365-3083.2009.02266.x?utm_source=openai))

Novelty and prior art check (as of August 11, 2026)
- No randomized KOA trials of α7-PAMs identified; α7-PAMs show antinociceptive/anti-inflammatory activity preclinically and human CNS safety in other indications. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22536953/?utm_source=openai))
- Neural engagement of the same pathway (vagus nerve stimulation) improves RA and shows early OA signals, supporting the tractability of the target circuit but not duplicating the proposed pharmacologic, biomarker-enriched approach. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12823386/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no-go milestones
- At 12 weeks: ≥15% reduction in synovial TSPO SUVratio vs placebo and significant improvement in QST composite.
- At 24 weeks: ≥0.35 SD improvement over placebo in WOMAC Pain, with concordant decreases in sCD14/sCD163.
- At 52 weeks: Slower medial compartment cartilage thinning vs placebo with mediation by earlier synovitis reduction.

Anticipated effect size beyond placebo
- Biomarker-driven selection (high TSPO, high sCD14/sCD163, adequate HRV), objective imaging co-primary, and a mechanism that couples resolution to nociception aim to mitigate high OA placebo responses that otherwise obscure analgesic signals. ([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2797073?utm_source=openai))

Contingencies
- If HRV is low despite synovitis, a brief standardized autonomic activation maneuver (deep-breathing protocol during dosing) will be tested as an exploratory covariate; device-based neuromodulation is not part of the interventional package to preserve atomicity.
- If type I PAM exposure fails to engage targets, consider next‑gen α7 PAMs with improved pharmacokinetics while maintaining activity dependence.

Translational impact
A single, state‑dependent molecular perturbation—amplifying α7nAChR signaling where inflammation has engaged cholinergic tone—links reduction of synovitis (a driver of cartilage loss) to normalization of nociceptive input and central sensitization. This satisfies mechanistic co‑primaries, preserves homeostasis, enables responder preselection, and provides a credible joint‑specific narrative under systemic dosing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4546521/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title: Epitope-fingerprint decoy of the aggrecan 32-mer to couple pain relief with slowed structural progression in osteoarthritis

Hypothesis-and-goal (inseparable)
- In knee/polyarticular OA patients with high flux of aggrecanase-derived neo-epitopes, a systemically administered, fragment-specific decoy that sequesters the aggrecan 32-mer (and predefined companion neo-epitopes) at joint nociceptor/synovial interfaces will (i) extinguish DAMP→TLR2 signaling that drives peripheral input and sensitization, and (ii) dampen local catabolic amplification that accelerates cartilage loss; together yielding clinically meaningful pain reduction and measurable slowing of structural progression. The 32-mer is a validated TLR2 ligand that excites a subset of joint-innervating nociceptors and mediates OA pain, establishing a causal fragment→receptor→pain pathway to intercept. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5926921/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
- Use epitope exposure as a disease fingerprint: bind and neutralize a single, pathology-restricted ligand (the aggrecan 32-mer), not the receptors or the broad protease families that have essential homeostatic roles elsewhere.

Intervention modality
- Systemic 32-mer–trap protein (Decoy-32):
  - Binding domain: humanized, high-affinity binder specific for the 32-mer neo-epitope; cross-reactivity panel pre-specified to include ARGS/NITEGE-bearing aggrecan fragments that co-traffic with the 32-mer but exclude intact aggrecan.
  - Disease-chemistry gating (optional, for safety): intramolecular autoinhibition relieved by mildly acidic, oxidizing, lactate-rich conditions typical of inflamed joints, to minimize off-joint activity under systemic exposure. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26213210/?utm_source=openai))
  - Pericellular enrichment (optional): low-affinity heparan-sulfate–binding motif to transiently dwell in synovial lining and nociceptor glycocalyx, increasing interception probability without stable receptor blockade.
  - Dosing: subcutaneous every 2–4 weeks; systemic by design (intra-articular excluded).

Causal pathway and why this normalizes sensitization and slows structural loss
- Structural cleavage of aggrecan (by ADAMTS-4/5, MMPs) in the interglobular domain releases a defined 32-mer; this fragment activates TLR2 on nociceptors and immune-lineage cells, driving peripheral firing and local mediator release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5926921/?utm_source=openai))
- Other ECM matrikines (e.g., fibronectin fragments) similarly engage TLR2/MyD88 to upregulate inflammatory/catabolic genes; reducing the dominant fragment’s availability weakens this feed-forward loop and lowers protease induction pressure. ([journals.physiology.org](https://journals.physiology.org/doi/full/10.1152/ajpcell.00464.2022?utm_source=openai))
- Removing the upstream fragment signal decreases peripheral drive so downstream central sensitization can renormalize over time; concurrently, reduced DAMP signaling decreases catabolic tone, slowing further cartilage degradation.

Prospective patient selection and pharmacodynamic (PD) confirmation
- Select patients with elevated aggrecanase activity by measuring ARGS and/or NITEGE neo-epitopes in serum (and optionally synovial fluid); these assays are established, quantifiable, and stable enough for enrichment and PD tracking. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24583346/?utm_source=openai))
- On-treatment PD: proportionate fall in circulating/synovial ARGS (and 32-mer if assayable) and reduction in TLR2-driven cytokine signature in synovial fluid cell pellets.

Study plan

Aim 1. Human mechanistic validation (ex vivo)
- Question: Does selective removal of 32-mer from human OA biofluids abrogate nociceptor activation and TLR2-dependent signaling?
- Methods:
  - Collect knee OA synovial fluid (SF) from phenotyped patients; fractionate and quantify ARGS/NITEGE and 32-mer.
  - Use human iPSC-derived nociceptors and primary human DRG neurons in Ca2+-imaging and patch-clamp assays. Compare responses to whole SF, 32-mer–immunodepleted SF, and SF spiked with synthetic/hPLC-purified 32-mer; rescue with Decoy-32.
  - Assess TLR2 dependence via blocking antibody and MyD88 pathway readouts in nociceptors and SF macrophages/fibroblast-like synoviocytes.
- Primary endpoints: reduction of SF-evoked nociceptor firing after 32-mer depletion or Decoy-32; reduction in NF-κB target transcripts in SF cell populations.
- Success criteria: ≥50% reduction in nociceptor activation in high-ARGS SF after Decoy-32; dose–response aligned with measured 32-mer burden.

Aim 2. Engineering and in vivo proof-of-concept
- Question: Can a systemic, fragment-selective decoy reduce pain behavior and structural deterioration with joint specificity?
- Construct engineering:
  - Affinity maturation against authentic human 32-mer; verify no binding to intact aggrecan/G1–G3 domains; evaluate cross-reactivity to ARGS/NITEGE carriers.
  - Incorporate pH/ROS/lactate-responsive autoinhibition; confirm activation only under OA-like conditions. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26213210/?utm_source=openai))
- Rodent models:
  - DMM mouse (cartilage degeneration) and rat MIA (high aggrecanase flux) with systemic Decoy-32 vs control. Serial SF/serum ARGS and 32-mer (if assayable). Weight-bearing asymmetry, von Frey thresholds, gait kinematics for pain; histology and µMRI for structure.
  - Biodistribution: quantify Decoy-32 in joint vs plasma; determine target-mediated drug disposition driven by local fragment concentrations.
- Success criteria: Clinically meaningful pain reduction (≥30% vs placebo) sustained over weeks plus significant reduction in aggrecan neo-epitope flux and improved histologic cartilage integrity.

Aim 3. Translational signal-finding trial (Phase 1b/2a, systemic administration)
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, enriched for high baseline serum ARGS (e.g., top tertile) and MRI risk features; N≈120; SC dosing Q2W for 24 weeks with blinded extension to 48 weeks for structure.
- Endpoints:
  - Primary (Week 12–24): WOMAC pain and KOOS pain responder rates; neuropathic descriptors tracked to monitor central sensitization normalization.
  - Key PD: change in serum ARGS (and 32-mer, if assayable) vs baseline; correlation with pain response.
  - Structural (Week 48): MRI cartilage thickness/volume and T2* mapping; reduced progression vs placebo.
- Joint-specificity narrative under systemic dosing: mass-action partitioning to diseased joints due to high local fragment flux (binding-dependent retention); optional metabolite gating increases functional activity only within inflamed synovial microenvironments. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24583346/?utm_source=openai))
- Placebo-exceeding strategy: mechanistic enrichment by ARGS high-burden phenotype; interim PD futility/continuation rules based on fragment suppression.

Safety and homeostasis
- Avoid receptor blockade and broad protease inhibition; intercept a pathology-restricted fragment. TLR and protease homeostasis elsewhere are preserved; systemic safety is enhanced by disease-chemistry–gated activation. Comparison benchmark: enzyme-directed ADAMTS-5 inhibition is clinically explored, but fragment interception is orthogonal and less likely to perturb normal matrix turnover. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11016567/?utm_source=openai))

Assays and tools
- Biomarkers: validated ELISAs for ARGS/NITEGE in SF and serum; develop LC–MS immuno-enrichment assay for 32-mer to quantify target engagement and exposure–response. ([oarsijournal.com](https://www.oarsijournal.com/article/S1063-4584%2810%2900214-1/fulltext?utm_source=openai))
- Mechanism readouts: ex vivo TLR2 pathway activation; SF cytokine panels.

Go/No-Go criteria
- Go: In Aim 1, ≥50% reduction of nociceptor activation by Decoy-32 in high-ARGS SF and a monotonic relation between 32-mer burden and Decoy-32 effect; in Aim 2, concurrent pain improvement and ARGS suppression with structural benefit trend; in Phase 1b/2a interim, predefined PD drop and ≥15-point placebo-adjusted improvement on WOMAC pain in the enriched subset.
- No-Go: Absent coupling between fragment suppression and pain endpoints; off-target binding to intact aggrecan; systemic safety signals at exposures required for PD effects.

Why this is distinct and feasible
- It directly neutralizes a causative, cartilage-derived DAMP that links structural damage to nociceptor input and catabolic amplification, rather than modulating broad inflammatory axes or blocking nociception. The 32-mer→TLR2→pain mechanism has been demonstrated in relevant models; other matrikines via TLR2/MyD88 support the feed-forward logic we intend to disrupt. The joint microenvironment provides chemical gates for on-target activation, and ARGS/NITEGE assays enable prospective enrichment and real-time PD verification. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5926921/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Systemic, LMW‑hyaluronan–selective decoy to restore joint “pain volume control” in osteoarthritis by keeping DAMP concentrations below PRR activation thresholds

Central hypothesis–question (co-equal)
If low–molecular‑weight hyaluronan (LMW‑HA) fragments generated in osteoarthritic joints are the dominant upstream danger signals that lower nociceptor thresholds via TLR2/4-MyD88 pathways, then systemically administering a high‑affinity, LMW‑HA–selective decoy that preferentially accumulates in diseased joints and hands captured fragments to endogenous scavenger receptors will (a) lower joint DAMP concentrations below pre‑specified receptor activation thresholds; (b) normalize peripheral and central sensitization; and (c) secondarily reduce structural progression—specifically in a biomarker‑defined subset with elevated synovial or serum LMW‑HA:HMW‑HA ratio. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2902571/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Pre-emptive, sub‑threshold DAMP control: maintain in‑joint LMW‑HA concentrations continuously below the TLR2/4 activation regime by selective sequestration and silent clearance, rather than blocking receptors or broadly suppressing inflammation. This preserves beneficial HMW‑HA signaling and joint lubrication while normalizing sensitization drivers. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175954/?utm_source=openai))

Agent concept
- Modality: Systemic biologic “HA-Lite,” a dimeric Fc-silent hyaladherin decoy built from a TSG‑6 Link‑module variant with kinetic preference for short HA oligomers (e.g., 6–40mers) over HMW‑HA. Effector-silent IgG4 Fc (LALA-PG) avoids complement/ADCC. Decoy–LMW‑HA complexes are cleared primarily by Stabilin‑2/HARE in liver/lymph node sinusoidal endothelium and by LYVE‑1 on lymphatic endothelium (“silent scavenging”). No intra-articular delivery. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0969212600001635?utm_source=openai))
- Joint specificity narrative: Preferential exposure and retention in diseased joints via increased synovial permeability and avid, reversible interactions with exposed glycosaminoglycans; on-target engagement occurs where LMW‑HA is produced and retained. Optional cartilage‑anchoring variant (WYRGRL tag) will be explored only after demonstrating adequate joint exposure, to increase dwell time in cartilage‑adjacent compartments. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8101446/?utm_source=openai))
- Constraint checks: Avoids IL‑1 axis, MMP inhibition, and NGF blockade; spares HMW‑HA functions; normalizes sensitization upstream of nociception; systemic route only; target is a pathology‑generated ligand rather than an essential homeostatic pathway. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175954/?utm_source=openai))

Mechanistic evidence base anchoring the question
- LMW‑HA is an endogenous DAMP in OA that activates TLR2/4–MyD88 and drives catabolic and inflammatory programs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2902571/?utm_source=openai))
- TLR4 is expressed by primary sensory neurons, and DAMPs can directly excite nociceptors via TLR4; these signals also propagate through synovial innate cells to sensitize nociceptors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3519737/?utm_source=openai))
- HMW‑HA exerts anti‑hyperalgesic effects via CD44/TLR4 crosstalk; therefore, sparing HMW‑HA is desirable. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175954/?utm_source=openai))
- HA molecular weight distribution in synovial fluid is measurable and associates with OA progression, enabling prospective enrichment by an elevated LMW‑HA:HMW‑HA ratio. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375131/?utm_source=openai))
- Stabilin‑2/HARE and LYVE‑1 mediate endocytic clearance of HA and HA complexes, providing native, noninflammatory sinks for decoy–fragment complexes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7279005/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Specify the causal pathway and activation thresholds in human-relevant matrices.
- Determine LMW‑HA concentration–response curves for TLR2/4 activation (NF‑κB reporter) in human synovial macrophage/fibroblast co‑cultures and DRG‑neuron/Schwann cell co‑cultures using size‑fractionated human OA synovial fluid (SEC‑MALS). Define pre‑specified “activation thresholds” and verify reversal with HA‑Lite. Link to neuronal outcomes (Ca2+ imaging, rheobase, TRPV1/TRPA1/Nav1.7 expression). Controls: TLR2/4 antagonism and MyD88 inhibition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375131/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer and validate an LMW‑HA–selective decoy that spares HMW‑HA and routes complexes to silent scavenging.
- Protein engineering: Start with human TSG‑6 Link‑module scaffold; tune oligomer-length selectivity by mutating aromatic/basic residues in the Link groove; screen by SPR/biolayer interferometry using defined HA oligomers versus HMW‑HA; down‑select variants with ≥50‑fold preference for oligomers ≤40mers. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0969212600001635?utm_source=openai))
- Fc engineering: IgG4‑S228P LALA‑PG to ablate FcγR/C1q; confirm no immune complex effector activity.
- Scavenger handoff: Demonstrate rapid uptake of fluorescent decoy–LMW‑HA complexes by Stabilin‑2/HARE and LYVE‑1 cell lines and primary liver/lymphatic endothelial cells; block with anti‑Stabilin‑2 or LYVE‑1 siRNA to prove pathway. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7279005/?utm_source=openai))
- Sparing of HMW‑HA biology: Verify preserved CD44/TLR4‑dependent anti‑hyperalgesic signaling and lubrication surrogates in vitro when HMW‑HA is present. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175954/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Demonstrate pharmacology, joint selectivity, and analgesic–structural coupling in vivo.
- Models: DMM mouse (structural OA) and collagenase‑induced OA rat (synovitis‑rich). Dose HA‑Lite IV q1–2 weeks.
- PK/BD: Whole‑body and joint biodistribution; synovial versus plasma target engagement (free versus bound LMW‑HA); optional WYRGRL‑tagged variant if joint exposure is suboptimal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8101446/?utm_source=openai))
- Pharmacodynamics along the pre‑specified pathway: 
  1) Lower synovial LMW‑HA:HMW‑HA ratio (SEC‑MALS). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375131/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Reduced TLR2/4 pathway activation in joint tissue lysates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2902571/?utm_source=openai))
  3) Normalized nociceptor excitability (ex vivo DRG electrophysiology) and decreased spinal dorsal horn pERK/IBA1 (central sensitization proxies). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4626273/?utm_source=openai))
  4) Structural slowing: MRI‑based cartilage thickness/T2 mapping and histologic OARSI scores at 8–12 weeks.
- Behavior: Weight‑bearing asymmetry, spontaneous activity, and conditioned pain modulation readouts to capture peripheral–central coupling.
- Safety: Hematology/chemistry, glycosaminoglycan panels, liver function; monitor global HA homeostasis.

Aim 4. Early clinical test in a biomarker‑enriched OA endotype.
- Design: Phase 1b/2a, randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled, 16 weeks, IV HA‑Lite q3 weeks.
- Population: Symptomatic knee OA (KL 2–3), MRI‑synovitis present, and elevated LMW‑HA:HMW‑HA ratio in synovial fluid or serum (assay validated in Aim 1; fallback to minimally invasive serum test if SF unavailable). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375131/?utm_source=openai))
- Primary endpoint: Change in WOMAC Pain and quantitative sensory testing (pressure pain thresholds, temporal summation).
- Key secondary: MRI cartilage thickness/T2; change in synovial LMW‑HA:HMW‑HA; ex vivo whole‑blood TLR4 reporter activity; rescue‑medication sparing.
- Causal‑pathway success criteria (all must move in the predicted direction): 
  1) ≥40% reduction in free LMW‑HA in SF/serum; 
  2) ≥30% reduction in TLR reporter activity; 
  3) increased nociceptive thresholds on QST; 
  4) slowed cartilage thinning versus placebo.
- Placebo‑mitigation strategy: Endotype enrichment by HA‑MW distribution; objective biochemical and imaging co‑primary/secondary endpoints; pre‑registered thresholds.

Key experimental methods and analytics
- HA size fractionation/quantification: SEC‑MALS and agarose‑gel electrophoresis; exploratory nanopore sizing for heavy‑chain–modified HA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4721052/?utm_source=openai))
- DRG assays: Calcium imaging/electrophysiology with LMW‑HA fractions; TLR‑dependence confirmed pharmacologically and by siRNA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3519737/?utm_source=openai))
- Scavenger uptake imaging: Live‑cell confocal with HARE/LYVE‑1 lines; liver sinusoidal endothelial cell uptake kinetics. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7279005/?utm_source=openai))

Joint selectivity rationale to be prospectively tested
- Disease‑localized ligand production and retention (LMW‑HA enriched in OA synovia); 
- Inflamed synovium permeability increases local decoy exposure; 
- Optional cartilage anchoring (WYRGRL) to extend joint dwell if necessary. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4375131/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Off‑target sequestration of HMW‑HA: address via length‑selective engineering and competitive binding assays; stop‑rules if serum viscosity or HA physiology changes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175954/?utm_source=openai))
- Immune complex deposition: minimized by Fc‑silent design and rapid handoff to HARE/LYVE‑1 clearance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7279005/?utm_source=openai))
- Systemic immunomodulation: monitor cytokines; mechanism does not block TLRs, it lowers one DAMP below threshold.

Go/no‑go gates
- Go to IND‑enabling if: (a) ≥10‑fold in vivo reduction of free LMW‑HA in OA joints vs. plasma; (b) ≥30% normalization of DRG excitability and ≥30% reduction in spinal pERK; (c) significant analgesia with concordant reductions in DAMP/TLR biomarkers; (d) structural benefit trend in MRI/histology at 8–12 weeks. 
- No‑go if HMW‑HA signaling is impaired or systemic HA homeostasis perturbed.

Why this proposal is the right test of the question
- It operationalizes a single global perturbation—keep a joint‑generated DAMP below its activation threshold—to re‑establish endogenous “volume control” over pain without broad immunosuppression, aligns with measurable activation thresholds and endotype selection, and provides a coherent causal chain from structure → DAMPs → receptor activation → sensitization → pain, with built‑in structural readouts. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2902571/?utm_source=openai))

Title
Orthogonal marrow niche rewiring with localized immune polarity inversion to eradicate LSCs under non‑genotoxic allo‑HSCT conditioning

Central question/hypothesis
Can we convert the bone marrow into a privileged survival niche for donor HSCs that LSCs cannot use, and simultaneously localize multi‑axis immune pressure (anti‑PD‑1/PD‑L1, anti‑CD47, NK recruitment) within the marrow, so that reduced‑intensity allo‑HSCT achieves relapse control comparable to or better than MAC without systemic genotoxicity or excess GVHD? The hypothesis rests on: (i) LSC retention and quiescence via CXCL12/CXCR4, VLA‑4/VCAM‑1, E‑selectin and trophic inputs including SCF/c‑KIT, THPO/MPL, and Ang‑1/Tie2; (ii) immune escape after allo‑HCT via HLA loss/downregulation and checkpoint upregulation; and (iii) the capacity of NK effectors to mediate GVL with relatively low GVHD risk. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai)) ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18371409/?utm_source=openai)) ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/133/12/1290/260469/Mechanisms-of-immune-escape-after-allogeneic?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Recode niche compatibility: provide donor HSCs with an orthogonal trophic axis (engineered receptor–ligand pairs) that is unavailable to LSCs, while locally suppressing native SCF/THPO/Ang‑1 signals and inverting immune signaling polarity in the marrow (recruit effectors and neutralize evasion cues in situ). This single change of “who can read the niche signals” forces LSCs off their survival supports and exposes them to localized, multi‑mechanism immune killing, compensating for the loss of MAC cytotoxicity. Orthogonal cytokine–receptor pairs are clinically plausible from prior IL‑2/IL‑2R work and can be adapted conceptually to hematopoietic trophic axes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build an orthogonal trophic channel for donor HSCs and withdraw native trophic support from LSCs within marrow.
- Engineer donor HSCs ex vivo to express orthogonal variants of key trophic receptors (prototype: MPL*, KIT*), and deliver marrow‑anchored orthogonal ligands (THPO*, SCF*) via ECM‑binding fusions to confine activity to bone marrow. As a counter‑field, locally neutralize native THPO/SCF/Ang‑1 signals with marrow‑anchored decoys/aptamers activated by leukemia‑associated proteases. Readouts: donor HSC engraftment/lineage reconstitution; loss of LSC quiescence, detachment from niche, and apoptosis/clearance; preservation of host stromal integrity.
- Rationale: THPO/MPL, SCF/c‑KIT and Ang‑1/Tie2 sustain HSC quiescence and are co‑opted by AML/LSCs; depriving native inputs selectively stresses LSCs, while orthogonal ligands maintain donor HSC fitness. Engineered ligand biasing of c‑KIT signaling and orthogonal IL‑2/IL‑2R precedents support feasibility of selective trophic wiring. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18371409/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5526607/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Create a bone‑marrow–anchored “polarity inversion” field that co‑recruits effectors and disables evasion locally.
- Construct a marrow‑retained chemo‑immunologic scaffold that: (i) displays ECM‑tethered chemokines (e.g., CXCL9/10 motifs) to recruit CXCR3+ donor NK/T effectors; (ii) presents protease‑activated PD‑L1 “Probody” traps and SIRPα decoys to neutralize PD‑1/PD‑L1 and CD47 “don’t‑eat‑me” signals where leukemia remodeling is highest; and (iii) includes collagen‑binding cytokine modules (e.g., IL‑15/IL‑12 analogs) to sustain NK cytotoxicity without systemic exposure. Readouts: spatial drug activation, local checkpoint consumption, NK recruitment/activation, phagocytosis, minimal systemic cytokinemia, and GVHD indices.
- Rationale: Protease‑activatable anti‑PD‑L1 agents demonstrate intratumoral activation; collagen‑anchored immunocytokines increase local bioavailability and reduce systemic toxicity; SIRPα decoys trigger macrophage phagocytosis and can aid NK activity. Bone/marrow anchoring can be achieved through ECM‑binding domains and/or bisphosphonate‑based hydroxyapatite targeting. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8311335/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7811803/?utm_source=openai)) ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/27/8/2190/672069/Phase-I-Study-of-the-CD47-Blocker-TTI-621-in?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9195145/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Test temporal uncoupling: transiently dismantle physical retention before delivering a short‑lived donor NK pulse.
- Evaluate marrow‑localized CXCR4 and/or E‑selectin antagonism to transiently release LSCs from protective contacts, followed by a brief infusion of donor NK or CAR‑NK cells targeting an LSC‑restricted antigen (e.g., CLEC12A) with built‑in safety off‑switch. Readouts: LSC mobilization kinetics, niche occupancy changes, NK infiltration and kill, MRD clearance, and GVHD safety.
- Rationale: CXCR4/E‑selectin antagonists mobilize AML cells and have been combined with therapy; allo‑NKs can target HLA‑loss clones with lower GVHD liability than T cells, complementing localized checkpoint/CD47 blockade. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7499473/?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Study design overview
- Platform: RIC/NMA allo‑HSCT in preclinical humanized AML models and an early‑phase clinical pilot in high‑risk AML candidates for RIC allo‑HCT. No genotoxic conditioning beyond standard RIC/NMA backbones; exclude busulfan/TBI per constraint.
- Modules and sequence: (1) Orthogonal donor HSCs + marrow‑anchored orthogonal ligands (engraftment privilege); (2) marrow‑anchored polarity inversion scaffold (checkpoint/CD47 traps + chemokine/cytokine recruitment); (3) timed, short‑persistence donor NK/CAR‑NK pulse post‑displacement.
- Controls: matched RIC allo‑HSCT alone; RIC + NK without niche rewiring; and, where ethical, MAC historical benchmarks for relapse. Co‑primary endpoints: 1‑year relapse incidence and GVHD grade II–IV. Key secondary endpoints: MRD negativity at day +100, donor chimerism, time to neutrophil/platelet engraftment, non‑relapse mortality, and immune biomarker spatial gradients.

Mechanistic validation and readouts
- Niche compatibility switch: single‑cell RNA/ATAC and phospho‑signaling of donor HSCs and LSCs under native vs orthogonal trophic inputs; in situ proximity ligation to confirm orthogonal receptor engagement only on donor HSCs; functional readouts of quiescence exit/apoptosis in LSCs.
- Polarity inversion: spatial proteomics to quantify PD‑L1 trap activation and CD47 blockade in marrow; intravital microscopy for NK recruitment and phagocyte synapse formation; systemic cytokine profiling for off‑target activation.
- Temporal uncoupling: live‑tracking of LSC mobilization vs NK arrival; kill efficiency vs simultaneous delivery.

Statistical/scientific milestones
- Go/no‑go 1: donor engraftment non‑inferior to RIC controls with reduced LSC markers in marrow niches (power for 20–30% relative reduction). 
- Go/no‑go 2: localized checkpoint/CD47 target occupancy ≥ predefined intramarrow threshold with minimal systemic engagement; absence of excess acute GVHD vs RIC.
- Go/no‑go 3: composite relapse endpoint at 12 months non‑inferior to MAC historical rates with equal or lower grade III–IV GVHD.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Orthogonal axis specificity: risk of cross‑talk with native receptors. Mitigation: use validated orthogonal design principles (loss‑of‑function in native binding interface plus gain‑of‑function complementary mutations) and marrow‑anchored ligands to confine exposure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))
- LSC trophic heterogeneity: some clones may be less dependent on THPO/SCF/Tie2. Mitigation: combine trophic withdrawal with polarity inversion and NK pulse; stratify by MPL/Tie2/KIT expression and CXCR4/VLA‑4/E‑selectin levels. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9820412/?utm_source=openai))
- Checkpoint/CD47 blockade toxicity: anemia/thrombocytopenia and systemic inflammation. Mitigation: marrow anchoring and protease‑activated traps to limit peripheral exposure; select SIRPα decoy formats with minimal erythrocyte binding. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/23/4/1068/122917/TTI-621-SIRP-Fc-A-CD47-Blocking-Innate-Immune?utm_source=openai))
- Mobilization‑related leukostasis: employ local marrow‑retained antagonists and monitor mobilization kinetics; sequence NK infusion after transient displacement window based on biomarker timing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7499473/?utm_source=openai))
- NK persistence/efficacy: insufficient dwell time. Mitigation: local IL‑15/12 support via collagen‑anchored modules; CAR specificity to CLEC12A where appropriate; preserve safety with short‑lived products/suicide switches. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11292205/?utm_source=openai))

Why this fulfills the constraints
- Compensates for lost MAC cytotoxicity by removing LSC trophic supports and adding localized, multi‑axis immune pressure without systemic genotoxic injury. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai))
- Excludes busulfan/TBI; interventions are signaling/microenvironmental and spatially confined.
- LSC‑selectivity with preserved HSC engraftment via orthogonal niche privilege. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5947856/?utm_source=openai))
- Overcomes marrow sanctuary: dismantles adhesion (temporal uncoupling) and replaces survival cues LSCs rely on, while recruiting effectors into those microdomains. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7367216/?utm_source=openai))
- Counters immune evasion in parallel: HLA‑loss addressed by NK; PD‑L1 and CD47 neutralized locally. ([ashpublications.org](https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/133/12/1290/260469/Mechanisms-of-immune-escape-after-allogeneic?utm_source=openai)) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8311335/?utm_source=openai))
- Enhances GVL without exacerbating GVHD by marrow localization and NK‑favored biology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12482124/?utm_source=openai))

Anticipated impact
If successful, this program establishes niche‑level compatibility engineering plus localized polarity inversion as a generalizable, non‑genotoxic path to eradicate LSCs in RIC/NMA allo‑HSCT, matching or surpassing MAC relapse control while reducing systemic toxicity and GVHD.

Title
Marrow-confined, replication-gated oncolytic adenovirus to restore MAC-grade graft-versus-leukemia under antibody-only conditioning in AML

Question/Hypothesis (undistinguished)
Can an intramedullary, leukemia-selective oncolytic adenovirus that locally expresses a CLL-1–directed T‑cell engager, a CD47 checkpoint trap (SIRPα‑Fc), and the CXCR3 chemokine ligand CXCL10 convert the leukemia-permissive marrow niche into a confined immune “hot spot,” thereby restoring or exceeding myeloablative-conditioning (MAC)–level disease control while preserving donor HSC engraftment and avoiding GVHD under non-genotoxic, antibody-based conditioning? This rests on three established premises: (i) RIC/NMA increases relapse versus MAC due to weaker cytotoxic/inflammatory priming; (ii) CLL‑1 (CLEC12A) is present on AML blasts/LSCs and largely absent on normal HSCs; (iii) oncolytic vectors can safely deliver BiTEs/checkpoint traps/chemokines for localized, multi-axis immune activation. ([astctjournal.org](https://www.astctjournal.org/article/S2666-6367%2821%2900718-1/fulltext?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Replace MAC’s systemic cytotoxic priming with a single, spatially confined switch: intramedullary, replication‑gated virotherapy that ignites multi-pronged, HLA‑independent, macrophage‑ and T‑cell–mediated GVL within marrow while leaving non-marrow tissues—and thus GVHD risk—unperturbed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8411207/?utm_source=openai))

Rationale and background
- Relapse after allo‑HCT remains higher with RIC/NMA than with MAC across myeloid malignancies; the survival advantage of MAC often reflects superior relapse control despite more toxicity. The proposal aims to deliver MAC‑equivalent GVL without MAC’s systemic genotoxicity. ([astctjournal.org](https://www.astctjournal.org/article/S2666-6367%2821%2900718-1/fulltext?utm_source=openai))
- The marrow niche protects LSCs via retention and quiescence; effective targeting must work in situ. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery/article/9/5/OF11/42067/CXCL12-Has-Niche-Specific-Roles-in-Leukemia-Stem?utm_source=openai))
- CLL‑1 (CLEC12A, CD371) is present on most AML blasts and a majority of LSC‑enriched fractions but is not detected on CD34+CD38− normal HSCs—affording LSC selectivity critical for preserving engraftment. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8457079/?utm_source=openai))
- Oncolytic vectors can express BiTEs, SIRPα‑Fc, and CXCL9/10‑CXCL10 to recruit and enable donor effectors while keeping checkpoint/anti‑phagocytic blockade local—mitigating the known GVHD risk of systemic checkpoint blockade post‑allo‑HCT. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/doi/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-17-2651/352753/p/Targeted-BiTE-Expression-by-an-Oncolytic-Vector?utm_source=openai))
- Intramedullary delivery and replication gating (tumor‑selective promoters; miRNA detargeting) are established methods to confine activity to marrow leukemia and spare HSCs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4852145/?utm_source=openai))
- Non‑genotoxic antibody conditioning (e.g., anti‑CD117/briquilimab) can enable engraftment without busulfan/TBI and fits the constraint set. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9118867/?utm_source=openai))

Study objective
Demonstrate that marrow-confined OV‑GVL achieves relapse incidence ≤ MAC while maintaining donor HSC engraftment and low GVHD under antibody-only conditioning.

Intervention: OV design, targeting, and gating
- Vector: E1A/E1B-competent oncolytic adenovirus (Ad5/Ad5F35) with AML‑selective replication (survivin/BIRC5 promoter or E2F‑responsive control of E1A) and miRNA detargeting using HSC‑high miR‑126 targets in essential viral transcripts to suppress replication in normal HSCs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6542078/?utm_source=openai))
- Transgenes (polycistronic, 2A-linked):
  1) Anti‑CD3×anti‑CLL‑1 BiTE for HLA‑independent T‑cell killing of CLL‑1+ LSCs/blasts. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2020.599933/full?utm_source=openai))
  2) Secreted SIRPα‑Fc to neutralize CD47 locally and license macrophage phagocytosis and cross‑presentation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7053234/?utm_source=openai))
  3) CXCL10 to attract CXCR3+ donor CD8/NK/NKT cells to the marrow where the virus is present. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9450898/?utm_source=openai))
- Delivery: Intramedullary (femoral/iliac) injections into leukemia‑involved sites under imaging guidance 72–48 h before graft infusion to allow initial oncolysis/antigen release; a second dose at day +7 in high‑burden models if required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4852145/?utm_source=openai))
- Conditioning: Anti‑CD117 (briquilimab/JSP191)–based, busulfan/TBI‑free platform ± minimal immunosuppression per antibody‑conditioning protocols; avoid systemic checkpoint inhibitors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9118867/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims and experiments

Aim 1: Engineer and validate marrow‑confined AML‑selective OV.
- Construct and test replication control (survivin/E2F promoters; miR‑126 detargeting) for selective lysis of primary human AML/LSC‑enriched fractions while sparing CD34+CD38− HSCs from healthy donors in 3D vascularized marrow‑on‑a‑chip and co‑culture with stromal cells. Endpoints: replication (qPCR), cytolysis, HSC colony formation, off‑target cytotoxicity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6542078/?utm_source=openai))
- Verify functional secretion/binding of SIRPα‑Fc and BiTE and expression of CXCL10; demonstrate enhanced macrophage phagocytosis of AML and T‑cell cytotoxicity in the presence of BiTE; note that OV‑encoded BiTEs and SIRPα‑Fc are validated modalities in prior studies. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/doi/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-17-2651/352753/p/Targeted-BiTE-Expression-by-an-Oncolytic-Vector?utm_source=openai))

Go/no‑go criteria: ≥2‑log selective kill of AML versus normal HSCs; no impairment of HSC CFU beyond vehicle; nanomolar-range BiTE activity; local (culture supernatant) but not “systemic” (media exchange reservoir) checkpoint trap accumulation in chip.

Aim 2: Define safe/efficacious intramedullary dosing and timing in vivo relative to allo‑HCT.
- Models: (i) NSG mice engrafted intrafemorally with primary human AML; (ii) immunocompetent AML models (e.g., C1498) transduced to express human CLL‑1 for BiTE engageability.
- Intervention: Intramedullary OV vs vehicle 72–48 h pre‑transplant; conditioning with anti‑CD117‑based antibody regimen (murine surrogate) without busulfan/TBI; then transplant allogeneic marrow and T cells (dose‑ranged to model clinical allo). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4852145/?utm_source=openai))
- Readouts: 
  - On‑target confinement: biodistribution (qPCR) shows marrow>>blood/liver/lung.
  - Engraftment: donor chimerism; CFU‑spleen; HSC homing.
  - Niche immunity: marrow CXCL10 gradient; influx of CXCR3+ CD8/NK; macrophage phagocytosis markers; absence of systemic cytokinemia.
  - Safety: GVHD scores/pathology; hematologic toxicity to donor HSCs.
- Rationale: Intratumoral/marrow‑local transgene expression mitigates systemic PD‑1/PD‑L1 blockade–associated GVHD risks reported post‑allo‑HCT. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39635535/?utm_source=openai))

Go/no‑go criteria: No delay in neutrophil/platelet recovery vs antibody‑conditioning control; GVHD not increased; ≥1‑log marrow AML reduction at day +21; virus confined to injected bones and draining marrow.

Aim 3: Efficacy versus RIC alone and versus MAC benchmark; mechanism of relapse prevention.
- Arms: (A) Antibody conditioning + allo‑HCT (control), (B) + intramedullary OV (test), (C) MAC (busulfan/TBI) + allo‑HCT (historical and small‑animal MAC positive control). Primary endpoint: 90‑day relapse incidence; secondary endpoints: OS, LSC frequency (limiting dilution xenograft), MRD negativity, GVHD.
- Mechanism: necessity tests with macrophage depletion, T‑cell depletion, and CLL‑1 blockade; rescue with BiTE‑negative or SIRPα‑Fc–negative virus variants to quantify contribution of each payload.

Success criteria aligned to research goal
- Relapse rate (and time‑to‑relapse) in Arm B statistically non‑inferior to or better than Arm C (MAC) with equal/less GVHD and preserved engraftment; Arm B superior to Arm A (antibody conditioning alone). ([astctjournal.org](https://www.astctjournal.org/article/S2666-6367%2821%2900718-1/fulltext?utm_source=openai))

Key design safeguards
- Target choice to preserve engraftment: CLL‑1 absent on CD34+CD38− HSCs reduces on‑target HSC toxicity risk; CD123 avoided for BiTE cargo due to known HSPC depletion potential. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/25/4/1358/9696/An-Anti-CLL-1-Antibody-Drug-Conjugate-for-the?utm_source=openai))
- Replication gating: survivin/E2F promoters plus miR‑126 detargeting to abort replication in HSCs. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6542078/?utm_source=openai))
- Spatial gating: intramedullary delivery limits systemic exposure; supports localized chemokine and checkpoint‑trap gradients. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4852145/?utm_source=openai))
- Immunobiology: local SIRPα‑Fc and BiTE avoid systemic checkpoint/CD47 blockade that can provoke GVHD; CXCL10 focuses donor CXCR3+ effectors into marrow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7053234/?utm_source=openai))

Statistical and operational plan
- Power: For murine relapse endpoints, n≥12/arm yields ≥80% power to detect 35% absolute relapse reduction (two‑sided α=0.05). Survival by log‑rank; competing risk for relapse vs NRM; GVHD grade by ordinal models.
- Manufacturability: Ad5/Ad5F35 backbone; payload size within adenoviral capacity; GMP‑compatible producer cell lines and purification.
- Safety monitoring: viral shedding PCR; anti‑adenovirus neutralizing antibodies; off‑target transgene in serum; stopping rules for GVHD, delayed engraftment, or systemic cytokines.

Contingencies
- Antigen escape: switch/stack BiTE against CD33 or dual CLL‑1/CD33 CODV; track with flow/MRD. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2162402X.2021.1945803?utm_source=openai))
- Inadequate T‑cell recruitment: replace/add CXCL9 or IL‑15 “cassette” in the same locus; both are validated in OV platforms. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6951834/?utm_source=openai))
- Residual systemic exposure: tighten detargeting by adding additional HSC‑high miRNA targets; reduce infectious dose.

Milestones
- Year 1: Complete vector engineering; in vitro selectivity and function; marrow‑chip safety. 
- Year 2: Intramedullary dosing/timing and biodistribution; proof of preserved engraftment and low GVHD in allo‑HCT models. 
- Year 3: Head‑to‑head efficacy versus MAC benchmark; IND‑enabling tox (biodistribution, shedding, germline).

Anticipated impact
If successful, this marrow‑confined OV strategy provides a non‑genotoxic path to MAC‑grade relapse control by restoring multi‑axis GVL exactly where LSCs live, while maintaining engraftment and avoiding GVHD‑amplifying systemic immunotherapy exposures. It directly addresses LSC sanctuary, HLA loss, anti‑phagocytic signaling, and T‑cell exclusion through a single, local, programmable agent. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery/article/9/5/OF11/42067/CXCL12-Has-Niche-Specific-Roles-in-Leukemia-Stem?utm_source=openai))

Appendix: key evidence points supporting feasibility
- RIC relapse disadvantage vs MAC; need for safer GVL restoration. ([astctjournal.org](https://www.astctjournal.org/article/S2666-6367%2821%2900718-1/fulltext?utm_source=openai))
- CLL‑1 as LSC target absent on normal HSCs. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/25/4/1358/9696/An-Anti-CLL-1-Antibody-Drug-Conjugate-for-the?utm_source=openai))
- OV‑encoded BiTEs, SIRPα‑Fc, and CXCL9/10 validated preclinically; local expression mitigates systemic toxicity. ([aacrjournals.org](https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/doi/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-17-2651/352753/p/Targeted-BiTE-Expression-by-an-Oncolytic-Vector?utm_source=openai))
- Intramedullary viral delivery is operationally routine in mice and translatable to targeted human marrow access. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4852145/?utm_source=openai))
- Systemic PD‑1/PD‑L1 blockade around allo‑HCT raises GVHD risk; local expression is preferred. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39635535/?utm_source=openai))
- Antibody‑only conditioning (anti‑CD117) offers non‑genotoxic engraftment platform compatible with the constraints. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9118867/?utm_source=openai))
