text:
Title
Intracellular temporal archiving of mRNA using time‑gated mesoporous silica nanocarriers for per‑cell multi‑timepoint transcriptomics

Hypothesis–question
Can programmable in‑cell temporal archiving of cytosolic mRNA—implemented by mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) that expose RNA‑capture surfaces at log‑spaced moments—yield accurate, same‑cell transcriptome trajectories over 0.5–24 h after a defined perturbation, and thereby provide a ground‑truth dataset to evaluate whether sparse, non‑destructive live measurements can reconstruct full cellular response movies? We posit that replacing repeated extraction with in‑cell storage overcomes the viability and throughput limits of serial aspiration while remaining mechanistically distinct from photoactivated single‑shot capture, metabolic labeling, or pseudotime inference. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05046-9?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Record first, read once: embed a multi‑gate “flight recorder” inside each living cell that, at seven programmed times, transiently presents barcoded capture chemistries to sequester and protect a small, minimally perturbative fraction of the cytosolic mRNA pool. After the final timepoint, perform one terminal lysis and sequencing to recover the per‑cell, per‑timepoint transcriptome series.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer time‑gated RNA‑capture MSNs for intracellular temporal archiving.
- Particle architecture: 80–120 nm MSNs with seven spatially segregated pore domains. Each domain bears an inner surface of mixed capture oligos (poly(dT) for polyadenylated mRNAs plus partially degenerate primers to sample non‑polyA tails), covalently linked to a unique DNA time‑barcode (T1–T7). Pore mouths are occluded by orthogonal, biocompatible molecular gates that open on command at t = 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h. Visible‑light photocleavable ruthenium complexes and/or bioorthogonal cleavage chemistries provide wavelength/trigger selectivity with low phototoxicity. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32481603/?utm_source=openai))
- Cytosolic access: surface coatings (low‑MW PEI or PAMAM dendrons) and/or photochemical endosomal‑escape modules (red/NIR photosensitizers) promote escape following endocytosis, with parameters tuned to minimize toxicity. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nn900918w?utm_source=openai))
- RNA preservation: adsorption within silica mesopores stabilizes RNA against nucleases until endpoint extraction, supporting delayed readout without degradation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3511576/?utm_source=openai))
Deliverable: a validated MSN formulation demonstrating orthogonal, seven‑step gating and cytosolic residency with cell viability >90% over 24 h.

Aim 2. Calibrate capture efficiency, perturbation load, and temporal fidelity in living cells.
- Model system: clonal HEK293T and one primary‑like line (e.g., RPE1). At t = 0, administer a defined perturbation (drug or CRISPRi/a inducer). Apply the seven triggers at logarithmically spaced times. At 24 h, lyse and perform library prep that preserves the time‑barcode on each captured molecule.
- Controls and references:
  1) Single‑shot photoactivated mRNA capture (TIVA) at select timepoints to benchmark on‑demand intracellular capture without multi‑bin archiving. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))
  2) Sequential Live‑seq on matched conditions to compare against invasive serial cytoplasmic biopsies. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05046-9?utm_source=openai))
  3) Bulk metabolic‑labeling controls (no single‑cell trajectories) to ensure the perturbation elicits expected kinetic waves.
- Calibration outcomes:
  • Per‑bin capture fraction and bias: estimate gene‑length, GC, and half‑life dependencies; adjust oligo composition and pore density to keep sink fraction low (target <1–2% of cellular mRNA per bin).  
  • Timing accuracy: quantify gate opening kinetics and effective sampling window per bin by co‑encapsulated fluorogenic sentinels.  
  • Minimal perturbation: verify unaltered growth and pathway readouts versus MSN‑free cells and versus TIVA single‑activation.
Success criteria: per cell, cumulative detection of ≥3,000 genes across bins with per‑bin UMIs sufficient to reconstruct coarse dynamics; inter‑bin consistency with independent destructive scRNA‑seq at those times (Pearson r ≥ 0.7 at pseudo‑bulk level).

Aim 3. Generate same‑cell response trajectories at scale and test reconstruction from sparse live signals.
- Data production: process ≥10,000 cells per condition, yielding seven‑timepoint trajectories per cell under one or more perturbations at t = 0. Log‑spaced gates capture fast induction and slow relaxation phases.
- “Reference movie” and decoding test: Fit a dynamical state‑space model to clonal replicate cells’ multi‑bin data to obtain a high‑fidelity ground truth of response trajectories. Then, prospectively evaluate whether partial, non‑destructive live measurements (e.g., intracellular SERS nanoprobes for a small, pathway‑tiled miRNA/mRNA panel) suffice to reconstruct full transcriptomes when decoded against the ground truth. Prior work demonstrates intracellular SERS/aptamer sensing of nucleic acids; here it is used only as a compressed, repeatable channel against which to test reconstruction fidelity. Primary endpoint is reconstruction error versus the archived trajectories, not SERS per se. ([opg.optica.org](https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=as-56-2-150&utm_source=openai))
Success criteria: with seven repeated live reads per cell, compressed‑signal decoding achieves gene‑set–level (pathway) dynamics within 10–20% error relative to MSN‑archived trajectories; single‑gene dynamics recovered for fast responders with F1 ≥ 0.7.

Experimental plan and methods
1) Synthesis and characterization
- Fabricate MSNs with seven gated domains by spatially selective functionalization (masked deposition or sequential orthogonal silanization) to segregate capture surfaces and triggers. Confirm pore size (8–12 nm), surface chemistries, and gate integrity by TEM, nitrogen sorption, and fluorogenic gate‑opening assays.
- Attach time‑barcoded capture oligos via stable linkers; validate sequence retention after simulated intracellular conditions.

2) Cell delivery and cytosolic access
- Optimize coatings for uptake and endosomal escape (PEI, PAMAM dendrons; photosensitizer‑mediated escape). Quantify cytosolic localization by split‑GFP cytosol reporters and endosome markers; titrate dose to maintain viability. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nn900918w?utm_source=openai))

3) Temporal gating
- Use seven triggers: either wavelength‑multiplexed visible‑light photocleavage or a hybrid schedule (two light triggers + five small‑molecule cleavages). Measure opening half‑times in cells and align to a 0.5–24 h log grid. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32481603/?utm_source=openai))

4) Library preparation and sequencing
- At end of timeline, lyse single cells, magnetically isolate MSNs, elute captured RNAs, and build sequencing libraries that retain the time‑barcode as a read index. Demultiplex to obtain per‑cell, per‑timepoint expression matrices.

5) Reconstruction test with sparse live readouts (optional)
- Introduce a small panel (10–50) of intracellular SERS nanoprobes targeting mRNAs/miRNAs across early, intermediate, and late pathways. Perform low‑power Raman reads at the same seven times. Train a decoder mapping SERS vectors to full expression states using MSN‑archived trajectories as supervision. Evaluate generalization on held‑out cells and perturbations. ([opg.optica.org](https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=as-56-2-150&utm_source=openai))

Data analysis
- Quality control per bin; normalization across bins using spike‑in captured standards embedded in each domain.
- Dynamics inference: fit per‑cell ODE‑regularized models to denoise bin‑wise counts while preserving temporal order; estimate response onsets, peaks, and relaxation times for each gene and pathway.
- Heterogeneity analysis: cluster trajectories; quantify variability in timing and amplitude; relate to cell‑cycle phase and baseline chromatin markers if available.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Low capture yield per bin: increase pore density and the number of particles per cell while keeping sink fraction <2%; enrich for polyA+ with higher‑affinity oligos; extend read depth.  
- Endosomal retention: employ combined PEI/PAMAM and photochemical escape; redesign particles with fusogenic lipids. ([pubs.acs.org](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/nn900918w?utm_source=openai))  
- Phototoxicity or off‑target gate opening: shift to visible/NIR‑responsive gates; calibrate light dose; include dark controls. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32481603/?utm_source=openai))  
- Novelty overlap: contrasts with TIVA (single photoactivation, no multi‑bin archive), Live‑seq (serial aspiration), and RNA timestamps (genetic editing clocks on specific RNAs rather than direct multi‑timepoint capture). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones
- Month 6: Seven‑gate MSN with verified orthogonal opening and cytosolic localization; per‑bin spike‑in recovery CV <15%.  
- Month 12: Demonstrate seven‑bin, same‑cell trajectories for a benchmark perturbation; per‑bin agreement to destructive scRNA‑seq r ≥ 0.7 (pseudo‑bulk).  
- Month 18: Scale to ≥10,000 cells; deliver ground‑truth trajectory atlas and evaluate sparse live decoding performance against it.

Impact
This work establishes a mechanism‑agnostic route to true same‑cell, multi‑timepoint transcriptomics by internal temporal archiving, providing a principled ground truth for testing whether non‑destructive sparse measurements can stand in for full destructive snapshots—an essential step toward longitudinal single‑cell omics at scale. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))

label: baseline
text:
Title
Chrono-APEX: same-cell, 7+ timepoint transcriptome trajectories via orthogonal, pulsed RNA proximity-labeling and single end-point single-cell readout

Hypothesis and research goal
A cell-internal, pausable recorder that appends orthogonal, durable chemical handles to endogenous RNAs during brief windows after a t=0 perturbation will enable reconstruction of same-cell transcriptome trajectories (≥7 log-spaced timepoints over 30 min–24 h) from a single end-point single-cell sequencing readout. We ask whether peroxidase-catalyzed RNA proximity labeling (APEX-seq chemistry) can be reformulated into an orthogonal, multi-pulse temporal stamping system in living cells without compromising viability or transcriptome coverage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
Encode “time” as covalent, bioorthogonal handles installed directly on RNAs in sub-minute APEX labeling bursts; decode “time” at the end by orthogonal click-ligation of DNA time-barcodes to those handles during single-cell library preparation, co-reading cellular identity and the time labels. APEX2 provides fast, compartment-targetable, in-cell RNA labeling; orthogonal phenol/tyramide substrates carrying distinct handles (alkyne, azide, trans-cyclooctene, bicyclononyne, etc.) allow seven unique pulses; CuAAC, SPAAC, and SPIEDAC chemistries then attach corresponding DNA indices for each pulse. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build a minimally perturbative, multi-pulse RNA stamping framework in live cells.
- Engineer APEX2 targeted to nucleus and cytosol (NLS-APEX2, NES-APEX2). Validate correct localization.
- Define a 7-pulse, logarithmic schedule after t=0 (e.g., 0.5 h, 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h, 16 h, 24 h). Each pulse: 30–60 s labeling with substrate Si + H2O2, immediate quench.
- Substrate panel S1–S7: alkyne-phenol (AP1), tyramide-azide (Tz-N3), tyramide–trans-cyclooctene (Tz‑TCO), tyramide–bicyclononyne (Tz‑BCN), and additional commercially feasible bioorthogonal handles (e.g., cyclopropene-tyramide; norbornene-tyramide; second-generation alkyne-phenol variant with altered scaffold) to complete seven orthogonal click-pair classes. Assess single-pulse toxicity and cumulative viability across 7 pulses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Establish ex vivo handle-to-DNA time-barcoding with orthogonal, sequential click chemistries compatible with RNA/cDNA and single-cell workflows.
- After endpoint lysis (single-cell), perform sequential, orthogonal clicks in one pot:
  1) SPAAC: azide-labeled RNAs → DBCO–DNA barcode B(azide). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13015407/?utm_source=openai))
  2) SPIEDAC: TCO-labeled RNAs → tetrazine–DNA barcode B(TCO). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5485739/?utm_source=openai))
  3) CuAAC (degassed, RT-protective conditions): alkyne-labeled RNAs → azide–DNA barcode B(alkyne). Include copper-free alternatives (DBCO-biotin) where required. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4940987/?utm_source=openai))
  4–7) Additional orthogonal ligations for BCN, cyclopropene, and norbornene handles with matched DNA barcodes using established orthogonal pairs (e.g., azide–BCN, tetrazine–cyclopropene). Validate minimal cross-reactivity in cellular RNA matrices. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-36658-y?utm_source=openai))
- Convert RNA–DNA conjugates to sequencing libraries: adapt Click-Seq-style workflows to ensure reverse transcription reads through triazole linkages; benchmark with spike-ins. Integrate with combinatorial indexing (sci-RNA-seq) to retain cell-of-origin. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022283615003514?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3. Calibrate temporal fidelity and demonstrate same-cell trajectories under a defined perturbation.
- Per-cell timebase: co-express synthetic locus(s) targeted by orthogonal base editors that fire only when each APEX pulse is triggered (brief, colocated activation). This writes a durable DNA audit trail of which pulses executed in each cell to correct for delivery or timing variability. ([yeolab.github.io](https://yeolab.github.io/papers/2020/Porto_NatRevDD.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmark experiment: EGF or TNF-α at t=0 in human cells. Read out single-cell transcriptomes with per-molecule time barcodes and the DNA timebase. Reconstruct within-cell response trajectories (immediate-early induction, export, stabilization/decay phases) across 30 min–24 h. Compare with standard APEX-seq enrichment profiles to confirm spatial specificity and with TRIBE/STAMP controls to contrast with RNA-editing-based interaction records (not time-resolved multi-pulse). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Experimental design and methods
- Cell lines and targeting: HEK293T and a disease-relevant line (e.g., MCF10A). Stable expression of NLS-APEX2 and NES-APEX2; confirm function by single-pulse APEX-seq controls. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))
- Pulse chemistry and quench: For each timepoint i, add Si (100–500 μM), H2O2 (0.5–1 mM) for 30–60 s; quench with ascorbate/thiourea/Trolox; validate minimal oxidative stress by viability and ROS assays. Short APEX pulses are established in cells; cumulative 7-pulse toxicity will be quantified and minimized. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))
- Handle set S1–S7: start with validated AP1 (alkyne-phenol) and tyramide-azide; incorporate TCO-tyramide and BCN-tyramide (commercially available or synthesized) plus two additional strain-alkene/alkyne tyramides (cyclopropene-, norbornene-). Confirm peroxidase compatibility and orthogonality in situ. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13015407/?utm_source=openai))
- Ex vivo barcoding: Single-cell lysis (mild, RNase-free), then four to seven sequential clicks under orthogonal conditions, each with a short ssDNA barcode bearing: (i) a unique time index, (ii) a UMI, (iii) a primer-binding site. Use CuAAC only after completing all copper-free reactions to protect RNA integrity; conditions validated in RNA–DNA conjugation literature and adapted from APEX-seq2 (DBCO-biotin derivatization). ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13015407/?utm_source=openai))
- Library prep and sequencing: Reverse transcribe with primers to both poly(A) and barcode scaffolds; construct joint libraries capturing gene identity, cell barcode, UMI, and time indices. Apply combinatorial indexing to scale to 10^4–10^5 cells per run. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15400?utm_source=openai))
- Controls:
  - No-APEX, no-substrate, and no-H2O2 controls to assess background.
  - Single-substrate, single-pulse controls to quantify per-handle efficiency and RNA coverage.
  - APEX-seq single-pulse benchmark (biotin-phenol/AP1) to ensure transcriptome capture matches published localization maps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))
  - TRIBE/STAMP editor fusions as orthogonal comparators for mechanism (RBP proximity editing vs time stamping). ([rnajournal.cshlp.org](https://rnajournal.cshlp.org/content/29/8/1230.full?utm_source=openai))

Data analysis
- Read parsing: assign reads to cells (cell barcodes) and to timepoints (detected DNA time indices). A read can carry multiple time indices if its RNA molecule persisted across multiple pulses; per-molecule multi-labels encode presence across windows.
- Per-gene per-cell timecourses: aggregate UMIs by time index to reconstruct within-cell trajectories, compute response latencies, peak times, decay constants.
- Calibration: use per-cell DNA timebase editor signatures to (i) confirm which pulses fired in that cell, (ii) correct for missed/attenuated pulses, and (iii) align cells to absolute time. ([yeolab.github.io](https://yeolab.github.io/papers/2020/Porto_NatRevDD.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- Validation: compare trajectory features with expected immediate-early gene kinetics and APEX-seq spatial enrichments for nucleus vs cytosol. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Demonstrate ≥7 orthogonal RNA handle installations with <15% cross-reactivity and >80% cumulative cell viability after 24 h, measured by LC–MS adduct profiling and dot-blot clicks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11429957/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Show efficient, sequential click-ligation of seven distinct DNA barcodes to total cellular RNA bearing the corresponding handles with <5% misassignment in spike-in mixtures. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4940987/?utm_source=openai))
- M3: Recover same-cell, 7-point gene trajectories after a t=0 perturbation in ≥5,000 cells with >70% of detected genes assigned to at least two timepoints. Use the DNA timebase to verify correct pulse execution per cell. ([yeolab.github.io](https://yeolab.github.io/papers/2020/Porto_NatRevDD.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and alternatives
- Limited handle orthogonality or incomplete barcoding: Start with a conservative 4–5 handle panel (AP1, azide, TCO, BCN, cyclopropene) with strong literature support; if seven are not practical in v1, use 4–5 pulses and add 2–3 pulses using split-APEX reconstitution (rapamycin-gated) that deposits an additional, decodeable handle class, maintaining orthogonality. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6548188/?utm_source=openai))
- RNA/cell damage by copper: prioritize copper-free SPAAC/SPIEDAC first; if CuAAC is required, employ protected, degassed protocols and/or perform CuAAC after cDNA synthesis (Click-Seq) to avoid RNA oxidation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4523409/?utm_source=openai))
- Off-target biology: APEX pulses are short; APEX-seq literature demonstrates feasibility for RNA labeling in live cells; nonetheless, evaluate transcriptome perturbation by bulk RNA-seq post-labeling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))

Differentiation from prior art
- Not computational inference (pseudotime) or metabolic RNA labeling: time is physically encoded on endogenous RNAs via orthogonal covalent handles. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))
- Not limited-gene reporters: transcriptome-wide capture with single-cell resolution.
- Extends APEX-seq (single-pulse spatial RNA labeling) to a multi-pulse, orthogonally encoded temporal recorder; introduces an end-to-end decoding workflow that converts chemical time marks into DNA indices co-read with scRNA-seq. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6786773/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinct from TRIBE/STAMP (RBP-targeted editing) by recording absolute timing across the transcriptome rather than interaction footprints. ([rnajournal.cshlp.org](https://rnajournal.cshlp.org/content/29/8/1230.full?utm_source=openai))

Expected outcome
A validated, mechanism-agnostic platform that encodes ≥7 temporal snapshots of the same living cell’s transcriptome into durable molecular marks, decodes them in a single end-point single-cell assay, and enables statistical analysis of inter-cell heterogeneity in response trajectories over 30 min–24 h.

label: baseline
text:
Title
Time-keyed competitive DNA writing to reconstruct single-cell transcriptome trajectories after perturbation

Hypothesis/goal
An orthogonal time key that opens a fixed number of genome-integrated recording “slots” at pre-set times, combined with deliberate competition among many transcript-responsive writers for these scarce slots, will compress each cell’s transcriptome state into a time-ordered edit code that can be decoded into transcriptome-level trajectories after a single end-point sequencing. We ask whether such a competitive, append-only recorder can capture ≥7 same-cell snapshots at logarithmic intervals from 30 minutes to 24 hours after a t=0 perturbation.

Atomic strategy
Separate “when” from “what.” Use autonomous, preloaded molecular time keys to gate seven non-overlapping write windows; within each window, enforce a hard cap on write capacity so that many transcript-driven writers must compete for few addresses. The multinomial outcome per window is a low-dimensional “sketch” of that cell’s high-dimensional transcriptome for that time, and a sequence of sketches reconstructs its trajectory.

Prior work and novelty check
- Nucleic acid strand-displacement circuits can operate in mammalian cytosol; heterochiral l-DNA components improve intracellular robustness and orthogonality, but complex autonomous dynamics in vivo remain limited relative to in vitro systems. Timer/delay circuits based on strand displacement are established in vitro. This supports feasibility of intracellular delay-based time keys while highlighting the novelty/risk of multi-pulse DNA timers in cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7254870/?utm_source=openai))
- Sequential, append-only genome editors such as DNA Typewriter and peCHYRON provide durable, ordered DNA tapes in mammalian cells and are standard media for multi-event recording. We will adopt these as the write substrate rather than inventing a new ligase-based medium. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04922-8?utm_source=openai))
- RNase H–independent hybridization chemistries (e.g., PNA; 2′-O‑modified/LNA steric blockers) bind RNA without degrading it, supporting non-destructive sensing that can be coupled to writer activation. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/24/3/494/2359651?utm_source=openai))
- Compressed transcriptome inference from limited landmarks (L1000) is validated; we will decode competitive edit patterns with similar priors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990023/?utm_source=openai))

Research plan

System overview
- Medium: A genome-integrated prime-editing recording array (Typewriter-like DNA Tape) that accepts sequential pegRNA-driven insertions to delimit ordered frames F1…F7+.
- Time (when): A set of seven autonomous, intracellular “one-shot” time keys that become available at logarithmically spaced delays after t=0 and each open exactly one frame for a short window (5–15 minutes).
- Content (what): A library of 300–1000 “hash-pegRNAs,” each conditionally activatable by non-destructive hybridization to abundant mRNA sequence features. During an open window, many hash-pegRNAs compete to edit a single active frame on the Tape, but total edits per frame are enforced to be small (e.g., 5–15), yielding a compressed signature of the cell’s transcriptome for that time.
- Readout: After 24 hours, sequence the Tape in bulk; per cell, recover a 7×M sparse matrix (time frames × hash IDs) and decode to transcriptome trajectories with landmark-based priors.

Aim 1. Build and calibrate autonomous intracellular time keys with logarithmic scheduling
- Design: Implement seven independent l-DNA strand-displacement delay modules (Key-0.5h, Key-1h, Key-2h, Key-4h, Key-8h, Key-16h, Key-24h). Each module is a nuclease-resistant hairpin/fuel pair (l-DNA or mixed chirality) that releases a unique d-DNA “key” oligo after a tunable delay; delays are set by fuel stoichiometry and rate-balanced to target window onsets. Use co-localizing nanoscaffolds to boost effective concentrations and reduce host interactions.
- Intracellular operation: Transfect/stably load modules; quantify key release kinetics using fluorogenic reporters in live mammalian cells (e.g., HEK293T). Benchmark drift, cell-to-cell variability, and temperature dependence over 24 h.
- Risk mitigation: If multi-hour precision is insufficient, fall back to a protein oscillator (CRISPR/dCas9 ring or TF-based) plus a small recombinase counter to subsample phases into seven effective windows. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7254870/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 2. Engineer competitive content encoders that sense transcript abundance without destruction
- Hash-pegRNA design: Each pegRNA is “caged” by a short antisense oligo (antago-oligo; 2′-O‑methyl/LNA or PNA) that base-pairs to its spacer/extension to block prime editing. Antago-oligos carry a 10–12-nt “unlock” sequence that is sequestered until they transiently bind one of many cognate k-mer motifs on cellular mRNAs; binding rearranges the antago-oligo hairpin and exposes the unlock.
- Non-destructive sensing: Because PNA and many 2′-modified oligos do not activate RNase H, mRNAs are not degraded; unlocked antago-oligos then dissociate, freeing the pegRNA to participate in editing—but only if a frame is open (Aim 3). Titrate antago-oligo/pegRNA ratios to keep basal activation low. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/24/3/494/2359651?utm_source=openai))
- Library coverage: Choose 300–1000 k-mer–mapped hashes to span common transcripts and accessible regions (UTRs/coding hotspots), optimizing dissimilarity among hash targets to improve decoding identifiability.

Aim 3. Time-gated, scarcity-enforced writing on a genome-integrated DNA Tape
- Tape medium: Integrate a tandem “DNA Tape” array (Typewriter) at a safe harbor locus. Configure pegRNAs so that each frame F_i is addressed by a unique short “frame opener” sequence. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04922-8?utm_source=openai))
- Time gating: The d-DNA key released by time module i activates F_i by strand-displacing a complementary DNA lock oligo that otherwise blocks the pegRNA’s primer-binding site for that frame. Keys are consumed (toehold exchange) so frames close automatically as key is titrated/sequestered.
- Enforce scarcity: Limit per-frame editor throughput by (i) restricting prime editor expression to the open-window via an RNA-level gate (e.g., an aptazyme-processed 5′ UTR with key-dependent stabilization), and (ii) capping the number of editable addresses per frame (short symbol slots). This bounds total edits per window to 5–15 events across the competing hash-pegRNAs.
- Single-cell capacity: With 7 frames × ~10 edits/frame, each cell yields ~70 irreversible, time-stamped insertions, sufficient for trajectory reconstruction while minimizing load on editing machinery.
- Controls: Include two sentinel pegRNAs that fire constitutively whenever a frame is open to report window integrity and missed/merged windows.

Aim 4. Decoding and validation
- Model: Treat each frame’s edit counts across hashes as a Poisson-multinomial draw proportional to underlying hash-specific “activation propensities,” which are functions of target transcript abundances and accessibility. Fit a calibration model by sacrificing small cell cohorts at defined times for scRNA-seq and computing the mapping from hash counts to transcriptome using L1000-style inference priors. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990023/?utm_source=openai))
- Reconstruction: For each recorded cell, infer per-frame transcript abundance vectors; assemble trajectories and analyze heterogeneity and response classes after the t=0 perturbation.
- Benchmarks: Compare against destructive time-series scRNA-seq; quantify concordance in early/late response genes, half-life–dependent lag structure, and clustering of response modes.

Key design details and justifications
- Orthogonality of time base: l-DNA circuits reduce nuclease degradation and off-target binding compared with d-DNA; operation of multi-component heterochiral strand displacement in living cells has been demonstrated, supporting intracellular feasibility for delay modules. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7973774/?utm_source=openai))
- Durable, ordered memory: Prime editing–based Typewriter/peCHYRON provide ordered, non-overwriting edits in mammalian cells over weeks; here they delimit minutes–hours frames in a single day. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04922-8?utm_source=openai))
- Non-destructive sensing: PNAs and many 2′-modified oligos do not trigger RNase H, preserving transcripts during sensing windows. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/24/3/494/2359651?utm_source=openai))
- Compression sufficiency: Landmark-based inference from ~1000 measurements recovers most of the transcriptome variance; our competitive hash counts serve as analogous compressed measurements with temporal indexing. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5990023/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones and decision gates (12–24 months)
- M1: Demonstrate intracellular l-DNA delay modules releasing distinct keys with CV <20% at 0.5–8 h delays; quantify drift (n>500 cells). Go/no-go: if CV >40% or toxicity observed, switch to protein oscillator + counter fallback. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12042877/?utm_source=openai))
- M2: Show frame-specific opening on DNA Tape upon exogenous delivery of each key and closure within 20 min after key consumption; no cross-frame edits.
- M3: Validate competitive encoding: as transcript abundance of a spike-in RNA is titrated, its cognate hash-pegRNA captures a larger share of fixed per-frame edits with a saturating response; other hashes are proportionally displaced.
- M4: End-to-end single-cell trajectory capture over 24 h with ≥7 frames; decode and correlate with matched destructive scRNA-seq checkpoints (0.5, 2, 8, 24 h), achieving ≥0.7 Pearson correlation on landmark genes.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- Time-base fragility: If DNA delays are too noisy, replace with a mammalian synthetic oscillator (e.g., CRISPR/dCas9 ring) driving periodic editor availability; subdivide phases into seven effective windows via recombinase gating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7430638/?utm_source=openai))
- Editor load/off-targets: Use high-fidelity PE variants and minimize exposure windows; monitor off-target editing by targeted capture.
- Hash library crosstalk: Filter hash sequences to minimize unintended binding; empirically trim library to well-behaved hashes during calibration.

Expected outcomes and impact
- A same-cell, end-point-read recorder delivering ≥7 time-indexed, compressed snapshots over 30 minutes–24 hours, enabling per-cell response trajectories under t=0 perturbations at scale.
- A general methodology—time keys plus competitive writing—that is orthogonal to cellular gene regulation and distinct from metabolic labeling or inference-only approaches, with clear paths to increased frame counts or alternative writers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6492567/?utm_source=openai))

text:
Title
Programmable condensate-coupled vesicular sampling for longitudinal transcriptomics from the same single cells

Research question as hypothesis
Can transient, low-affinity, optogenetically gated RNA-condensate “samplers” positioned at the plasma membrane and coupled to ESCRT-mediated microvesicle budding externalize a minimally biased aliquot of the cytosolic mRNA pool on command, enabling ≥7 longitudinal transcriptome snapshots from the same living single cells after a defined perturbation?

Atomic strategy
Exploit rapid mRNA exchange kinetics with weak, reversible RNA–protein condensates to momentarily concentrate a representative sliver of the local polyadenylated transcript pool at the cell periphery, then hand off that cargo to ESCRT-driven outward budding to produce time-stamped, cell-localized vesicles that are captured immediately above each cell. This converts intracellular expression dynamics into periodic extracellular readouts without re-entering or lysing the cell. mRNAs in EVs broadly reflect cellular abundance profiles, supporting their use as proxies when sampling is controlled. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6496347/?utm_source=openai))

Background and rationale
- EVs carry diverse RNAs and, at the mRNA level, EV abundance correlates with donor-cell abundance (r≈0.86), indicating that EV RNA can reflect intracellular transcriptomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8944098/?utm_source=openai))
- ESCRT recruitment by short “late domains” (PTAP→TSG101; YPXnL→ALIX; PPXY→NEDD4) executes outward membrane scission in viral budding and cellular microvesicle pathways; ARRDC1 uses a PSAP motif to recruit TSG101 and drive plasma-membrane microvesicle release. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3819203/?utm_source=openai))
- mRNAs and RBPs exchange with RNA granules on seconds-to-minutes timescales (FRAP), enabling transient enrichment without durable sequestration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6496347/?utm_source=openai))
- Optogenetic phase-separation (optoDroplets) provides millisecond–minute control over condensate nucleation/dispersion in living cells. ([condensates.com](https://condensates.com/publications/spatiotemporal-control-of-intracellular-phase-transitions-using-light-activated-optodroplets/?utm_source=openai))
- Single-cell devices can spatially capture secreted EVs from individual cells over time by placing a functionalized slide 50–100 μm above each cell, preserving cell identity across serial collections. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5023418/?utm_source=openai))
- Related work: Live-seq samples cytoplasm by aspiration to obtain two time points per cell; TRACE-seq and recent Gag-based NTVE systems export RNAs via EVs at the population scale but do not deliver single-cell–resolved, repeated trajectories with controlled, unbiased sampling. Our design explicitly targets same-cell identity and tunable, low-burden sampling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))

Objectives
1) Engineer a membrane-proximal, low-affinity RNA-condensate sampler with optogenetic gating and quantify its sampling neutrality and cellular burden.
2) Couple the sampler to ESCRT-mediated outward budding to package and export the sampled RNA as microvesicles on command.
3) Build a single-cell microchamber platform with removable, time-barcoded capture slides to collect and index vesicles from the same cells at logarithmically spaced times after t=0 perturbation.
4) Demonstrate ≥7 longitudinal transcriptome snapshots per cell (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h) and quantify single-cell response trajectories and heterogeneity.

System design
- Sampler scaffold
  - Core: A low-valency RNA-binding module (e.g., PABP RRM1-2 affinity-attenuated mutant) fused to an intrinsically disordered region tuned just below the phase-separation threshold at baseline; CRY2-based oligomerization provides light-gated, minute-scale condensate nucleation/dispersion. Target FRAP half-times for scaffold and co-enriched mRNA: 2–60 s; duty cycle ≤10 min per pulse to limit sequestration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6496347/?utm_source=openai))
  - PM positioning: A mild PM-tether (e.g., CAAX box) localizes condensate nucleation to the cortex, where outward budding will sample the adjacent cytosol.
- Vesicle export module
  - ESCRT recruitment: Embed PTAP and YPXnL late domains within the scaffold and/or co-recruit ARRDC1 (PSAP–TSG101) to trigger ESCRT-dependent microvesicle budding at the PM during light pulses. Include minimal ubiquitinizable lysines to enhance ESCRT sensitivity if needed. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3819203/?utm_source=openai))
  - Extraction fraction control: Tune light intensity, pulse length, and scaffold valency to keep exported mRNA per pulse below 0.3–0.5% of cellular mRNA (estimated from vesicle counts and mRNA-per-vesicle benchmarks), preserving viability and steady-state gene expression.
- Single-cell capture and time indexing
  - Culture each cell in a microchamber aligned under a removable glass capture slide bearing spatially arrayed anti-vesicle binders and a unique time barcode (one slide per time point). Slides are exchanged at scheduled times to encode time without intracellular barcoding. Geometry and capture precedent follow established single-cell EV capture assays. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5023418/?utm_source=openai))
  - After the final time point, all slides are processed for RNA-seq with slide-borne barcodes encoding cell location and time.

Experimental plan and milestones
Aim 1: Sampler neutrality and kinetics
- Construct variants spanning RNA-binding affinity and IDR valency; quantify condensate formation thresholds and FRAP in HEK293T and one primary cell model.
- Metrics: FRAP t1/2 (2–60 s), condensate lifetime (≤10 min on-pulse), global translation rate (puromycin incorporation), viability (>95%), stress markers (eIF2α-P).
- Acceptance: No significant differential expression due to sampler in unpulsed cells; reversible condensates on light OFF within 5–10 min.

Aim 2: ESCRT-coupled export
- Add PTAP/YPXnL motifs and/or ARRDC1 co-recruitment domain; confirm ESCRT dependence via dominant-negative VPS4 and TSG101/ALIX knockdown.
- Quantify vesicle production and RNA cargo per pulse; benchmark against NTVE-like positive controls. Expect outward microvesicles with EV markers and ESCRT dependence. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3306724/?utm_source=openai))
- Acceptance: 10^2–10^3 vesicles/cell/pulse with detectable poly(A)+ RNA; exported RNA composition correlates with donor lysate (r≥0.7 across genes), consistent with EV–cell concordance. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8944098/?utm_source=openai))

Aim 3: Single-cell platform and time indexing
- Fabricate PDMS microchambers and removable, oligo-barcoded capture slides positioned 100 μm above cells; validate one-to-one mapping of captured vesicles to underlying cells by fluorescent vesicle labeling, following the geometry of prior single-cell EV capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5023418/?utm_source=openai))
- Perform a step perturbation at t=0 (e.g., EGFR inhibitor); collect 7 time points at logarithmic intervals by swapping slides; sequence each slide.

Aim 4: Biological validation of longitudinal trajectories
- Compare per-cell vesicle RNA-seq to terminal lysate scRNA-seq of the same cells (post-24 h) to audit bias; include exogenous spike-ins during each pulse for between-time calibration.
- Test-retest: run two independent perturbations and replicate trajectories.
- Benchmark against Live-seq two-point sampling and population NTVE/TRACE paradigms to demonstrate added value: same-cell identity across ≥7 points with controlled extraction and minimal bias. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))

Key readouts and success criteria
- Technical
  - Per-time-point library complexity ≥3,000 genes/cell; cross-time cell viability ≥90%.
  - Extraction fraction per pulse ≤0.5%; negligible induction of mitochondrial RNA leakage.
  - EV–cell expression correlation r≥0.7; low length and 3′-bias relative to controls.
- Biological
  - Detect known early (≤1 h) and late (≥8 h) transcriptional waves after drug addition within the same cells.
  - Quantify inter-cell heterogeneity (e.g., differential adaptation trajectories) with ≥100 cells in parallel.

Controls
- No-light controls; optogenetic light-only controls.
- ESCRT dependency: TSG101/ALIX knockdown, VPS4 dominant negative.
- Positive control: NTVE_PABP-like export at population scale; Negative control: sampler without late domains.
- Orthogonal validation: end-point scRNA-seq of same cells, and, where feasible, Live-seq two-point comparison. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))

Risk mitigation
- Low export yield: increase pulse duration or scaffold valency modestly; add PPXY→NEDD4 route if PTAP/YPXnL insufficient. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2958808/?utm_source=openai))
- Sampling bias: tune RNA-binding domain to weaker affinity; mix poly(A)- and AU-biased binders; audit with spike-ins.
- Cellular stress: shorten pulses; reduce expression; verify stress pathways.

Differentiation from prior art
- Unlike Live-seq (invasive aspiration, typically two points), this approach is non-destructive and scales to ≥7 points/cell. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Unlike TRACE-seq and NTVE (population-level EV export with specific adapters or Gag-based budding), this design delivers single-cell–resolved trajectories by spatial capture and aims for minimally biased, low-occupancy sampling via transient condensates rather than strong sequence-specific loading. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8844816/?utm_source=openai))

Expected impact
A general, mechanism-agnostic platform to follow single-cell drug-response trajectories without cell destruction, enabling direct measurement of intra-cellular dynamics and inter-cell heterogeneity in real time, with straightforward integration into perturbation screens and primary-cell assays.

text:
Title
ReCap-seq: Reversible-capture nanoperfusion patch for longitudinal, transcriptome-wide sampling of the same living cell

Premise and gap
- Existing longitudinal single-cell transcriptomics aspirate cytoplasm (FluidFM/Live-seq) or extract through nanostraws/electroporation; they can work but still remove bulk material and require active extraction flows, which may confound recovery kinetics and scaling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Intracellular capture chemistries (e.g., TIVA) prove that poly(A)+ RNAs in live cells can be hybridized by oligo-based probes, but they require destructive endpoints and are not designed for repeated same-cell sampling. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))
- Solid-phase oligo-dT capture is robust in microfluidic contexts, but only after lysis. A non-aspirative, reversible capture interface that briefly “touches” the cytosol and releases captured RNAs with a time-point barcode has not been demonstrated. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3923508/?utm_source=openai))

Atomic strategy
- Replace extraction with reversible, near-equilibrium hybridization at a sealed, intracellularly addressed nanointerface. Present high-density, photocleavable oligo-dT brushes on a nanoporous membrane that forms a transient nanoscale conduit into the cytosol. During brief windows, a subpercent fraction of poly(A)+ RNAs binds and is then released to the chip with a time barcode. No bulk aspiration; capture fraction is set by surface density and dwell time, not volume withdrawal. Stable nanoscale access is supported by prior nanowire/nanostraw membrane interfaces. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms4613?utm_source=openai))

Hypothesis–goal (deliberately inseparable)
- A cell-attached, reversible-capture nanoperfusion patch can provide minimally perturbative, ≥7-point, log-spaced (0.5–24 h) transcriptome sampling from the same living cell after a defined t=0 perturbation, with per-timepoint molecular yields sufficient for gene-level dynamics and inter-cell heterogeneity analyses, while introducing less perturbation than aspiration-based methods. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Engineer the reversible-capture nanoperfusion patch (ReCap patch)
- Fabricate an ultrathin (≤200 nm) nanoporous membrane (50–150 nm pores) integrated in a microdome that seals to a 2–5 µm patch of plasma membrane on adherent cells in microchambers.
- Functionalize pore interiors with dense, photocleavable oligo-dT(24–30) primers bearing UMIs and a timepoint barcode (TPB-k). Surface chemistry and release conditions are tuned to achieve rapid hybridization and quantitative elution.
- Validate nanoscale access and seal integrity (dye exclusion; FRAP of cytosolic GFP near pores; electrical impedance). Confirm that capture proceeds without net suction or electroporation.

2) Establish longitudinal, same-cell transcriptome sampling with defined time bins
- Protocol: administer perturbation at t=0; at t = 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h, land the ReCap patch for 2–5 min under physiological buffer; stop-flow for 30–60 s to favor boundary-layer hybridization; photorelease TPB-k–primed RNA into an on-chip lane; lift patch. Repeat on the same cell.
- Library: pool all seven eluates per cell; perform template-switching cDNA with TPB-k and UMI annotation; sequence 3′ ends.
- Metrics: per-timepoint UMI counts; gene detection; technical noise via ERCC spike-ins in the elution lane.

3) Benchmark perturbation, fidelity, and scalability
- Perturbation: compare growth rate, division, and an 8 h end-point scRNA-seq profile of ReCap-sampled cells vs. matched unsampled controls; benchmark against Live-seq (FluidFM) and nanostraw nanoelectroextraction (NEE) sampled cells on the same lines and schedules. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Fidelity: in synchronized inductions (e.g., TNFα response), compare ReCap-seq trajectories to parallel destructive time courses from sister cultures; quantify bias toward 3′ UTR and AU-rich transcripts; compare gene-wise dynamics to Live-seq/NEE references. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5347600/?utm_source=openai))
- Scalability: operate 256–1024 microchambers with automated patch positioning; evaluate cross-contamination by swapping TPB-k schedules on neighboring cells.

Experimental design and methods
- Device and chemistry
  - Nanoporous membrane: SiN or parylene-C; pore density ~10^8 m−2 to set capture capacity; dome gasket is soft elastomer ring for reversible sealing.
  - Capture layer: photocleavable linker–oligo-dT–UMI–TPB-k immobilized by click chemistry; photorelease with 365–405 nm at ≤1 mJ/cm^2. Elution routed to a per-cell serpentine channel with on-valve mixing of ERCCs.
  - Hybridization control: capture dwell ≤5 min at 33–37°C; high local probe density drives near-equilibrium binding of a small fraction of freely diffusing poly(A)+ RNAs in cytosol adjacent to pore mouths; restore flow to re-equilibrate unbound RNAs.
- Cells and perturbations
  - Model lines: RAW264.7 (LPS), NIH-3T3 (serum restimulation), and primary human macrophages (LPS+IFNγ). These have established Live-seq and/or nanostraw precedents for longitudinal sampling and viability benchmarking. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Controls
  - Zero-light controls (capture layer intact) to quantify nonspecific adsorption.
  - Dummy-oligo controls (polyC) to assess poly(A)-specificity.
  - Immediate post-capture qPCR of housekeeping and IEGs to confirm rapid on-chip stabilization.
- Data analysis
  - Alignment to 3′ ends; UMI collapsing per TPB-k; per-gene generalized additive models across timepoints within each cell; hierarchical models to partition within-cell vs between-cell variance.

Power and performance targets
- Per timepoint per cell: ≥1,000–3,000 UMIs; ≥800 genes detected.
- Longitudinal per cell: ≥7 timepoints; cumulative mRNA removed ≤3–4% (substantially below typical perturbations reported for aspiration-based biopsies), maintaining viability and transcriptional stability outside intended perturbation responses. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Scale: ≥500 cells per condition to quantify inter-cell heterogeneity.

Validation and benchmarking
- Compare ReCap-seq to:
  - Live-seq (FluidFM cytoplasmic biopsy). Expect lower cell cycle delay and faster recovery due to non-aspirative capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
  - Nanostraw sampling/NEE. Expect comparable or lower perturbation because there is no electroporation and no convective extraction. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5347600/?utm_source=openai))
  - TIVA-tag endpoint capture. Demonstrate repeated, same-cell time-binning absent in TIVA. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Low RNA yield: increase local probe density, extend dwell to 5 min, multiplex two patch contacts per time bin, or pool two adjacent pores; confirm saturation curves.
- Membrane stress: minimize dwell force; use soft gaskets; monitor Ca2+ spikes; abort if repair markers rise.
- 3′ bias: incorporate minority randomers (N9–N12) appended beyond poly(dT) to mitigate extreme 3′ skew; rely on UTR annotation in analysis.
- Phototoxicity: use minimal UV dose; validate by ROS assays; consider red-shifted photocleavable linkers if needed.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1 (months 0–6): Fabricate ReCap patch; demonstrate reversible, barcodeable elution from fixed RNA standards; show membrane seal with no dye leakage.
- M2 (months 6–12): Achieve ≥7 timepoint sampling from the same NIH-3T3 cell with ≥1,000 UMIs/timepoint and preserved proliferation vs unsampled controls.
- M3 (months 12–18): Benchmark against Live-seq and NEE in RAW264.7 LPS response; show comparable gene dynamics with lower perturbation signatures.
- M4 (months 18–24): Scale to ≥500 cells/condition; quantify inter-cell trajectory heterogeneity.

Differentiation and impact
- Distinct from aspiration (Live-seq) and nanostraw extraction: no volumetric withdrawal or electroporation; capture is governed by reversible hybridization kinetics at a sealed nanointerface. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9402441/?utm_source=openai))
- Distinct from TIVA: repeated, same-cell, absolute-time bins rather than single destructive capture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3964595/?utm_source=openai))
- Uses established building blocks (oligo-dT solid-phase capture; stable nanoscale cell–nanostructure interfaces) in a new configuration optimized for longitudinal, minimally perturbative, transcriptome-wide measurement in the same living cell. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3923508/?utm_source=openai))

Deliverables
- An open, validated ReCap-seq platform (device, surface chemistry, and software) enabling absolute-time, ≥7-point, same-cell transcriptomics under defined perturbations at scale.

text:
Title
Gate-and-catch longitudinal transcriptomics: reversible electroporation-driven outward RNA sampling with environmental time encoding

Hypothesis-question
Can a living cell’s plasma membrane be used as a periodically re-openable gate to divert a trace, non-lethal fraction of its cytosolic mRNA into a proximal, time-barcoded capture surface, so that the same cell’s transcriptome can be read at ≥7 time points from 30 min to 24 h after a defined perturbation? Reframed: does coupling reversible, localized electroporation (as the gate) with electrophoretic RNA capture onto sequentially activated barcoded substrates (as the catch) yield faithful, longitudinal, same-cell transcriptomes without aspiration or genetic export machinery?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the brief window of reversible, localized membrane permeability to drive a controlled outward flux of polyadenylated mRNA toward a nearby high-affinity, time-addressable capture surface using short electric pulses; membrane reseals within seconds to minutes, keeping the cell viable. This converts intracellular temporal changes into an external, barcoded physical record that is decoded at a single endpoint. Reversible electroporation is established to create transient nanoscale pores with rapid resealing; localized formats and on-chip extraction of intracellular contents have been demonstrated, and electric-field–assisted RNA capture onto surfaces is efficient. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9031838/?utm_source=openai))

Specific aims
1) Build an addressable “gate-and-catch” microarray that pairs single-cell reversible electroporation electrodes with annular, photo-activatable, barcoded RNA-capture hydrogels positioned 10–50 µm from the cell edge.
2) Demonstrate longitudinal, same-cell mRNA profiling at 7 log-spaced time points (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 h) after t=0 perturbation, across ≥1,000 cells in parallel.
3) Quantify fidelity, bias, and impact on viability by benchmarking against destructive scRNA-seq at 24 h and against existing longitudinal sampling methods (Live-seq and nanostraw sampling).

Platform design and workflow
- Cell arraying and identity: Adherent cells are seeded onto a microelectrode array with one electrode under each microtrap. Each site has a fixed spatial cell ID.
- Time encoding by environmental barcodes: Around each cell, a ring of 7 hydrogel sectors contains masked oligo(dT) capture probes with unique time barcodes (T0–T6). At each target time, a DMD projects patterned light to uncage only the sector for that window, enabling capture during a 5–10 min interval; other sectors remain inactive.
- Gate actuation and capture: Immediately after uncaging, a burst of 2–5 sublytic, microsecond pulses (field 100–300 V/cm at the cell–electrode interface) is applied for <1 s to nucleate reversible pores. While pulses are on, polyanionic RNAs experience electrophoretic drift toward the hydrogel; post-pulse, a local concentration gradient sustains short-range diffusion into the activated sector. Hydrogels incorporate poly(d-lysine) to increase electrophoretic concentration and capture efficiency. RNase inhibitors are included in a thin overlayer. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9031838/?utm_source=openai))
- Resealing and recovery: Cells remain in standard medium; resealing occurs within seconds-to-minutes via canonical repair, minimizing stress.
- Library prep: At 24 h, all sectors are retrieved. cDNA is prepared with 3′-end counting chemistry, reading both the cell’s spatial ID and the sector’s time barcode. One sequencing run yields per-cell, per-time transcriptomes.

Experimental plan
- Model system and perturbation: Use an inducible NF-κB activation in HEK293 or macrophage-like cells. At t=0, add TNFα; log-spaced captures follow.
- Throughput and heterogeneity: Pattern 1,500–3,000 addressable sites; sample ≥1,000 cells passing QC (viability and capture yield thresholds) to quantify inter-cell trajectory heterogeneity.
- Controls:
  - No-pulse, uncaged sector controls to measure background adsorption.
  - Pulse, caged sector controls to measure non-specific loss.
  - ERCC spike-ins preloaded in sectors for library normalization, not extraction yield.
  - Sentinel Live-seq at 2–3 time points in a subset of cells to cross-validate with an orthogonal, minimally invasive longitudinal method; nanostraw sampling used similarly in a matched culture. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05046-9?utm_source=openai))
- Benchmarks and acceptance criteria:
  - Viability ≥90% at 24 h; cell cycle distribution unchanged vs. non-pulsed neighbors.
  - Per time point, ≥2,000 genes detected at >1 UMI in ≥70% of cells.
  - Concordance: At 24 h, Pearson r ≥0.8 in gene-level abundance vs. matched destructive scRNA-seq after correcting for capture depth.
  - Longitudinal coherence: Known NF-κB target dynamics (early vs. late genes) resolved in single cells; between-cell variance decomposes into baseline-state vs. response-timing components.

Key technical details and justifications
- Electroporation parameters: Use addressable microelectrodes to restrict fields to each cell. Reversible electroporation at microscale yields transient pores that reseal quickly; localized systems have already extracted intracellular enzymes repeatedly while maintaining viability, supporting outward sampling feasibility when the capture sink is proximal. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9031838/?utm_source=openai))
- Capture physics: The electric field serves two purposes—pore formation and electrophoretic focusing of RNAs toward the activated hydrogel. Prior work shows electric-field–assisted mRNA capture onto surfaces is effective and is enhanced by poly(d-lysine), which we implement in the sectors. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-022-01455-3?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation from existing approaches:
  - Not aspiration: Unlike Live-seq (FluidFM cytoplasmic biopsy), no nanopipette enters the cell; the gate is the membrane itself and the readout is environmental. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05046-9?utm_source=openai))
  - Not nanostraw sequential aspiration: No permanent nanochannels traverse the membrane; access is transient and field-gated. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28223521/?utm_source=openai))
  - Not vesicular export (NTVE): No engineered exporters or vesicle trafficking dependencies; sampling is physical and immediate, minimizing packaging biases. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72072-w?utm_source=openai))

Bias, safety, and failure mode analysis
- Extraction fraction and burden: Target <1–2% cytosolic mRNA per event, estimated from UMI counts and ERCC-normalized yields. Monitor stress signatures and proliferation; titrate pulse amplitude and count to minimize perturbation.
- Molecular bias: Larger/structured RNAs may drift less efficiently; model electrophoretic mobility and adjust pulse trains. Empirically derive gene-level correction factors by comparing against Live-seq and end-point scRNA-seq.
- Cross-window contamination: Use rapid perfusion and quench steps; verify <5% carryover by exposing decoy sectors after each window and sequencing their barcodes.

Data analysis
- Per-cell trajectory inference uses absolute time labels; mixed-effects models decompose within-cell vs. between-cell variance. Differential dynamics are tested by gene-wise functional ANOVA across time with per-cell random intercepts. Identify response archetypes and map them back to baseline predictors measured at t=−0.1 h (imaging-derived cell size, cell-cycle proxy).

Milestones
- M1 (Month 3): Device yield >90%; per-pulse viability >98% and resealing verified by dye exclusion.
- M2 (Month 6): ≥7 time points captured with median 2,500 genes/time/cell in HEK293; NF-κB kinetics resolved in bulk-average.
- M3 (Month 9): Per-cell trajectories across ≥1,000 cells; concordance with destructive 24 h scRNA-seq r ≥0.8.
- M4 (Month 12): Cross-validation with Live-seq at two time points; trajectory-class predictors identified.

Expected impact
This study establishes a general, genetics-free route to same-cell longitudinal transcriptomics by turning the membrane into a controllable export valve and encoding time in the environment. It complements aspiration-based (Live-seq) and conduit-based (nanostraw) methods and avoids dependencies of vesicular export, enabling scalable trajectory mapping of perturbation responses in living cells. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05046-9?utm_source=openai))

Title
Closed-loop auricular vagus nerve stimulation to normalize gastric neuroimmune tone in chronic stress-induced gastritis

Integrated research question-hypothesis
If stress-induced gastritis is driven by a maladaptive neuroimmune setpoint—characterized by CRF-driven mast cell activation, sympathetic vasoconstriction, impaired mucosal perfusion, and barrier failure—then time-locked activation of vagal afferents, delivered only during physiological signatures of stress, will restore mucosal blood flow, suppress mast cell–mediated inflammation via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, stabilize epithelial tight junctions, and reduce mucosal injury and symptoms without increasing acid output.

Atomic strategy
A single perturbation: closed-loop, afferent-selective auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) triggered by real-time stress physiology (heart-rate-variability and gastric myoelectric markers) to engage the vagal anti-inflammatory reflex and reset gastric mucosal neuroimmune tone.

Mechanistic rationale
- Stress activates hypothalamic CRF pathways and sympathetic outflow → mucosal mast cell degranulation, cytokine release, microvascular constriction, oxidative stress, and barrier disruption.
- Afferent vagal activation (auricular branch → NTS) reduces hypothalamic CRF drive, shifts autonomic balance parasympathetic, and engages the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex (α7nAChR on mucosal immune cells), improving perfusion and barrier integrity.
- Parameterization emphasizing afferent recruitment minimizes efferent cholinergic drive to parietal cells, limiting acid hypersecretion risk.

Specific aims
1) Define person-specific physiological signatures linking stress to gastric mucosal injury.
2) Engineer and validate a closed-loop taVNS algorithm that maximizes mucosal perfusion and barrier stability while avoiding acid upregulation.
3) Test clinical efficacy and mechanistic mediation in chronic stress-induced gastritis.

Study design
- Phase 1 mechanistic mapping (n=30): Observational, repeated-measures profiling across stress exposures and recovery.
- Phase 2 device optimization (n=24): Double-blind, crossover parameter sweep with real-time gastric readouts.
- Phase 3 efficacy trial (n=120): Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled parallel trial (12 weeks), with a preplanned N-of-1 subprogram for responders/nonresponders.

Participants
Adults with endoscopically confirmed non-erosive or erosive gastritis, symptom chronicity >6 months, elevated perceived stress, and exclusion of H. pylori, NSAID overuse, and significant psychiatric instability. Standard-of-care acid suppression allowed if stable ≥4 weeks.

Sensing and triggers
- Autonomic stress index: rolling composite of reduced HRV (RMSSD drop, LF/HF rise), elevated skin conductance, and pupil diameter (optional camera).
- Gastric state index: cutaneous electrogastrography (EGG) bradygastria/tachygastria, and ingestible pH capsule for real-time gastric acidity.
- Trigger rule: deliver stimulation when autonomic stress index exceeds personalized threshold and gastric state index predicts perfusion vulnerability, with refractory periods to avoid overstimulation.

Stimulation parameters (initial, refined in Phase 2)
- Site: auricular cymba conchae (afferent-dominant).
- Waveform: charge-balanced biphasic; 20–25 Hz; 200–300 μs pulse width; intensity titrated to sensory threshold +10% without pain.
- Duty: 2–3 min bursts, auto-terminated when HRV normalizes; maximum 20 min/session; up to 3 sessions/day during stress windows; nightly prophylaxis 10 min before sleep if nocturnal symptoms predominate.
- Sham: earlobe stimulation, identical sensation profile without vagal engagement.

Endpoints
- Primary (Phase 3): Change in endoscopic gastritis activity (updated Sydney score) at 12 weeks.
- Key secondaries: symptom burden (GSRS-dyspepsia subset), mucosal perfusion (laser speckle contrast during endoscopy), histologic mast cell activation (tryptase density), mucosal cytokines (TNF, IL-1β, IL-6), tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin), oxidative stress markers, HRV normalization index, and days rescued from on-demand antacids.
- Safety: bradycardia, syncope, worsened reflux, sleep disturbance, skin irritation; continuous monitoring of heart rate and periodic 24-hour pH-impedance in a subset.

Mechanistic mediation tests
- Ex vivo biopsies pre/post intervention: α7nAChR pathway engagement via ACh/epibatidine challenge with and without α7 antagonism; cytokine readouts.
- CRF axis modulation: salivary cortisol diurnal slope change.
- Perfusion–injury coupling: correlation of perfusion gain with reductions in neutrophil infiltration and symptom relief.

Analytic plan
- Phase 1: Mixed-effects models to identify individualized thresholds linking stress indices to perfusion and pH changes.
- Phase 2: Bayesian adaptive parameter optimization (multi-armed bandit) maximizing perfusion and minimizing acid output.
- Phase 3: Intention-to-treat analysis; mediation by perfusion change and mast cell markers; predefined minimal clinically important difference in GSRS of 0.4 and Sydney score reduction ≥1 grade in ≥2 regions.

Repeated applicability and scalability
- Daily or event-triggered use with wearable sensing; home-based, noninvasive, and titratable.
- Algorithm personalization enables ongoing efficacy despite fluctuating stress loads.

Innovation
- Single-perturbation, closed-loop neuromodulation targeted to a mucosal neuroimmune endpoint rather than generic symptom suppression.
- Afferent-selective engagement of the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex in the stomach with real-time physiological gating.

Risk mitigation
- Acid secretion risk: afferent-focused parameters; real-time pH safeguards that suspend stimulation if acid rises >0.5 pH units below baseline.
- Autonomic adverse events: heart rate floor safety lockout; screening for conduction disease.
- Nonresponse: switch to nightly prophylaxis plus daytime event-triggered bursts; stratify by baseline α7nAChR expression and mast cell density.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1 (6 months): Feasible stress-trigger detection (AUROC ≥0.8) and safe home use.
- M2 (12 months): Parameter set that increases mucosal perfusion ≥20% without lowering mean gastric pH versus baseline or sham.
- M3 (24 months): Phase 3 primary endpoint met; effect size ≥0.5 SD vs sham; mediation by perfusion and mast cell markers confirmed.
- No-go: inability to prevent acid lowering, or absence of perfusion/biomarker change despite symptom improvements.

Translational extensions
- Combine with low-dose PPI taper protocol to test PPI-sparing potential.
- Explore α7nAChR-positive allosteric modulators delivered as gastric-retentive, nonabsorbable formulations to mimic the neuromodulatory anti-inflammatory signature.

Data and ethics
- Pre-registration; blinded adjudication of endoscopic outcomes; device logs and raw physiology signals shared under controlled access.
- Patient-centered outcomes integrated via ecological momentary assessment.

Impact
A repeatedly applicable, mechanism-anchored therapy that targets the neuroimmune root of stress-induced gastritis and reduces reliance on chronic acid suppression.

Title
Firebreak gastric mucosal patches: postbiotic-trained organoid sheets that locally inoculate the stomach against stress signals

Hypothesis–Goal
A brief ex vivo exposure of human gastric epithelial organoids to a defined “stress‑resilience postbiotic” mixture durably imprints a cytoprotective state that, after endoscopic engraftment as mucosal patches, creates local firebreak zones that resist brain‑derived stress signals and paracrinally shield adjacent native mucosa. The therapeutic goal is a repeatedly applicable, localized intervention that prevents stress‑induced gastritis flares without altering central stress circuitry or the global microbiome.

Atomic Strategy
Exploit microbial metabolite–driven epigenetic training (via Nrf2/HIF/PPAR pathways) to program gastric epithelial cells into a stable, high‑mucin, high‑PGE2, antioxidant, tight‑junction–fortifying state that also secretes protective extracellular vesicles (EVs) and trefoil factors, thereby extending protection beyond the graft margins.

Biological Rationale
- Stress injury pathogenesis: sympathetic/CRF signaling → mucosal ischemia, barrier breakdown (tight junction loss), oxidative damage, and reduced prostaglandins.
- Protective levers: gut‑microbe metabolites from stress‑resilient hosts (e.g., butyrate, indole derivatives, spermidine, secondary bile acids, lactate, GABA) activate epithelial Nrf2/HIF/PPAR, enhance COX‑dependent PGE2, TFFs, and mucins (MUC5AC), and tighten junctions (ZO‑1/occludin).
- Trained phenotype: short, intense postbiotic exposure can induce durable chromatin and metabolic states in epithelia; trained cells can export protection via EVs and secreted factors to neighboring tissue.

Specific Aims
1) Define and standardize a Stress‑Resilience Postbiotic Cocktail (SRPC).
2) Induce and verify a durable, transferable protective program in human gastric organoids.
3) Engineer endoscopically deployable organoid sheets and test in stress‑gastritis models for on‑patch and off‑patch protection (“firebreak radius”).
4) Establish repeat‑application logistics and in vivo boosting to maintain protection over chronic courses.

Aim 1: SRPC definition and standardization
- Source: stool ultrafiltrates (<50 kDa) from verified stress‑resilient donors (behavioral/physiologic assays).
- Fractionation: orthogonal separations (size, polarity) → targeted metabolomics → reconstitution to identify a minimal effective set (MES).
- Functional screen: human gastric epithelial monolayers/organoids challenged with norepinephrine/CRF + acid/hypoxia/ROS.
- Criteria: acute induction of Nrf2 targets (HO‑1/NQO1), PGE2, mucin/TFF expression, TEER↑, permeability↓, apoptosis/ROS↓.
- Output: GMP‑amenable MES (SRPC) and dose–time training schedule (e.g., 24–48 h pulse).

Aim 2: Train organoids and prove durability and paracrine transfer
- Cells: autologous gastric organoids from endoscopic biopsies or hiPSC‑derived gastric epithelium.
- Training: SRPC pulse; washout; maturation on gastric ECM.
- Durability assays:
  - Epigenetics: H3K27ac/H3K4me3 at cytoprotective loci; ATAC‑seq accessibility; DNA methylation at tight‑junction/mucin genes.
  - Functional: repeated stress challenges over 30–60 days post‑training without re‑exposure.
- Paracrine transfer:
  - Conditioned media and EVs applied to naïve epithelia; measure protection.
  - Necessity tests: EV depletion; EP4 (PGE2) antagonism; Nrf2 inhibition in recipients.
- Success threshold: ≥50% reduction in permeability and apoptosis vs. controls across ≥3 stress cycles; protection transferable via EVs/secretome.

Aim 3: Patch engineering and in vivo efficacy
- Construct: confluent 2D epithelial sheets from trained organoids on thin collagen/fibrin or decellularized gastric ECM; no exogenous cells beyond epithelium to keep the intervention atomic.
- Delivery: endoscopic placement on lightly abraded mucosa with fibrin sealant; grid of 5–10 mm patches to create overlapping firebreaks.
- Models: water‑immersion restraint stress and restraint‑cold stress in rodents; large‑animal confirmatory model as needed.
- Readouts:
  - On‑patch: histologic injury score, mucus thickness, TEER ex vivo, local PGE2, antioxidant tone.
  - Off‑patch (firebreak effect): gradient mapping 0–20 mm from patch edge for junction proteins, oxidative injury, and EV uptake.
  - Physiology: mucosal blood flow (laser Doppler), gastric pH/acid output, motility.
- Durability: weekly stress cycles for 8–12 weeks; patch survival and function; define booster schedule if needed.
- Success threshold: ≥40% reduction in cumulative erosions and ≥20% protection radius beyond patch margin, sustained across ≥6 stress cycles.

Aim 4: Repeatability and in vivo boosting
- Banking: manufacture and cryopreserve multiple autologous trained sheets per patient from a single biopsy session.
- Redeployment: endoscopic replacement at 3–6 month intervals based on biomarker drift.
- In vivo boosting: brief luminal SRPC perfusion during surveillance endoscopy to refresh training without replacing the patch; confirm re‑induction of cytoprotective transcription.

Key Mechanistic Tests (falsifiable)
- Is Nrf2 activation necessary? CRISPRi/shRNA knockdown before training should abrogate training benefits.
- Is PGE2/EP4 signaling required for paracrine spread? EP4 blockade should shrink firebreak radius without eliminating on‑patch resilience.
- Are EVs key carriers? EV depletion (ultracentrifugation) should reduce off‑patch protection but spare on‑patch effects.

Safety and Risk Mitigation
- Autologous cells minimize rejection; genomic stability (karyotype/oncogene panels), off‑target proliferation assays, and soft‑agar tests.
- Acid exposure: pre‑ and post‑engraftment PPI cover during initial adhesion; then step‑down to avoid global acid suppression chronically.
- Hypersecretion risk: monitor basal/meal‑stimulated acid; limit patch area to <10% mucosal surface to preserve physiology.
- Microbial overgrowth: monitor local microbiota; mucin glycosylation profiling.
- Dysplasia surveillance: scheduled biopsies at and around patches.

Endpoints and Biomarkers
- Molecular: Nrf2 target expression, mucin/TFF levels, tight‑junction proteins, EV miRNA cargo (e.g., miR‑146a).
- Functional: TEER, FITC‑dextran flux, apoptosis/ROS markers.
- Physiologic: endoscopic lesion scores, microvascular flow.
- Secreted: gastric juice PGE2 and EV counts as noninvasive patch function proxies.

Manufacturing and Deployment
- cGMP pipeline: biopsy → organoid expansion → SRPC training → QC (omics + function) → sheet assembly → cryopreservation → just‑in‑time thaw and delivery.
- Standardized SRPC kit co‑developed with defined MES; lot‑to‑lot fingerprinting.

Milestones
- Year 1: SRPC/MES defined; training protocol and durability window established.
- Year 2: Patch engineering finalized; in vivo efficacy and firebreak radius demonstrated; booster regimen defined.
- Year 3: GLP safety, dose/coverage mapping, and repeat‑application protocol; readiness for first‑in‑human feasibility (endoscopic safety and biomarker endpoints).

Decision Rules
- Advance if the trained phenotype persists ≥8 weeks post‑engraftment and protection extends ≥10 mm beyond patch edges.
- Pivot (ideation failed) if training requires continuous metabolite presence or fails to transfer paracrinally.

Expected Impact
A localized, repeatable, mechanism‑grounded therapy that installs durable “firebreaks” against stress injury—transforming management of stress‑induced gastritis from systemic suppression to precision mucosal resilience.
