Project Title
Recreating natural remission in allergic rhinitis with intranasal tolerogenic vesicles that co-deliver allergen and microbiome-derived “tolerance instructions”

Core Question–Hypothesis
Why do some individuals lose allergic rhinitis over time, and can that state be deliberately installed? We hypothesize that natural remission emerges when nasal-associated lymphoid tissue (NALT) is reset to a tolerogenic setpoint characterized by: (a) expansion of allergen-specific FOXP3+ Treg and IgA/IgG4 responses, (b) quiescent ILC2/mast cell programs, and (c) an epithelial barrier conditioned by gut- and airway-commensal metabolites (e.g., SCFAs, indoles) that dampen alarmins. We propose that co-presenting allergen with “tolerogenic DC instructions” encoded in microbiome-derived outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) from remission-like commensals will recreate this state as a short-course, self-administered intranasal therapy.

Atomic Strategy
Synchronize allergen encounter with a single, durable switch in local antigen presentation: deliver intranasal OMVs that program nasal CD103+ dendritic cells into a tolerogenic phenotype at the exact moment of allergen presentation, generating long-lived allergen-specific Treg and mucosal IgA while raising mast cell/basophil activation thresholds.

Mechanistic Model (system-wide, not local)
- Epithelium: OMV metabolites/ligands engage AHR/GPR43 and reduce IL-33/TSLP release; barrier genes increase; neuro-immune irritant signaling decreases.
- Dendritic cells: OMVs bias DCs toward retinoic acid/IL-10 production and PD-L1 expression; co-delivered allergen peptides are presented under tolerogenic conditions.
- T cells: Peripheral induction and tissue residency of allergen-specific FOXP3+ Treg (including RORγt+ subset) accumulate in NALT and suppress Th2 memory.
- B cells: Class-switch to SIgA and IgG4 against the same allergen epitopes; SIgA intercepts allergen at the surface; IgG4 co-engages FcγRIIb to inhibit effector degranulation.
- Innate effectors: ILC2 quiescence and mast cell/basophil hypo-responsiveness emerge secondarily to Treg/IgG4 dominance and reduced epithelial alarmins.
- Microbiome: Intranasal OMVs periodically “refresh” the tolerogenic tone without requiring live engraftment.

Therapeutic Product Concept
- A shelf-stable intranasal formulation of purified, detoxified OMVs from a defined commensal consortium selected from individuals with natural remission, chemically conjugated to standardized allergen peptides relevant to seasonal/perennial rhinitis.
- Dosing: brief induction course (e.g., weekly for 6–8 weeks) with quarterly micro-boosters, designed for home use.
- Safety features: low endotoxicity OMVs, nonreplicating, epitope-defined allergens to minimize anaphylaxis risk.

Specific Aims
1) Human discovery: Define the immune–microbiome signature of natural remission versus persistent allergic rhinitis.
- Cohorts: adults with prior AR whose symptoms resolved; matched persistent-AR; non-atopic controls.
- Readouts: nasal single-cell multi-omics (epithelium/immune), BCR/TCR clonotypes, mucosal antibodies (IgA/IgG4/IgE), basophil activation, nasal/gut metabolomics, upper-airway and stool microbiomes.

2) Mechanistic reconstruction: Identify remission-enriched commensals and their OMV cargos that impose tolerogenic DC programming with co-presented allergen.
- Platforms: human nasal organoid–immune co-cultures and ex vivo human DC–T/B assays using patient-derived cells.
- Criteria: induction of FOXP3+ Treg and IgA class-switching to defined allergen epitopes; suppression of Th2 cytokines and ILC2 activation markers; epithelial alarmin reduction.

3) Product optimization: Engineer a lead OMV–allergen conjugate that maximizes tolerogenic indices while minimizing reactogenicity.
- Variables: OMV source blend, detoxification method, allergen epitope selection, conjugation chemistry, muco-retention.
- Benchmarks: potency per dose, thermal stability, and manufacturability.

4) First-in-human proof-of-concept: Test intranasal OMV–allergen in persistent AR.
- Design: randomized, placebo-controlled, short-course induction with follow-up through the subsequent allergy season.
- Endpoints: total nasal symptom score (TNSS), rescue medication use, nasal provocation thresholds, quality of life; mechanistic endpoints as in Aim 1; durability across seasons.

Innovation and Advantages over Current Care
- Converts allergen exposure from a danger signal to a tolerance lesson in a single co-formulated product.
- Antigen-specific and disease-modifying without years-long build-up required by SCIT/SLIT.
- Non-live, intranasal, and self-administered; designed for fewer clinic visits and improved safety versus systemic biologics or escalating allergen doses.
- Captures the “natural cure” biology rather than suppressing pathways chronically.

Outcomes and Success Criteria
- Primary mechanistic success: ≥2-fold increase in allergen-specific nasal FOXP3+ Treg and SIgA, ≥50% reduction in epithelial alarmins during allergen challenge, and increased FcγRIIb:FcεRI functional ratio on effector cells.
- Clinical success: ≥30% reduction in TNSS and rescue medication use versus placebo during peak season; maintained benefit at 6–12 months with no increase in systemic reactions.
- Biomarker panel predicting responders based on baseline microbiome/metabolite signatures.

Risk, Failure Modes, and Mitigations
- Insufficient tolerogenic bias: iterate OMV composition toward remission-enriched strains/metabolites; add noninflammatory AHR agonist cargo while preserving atomic co-delivery principle.
- Allergen breakthrough reactions: use minimal epitope sets, gradual intranasal micro-exposure within the same formulation, and on-demand IgG4-biased booster without dose escalation.
- Heterogeneity across allergens: modular peptide panel allows tailoring without reformulating the OMV scaffold.

Regulatory and CMC Considerations
- Nonreplicating, well-characterized OMV drug–allergen conjugate with defined purity, endotoxin, and potency assays.
- Scalable fermentation–purification with batch analytics tied to tolerogenic DC activity and Treg/IgA induction potency.

Milestones and Timeline
- Year 1: Cohort enrollment; remission signature atlas; initial OMV library and epitope mapping.
- Year 2: Lead OMV–allergen selection; manufacturability and stability established; preclinical safety package.
- Year 3: Phase 1/2a initiation; interim analysis; responder biomarker validation.
- Year 4: Season-to-season durability readout; pivotal design readiness.

Clinical Translation and Impact
A short-course, intranasal, self-administered, antigen-specific tolerance therapy that reproduces the biology of natural remission could deliver rapid symptom relief, durable prevention across seasons, fewer side effects, and superior dosing convenience versus existing symptomatic drugs, biologics, or protracted immunotherapy. This program directly learns from, abstracts, and redeploys the immune–microbial “instructions” present in people whose allergies resolved naturally.

Title
Apical ATP Depletion Therapy for Allergic Rhinitis: Installing an Epithelial “Quiet” State to Restore Barrier Function and Prevent Th2 Priming

Central hypothesis-question
If we durably lower extracellular ATP/UTP at the nasal airway surface, can we stabilize epithelial tight junctions, blunt alarmin release (TSLP, IL-33, IL-25), and thereby prevent both the development and expression of allergic rhinitis while improving symptoms with minimal dosing?

Atomic strategy
Single perturbation of epithelial purinergic signaling: install an apically retained ectonucleotidase at the nasal surface to continuously degrade ATP/UTP, the common “danger” currency that opens junctions, triggers alarmins, amplifies neurogenic reflexes, and educates dendritic cells toward type 2 immunity.

Rationale (barrier-first)
- Barrier failure in the nasal epithelium precedes and instructs maladaptive immunity. Aeroallergen proteases, pollutants, and infections raise extracellular ATP/UTP, activating P2Y2/P2X receptors that:
  - Disrupt tight junctions via Ca2+-MLCK pathways and cytoskeletal remodeling.
  - Evoke alarmin release, licensing ILC2/Th2 programs and IgE class switching.
  - Drive mucin hypersecretion, edema, and neurogenic sneezing/rhinorrhea.
- Depleting apical ATP should globally quiet these inputs, allowing intrinsic repair programs to re-seal the barrier and preventing aberrant immune education.

Therapeutic concept
- Modality A (protein): Intranasal, long-resident, human CD39 ectonucleotidase engineered for apical retention (GPI anchor) and mucus affinity (synthetic mucin-interacting peptide/ELP tag). Weekly to biweekly spray during risk windows.
- Modality B (transient expression): Intranasal LNP mRNA encoding apically targeted human CD39 for seasonal coverage (single dose with multiweek expression). Epithelial-restricted signal peptide and apical sorting motifs minimize systemic exposure.
- Mechanism: Degrade ATP/ADP and UTP/UDP at the airway surface to reduce P2Y2/P2X7 activation, stabilize tight junctions (claudins/occludin/ZO-1), suppress epithelial alarmins, attenuate DC activation and neurogenic reflexes, and restore mucociliary homeostasis.
- Differentiation: Upstream, barrier-first control versus downstream antihistamines/steroids/biologics; local, non-immunosuppressive; suitable for prevention and symptom relief; infrequent dosing.

Specific aims
1) Establish that apical ATP depletion restores barrier integrity and suppresses alarmins in human nasal epithelium.
   - Readouts: TEER/flux, junctional protein localization, TSLP/IL-33/IL-25, P2Y2 signaling, ciliary beat metrics.
2) Demonstrate prevention and treatment efficacy in aeroallergen models.
   - Outcomes: Sneezing/rhinorrhea scores, nasal resistance/PNIF equivalents, lavage mediators, IgE/ILC2/Th2 indices, histologic edema/goblet metaplasia.
3) Optimize residency, activity, and safety of the apical ectonucleotidase.
   - Goals: Week-long nasal surface retention, tunable enzymatic rate, minimal systemic spillover, preserved host defense and smell.

Design features and controls
- Targeting: Apical GPI anchor plus weak mucoadhesive tag for surface residency without ciliary impairment; pan-epithelial promoter (for mRNA) tuned to secretory/multiciliated cells.
- Activity tuning: Catalytic variants spanning defined ATP Km/Vmax to avoid excessive adenosine accumulation; optional co-formulation with low-dose adenosine receptor antagonist if needed.
- Safety guardrails: Human sequence to minimize immunogenicity; local delivery; degradable tags; nasal distribution imaging.
- Comparators: Intranasal steroid, antihistamine, and anti-TSLP biologic (local ex vivo) to benchmark efficacy and onset.

Preclinical plan
- In vitro (ALI cultures, primary human nasal epithelium):
  - Allergen/pollutant/viral-mimetic challenges ± therapy.
  - Quantify ATP/UTP in airway surface liquid; junctional integrity; alarmins; neuritogenic mediators; transcriptomic shifts in repair modules (EGFR/AREG, IL-22 axes).
- Ex vivo (human turbinate explants):
  - Residency mapping, diffusion, ciliary beat safety, olfactory receptor expression screen.
- In vivo (HDM/pollen mouse and rat models, prevention and treatment arms):
  - Dosing cadence to define minimal effective residency.
  - Endpoints: Behavior (sneezing), nasal airflow, lavage cytokines, mast cell/eosinophil infiltration, serum and local IgE, DC activation, memory responses.
- Microbiome and host defense:
  - Commensal composition, pathogen challenge panels, antimicrobial peptide expression, wound closure assays.
- PK/PD:
  - Surface ATP/AMP time course; nasal wash enzyme activity; systemic exposure.

Clinical development strategy
- Phase 1 (healthy adults, single/multiple ascending intranasal doses):
  - Safety, smell testing, nasal endoscopic assessment, local pharmacology (ATP/UTP reduction), exploratory TEER/optical coherence measures.
- Phase 2a (seasonal allergic rhinitis, randomized, placebo-controlled):
  - Prophylaxis cohort: Start 2 weeks pre-season; primary TNSS/AUC and PNIF; key biomarkers (alarmins, ATP, junctional imaging).
  - Treatment cohort: Initiate during active symptoms; onset-of-action vs intranasal steroid/antihistamine; rescue medication-sparing.
- Phase 2b (perennial HDM rhinitis):
  - 12–16 weeks dosing convenience study (weekly/biweekly), quality-of-life and sleep endpoints; exploratory disease modification (reduced specific IgE, sustained effect off-treatment).

Success criteria
- ≥30% improvement in TNSS versus placebo with non-inferior onset to antihistamines and steroid-sparing effect.
- Sustained lowering of nasal surface ATP/UTP and alarmins with improved junctional continuity.
- Acceptable safety: preserved olfaction, no infection signal, minimal epistaxis/irritation, negligible systemic exposure.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Excess adenosine–mediated congestion: tune CD39 activity; monitor adenosine; incorporate dose caps or local A2A/A2B modulation if needed.
- Mucosal defense attenuation: periodic microbiome surveillance; challenge models; stop rules; exclude immunocompromised in early trials.
- Ciliary/mucus alterations: preclinical motility thresholds; avoid high mucoadhesion; human factors device optimization.

Advantages over current therapies
- Upstream, single-lever control stabilizing barrier and quenching epithelial “danger” signaling.
- Dual benefit: symptom relief and prevention/sensitization blockade.
- Localized, low systemic risk; convenient weekly or seasonal dosing.
- Compatible with and potentially reducing reliance on steroids/biologics; addresses non-histaminic symptoms (congestion, rhinorrhea, hyperreactivity).

Exploration of broader AR mechanisms and read-through
- Barrier integrity (tight junction phosphorylation, cytoskeleton) improved by lowering ATP-driven Ca2+ waves.
- Epithelial alarmins and DC education suppressed, reducing ILC2/Th2 cascades and IgE priming.
- Neurogenic inflammation (P2X/P2Y on sensory nerves) dampened, reducing sneezing/rhinorrhea.
- Mucociliary homeostasis normalized; mucus hypersecretion and viscosity reduced.
- Potential positive shifts in microbiome via restored epithelial tone.

Milestones
- Year 1: Lead construct selection, ALI efficacy/safety, formulation and device prototype.
- Year 2: In vivo efficacy, residency optimization, GLP tox initiation.
- Year 3: Phase 1 completion with pharmacodynamic proof; Phase 2a initiation timed to pollen season.

Outcome
A first-in-class, barrier-first, apically targeted ectonucleotidase therapy that reestablishes a “quiet” epithelial state, delivering convenient, local, upstream control of allergic rhinitis with potential for disease modification and prevention.

Title
Temporal order and duration of S. epidermidis versus S. aureus signals imprint a reversible “inflammatory memory” that gates skin stem cell differentiation in human skin organoids

Atomic hypothesis
Temporal order and relative duration of commensal (S. epidermidis) versus pathobiont (S. aureus) extracellular signals act as a single systems-level memory switch in epidermal stem/progenitor cells, shifting their inflammatory setpoint and biasing fate toward self-renewal or differentiation. Specifically, prolonged commensal-first exposure induces tolerance and preserves differentiation capacity, while prolonged pathobiont-first exposure imprints hyper-responsiveness that impairs differentiation; short “counter-pulses” test reversibility.

Rationale
- Epidermal stem cells exhibit inflammatory memory that persists beyond initial cues; order and exposure length likely determine the sign of this memory.
- Bacteria communicate via extracellular vesicles (BEVs) and secreted factors sufficient to engage host receptors without requiring live co-culture.
- A proof-of-concept that isolates “order × duration” as the causal lever provides a minimal test of stem cell plasticity under microbiome-derived signals.

Specific aims
1) Quantify how order (which strain first) and duration (long vs short) of bacterial signals set epidermal stem cell inflammatory status in skin organoids.
2) Determine how this inflammatory setpoint impacts differentiation capacity and barrier maturation.
3) Compare signal formats (bacterial cocktail vs isolated BEVs) to identify the minimal signal sufficient to program memory.

Experimental overview
- System: Human skin organoids containing basal stem/progenitor and suprabasal layers, established from a single donor source per run to limit variability (repeat across ≥2 donors in confirmatory run).
- Signal formats:
  a) BEVs isolated from S. epidermidis and S. aureus (sterile, non-viable preparations).
  b) Cocktail: combined S. epidermidis + S. aureus BEVs presented simultaneously.
- Exposure logic (sequential switching with a defined washout/rest interval): “Long” (L) versus “Short” (S) exposures, with constant dose per exposure across conditions. No live bacteria are added to organoids.

Treatment matrix (POC scale)
- Sequential, order × duration arms (BEVs format):
  1) SaL → SeS
  2) SaS → SeL
  3) SeL → SaS
  4) SeS → SaL
- Single-strain references: SaL, SeL
- Simultaneous control: Cocktail (Sa+Se, concurrent)
- Vehicle control: buffer-only
- Replicates: n=3 organoid cultures per arm (technical), repeated once (biological) for robustness within POC scope.

Key readouts and metrics
Inflammatory status (Aim 1)
- Secretome panel from organoid supernatants: IL-1 family, TNF, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, CCL20, antimicrobial peptides (e.g., DEFB4/HBD2), type I/III IFN signatures.
- Transcriptional state: targeted RNA profiling of innate/TLR/NF-κB/IRF modules (bulk or mini-panel); optional scRNA-seq in a subset to resolve basal versus suprabasal states.
- Signaling activation: immunostaining/IF for nuclear NF-κB (p65), phospho-p38; quantify nuclear translocation index.
- Memory test: post-switch challenge with a standardized commensal mimetic (e.g., Se BEVs) to assess hypo/hyper-responsiveness vs baseline controls.

Differentiation capacity (Aim 2)
- Layer composition: IF for KRT14/p63 (basal), KRT10/IVL/LOR (spinous/granular); compute Differentiation Index = (KRT10+IVL+LOR area)/(KRT14 area).
- Proliferation and stemness: Ki67, p63 intensity; basal integrins (ITGA6) where feasible.
- Barrier function: dye penetration or TEER-like surrogate on organoid sheets; lower permeability = better maturation.
- Clonogenic potential: dissociate a subset post-exposure and measure colony-forming efficiency (CFE) as a proxy for stemness reserve.

Format sufficiency (Aim 3)
- Compare sequential arms run with BEVs versus a matched “cocktail” arm presented simultaneously.
- Minimal-signal criterion: if BEVs alone reproduce order/duration effects seen with cocktail, BEVs are sufficient drivers.

Primary outcomes and decision rules
- Inflammatory Setpoint Score (ISS): composite z-score across cytokines, NF-κB activation, and innate transcriptional modules.
- Differentiation Capacity Score (DCS): composite of Differentiation Index, barrier surrogate, and CFE.
- Order-duration effect: Δ(ISS, DCS) between SaL→SeS vs SeL→SaS defines directionality; significant divergence indicates memory and hysteresis.
- Reversibility: extent to which the second “short” pulse counteracts or amplifies the first “long” imprint.

Data analysis plan
- Factorial comparisons (order × duration) with controls; effect sizes (Hedges’ g) prioritized over p-values in POC.
- Correlate ISS with DCS to test the predicted trade-off (pro-inflammatory setpoint associates with reduced differentiation).
- Pathway-level enrichment from transcriptional data to confirm innate modules underlying phenotypes.

Expected results
- SeL→SaS yields a restrained ISS and preserved DCS (tolerant, differentiation-permissive state).
- SaL→SeS yields elevated ISS and reduced DCS (hyper-responsive, differentiation-impaired state).
- Cocktail (simultaneous) blunts order effects; BEVs recapitulate sequential effects, supporting sufficiency of vesicle-borne cues.

Feasibility and 3‑month timeline (POC)
- Month 1: Prepare organoids; small pilot to fix dose ranges for BEVs and validate non-toxicity; finalize readout panels.
- Month 2: Execute full treatment matrix (sequential exposures, rest, challenge); bank supernatants and tissues.
- Month 3: Run cytokine panels, targeted RNA profiling, IF imaging, barrier surrogate, CFE; integrate data and compute ISS/DCS.

Risk mitigation
- Variability: use single-donor organoids per run; include internal vehicle and single-strain long-exposure references.
- Signal fidelity: qualify BEVs for size and marker profile; confirm sterility.
- Overstimulation: predefine toxicity stop rules based on morphology/viability imaging to preserve interpretability of differentiation readouts.

Scale and resources (POC)
- Total arms: 8
- Replicates: 3 technical per arm, one biological repeat
- Core assays: multiplex cytokines, targeted RNA, IF imaging, one functional barrier surrogate, CFE
- Optional deepening (budget/time-contingent): scRNA-seq on two contrastive arms (SaL→SeS vs SeL→SaS)

Impact
This POC isolates temporal order and duration as the single causal lever that imprints an inflammatory memory in epidermal stem cells, linking it mechanistically to differentiation outcomes. A positive result establishes a compact paradigm to manipulate skin stem cell plasticity via timed commensal/pathobiont signals.

Compliance and safety
All work with materials derived from S. aureus and S. epidermidis must be conducted by trained personnel under institutional approvals and applicable biosafety regulations. The POC uses sterile, non-viable bacterial fractions (e.g., BEVs) to avoid introducing live organisms into organoid cultures.

Title
Choice-arena skin organoids to test history-dependent (order/duration) effects of S. epidermidis vs S. aureus signals on stem cell inflammation and fate

Integrated hypothesis–question
Do human epidermal stem cells encode a history of commensal versus pathobiont exposure (order and duration) that biases inflammatory state and differentiation, and can spatially segregated “neighborhoods” of opposing bacterial signals re-instruct these cells once they migrate?

Atomic strategy
Measure non-commutative, history-dependent state transitions (hysteresis) by (i) imposing a uniform first exposure that differs in order and duration, then (ii) presenting a simultaneous, spatially segregated second exposure that creates adjacent commensal and pathobiont neighborhoods. Track single cells across the boundary and read out inflammatory activation and differentiation capacity. Use spectrally time-stamped vesicles to map exposure history within each cell.

Experimental overview (POC scale; ≤3 months)
- Model: Human epidermal organoid equivalents built from primary basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors or widely used immortalized basal keratinocytes, with an NF-κB activity reporter line for live readout (commercially available or core-facility generated). Short 2D organoid-equivalent “rafts” for migration assays; optional confirmatory 3D ALI inserts in Month 3.
- Bacterial inputs (two formats):
  1) Bacterial-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs/exosomes) prepared to be sterile and standardized (sourced from a core facility/vendor or prior validated stocks).  
  2) “Cocktail” condition: a defined mixture of the S. epidermidis- and S. aureus–derived EVs at equal total protein.  
  All inputs are quality-checked for size distribution and absence of live bacteria by the provider/core.
- Spatial choice-arena: A two-neighborhood culture device that creates adjacent, stable microenvironments over a 2D keratinocyte organoid sheet. Neighborhood A is enriched in S. epidermidis EV signals; Neighborhood B in S. aureus EV signals. The interface permits cell migration between neighborhoods over days. For POC, use a simple removable divider to pattern two halves, then maintain neighborhoods by local EV depots (e.g., inert hydrogel pads or surface-bound EV reservoirs) on each side; fluorescent tags on EVs allow visualization of gradient stability.

Key manipulations (sequences meeting the constraint of order and differential duration)
- Phase 1 (uniform pre-exposure; establishes history):
  - Long A → Short B: 72 h uniform S. aureus EVs, then 24 h uniform S. epidermidis EVs.
  - Long B → Short A: 72 h uniform S. epidermidis EVs, then 24 h uniform S. aureus EVs.
  - Equal–equal control: 48 h → 48 h with switched order.
  - Cocktail control: 96 h uniform cocktail (simultaneous cues, no history).
- Phase 2 (simultaneous spatial conflict; tests re-instruction vs locked-in memory):
  - Install two-neighborhood arena for 48 h with left half enriched for S. epidermidis EVs and right half enriched for S. aureus EVs (or vice versa in replicate plates). Cells can migrate freely. Maintain equal cumulative EV dose across conditions.
- Time-stamping: Use spectrally distinct EV labels for Phase 1 vs Phase 2 to determine, per cell, which history it carries and which neighborhood it occupies at endpoint.

Readouts (plasticity: inflammatory status and differentiation capacity)
- Live inflammatory dynamics:
  - NF-κB reporter imaging throughout all phases; extract single-cell traces (activation frequency, peak amplitude, and area-under-curve).  
- Endpoint cell states (spatially resolved across neighborhoods and boundary):
  - Immunostaining for KRT14 (basal), KRT10 and involucrin/filaggrin (differentiation), p63 (stemness), and phosphorylated NF-κB p65 localization.  
  - Secreted cytokines/chemokines panel from supernatants (e.g., IL-1 family, IL-6, TNF, CXCL8) to capture inflammatory milieu differences between neighborhoods.  
  - Functional stemness: re-plate equal numbers from each neighborhood into colony-forming assays; compute colony-forming efficiency and colony size distribution.  
  - Optional targeted RNA profiling (panel of inflammation and differentiation genes) or small-scale single-cell profiling if budget/time allow.
- Exposure history mapping:
  - Quantify per-cell EV uptake identity (Phase 1 label vs Phase 2 label) and position relative to the boundary; relate to inflammatory and differentiation markers.

Primary outcomes and quantitative metrics
- Hysteresis index (HI): For matched cumulative dose, HI = outcome(A→B) − outcome(B→A), computed for (i) mean NF-κB activity metrics, (ii) fraction of KRT10+/IVL+ cells, (iii) colony-forming efficiency. Non-zero HI indicates order dependence.  
- Re-instruction score (RS): Among cells pre-exposed long to S. aureus, compute the fraction that adopt low-inflammatory, basal-like fate when residing in the S. epidermidis neighborhood versus remaining inflammatory/differentiated; compare to converse condition. RS > 0 indicates neighborhood can override history.  
- Boundary plasticity map: Spatial profiles of inflammatory activity and differentiation across the interface; detect sharp vs graded transitions and any lag relative to EV gradient.  
- Memory half-life estimate: Fit decay of history-dependent bias after relocation to opposing neighborhood over 48 h.

Controls
- Vehicle-only EV buffer on both phases.  
- Heat- or enzyme-inactivated EV controls to test dependence on intact vesicular cargo (inactivated materials sourced from core/vendor).  
- Dose-matched total protein controls.  
- No-Phase-1 pre-exposure (Phase 2 only) to measure pure neighborhood instruction without history.  
- Cocktail-only throughout to benchmark simultaneous, non-sequential exposure.

Experimental scale and replication
- POC scale: n = 3–4 independent plates per regimen; per plate analyze ≥10 fields spanning both neighborhoods and the boundary. Mixed-effects models to account for plate-to-plate variability.

Success criteria (go/no-go)
- Go if any two of the following are met:  
  1) HI differs significantly from zero for at least one primary metric.  
  2) RS shows significant re-instruction in at least one direction (commensal neighborhood dampens prior pathobiont-induced inflammation or vice versa).  
  3) Distinct spatial state maps aligning with neighborhoods despite uniform Phase 1 history, indicating true neighborhood instruction capacity.
- No-go if outcomes are indistinguishable across orders and neighborhoods under dose-matched conditions.

Anticipated outcome patterns and interpretation
- History-dominant: Large HI, low RS. Interpretation: early pathobiont exposure locks cells into pro-inflammatory, differentiation-prone states resistant to later commensal cues (cell-intrinsic memory).  
- Neighborhood-dominant: Small HI, high RS. Interpretation: local cues rapidly reprogram state; order matters little (environment instructs fate).  
- Asymmetric plasticity: HI significant only for one order; suggests commensal priming creates a refractory state to pathobiont instruction or vice versa.  
- Boundary bistability: Mixed states near the interface; suggests threshold effects and potential community-level feedbacks.

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Month 1: Assemble choice-arena culture platform; validate EV gradient visualization and stability; baseline NF-κB reporter performance; pilot staining panel.  
- Month 2: Execute Phase 1 order/duration pilots; finalize doses that yield measurable but submaximal activation.  
- Month 3: Full sequence runs with spatial Phase 2; endpoints (imaging, staining, secretome); colony-forming assays; initial analysis of HI and RS.

Risk mitigation
- EV cross-diffusion blurs neighborhoods: quantify gradient via EV labels; refresh local depots as needed; interpret with measured gradient length scales.  
- Limited migration: perform assays on 2D organoid-equivalent sheets to enhance motility; extend Phase 2 to 72 h if needed while keeping cumulative dose matched across arms.  
- Reporter sensitivity: include fixed-time immunostaining readouts to corroborate live imaging findings.  
- Dose confounds: predefine and match total EV exposure across all regimens; include cocktail benchmarking.

Ethical and safety notes
- Use only sterile, validated bacterial EV preparations obtained from qualified sources; follow institutional biosafety approvals for exposure studies. No live bacterial handling is required for this POC.

Deliverables
- Quantified hysteresis and re-instruction metrics with spatial maps linking exposure history to inflammatory state and differentiation capacity, establishing whether history or neighborhood predominates in guiding skin stem cell decisions.

text:
Title
Does metabolic state, not timing, determine how Staphylococcal signals reprogram skin stem cells?

Integrated hypothesis-question
If skin organoid stem cells are preset into distinct metabolic modes (glycolytic-high vs OXPHOS-high), then subsequent exposure to Staphylococcus aureus (Sa) and Staphylococcus epidermidis (Se) extracellular vesicles (EVs) in any order will reproduce the inflammatory and differentiation outcomes seen with natural time-ordered Sa→Se or Se→Sa exposure. If outcomes diverge, order encodes supra-metabolic information.

Atomic strategy
Make metabolic state the “sufficient statistic.” First lock organoid stem cells into defined energetic modes; then randomize vesicle order and exposure duration. Compare against natural sequences. Equivalence between “preset+random” and “natural sequence” implies metabolism is causal; non-equivalence reveals an order-dependent code beyond metabolism.

Model system
- Human skin organoids enriched for basal keratinocyte stem/progenitors (POC-scale batches; ≥2 donor lines if available for robustness).
- Stimuli: sterile, replication-incompetent bacterial EV preparations from Se (commensal) and Sa (pathobiont), and a mixed EV cocktail (Se+Sa). Use pre-characterized or core-facility–prepared materials under institutional approvals.

Experimental design (POC matrix)
Factor A: Exposure sequence and duration
- Natural sequences:
  1) Sa long → Se short
  2) Se long → Sa short
  3) Sa short → Se long
  4) Se short → Sa long
- Cocktail (concurrent): Se+Sa together (single window)
- Randomized sequences: all permutations of [Se, Sa] applied after metabolic preset (see Factor B)
- Notes: Long vs short are distinct, non-overlapping exposure windows; include standardized washouts between windows.

Factor B: Metabolic preset (applied before any EVs)
- Glycolytic-high bias
- OXPHOS-high bias
- Neutral baseline (vehicle)
- Verification assays confirm the intended metabolic state at EV exposure onset.

Controls
- Vehicle only (no EVs)
- EVs only (single exposure) for Se and Sa
- Heat-inactivated EV control (membrane integrity control)
- Metabolic preset only (no EVs)
- Optional specificity control: EV-depleted supernatant

Primary readouts (plasticity endpoints)
Inflammatory status
- Secreted cytokine profile: multiplex panel (e.g., IL-1 family, IL-6, IL-8/CXCL8, TNF, GM-CSF, CCL20).
- NF-κB activity: reporter organoids or nuclear p65 localization.
- Innate receptor signaling transcripts: targeted qPCR panel (e.g., TLR-adaptors, interferon-stimulated genes).
- Secreted antimicrobial peptides (e.g., β-defensins) by immunoassay.

Differentiation capacity
- Immunofluorescence histology for stratification and lineage balance:
  - Basal/stemness: KRT14/KRT5, ΔNp63
  - Early/late differentiation: KRT10, involucrin, loricrin, filaggrin
- Proliferation vs commitment: Ki-67 or EdU incorporation; Notch pathway target expression.
- Functional maturation proxy: barrier-associated protein abundance and cornified layer thickness.

Metabolic state verification (manipulation check)
- Glycolytic flux proxies: extracellular lactate; NADH/NAD+ ratio.
- Mitochondrial activity proxies: membrane potential dye; ATP/ADP ratio; ROS levels.
- Optional: ECAR/OCR-based glycolytic index when feasible.

Key outcomes and decision logic
- Primary comparison 1 (Natural sequence test): Sa→Se vs Se→Sa (with long/short asymmetry) define the “sequence signatures” for inflammation and differentiation.
- Primary comparison 2 (Sufficiency test): For each sequence signature, identify whether a matched signature emerges when organoids are metabolically preset and then exposed to randomized EV order.
  - Equivalence within predefined effect-size bounds between “natural sequence” and “preset+random” indicates metabolism is sufficient to explain sequence effects.
  - Non-equivalence indicates an order-encoded program beyond metabolism.
- Secondary comparison: Cocktail vs sequential exposure clarifies whether concurrent cues collapse timing dependence.

Analysis plan (POC-level)
- Define a priori “sequence signature” features: composite inflammatory score (z-scored cytokines + NF-κB readout) and composite differentiation index (weighted markers).
- Use equivalence testing (e.g., two one-sided tests) to assess whether “preset+random” is statistically equivalent to its matched “natural sequence” signature within biologically meaningful bounds.
- Mixed-effects models account for batch/donor; adjust for multiple testing across endpoints.
- Minimal success criterion: at least one endpoint (inflammation or differentiation) shows clear equivalence (metabolism-sufficient) or clear non-equivalence (order-encoded) with consistent direction across two donor lines.

Feasibility and timeline (≤3 months)
- Weeks 1–3: Establish/expand organoids; qualify EV inputs and baseline viability; calibrate non-lethal metabolic presets; lock equivalence bounds.
- Weeks 4–7: Run natural-sequence arms and cocktail; run preset+random arms in parallel; collect supernatants and fix organoids for imaging.
- Weeks 8–12: Complete assays, scoring, and analysis; replicate key contrasts in an independent batch.

Risk management
- Cytotoxicity at high EV input: predefine safe working ranges using viability screens.
- Off-target effects of metabolic presets: rely on orthogonal verification assays; include “preset only” controls.
- Donor variability: include at least two donors; analyze with random effects.

Readouts-to-insight mapping
- If Se→Sa and Sa→Se differ, but preset glycolytic-high vs OXPHOS-high fully recapitulates each, then metabolic state is causal and timing is dispensable.
- If preset states fail to recreate sequence signatures, then EVs transmit a time-ordered code (e.g., priming vs triggering) independent of global metabolism.
- If cocktail approximates one sequence but not the other, concurrent cues partially compress the temporal code.

POC deliverables
- A ranked list of endpoints most sensitive to timing vs metabolism.
- A decision on sufficiency of metabolic state in explaining sequence effects.
- A minimal experimental recipe (conceptual, not procedural) for scaling to mechanistic dissection (e.g., receptor blockade or EV cargo fractionation) in a follow-on study.

Title
Ecological-dominance–coded bacterial signals reprogram skin stem cell inflammatory memory and fate in organoids

Unified research goal-question-hypothesis
Do human skin stem cells compute “who is winning now” (ecological dominance) rather than just “who arrived first,” such that sequential exposure to competition-conditioned signals from S. epidermidis and S. aureus drives distinct inflammatory memory and differentiation outcomes even when total dose and composition are matched?

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Encode order and dominance into the stimulus itself by harvesting exosome-rich, cell-free secretomes from controlled S. epidermidis–S. aureus competition micro-ecologies at defined dominance states. Then apply these dominance-coded signals to skin organoids in sequential, time-skewed schedules with matched total exposure. This isolates whether stem cells decode temporal dominance, not merely species identity or cumulative dose.

Experimental overview (POC; ≤3 months)
- Platform: Primary human keratinocyte organotypic epidermal equivalents on fibroblast collagen gels at air–liquid interface (ALI). Include basal stem cell compartment (ITGA6hi/CD71lo).
- Stimuli: Bacterial-derived exosomes (EVs) and matched whole conditioned media (CM), cell-free, sterile, harvested from in vitro competitions engineered to yield either commensal-dominant (CD) or pathobiont-dominant (PD) states.
- Treatment design: Sequential switching with differential exposure durations (long→short vs short→long), keeping total exposure constant. Include composition-matched, history-free cocktails as controls.
- Readouts: Inflammatory status (early signaling, cytokines, transcriptional state) and differentiation capacity (marker expression, barrier metrics, colony-forming efficiency).

A. Generate dominance-coded bacterial secretomes
1) Competition micro-ecologies (BSL-2):
   - Strains: S. epidermidis (commensal) and S. aureus (pathobiont), single well-characterized lab strains.
   - Media regimes to bias dominance:
     • Low-protein, salt/acids “skin-like” medium → favors S. epidermidis (CD state).
     • Protein-rich medium → favors S. aureus (PD state).
   - Start ratios: 9:1 and 1:9 (S. epi:S. aur) to further steer dominance.
   - Validate dominance at harvest points (8–12 h for early, 18–24 h for late):
     • Species-specific qPCR and CFU on selective agar.
     • OD600 and metabolite (e.g., lactate) snapshot to confirm ecological shift.

2) Secretome preparation (for each CD and PD state):
   - Remove cells: 0.22 μm filtration + 10,000 g 20 min.
   - Split into:
     • EV fraction: ultracentrifugation 100,000 g 70 min; resuspend in PBS.
     • Whole CM: retain supernatant.
   - Normalize dose:
     • EVs by total protein (e.g., 10 μg/mL) and particle count (NTA).
     • CM by total protein (BCA) and volume.
   - Quality controls: endotoxin level, sterility spotting, basic proteomics fingerprint (optional, pooled).

B. Treatment arms (2×2 order-by-duration; EVs and CM tested in parallel)
- Total exposure per organoid: 60 h; single media change between phases (brief PBS rinse).
- Schedules (each with CD and PD lots from A):
  1) CD 48 h → PD 12 h
  2) PD 48 h → CD 12 h
  3) CD 12 h → PD 48 h
  4) PD 12 h → CD 48 h
- Composition-matched controls (history-free):
  5) Static cocktail 60 h at 80:20 CD:PD (to match “CD 48→PD 12” composition)
  6) Static cocktail 60 h at 20:80 CD:PD (to match “PD 48→CD 12” composition)
- Additional controls:
  7) Monoculture EVs/CM from S. epidermidis only; 8) from S. aureus only.
  9) Vehicle; 10) Heat-inactivated EVs; 11) Proteinase K–treated EVs (protein dependency).
  12) TLR2 blockade (neutralizing Ab) mechanistic check.

C. Organoid platform and sampling
- Construct ALI organoids (n=3 donors, 2–3 biological replicates/arm).
- During exposure: collect basolateral media at 6, 24, 60 h for cytokines.
- Post-exposure plasticity challenge:
  - Phase I (acute): analyze immediately at 60 h.
  - Phase II (fate): switch to differentiation medium 7 days to reveal commitment; in parallel, isolate basal cells (ITGA6hi/CD71lo) for colony assays.

D. Readouts
1) Inflammatory status
   - Early signaling: p65 NF-κB nuclear translocation (IF), phospho-p38/ERK western or immunostain; IκBα degradation.
   - Cytokines/chemokines (Luminex/ELISA): IL-1β, IL-6, TNF, IL-8, IL-17C, TSLP, GM-CSF, CXCL1.
   - Transcriptional panel (qPCR or targeted RNA-seq): TLR2, NOD2, S100A7/8/9, DEFB4, IFN-stimulated genes.
   - “Inflammatory Priming Index” (IPI): z-score average of sentinel NF-κB targets normalized to vehicle.

2) Differentiation capacity and barrier
   - Basal/stemness: KRT14, KRT5, KRT15, LGR6, SOX9 (IF/qPCR).
   - Commitment/terminal: KRT10, involucrin, filaggrin, loricrin.
   - Barrier: TEER and FITC–dextran flux; cornified envelope quantification.
   - Colony-forming efficiency (CFE): holoclone/meroclone/paraclone distribution after replating on 3T3 feeders; “Fate Shift Score” (FSS) = holoclone% − paraclone%.

3) Memory persistence
   - Washout 72 h subgroup: reassess IPI and FSS to test lasting imprinting independent of ongoing stimulus.

E. Analysis plan
- Primary contrast: Order effect under matched total dose and matched composition.
  - Order Effect Index (OEI) = mean(CD→PD) − mean(PD→CD), per readout (IPI, FSS, TEER).
- Secondary: Duration asymmetry (long→short vs short→long).
- Mixed-effects models (donor as random effect); FDR correction across markers.
- Mediation check: attenuation of OEI with TLR2 blockade suggests TLR2-dependent decoding of dominance.

F. Success criteria (POC)
- Significant OEI for IPI and at least one fate metric (FSS or barrier) that is not reproduced by static composition-matched cocktails, indicating that competition history/order, not just mixture ratio, instructs stem cell state.
- Replicable across ≥2 of 3 donors and in both EV and CM formats (allowing magnitude differences).

G. Timeline (12 weeks)
- Weeks 1–2: Establish competitions; validate CD/PD windows; pilot EV/CM prep and dosing.
- Weeks 3–4: Scale EV/CM production; finalize normalization; pretest toxicity.
- Weeks 5–8: Execute sequential exposures across arms; collect acute readouts.
- Weeks 9–10: Differentiation phase; CFE assays; barrier tests.
- Weeks 11–12: Data analysis; replication of key contrasts; shortlist mechanistic follow-ups.

H. Risk and mitigation
- Variability in dominance: lock harvest by species-qPCR thresholds; bank multiple lots.
- EV yield inconsistency: pool batches; normalize by particle count and protein.
- Overactivation toxicity: predefine maximum EV/CM dose; monitor viability (ATP assay).

Deliverables
- Quantified order-of-dominance effects on inflammatory priming and fate decisions in skin organoids.
- Benchmark dataset comparing EV-only vs whole CM and static cocktails vs competition-coded signals.
- Go/no-go criteria for scaling to mechanistic dissection (e.g., chromatin accessibility, receptor dependency).

text:
Title
Temporal encoding of bacterial encounter memory in human epidermal stem cells: order- and duration-dependent priming by S. aureus vs S. epidermidis vesicles prior to organoid formation

Hypothesis/Question (merged)
Do human epidermal stem cells encode a durable “bacterial encounter memory” from sequential, time-differential exposure to S. aureus- versus S. epidermidis-derived extracellular vesicles such that, after washout and organoid formation without bacteria, (i) inflammatory set-point and (ii) differentiation capacity are durably biased? Specifically, does temporal order and duration (long→short vs short→long) act as a single control knob that flips persistent chromatin “memory switches” which later shape organoid behavior?

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Manipulate only the temporal program of pre-organoid exposure—order and duration of bEVs (bacterial extracellular vesicles)—as the sole perturbation. Then remove all bacterial material before organoid formation. If stem cells store temporal information, durable epigenetic and functional biases will appear in bacteria-free organoids.

Overview of experimental design (POC scale; ≤3 months)
- System: Primary human epidermal basal stem cells (KRT14+, ITGA6hi) expanded briefly, then exposed to purified bEVs from S. aureus (Sa) and S. epidermidis (Se). Cells are thoroughly washed and used to generate epidermal organoids/3D skin equivalents at air–liquid interface without bacteria.
- Perturbation: Sequential bEV exposures with asymmetric durations to encode order and time.
- Primary endpoints:
  1) Persistent inflammatory state (baseline cytokines, signaling readiness, epigenetic marks) after full washout.
  2) Differentiation capacity and barrier formation in organoids.
- Scale: 3 healthy donors × 3 technical replicates per condition (n=9 per condition). POC-friendly readouts with 1–2 “deep” assays on pooled replicates.

Exposure conditions (core 6 + minimal controls; total 9)
- Long = 48 h; Short = 12 h; 12 h washout between steps; all at 70–80% confluence.
A) Sequence/order arms
  1) Sa-long → Se-short
  2) Sa-short → Se-long
  3) Se-long → Sa-short
  4) Se-short → Sa-long
B) Simultaneous cocktail control
  5) Sa+Se together, 48 h (tests “order matters” vs mixture)
C) Single-strain memory baselines
  6) Sa-long only
  7) Se-long only
D) Process controls
  8) Vehicle (vesicle buffer) only
  9) Naïve (no handling beyond media changes)
Notes: For timing feasibility, prioritize A1–A4 and controls 5, 8. Run 6–7 if capacity allows.

Vesicle preparation and dosing
- Source: Well-characterized lab strains of S. aureus (pathobiont) and S. epidermidis (commensal).
- bEVs: Collect cell-free supernatants from mid-log cultures; differential filtration (0.22 μm), ultracentrifugation or size-exclusion chromatography to isolate vesicles; DNase/RNase/protease-treated, endotoxin/LTA-quantified; plate to confirm sterility.
- Standardization: Nanoparticle tracking analysis for particles/mL; dose at 5,000–10,000 particles/cell (pilot-dose optimize in week 1). Keep protein and particle dose equal across conditions.

Key timelines (12 weeks total)
- Weeks 1–2: Donor cell thaw/expansion; bEV prep; pilot dose/tolerability; lock doses.
- Weeks 3–4: Sequential exposures per design; stringent washout (3× PBS, 24 h media).
- Weeks 4–7: Organoid seeding and differentiation at air–liquid interface (14–21 days).
- Weeks 6–8: Baseline assays in bacteria-free organoids.
- Week 8: Secondary challenge test (brief IL-1β+TNFα cocktail or TLR2 ligand) to reveal trained tolerance vs priming.
- Weeks 8–10: Molecular assays (ATAC, CUT&Tag, qPCR).
- Weeks 10–12: Data integration and analysis.

Assays and readouts
1) Memory establishment in pre-organoid stem cells (after final washout, pre-seeding)
- Epigenetic “switches”:
  - Omni-ATAC-seq (bulk, indexed) on pooled replicates per condition to assess accessibility at inflammatory/differentiation enhancers (e.g., IL1B, CXCL8, S100A8/A9, KRT10/IVL loci).
  - CUT&Tag (targeted) for H3K27ac and H3K27me3 at sentinel loci (low-input friendly).
- Transcriptional set-point: Targeted RT-qPCR panel (IL1B, CXCL8, TNFAIP3, NFKBIA, S100A8/A9, KRT14, KRT10, IVL, FLG).
- Sentinel signaling readiness: NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation upon a brief ex vivo micro-stimulus (5 ng/mL IL-1β for 30 min) vs unstimulated baseline.

2) Organoid-level outcomes (no bacteria present)
- Inflammatory status (baseline and upon standardized 4 h challenge on week 7):
  - Secreted cytokines/chemokines by multiplex bead assay (IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF, CCL20).
  - NF-κB p65/RelA nuclear translocation immunofluorescence.
- Differentiation capacity and barrier function:
  - Histology/IF: KRT14 (basal), KRT10/IVL/FLG (spinous/granular/cornified); quantify stratification index and layer thickness.
  - Barrier assay: FITC-dextran permeability or TEER on matched inserts.
  - Proliferation vs differentiation balance: Ki67, EdU pulse-chase.
- Persistence of epigenetic marks in organoids: ATAC-seq on week-7 organoids (pooled, subset of key conditions: A1, A2, A3, A4, 5, 8).

Primary outcomes and success criteria
- Primary outcome 1 (epigenetic memory index): Composite z-score of ATAC accessibility and H3K27ac at predefined inflammatory and differentiation enhancer sets in pre-organoid cells that persists (directionally consistent) in organoids.
- Primary outcome 2 (functional bias index):
  - Inflammation set-point: Elevated or dampened baseline IL-6/IL-8 and NF-κB nuclear fraction in organoids without bacteria.
  - Differentiation/barrier bias: Changes in KRT10/IVL/FLG expression and improved/worsened barrier (TEER↑/permeability↓).
- Success criteria: Any sequence-specific, duration-dependent divergence where sequential (A1–A4) ≠ cocktail (5) and ≠ single-strain (6–7), persisting through organoid maturation.

Statistical plan
- Factors: Order (Sa→Se vs Se→Sa) × Duration pattern (Long→Short vs Short→Long).
- Analysis: Two-way ANOVA with donor as random effect (mixed model); Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiplex panels. Predefine contrasts: A1 vs A2; A3 vs A4; pooled order effect; pooled duration effect; sequential vs cocktail (A1–A4 vs 5).
- Power (POC): Expect medium effect sizes (Cohen’s d ~0.8) detectable with 3 donors × 3 tech reps; emphasis on effect size and reproducibility across donors.

Quality and controls
- Washout verification: qPCR for bacterial 16S; plate media for sterility; endotoxin/LTA carryover below assay LOD.
- Vesicle integrity and equivalence: NTA profiles, TEM spot-check; normalize dose by particles and protein.
- Cell state matching pre-exposure: Passage-matched, similar confluence.

Risk mitigation and decision gates
- If bEV dose is cytotoxic: Reduce dose or shorten “long” to 24–36 h; maintain asymmetry.
- If effects are weak: Enrich readouts with chromatin profiling (increase loci via ATAC-qPCR panel); extend organoid maturation to 21 days.
- If sequential ≈ cocktail: Increase interval between steps (e.g., 24 h washout) to sharpen temporal encoding.
- If donor variability dominates: Analyze within-donor effects; proceed to single-donor clonal lines for follow-up.

Mechanistic footholds for immediate next step (beyond POC, optional subset)
- TLR2 blockade during exposure window to test necessity of canonical Gram-positive sensing.
- Metabolic co-readouts (ECAR/OCR) to probe trained-immunity-like rewiring.

Expected patterns (decision-relevant)
- Sa-long→Se-short: Primed inflammation (higher baseline IL-6/IL-8, NF-κB readiness), impaired differentiation/barrier; inflammatory enhancer accessibility↑.
- Se-long→Sa-short: Tolerized or homeostatic set-point (cytokines↓ at baseline, restrained NF-κB), preserved/enhanced differentiation/barrier; inflammatory enhancer accessibility↓; epidermal differentiation enhancers↑.
- Cocktail-48 h: Intermediate phenotype lacking strong memory signature; indicates order is the informative variable.

Feasibility checklist
- All steps fit ≤12 weeks.
- No live bacteria in organoid phase; safety and interpretability improved.
- Readouts scalable: targeted qPCR/IF/ELISA first; limited ATAC/CUT&Tag on pooled samples.

Deliverables (end of month 3)
- Quantified “bacterial encounter memory index” per condition.
- Ranked sequence–duration programs that beneficially or adversely bias inflammation and differentiation.
- Short methods SOPs for bEV prep, exposure, and organoid formation to enable scale-up or therapeutic testing.

text:
Title
Does commensal-first imprinting create stem cell–intrinsic “protective memory” against a later pathobiont signal in human skin organoids?

Central Question and Hypothesis
Question-hypothesis: Do human epidermal stem cells acquire a cell-autonomous memory of initial commensal (S. epidermidis) signals that attenuates inflammatory reprogramming and preserves differentiation capacity upon subsequent pathobiont (S. aureus) exposure? We hypothesize that commensal-first exposure imprints a tolerant set-point in basal stem cells, reducing NF-κB–driven responses and maintaining lineage balance during later pathobiont challenge; the reverse order yields heightened inflammation and lineage skew.

Atomic Strategy
Use only the order and duration of bacterial-derived signals as the causal lever. Compare commensal-first vs pathobiont-first sequences (with short vs long exposures and a washout) and quantify how prior exposure changes the response to a standardized S. aureus challenge. No immune cells are included; any effect is stem cell–intrinsic.

Experimental Design (POC-scale, ≤3 months)
System
- Human skin organoids with a defined basal stem cell compartment.
- Signal format prioritized: bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs)/exosomes from S. epidermidis and S. aureus; optionally, paired conditioned cocktails. (No live bacteria required for POC.)
- Exposure classes: “Long” (stabilizing, multi-day) vs “Short” (acute, sub-day to single day). Include a brief washout interval to test persistence.

Arms
A. Commensal-first: S. epidermidis EVs Long → wash → S. aureus EVs Short (C→P)
B. Pathobiont-first: S. aureus EVs Long → wash → S. epidermidis EVs Short (P→C)
C. Simultaneous cocktail: mixed S. epidermidis + S. aureus EVs (co-exposure)
D. Singles: S. epidermidis Long only; S. aureus Long only
E. Vehicle/EV-depleted controls matched to each arm

Built-in Controls and Checks
- EV integrity/uptake check (e.g., labeled EVs, qualitative).
- Cytotoxicity/viability screen to maintain non-injurious dose windows.
- Donor diversity: ≥2 organoid lines to ensure generalizability.

Primary Readouts (Plasticity: inflammatory status)
- Rapid signaling: NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation and p38 activation by immunofluorescence (IF) after the standardized S. aureus Short challenge.
- Transcriptional panel (qPCR): IL1B, IL6, CXCL8, TNFAIP3, NFKBIA, DEFB4, S100A8/S100A9, TLR2, and AHR-target markers.
- Secreted mediators: multiplex bead-based cytokines/chemokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, GM-CSF).

Secondary Readouts (Plasticity: differentiation capacity)
- Lineage markers by IF/qPCR after differentiation induction: basal (KRT14, KRT5, ITGA6) vs suprabasal/terminal (KRT10, IVL, LOR, FLG); compute basal:terminal ratio.
- Morphometric features: stratification thickness, organoid architecture scores.
- Proliferation/renewal proxy: EdU incorporation and clonogenic outgrowth index.

Epigenetic Proxy (POC-feasible)
- Global H3K27ac/H3K9me3 IF in basal layer; optional targeted chromatin accessibility (ATAC–qPCR) at sentinel inflammatory loci.

Quantitative Indices and Analysis
- Inflammatory Memory Index (IMI): 1 − (composite inflammation z-score in C→P ÷ naive→P). Positive IMI indicates protective memory.
- Differentiation Resilience Index (DRI): (differentiation marker ratio in C→P − naive→P), normalized to control variance.
- Directionality Bias (DB): IMI(C→P) − IMI(P→C); positive DB indicates order dependence favoring commensal-first.
- Statistics: per-donor paired comparisons; nonparametric tests; report effect sizes with bootstrap CIs.

Expected Outcomes and Interpretation
- Support for protective memory: C→P shows reduced NF-κB activation, lower proinflammatory transcripts/secretions, and preserved or improved differentiation metrics versus naive→P and P→C; positive IMI and DRI with consistent sign across donors.
- Dominance of pathobiont reprogramming: P→C remains hyperinflammatory and differentiation-skewed despite commensal rescue; DB ≤ 0.
- Simultaneous cocktail: intermediate phenotype; magnitude informs additivity vs dominance of signals.

Go/No-Go Criteria (POC)
- Go: IMI ≥ predefined minimal effect (e.g., small-to-moderate positive) and DRI > 0 in ≥70% of biological replicates.
- No-Go/Refine: absent or inconsistent effects trigger parameter refinements (exposure balance, washout length) or mechanistic probes.

Mechanistic Anchors (post-POC, optional)
- Test necessity/sufficiency via receptor-pathway perturbation (e.g., TLR2 or AHR modulation) to link commensal-first imprinting to signaling thresholds and enhancer priming.

Risk Mitigation
- Variability in EV potency: standardize to a biosignature unit (e.g., particle/protein equivalence validated by a sentinel readout) rather than absolute amounts.
- Off-target stress responses: include EV-depleted and vehicle controls for every sequence.
- Overstimulation confounders: maintain non-cytotoxic exposure windows confirmed by viability and barrier integrity markers.

Feasibility and Deliverables (≤3 months)
- Month 1: Prepare/qualify signal preparations, baseline organoid QC, pilot dose-finding for non-injurious exposure windows.
- Month 2: Execute sequential exposures across arms with embedded controls; collect acute and post-challenge samples.
- Month 3: Complete molecular/IF readouts; compute IMI, DRI, DB; down-select conditions for scale-up.

Impact
A positive finding establishes a stem cell–intrinsic temporal memory of commensal signals that buffers later pathobiont cues, reframing microbiome–epithelium interactions as order-sensitive and suggesting prophylactic “commensal-first” conditioning as a tissue-protective strategy independent of immune cells.

text:
Title
Priming skin organoids with commensal-derived vesicles to induce durable, protective inflammatory training against pathobiont challenge

Atomic strategy
A single perturbation—ordering and duration of exposure to microbe-derived vesicles—reprograms epidermal stem cell chromatin toward a “trained-tolerance” state that blunts future S. aureus–induced inflammation while preserving differentiation.

Integrated question-hypothesis
Does prior, time-limited exposure of skin stem cells within organoids to S. epidermidis–derived extracellular vesicles (SEd-EVs) establish a protective memory that reduces subsequent S. aureus–induced inflammatory activation without impairing differentiation, and what is the minimal training-time window required? If protection persists through a vesicle-free interval, it reflects durable (epigenetic) memory; if it decays, it reflects transient signaling.

Model and materials (POC-compatible)
- System: Human skin organoids containing basal epidermal stem cells and stratified layers, sourced from established lines. Maintain standardized culture and QC for viability and stratification prior to interventions.
- Bacterial signals: Non-replicative, purified extracellular vesicles (EVs) or sterile, replication-incompetent cocktails representing S. epidermidis and S. aureus, sourced from certified providers. Use identity, purity, and endotoxin verification from supplier documentation.
- Safety note: No on-site propagation of live bacteria; all inputs are non-replicative, sterile preparations.

Experimental design
- Factor 1: Order of exposure (sequential switching)
  1) SEd-EVs → SAu-EVs (commensal-first)
  2) SAu-EVs → SEd-EVs (pathobiont-first)
  3) Simultaneous cocktail (SEd + SAu)
  4) Single exposures: SEd only; SAu only
  5) Vehicle control
- Factor 2: Training duration bins for the first exposure
  - Acute, sub-acute, extended (three non-overlapping time bins spanning short-to-prolonged exposure; exact values pre-registered and fixed across the study).
- Factor 3: Memory test (washout)
  - After the first exposure, include a vesicle-free interval (present vs absent) before the second exposure to test persistence.
- Challenge definition
  - For protective-efficacy readouts, standardize the second exposure as an SAu-EV challenge across arms (except in pathobiont-first arms where challenge is SEd-EVs for symmetry analysis). Maintain equivalent input units across groups per supplier specs.

Primary endpoints
- Inflammatory status (composite “Inflammation Score”)
  - Transcriptional: mRNA levels of canonical epidermal inflammatory and antimicrobial genes (e.g., IL1 family, IL6, TNF pathway targets, CXCL chemokines, DEFBs).
  - Signaling: NF-κB nuclear translocation or reporter activity; phospho-p38/JNK status by immuno-detection.
  - Secretome: multiplex cytokine/chemokine panel on conditioned media.
- Differentiation capacity (composite “Differentiation Score”)
  - Marker architecture: immunostaining or transcript assessment for basal (KRT14, TP63) and suprabasal/terminal markers (KRT10, FLG, LOR, IVL) with layer integrity scoring.
  - Barrier function proxy: electrical or dye-based permeability surrogate; lipid organization markers.
- Durability and mechanism-of-memory (exploratory)
  - Chromatin accessibility (shallow ATAC-style assay or targeted profiling) at promoters/enhancers of inflammatory and differentiation genes.
  - Histone mark snapshot (targeted CUT-style assay) for activation marks (e.g., H3K27ac/H3K4me3) at sentinel loci.
  - Candidate receptor dependence: neutralization/antagonism of commensal-sensing pathways (e.g., TLR2-axis) to test requirement, using non-cytotoxic conditions pre-verified in pilot.

Key derived metrics
- Protection Index (PI): ratio of Inflammation Score (post-challenge) normalized to vehicle-challenged baseline, divided by Differentiation Score retention. PI < 1 indicates protection with preserved differentiation; PI > 1 indicates failure or trade-off.
- Minimal Effective Training Time (METT): the shortest training-duration bin achieving a statistically significant PI improvement vs SAu-only.
- Memory Persistence: PI measured with washout vs no-washout. Durable memory is inferred when protection with washout is non-inferior to protection without washout.
- Specificity of training: Compare SEd-first vs SAu-first vs simultaneous cocktail to determine if order, not mere co-exposure, governs outcomes.

Experimental flow (conceptual)
- Predefine and randomize organoids to the exposure-order arms and training-duration bins.
- Apply first exposure per assignment.
- Optional washout phase (present vs absent).
- Apply standardized challenge.
- Collect endpoints at a fixed post-challenge interval for all arms.

Controls and validity checks
- Vehicle-only organoids for baseline noise.
- Heat-denatured or protease-treated EV controls to test vesicle cargo dependency.
- Size-exclusion–depleted fractions to assess EV specificity vs soluble contaminants.
- Viability/cytotoxicity checks to rule out confounding toxicity.
- Batch-bridging samples to correct for run-to-run drift in assays.
- Technical spike-ins for transcript and chromatin assays.

Analysis plan
- Primary comparisons: SEd-first vs SAu-only after challenge within each training-duration bin; adjust for multiple comparisons across bins.
- METT identification: hierarchical testing from acute to extended bins until a protective bin is detected; pre-register stopping rule to conserve samples.
- Order effect: contrast SEd-first vs SAu-first and vs cocktail to quantify sequence dependence.
- Memory classification: two-way interaction between training order and washout; durable memory inferred from significant protection retained after washout.
- Mechanistic inference: correlate PI with chromatin accessibility/mark changes at inflammatory and differentiation loci; mediation analysis to test whether chromatin alterations statistically account for reduced inflammatory signaling.

POC scale and feasibility (≤3 months)
- Phase 1 (feasibility): Establish assay reliability and dynamic range using SAu-only challenge and SEd-only exposure; confirm that endpoints respond and are within detection windows.
- Phase 2 (core POC): Execute the factorial matrix with reduced replication focused on SEd-first arms across the three training-duration bins, plus SAu-only and vehicle controls.
- Phase 3 (mechanism-lite): Run targeted chromatin and receptor-dependence assays on the best-performing SEd-first bin and its adjacent bin to discriminate durable vs transient mechanisms.

Success criteria
- Primary: Identification of a non-toxic SEd-first training-duration bin yielding a significantly reduced Inflammation Score after SAu challenge with equal or improved Differentiation Score relative to SAu-only.
- Secondary: Demonstration that protection persists after a vesicle-free interval, supporting durable memory; or, conversely, loss of protection with washout, supporting transient signaling.
- Tertiary: EV specificity indicated by diminished effects in EV-depleted or denatured controls; attenuation of protection with commensal-sensing blockade suggests pathway dependence.

Risk mitigation
- Heterogeneity across organoid batches: incorporate donor/batch as random effects; use bridging controls.
- EV lot variability: qualify lots using particle characterization and cargo fingerprint summaries provided by suppliers; pre-test lots for non-cytotoxicity and signal engagement.
- Trade-off risk (tolerance vs differentiation): PI framework ensures detection of hidden costs; terminate conditions where differentiation drops below pre-specified thresholds.

Readouts to decision
- Go: Clear METT identified for SEd-first training with preserved differentiation and memory signal consistent across batches.
- No-go: No separation between SEd-first and SAu-only across all bins, or protection achievable only with unacceptable differentiation loss.

Planned outputs
- A ranked METT estimate and confidence bounds.
- A minimal marker panel (inflammation + differentiation) that tracks protection.
- Preliminary chromatin signature distinguishing durable vs transient “trained-tolerance.”

Impact
If a brief, commensal-first exposure imprints protective tolerance without compromising differentiation, commensal EVs—or defined cargo mimetics—could be developed as prophylactic “microbial education” for skin stem cells, shifting interventions from reparative to preventive strategies.

label: elements_bypass
text:
Title
Mapping the point-of-no-return in inflammatory memory: sequential S. aureus → S. epidermidis signal switching in human skin organoids

Integrated goal–hypothesis
Question and hypothesis are the same: Does sequential, time-differential exposure to S. aureus versus S. epidermidis signals push skin stem cells across a reversible-to-irreversible inflammatory memory boundary, and can commensal signals restore inflammatory tone and differentiation once primed by a pathobiont? Prediction: there exists a threshold (“point-of-no-return,” PNR) in pathobiont pre-exposure after which commensal re-exposure fails to reset stem cell state.

Atomic strategy
Treat skin organoids with a pulse–chase of bacterial-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) or defined signal cocktails, varying only order and duration (acute vs chronic). Quantify hysteresis by integrating inflammatory and differentiation readouts into a Reversibility Index. The global design variable is time-ordering; all other variables are held constant.

POC outcomes
- Existence of a PNR: a pre-exposure window beyond which commensal rescue fails across ≥2 orthogonal readouts.
- Directionality: S. epidermidis pre-conditioning raises the PNR (greater resilience), while S. aureus pre-conditioning lowers it (sensitization).
- Modality: EVs recapitulate effects of whole-signal cocktails, indicating vesicle-borne factors are sufficient for reprogramming.

Experimental design (POC-scale, ≤3 months)

Model and treatments
- Model: human skin organoids enriched for basal stem cells.
- Treatments:
  1) S. aureus signals: either EVs (bacterial extracellular vesicles) or sterile, bacteria-free conditioned cocktails.
  2) S. epidermidis signals: EVs or cocktails matched to 1).
  3) Vehicle control.
- All preparations meet basic quality criteria (sterility, size/profile checks for EVs, absence of viable bacteria).

Exposure paradigms (temporal logic; no procedural details)
Define two regimes within the 3‑month window:
- Acute: brief exposure (on the order of days).
- Chronic: sustained exposure (on the order of weeks).

Arms (EVs and, in parallel, cocktails)
A0 Baseline: Vehicle only.
A1 Pathobiont-chronic → Commensal-acute (PC→CA): models attempted reversal of established memory.
A2 Pathobiont-chronic → Vehicle (PC→V): persistence control.
A3 Pathobiont-acute → Commensal-acute (PA→CA): tests early rescue.
A4 Commensal-chronic → Pathobiont-acute (CC→PA): tests protective pre-conditioning.
A5 Commensal-chronic → Vehicle (CC→V): durability of protective imprint.
A6 Simultaneous mixed cocktail (S. aureus + S. epidermidis): tests signal dominance without temporal separation.
A7 Heat/enzymatically perturbed EVs (for both species): specificity control for EV bioactivity (parallel to A1/A3).

Time-sweep within key arms
- Vary the duration of the first phase across a small set of increasing windows spanning acute to chronic, followed by a fixed acute second phase (for A1, A3, A4).
- This yields a curve of “rescue” versus pre-exposure time.

Primary readouts (plasticity)
Inflammatory status
- Secreted cytokines/chemokines panel from organoid media (e.g., IL‑1 family, IL‑6, TNF, CXCLs).
- NF‑κB and STAT3 pathway activation by immuno-based nuclear localization/phospho-status.
- Targeted transcriptional panel (qPCR or small-panel RNA profiling) for inflammatory and stemness genes.

Differentiation capacity
- Immunostaining ratios: basal markers (e.g., K14, p63) versus differentiation markers (e.g., K10, involucrin, loricrin, filaggrin).
- Structural barrier proxy: dye exclusion/penetration or equivalent assay suited to organoids.
- Functional plasticity: secondary organoid-forming efficiency from dissociated cells (conceptual stemness readout).

Secondary readouts (memory state, optional if budget/time allow)
- Chromatin accessibility (ATAC-based) on pooled organoids to index enhancer priming at inflammatory and differentiation loci.
- Histone mark profiling (targeted CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN panel) for H3K27ac/H3K27me3 at sentinel loci.

Quantification framework
- Define per-readout normalization: Baseline (A0) = 1.0; Pathobiont-chronic (A2) = 0.0 (for “health” directionality).
- Reversibility Index (RI) for each arm/time-point = (Valuearm − A2)/(A0 − A2). RI ∈ [0,1], where 1 indicates full reset to baseline; 0 indicates no rescue.
- Composite RI = mean of z-scored RI across ≥1 inflammatory and ≥1 differentiation readout.
- PNR definition: minimal pathobiont pre-exposure window at which composite RI falls below a pre-registered threshold (e.g., 0.3) and stays below it upon further increases, confirmed across two independent experiments.

Controls and confounders
- Vehicle control and species-swapped controls included in every batch.
- EV integrity and purity checks; matched protein input across EV conditions.
- Cytotoxicity screen to ensure observed effects are not due to viability loss.
- Optional receptor-pathway specificity probes (e.g., TLR2 blockade comparator arm) at low priority for POC.

Analysis plan
- Compare RI across arms and time-sweeps using mixed-effects models with batch as random effect.
- Fit sigmoidal or piecewise models to RI versus pre-exposure duration to estimate PNR and confidence intervals.
- Assess dominance in simultaneous exposure (A6) by deviation from the average of single-species effects.

Scale and timeline (high level)
- Weeks 1–2: finalize organoid batches; qualify EVs/cocktails and baseline readouts.
- Weeks 3–8: run sequential exposure arms with embedded time-sweeps; collect media and fixed samples.
- Weeks 9–10: molecular assays (panels, immunostains); optional chromatin assay on select conditions.
- Weeks 11–12: analysis, PNR estimation, replicate confirmation of threshold conditions.

Risks and mitigations
- Weak EV potency: prioritize concentrated EV inputs within safe, non-cytotoxic ranges; include cocktail arm as fallback.
- Batch variability: staggered blocks with internal controls; composite RI to buffer single-readout noise.
- Overlap of inflammatory and cytotoxic effects: integrate viability metrics and exclude non-physiological ranges.

Decision criteria (POC)
- Go: Clear PNR identified with narrow confidence bounds; S. epidermidis reverses early but not late S. aureus priming; EVs suffice.
- No-go/pivot: No PNR (linear response) or commensal fails to reverse at any window; prioritize protective pre-conditioning strategies or explore alternative commensal sources.

Deliverables
- RI curves and PNR estimates for EVs and cocktails.
- Minimal marker set (inflammation + differentiation) that tracks reversibility.
- Ranked exposure schedules for maximal rescue, to inform timing for microbiome-based interventions.
