text:
Title
Dynamic Microenvironment Pacing to Exhaust Phenotypic Plasticity in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer

Central question/hypothesis
Can externally paced, cyclical shifts in tumor microenvironmental acidity and oxygenation convert TNBC’s phenotypic plasticity into a selective liability—driving energetic/redox collapse, blocking dormancy, and eliminating residual disease—while sparing normal mammary tissue that is evolutionarily adapted to physiological cycles?

Atomic strategy
Exploit adaptation hysteresis: impose controlled, repeated pH and pO2 oscillations that force TNBC cells to continually transition between metabolic and epithelial–mesenchymal states faster than they can stably reprogram, creating predictable windows of vulnerability that culminate in ferroptotic and mitotic failure.

Rationale
- Intrinsic TNBC features: high genomic instability, metabolic rewiring (glycolysis↔OXPHOS switching), EMT/MET plasticity, and elevated basal ROS create a narrow redox/energetic margin.
- Physical/anatomical leverage: the breast is superficial and compartmentalized; local implants can precisely modulate microenvironments over centimeter scales with rapid kinetics. Post-lactational involution and ductal physiology already expose mammary epithelium to acidity, hypoxia/reoxygenation, and stromal remodeling—cycles normal cells better tolerate than TNBC.
- Systems insight: repeated state switching is metabolically expensive and induces mismatch between transcriptional programs and microenvironment (hysteresis). At defined amplitudes/frequencies, this produces energy debt (AMPK↑), lipid peroxidation (ACSL4-dependent), replication stress, and cytokine/DAMP release that together kill plastic, high-ROS TNBC while avoiding global toxicity.

Therapeutic system: Microenvironment Pacer Implant (MPI)
- Form factor: soft, bioresorbable, mesh-like implant (1–2 cm) placed intratumorally or in the post-lumpectomy cavity; percutaneous power/telemetry during therapy; autonomous thereafter; resorbs over weeks.
- Sensing: integrated microelectrodes and optical probes for pH, pO2, lactate, temperature; closed-loop control.
- Actuation:
  1) Iontronic pH modulation: solid-state proton pumps generate transient acidification (target pH nadir 6.5–6.7) followed by neutralization (pH 7.2–7.4) via local bicarbonate exchange.
  2) Oxygen cycling: on-demand hypoxia induction (vascular tone microstimulation and enzymatic O2 consumption) followed by reoxygenation via microbubble/oxygen-permeable reservoir release (target pO2 10–60 mmHg range).
- Waveforms: duty-cycled, non-harmonic oscillations (period 1–6 hours; occasional “burst” cycles) to prevent tumor entrainment; safety clamps limit extremes in adjacent normal tissue.
- Selectivity enhancers: positioning within tumor mass (steeper diffusion gradients), stochastic micro-zonation to preferentially stress hypoxic acidic cores, and failure-responsive amplitude throttling.

Specific aims and experiments

Aim 1. Define lethal oscillation regimes that selectively collapse TNBC adaptation.
- Models: patient-derived TNBC organoids and matched normal mammary organoids; multicellular co-cultures (fibroblasts, macrophages).
- Platform: benchtop microfluidic “pH/pO2 cycler” replicating MPI waveforms.
- Parameter sweep: amplitude, period, rise-time, duty cycle.
- Readouts: viability; ATP/AMPK; OCR/ECAR; mitochondrial potential; lipid ROS (BODIPY-C11), malondialdehyde; ferroptosis rescue (ferrostatin-1, liproxstatin-1); mitotic errors (pH3, micronuclei); single-cell RNA-seq to map state transitions (EMT/MET markers, metabolic programs); dormancy markers (NR2F1, DEC2).
- Success criteria: identification of ≥1 waveform that kills ≥70% TNBC organoids with ≤20% viability loss in normal organoids; increased lipid peroxidation not rescued by caspase inhibitors but rescued by ferroptosis inhibitors.

Aim 2. Engineer and validate the MPI for intramammary deployment and closed-loop control in vivo.
- Device milestones: biocompatibility, stable sensing (±0.05 pH units; ±5 mmHg pO2), actuation reproducibility, and thermal neutrality.
- Models: orthotopic TNBC xenografts and syngeneic models with dorsal window chambers for intravital mapping of pH, pO2, and perfusion; post-lumpectomy minimal residual disease models.
- Protocol: daily 8–16-hour pacing for 7–14 days versus constant conditions; longitudinal MRI/photoacoustic O2 mapping; microdialysis for lactate, cytokines, and lipid peroxidation adducts.
- Endpoints: tumor regression; residual disease burden; CTC counts; spontaneous metastasis; histologic necrosis; immune infiltration (CD8, NK, M1/M2 ratios) and interferon signatures post-reoxygenation.
- Success criteria: ≥50% reduction in residual disease and metastasis, improved survival, and no grade ≥3 local tissue injury.

Aim 3. Mechanistic validation of adaptation hysteresis and dormancy blockade.
- Track lineage and state switching with barcoded TNBC lines; measure transition kinetics under different waveform frequencies.
- Quantify “resonant lethality”: frequency at which mismatch between transcriptional reprogramming half-time and environmental cycle maximizes death.
- Test dormancy prevention: label-retaining/quiescent cell assays; recurrence after therapy cessation.
- Success criteria: defined hysteresis window linked to death phenotypes; suppression of dormancy markers and delayed/absent recurrence compared to controls.

Safety and tumor selectivity strategy
- Spatial selectivity: intratumoral mesh confines strongest gradients to tumor cores; real-time mapping prevents spillover.
- Physiological guardrails: pH floor ≥6.5 and pO2 floor ≥10 mmHg at tumor-normal interface; adaptive control reduces amplitude near sensitive tissue.
- Temporal selectivity: treatment windows aligned with patient circadian rhythms to favor host resilience.
- Material strategy: bioresorbable polymers yielding neutral byproducts; infection-resistant coatings; on-demand shutdown.

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1 (Months 0–12): Lethal-selective waveform identified in organoids; device benchtop validation. Go if TNBC:normal kill ratio ≥3.5.
- M2 (Months 12–24): In vivo efficacy with closed-loop control; safety within predefined guardrails. Go if residual disease and metastasis reduced ≥50% without significant toxicity.
- M3 (Months 24–36): Mechanistic confirmation of resonant lethality and dormancy blockade; GLP biocompatibility and manufacturability package for first-in-human feasibility.

Risk assessment and contingencies
- Risk: Normal tissue injury from over-acidification/hypoxia. Mitigation: conservative clamps, spatial modeling, rapid neutralization modules, and short-cycle testing.
- Risk: Tumor entrains to fixed patterns. Mitigation: waveform variability (aperiodic sequences), multi-point phasing.
- Risk: Heterogeneous penetration. Mitigation: arrayed micro-implants; peri-ductal placement leveraging ductal conduits.
- Risk: Non-ferroptotic escape. Mitigation: adjust waveform to intensify reoxygenation spikes; explore safe local iron supplementation within implant reservoir to bias lipid peroxidation, if needed, under strict safety thresholds.

Clinical path and use cases
- Neoadjuvant shrinkage and margin sterilization to reduce resection volume.
- Post-lumpectomy cavity pacing to eradicate residuals and prevent dormancy-driven recurrence.
- Implantation via minimally invasive percutaneous approach under ultrasound; therapy over 1–2 weeks; device resorption thereafter.

Expected outcome and impact
A first-in-class, device-driven, target-agnostic therapy that reframes TNBC plasticity from an advantage to a fatal vulnerability, leveraging mammary physiology and tumor biophysics to achieve selective tumor control, prevent dormancy, and reduce recurrence with minimal systemic toxicity.

Title
Ecological Polarity Trap (PoLET) for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer

Central hypothesis-question
Can a transient, localized restoration of mammary tissue polarity and physiological softness at the tumor–stroma interface force highly plastic TNBC cells into a myoepithelial-like, non-proliferative state that persists after the cue is withdrawn?

Atomic strategy
Impose a single, global microenvironmental change—basement-membrane polarity plus low tissue stiffness—to turn off mechanotransduction-driven plasticity (e.g., YAP/TAZ) and lock TNBC into a terminal, non-invasive myoepithelial phenotype.

Rationale
- TNBC cells exhibit high phenotypic plasticity and depend on mechanosensing of stiff, disorganized extracellular matrix to maintain proliferation, EMT, and invasion.
- Normal mammary epithelium is growth-restrained by apico–basal polarity cues from a soft, laminin-rich basement membrane and intact cell–cell junctions.
- A brief period of correct polarity and softness can trigger chromatin reprogramming toward a differentiated, contractile myoepithelial-like state; once established, this state can be self-maintaining due to epigenetic feedback and reinforced junctional architecture.
- The breast’s superficial location enables precise, local modulation of the tumor microenvironment with minimal systemic exposure.

Therapeutic concept
A conformal, peritumoral basement-membrane–mimetic hydrogel “cap” that:
- Presents laminin-rich polarity cues to tumor edges and ducts.
- Matches physiological mammary softness.
- Restores tissue architecture by guiding epithelial alignment and hemidesmosome formation.
- Is applied in short pulses to exploit plasticity windows and induce an epigenetically locked, myoepithelial-like, non-proliferative state that persists after gel degradation.

Specific aims

Aim 1 — Define the polarity–softness window that triggers a stable trap state.
- Build 3D TNBC organoid and ex vivo patient-slice systems with tunable hydrogels that independently vary: (a) laminin presentation and spatial orientation; (b) stiffness within the physiological mammary range; (c) epithelial alignment topology (duct-like curvature).
- Readouts: nuclear-to-cytoplasmic YAP/TAZ, junctional organization (E-cadherin, α6β4), myoepithelial markers (SMA, calponin, p63), chromatin/accessibility (ATAC-seq), cell-cycle exit (Ki-67, EdU), invasion in collagen, and reversibility after cue withdrawal.
- Deliverable: quantitative “trap map” specifying minimal polarity/softness parameters and exposure timing that yield irreversible growth arrest and invasion block.

Aim 2 — Demonstrate epigenetic locking and escape-proofing.
- Lineage-trace single TNBC cells through trap induction and withdrawal to test persistence across cell divisions.
- Identify epigenetic features that predict permanence (e.g., heterochromatin spreading at mechano-responsive loci, H3K27me3/H3K9me3 redistribution, lamina-associated domain engagement).
- Test perturbation-resilience: re-expose trapped cells to stiff matrices, EMT-inducing cytokines, and metabolic stress to assess escape frequency.
- Deliverable: biomarkers and a minimal pulse schedule that maximize lock-in and minimize escape.

Aim 3 — Validate local, tumor-selective trapping in vivo using the breast’s accessible anatomy.
- Orthotopic TNBC PDX models: apply a conformal, degradable peritumoral hydrogel cap post-tumor exposure (or post-lumpectomy to coat margins).
- Integrate noninvasive compliance-matched external support (soft compression garment) to maintain contact without increasing bulk stiffness.
- Endpoints: tumor growth arrest, invasion depth, ductal re-alignment, metastasis reduction, durability after gel resorption, and off-target effects in adjacent normal mammary tissue.
- Immune context: profile whether trapping reduces pro-metastatic inflammation and unmasks neoantigen presentation without immunosuppression.

Selectivity and safety
- Tumor-selective dependency: TNBC relies on stiff, disorganized ECM to sustain plasticity; normal ducts are already polarized and quiescent, thus relatively insensitive to added polarity cues.
- Local delivery: peritumoral confinement minimizes systemic exposure and spares distant tissues.
- Non-cytotoxic mechanism: growth restraint via architecture and mechanotransduction normalization reduces collateral damage versus cytolysis.

Treatment workflow (preclinical-to-clinical path)
- Diagnostic planning: imaging-guided 3D map of tumor–duct geometry to design gel coverage.
- Trap induction: brief, repeated applications of the conformal gel cap to re-establish polarity and softness at tumor boundaries and along at-risk ducts.
- Verification: bedside-compatible readouts (e.g., elastography for stiffness normalization; immunofluorescent cytology from fine-needle brushing for YAP/TAZ localization and myoepithelial markers).
- Maintenance: no chronic device; rely on epigenetic locking. Re-apply only if escape biomarkers emerge.

Milestones and success criteria
- In vitro/ex vivo: ≥80% of TNBC cells enter sustained cell-cycle exit and lose invasive capacity for multiple population doublings post-cue withdrawal; stable myoepithelial-like transcriptome and chromatin signatures.
- In vivo: durable suppression of growth and metastasis with preserved normal tissue architecture and function; absence of fibrosis or chronic inflammation.
- Translational readiness: manufacturable, biocompatible gel with controlled degradation; imaging-based intraoperative placement protocol; biomarker panel for on-treatment confirmation.

Risk, falsification, and contingency
- Risk: Insufficient permanence after cue withdrawal. Falsification: high escape rates despite optimal parameters.
- Contingency: augment polarity stabilization without receptor-targeted drugs by adding transient, non-pharmacologic mechanical entrainment (low-intensity therapeutic ultrasound to further sequester YAP/TAZ) during gel application, while keeping the atomic strategy—restored polarity/softness—the core driver.

Impact
If successful, PoLET converts TNBC’s plasticity from an advantage to a liability, using a single, local, architecture-restoring perturbation to force cells into a dead-end, non-proliferative myoepithelial-like state—leveraging intrinsic mechanobiology and the breast’s anatomy to achieve selectivity with minimal toxicity.

Title
Topical, ROS-gated DNA-damage amplification for TNBC using a thermoresponsive cream and mild hyperthermia

Central hypothesis-question
If we locally push oxidative DNA lesions just past the repairable threshold only inside tumor cells, can we selectively eliminate superficial TNBC while sparing normal breast tissue? We posit that a cream-delivered, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activated prodrug that amplifies single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs), combined with brief mild hyperthermia, will trigger synthetic-lethal collapse in homologous-recombination–deficient (HRD) TNBC, with minimal systemic exposure.

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Exploit TNBC’s intrinsic HR repair weakness by locally amplifying endogenous oxidative SSBs above the repair capacity using a ROS-activated prodrug; heat serves only to concentrate and time-lock delivery, not to kill by itself.

Rationale
- Biological selectivity: Many TNBCs exhibit HRD/replication stress, making them hypersensitive when SSBs convert to double-strand breaks (DSBs) during replication. Elevated basal ROS and redox cycling further predispose TNBC cells to oxidative DNA lesions that normal mammary epithelium better tolerates.
- Anatomical selectivity: Breast tumors are often close to the skin; the nipple–areolar complex and hair follicles provide natural conduits for local delivery with low systemic exposure.
- Physiological selectivity: Brief mild hyperthermia (41–43°C) transiently suppresses HR-mediated repair and increases membrane permeability, enhancing local deposition and potency at the application site while remaining tolerable to normal tissue.

Therapeutic concept
- Payload: A small-molecule prodrug that is inert in normoxic, low-ROS environments and rapidly unmasks under tumor-level ROS. Lead class: boronate-caged SSB generators (e.g., boronic-ester–masked Topoisomerase I poison or an abasic-site–amplifying scaffold) that release the active species upon H2O2/peroxide-triggered cleavage. The active drug increases SSBs and stalled replication forks, driving DSB accumulation in HRD cells.
- Formulation: A thermoresponsive, oil-in-water hydrogel cream (e.g., Pluronic-like matrix) embedding phase-change solid-lipid nanoparticles tuned to soften at 41–42°C. Particles carry the prodrug and penetration enhancers optimized for follicular and ductal entry. Heat acts as a spatial-temporal “gate” for release without systemic burst.
- Application and activation: Topical application over tumor-bearing breast or post-lumpectomy margins; optional areolar-focused application to leverage ductal transport. A brief, localized heat session follows each application to (i) increase stratum corneum permeability, (ii) soften carriers for payload release, and (iii) transiently depress HR.
- Mechanism of tumor selectivity (four filters):
  1) Local placement to breast skin/ducts limits exposure elsewhere.
  2) Heat-gated release confines availability to treated loci.
  3) ROS-gated chemical unmasking confines activation to high-ROS tumor cells.
  4) HRD-dependent lethality ensures that unrepaired lesions preferentially kill TNBC.

Intended clinical use-cases
- Superficial or subcutaneous TNBC lesions and chest-wall recurrences.
- Post-lumpectomy margin sterilization to reduce local recurrence.
- Inflammatory or dermal lymphatic involvement where skin-directed therapy is feasible.

Specific aims
1) Engineer and validate a ROS-activated, thermogated topical system for breast delivery.
   - Select and synthesize a boronate-caged SSB amplifier with high ROS/unmasking rate and low background cleavage.
   - Formulate a thermoresponsive cream with phase-change nanoparticles achieving on-demand release at 41–42°C.
   - Optimize transdermal and ductal penetration while maintaining skin tolerability; quantify depth profiles in ex vivo human breast skin and nipple–areolar tissue.

2) Demonstrate tumor-selective activation and synthetic lethality in HRD TNBC under mild hyperthermia.
   - In vitro panels: HRD TNBC cell lines versus normal mammary epithelial cells and HR-proficient breast cancer controls.
   - Mechanistic biomarkers: ROS-dependent unmasking (fluorogenic surrogate), γH2AX and 53BP1 foci (DSBs), RAD51 foci suppression (HR impairment by heat), PARylation dynamics, replication fork stalling (DNA fiber assay), and comet assays.
   - Causality tests: Rescue with antioxidants (e.g., catalase mimetics) and HR restoration (e.g., RAD51 overexpression) to confirm ROS-gated/HRD dependency. Compare ±hyperthermia to isolate the contribution of heat-gated delivery.

3) Establish preclinical efficacy, exposure, and safety with localized heating.
   - Superficial orthotopic and chest-wall TNBC models; topical dosing followed by controlled mild hyperthermia sessions.
   - Endpoints: Tumor regression, local recurrence-free interval (post-resection margin model), intratumoral active-drug levels, systemic PK/PD (plasma and distant organs), skin tolerability.
   - Selectivity: Spatial mapping of unmasked drug versus intact prodrug across skin–tumor interface; histologic damage restricted to tumor zones.

Innovation
- Mechanistic minimalism: One biological switch (ROS) + one physical gate (heat) drives selectivity; no dependence on ER/PR/HER2.
- Anatomical route: Exploits ductal and follicular conduits of the breast for high local concentration without invasive devices or systemic dosing.
- Synthetic-lethal framing: Converts existing oxidative burden and HRD into a precise local vulnerability.

Research plan and key experiments (high level)
- Chemistry and stability: Tune boronate electronics to match tumor-range ROS for rapid unmasking while remaining stable in normal tissue. Confirm by kinetic assays in controlled ROS milieus and human skin homogenates.
- Formulation physics: Map release versus temperature; ensure negligible release at 32–37°C and rapid release at 41–42°C. Optimize particle size and cream rheology for residence within follicles/ducts.
- Transport and deposition: Use ex vivo human breast skin/areolar tissues and confocal/mass-spectrometry imaging to quantify depth and intraductal distribution; benchmark with and without heat.
- Cellular pharmacology: Determine IC50 shifts with ROS modulation and HR status; quantify replication catastrophe under synchronized S-phase conditions; demonstrate that normal epithelial cells tolerate exposures that kill HRD TNBC.
- In vivo pharmacology: Define local exposure gradients, systemic exposure (should be low), and on-target PD (γH2AX, reduced RAD51 foci post-heat). Evaluate efficacy in superficial TNBC xenografts and in a resection–reimplantation margin model to emulate clinical margin sterilization.
- Safety: Assess skin irritation, barrier recovery, wound healing, and sensory tolerance of mild heat. Monitor off-target toxicity in distant organs; confirm minimal circulating active drug.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- Chemistry: ≥50-fold faster unmasking at tumor-mimetic ROS versus normal-tissue ROS; <5% spontaneous activation in serum/physiologic buffers.
- Formulation: <10% release at ≤37°C over 2 hours; >70% release within 20 minutes at 41–42°C.
- Selectivity in vitro: ≥10-fold TNBC:normal selectivity index under heat; loss of effect with antioxidants or HR restoration.
- In vivo: ≥60% tumor volume reduction or statistically significant margin-sterilization benefit with no grade ≥2 skin toxicity and negligible systemic exposure.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Heterogeneous ROS: Pre-therapy selection via noninvasive redox imaging or tissue redox assays; adapt by modestly increasing heat sessions to enhance local ROS and delivery; reserve alternative caging chemistries responsive to hypoxia if needed.
- Tumor depth beyond diffusion: For deeper lesions, combine cream with nonablative focused superficial ultrasound to push carriers/heat several millimeters deeper while retaining local control.
- Variable HR status: Use RAD51 functional assays from tumor swabs/biopsies to identify HRD-enriched candidates most likely to benefit.

Translational path
- Indication: Superficial TNBC, chest-wall recurrence, and positive-margin settings where local control is critical.
- Early clinical readouts: On-treatment core-needle or surface biopsies for active-drug detection, γH2AX mapping, and RAD51 foci suppression; dermal tolerability scoring; circulating exposure profiling.
- Device synergy: A low-cost, feedback-controlled heating patch ensures reproducible temperature windows and patient comfort.

Expected outcome and impact
This strategy should achieve potent local tumor kill by leveraging two stable, tumor-intrinsic properties—elevated ROS and HR repair weakness—while using the breast’s superficial anatomy for targeted delivery. The result is a noninvasive, organ-sparing therapy that minimizes systemic toxicity and could become a practical option for superficial TNBC, chest-wall disease, and margin sterilization after breast-conserving surgery.

Title
Closed-loop “Soft-State Entrapment” of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer by Elastography-Guided Focused Ultrasound

Central hypothesis
Metastatic competence in TNBC requires the tumor microenvironment (TME) to exceed a stiffness set point that sustains integrin–FAK–Rho/ROCK–YAP/TAZ signaling, EMT programs, and intravasation. Maintaining the breast tumor and peritumoral stroma below this mechanical threshold traps TNBC cells in a low-motility, non-intravasive state that is locally resectable.

Atomic strategy (single conceptual lever)
Impose and actively maintain a local storage modulus “softness set point” in the tumor-bearing breast (G′target in the physiological mammary range) using noninvasive, closed-loop control. The only dial we turn is tissue stiffness.

Objectives
- Define the metastasis-permissive vs. -restrictive stiffness threshold for TNBC.
- Build a real-time, patient-specific “softness switch” using elastography-guided focused ultrasound to keep tumor stiffness below threshold.
- Demonstrate suppression of dissemination (CTCs and distant lesions), while preserving or improving surgical margins and minimizing toxicity to normal breast tissue.

Rationale and selectivity
- Biology: TNBC’s phenotypic plasticity, EMT propensity, and reliance on mechano-transduced YAP/TAZ make it uniquely susceptible to stiffness control. Soft matrices downshift cytoskeletal tension, nuclear mechanotransduction, and chromatin accessibility at pro-metastatic enhancers.
- Anatomy/physics: The breast’s superficial location enables precise acoustic focusing with low attenuation and bedside shear-wave elastography for closed-loop feedback.
- Tumor selectivity: Only stiffer voxels (tumor/desmoplastic rim) are targeted; normal parenchyma is already within the G′target and is spared by threshold-based control.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Quantify the stiffness set point that governs TNBC dissemination.
- Establish stiffness–state maps by culturing TNBC organoids and patient-derived explants in tunable hydrogels spanning normal breast (~0.2–1 kPa) to desmoplastic ranges (>2–10 kPa).
- Identify G′crit at which YAP/TAZ nuclear localization, EMT markers, traction forces, transendothelial migration, and intravasation proxies switch on/off.
- Derive a minimal biomarker panel (e.g., cytoplasmic YAP/TAZ index, collagen alignment score) that reports whether G′ < G′crit in vivo.

Aim 2. Engineer a closed-loop “softness switch” using elastography-guided focused ultrasound (FUS).
- Integrate shear-wave elastography to generate 3D stiffness maps and drive an adaptive FUS controller that selectively treats voxels with G′ ≥ G′crit.
- Use nonablative acoustic regimes to disrupt collagen alignment and stromal contracture without thermal necrosis; validate on-target softening, persistence, and reversibility.
- Confirm on-target mechanotransduction shutdown (YAP/TAZ export, pFAK↓, RhoA/ROCK tone↓) and preservation of tissue architecture.

Aim 3. Test dissemination control and surgical conversion in vivo and in patients.
- In orthotopic TNBC models, compare closed-loop FUS vs. sham on: circulating tumor cells (CTCs), spontaneous metastasis burden, margin status, and time-to-metastasis.
- Implement a perioperative “stability window”: initiate softness control at diagnosis, maintain G′ < G′crit through resection, and monitor rebound dynamics.
- First-in-human feasibility: safety, stiffness control accuracy, pharmacodynamic biomarker changes, and early signals of dissemination suppression.

Study design and endpoints
- Primary endpoint: proportion of time tumor voxels remain below G′crit (mechanical control fidelity).
- Key biological endpoints: YAP/TAZ cytoplasmic fraction, EMT/MET marker reversal, reduced endothelial transmigration, CTC reduction, and diminished collagen fiber alignment (SHG imaging).
- Clinical endpoints: downstaging to resectable disease, negative-margin rates, local recurrence-free and metastasis-free intervals.
- Safety: skin/subcutaneous injury, pain, milk duct integrity (where applicable), and off-target softening.

Mechanistic checks and global-system fit
- CAF contracture rebound: track stromal tension markers; if rebound detected, increase treatment frequency rather than add new agents, preserving the single mechanical control variable.
- Perfusion effects: monitor vascular leak/intravasation; ensure acoustic parameters that soften matrix without promoting vascular rupture.
- Immune contexture: record T-cell infiltration and myeloid phenotypes as secondary outcomes; a softer matrix is expected to reduce physical exclusion without adding immunotherapies.

Go/no-go milestones
- Go: Robust identification of G′crit with concordant YAP/TAZ/EMT switching; ≥70% on-target voxel softening maintained for >72 hours without tissue injury; ≥50% CTC reduction vs. sham.
- No-go: Inability to sustain sub-threshold stiffness without collateral damage or paradoxical increase in dissemination.

Advantages over target-based therapy
- Mechanism-agnostic to ER/PR/HER2 status; exploits TNBC’s dependence on mechanotransduction rather than canonical receptors.
- Physical-state control limits evolutionary escape routes common in genomically unstable TNBC; a global constraint outcompetes pathway-specific resistance.

Anticipated impact
By enforcing a breast-local mechanical state below the metastasis-permissive threshold, this approach aims to convert aggressive TNBC into a contained, surgically curable disease while minimizing toxicity to normal tissue. The “softness switch” reframes metastasis prevention as a controllable physical variable rather than a moving molecular target.

text:
Project title
POLQ-gated DNA cassettes that exploit TNBC genomic instability to make tumors self-soften and self-normalize their stroma

Central hypothesis
TNBC’s addiction to alternative end-joining (POLQ/MMEJ) and chronic replication stress creates a DNA-repair “door” that normal mammary cells keep shut. Short, microhomology-ended DNA cassettes can pass through this door only in TNBC cells, where they become stably expressed, instructing those cells to emit stromal-normalizing signals (primarily collagen-suppressive miR-29) that soften the tumor, decompress interstitial pressure, and reopen immune and drug access.

Atomic strategy
Gate therapeutic DNA expression on a repair operation TNBC uniquely overuses—POLQ-driven microhomology-mediated end joining—so that payload uptake and functionalization occur in TNBC but fail in normal tissue.

Innovation
- Mechanism-level selectivity: functional “permission” requires POLQ/MMEJ, not conventional ER/PR/HER2 targets.
- Tumor uses itself as a bioreactor: edited TNBC cells secrete miR-29–rich extracellular vesicles that reprogram fibroblasts and reduce collagen crosslinking.
- Anatomy leveraged: intratumoral/peritumoral dosing in the breast’s superficial site provides physical containment and dose control.

Therapeutic design
- Vector: short double-stranded DNA cassettes with paired microhomology termini and a built-in dependency on POLQ/MMEJ to resolve an expression-blocking lesion. In HR-proficient, POLQ-low cells, the cassette remains nonfunctional and is cleared.
- Promoter logic: stress- and hypoxia-responsive regulatory elements to confine expression to the hostile TNBC microenvironment.
- Payload v1 (primary): a compact transcript that loads miR-29 family mimics into secreted extracellular vesicles, biasing CAFs toward a low-collagen, low-LOX state and reducing YAP/TAZ mechanotransduction in tumor cells.
- Optional payload v2 (secondary arm for comparison): an EV-enriched miR program that nudges macrophages toward M1-like states without systemic cytokines.
- Physical delivery: image-guided intratumoral/peritumoral administration using a biodegradable depot to localize DNA in the mammary stroma; optional brief, low-energy electroporation or ultrasound to increase tumor-only uptake.

Predicted system-level effects
- Selective functionalization in POLQ-high, HR-deficient TNBC cells; negligible expression in normal mammary epithelium and adipocytes.
- CAF reprogramming → reduced fibrillar collagen/IHF, lowered LOX activity, decreased matrix stiffness and interstitial fluid pressure → improved perfusion, T-cell infiltration, and drug penetration.
- Feedback dampening of invasion by reducing stiffness-driven YAP/TAZ signaling and EMT cues.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Establish repair-gated selectivity in human TNBC models.
- Build a reporter cassette whose expression requires POLQ/MMEJ resolution; quantify activation across TNBC lines (HRD/POLQ-high) versus normal mammary organoids and fibroblasts.
- Perturbation controls: POLQ inhibition/knockdown to confirm gate dependency; HR restoration in TNBC to test loss of function.
- Endpoint: ≥20-fold TNBC:normal functionalization ratio and on-target genomic repair signatures consistent with MMEJ.

Aim 2. Program TNBC cells to secrete miR-29–rich vesicles and quantify stromal normalization.
- Deploy the gated cassette encoding an EV-loading scaffold for miR-29 family.
- Measure EV cargo, CAF transcriptomic shifts (collagens, LOX/LOXLs, ACTA2), and matrix remodeling in co-culture and 3D organotypic gels.
- Biophysical readouts: atomic force microscopy stiffness maps, interstitial pressure, and diffusion assays for macromolecules.
- Endpoint: ≥30% reduction in bulk stiffness and ≥2× increase in macromolecular diffusivity without increased invasion in organoids.

Aim 3. Test intramammary delivery, efficacy, and safety in vivo.
- Orthotopic TNBC xenograft and syngeneic models with image-guided intratumoral/peritumoral dosing via biodegradable depot.
- Outcomes: cassette functionalization restricted to tumors; decreased second-harmonic collagen, lower LOX activity, enhanced CD8+ infiltration, improved small-molecule and antibody delivery, and tumor control.
- Safety: histology of adjacent mammary/adipose tissue, liver, and lung; systemic EV and miRNA levels; behavior and weight.
- Stopping rules: any evidence of increased metastasis or off-tumor functionalization triggers payload swap to a purely CAF-quiescence program and/or promoter tightening.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Demonstrate POLQ-gated selectivity ex vivo with predefined activation ratio and MMEJ signature.
- M2: Show stromal normalization (stiffness, diffusivity, collagen/LOX downregulation) without pro-invasive phenotypes.
- M3: Achieve in vivo tumor-selective functionalization with improved immune/drug access and ≥50% tumor-growth delay as monotherapy; combinatorial benefit with standard chemo or checkpoint blockade.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Risk: ECM softening could facilitate invasion in some contexts. Mitigation: real-time invasion metrics; payload variants that primarily suppress crosslinking (LOX) without bulk degradation; ability to pivot to immune-reprogramming payload.
- Risk: Residual functionalization in proliferative normal cells. Mitigation: local delivery, stress/hypoxia promoters, and inclusion of a drug-inducible safety switch for selective ablation of edited cells if needed.
- Risk: Heterogeneity in POLQ/MMEJ dependence. Mitigation: preselect patients by POLQ expression/MMEJ reporter biopsy; adapt cassette microhomology architecture to maximize gate stringency.

Patient-selection and translation
- Biomarker panel: POLQ expression/activity, HRD score, mutational signatures indicative of MMEJ/APOBEC activity, ECM stiffness imaging.
- Procedure: outpatient, image-guided intratumoral/peritumoral injections enabled by superficial breast anatomy, with repeat dosing aligned to tumor size and stiffness metrics.

Impact
By turning TNBC’s genomic instability into a key that unlocks therapeutic DNA only inside the tumor, this approach creates a self-softening, self-normalizing lesion that is easier for drugs and immune cells to penetrate—achieving selectivity through a repair dependency rather than conventional receptor targets, while leveraging the breast’s anatomical accessibility for localized, controllable therapy.

text:
Title: FERRO-SCAN-FUS: Label-free vulnerability mapping and selective ultrasound tipping of ferroptosis in TNBC

Unified hypothesis-goal:
TNBC cells that accumulate peroxidized membrane lipids and labile iron exhibit a mechanically fragile state that can be identified noninvasively and selectively collapsed by parameter-tuned focused ultrasound, inducing ferroptosis while sparing normal mammary tissue. We will develop a closed-loop, drug-free, marker-free theranostic system that detects this vulnerable state in real time and pushes only those regions over the ferroptotic threshold.

Atomic strategy:
Exploit endogenous lipid peroxidation as both target identifier (label-free contrast) and Achilles’ heel (lowered mechanical failure threshold) to enable ultrasound-selective ferroptotic kill.

Rationale (systems view):
- Intrinsic TNBC features—PUFA-rich membranes, high oxidative flux, iron dysregulation, and redox-buffer limitations—periodically place subpopulations near a ferroptosis tipping point.
- Lipid peroxidation reduces membrane line tension and increases compressibility/viscous loss, creating an ultrasound pressure window that disrupts peroxidized membranes but not healthier, less peroxidized ones.
- Breast tumors’ superficial location allows high-frequency imaging and tightly focused therapy with minimal path attenuation and real-time monitoring.

Specific aims:
1) Define the ultrasound vulnerability window of peroxidized membranes.
2) Build a label-free “ferro-vulnerability map” using multimodal acoustic signatures.
3) Create a closed-loop focused ultrasound controller that treats only mapped vulnerable regions and confirms selective ferroptotic death in vivo.
4) Establish safety/selectivity margins and translational dosimetry in orthotopic TNBC models.

Aim 1: Biophysical thresholding of peroxidized membranes
- Model systems: giant unilamellar vesicles and cell monolayers with controlled PUFA content and graded endogenous peroxidation (enzymatic and metabolic manipulations; no exogenous contrast agents in readouts).
- Readouts (label-free/orthogonal): AFM nanoindentation, Brillouin/ultrafast acoustics for viscoelasticity; lipidomics for oxidized phospholipid species; iron speciation assays.
- Ultrasound parameter sweep: 5–15 MHz; burst length 5–50 cycles; peak negative pressure 0.3–3 MPa; PRF 100–1000 Hz; thermal index ≤0.5. Determine pressure-time integral and mechanical index ranges that cause membrane poration/rupture only in high-peroxidation conditions.
- Deliverable: Vulnerability transfer function linking peroxidation level to mechanical failure probability.

Aim 2: Label-free ferro-vulnerability mapping in tissue
- Imaging suite:
  - Quantitative ultrasound backscatter and spectral slope/intercept to sense microstructural disorder from peroxidized domains.
  - Shear-wave elastography for viscoelastic loss tangent (peroxidation-associated softening/viscous increase).
  - Multispectral photoacoustic imaging (no contrast agents) near lipid overtone bands to quantify lipid abundance and oxidation-dependent spectral shifts; hemoglobin spectra for local oxygenation (modulates peroxidation kinetics).
- Data model: Train a multimodal classifier to output a “Ferro-V score” per voxel (0–1 probability of being within 20% of ferroptotic threshold), cross-validated against ex vivo lipidomics and electron micrographs.
- Deliverable: Real-time 3D vulnerability map with sensitivity ≥80% and specificity ≥80% for imminent ferroptotic transition.

Aim 3: Closed-loop selective tipping via focused ultrasound
- Controller logic:
  - Sensing: Interleave brief mapping sequences with therapy bursts.
  - Actuation: Apply sub-cavitational stress bursts within the Aim 1 window to Ferro-V hotspots until a confirmation signature is observed.
  - Confirmation: Real-time indicators—rise in passive acoustic emissions at harmonic/ultraharmonic bands consistent with membrane failure; photoacoustic increase from oxidized lipid adduct accrual followed by signal collapse; elastography shift reflecting necrotic softening.
- In vivo testbed: Orthotopic TNBC xenografts and syngeneic models in the mammary fat pad; skin-sparing acoustic coupling and high-frequency transducers suited for the breast.
- Endpoints: Tumor control ratio, spatially resolved ferroptosis markers (iron-dependent lipid peroxide adducts, ultrastructural morphology), minimal apoptosis/necrosis in adjacent normal tissue.

Aim 4: Safety, selectivity, and translational dosimetry
- Off-target analysis: Skin, ducts, neurovascular bundles, and adipose; lactational function in appropriate models.
- Selectivity enhancers (no drugs): Respiratory-gated oxygenation modulation and pulse timing; adaptive beamforming to avoid vasculature-rich normal lobules; acoustic pressure ceiling = 80% of normal-tissue failure threshold.
- Deliverable: Clinical protocol template with patient-specific acoustic planning for early-phase trials.

Methods overview:
- Hardware: Co-registered high-frequency US/PA imaging probe and a concentric FUS therapy transducer; passive cavitation detector.
- Software: Real-time GPU pipeline for Ferro-V mapping and adaptive dosing.
- Analytics: Spatial Bayesian updating of Ferro-V during therapy; causal mediation to attribute tumor control to ferroptotic, not thermal, mechanisms (strict thermal index monitoring).

Selectivity safeguards:
- Energy windowing derived from Aim 1 ensures PNP values below normal-tissue poration threshold.
- Closed-loop stop rules on detection of off-target mechanical signatures.
- Spatial gating to fibro-fatty septa and tumor core; avoidance zones for skin and Cooper’s ligaments.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria:
- M1: Vulnerability transfer function with >10x differential failure probability between high- vs low-peroxidation membranes at fixed PNP. Go if achieved.
- M2: Ferro-V map AUROC ≥0.85 against ex vivo lipidomics. Go if achieved; refine otherwise.
- M3: In vivo selective kill: ≥60% reduction in viable tumor volume with ≤5% histologic injury to adjacent normal tissue. Proceed to expanded cohorts if met.
- M4: Reproducible closed-loop control in moving/respiring subjects with treatment times ≤30 minutes per lesion.

Risk mitigation:
- If PA peroxidation contrast is insufficient, weight the map toward elastography/QUS features and temporal hemodynamic reactivity.
- If cavitation-free poration is inadequate, use short pulse sequences that exploit stable endogenous nuclei while keeping MI below skin safety thresholds.
- If heterogeneity blunts selectivity, adopt fractionated sessions that exploit daily metabolic swings toward peroxidation.

Success metrics:
- Therapeutic index improvement ≥3x over thermal FUS at equal tumor control.
- Durable ferroptosis-dependent control verified by rescue/failure upon systemic iron chelation in exploratory arms (preclinical only).
- No exogenous drugs or markers required for target identification or treatment in the core protocol.

Impact:
This proposal operationalizes a single, global perturbation—tuning acoustic stress to the intrinsic mechanical fragility created by TNBC’s lipid peroxidation state—turning tumor metabolism into both the targeting system and the kill switch, leveraging the breast’s superficial anatomy for precise, noninvasive, selective therapy.

Title
cGAMP-Gated Therapeutic Cells for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: Exploiting Paracrine Signatures of Genomic Instability with Localized, Fail-Safe Activation

Central Hypothesis and Research Goal
TNBC’s pervasive chromosomal instability generates tumor-confined paracrine danger signals—particularly extracellular 2′3′-cGAMP derived from cGAS sensing of mislocalized DNA. We hypothesize that extracellular cGAMP is a reliable, spatially restricted proxy for TNBC “DNA chaos” that can be harnessed to turn engineered therapeutic cells on only within the tumor. The goal is to create cGAMP-gated therapeutic cells that remain quiescent systemically but, upon entering the cGAMP-rich tumor microenvironment, activate a tightly controlled anti-tumor program with minimal off-tumor toxicity. The superficial anatomy of the breast enables image-guided local delivery and containment, further improving selectivity.

Atomic Strategy
Use extracellular cGAMP as a universal, tumor-intrinsic activation cue. Engineer therapeutic cells with a STING-responsive genetic switch that converts cGAMP uptake into transient, localized expression of a bystander-killing module (e.g., a clinically validated prodrug-converting enzyme or apoptotic ligand) restricted to the tumor microenvironment.

Mechanistic Rationale
- Genomic instability → cytosolic dsDNA/micronuclei in TNBC cells → cGAS activation → 2′3′-cGAMP production.
- Tumor cells export cGAMP; stromal ENPP1 limits its diffusion, confining signal to tumor regions.
- Therapeutic cells engineered to efficiently import and sense cGAMP engage STING→IRF3/NF-κB transcriptional response only in cGAMP-high niches.
- The switch drives expression of a short-lived, locally acting effector that kills adjacent tumor cells (including antigen-negative variants) via a bystander effect.
- In normal tissues (low extracellular cGAMP), cells remain inert; local administration to the breast further reduces systemic exposure.

Research Plan

Aim 1: Establish extracellular cGAMP as a spatially restricted marker of TNBC genomic instability.
- Quantify and map extracellular cGAMP in TNBC versus normal mammary tissue using orthotopic models and freshly obtained surgical samples; co-register with genomic instability markers (HRD scores, micronuclei burden) and microenvironmental features (acidity, hypoxia).
- Define activation thresholds and temporal dynamics of cGAMP in response to clinically feasible “primers” that increase DNA chaos (e.g., low-dose radiation or PARP inhibition) without relying on ER/PR/HER2.

Milestone: Demonstrate that extracellular cGAMP is consistently enriched within TNBC lesions, with a concentration-time profile suitable for switchable cell activation and negligible levels in matched normal tissue.

Aim 2: Build and validate cGAMP-gated therapeutic cells (STING-Switch Cells; SSCs) with tumor-only activation.
- Construct a human-cell therapeutic chassis (e.g., macrophage-like or NK-like) harboring a STING-responsive regulatory module controlling a locally acting effector (such as a prodrug-activating enzyme with a short diffusion radius, or a membrane-tethered apoptosis ligand).
- Engineer inertness outside tumors via: (i) strict dependence on cGAMP-triggered transcription; (ii) rapid effector turnover; (iii) a drug-inducible safety off-switch.
- In co-culture with TNBC versus normal mammary epithelial cells, quantify switch fidelity, activation kinetics, effector output, and bystander kill radius. Confirm quiescence in cGAMP-low settings and full deactivation after signal withdrawal.

Milestone: ≥100-fold on/off activation ratio in response to physiologic cGAMP; potent TNBC killing with no measurable cytotoxicity in normal co-cultures; rapid return to baseline after signal cessation.

Aim 3: Leverage breast tumor anatomy for safe, effective delivery and containment; demonstrate in vivo efficacy.
- Localize SSCs via ultrasound-guided intratumoral/peritumoral administration or a sutureable depot positioned against the tumor bed to minimize systemic circulation.
- Test efficacy in orthotopic TNBC models with and without priming (low-dose radiation or PARP inhibition) to amplify genomic-instability signals. Use a companion orally available prodrug if employing a prodrug-activating effector, restricting active drug generation to SSC-activated zones.
- Endpoints: tumor regression, survival, spatial pharmacodynamics (effector expression confined to cGAMP-rich regions), systemic cytokine levels, and off-target tissue histology.

Milestone: Significant tumor control or eradication with minimal systemic cytokine induction and no histopathologic injury to distant organs; containment of SSCs within the breast compartment.

Safety and Selectivity Architecture
- Biological selectivity: dependence on a tumor-intrinsic, instability-derived paracrine signal (cGAMP) absent in normal tissues.
- Anatomical selectivity: superficial breast location enables image-guided local dosing and retrieval of depots if needed.
- Pharmacological selectivity: bystander-kill module restricted by short half-life or prodrug gating.
- Device-level selectivity: depot materials that physically confine cells to the tumor bed.
- Fail-safes: drug-inducible global off-switch; predefined stop criteria based on serum biomarkers.

Validation of Generalizability and Resistance Barriers
- Heterogeneity: test across TNBC subtypes and patient-derived xenografts; evaluate killing of receptor-negative clones.
- Evolutionary robustness: because activation depends on the fundamental cost-of-instability signal rather than a single surface antigen, escape via antigen loss is disfavored; potential escape via reduced cGAMP export is countered by priming regimens that re-elevate DNA chaos.

Expected Impact
This strategy reframes TNBC therapy around a fundamental systems-level weakness—genomic instability—by converting a tumor-confined, paracrine “danger currency” (cGAMP) into a precise activation trigger for therapeutic cells. Coupled with local delivery enabled by breast anatomy, it aims to achieve high tumor selectivity, address intratumoral heterogeneity through bystander effects, and minimize toxicity to normal tissues without relying on ER, PR, or HER2.

Title
Photo-FerroRx: Spatially gated photoperoxidation to drive ferroptosis in triple-negative breast cancer

Atomic insight
Push TNBC cells past the ferroptotic threshold by confining singlet-oxygen–driven lipid peroxidation to tumor membranes with light, leveraging the breast’s superficial anatomy for spatial control and TNBC’s intrinsic ferroptosis susceptibility for biological selectivity.

Hypothesis and research question
If red/NIR light is used to activate a membrane-localizing photosensitizer within superficial TNBC lesions, the resulting localized lipid peroxidation will overwhelm GPX4-dependent defenses and trigger ferroptosis selectively in TNBC cells, sparing adjacent normal breast tissue. What illumination and drug parameters maximize ferroptosis-based tumor kill while minimizing collateral damage in vivo?

Rationale
- Biological vulnerability: TNBC exhibits high basal ROS, labile iron pools, PUFA-rich phospholipids (ACSL4-high), and dependency on GPX4/FSP1 buffering, lowering the threshold for ferroptosis.
- Anatomical advantage: Most breast tumors are within 5–15 mm of the skin or along ductal trees, enabling precise, outpatient light delivery (surface patch or micro-fiber interstitial/intraductal) to confine photochemistry to the tumor.
- Mechanistic fit: Photodynamic activation produces singlet oxygen that preferentially peroxidizes PUFA-phospholipids—the initiating lesion for ferroptosis—without requiring canonical receptor targets.

Therapeutic concept
A clinically established, lipophilic photosensitizer (e.g., 5-ALA–induced PpIX or verteporfin) is administered at doses that enrich membranes of TNBC cells. Image-guided red/NIR illumination (surface conformal patch for ≤10 mm depth; micro-fiber interstitial or intraductal for deeper/periductal foci) generates singlet oxygen in situ, driving phospholipid peroxidation beyond the ferroptotic threshold specifically where light is applied.

Specific aims
1) Establish ferroptosis as the dominant death mode after PDT in TNBC.
- Determine dependency on lipid peroxidation (BODIPY-C11 oxidation), iron (modulation by iron chelation/supplementation in vitro), and GPX4/FSP1 buffering (rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors; sensitization by GPX4 knockdown).
- Benchmark against normal mammary epithelial cells for therapeutic index.

2) Optimize illumination to maximize ferroptosis with minimal off-target damage.
- Compare continuous versus low-irradiance/fractionated red/NIR light to sustain oxygen and favor non-thermal, lipid-focused photochemistry.
- Map photochemical action depth and fluence–response in superficial tissue phantoms and ex vivo breast specimens.

3) Validate efficacy, selectivity, and safety in orthotopic TNBC.
- Test in immunocompetent and xenograft models with surface patch illumination or fiber-assisted delivery.
- Quantify tumor control, ferroptosis biomarkers in situ, and normal-tissue histology and function.
- Profile immune consequences (DAMPs, antigen-presenting cell activation, CD8+ infiltration) to assess potential immunogenic ferroptosis.

Study design and methods (high level)
- Photosensitizer selection: Compare 5-ALA/PpIX (tumor-preferential accumulation via heme synthesis dysregulation) versus verteporfin (690 nm activation, deeper reach). Choose the agent yielding the widest ferroptotic window in TNBC over normal cells.
- Light delivery: 
  - Superficial lesions: flexible, conformal LED patch at the target wavelength with dosimetry guided by real-time fluorescence imaging of PS accumulation.
  - Deeper/periductal lesions: 200–500 µm micro-fiber for interstitial or intraductal illumination guided by ultrasound/ductoscopy to confine dose to tumor volume.
- Readouts of ferroptosis: membrane lipid peroxidation (BODIPY-C11), 4-HNE/MDA adducts, labile iron assays, GPX4/FSP1 levels, ACSL4 expression, and ferroptosis-rescue/activation controls (e.g., ferrostatin-1 versus caspase inhibitors). Distinguish from apoptosis/necrosis by marker panels and EM morphology.
- Safety/PK-PD: Co-register PS fluorescence with delivered light to define safe margins; monitor skin and parenchyma for edema, pain, thermal rise, and function.

Tumor selectivity strategy
- Spatial gating: Only illuminated tissue is exposed to ROS; beam shaping and dosimetry constrain chemistry to tumor geometry.
- Pharmacologic bias: Preferential tumor PS accumulation (e.g., PpIX) enhances on-target ROS yield.
- Biological differential: TNBC’s iron/PUFA/GPX4 dependence lowers the peroxidation threshold; normal mammary epithelium, with lower iron and stronger redox buffering, remains below threshold at therapeutic fluences.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: In vitro TNBC-to-normal selectivity index ≥3 for ferroptotic death with confirmed rescue by ferroptosis inhibitors; proceed to in vivo.
- M2: In vivo local control ratio ≥70% with histologic confirmation of ferroptosis and ≤10% Grade ≥2 local toxicity; proceed to optimization.
- M3: Durable control and immune activation (increased CD8+/granzyme B, reduced exhausted phenotypes) without systemic toxicity; nominate regimen for feasibility trial planning.

Risk and mitigation
- Risk: Hypoxia may limit ROS yield. Mitigation: fractionated/low-irradiance illumination to allow oxygen replenishment; consider supplemental oxygenation during treatment.
- Risk: Off-target skin inflammation. Mitigation: strict fluorescence-gated dosimetry, cooling, and shielding.
- Risk: Heterogeneous PS uptake. Mitigation: real-time PS fluorescence mapping to adapt fluence; if needed, intratumoral or intraductal PS delivery for uniform distribution.

Expected outcomes
- Mechanistic validation that PDT can be tuned to induce bona fide ferroptosis in TNBC.
- A clinically translatable, receptor-agnostic, spatially selective therapy exploiting breast anatomy and TNBC’s ferroptosis vulnerability.
- A platform for combination with immune checkpoint blockade in future studies if immunogenic ferroptosis is confirmed.

text:
Title
Same-day Autologous Hematopoietic Shielding (SAHS) to bypass LSC/HSC selectivity in AML

Central hypothesis (question-as-hypothesis)
If long-term repopulating HSC are made temporarily absent from the body during anti-leukemic treatment and then immediately returned as a purified autologous graft, we can deliver LSC-lethal therapy without the constraint of myelotoxicity, achieving durable leukemia control while shortening and stabilizing hematopoietic recovery.

Atomic strategy
Change the system boundary: remove the shared vulnerable population (patient’s own HSC) from exposure, treat the leukemia in vivo, then restore hematopoiesis. This bypasses the need to molecularly distinguish LSC from HSC.

Specific aims
1) Build a rapid, marker-minimal HSC capture-and-return workflow that yields an LSC-depleted, HSC-enriched autologous graft within 6–8 hours.
2) Establish an in vivo treatment window in which marrow-directed, LSC-lethal therapy can be administered unconstrained by HSC toxicity.
3) Test feasibility, safety, hematopoietic recovery, and anti-leukemic efficacy of SAHS in a first-in-human pilot.

Rationale
- The selectivity barrier arises because LSC and HSC share markers, signaling, and niches. Rather than searching for new molecular differences, SAHS removes HSC from harm’s way.
- Autologous HSC rescue is clinically validated to reconstitute hematopoiesis within ~10–14 days; applying it as a same-day, front-line shielding maneuver reframes induction/consolidation around a protected stem cell reserve.
- Purification relies on label-free biophysical/functional enrichment so the approach does not depend on discovering new targets.

Approach

Aim 1: Rapid HSC capture-and-return (preclinical optimization; then clinical deployment)
- Mobilization and collection (2–3 hours total):
  - Plerixafor-only mobilization timed to circadian peak of CD34+ egress (± short, light exercise). Avoids multi-day G-CSF and minimizes blast surge.
  - Large-volume leukapheresis to collect circulating progenitors.
- Graft enrichment without new target discovery (2–3 hours):
  - Primary: clinical-grade CD34 selection (permitted, not discovery) to reduce lymphoid/myeloid bulk.
  - Adjunct, marker-agnostic, label-free purging modules run in parallel:
    - Deterministic lateral displacement + inertial microfluidics to deplete larger/softer blasts.
    - Real-time deformability cytometry or dielectrophoresis to enrich quiescent, small, stiff HSC-like cells.
    - 2-hour hypoxic, growth-factor–free hold (1–3% O2) as a functional stress test favoring quiescent HSC survival over metabolically demanding blasts.
- Release criteria (rapid assays, ≤60 minutes total):
  - Viability and dose (target ≥5 × 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg).
  - Absence or low burden of leukemic driver by rapid droplet-digital PCR on small aliquots.
  - Morphology/flow for blast depletion using standard panels (no discovery).
- Contingency:
  - If yield or purity is inadequate, store product and abort SAHS for that cycle; proceed with standard-of-care.

Aim 2: HSC-absent therapy window (in vivo, 3–6 hours)
- Immediately after collection, administer therapy that would otherwise be HSC-limited:
  - Myeloablative-intensity chemotherapy (e.g., high-dose cytarabine- or melphalan-based) or
  - Regionally intensified, marrow-directed delivery (e.g., bilateral intraosseous iliac infusions with systemic exposure constraints), or
  - Non–target-discovery modalities such as targeted marrow irradiation with total-marrow-sparing techniques.
- Supportive measures:
  - Renal/hepatic protection per agent.
  - Real-time pharmacokinetic monitoring to define the safe reinfusion window (drug level thresholds pre-specified).
- Reinfusion:
  - Return autologous HSC graft same day once circulating drug levels drop below pre-specified thresholds for stem cell exposure.
  - Cryopreserve excess product for rescue or subsequent cycles.

Aim 3: First-in-human pilot (n=18, single-arm, multi-cycle feasibility)
- Population: Adults with newly diagnosed or relapsed AML without hyperleukocytosis emergency; exclude rapidly progressive DIC/AML-M3.
- Intervention:
  - Up to two SAHS cycles integrated with standard induction/consolidation timing.
- Endpoints:
  - Feasibility: ≥80% completion of full SAHS workflow in ≤8 hours.
  - Safety: procedure-related SAE rate ≤10%; no reinfusion-related blast flare; day-100 non-relapse mortality ≤5%.
  - Hematologic recovery: ANC ≥500/µL by day ≤12 post-reinfusion; platelets ≥20k/µL by day ≤14 without transfusion (per cycle).
  - Anti-leukemic efficacy: MRD negativity (flow or NGS) post-SAHS; composite CR rate; event-free survival at 6 months.
  - Purity control: leukemic mutation VAF in graft below pre-specified threshold (e.g., <0.01).

Key methods and controls
- Process controls:
  - Blinded back-to-back comparisons of label-free purging modules to optimize LSC depletion while maintaining CFU-GEMM and LTC-IC output.
  - Pharmacokinetic safety gates for reinfusion, validated in a large-animal model with autologous CD34+ reinfusion.
- Biological validation:
  - Paired xenotransplantation of small aliquots from pre- and post-purged products in NSG mice (exploratory, not release-criteria).
- Clinical comparators:
  - Matched retrospective cohort receiving standard induction without SAHS for descriptive comparisons of cytopenia duration, infections, and MRD.

Risk management
- Risk: Reinfusing occult LSC.
  - Mitigation: Orthogonal depletion (size/deformability + CD34 selection), rapid ddPCR VAF gate, reserve product quarantine if threshold exceeded.
- Risk: Insufficient CD34+ dose.
  - Mitigation: Mobilization timing optimization; contingency cryopreservation from prior cycle; option for pooled two-day collection in subsequent cycle.
- Risk: Delayed engraftment.
  - Mitigation: Target high CD34+ dose; co-infuse early progenitors (CD34+CD38+) retained by process; growth factor support post-reinfusion (not part of discovery).
- Risk: Therapy exposure of residual circulating HSC.
  - Mitigation: Real-time PK monitoring and a fixed “washout-to-reinfusion” interval validated preclinically.

Milestones and success criteria (go/no-go)
- M1: Preclinical module integration achieves ≥3-log blast depletion with ≥70% retention of CFU-GEMM and LTC-IC (go).
- M2: Large-animal PK/reinfusion study shows engraftment without toxicity at pre-specified thresholds (go).
- M3: First 6 patients complete SAHS with median ANC recovery ≤12 days and no graft-related SAEs (continue).
- Success: ≥60% MRD negativity after SAHS cycles with infection days reduced by ≥30% vs matched controls, and day-30 hematologic recovery meeting targets.

Expected outcomes and impact
- Operationally removes HSC from the therapeutic constraint set, allowing intensified LSC killing without inventing new targets.
- Shortens and stabilizes hematopoietic recovery through immediate autologous rescue, directly reducing myelotoxicity-driven morbidity.
- Provides a platform adaptable to diverse LSC-lethal modalities (chemotherapy, radiation, physical energies) while remaining agnostic to molecular selectivity.
- If validated, reframes AML therapy from “find a selective target” to “control exposure by redesigning system boundaries,” generalizable to other stem cell–proximal malignancies.

text:
Title
Sanctuary-first AML therapy: temporary ectopic niches that hide autologous HSCs and leave LSCs exposed

Hypothesis–Question
Can a retrievable, ectopic “safe-niche” that sequesters and maintains autologous HSCs in deep dormancy outside the marrow during cytotoxic therapy eliminate the need to distinguish LSC from HSC, thereby reducing myelotoxicity while allowing conventional regimens to debulk leukemia?

Atomic Strategy
Externalize selectivity: physically decouple healthy HSCs from the marrow by moving them into a field-addressable, macroporous, soft, hypoxia-maintaining niche outside systemic drug exposure; leave all malignant cells in situ and vulnerable.

Overview of the Proposed System
- Shelter: a subcutaneous, macroporous cryogel (elastic modulus ~0.2–1 kPa; pore size 50–150 μm) that passively maintains low-O2 microdomains (∼1–3%) and minimal nutrient flux to enforce quiescence.
- Addressability: embedded superparamagnetic particles enable on-demand capture/retrieval and positional control with an external magnet.
- HSC capture: autologous HSCs are procured (clinical standard mobilization + apheresis), short-term loaded with clinically used iron-oxide (for field guidance), and seeded into the device ex vivo before implantation; no new molecular markers are required.
- Protection principle: spatial separation plus quiescence reduces exposure to myelotoxic drugs and radiation; malignant cells remain in marrow and are treated conventionally.
- Return: after therapy, the device is retrieved; HSCs are released and reinfused or allowed to egress after in situ device dissolution.

Specific Aims
Aim 1. Build a minimal, quiescence-enforcing ectopic niche that preserves long-term HSC function in vivo.
- Criteria: >80% viability at 4–6 weeks; >70% Ki67−/G0; preserved colony-forming capacity and serial repopulation equal to pre-load baseline.

Aim 2. Demonstrate malignant exclusion.
- Test whether AML LSCs fail to co-occupy or persist within the niche when present in circulation.
- Criteria: <0.1% leukemic contamination by flow/NGS; no leukemic engraftment from explanted shelters on serial transplantation.

Aim 3. Prove therapeutic window expansion.
- In AML-engrafted mice, compare standard chemo ± radiomimetic dosing with vs without HSC sanctuary.
- Endpoints: nadir ANC/platelets, time to count recovery, overall survival, leukemia burden (flow/bioluminescence), and functional HSC engraftment after sanctuary release.

Design and Methods
- Materials: PEG- or alginate-based cryogels fabricated at subzero temperatures for interconnected macropores; stiffness tuned via crosslinking; oxygen microdomains sustained by geometry and diffusion path length (no exogenous factors required).
- Ex vivo HSC preparation: clinical CD34+ selection and brief iron-oxide loading (ferumoxytol-equivalent) under conditions that do not alter stemness; seed 1–5×10^6 cells/device.
- Implantation: subcutaneous pocket; external magnet secures device in stable location.
- In vivo maintenance: no growth factors; low-nutrient perfusion from avascular pocket and soft matrix enforce dormancy; periodic imaging (MRI) tracks device and cell load.
- Malignancy exclusion test: co-inject fluorescently barcoded AML cells IV; sample device and marrow serially; quantify leukemic barcodes in device vs blood/marrow.
- Therapy challenge: deliver daunorubicin/cytarabine or other myelotoxic regimens; monitor blood counts and marrow histology; after treatment, retrieve device magnetically or via small incision; release cells by enzymatic or pH-triggered dissolution; reinfuse IV; assess long-term, multilineage engraftment and serial repopulation.

Readouts
- Quiescence/quality: Ki67/DAPI, H2B-GFP label retention, RNA velocity; ROS levels; mitochondrial membrane potential.
- Function: CFU assays; primary and secondary NSG repopulation; lineage balance.
- Safety: device sterility, local inflammation, iron load/biodistribution; absence of leukemic take from device-derived cells.
- Efficacy: nadir depth, recovery time, leukemia burden, survival.

Key Controls
- No-device controls; device without cells; cells in device with normal-O2 pores; sham ferumoxytol-free cells.
- Leukemia-spiked HSC preps to test decontamination by sanctuary workflow.
- Chemotherapy pharmacokinetics at device site vs plasma.

Go/No-Go Gates
- Go: Aim 1 success + <0.1% leukemic contamination (Aim 2).
- No-Go: loss of long-term repopulation or any leukemic engraftment from device; redesign to increase dormancy (softer matrix, reduced pore interconnectivity) and/or switch to fully closed immunoisolating microcapsules.

Risk Mitigation
- If in vivo malignant ingress occurs, pivot to fully sealed, oxygen-permeable microcapsules (retrievable by magnet) to prevent any external cell entry.
- If HSC yield is low, perform two short mobilizations with interim cryopreservation.
- If quiescence drifts, tune stiffness and diffusion path length; shorten in-device residence.

Milestones and Timeline
- Year 1: Fabricate device; validate quiescence and viability ex vivo/intradermal; MRI tracking.
- Year 2: Malignancy exclusion and contamination thresholds; closed-system variant if needed.
- Year 3: AML model therapeutic window study; survival benefit and hematologic recovery; pre-IND package components (manufacturing, sterility, toxicology).

Impact
By moving healthy HSCs out of harm’s way rather than distinguishing them from LSCs, this strategy reframes AML therapy as a spatial control problem. If validated, it enables higher-intensity, shorter courses of conventional treatment with reduced myelotoxicity, independent of new molecular targets.

label: elements_bypass
text:
Title
Programmable hematopoietic hibernation to bypass LSC–HSC selectivity in AML

Central hypothesis-as-question
Can a reversible, organism-level torpor program place healthy HSC into deep, temporary quiescence (“hibernation”) while AML cells remain cycling, enabling cycle-specific chemotherapy to spare HSC yet eliminate leukemia?

Atomic strategy
Exploit a conserved hypometabolic/torpor state with a short-acting torpor-mimetic agent (TMA) plus controlled cooling to push normal HSC into G0; deliver S-phase–dependent chemotherapy during this window; then pharmacologically and thermally reverse torpor to reinitiate hematopoiesis.

Why this reframes the selectivity problem
- Selectivity is shifted from molecular recognition to temporal physiology: protect what can sleep (HSC), attack what must stay awake (AML).
- No discovery of new markers or signaling targets is required; the intervention acts at the organismal/metabolic level.
- Myelotoxicity is reduced by pre-emptively removing HSC from the population susceptible to cycle-specific cytotoxics.

Intervention blueprint
- Induction (“sleep”): Administer a TMA that engages endogenous torpor circuitry (e.g., adenosine-axis agonism or 5′-AMP) plus targeted temperature management to 33–34°C for 6–12 hours.
- Cytotoxic window: Infuse S-phase–selective chemotherapy (e.g., cytarabine-based) during the nadir of metabolic rate and HSC cycling.
- Reversal (“wake”): Rewarm to normothermia and administer a xanthine antagonist (e.g., caffeine/theophylline) to disengage TMA effects; initiate controlled refeeding to accelerate hematopoietic recovery.

Specific aims
1) Define and validate hematopoietic hibernation.
2) Test differential “wakefulness” of AML under torpor conditions.
3) Demonstrate therapeutic index gain: preserved HSC function with superior leukemia kill.
4) Establish translational parameters and safety for first-in-human testing.

Aim 1: Define and validate hematopoietic hibernation
- Models: C57BL/6 mice; human CD34+ cord blood xenografts for HSC readouts.
- Protocol: TMA dose-finding with/without mild hypothermia; monitor core temperature, VO2/CO2, heart rate.
- Readouts:
  - Cell-cycle state: Ki-67/DAPI and EdU/BrdU incorporation in phenotypic HSC (Lin−Sca1+Kit+CD150+CD48−) and progenitors.
  - Metabolic state: marrow ATP/AMP ratio, mitochondrial membrane potential, ROS.
  - Function: colony-forming assays (CFU-GM/BFU-E/CFU-GEMM), competitive repopulation at 16–24 weeks.
- Success criteria: ≥70% reduction in HSC S/G2/M fraction, preserved long-term repopulation vs controls, reversibility within 24–48 hours post-wake.

Aim 2: Test AML “wakefulness” under torpor
- Models: MLL-AF9, FLT3-ITD; human AML PDX covering diverse genotypes.
- Protocol: Apply torpor regimen; measure proliferation during nadir.
- Readouts: EdU pulse-chase; mitotic index; replication stress markers; apoptosis after cytarabine exposure during torpor vs normothermia.
- Success criteria: AML maintains ≥40–60% S-phase fraction or exhibits heightened replication stress under torpor, indicating failure to enter protective quiescence.

Aim 3: Demonstrate therapeutic index gain
- Study arms (preclinical):
  1) Chemo alone.
  2) Torpor alone.
  3) Torpor → chemo during nadir → wake (primary test).
  4) Chemo at matched time but normothermia (timing control).
- Endpoints:
  - Myeloprotection: CBC nadirs, marrow CFU, competitive repopulation post-therapy, time to ANC/platelet recovery, transfusion needs.
  - Antileukemic efficacy: leukemic burden (flow cytometry of blasts/PDX human CD45+), event-free and overall survival.
  - Therapeutic index: efficacy normalized to HSC function (e.g., leukemia reduction per unit HSC depletion).
- Success criteria: ≥2× improvement in HSC functional preservation at equal or improved leukemia control; faster hematologic recovery (>30% reduction in neutropenia duration).

Aim 4: Translational parameters and safety
- Pharmacology: PK/PD of TMA, thermal dose (area-under-curve below 35°C), interaction with cytarabine exposure and intracellular Ara-CTP.
- Safety: hemodynamics, arrhythmia risk, renal/hepatic indices; neurobehavioral recovery post-wake.
- Biomarkers for bedside control: continuous temp/VO2; serum lactate/ketones; marrow EdU microdosing to confirm cycle suppression in HSC.
- Reversal protocol: standardized rewarming rate; xanthine dosing; glucose/insulin-controlled refeeding to trigger hematopoietic rebound.

Experimental considerations
- Chronopharmacology: synchronize induction with resting-phase to maximize baseline HSC quiescence.
- Nutritional preconditioning: 24-hour fasting-mimicking diet to amplify quiescence; standardized refeeding to accelerate “wake.”
- Chemo choice: prioritize S-phase agents (cytarabine, cladribine) and schedule anthracyclines to the torpor window’s mid-nadir.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: AML enters quiescence under torpor.
  - Mitigation: select AML subtypes with constitutive proliferative drive (e.g., FLT3-ITD) for initial translation; add low-dose priming (e.g., hypomethylating agent) 48–72 hours pre-torpor to enforce cycling.
- Risk: Reduced drug delivery in hypometabolism.
  - Mitigation: confirm marrow drug concentrations; adjust infusion rate or brief normothermic “pulses” without releasing HSC from G0.
- Risk: Incomplete HSC protection.
  - Mitigation: increase TMA dose or cooling depth within safety bounds; shorten chemo exposure to tight nadir window; confirm by real-time EdU.

Go/no-go milestones
- Go: reproducible ≥70% HSC cycle suppression with full functional recovery; AML maintains cycling or exhibits lethal replication stress under torpor; ≥2× therapeutic index improvement in at least two AML models.
- No-go: AML uniformly arrests with HSC; inability to safely reverse torpor within predefined hemodynamic limits.

First-in-human pilot (concept)
- Population: adults with de novo AML undergoing induction; exclude cachexia or high cardiac risk initially; enrich for proliferative genotypes.
- Design: single-arm safety/feasibility of torpor-programmed induction vs historical controls.
- Primary endpoints: safety (hemodynamic stability), feasibility (≥90% protocol adherence), hematologic recovery time vs matched controls.
- Secondary endpoints: CR rate, MRD negativity, transfusion burden, mucositis/neutropenic infection rates.

Impact
- Converts the selectivity bottleneck into a temporal-physiology problem, reducing myelotoxicity without new target discovery.
- If validated, establishes a programmable “sleep–hit–wake” platform applicable across cytotoxic regimens and potentially other marrow-toxic therapies.
