text:
Title
The Glyco-Epigenetic Checkpoint (GEC): Histone dicarbonyl glycation as a binary metabolic memory gate and its erasure via endogenous deglycation

Central hypothesis and research goal
Metabolic stress (transient glucose/lipid surges) drives nuclear accumulation of reactive dicarbonyls (methylglyoxal/glyoxal), which nonenzymatically glycate histone lysine/arginine residues. Above a quantized occupancy threshold on specific chromatin domains, histone glycation displaces canonical acyl marks, disrupts chromatin readers, and locks transcription into a pro-inflammatory, fibrotic, and insulin-resistant state across tissues. This threshold defines a metabolic “point of no return” (the GEC) that converts reversible dysfunction into disease commitment. Enhancing endogenous nuclear deglycation and dicarbonyl detoxification below this threshold will erase the chromatin “scar” and reset cells to a pre-injury state. The research goal is to define, validate, and therapeutically modulate the GEC for disease interception.

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single, druggable erasure mechanism: amplify nucleus-localized deglycation of histone dicarbonyl adducts (via DJ-1/PARK7 and FN3K) and pre-glycation detox (GLO1/2–GSH axis) to drive histone glycation occupancy below the commitment threshold, thereby resetting chromatin programs independent of upstream nutrient-sensing pathways.

Mechanistic model (checkpoint properties)
- Input: episodic excess glycolytic/β-oxidation flux → dicarbonyl production (MGO/GO).
- Buffer: nuclear GLO1/2–GSH detox and histone/protein deglycation (DJ-1, FN3K).
- Nonlinearity: when dicarbonyl generation surpasses detox/deglycation capacity, histone glycation rapidly rises on promoters/enhancers controlling inflammation, ECM, lipogenesis, and secretory stress.
- Commitment: glycation impairs histone acylation readers/writers, perturbs nucleosome dynamics, and can modify detox enzymes themselves, creating positive feedback (hysteresis). State persists after stress removal.
- Erasure: boosting nuclear deglycation/detox below a defined occupancy threshold restores acylation balance, chromatin accessibility, and transcriptional homeostasis.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define the GEC threshold and hysteresis across tissues.
- Models: Primary human hepatocytes, adipocytes, pancreatic islet cells, gut organoids, and cardiac fibroblasts; mouse and human PBMCs for systemic readouts.
- Protocol: Pulsed high glucose/palmitate ± recovery to mimic real-life dietary spikes. Time-resolved sampling.
- Readouts:
  - Quantitative proteomics of histone adducts (LC–MS/MS) to map MGO/GO-derived glycation stoichiometry at specific lysines/arginines.
  - Multi-omics: ATAC-seq, ChIP-RIME for bromodomain/reader displacement, RNA-seq for gene programs.
  - Live-cell chromatin compaction (FLIM–FRET/Hi-D), and metabolic flux (13C tracing).
- Analysis: Fit sigmoidal models of glycation occupancy vs. phenotypic outputs; define half-max threshold (GEC50) and hysteresis width after stress withdrawal.

Milestone: Identify a conserved occupancy threshold on disease-relevant loci that predicts irreversibility across ≥3 tissues.

Aim 2. Map endogenous erasers of the scar and quantify erasure kinetics.
- Perturbations: CRISPRa/CRISPRi of DJ-1, FN3K, GLO1/2; nucleus-targeted overexpression and catalytically dead controls.
- Metrics: Erasure half-time (t1/2) for histone glycation versus restoration of acyl marks; recovery of transcriptional and functional phenotypes (insulin signaling, secretory capacity, ECM normalization).
- Mechanism: Determine whether deglycation alone (no change in upstream flux) resets programs below GEC.

Milestone: Demonstrate that elevating nuclear deglycation reduces glycation occupancy below threshold and restores function after stress.

Aim 3. Therapeutic modality discovery focused on nuclear erasure.
- Biochemical screening:
  - Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of DJ-1 deglycase; stabilizers of active dimer; activity assays with glycated histone peptides.
  - FN3K activators that enhance ATP turnover on fructosamine adducts.
  - GLO1 activators and GSH-sparing cofactors to reduce nuclear dicarbonyl load.
- Chemistry and targeting:
  - Nucleus-penetrant carnosine analogs resistant to carnosinase (CNDP1/2), with DNA-binding–independent nuclear localization tags.
  - Redox-neutral MGO “sponge” prodrugs that unmask in the nucleus (aldehyde-reactive warheads with nuclear retention motifs).
- Cellular screening cascade: High-content imaging for glycation marks, reader relocalization, and chromatin accessibility; off-target counterscreens (HDAC/BET, PARP, sirtuins) to ensure novelty.
- PK/PD: Nuclear target engagement biomarkers (see Aim 4).

Milestone: ≥2 chemical series with on-target nuclear deglycation, no HDAC/BET cross-reactivity, EC50 < 500 nM in cells.

Aim 4. Biomarkers and patient selection for interception.
- Circulating/accessible biomarkers:
  - PBMC histone glycation occupancy by targeted LC–MS as a surrogate for tissue GEC state.
  - Plasma dicarbonyls and AGE signatures; RBC FN3K activity; DJ-1 oxidation state.
- Dynamic stress test: Standardized mixed-meal or lipid challenge, with pre/post PBMC histone glycation to detect hysteresis and proximity to threshold.
- Imaging/omics endpoints: Noninvasive liver MRI-PDFF and serum fibrosis panels aligned to PBMC GEC readouts.

Milestone: Validate a composite “GEC score” that stratifies individuals at the interception window (prediabetes/NAFLD without fibrosis, early diastolic dysfunction, islet compensation).

Aim 5. In vivo interception and reversal before irreversible remodeling.
- Models: Diet-induced and intermittent high-sugar/fat mouse models; pre-fibrotic NASH; β-cell stress without decompensation; HFpEF of metabolic origin.
- Interventions: Lead DJ-1/FN3K PAMs; nucleus-targeted carnosine analog; GLO1 activator; engineered microbe (see below).
- Endpoints: Tissue histone glycation occupancy, transcriptomic reset, insulin sensitivity (clamp), islet secretory reserve, ECM reversal, and prevention of fibrosis/remodeling.
- Timing: Intervene after establishment of dysfunction but before fibrosis to model interception.

Milestone: Durable phenotypic rescue with confirmed chromatin erasure below threshold and reduced hysteresis.

Therapeutic modalities and delivery
- Small molecules: DJ-1 and FN3K PAMs; GLO1 activators; nucleus-targeted dicarbonyl scavengers.
- Biologic: AAV-delivered nucleus-targeted FN3K/DJ-1 for high-risk focal tissues (liver/pancreas) with regulatable promoters for safety.
- Engineered microbe: Gut commensal expressing high-flux glyoxalase pathway to reduce systemic dicarbonyl burden without altering glycemia.
- Combination logic: Short, pulsed “erasure therapy” to reset chromatin, followed by lifestyle/metabolic standard care; avoid chronic interference with physiological signaling.

Safety and off-target strategy
- Maintain redox neutrality; exclude broad HDAC/BET/PARP/SIRT modulation.
- Genome integrity: Monitor DNA damage, PARylation, replication stress.
- Metabolic homeostasis: Continuous glucose, lipidomics, mitochondrial function.
- Immunology: Cytokine panels and trained-immunity markers to avoid immune suppression.

Translational plan and decision gates
- Go/no-go 1: Existence of a conserved, quantized histone glycation threshold predicting irreversibility across ≥3 tissues.
- Go/no-go 2: Pharmacologic erasure drives occupancy below threshold with transcriptional and functional reset in ≥2 human primary cell types.
- Go/no-go 3: In vivo interception with biomarker-linked PD in ≥2 models without fibrosis progression.
- Candidate selection: Single agent with oral bioavailability or depot durability, nuclear target engagement in PBMCs, and clean safety pharmacology.

Why this is novel and checkpoint-like
- Target class: nonenzymatic histone dicarbonyl glycation and its endogenous erasers—distinct from canonical nutrient sensors (AMPK/mTOR/PPARs/GLP-1R/FGF21).
- Binary gating: occupancy-driven, hysteretic commitment switching that is separable from continuous metabolic signaling.
- Erasable memory: leverages intrinsic deglycation/detox pathways as a biological “delete button” to reset chromatin state.

Expected impact
A tissue-agnostic, first-in-class interception therapy that prevents progression from metabolic dysfunction to irreversible disease by erasing the chromatin record of prior injury, restoring flexibility of metabolic and inflammatory programs before fibrosis, β-cell exhaustion, or cardiac remodeling.

Title
The Lactate–Lactylation Commitment Node (LLCN): a threshold epigenetic-metabolic checkpoint for disease interception and closed-loop control

Central hypothesis
Sustained lactate elevation beyond a concentration–pH–duration threshold triggers a switch-like increase in histone and non-histone protein lactylation that commits tissues to fibrogenic, pro-inflammatory, and metabolically inflexible states; keeping lactate below this “lactylation onset threshold” (LOT) or rapidly reversing lactylation prevents irreversible progression across liver, adipose, heart, kidney, and pancreas.

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Treat the conversion of excess lactate into lactylation marks as the discrete checkpoint. Sense when intracellular/extracellular lactate and pH approach the LOT and clamp lactate just below this threshold—or actively de-lactylate chromatin—thereby preventing commitment while preserving physiological lactate signaling.

Rationale
- Lactate is a Goldilocks metabolite: essential carbon/redox shuttle and signaling cue at modest levels; at high, sustained levels it drives epigenetic reprogramming via protein lactylation.
- Lactylation exhibits threshold-like behavior because it depends nonlinearly on: (i) lactate availability and cellular pH; (ii) acyl-donor formation; (iii) writer (e.g., p300/CBP family) kinetics; (iv) limited capacity of delactylases (class I HDACs and sirtuins) under low NAD+ and acidic conditions. This creates positive feedback and hysteresis—a commitment feature.
- The same switch can operate in multiple tissues exposed to metabolic stress, hypoxia, or inflammation, providing a tissue-agnostic interception point.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define the lactylation onset threshold (LOT) and commitment dynamics across cell types.
- Deliverables
  - LOT maps (concentration–pH–exposure time) for hepatocytes, stellate cells, adipocytes, adipose tissue macrophages, cardiac fibroblasts, renal tubular cells, islet endocrine and immune cells.
  - Commitment criteria: persistence of lactylation/gene programs ≥72 h after lactate normalization (hysteresis index).
  - A quantitative “LLCN score” integrating nuclear H3/H4 lactylation, chromatin accessibility, and sentinel gene expression.
- Approach
  - Titrate lactate and pH using controlled microfluidics, apply time-varying pulses to detect tipping points.
  - Multi-omic readouts: targeted proteomics of lactyl-lysine, cfChIP-seq for key lactyl marks (e.g., H3K18la), ATAC-seq, nascent RNA-seq time courses pre- and post-washout.
  - Kinetic modeling of writer/delactylase saturation to infer feedback strength and hysteresis.
  - Identify lactylation readers by lactyl-peptide pulldown/MS to reveal chromatin complexes that lock the state.

Aim 2. Establish causality between LLCN crossing and irreversible pathology in vivo; define interception windows.
- Models
  - Diet-induced NASH/fibrosis; pressure-overload or metabolic HFpEF; diabetic kidney disease; obesity-induced adipose inflammation; beta-cell stress models.
- Readouts
  - Intravital lactate and pH imaging (genetically encoded sensors), tissue lactyl-proteome, single-nucleus cfChIP from plasma for organ-origin lactyl marks, fibrosis/inflammation indices, metabolic flux.
- Experiments
  - Programmed lactate clamps to artificially cross/not cross the LOT with matched glycemia/oxygenation.
  - Test reversibility: normalize lactate after crossing and quantify persistence of lactylation and pathology.
  - Define earliest interception time that averts fibrosis or endocrine cell failure.

Aim 3. Therapeutic modulation of the LLCN.
- Small molecules
  - Writer-selective lactylation blockers: optimize p300/CBP catalytic pocket ligands for preferential inhibition of lactyl transfer over acetyl transfer (structure-guided).
  - Delactylase potentiators: identify/engineer selective activators or targeted recruitment (PROTACs/MOSAICs) of class I HDACs to lactylated loci.
  - Lactyl-donor scavengers: nucleophile-based traps for reactive lactyl donors; medicinal chemistry to ensure intracellular delivery without global acyl-scavenging.
  - Redox/pH microclampers: NAD+ regeneration couplers and localized buffering to raise delactylase capacity without suppressing physiological lactate transients.
- Biologic/engineered modalities
  - Organelle-targeted delactylases (mito- and nucleo-anchored) delivered by LNPs or AAV with disease-inducible promoters.
  - Monoclonal/biologic readers-blockers: disrupt lactyl-lysine reader interactions discovered in Aim 1 to break feed-forward stabilization.
- Engineered microbe/device
  - “Lactate Guard”: an autonomous probiotic (e.g., E. coli Nissle or Lactobacillus) engineered with a lactate/pH logic gate controlling expression of a lactate sink module (LDHB + NADH oxidase + catalase) to convert lactate to pyruvate/H2O safely in gut lumen, throttling portal lactate spikes to the liver.
  - An implantable subcutaneous micro-bioreactor encapsulating sentinel cells expressing Laconic+pHluorin that, above LOT, actuate a membrane-bound LDHB/NAD+ recycler; failsafes cap maximal lactate removal rate to preserve exercise physiology.

Aim 4. Translation: human biomarkers, stratification, and closed-loop thresholds.
- Biomarkers
  - Plasma cfChIP for H3K18la/H4K8la with tissue-of-origin deconvolution.
  - Lactate–pH exposure integrals from continuous interstitial monitors to compute a patient-specific LOT proximity score.
- Early clinical testing
  - Short-term interception studies in high-risk NAFL/NASH, HFpEF with obesity, and DKD patients: test probiotic/device clamps or short-course lactylation blockers; endpoints include change in cfChIP lactyl marks, ELF score/MRE stiffness (liver), E/e′ and ECV (heart), and albuminuria/eGFR slope (kidney).

Innovation and novelty
- Defines a discrete, druggable checkpoint (LLCN) based on a metabolite-driven epigenetic switch, not a canonical nutrient sensor pathway.
- Introduces LOT as a quantitative, actionable threshold to trigger closed-loop control, aligning with the Goldilocks paradigm.
- Couples epigenetic state surveillance (cfChIP lactyl marks) with autonomous metabolite clamping—an interception-first therapeutic window.

Therapeutic window and safety
- Preserve physiologic lactate signaling (exercise, wound healing) by:
  - Patient- and tissue-specific LOT mapping.
  - Devices/microbes with upper-bound removal rates and reversible actuation.
  - Short pulse dosing of writer blockers around predicted LOT crossings rather than chronic suppression.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- Year 1: LOT maps and LLCN score across target cell types; identification of at least one lactylation reader complex.
- Year 2: In vivo demonstration that transient LOT crossing induces persistent pathology; interception by pre-emptive clamp prevents commitment.
- Year 3: Lead molecules that block lactylation with ≥5× selectivity over acetylation; engineered microbe/device achieving ≥30% reduction of portal or interstitial lactate spikes without affecting exercise tolerance.
- Year 4: First-in-human LOT proximity assay validated; pilot interception study shows ≥20% reduction in cfChIP lactyl marks and improvement in a prespecified organ-specific surrogate endpoint.

Anticipated outcomes and decision gates
- If lactylation lacks hysteresis in a given tissue, pivot to tissues where hysteresis is strongest and prioritize reader blockade (locking mechanism) over lactate clamping.
- If systemic clamping impairs physiology, deploy organ-restricted strategies (gut-first portal clamping; liver-targeted p300 inhibitors; fibroblast-tropic delactylases).

Impact
A validated LLCN will provide a unified, tissue-agnostic metabolic checkpoint and an accompanying closed-loop therapy to keep patients on the safe side of the lactate Goldilocks zone—intercepting disease before fibrosis, beta-cell exhaustion, or cardiac remodeling become irreversible.

Title: The GLiP Checkpoint — A galectin–N-glycan lattice percolation switch that commits tissues to metabolic pathology and is therapeutically resettable

Central hypothesis and goal
- Hypothesis: The cell-surface galectin–N-glycan lattice undergoes a percolation transition (the GLiP checkpoint) as metabolic debt accumulates. Crossing a critical lattice density commits cells to a supercritical state that stabilizes pro-pathology receptors and transporters at the membrane, suppresses receptor turnover and lysosomal flux, and locks tissues into chronic metabolic dysfunction. Transiently pushing the lattice below the percolation threshold triggers a global “reset” characterized by bulk endocytosis, lysosomal cleanup, and a brief reduction in nutrient/hormone signaling (a metabolic pause) that clears accumulated damage and restores reversibility.
- Goal: Discover, quantify, and drug the GLiP checkpoint to intercept metabolic disease before irreversible remodeling (fibrosis, beta-cell exhaustion, cardiovascular remodeling).

Atomic strategy
- Single insight: Treat the emergent percolation state of the galectin–N-glycan lattice as a binary, druggable metabolic checkpoint. Modulate its criticality with short pulses of galectin–glycan interface antagonists to intentionally cross below the critical threshold, thereby synchronously activating cleanup (lysosomal/autophagic flux) and inducing a temporary metabolic pause.

Rationale: why GLiP encodes metabolic debt and shows switch-like behavior
- Multistress integration: UDP-GlcNAc (from glucose, glutamine, acetyl-CoA) drives N-glycan branching; inflammatory cues increase galectin abundance; ER/proteostasis stress raises glycoprotein load. These orthogonal “debts” converge multiplicatively on lattice valency and occupancy.
- Thresholding: Percolation of multivalent galectins on branched N-glycans exhibits a sharp critical threshold (φ*). Below φ*, receptors and transporters diffuse and recycle; above φ*, a supercritical lattice traps them, prolonging signaling, reducing endocytosis and lysosomal routing, and reinforcing damage accumulation.
- Reset logic: Briefly reducing effective lattice valency/occupancy (subcritical) triggers synchronized receptor internalization and lysosomal engagement, which both clears damaged cargo and imposes a transient nutrient/hormone signaling pause.

Therapeutic concept
- Modality: Short-acting galectin–CRD (carbohydrate recognition domain) antagonists or multivalent glycomimetics with high on-rate and fast off-rate, dosed in pulses to avoid chronic immune/metabolic suppression.
- Alternative/adjunct: Transient, partial inhibition of MGAT5-mediated β1,6-branching or competitive decoys (soluble glycopolymers) to momentarily reduce lattice connectivity; engineered microbes that sequester circulating galectin ligands to fine-tune systemic galectin availability.
- Companion diagnostic: A peripheral blood GLiP score quantifying near-threshold lattice state to time pulses before commitment to pathology.

Measurable definition of the GLiP checkpoint
- State variable: S ∈ {subcritical, supercritical} defined by L = B × G × V, where B is mean β1,6-branching per glycoprotein, G is local galectin density, and V is effective valency/affinity; S switches when L crosses φ*, exhibiting hysteresis.
- Readouts:
  - Live-cell lattice mapping: fluorescent galectin probes + super-resolution imaging to quantify cluster size distribution and extract φ*.
  - Single-particle tracking/FRAP of insulin receptor, cytokine receptors, and nutrient transporters to measure diffusion/trapping transitions.
  - Lysosomal/autophagic flux after lattice dissolution (TFEB nuclear translocation, LC3-II flux, LTR fluorescence).
  - “Metabolic pause” markers: acute reductions in glucose/fatty acid uptake and downstream signaling amplitudes with preserved viability.

Experimental plan

Aim 1 — Establish GLiP as a discrete, tissue-agnostic metabolic checkpoint and map φ*
- Build in vitro models (primary hepatocytes, adipocytes, beta cells, endothelial cells, macrophages) spanning nutrient surplus, lipotoxicity, and proteotoxic stress to titrate B, G, and V independently.
- Derive φ* from cluster-size scaling and receptor mobility inflection points; validate bistability/hysteresis by ramp-up/ramp-down of branching and galectin levels.
- Link GLiP state to metabolic debt metrics: acylcarnitines, O-GlcNAc, protein carbonyls, misfolded glycoprotein burden.

Aim 2 — Test causality: pulse-driven subcritical crossing resets cells
- Interventions: short pulses (15–120 min) of fast-off galectin-3/9 antagonists or glycomimetic decoys at doses calibrated to cross below φ* without prolonged suppression.
- Outcomes:
  - Cleanup: surge in receptor/cargo endocytosis and lysosomal degradation; removal of damaged mitochondria/proteins; restoration of proteostasis markers.
  - Pause: acute, reversible dampening of nutrient transporter surface density and anabolic signaling; recovery to baseline within hours post-pulse.
  - Reversibility: reduced ROS, improved redox and mitochondrial function 24–72 h post-pulse without cytotoxicity.
- Controls: chronic antagonist exposure (to show harm of persistent suppression), lattice-irrelevant ligands, and MGAT5 knockdown to modulate B directly.

Aim 3 — Interception in vivo and therapeutic windowing
- Models: diet-induced pre-NASH, pre-diabetes, pressure-overload cardiometabolic stress. Enrich for near-threshold GLiP by baseline PBMC GLiP score and tissue galectin imaging.
- Dosing logic: weekly or biweekly pulses during high-risk windows (e.g., postprandial peaks, circadian vulnerability) guided by GLiP score dynamics.
- Endpoints: prevention of fibrosis (liver, heart), preservation of beta-cell function, improved insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammatory tone—without weight loss as primary driver.
- Safety: immune competence, wound healing, infection surveillance, and off-target glycan perturbation panels.

Biomarkers and diagnostics
- GLiP score (blood): ex vivo galectin probe binding to PBMCs + glycomics of β1,6-branching; soluble galectin-3/9 levels; model-derived L relative to φ*.
- Imaging: targeted galectin probes for tissue lattice mapping (liver/adipose PET or optical in preclinical).
- Pharmacodynamic markers: spike in lysosomal flux and transient transporter endocytosis following pulses; recovery kinetics.

Druggability and delivery
- Small molecules/glycomimetics: optimized for high on-rate, rapid systemic clearance, and limited CNS exposure; inhaled or parenteral routes depending on PK needs.
- Biologics: soluble galectin traps with tunable valency; glycopolymers with defined spacing to adjust the effective V.
- Engineered microbe (adjunct): secretes non-absorbable galectin-binding oligosaccharides that titrate systemic galectin availability with minimal systemic exposure.

Risk mitigation and falsification
- If lattice dissolution fails to trigger cleanup, pair subcritical crossing with a low-dose lysosome-activating cue only during pulses; if cleanup occurs without a pause, tune pulse intensity/duration to increase transporter internalization.
- Falsification: if φ* cannot be identified (no scaling inflection) or if subcritical crossing does not produce synchronized endocytosis and lysosomal activation across tissues, reject GLiP as a checkpoint.

Milestones and deliverables (36 months)
- Year 1: Quantified φ* across cell types; validated GLiP score in blood.
- Year 2: Proof-of-concept pulses that reset cells ex vivo and in two tissues in vivo; defined safety margins.
- Year 3: Lead antagonist/decoy with humanized PK/PD; interception efficacy in two preclinical models; IND-enabling plan plus companion diagnostic prototype.

Impact
- Establishes a binary, tissue-agnostic metabolic checkpoint grounded in an emergent biophysical transition rather than a single canonical pathway.
- Provides a precision interception strategy that preempts irreversible remodeling by coupling a timed metabolic pause with synchronized cellular cleanup.
- Opens a new therapeutic class: percolation modulators for metabolic disease prevention and reversal.

Title: MR1–MAIT ligand gating as a metabolic checkpoint for disease interception

Core hypothesis-goal (inseparable):
A host–microbiome co-metabolite threshold that determines MR1 occupancy by ultra-agonists versus antagonists serves as a switch-like checkpoint controlling whether transient metabolic stress (e.g., obesity, hyperglycemia) becomes self-resolving or progresses to irreversible metabolic disease; modulating MR1 ligand state will intercept disease progression.

Atomic strategy:
Recode the transition from reversible to irreversible metabolic dysfunction as a binary MR1 ligand competition problem: when the formation rate of potent MAIT-activating ligands (e.g., 5-OP-RU class produced from microbial riboflavin intermediates plus host methylglyoxal) exceeds a threshold relative to non-activating MR1 ligands (e.g., Ac-6-FP-like), MR1 becomes predominantly agonist-occupied, driving durable MAIT activation and inflammatory remodeling across tissues. Preventing agonist dominance—or enforcing antagonist dominance—halts commitment to pathology.

Why this is a checkpoint:
- Switch variable: MR1 occupancy state (agonist-bound vs antagonist-bound).
- Threshold behavior: non-linear formation of ultra-agonists depends on the product of two inputs that rise during stress (microbial 5-A-RU supply and host dicarbonyl stress via methylglyoxal). Crossing a formation threshold flips MAIT cells into a stable pro-inflammatory, tissue-retentive state that sustains metabolic inflammation.
- Tissue-agnostic: MAIT cells survey gut, liver, adipose, and pancreas, exporting a common cytokine/inflammation program (IFN-γ, IL-17, GM-CSF) that amplifies macrophage and stromal scarring responses.
- Druggable: MR1-binding small molecules/biologics, engineered microbes to shift ligand ecology, and host dicarbonyl modulators.

Study population framing (natural experiment):
Exploit rare individuals who experience temporary obesity, hyperglycemia, or steatohepatitis but completely remit without chronic disease (“spontaneous resolvers”), contrasted with matched individuals who progress. This design lets nature reveal protective MR1 ligand ecologies and MAIT states associated with resilience.

Specific aims:
1) Define the MR1 ligandome threshold that separates resolvers from progressors.
2) Map MAIT cell state transitions that encode commitment to metabolic pathology.
3) Establish causality by reprogramming MR1 ligand competition ex vivo and in vivo.
4) Build a first-in-class interception therapy that enforces antagonist-dominant MR1 occupancy in at-risk humans.

Aim 1: Human discovery of the MR1 ligand checkpoint
- Cohorts:
  - Resolving cohort: adults with documented transient metabolic derangements (e.g., BMI increase with subsequent ≥10% weight loss and normalization of HOMA-IR within 12–24 months; or transient NAFLD with ≥30% MRI-PDFF reduction without pharmacotherapy).
  - Progressor cohort: matched individuals advancing to persistent T2D/NAFLD/fibrosis over the same interval.
- Measurements (paired baseline and follow-up):
  - Circulating and urinary MR1-ligand fingerprints by targeted stable-isotope LC–MS/MS: quantify ultra-agonist adducts (5-OP-RU/5-OE-RU surrogates), non-activating ligands, and unknown binders via MR1 pull-down competition.
  - Dicarbonyl stress panel: methylglyoxal, glyoxal; protein adducts (MG-H1); glyoxalase system activity (GLO1).
  - Shotgun metagenomics/metatranscriptomics: riboflavin pathway flux capacity (ribA/ribB/ribD/ribH expression), 5-A-RU generation potential, and predicted production of MR1 antagonists.
  - MAIT profiling across blood and accessible tissues (adipose biopsies, liver fine-needle aspirates when available):
    - MR1 tetramer+ TCR Vα7.2+ cells; activation/exhaustion markers; cytokine potential; tissue-retention (S1PR1↓, CD69↑, CXCR6↑).
    - Single-cell RNA/ATAC-seq to identify stable pro-inflammatory vs quiescent states and epigenetic hysteresis.
  - Clinical/metabolic phenotypes: OGTT with insulin secretion/sensitivity indices, MRI-PDFF, elastography, continuous glucose monitoring variability metrics.
- Analyses:
  - Identify a composite “MR1 agonist dominance index” (ADI) = (agonist ligand pool)/(antagonist ligand pool), and estimate a threshold (ADI*) that best separates resolvers vs progressors.
  - Integrate ADI with dicarbonyl burden and microbiome riboflavin flux to infer formation kinetics and tipping points.

Aim 2: Mechanistic mapping of commitment biology
- Ex vivo human tissue systems:
  - Adipose and liver slices co-cultured with autologous or allogeneic MAIT cells under tunable MR1 ligand ratios; quantify switch-like induction of fibrogenic and inflammatory programs in stromal and myeloid compartments.
  - Perturbations: adjust methylglyoxal, add/remove riboflavin precursors, spike defined MR1 antagonists.
- Readouts:
  - Non-linear response curves and hysteresis (forward vs reverse titration) in MAIT activation and downstream tissue programs; define conditions where returning below ADI* fails to reverse MAIT/tissue state (commitment).
  - Map feed-forward loops (e.g., MAIT cytokines suppress glyoxalase activity or remodel microbiota), explaining irreversibility.

Aim 3: Causality and druggability
- Ligand competition toolkit:
  - Small-molecule MR1 antagonists optimized for stability and oral exposure; MR1-blocking antibodies for short pulses.
  - Dicarbonyl modulators: methylglyoxal scavengers and GLO1 inducers to reduce ultra-agonist formation.
  - Engineered live biotherapeutics: microbes that (a) degrade 5-A-RU precursors; (b) secrete MR1 antagonists; or (c) export riboflavin overproduction buffers that minimize reactive adduct formation.
- In vivo validation:
  - Humanized MAIT mouse models with diet/obesity or NAFLD settings; impose ligand ecologies that mirror human ADI strata; intervene to cross below ADI* and test reversal of MAIT/tissue states, insulin sensitivity, and fibrotic gene programs.
  - Short pulse-blockade tests to show that transient enforcement of antagonist dominance prevents long-term commitment if given before the hysteresis window closes.

Aim 4: Translation to interception trial
- Companion diagnostics:
  - MR1 ligandome panel (ADI), methylglyoxal adducts, microbiome riboflavin flux score, circulating activated MAIT frequency.
- First-in-human strategy (Phase 1b/2a, interception):
  - Population: prediabetes or early NAFLD with elevated ADI and activated MAIT signature but no advanced fibrosis or beta-cell failure.
  - Interventions (randomized arms):
    1) Oral MR1 antagonist.
    2) MR1 antagonist + dicarbonyl scavenger.
    3) Engineered microbial consortium producing MR1 antagonists.
  - Duration: 12–24 weeks with follow-up at 48 weeks for durability.
  - Endpoints: change in ADI and MAIT activation (primary pharmacodynamic), insulin sensitivity (hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp or surrogate), MRI-PDFF, liver stiffness, beta-cell function indices, inflammatory and fibrotic biomarkers.

Therapeutic product concepts
- Small molecules: high-affinity, non-activating MR1 binders that outcompete ultra-agonists and stabilize a non-signaling MR1 conformation; oral, gut-liver targeted.
- Biologics: MR1-blocking antibody or soluble MR1 decoy for short-course pulses around high-risk transitions (acute weight gain, postpartum, steroid exposure).
- Engineered microbes: chassis strains that deplete 5-A-RU precursors and secrete MR1 antagonists; designed for colonization windows to re-establish a protective ligand ecology.
- Host co-therapies: methylglyoxal scavengers or GLO1 inducers to depress ultra-agonist formation below the threshold.

Safety and selectivity
- Temporal targeting: short-course or intermittent dosing to avoid broad MAIT suppression.
- Tissue targeting: gut-restricted exposure or liver-targeted chemistries to minimize systemic immune impact.
- Immune surveillance safeguards: vaccination titer monitoring; infection surveillance; stop rules for febrile illnesses.

Biomarkers and success criteria
- Checkpoint engagement: ≥50% reduction in ADI with concordant fall in MR1 tetramer+ activation markers.
- Reversal of commitment: shift of MAIT transcriptome from inflammatory to quiescent; restoration of glyoxalase activity; reduction in stromal fibrogenic signatures.
- Clinical signals: improved insulin sensitivity, reduced liver fat and stiffness, stabilized or improved beta-cell function.

Milestones and decision gates (Years 1–4)
- Year 1: Establish ADI*, validate ligandomics assay, show separation of resolvers vs progressors; Go if AUROC ≥0.8.
- Year 2: Demonstrate hysteresis and reversibility ex vivo; nominate two MR1 antagonists and one microbial product.
- Year 3: Show in vivo interception and durability with pulse therapy in humanized models; finalize CMC for lead assets.
- Year 4: Launch Phase 1b/2a interception study with companion diagnostic.

Key risks and mitigations
- Risk: MR1-independent drivers dominate in some patients. Mitigation: stratify by ADI and MAIT signature; combination with dicarbonyl control.
- Risk: Incomplete tissue penetration. Mitigation: gut-first approach plus liver-targeted chemistries; consider local delivery (enteric, portal).
- Risk: Infection susceptibility. Mitigation: time-limited dosing, exclusion criteria, rapid reversal agents (ligand washout, decoy MR1).

Outcome
If validated, the MR1 ligand occupancy state becomes a druggable, tissue-agnostic metabolic checkpoint. Enforcing antagonist-dominant MR1 binding during windows of metabolic stress intercepts progression to irreversible disease by preventing MAIT-driven chronic inflammation and fibrotic remodeling.

text:
Title
The Homocysteinylation Threshold as a Metabolic Checkpoint: Intercepting Homocysteine Thiolactone to Unlock Reversible Disease States

Central hypothesis
A binary, threshold-driven accumulation of irreversible N-homocysteinyl-lysine adducts on a small set of metabolic hub proteins converts reversible metabolic stress into a self-sustaining pathological state across tissues. This “homocysteinylation checkpoint” is crossed when the precursor homocysteine thiolactone (HTL) exceeds local detox capacity, driving covalent protein locking, proteostatic overload, and innate/adaptive immune activation. Preemptive enzymatic destruction of HTL reverts the system to a healthy attractor before fibrosis, beta-cell failure, or cardiovascular remodeling.

Atomic strategy
Break the lock by eliminating the key: create a high-efficiency, systemically available thiolactonase to destroy HTL before it N-homocysteinylates proteins, thereby reversing the checkpoint without broad suppression of upstream metabolism.

Why this is a checkpoint
- Switch-like trigger: HTL production rises nonlinearly with translational stress and methionine flux; once detox capacity is saturated, N-homocysteinylation of specific lysines climbs steeply (cooperative adduct accumulation).
- Irreversibility: Nε-lysine homocysteinylation forms a stable amide; reversal requires protein turnover, locking networks despite removal of upstream stressors.
- Self-amplification: Adducted proteins in insulin signaling, mitochondrial respiration, lipoprotein trafficking, and ECM/homeostasis propagate dysfunction and expose neoepitopes that sustain inflammation.

Drug target
The reactive intermediate homocysteine thiolactone (HTL), not canonical signaling nodes. HTL is absent/low in health, rises with metabolic stress, circulates systemically, and is chemically unique (strained thio-lactone ring), enabling selective detection and degradation.

Therapeutic modality
- Lead: Engineered soluble humanized thiolactonase (sHTLase) with high kcat/KM for HTL, hepatocyte-secreted to plasma (AAV8/AAV-LK03 or LNP-mRNA liver-targeted expression). Scaffold: evolved paraoxonase/lactonase variants retuned for HTL specificity.
- Adjuncts: 
  - Allosteric activators of endogenous serum paraoxonase HTLase activity (small molecules).
  - Gut-deployed engineered microbe that lowers systemic homocysteine flux (methionine-sparing assimilation and B12-dependent remethylation), serving as an HTL precursor sink in high-protein diets.

Disease interception window
- Prediabetes/early T2D with insulin resistance but preserved beta-cell reserve.
- NAFLD/NASH without bridging fibrosis.
- Metabolic syndrome with subclinical vascular dysfunction (arterial stiffness, microvascular rarefaction).
- Post-gestational diabetes and postpartum cardiometabolic risk.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Establish the homocysteinylation threshold and its switch-like behavior across tissues.
- 1.1 Adductome mapping: Develop targeted LC–MS3 adductomics to quantify N-homocysteinyl-lysine (N-Hcy-Lys) site occupancy and HTL levels in plasma, EVs, liver, adipose, skeletal muscle, endothelium. Build a cross-tissue panel of “hub” proteins a priori (insulin receptor β, IRS1/2, PI3K p85, AKT1/2 K-sites; VDAC1, ATP5A; ApoB/ApoA1; collagen I/III; SERCA2; Rab GTPases).
- 1.2 Tipping-point kinetics: Titrate HTL in primary human hepatocytes, adipocytes, myotubes, and endothelial cells while tracking N-Hcy-Lys occupancy, insulin signaling gain (pAKT vs insulin), mitochondrial respiratory control ratios, and inflammatory readouts. Fit Hill coefficients and identify a critical occupancy fraction (fc) that coincides with functional collapse and hysteresis.
- 1.3 In vivo validation: Use mice with altered HTL balance:
  - PON1 loss/gain models to modulate endogenous HTL detox.
  - Liver-specific MetRS editing-domain hypomorphs to elevate intracellular HTL.
  - High-methionine/low-B vitamin diets ± oxidative stressors to elevate HTL.
  Map the fc at which multi-tissue metabolic inflexibility and glucose intolerance emerge.

Aim 2. Prove causality: show that selective HTL destruction reverts the checkpoint after it is crossed.
- 2.1 Enzyme engineering: Evolve sHTLase variants with >10^6 M−1 s−1 for HTL, >1000-fold selectivity versus physiologic lactones and acyl-CoAs; humanize and GPI-anchor or secrete via ApoE leader. Confirm no activity on peptide bonds or glutathione thioesters.
- 2.2 Rescue experiments: In cell and mouse models driven past fc, deliver sHTLase (LNP-mRNA or AAV) and measure:
  - Depletion of free HTL, halt of new N-Hcy-Lys formation, and net decline in adduct burden via accelerated proteostasis.
  - Restoration of insulin signaling gain, mitochondrial coupling, and vascular tone.
  - Loss of N-Hcy-Lys neoepitope IgG and reduction in tissue-resident macrophage activation.
- 2.3 Hysteresis reversal: Demonstrate that sustained HTL removal collapses the diseased attractor without imposing upstream dietary or hormonal changes; quantify time-to-reversal versus protein half-lives of adducted hubs.

Aim 3. Build a translational biomarker and stratification toolkit.
- 3.1 Blood markers: Quantify plasma HTL, N-Hcy-Lys in ApoB and EV cargo, and serum HTLase activity. Construct a composite “HcyLock score” predicting fc proximity.
- 3.2 Imaging/functional readouts: Hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp with tracers; liver MRI-PDFF and elastography; flow-mediated dilation and pulse wave velocity.
- 3.3 Patient selection: Identify individuals with high HcyLock score but pre-fibrotic livers or preserved C-peptide to maximize reversibility.

Aim 4. Safety, selectivity, and manufacturability.
- 4.1 Off-target chemistry: Screen sHTLase against >200 metabolites (lactones, acyl-CoAs, cyclic thioesters). Confirm no hydrolysis of coenzyme A thioesters or lipid mediators.
- 4.2 Immunogenicity: Human sequence backbone, deimmunized surfaces, transient mRNA dosing to assess anti-drug antibodies; monitor complement and cytokines.
- 4.3 Microbiome adjunct: Engineer a probiotic chassis with methionine/HTL assimilation modules under diet-inducible promoters; confinement via auxotrophy and kill-switches.

Mechanistic model
- Order parameter: φ = mean occupancy of N-Hcy-Lys across hub set S.
- Dynamics: dφ/dt = kform[HTL](1−φ) − kturn φ, with [HTL] governed by production (MetRS error, oxidative stress) and clearance (PON1/sHTLase/renal). A critical φc produces discontinuous loss of network controllability in insulin and mitochondrial modules; removing HTL decreases kform and returns φ below φc, restoring function after protein turnover.

Key deliverables and milestones
- Year 1: HTL/N-Hcy-Lys assays validated; fc and Hill slopes defined in cells; initial sHTLase with >10^5 M−1 s−1.
- Year 2: In vivo fc defined; proof-of-concept reversal with sHTLase in two tissues; HcyLock score trained.
- Year 3: IND-enabling package for LNP-mRNA sHTLase; phase 0/biomarker trial in high HcyLock score, pre-fibrotic NAFLD or insulin-resistant subjects.

Falsifiable predictions
- Crossing fc will show hysteresis: withdrawing HTL without degrading existing adducts will not fully restore function until proteostasis clears adducted hubs.
- sHTLase will reduce new N-Hcy-Lys formation within hours and restore signaling over protein half-life timescales (days–weeks), preceding fibrosis regression.
- Individuals with high HTL/low endogenous HTLase activity will respond most to sHTLase; those with low φ at baseline will show minimal benefit.

Risk assessment and alternatives
- If intracellular HTL dominates and secreted sHTLase is insufficient, deploy cell-penetrant sHTLase (CPP-fusion) or hepatocyte-targeted intracellular expression.
- If MetRS editing governs HTL more than clearance, screen for small-molecule enhancers of MetRS editing to complement sHTLase.
- If N-Hcy-Lys is not enriched on hubs, broaden S or pivot to parallel irreversible adduct classes (e.g., γ-ketoaldehyde isoketal-lysine) with analogous “key elimination” enzymes.

Translational positioning
This tissue-agnostic checkpoint targets a chemical singularity—HTL—that only becomes abundant as disease emerges. By destroying the key before it locks essential proteins, we intercept progression and reopen a path to physiologic reversal without chronic pathway blockade.

Title
META-LOCK: A synthetic non-enzymatic acylation burden checkpoint for intercepting metabolic disease

Hypothesis and research goal
A programmable, bistable checkpoint that monitors the intracellular burden of non-enzymatic protein acylation and carbonyl adducts (the “acylation burden”) can act as a switch that commits cells to either reversible repair or irreversible dysfunction. Installing a synthetic checkpoint that flips ON only when acylation burden crosses a calibrated threshold will halt or reverse progression to metabolic disease across tissues.

Atomic strategy
Exploit non-enzymatic acylation burden as a universal danger signal of metabolic overflow, and encode it into a synthetic Schmitt trigger that converts continuous metabolite-derived damage into a binary decision: trigger a coordinated “repair and unload” program when and only when the burden exceeds a preset threshold, and return to OFF once burden normalizes.

Rationale and novelty
- Checkpoint primitive: Non-enzymatic acylations (succinyl-, malonyl-, lactyl-lysine) and advanced glycation/lipoxidation end-products (AGE/ALE adducts such as CML/CEL/HNE-adducts) rise nonlinearly when carbon flux, redox stress, and CoA scarcity converge. This accumulation is upstream of, and orthogonal to, canonical sensors (AMPK, mTOR, PPARs).
- Threshold behavior: Damage accrues gradually, but proteome modification shows cooperative, system-level tipping once detox and buffering saturate—well-suited to a binary gate.
- Tissue-agnostic: Acylation burden emerges in liver, adipose, muscle, heart, kidney, and β-cells under nutrient excess, hypoxia, and inflammation.
- Druggability: The switch is encoded by gene therapy; its set-point and duty cycle are tuned by small-molecule dimerizers or competitive ligands; burden itself is modifiable by metabolite analogs or engineered microbes.

System architecture (the META-LOCK checkpoint)
1) Input module: Intracellular acylation-burden readers
- A tandem array of metabolite-modification binders expressed as stable intrabodies/nanobodies:
  a) Anti–succinyl-lysine and anti–malonyl-lysine binders (non-enzymatic TCA overflow signal).
  b) Anti–lactyl-lysine binder (glycolytic overflow/hypoxia signal).
  c) Anti–CML/CEL or HNE-lysine binder (carbonyl/lipoxidation stress).
- Readers are fused to oligomerization-prone scaffolds with defined valency to convert many low-affinity binding events into a cooperative cluster proportional to global burden.

2) Digitizer: Proximity-gated protease that implements a Schmitt trigger
- Split protease (e.g., TEV or 3C) halves are each fused to distinct reader scaffolds. High local avidity at elevated burden reconstitutes active protease.
- Hysteresis is built by:
  a) Protease liberating a transcriptional activator from a degron only after a defined integration time (via slow-accumulating protease substrate).
  b) A positive feedback loop where the output transiently stabilizes the active state, creating ON stability and filtering noise.
- A paired “OFF-restorer” substrate with slower kinetics ensures the system reverts only after burden falls below a lower threshold.

3) Output module: Coordinated “repair and unload” program (pathway-level, not single targets)
- Detoxify and repair
  a) Upregulate glyoxalase and aldo-keto reductases (clear carbonyls).
  b) Enhance thiol repair and glutathione/NADPH regeneration modules.
  c) Activate mitophagy/lipophagy/ER-phagy effectors to remove damaged organelles and lipid droplets.
- Reduce future acylation flux
  a) Temporarily repress cytosol-to-nucleus acetyl–carbon feeders (e.g., ACLY/ACSS2) and citrate export (SLC25A1) using CRISPRi with safety caps (dose-limited guides).
  b) Induce CoA replenishment (PANK pathway) and peroxisomal β-oxidation throttling to rebalance acyl-CoA pools.
- Restore metabolic flexibility
  a) Promote UPRmt/mitochondrial biogenesis factors to reset oxidative capacity.
- Outputs are delivered via compact transcriptional units controlled by the protease-gated activator; all effectors are drug-tunable (see below).

4) Therapeutic control and druggability
- Threshold tuning: An oral small molecule that transiently stabilizes split protease dimerization increases sensitivity; a competing intracellular peptide (cell-permeant) raises the threshold by occupying reader interfaces.
- Duty-cycle control: A clinically approved dimerizer (rapalog-like) gates the activator’s nuclear entry, allowing physician control over ON-duration.
- External brake: A kill-switch protease substrate responsive to a separate, clinician-dosed small molecule instantly disables the output.

5) Delivery formats
- Interception-grade, transient: LNP-mRNA for high-risk windows (e.g., during rapid weight gain, chemotherapy, pregnancy diabetes risk).
- Durable, adjustable: AAV with compact cassettes and systemic tropism variants; inclusion of a small-molecule gate ensures control across tissues.

Therapeutic window and indications
- Prediabetes and early T2D (before β-cell exhaustion).
- NAFLD/NASH stages F0–F2 (pre-fibrotic to early fibrotic).
- Early HFpEF/metabolic cardiomyopathy (before structural remodeling hardens).
- Diabetic kidney disease at microalbuminuria onset.
The checkpoint turns ON during high-burden episodes, executes repair/unload, and turns OFF once normalized—preventing commitment to irreversible remodeling.

Specific aims and experiments
Aim 1. Build and calibrate the acylation-burden readers
- Generate intrabodies/nanobodies specific for succinyl-, malonyl-, lactyl-lysine and CML/CEL/HNE adducts; quantify affinity and selectivity on modified peptide arrays and in live-cell proteomes.
- Engineer multivalent scaffolds (defined valency/spacing) and measure clustering versus global burden in cells challenged with nutrient excess, hypoxia, or carbonyl donors.
- Define the composite “burden index” and threshold that best predicts mitochondrial dysfunction, proteostatic stress, and loss of insulin signaling.

Go/no-go: Achieve a steplike reader clustering response (Hill coefficient >3) and predictive ROC AUC >0.8 for impending mitochondrial depolarization.

Aim 2. Implement the Schmitt trigger and validate binary behavior
- Construct reader-fused split protease and degron-shielded activator. Calibrate ON threshold and hysteresis via protease kinetics and feedback strength.
- Demonstrate digital ON/OFF outputs with time integration and noise rejection in fluctuating burden environments.
- Verify reversibility: ON at high burden; OFF once burden sustained below lower threshold.

Go/no-go: Hysteresis width ≥20% of threshold and false-ON rate <1% under physiological noise.

Aim 3. Program the repair/unload outputs and test causality
- Assemble output modules (detox, unload, flexibility) under a single protease-gated promoter; cap maximal repression of feeder pathways to avoid hypometabolism.
- In human hepatocyte, adipocyte, cardiomyocyte, β-cell, and renal proximal tubule models, test whether META-LOCK ON restores:
  a) Mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration flexibility, and NAD(P)H balance.
  b) Proteome acylation/carbonyl adduct levels.
  c) Insulin signaling and stress-response normalization.
- Benchmark against non-digital, constitutive activations to show superiority of thresholded, transient action.

Go/no-go: ≥50% restoration of mitochondrial and insulin signaling metrics with ≤10% reduction in basal ATP during OFF state.

Aim 4. Disease interception in vivo and cross-tissue generality
- Deliver META-LOCK via LNP-mRNA to diet-induced obese and db/db mice at prediabetic and early disease windows; via AAV for longer-term studies.
- Primary endpoints: prevention/reversal of early fibrosis (liver/kidney/heart), improved glucose tolerance/insulin sensitivity, reduced AGE/acylation burden, preserved β-cell mass and diastolic function.
- Test in cardiac pressure-overload with metabolic stress and in early CKD models to show tissue-agnostic benefit.

Success criteria: Significant interception of progression versus controls and superiority to matched non-digital interventions.

Aim 5. Safety, control, and translational engineering
- Off-target binding profiling of intrabodies; immunogenicity minimization (humanized scaffolds).
- Off-switch and threshold-tuner pharmacology; PK/PD modeling of ON-duty cycles compatible with outpatient dosing.
- Companion diagnostic: plasma AGE/acyl-lysine adduct panels and wearable-derived metabolic stress episodes to schedule transient dosing.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Reader specificity: Use dual-input coincidence (e.g., succinyl-lysine AND CML) to reduce false positives from isolated perturbations.
- Overcorrection risk: Hard caps on CRISPRi guide potency; ON-window limits via drug-gated nuclear localization.
- Heterogeneous tissue thresholds: Encode tissue-context minimal promoters and modular readers to tune local set-points.

Milestones to de-risk translation
- Year 1: Achieve digital thresholding with hysteresis in vitro; define therapeutic burden index.
- Year 2: Demonstrate interception in at least two tissues in mice with drug-tunable control.
- Year 3: Large-animal delivery feasibility, safety, and companion diagnostic validation.

Therapeutic product concept
A programmable gene therapy delivering META-LOCK plus an oral threshold-tuner. Positioned for disease interception: a safety switch that senses when metabolic damage is about to become irreversible and transiently executes a coordinated, system-level repair—then stands down.

Title
The Lactate–Lactylation Latch (LLL): a bistable metabolic checkpoint and its interception window

Core hypothesis and goal
A positive-feedback loop between intracellular lactate accumulation and histone lysine lactylation (Kla) forms a bistable “latch” that commits diverse cell types to pathological metabolic remodeling (insulin resistance, fibrogenesis, β-cell failure, cardiac remodeling). The research goal is to discover, instrument, and therapeutically modulate this latch using synthetic, thresholded intracellular sensors that define the commitment boundary in time and state space, enabling interception by brief, low-intensity metabolic nudges before irreversible damage.

Atomic strategy
Define the checkpoint not as a single protein target but as a switch-like state transition governed by two coupled variables—nuclear lactate concentration and chromatin Kla occupancy—that self-reinforce to create hysteresis. Build orthogonal, digital reporters for each variable and a genetic AND-gate “commitment recorder” to pinpoint the separatrix (point-of-no-return). Use this timing to deliver short, druggable interventions that push cells back across the boundary before the latch locks.

Mechanistic model (to be tested)
- Driver: metabolic stressors (overnutrition, hypoxia, cytokines, lipotoxicity, microbiome metabolites) elevate glycolytic flux, cytosolic NADH, and lactate; nuclear lactate rises via monocarboxylate transporters/shuttles.
- Writer/eraser balance: elevated lactate (or lactyl–CoA) increases histone Kla on metabolic/fibrogenic loci; reduced delactylation capacity under oxidative/redox stress sustains Kla.
- Positive feedback: Kla enhances transcription of glycolysis, lactate production/efflux programs and pro-fibrotic/inflammatory genes, further increasing lactate and Kla.
- Checkpoint property: once Kla and nuclear lactate exceed a critical threshold for a critical dwell time, the system enters a stable, pathological attractor with hysteresis; subthreshold, the state remains reversible.

Therapeutic premise
Transiently reducing nuclear lactate and/or accelerating delactylation before the latch “locks” restores a healthy attractor. Candidate nudges include brief dosing of metabolic flux modulators, delactylation enhancers, lactate transport modulators, and physicochemical buffers; these are low-burden, tissue-agnostic, and druggable.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Build intracellular, thresholded sensors and a digital commitment recorder
- Nuclear lactate sensor: retargeted genetically encoded fluorescent sensor to the nucleus with tunable dynamic range; ratiometric readout.
- Chromatin Kla sensor: evolve a high-specificity single-domain binder for Kla (anti-Kla sdAb) and fuse to split-luciferase or split-TEV; complement only in chromatin context using histone-tail tethers to yield Kla-dependent light or protease activity.
- Digital AND-gate recorder: integrate nuclear lactate-high AND Kla-high into a recombinase-based memory circuit (Cre/lox or Bxb1) with time integration (ultrasensitive promoter + protease timer). Output is an irreversible color/barcode switch marking cells that have crossed the separatrix.
- Calibration: engineer synthetic band-pass thresholds (Hill coefficient tuning, degron-controlled timers) so each module behaves digitally with defined setpoints. Validate orthogonality and minimal metabolic load.

Aim 2. Map the separatrix across tissues and contexts
- Systems to profile: human iPSC-derived hepatocytes, adipocytes, β-cells, cardiac myocytes, and macrophages; primary mouse cells; multi-tissue organoid co-cultures.
- Stress landscapes: factorial combinations of glucose/FA oversupply, hypoxia oscillations, cytokines (TNFα/IL-1β), endotoxin/bile acids/TMAO/SCFAs, and circadian phase.
- Readouts: single-cell commitment maps (recorder on/off), live nuclear lactate trajectories, Kla sensor kinetics, bulk/SC multi-omics (RNA-seq, ATAC, ChIP for Kla, acyl-proteomics), lactate fluxomics (13C tracing).
- Modeling: fit a minimal two-variable bistable model with dwell-time dependence; estimate thresholds and hysteresis width per tissue; identify universal vs tissue-specific parameters.

Aim 3. Identify druggable nodes that shift thresholds without targeting canonical axes
- Genetic perturbations (CRISPRi/a) focused on:
  - Lactate handling: LDH isoform balance, monocarboxylate transporters (e.g., SLC16A family), nuclear-cytosolic redox shuttles (malate–aspartate, glycerol-3P).
  - Kla machinery discovery: unbiased chemoproteomics to identify lactylation writers (acyltransferase candidates) and erasers (delactylases); targeted mutagenesis of candidate acyl–CoA synthetases that could generate lactyl–CoA.
  - Nuclear buffering: carbonic anhydrases, lactate–proton cotransport coupling, histone acyl-reader domains that propagate Kla-driven transcription.
- Small-molecule/metabolite library screen using the AND-gate recorder as primary readout to find agents that: (i) raise the forward threshold (harder to commit), (ii) reduce dwell-time requirement, or (iii) widen the reversal window. Secondary assays confirm effects on nuclear lactate and Kla kinetics, not global cytotoxic suppression.

Aim 4. Define interception by brief “metabolic nudges”
- Candidate nudges (all administered as short pulses, minutes–hours): dichloroacetate-class PDH activators; mild MCT modulation to rebalance nuclear vs cytosolic lactate; NAD+ precursors to shift LDH equilibrium; bicarbonate/THAM micro-pulses to uncouple lactate–proton co-accumulation; tailored amino acid pulses (e.g., alanine/glycine) to drain pyruvate-lactate pools via transamination; oxygenation cycles; delactylase activators or writer inhibitors discovered in Aim 3.
- Optimization: response-surface designs align pulse amplitude, duration, and circadian phase with the precommitment interval defined by sensors; evaluate rebound risk and hysteresis crossing probability at single-cell resolution.
- Outcomes: proportion of “committed” cells reverted to the safe basin; durability of reversion; minimal dose/time achieving reversion with preserved cell function.

Aim 5. In vivo validation and translatability
- Reporter animals: knock-in LLL recorder mice (liver, adipose, heart, islets, macrophages) plus a blood-accessible secreted recorder for longitudinal sampling.
- Disease interception studies: diet-induced metabolic syndrome/NASH, pressure-overload cardiomyopathy, and β-cell stress models. Trigger stress, monitor latent commitment (recorder), and deliver optimized nudges before macroscopic disease endpoints.
- Endpoints: prevention of fibrosis and ECM remodeling; preservation of β-cell insulin secretory capacity; maintained cardiac compliance; systemic insulin sensitivity; safety/tolerability of nudges.

Therapeutic development paths
- Small molecules: (i) selective modulators of nuclear lactate handling (novel MCT allosteric modulators with nuclear bias), (ii) lactylation writer inhibitors identified by chemoproteomics, (iii) delactylase activators (hit-to-lead from Aim 3).
- Biologics: cell-penetrant binders that block Kla reader domains at pro-fibrotic loci; targeted protein degraders of lactylation writers.
- Engineered microbes: gut strains that buffer luminal lactate and deliver pH/anion equivalents or short-chain fatty acid programs that reduce systemic lactate/Kla susceptibility without malabsorption.
- Digital companion: sensor-driven dosing schedules that align nudges with individual-specific precommitment windows.

Milestones and success criteria
- Year 1: Validated nuclear lactate and Kla sensors; AND-gate recorder with ≤5% false positives; initial separatrix maps in two cell types.
- Year 2: Universal latch parameters across five tissues; evidence of hysteresis; ≥3 druggable nodes that shift thresholds without impairing viability.
- Year 3: Optimized nudge protocols that revert ≥60% of recorder-positive cells to recorder-off with durable function; in vivo early commitment detection.
- Year 4: Disease interception in two models with fibrosis/β-cell failure prevention using brief, well-tolerated nudges; candidate therapeutics with PK/PD supporting first-in-class LLL modulators.

Risk management and pivots
- If histone Kla lacks bistability, expand to a generalized “acylation latch” panel (succinylation, malonylation, glutarylation) using the same sensor/recorder framework and maintain lactate as one axis.
- If nuclear lactate is not the limiting axis, shift to redox-coupled proxies (nuclear NADH/NAD+ sensors) while retaining Kla sensing to preserve the latch architecture.
- If a single writer enzyme is not identifiable, pursue reader-domain antagonism or delactylase activation as primary drug strategies.

Impact
This program reframes the “metabolic checkpoint” as an emergent, druggable state transition—the Lactate–Lactylation Latch—measured and controlled in real time. By discovering and exploiting the narrow precommitment window with simple, time-precise nudges, it enables tissue-agnostic interception of metabolic disease progression before fibrosis, β-cell exhaustion, or cardiac remodeling become irreversible.

Title
MITO-SEAL: A mitochondrial DNA–containment checkpoint that preserves metabolic reversibility by preventing VDAC oligomerization and cGAS–STING commitment

Unified hypothesis–question
Does a binary mitochondrial checkpoint—the oligomerization state of the outer-membrane channel VDAC that governs mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) escape and cGAS–STING activation—determine whether severe metabolic stress remains reversible, and can pharmacologic stabilization of non-oligomeric VDAC keep tissues in a recoverable state across organs?

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Keep mtDNA inside mitochondria during metabolic stress by stabilizing VDAC in a non-oligomeric state. Preventing the mtDNA→cGAS–STING danger signal averts the switch into chronic inflammatory remodeling and fibrosis, maintaining reversibility even under profound metabolic perturbation.

Why this is a checkpoint and not a rheostat
- Trigger: VDAC oligomerization forms high-conductance pores that permit mtDNA extrusion. Below a threshold of mitochondrial lipid peroxidation/Ca2+/ROS, VDAC remains monomeric/low-order—no mtDNA escape.
- Commitment: Cytosolic mtDNA engages cGAS–STING, initiating a self-sustaining interferon/inflammasome program that locks tissues into fibrotic, insulin-resistant states.
- Binary behavior: The mtDNA leakage–STING pathway shows thresholded, switch-like activation; once engaged, it persists despite restoration of proximal metabolic parameters.
- Reversibility principle: Protected states (hibernation, extreme fasting, early post–bariatric surgery) are predicted to preserve low VDAC oligomerization despite stress, preventing commitment.

Therapeutic concept
Develop small molecules or cell-permeant, mitochondria-targeted macrocycles that bind VDAC at oligomerization interfaces (“VD-LOCK”) to prevent stress-induced oligomerization without impairing basal metabolite flux. Complement with cardiolipin-stabilizing lipid edits to raise the oligomerization threshold. Goal: disease interception across liver, adipose, muscle, islet, and heart.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Establish MITO-SEAL as the reversibility guardian in naturally protected states.
- Models: Hibernating ground squirrels; 72-hour fasting in mice; humans pre- and 1–4 weeks post–bariatric surgery; very–low-calorie diet responders.
- Readouts (multi-tissue: liver, adipose, muscle, islet proxies, PBMCs):
  - VDAC oligomerization by blue-native PAGE and in situ proximity ligation.
  - Cytosolic/serum mtDNA (qPCR for ND1/ND6) and DNase-resistant cf-mtDNA.
  - cGAS–STING activation (cGAMP, p-TBK1, ISG transcript score).
  - Fibrosis/ECM early remodeling signatures and macrophage state.
- Prediction: Protected states display low VDAC oligomerization and suppressed cGAS–STING under equal or greater metabolic stress versus unprotected controls.

Aim 2. Quantify the biophysical threshold that gates commitment.
- Build stress–response curves across gradients of lipid peroxidation, Ca2+, fatty-acyl CoAs, and ROS in primary hepatocytes, adipocytes, myotubes, and human islet clusters.
- Define the Hill coefficient and inflection point linking mitochondrial cardiolipin oxidation to VDAC oligomerization and mtDNA release.
- Map modifiers that shift the threshold: membrane cardiolipin unsaturation pattern, mtCa2+ buffering, mitochondrial GSH/GSSG, and specific VDAC cysteine PTMs (persulfidation, nitrosylation).
- Criterion for checkpoint behavior: cooperative transition with a discrete inflection; presence of hysteresis after transient activation.

Aim 3. Develop and validate VD-LOCK modulators that preserve reversibility in disease-prone settings.
- Chemistry: Optimize oligomerization-interface binders (starting from known chemotypes as inspiration but re-engineered for mitochondrial delivery and selectivity), and de novo macrocyclic/peptidomimetic binders with triphenylphosphonium or alternative mito-targeting motifs.
- Secondary modality: mitochondria-targeted cardiolipin stabilizers that prevent peroxidation and raise the oligomerization threshold; and selective STING antagonists as mechanistic comparators, not primary targets.
- In vivo interception tests:
  - NASH/fibrosis models (CDAA or GAN diet), diet-induced obesity with β-cell stress, and pressure-overload cardiometabolic remodeling.
  - Dosing initiated at pre-fibrotic, high–cf-mtDNA stage; endpoints include fibrosis blockade, β-cell function preservation, whole-body insulin sensitivity, and durability after drug washout.
- Mechanistic necessity/sufficiency: Genetic tethering of VDAC monomers or expression of oligomerization-deficient mutants; CRISPRa/CRISPRi of cGAS/STING to position checkpoint.

Aim 4. Translation: biomarker panel, patient selection, and early clinical PoC.
- Biomarker suite:
  - Plasma DNase-resistant cf-mtDNA and cGAMP.
  - Phospho-TBK1 ISG composite score in PBMCs.
  - VDAC oligomerization surrogate in platelets/PBMCs (proximity ligation index).
  - Cardiolipin oxidation adducts and 4-HNE–protein adducts.
- Stratification: enroll patients with high cf-mtDNA/ISG score but minimal fibrosis by MRI-PDFF/MRE or low ELF score.
- Window-of-opportunity trials (8–12 weeks) in NAFLD with insulin resistance: primary pharmacodynamic readouts are reductions in cf-mtDNA and ISG score; secondary metabolic endpoints include HOMA-IR, OGTT AUC, MRI-PDFF, and noninvasive fibrosis markers.

Mechanistic falsification tests (corrigibility)
- If cGAS–STING remains low despite disease progression, search for alternative mtDNA sensors or parallel DAMP pathways; reframe checkpoint to “mtDNA containment” independent of STING.
- If VD-LOCK improves inflammation but not metabolic endpoints, evaluate off-target constraints and consider combination with lipid-flux normalization (without invoking AMPK/mTOR/PPARs).

Safety and selectivity
- Preserve basal VDAC transport: screen against ATP/ADP exchange kinetics and metabolite flux; require normal respiration and calcium handling at rest.
- Stress-selective action: efficacy emerges only under peroxidative/Ca2+ load; no mitochondrial depolarization or apoptosis in quiescent cells.
- Off-tissue monitoring: hematologic ISG normalization without immunosuppression; no interference with antiviral responses in vaccine-challenge assays.

Operational plan and milestones
- Year 1: Validate checkpoint signature in protected states; define thresholds and hysteresis; nominate chemical series and mitochondrial delivery strategy.
- Year 2: Demonstrate interception in two disease models with biomarker reversal preceding histology; establish safety margins; finalize clinical biomarkers.
- Year 3: IND-enabling studies for lead VD-LOCK; initiate first-in-human PD study in biomarker-selected NAFLD.

Go/no-go criteria
- Go: Demonstrate cooperative VDAC oligomerization threshold (Hill coefficient ≥2) that coincides with mtDNA release and ISG engagement in ≥3 tissues; show that VD-LOCK shifts this threshold rightward and prevents commitment with ≥30% reduction in fibrosis score and preserved β-cell function versus control.
- No-go: Linear, non-cooperative responses; inability to separate basal flux from oligomer blockade; lack of translational biomarker movement in protected states or treatment.

Expected impact
Positioning VDAC oligomerization as a druggable mitochondrial DNA–containment checkpoint reframes metabolic disease interception: by sealing mitochondria under stress, we prevent inflammatory commitment and keep systemic metabolism in a recoverable, therapy-responsive regime across organs.

text:
Project title
The Z-RNA/ZBP1 distress-gate: a binary metabolic checkpoint that commits tissues to inflammatory cell death and fibrotic remodeling, and a therapeutic “Z‑Lock” to intercept it

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Metabolic stress forces endogenous RNAs into the left-handed Z-RNA conformation within cells and extracellular vesicles. Once Z-RNA abundance crosses a threshold, it engages the Zα-domains of ZBP1 to trigger PANoptosis and feed-forward inflammatory signaling. This Z-RNA→ZBP1 engagement is a discrete, druggable gate that converts reversible metabolic dysfunction into irreversible tissue remodeling. Therapeutically blocking Z-RNA sensing—rather than downstream inflammation—prevents organs from synchronizing distress responses.

Central hypothesis and research goal
Hypothesis and goal are the same: Z-RNA accumulation and inter-organ transfer act as a binary “point-of-no-return” signal in metabolic disease, gated by ZBP1 binding. We will discover, validate, and pharmacologically block this checkpoint to intercept progression before fibrosis, β-cell exhaustion, and cardiovascular remodeling.

Why this is novel and fits constraints
- Mechanistic class: topology-specific nucleic acid danger signal (Z-RNA) and its sensor ZBP1—not canonical metabolic nodes (AMPK, mTOR, etc.).
- Checkpoint character: a threshold, switch-like engagement of Zα domains that commits cells to PANoptosis and chronic inflammation.
- Tissue-agnostic: hepatocytes, adipocytes, myocytes, endothelium, and tissue macrophages all express the machinery; Z-RNA is trafficked systemically via EVs.
- Druggable: interface-blocking macrocycles/small molecules, decoy mini-proteins (Zα mimetics), and nucleic-acid topology stabilizers/destabilizers.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Define Z-RNA as an irreversible-stress signal across metabolic tissues and the microbiome–host axis.
- 1.1 Build conformation-specific capture assays: develop Z-RNA–selective binders (engineered Zα domains and Z-RNA antibodies) for pulldown from cells, plasma, and EVs under lipotoxic, glucotoxic, and hypoxic stress.
- 1.2 Identify sequence/structure motifs that flip to Z under stress: long-read and structure-aware RNA-seq of captured material to map endogenous repeats (e.g., SINE/LINE), tRNA-derived fragments, and microbiome-derived RNAs.
- 1.3 Quantify threshold behavior: titrate metabolic stressors in primary hepatocyte, adipocyte, myotube, and islet models; derive ultrasensitivity curves (Hill coefficients) for Z-RNA emergence and EV export.

Decision point: If no ultrasensitivity (Hill n<2) is observed, ideation failed; pivot to alternative topology-specific sensors (e.g., ADAR1 editing collapse as checkpoint).

Aim 2. Demonstrate that Z-RNA→ZBP1 binding is the gate that commits tissues to PANoptosis and fibrotic programming.
- 2.1 Engineer ZBP1 sensor lines: split-luciferase or fluorescence resonance energy transfer reporters that quantify Zα-domain occupancy; CRISPR point mutants disrupting Zα binding define specificity.
- 2.2 Reconstitute inter-organ signaling: EVs from stressed donor cells (liver, adipose, muscle, gut epithelium) and from gnotobiotic microbiomes challenge recipient macrophages, endothelium, β-cells, and stellate cells; measure switch-like activation of PANoptosis (caspase/gasdermin, RIPK3/MLKL) and profibrotic signatures.
- 2.3 In vivo thresholding: diet-induced metabolic stress models instrumented with longitudinal plasma Z-RNA-EV index and tissue ZBP1 occupancy; test hysteresis and commitment (irreversibility after transient blockade release).

Go/no-go: If ZBP1 loss or Zα disruption abrogates switch-like cell death and remodeling in ≥3 tissues, proceed to Aim 3.

Aim 3. Create “Z‑Lock” therapeutics that intercept Z-RNA sensing before organ-to-organ coordination occurs.
- 3.1 Decoy mini-proteins: stabilize, dimerize, and humanize Zα domains with Fc or albumin-binding scaffolds to sequester Z-RNA (extracellular and endosomal) and blunt uptake-driven signaling.
- 3.2 Interface antagonists: screen macrocyclic peptides and fragment libraries for binders to the ZBP1 Zα pocket; optimize for cell penetration and selectivity with structure-guided design and biophysical displacement assays.
- 3.3 Topology modulators: identify small molecules that disfavour B→Z transition of relevant RNAs without global transcriptional toxicity.
- 3.4 Interception window: dose Z‑Lock agents at pre-fibrotic stages (e.g., 6–10 weeks in diet models) and in islet stress priming; read out prevention of PANoptosis, stellate activation, and β-cell functional decline.

Aim 4. Translation package: biomarkers, patient stratification, and first-in-human path.
- 4.1 Plasma Z-RNA-EV index: Zα-capture ELISA coupled to structure-aware qPCR/short-read panels for minimal Z-RNA motifs; develop clinical-grade assay.
- 4.2 Companion pharmacodynamic markers: ZBP1 occupancy reporter in peripheral monocytes; circulating pMLKL fragments; EV cargo profiles; A-to-I editing deficit score as a susceptibility marker.
- 4.3 Human cohorts: cross-sectional and longitudinal sampling in prediabetes, NAFLD without fibrosis, early NASH, obesity with/without insulin resistance to define the interception window.

Mechanistic model to be tested
- Input: chronic nutrient excess, lipotoxic species, and microbiome shifts elevate polyamines/ionic strength and dsRNA burden (e.g., retroelements, tRNA fragments).
- Switch: B→Z transition generates Z-RNA beyond a threshold; ZBP1 Zα-domain engagement becomes cooperative.
- Commitment: ZBP1 triggers PANoptosis and amplifies sterile inflammation; EVs carrying Z-RNA broadcast the state to other organs, synchronizing failure programs (insulin resistance, stellate activation, endothelial dysfunction).
- Interception: blocking Z-RNA sensing restores reversibility by preventing the multi-organ “all-call.”

Therapeutic modalities and delivery
- Z‑Lock decoy mini-protein: Fc-fused Zα tandem with endosomal retention tag for EV-rich compartments; long half-life for systemic coverage.
- Macrocyclic peptide/small-molecule Zα antagonists: orally available candidates prioritized; liver-targeted GalNAc conjugates as backup for hepatic interception.
- Microbiome lever (adjunct): engineered probiotic degrading polyamines to raise the Z-RNA formation threshold; used only if systemic Z‑Lock is insufficient.

Disease interception window
- Pre-fibrotic NAFLD/NASH; insulin-resistant obesity before β-cell decompensation; early diabetic cardiomyopathy/remodeling. Dosing guided by rising plasma Z-RNA-EV index and declining A-to-I editing score.

Validation criteria
- Binary behavior: demonstration of steep, cooperative activation of ZBP1 and PANoptosis across tissues, with hysteresis consistent with a checkpoint.
- Causality: loss of ZBP1 Zα binding abolishes switch; adding back Z-RNA rescues it.
- Interception efficacy: Z‑Lock normalizes metabolic phenotypes and prevents fibrosis/β-cell failure without broad immunosuppression.
- Translatability: Z-RNA-EV index predicts progression and responds dynamically to Z‑Lock in animal models and ex vivo human tissues.

Risk and mitigation
- If Z-RNA is not the dominant ligand in some tissues, expand to additional topology-specific ligands (Z-DNA, editing-deficient dsRNA) while retaining Z‑Lock as first-line.
- Off-target antiviral effects: maintain innate immune tone by selective partial occupancy of Zα domains; monitor vaccine responses and interferon signatures.

Projected outcomes and impact
- A first-in-class metabolic checkpoint defined by nucleic acid topology, not a canonical pathway.
- A conformation-specific biomarker for the “point-of-no-return.”
- A therapeutic class (Z‑Lock) that prevents multi-organ synchronization of metabolic failure and enables true disease interception.
