Title
GlycoPASS: Reverse-gating circulating tumor cells through organ-mimetic endothelial glycocalyces to predict pan-cancer organotropism from blood

Central hypothesis–question (merged)
If organ-specific endothelial glycocalyces act as selective “gates” for extravasation, then a CTC’s high-dimensional glycan-binding/adhesion fingerprint to these gates uniquely encodes its organ destination. Can we capture and read this fingerprint from a single blood draw to prospectively predict the organ(s) of metastasis across cancers?

Atomic strategy
Exploit differential, shear-dependent adhesion of live CTCs to reconstructed, organ-specific endothelial glycocalyx surfaces as both the sorting and labeling mechanism; the same interaction that enables organ entry becomes the assay readout.

Specific aims
1) Build Organ-Glycocalyx Gates (OGGs): parallel microfluidic channels each presenting a defined, organ-mimetic glycocalyx.
2) Function-first sorting of CTCs: partition patient CTCs by real-time adhesion under physiological shear to each OGG and quantify an individual “adhesiotype vector.”
3) Decode the glycan passport: perform single-cell glycomics/glycoproteomics and multiplex lectin-barcoded profiling on OGG-sorted CTCs to identify minimal motif sets that predict organ capture.
4) Train and validate a predictive GlycoPASS Index that maps blood-derived glycan signals to an organ-specific metastasis probability distribution, with mechanistic verification via targeted glyco-gene perturbations.

Innovation
- Destination-first, function-first: predicts where, not whether, using the same glycocalyx interactions that mediate endothelial arrest and extravasation.
- Organ-mimetic glycocalyx as the assay substrate: converts vascular biology into a physical sorter and labeler of “organ-committed” CTCs.
- Pan-cancer by design: focuses on conserved glycan motifs and host gates rather than tissue-of-origin oncogenes.

Organ-Glycocalyx Gate (OGG) construction
- Substrates: inert microchannels with controlled shear (0.5–4 dyn/cm²).
- Glycocalyx printing: chemoenzymatically defined HS/CS fine structures, mucin-mimetic polymers with tunable sialylation/fucosylation densities, and immobilized host lectins/adhesion receptors enriched in target organs (e.g., selectins, galectins, Siglecs, ICAM/VCAM variants) at physiological surface densities.
- Organ panels (initial): lung, liver, bone marrow, brain, adrenal, lymph node. Each OGG optimized to recapitulate known endothelial glycan–lectin landscapes and sulfation patterns, plus organ-specific flow profiles.
- Quality control: quartz crystal microbalance and fluorescent lectin panels to verify motif density/availability; primary human microvascular endothelial vesicle–derived glycocalyx fractions for benchmarking.

CTC capture and adhesiotyping
- Input: 10–20 mL peripheral blood; negative depletion of leukocytes/erythrocytes; platelet disaggregation control.
- Run-through: mix introduced across parallel OGGs; real-time imaging to quantify rolling, tethering, firm adhesion, and transmigration surrogates; detach non-adherent cells for reuse.
- Output: per-patient adhesiotype vector = fraction and kinetics of CTC engagement across OGGs; adherent cells recovered from each OGG become organ-labeled CTC cohorts.

Glycan passport decoding
- Single-cell level:
  - scLectin-Seq with DNA-barcoded lectins (30–60 probes) to quantify motif abundance.
  - Targeted sc-glycoproteomics (enriched N-/O-glycopeptides via HILIC and stepped-HCD/EThcD).
  - Released glycan profiling (permethylated N-/O-glycans by LC-MS/MS) from pooled OGG bins when input is limiting.
- Integrative features:
  - Motifs (e.g., sLeX/sLeA variants; α2,3 vs α2,6 sialylation; core-1/2 O-glycans; HS N-/O-sulfation patterns; fucosylation branch points).
  - Carrier proteins (mucins, integrins, CD44 variants) where detectable.
  - Adhesion kinetics parameters from OGG (rolling velocity, arrest half-life) as functional priors.

Model building: GlycoPASS Index
- Training labels: OGG bin identity (functional label) plus longitudinal clinical outcomes (first-met site within 12–24 months).
- Architecture: multi-task probabilistic model integrating scLectin-Seq and glycoproteomic features with OGG kinetics to output P(metastasis to organ | blood draw).
- Minimal panel derivation: L1-regularization and Shapley-based selection to compress to a 10–20 reagent clinical lectin panel (and 3–5 confirmatory glycoprotein targets) deployable on a benchtop flow cytometry or sequencing readout.

Validation strategy
- Technical: spike-in organ-tropic reference cell lines to confirm OGG specificity and shear dependence; cross-lab reproducibility of glycocalyx printing.
- Biological: CRISPRi/a perturbation of key glyco-genes (e.g., FUT3/6, ST3GALs, GCNTs, NDSTs, HS2ST) in organ-tropic models; test shifts in OGG adhesion and in vivo organotropism (mouse xenografts).
- Clinical:
  - Discovery cohort (n≈200): breast, lung, colorectal, melanoma, prostate, kidney; baseline and on-therapy blood draws; train GlycoPASS.
  - Prospective test (n≈150): blinded prediction of first-met organ; primary endpoints: AUROC per organ, calibration, and decision utility for surveillance triage.
  - Orthogonal confirmation: cfDNA methylation and imaging for site-of-origin adjudication when tissue is unavailable.

Pan-cancer applicability
- Focus on conserved host–glycan gate interactions rather than tumor lineage markers.
- Stratified analyses ensure model holds across diverse oncogenic drivers; domain adaptation layers adjust for therapy-induced glycome shifts.

Deliverables
- OGG microfluidic sorter and SOPs for glycocalyx fabrication.
- A minimal, CLIA-ready GlycoPASS panel (lectin-barcoded assay) and software to output organ-specific risk vectors.
- Reference atlas: organ-specific CTC glycan passports across cancers.

Risk and mitigation
- Low CTC yield: enrich repeat draws; incorporate tumor-derived extracellular vesicles into adhesiotyping as a backup signal.
- Platelet cloaking: standardized anti-platelet unmasking protocol; model covariates for platelet signatures.
- Glycome plasticity under therapy: longitudinal sampling and time-aware modeling.

Milestones
- Month 0–12: OGG build/validation; spike-in benchmarks; initial patient feasibility.
- Month 12–24: Discovery cohort complete; GlycoPASS v1; minimal panel locked.
- Month 24–36: Prospective validation; mechanistic perturbation confirmation; preclinical utility study for organ-specific surveillance.

Success criteria
- Technical: >80% concordance of adhesiotype between replicate runs; stable OGG presentation over 30 days.
- Predictive: AUROC ≥0.80 for ≥3 major organs (lung, liver, bone) and calibrated probabilities (Brier score ≤0.15).
- Translational: Minimal panel turnaround ≤48 h; compatibility with 10 mL blood.

Title
Heparanase-labile stealth glycocalyx on therapeutic cells to convert endothelial injury remodeling into site-specific homing and transendothelial migration

Central premise
Endothelial injury universally upregulates heparanase and remodels the glycocalyx, shortening heparan sulfate (HS) chains, altering sulfation domains, and exposing core proteins while changing hyaluronan (HA) and chondroitin sulfate (CS) ratios. These compositional shifts create a biochemical signature absent from healthy vessels. If therapeutic cells carry an anti-adhesive, HS-like “stealth” layer that is trimmed only by endothelial heparanase at injury sites, their native adhesion receptors (e.g., VLA-4, LFA-1, CD44) become unmasked only where the glycocalyx is pathologically remodeled, yielding selective homing and extravasation without perturbing systemic vascular homeostasis.

Atomic strategy
Program the cell surface with a removable HS-mimetic brush whose sole trigger for de-shielding is endothelial heparanase activity enriched at injury sites. Outside injury zones the brush sterically and electrostatically suppresses nonspecific interactions; at the injury interface, enzymatic cleavage shortens/solubilizes the brush, restoring receptor accessibility and enabling physiologic arrest, crawling, and transendothelial migration.

Specific aims
1) Build and tune a heparanase-labile HS brush on cell membranes.
2) Demonstrate spatially confined unmasking and extravasation in endothelial microvascular models with graded glycocalyx injury.
3) Validate selective in vivo homing/extravasation and safety in multi-injury contexts, and adapt to endogenous stem cells via in-blood membrane transfer.

Approach

Aim 1: Construct and characterize the stealth HS brush
- Chemistry/format:
  - Non-genetic format for off-the-shelf cells: cholesterol- or DSPE-anchored HS oligomers (dp ~12–30) linked via PEG (2–5 kDa) for membrane insertion; sulfation patterns selected to be good heparanase substrates but below antithrombin-binding thresholds.
  - Optional genetic format for autologous products: a GPI-anchored, mucin-like scaffold (tandem repeats) engineered to bear HS via consensus Ser-Gly dipeptides; chain elaboration promoted by co-expressing HS biosynthetic enzymes; chains trimmed in situ by heparanase at injury.
- Tuning variables: chain length, N-/6-O-sulfation ratios, surface density (target 10^4–10^5 chains/cell), linker length, residence time.
- Readouts:
  - Brush presence/thickness: AFM force mapping, electron microscopy of shadowed replicas, fluorescence halo with labeled HS.
  - Masking efficacy: flow cytometry accessibility of VLA-4/LFA-1/CD44 epitopes and ligand-binding under static conditions.
  - Trigger specificity: loss of brush signal and restored receptor accessibility after exposure to recombinant heparanase versus hyaluronidase/chondroitinase; kinetics under physiological shear; resistance to plasma proteases.

Go/no-go for Aim 1: ≥80% reduction in ligand accessibility when brushed; ≥70% restoration within 10–30 min after heparanase exposure; negligible restoration with non-relevant enzymes.

Aim 2: Spatially confined activation and transendothelial migration in vitro
- Model: Microfluidic channels with human microvascular endothelial monolayers. Create adjacent regions with intact glycocalyx and injury-mimics (TNF-α + heparanase overexpression or pulsed heparanase/hyaluronidase exposure; confirm by HS/HA/CS staining and syndecan/glypican quantification).
- Assays under shear (1–20 dyn/cm2):
  - Arrest/rolling: quantify arrest density and rolling velocity for brushed vs unbrushed mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs), and immune cell therapeutics.
  - Crawling/TEM: measure time to diapedesis and fraction completing TEM; visualize junctional crossing and basement membrane penetration.
  - Confinement metrics: injury:healthy arrest ratio, TEM ratio, and event maps across gradients.
- Causality controls: heparanase inhibition (e.g., competitive inhibitors), heparanase knockdown endothelium, brush variants resistant to heparanase, and HA-/CS-targeted brushes to test specificity to HS remodeling.

Success criteria for Aim 2: ≥5-fold increase in injury:healthy arrest ratio and ≥3-fold increase in injury:healthy TEM ratio for brushed cells vs unbrushed, abolished by heparanase inhibition or heparanase-resistant brush.

Aim 3: In vivo selectivity, efficacy, and safety
- Models (disease-agnostic panel): unilateral hindlimb ischemia–reperfusion (sterile injury), localized photochemical vascular injury, and transient endotoxemia. Confirm endothelial glycocalyx remodeling by HS/HA/CS profiling and syndecan shedding.
- Endpoints:
  - Biodistribution: whole-body and organ imaging of labeled cells; injury:contralateral homing index at 6–48 h.
  - Extravasation: intravital microscopy and 3D tissue clearing to score luminal vs perivascular cell positions; TEM frequency.
  - Repair efficacy: perfusion recovery (laser Doppler), histological regeneration indices, functional scores appropriate to model.
  - Vascular integrity/homeostasis: Evans blue leakage, hematology, coagulation (aPTT/anti-Xa), blood pressure, cytokines.
- Endogenous stem cell extension: infusion of fusogenic liposomes bearing cholesterol-HS constructs for in-blood membrane transfer to circulating stem/progenitor cells; quantify coating levels, persistence, and injury-selective unmasking.

Milestones
- Phase I: Brush synthesis and tuning complete with validated heparanase-gated unmasking (months 0–6).
- Phase II: Microfluidic confinement and TEM enhancement achieved with predefined ratios and inhibitor reversibility (months 6–12).
- Phase III: In vivo injury-selective homing ≥3-fold and extravasation ≥2-fold vs controls, with unchanged systemic vascular parameters across models (months 12–24).

Mechanistic validation
- Demonstrate that enhanced adhesion requires restored integrin function: blockade with anti-VLA-4/LFA-1 abrogates effect post-unmasking.
- Show dependence on HS remodeling: no enhancement in heparanase-deficient or heparanase-inhibited animals; diminished effect where endothelial glycocalyx is experimentally preserved.
- Map local chemokine retention: quantify CXCL12/CXCL8 retention at injury regions; test whether unmasking increases chemokine capture via native cell receptors.

Safety and confinement features
- No endothelial manipulation; the trigger is endogenous heparanase concentrated at injury.
- HS chains selected to avoid antithrombin-binding motifs and excessive anticoagulant activity.
- Limited brush residence time (t1/2 8–24 h) to match homing window; reversible lipid insertion allows clearance.
- Off-target guardrails: lack of effect in healthy tissues, minimal complement activation, and no increase in systemic permeability.

Potential risks and contingencies
- Insufficient heparanase to unmask: increase substrate susceptibility by adjusting HS sulfation patterns/length or include secondary, injury-coincident triggers (mild ROS-labile crosslinks) while keeping heparanase as the primary gate.
- Rapid brush shedding in circulation: increase lipid anchor valency or add weak avidity tags to prolong residence without affecting activation logic.
- Anticoagulant side effects: further reduce 3-O-sulfation and chain size; cap chains to abolish antithrombin affinity.

Broad applicability
Because endothelial HS remodeling and associated HA/CS ratio changes occur across sterile, inflammatory, mechanical, and ischemic injuries, a heparanase-labile stealth glycocalyx converts a shared, tissue-level compositional signal into a precise, site-specific recruitment gate for both endogenous and exogenously administered therapeutic cells, without disrupting normal glycocalyx barrier function or systemic vascular homeostasis.

Title
Constitutive integrin activation as a dystrophin-independent mechanical bridge for DMD

Central hypothesis + research goal
A single, genetically encoded, membrane-tethered integrin activator that hardwires β1D-integrin into a high-affinity, actin-coupled state will substitute for dystrophin’s mechanical linkage, thereby reducing membrane fragility, downstream calcium overload, and secondary inflammation/fibrosis in skeletal and cardiac muscle of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), without targeting the dystrophin gene.

Atomic strategy
Install a synthetic, muscle-targeted, inside-out integrin activation module that constitutively stabilizes α7β1D–laminin adhesions and couples them to cortical actin, creating an alternative force-transmission axis at costameres.

Therapeutic construct (“MuTAct”)
- Single-gene, membrane-anchored cytoplasmic fusion protein comprising:
  - A transmembrane anchor for sarcolemmal localization.
  - An engineered talin-head–like integrin-activating domain that binds the β1D cytoplasmic tail to induce the high-affinity conformation and clustering of integrins.
  - A minimal vinculin-recruiting/actin-engaging motif to nucleate linkage to F-actin without relying on dystrophin/utrophin.
- Expression control:
  - Striated muscle–specific promoter supporting skeletal and cardiac expression.
  - Tunable expression via post-transcriptional regulation (e.g., inclusion of tissue-restrictive miRNA target sites) to minimize off-muscle exposure.
- Vector: muscle-tropic AAV serotype compatible with systemic delivery; total cassette size engineered to fit single-stranded AAV capacity.

Mechanism of action
- Primary: Constitutive inside-out activation and lateral clustering of α7β1D integrins at costameres increases laminin engagement, stiffens membrane–ECM adhesions, and creates a parallel mechanical bridge to transmit lateral forces during contraction.
- Secondary systems effects:
  - Reduced contraction-induced microtears lower pathological calcium influx, mitigating calpain activation and mitochondrial stress.
  - Diminished myofiber necrosis attenuates DAMP-driven inflammation, which in turn reduces TGF-β–driven fibrosis and fibro-adipogenic expansion.
  - Improved mechanical homeostasis supports satellite cell engraftment and regeneration by stabilizing the niche.
  - In cardiomyocytes, enhanced β1D engagement supports sarcolemmal integrity and may slow DMD cardiomyopathy progression.

Differentiation and novelty
- Distinct from dystrophin gene correction/re-expression and micro-dystrophin approaches.
- Distinct from prior compensatory strategies (e.g., utrophin upregulation, α7-integrin overexpression, GALGT2 glycosylation, myostatin/SERCA modulation, membrane-repair protein delivery). MuTAct does not merely increase integrin abundance or repair after injury; it installs a constitutive activation-and-coupling module that reprograms integrin conformation and linkage to actin, creating a persistent, dystrophin-independent mechanical pathway. To our knowledge, a membrane-tethered, talin-mimetic integrin activator targeted to β1D for DMD has not been evaluated preclinically or clinically.

Preclinical development plan (decision-focused)
- Design/validation
  - In silico and cellular validation of MuTAct variants to balance integrin activation with cell viability; select a lead showing robust integrin activation, focal adhesion maturation markers, and preserved contractility in human iPSC-derived myotubes and cardiomyocytes from DMD genotypes.
- Proof-of-concept in vivo
  - Systemic dosing in a standard murine DMD model with blinded, prespecified endpoints: membrane integrity (Evans blue/IgG uptake), calcium handling proxies, force drop under eccentric contractions, histopathology (necrosis, central nuclei, fibrosis), serum biomarkers, and arrhythmia surveillance.
  - Cardiac function by echocardiography and MRI where feasible.
  - Go/no-go criteria: ≥30% reduction in contraction-induced force loss and ≥50% reduction in membrane leak versus controls, without adverse remodeling.
- Translation-enabling studies
  - Biodistribution, expression durability, and immunogenicity characterization; manufacturability assessment at clinically relevant scales; off-target tissue exposure profiling.
  - Large-animal feasibility in a dystrophic canine model focusing on safety, skeletal/cardiac function, and biomarkers.

Safety and control features
- Muscle-specific promoter and microRNA de-targeting to limit expression outside striated muscle.
- Integrin activation domain tuned to avoid hyper-adhesion and unwanted fibrosis; inclusion of degron-based expression caps or regulatable expression architecture if needed.
- Cardiac monitoring to mitigate risks of altered mechano-signaling.
- Immunogenicity minimization through human-derived domains and deimmunization of novel junctions.

Clinical translation path
- Patient population: ambulatory/non-ambulatory males with confirmed DMD, including those ineligible for exon-skipping or micro-dystrophin.
- Administration: single systemic infusion of muscle-tropic AAV vector.
- Early-phase endpoints: safety; serum CK/ALT/AST; muscle MRI (T2, fat fraction); functional tests (e.g., NSAA/10MWT where appropriate); wearable-derived activity measures; biopsy-based pharmacodynamics (integrin activation/clustering signatures, costamere reinforcement markers); cardiac function (LVEF/GLS).
- Biomarker strategy: composite of membrane injury markers, pro-fibrotic cytokines, and mechanotransduction readouts to quantify mechanism engagement.

Risks and mitigations
- Excessive adhesion/fibrosis: mitigate by domain tuning and dose-finding; monitor ECM deposition signatures.
- Interference with myocyte plasticity: screen transcriptional programs for maladaptive shifts; prioritize variants with neutral global expression impact.
- Immune responses to vector or novel junctions: employ standard prophylaxis frameworks and sequence-level deimmunization; consider redosability strategies in platform evolution.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Lead construct shows sustained integrin activation with preserved contractility in human DMD myotubes and cardiomyocytes.
- M2: In vivo murine efficacy with prespecified functional and histological improvements and acceptable safety margin.
- M3: Large-animal feasibility with concordant mechanism biomarkers and no dose-limiting toxicities.
- M4: CMC readiness for GMP vector, regulatory package assembled for first-in-human study.

Why this could generalize across DMD genotypes
By bypassing dystrophin and reconstituting the membrane–ECM–actin linkage via constitutive β1D-integrin activation and actin engagement, MuTAct targets the shared, proximal mechanical failure underlying diverse DMD mutations, with downstream benefits on calcium handling, inflammation, fibrosis, and regeneration.

Title
Nature’s shock absorber: Ultra–high–molecular‑weight hyaluronan (uHMW‑HA) gene therapy to compensate for dystrophin loss in Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Premise and integrated hypothesis–question
Can installing, within human skeletal muscle, a pericellular coat of ultra–high–molecular‑weight hyaluronan—an adaptation leveraged by long‑lived, injury‑resistant mammals—mechanically and immunologically buffer dystrophin‑deficient myofibers enough to prevent membrane microtears, blunt Ca2+ overload, and suppress fibrosis/inflammation, thereby altering DMD progression without restoring dystrophin?

Atomic strategy
A single genetic perturbation: durable, myofiber‑restricted expression of a humanized hyaluronan synthase engineered to preferentially produce ultra–high–molecular‑weight chains (uHMW‑HA) at the sarcolemma, creating a lubricating, viscoelastic pericellular matrix that:
- Reduces shear‑induced membrane strain and microtears (primary pathology in dystrophin loss).
- Dampens mechanosensitive channel activation and pathological Ca2+ influx.
- Skews HA signaling toward anti‑inflammatory/anti‑fibrotic pathways by minimizing low‑MW HA fragments.
- Improves force transmission by evenly distributing load across the ECM.

Therapeutic concept
- Modality: In vivo gene addition/regulation.
- Cargo: Humanized HAS2 variant (HAS2‑uHMW) guided by comparative residues/motifs from species with naturally abundant uHMW‑HA, optimized for muscle membranes to favor longer polymer processivity.
- Vector/delivery: Muscle‑tropic AAV or LNP‑mRNA for skeletal muscle; myofiber‑specific promoter; detargeting elements to minimize cardiac/vascular expression; optional drug‑tunable expression domain to control HA levels.
- Product profile: One‑time or infrequent dosing; transgene size fits standard vectors; non‑dystrophin mechanism.

Why this can work system‑wide (first‑principles rationale)
- Mechanical: HA’s entangled, highly hydrated chains create a slip layer that reduces friction and peak strain at the sarcolemma during contraction, lowering the probability and extent of membrane ruptures.
- Ionic homeostasis: Fewer and smaller tears translate into fewer Ca2+ microdomains and less calpain activation, stabilizing excitation–contraction coupling.
- Immuno‑fibrotic axis: High‑MW HA biases signaling away from TLR‑driven inflammation and TGF‑β–mediated fibrosis, countering core DMD amplifiers.
- Regeneration: A permissive, non‑scar‑prone matrix can improve satellite cell migration and fusion dynamics.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Natural‑experiment validation of HA‑centric compensation
Question: Does uHMW‑HA confer dystrophin‑independent resilience?
- Strategy: Comparative, cross‑species myotube systems with matched dystrophin loss to query dependence on HA length/abundance. Modulate HA enzymatically/genetically and quantify membrane injury susceptibility, Ca2+ dysregulation, and inflammatory readouts.
Go/no‑go: uHMW‑HA elevation must reduce membrane injury and Ca2+ overload by prespecified margins versus controls.

Aim 2. Engineer a human‑compatible HAS2‑uHMW transgene
Question: Can we bias HA chain length safely in myofibers?
- Strategy: Create a human HAS2 backbone incorporating processivity‑enhancing motifs inferred from resilient species; ensure correct membrane localization; embed muscle‑specific transcriptional control and detargeting to reduce cardiac exposure; incorporate an optional small‑molecule–responsive attenuator for dose control.
Success criteria: Predominant uHMW‑HA distribution at the myofiber surface; no deleterious intracellular accumulation; tunable expression.

Aim 3. Demonstrate pathology‑level efficacy without dystrophin restoration
Question: Does pericellular uHMW‑HA correct key DMD pathologies in vivo and in human cells?
- Strategy: Evaluate in established dystrophin‑deficient models and patient‑derived myofibers for:
  - Membrane integrity and dye exclusion under eccentric load.
  - Ca2+ homeostasis and calpain activity.
  - Fibrosis and inflammatory signatures.
  - Muscle force, fatigue resistance, and gait metrics.
Success criteria: Concurrent improvement across membrane stability, Ca2+ handling, and fibrotic/inflammatory endpoints with meaningful functional gain.

Aim 4. Translation and manufacturability
Question: Is clinical deployment feasible and safe at scale?
- Strategy: Define dose/exposure bands achieving target HA levels without edema or impaired contractility; biodistribution and detargeting verification; immune risk assessment; CMC plan for vector at commercial scale; nonclinical safety focusing on ECM remodeling, thrombosis risk, and organ HA accumulation.
Milestones: Defined therapeutic index; scalable manufacturing process; regulatory‑aligned safety dossier.

Clinical path (phase‑appropriate, realistic)
- Initial indication: Ambulatory adolescents/young adults with confirmed DMD and preserved respiratory function to facilitate functional readouts; exclusion for advanced cardiomyopathy to de‑risk off‑target exposure.
- Primary biomarkers: MRI T2/T1rho for edema/fibrosis; microtear‑sensitive serum/urine markers; HA length distribution in muscle microdialysate or biopsy; CK reduction.
- Secondary endpoints: Quantitative muscle testing, timed function tests, wearable‑derived gait variability, patient‑reported outcomes.
- Safety monitoring: Tissue/serum HA levels, fluid balance, cardiac function, coagulation, liver enzymes; vector immunity; manageability of the tunable expression domain.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Excess matrix stiffness or edema: Use tunable expression and tight muscle‑specific control; predefined shutdown via small‑molecule switch or RNA‑mediated knockdown if thresholds exceeded.
- Cardiac exposure: Detargeting elements and dose partitioning; cardiac function surveillance.
- Immunogenicity: Humanized coding sequence; immune‑modulating prophylaxis per standard gene therapy practice.
- Efficacy ceiling: If mechanical buffering alone is insufficient, pre‑specified combination path with orthogonal, non‑dystrophin modules (for example, Ca2+ microdomain buffering) while preserving the atomic core.

Differentiation and novelty
- Does not restore or modulate dystrophin or utrophin.
- Leverages a single, nature‑derived physical–biological intervention (uHMW‑HA) to simultaneously address membrane instability, Ca2+ dysregulation, inflammation, and fibrosis.
- Gene therapy payload is compact, regulatable, and compatible with current delivery platforms.

Success criteria and timeline
- Year 1: Establish HA‑dependent resilience signal and finalize HAS2‑uHMW construct with control elements.
- Year 2: Demonstrate multi‑endpoint efficacy in dystrophin‑deficient models and human myofibers; define therapeutic window.
- Year 3: Complete GLP‑aligned safety, CMC readiness, and file for first‑in‑human.

Outcome
A first‑in‑class, dystrophin‑independent gene therapy that installs a pericellular “shock absorber,” transforming the mechanical and inflammatory landscape of dystrophin‑deficient muscle and providing a scalable, clinically practical alternative path to disease modification in DMD.

Title
Porting mouse “resilience state” to human muscle: multiplex enhancer reactivation gene therapy for DMD

Central research question-as-hypothesis
If the superior survival of mdx mice arises from coordinated activation of a small set of protective enhancers and their downstream genes, then re-creating this regulatory “resilience state” in human muscle stem cells and myofibers—without touching dystrophin—will stabilize membranes, normalize calcium handling, restrain fibrosis/inflammation, and sustain regeneration sufficiently to modify DMD progression.

Atomic strategy
Transfer regulatory state, not genes: a single, deliverable multiplex epigenome-editing therapy that selectively boosts human orthologs of mdx-activated protective modules (and silences human-specific pathological modules) by targeting their native enhancers/promoters with pooled CRISPRa/CRISPRi guides. This replays the mouse’s endogenous compensation program in human tissue.

Therapeutic concept
- Modality: Non-cutting, transient or controllable epigenome editing (CRISPR-based activation/repression) delivered to skeletal muscle and satellite cells.
- Target class: Conserved, muscle-restricted enhancer/promoter modules that drive:
  1) Membrane stabilization/costamere reinforcement (e.g., α7β1 integrin axis, sarcospan complex).
  2) Acute membrane repair (e.g., annexin-driven repair machinery).
  3) Calcium homeostasis and mechano-transduction setpoint (e.g., repression of stretch-activated channel overdrive).
  4) Anti-fibrotic and pro-resolving inflammation programs (e.g., dampening profibrotic cues; boosting pro-resolving lipid mediator enzymes).
  5) Regeneration capacity safeguards in satellite cells (e.g., telomere/shelterin protection or stress-quiescence balance).
- Key design choice: Multiplex guide array targeting 6–10 prioritized regulatory elements to shift the whole network, rather than overexpressing any single factor.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define the mdx “resilience enhancer atlas” and its human orthologs.
- Comparative single-nucleus multiome (chromatin accessibility + transcriptome) under standardized contraction/injury contexts in mdx vs wild-type mouse muscle stem cells and myofibers; integrate with perturbation data to identify enhancer modules whose activity correlates with membrane integrity, calcium stability, fibrosis restraint, and regeneration.
- LiftOver and motif grammar analysis to nominate orthologous human elements; prioritize elements with strong muscle specificity, evolutionary conservation of TF syntax (MEF2, TEAD, NFAT, SRF modules), and therapeutic leverage on the four DMD pathologies above.
- Build a ranked target list with minimal sufficient module sets that recapitulate the mouse resilience state in silico.

Aim 2. Engineer a compact, muscle-restricted multiplex CRISPRa/CRISPRi therapy that installs the resilience state in human cells.
- Construct pooled guide arrays (one cassette per module) to activate protective elements and repress pathogenic ones; include an inducible, muscle-selective control layer so editing activity increases under mechanical/calcium stress and is quiescent at rest.
- Validate state transfer in human DMD myogenic cells: single-cell readouts of chromatin opening, target gene induction/repression, and network-level shift toward the mdx resilience signature.
- Optimize for parsimony: reduce to the smallest guide set that preserves efficacy and minimizes off-target transcriptome drift.

Aim 3. Demonstrate functional efficacy and safety in human-relevant DMD models.
- Function: Rescue assays in human DMD iPSC-derived myofibers and humanized xenograft muscle, measuring:
  - Membrane stability under controlled stretch/injury (e.g., dye exclusion, leak kinetics).
  - Calcium transient normalization and mitochondrial sparing during load.
  - Force production/fatigue resistance.
  - Fibrosis/inflammation biomarkers and extracellular matrix remodeling.
  - Satellite cell self-renewal and regenerative output after injury cycles.
- Safety: Genome-wide off-target binding screens for the editor and guides; transcriptomic boundary checks for oncogenic, myogenic lineage, and cardiac conduction pathways; reversibility and tunability of the epigenetic state.

Innovation and differentiators
- Network-first therapy: targets a minimal enhancer set to flip an entire protective program rather than single-gene add-backs.
- Cross-species regulatory porting: extracts and replays mdx enhancer grammar in human cells to mimic the mouse’s natural compensation.
- Dystrophin-agnostic: no editing, re-expression, or proxy miniaturization of dystrophin; compatible with, but independent of, dystrophin-restoring treatments.

Mechanistic coverage of DMD pathology
- Membrane instability: Reinforce costameres and repair machinery by upregulating integrin/sarcolemmal stabilizers and annexin-mediated resealing.
- Calcium dysregulation: Repress hyperactive stretch/mechano channels and tune mechano-transduction TF networks to lower pathological calcium influx.
- Fibrosis/inflammation: Downshift profibrotic drivers and boost resolution-phase effectors to reduce TGF-β/CCN2/SPP1-like scarring axes and neutrophil/monocyte persistence.
- Regeneration failure: Safeguard satellite cell fitness via enhancer-driven programs that maintain quiescence-exit balance and telomere/shelterin protection under chronic injury.

Translational plan
- Delivery: Muscle-tropic, non-integrating delivery of an inducible epigenome editor plus multiplex guide array; options include dual-vector strategies or transient RNA delivery for repeatable dosing. Muscle-specific regulatory control to restrict activity to target tissues.
- Dosing paradigm: Induction-on-demand architecture mitigates chronic exposure; retreatment remains feasible due to non-cutting modality.
- Manufacturability: Guides are short and fully synthetic; editor payload standardized across indications; scalable vector production aligns with current muscle gene therapy platforms.
- Clinical path: Initial focus on ambulatory adolescents to test functional endpoints with lower fibrosis burden; biomarkers include a composite panel of membrane injury, calcium homeostasis, and fibrosis markers alongside quantitative MRI and strength measures. Compatible with background standard-of-care and combinable with dystrophin-directed agents.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Off-target chromatin remodeling: Use high-specificity guides, orthogonal validation, inducible control, and dose titration; predefine transcriptomic safety guardrails.
- Overcorrection/imbalances (e.g., excessive adhesion or suppressed inflammation): Stress-inducible circuits and ceilinged activators; select targets with homeostatic negative feedback built into the module.
- Immune recognition of editor: Minimize exposure time, tissue-restrict expression, and consider retreatment strategies with alternating delivery formats.
- Heterogeneity across muscles: Include guides common to limb and respiratory muscles; stratify patient selection by baseline fibrosis/regeneration potential.

Go/no-go milestones
- Demonstrate in human DMD myofibers a ≥50% reduction in stretch-induced membrane leak and normalization of calcium transient area without impairing myogenesis.
- Achieve a predefined fibrosis/inflammation biomarker score reduction and force improvement in humanized xenograft muscle without transcriptomic breach of safety guardrails.
- Show reversibility/tunability of the edited epigenetic state in vitro and in vivo.

Expected outcome
A dystrophin-independent, regulatorily precise gene therapy that installs a mouse-like resilience program in human muscle, yielding clinically meaningful stabilization of muscle integrity and function with a realistic path to first-in-human testing.

Title
Regeneration-coupled “UTRN Lock-On” gene therapy: permanent activation of endogenous utrophin in human muscle stem cells to replace dystrophin function in Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Central hypothesis and research goal
If the endogenous utrophin (UTRN) locus in human muscle stem cells (satellite cells) is permanently reprogrammed to a high-expression, regeneration-coupled state, then every new myofiber produced across life will be utrophin-rich, stabilizing the sarcolemma, reducing calcium overload, limiting inflammation/fibrosis, and functionally substituting for dystrophin without touching the DMD gene. The research goal is to create and translate a one-time, somatic, genome-writing “on switch” at UTRN in satellite cells that is mitotically heritable yet editor-transient, thereby turning DMD from a progressive degeneration into a continuously self-repairing condition.

Atomic strategy
Rewrite a single cis-regulatory control point at the native UTRN locus in satellite cells—installing a compact, self-sustaining enhancer/promoter “Lock-On” element that couples utrophin to myogenic master regulators—so utrophin is durably high whenever satellite cells activate and differentiate, independent of fetal programs or upstream disease stress signals.

What makes this novel
- Targets regulation, not transgene addition: a minimal cis-regulatory edit that permanently elevates the patient’s own utrophin rather than introducing micro-utrophin or modulating dystrophin.
- Regeneration-coupled permanence: the edit is designed to be mitotically heritable in satellite cells, seeding waves of utrophin-high myofibers for decades without chronic drug exposure.
- Single-locus, multi-pathology impact: a physiological utrophin–glycoprotein complex at costameres restores membrane stability, secondarily normalizing calcium handling, reducing sterile inflammation, and decreasing fibrosis risk.
- To our knowledge, no in vivo, satellite cell–targeted genome editing approach has installed a persistent, synthetic enhancer at UTRN to couple adult myogenesis to utrophin expression.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Define the minimal “Lock-On grammar” for human UTRN.
- Map cis-elements controlling UTRN during human myogenesis and regeneration; derive a compact sequence that (a) recruits myogenic regulators, (b) establishes active chromatin marks, and (c) resists developmental silencing in adult muscle.
- Benchmark against endogenous promoters/enhancers in human myotube and satellite cell models to select a sub-200 bp element with high dynamic range and positional tolerance.

Aim 2. Build a genome-writing module that installs the Lock-On at UTRN and then clears.
- Use a transient, nuclease-free or low-DSB genome editor to make precise, small edits that either insert the Lock-On element or create de novo high-affinity sites for myogenic regulators at the native promoter/enhancer.
- Incorporate a “prime-and-lock” design: editor expression is brief; the resulting chromatin state and sequence reprogramming are mitotically heritable without ongoing editor presence.

Aim 3. Achieve selective in vivo delivery to human-relevant satellite cells.
- Engineer a delivery system with muscle/satellite-cell tropism and transient editor kinetics; restrict guide/regulatory cargo by a satellite cell–active transcriptional gate to minimize off-target cell editing.
- Validate biodistribution, edit fraction in satellite cells, and on-target durability in humanized muscle models.

Aim 4. Demonstrate disease modification across DMD pathologies.
- In dystrophin-null preclinical models, quantify: (a) utrophin protein at costameres/neuromuscular junctions; (b) membrane stability (e.g., dye exclusion, CK); (c) calcium homeostasis markers; (d) inflammation/fibrosis indices; (e) force production and fatigue resistance; and (f) satellite cell pool integrity and regenerative capacity over time.
- Establish dose–response and minimal effective edited-cell fraction required for functional benefit.

Mechanism of action
- The Lock-On element recruits myogenic master regulators during satellite cell activation and differentiation, installing and maintaining an active chromatin architecture at UTRN.
- Elevated, properly localized utrophin assembles the utrophin–glycoprotein complex at costameres, restoring mechanical coupling between the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix, reducing contraction-induced membrane tears.
- Stabilized membranes reduce pathological calcium influx and downstream necrosis; decreased damage lowers DAMP-driven inflammation and TGF-β–mediated fibrosis; improved fiber survival and niche health preserve the satellite cell pool, sustaining long-term muscle regeneration.

Safety and feasibility
- Utrophin is an endogenous self-protein; immunogenicity risk is low relative to dystrophin re-expression in null patients.
- Transient editor exposure limits off-target activity; the small edit footprint avoids large genomic insertions.
- Satellite cell–selective expression of editing guides and built-in editing “off-switches” reduce bystander editing in non-target tissues.
- Genotoxicity, off-target editing, and insertional risks are mitigated through unbiased genome-wide assays and long-term surveillance in large-animal models.

Translational plan
- Indication: ambulatory boys with DMD (early intervention to preserve/regenerate muscle), with expansion to non-ambulatory stages for limb/diaphragm targets.
- Administration: systemic delivery optimized for skeletal muscle with option for regional limb perfusion in early-phase trials to de-risk.
- Pharmacology: one to few doses to reach a threshold fraction of edited satellite cells; re-dosing feasible given transient, non-integrating payloads.
- Biomarkers: serial muscle biopsies for utrophin localization/intensity; noninvasive imaging for fibrosis; serum CK; standardized functional measures.
- Manufacturing: scalable, modular production of editor and guide cargos with release criteria emphasizing purity, potency (on-target edit rate), and residual editor clearance.

Milestones and go/no-go criteria
- M1: Identify a Lock-On sequence achieving >10× upregulation of endogenous UTRN in human myogenic cells with stable expression through ≥10 cell divisions. Go if achieved in ≥2 donor lines.
- M2: Achieve ≥15% on-target Lock-On installation in primary human satellite cells ex vivo with no detectable high-risk off-target events. Go if off-target profile passes predefined thresholds.
- M3: In dystrophin-null mouse, attain ≥10% edited satellite cells in limb muscles, with utrophin restoration to ≥40% of healthy levels at costameres and ≥30% increase in specific force. Go if functional and histological endpoints meet targets without safety signals.
- M4: Demonstrate durable benefit (≥9 months in mouse; ≥6 months in large animal) with stable satellite cell pool size and no clonal expansion. Proceed to IND-enabling studies.

Risk assessment and mitigation
- Satellite cell transduction efficiency: parallel capsid/ligand discovery and dosing paradigms; accept partial editing if threshold for functional rescue is met via muscle’s multinucleation and regeneration dynamics.
- Overexpression beyond physiological localization: require correct subcellular localization readouts; Lock-On grammar tuned to costamere-rich expression without ectopic accumulation.
- Editing mosaicism: leverage regenerative cycles—edited satellite cells clonally expand and seed edited myonuclei over time; longitudinal modeling guides dose and timing.
- Fibrosis-dominant late-stage muscle: incorporate inclusion criteria and, in later cohorts, combine with standard anti-fibrotic care without mechanistic coupling to dystrophin.

Why this can generalize
A single, regeneration-coupled, cis-regulatory rewrite converts a degenerative disease into a self-repairing state by exploiting the life-long renewal engine of skeletal muscle. The platform extends to other compensatory networks (e.g., integrin α7β1D, sarcospan) by swapping Lock-On grammar at their endogenous loci if additional stabilization is needed.

Success criteria
- Molecular: long-lived, mitotically stable activation of endogenous utrophin in human satellite cells and derived myofibers with correct membrane localization.
- Cellular/tissue: restored membrane integrity, normalized calcium indicators, reduced inflammatory/fibrotic signatures, preserved satellite cell pool.
- Functional: clinically meaningful improvements in muscle strength/endurance with acceptable safety in early human studies.

Summary
This proposal aims to permanently “flip on” utrophin at its native locus in muscle stem cells via a compact, regeneration-coupled Lock-On element installed by transient genome editing. By changing one regulatory control point, every subsequent myofiber becomes utrophin-rich, addressing the core biomechanical failure of DMD while secondarily normalizing calcium handling, inflammation, and fibrosis—without ever touching the dystrophin gene.

Title
DAMAGE-SENSE: A disease-state–activated, multiplex CRISPRa gene therapy that rewires endogenous compensation networks in Duchenne muscular dystrophy without dystrophin restoration

Unified hypothesis-goal
In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), damaged myofibers show convergent “stress signatures” (calcium overload, inflammation, ER/mitochondrial stress) that are largely absent in healthy muscle. If a genetic switch can be made to turn on only in this stressed state, we can drive a coordinated, multi-gene pro-resilience program that stabilizes membranes, normalizes calcium, dampens fibrosis/inflammation, and improves regeneration—without targeting dystrophin itself.

Atomic strategy
Exploit the disease state as the address label: build an AND-gated transcriptional activator that assembles only inside stressed myofibers and then program it (via CRISPRa) to upregulate a compact set of endogenous compensatory genes across three failure modes—membrane stability/repair, calcium/proteostasis, and niche reprogramming—thereby converting injury signals into a self-limiting therapeutic response.

System architecture

1) Stress-state sensor (muscle-specific AND gate)
- Logic: Muscle lineage AND (NF-κB/inflammatory) AND (NFAT/calcium-activated or UPR/ATF6).
- Implementation concept: a split, nuclease-dead CRISPR activator whose two halves are independently driven by stress-responsive promoters; reconstitution occurs only where both stress pathways are active. A muscle enhancer restricts baseline expression to myofibers and cardiomyocytes; microRNA detargeting reduces expression in liver/immune cells.
- Outcome: Therapeutic activity is silent in healthy muscle, switches on in damaged fibers, and turns down as stress resolves.

2) Programmable effector layer (CRISPRa network)
- Modality: A compact dCas-based activator with a multiplex guide RNA cassette targets endogenous loci; no genome cutting.
- Effector clusters (initial 6–8 targets; adjustable by guide selection):
  A. Membrane stability and repair
     - Itga7 (α7-integrin): reinforce costameres and laminin binding.
     - Sspn (sarcospan): strengthen dystrophin-independent adhesion complexes.
     - Trim72/Mg53 and Dysf (dysferlin): accelerate membrane resealing after injury.
  B. Calcium handling and proteostasis
     - Atp2a2 (SERCA2a) ± Atp2a1 (SERCA1): enhance Ca2+ reuptake.
     - Cast (calpastatin): inhibit Ca2+-activated proteases to limit myofibrillar damage.
     - Sod2 (mitochondrial SOD): reduce ROS from Ca2+-stressed mitochondria.
  C. Anti-fibrosis and immunomodulation (paracrine-in-myofiber origin)
     - Dcn (decorin): sequester TGF-β and limit collagen deposition.
     - Ltbp4: buffer active TGF-β bioavailability; human genetic data suggest protection.
     - Il10: tilt macrophage polarization toward resolution/repair.
- Rationale: Each target has supportive biology on its own; the novelty is disease-gated, simultaneous, modest upregulation across nodes for network-level resilience with lower risk than single supra-physiologic overexpression.

3) Delivery and manufacturability
- Vector: Dual AAV with muscle-tropic capsids (systemic delivery). Vector A carries the split stress-sensor halves and dCas activator; Vector B carries the multiplex gRNA cassette. Packaging stays within standard AAV capacities; components are modular for lot-to-lot tuning.
- Dosing concept: Dose-sparing is enabled by the damage-activated amplification; activity scales with disease burden.
- Redosability path: Alternate capsids or LNP for gRNA “software updates” if needed; core chassis remains constant.

4) Safety features
- Three-layer restriction: muscle-specific enhancer; dual stress-responsive gating; microRNA detargeting.
- No DNA cutting: dCas-based activation avoids double-strand breaks.
- Built-in ceiling: effect size limited by endogenous promoter capacity, reducing risk of overcorrection.
- External control: add a clinically familiar small-molecule–removable degron on the activator to allow pharmacologic shutdown if needed.

Research plan and milestones

Phase I: Engineering and in vitro proof-of-concept
- Build sensor variants and benchmark AND-gate fidelity in human DMD patient–derived myotubes versus healthy controls exposed to calcium/inflammatory stimuli. Readouts: nuclear translocation, reporter activation, off-state leak.
- Program the CRISPRa cassette with initial guide sets to the nine loci above. Quantify on-target upregulation, off-target transcriptional drift (RNA-seq), and functional rescue markers (membrane repair after laser injury, Ca2+ transients, myotube contractility, fibrosis/inflammatory cytokine profiles in co-culture with fibroblasts/macrophages).

Phase II: In vivo efficacy and dose-finding
- Small-animal models: mdx4cv and D2.mdx for skeletal pathology; assess diaphragm and limb; include mdx/utrn+/- for severity. Endpoints: force production, eccentric contraction protection, creatine kinase, membrane leak assays, fibrosis quantification, immune infiltrates, and transcriptional biomarker engagement.
- Cardiac evaluation: DMD cardiomyopathy models for ejection fraction, fibrosis, arrhythmia burden, and Ca2+ handling indices.
- Safety: biodistribution, vector copy number, liver/immune detargeting, cytokines, and off-switch response to degron ligand.

Phase III: Large-animal translation readiness
- GRMD (canine) feasibility: whole-body delivery, gait/respiration function, 6-minute walk surrogate, MRI fat fraction, and cardiac MRI.
- CMC scale-up: stable producer lines for both AAVs; analytics for guide integrity and activator expression; release assays keyed to sensor function.

Success criteria (stage gates)
- ≥10-fold on/off dynamic range of the stress sensor in vitro with <5% leak in healthy cells.
- Coordinated ≥1.5–3× upregulation at ≥6 targets with minimal transcriptional off-targets.
- ≥30% improvement in eccentric contraction tolerance and ≥30% reduction in fibrosis versus control in mdx/D2.mdx at a clinically plausible vector genome range.
- Demonstrated reversibility with external degron ligand and decay back to baseline as injury resolves.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: Immunogenicity to bacterial dCas components. Mitigation: humanized activator scaffolds where possible; transient immune modulation; shielded expression via muscle-restricted microenvironments; explore smaller Cas or human ZF-based activators as drop-in alternatives.
- Risk: Overactivation of single pathways (e.g., excessive IL-10 or integrin). Mitigation: guide titration to moderate endogenous-range gains; cap activation with weaker activator domains on sensitive nodes; retain external off-switch.
- Risk: Heterogeneity across patients. Mitigation: modular “guide palette” enabling personalized or cohort-optimized sets; pre-infusion ex vivo transcriptomic profiling to select best subset.

Clinical translation path
- Regulatory positioning: non-editing gene regulation with tissue- and disease-restricted activity; stepwise first-in-human in ambulatory adolescents with biomarker-led dose escalation.
- Patient selection/biomarkers: baseline inflammatory/Calcium-stress signature to predict sensor engagement; circulating CK and fibrosis imaging as early PD markers; RNA signatures from myobiospy to confirm target engagement.
- Scalability: Dual-AAV manufacturing within current industrial capacity; modularity allows rapid iteration of guide sets without revalidating the whole chassis.

What makes this novel
- The therapy does not correct or express dystrophin (or micro-dystrophin). Instead, it uses a disease-gated, logic-AND genetic switch to sense the DMD stress milieu and then rewires multiple endogenous, dystrophin-independent resilience pathways via CRISPRa, yielding whole-system compensation with built-in safety and a realistic route to manufacturing and clinical translation.

Title
Fibrosis-Insulated Myogenic Switch (FIMS): a synthetic CRISPR epigenetic circuit in human muscle stem cells that converts pro-fibrotic cues into durable myogenic commitment for DMD

Hypothesis and Research Goal
Hypothesis: Chronic inflammatory and TGFβ-rich milieus in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) bias human muscle stem cells (MuSCs; satellite cells) toward maladaptive fibrogenic fates, depleting regenerative capacity and accelerating scarring. Installing a single synthetic, signal-integrating genetic switch that senses pro-fibrotic signaling and automatically enforces a myogenic program—while epigenetically silencing fibrogenic determinants—will create “fibrosis-insulated” MuSCs that sustain muscle regeneration and resist scarring without restoring dystrophin.
Goal/Question: Can a compact, cell-type–restricted CRISPR-based epigenetic switch in MuSCs transduce disease-associated fibrotic/inflammatory signals into a self-stabilizing myogenic state that preserves regeneration, reduces fibrosis, and improves function in DMD?

Atomic Strategy
A single-locus synthetic switch that inverts pathology: when pro-fibrotic pathways (e.g., SMAD/NF-κB) are active, the switch simultaneously (a) CRISPRi-silences master fibrogenic regulators and (b) CRISPRa-boosts core myogenic determinants, installing a reversible epigenetic “myogenic-only” mode that persists through cell divisions but remains fail-safe controllable.

Disease Context and Rationale
- DMD pathogenesis combines membrane fragility, Ca2+ dysregulation, chronic inflammation, failed regeneration, and progressive fibrosis. Even with ongoing myofiber damage, outcomes track how well MuSCs can rebuild muscle while fibrosis is restrained.
- MuSC fate plasticity is sensitive to inflammatory and TGFβ-family cues. Persistent exposure skews stem/progenitor pools away from productive myogenesis and toward fibroblast-like states, amplifying scar deposition and limiting functional recovery.
- Rather than blocking scarring after it starts, preventing MuSC entry into fibrogenic trajectories stabilizes the regenerative engine itself—an upstream, system-level intervention that complements any future membrane-stabilizing or damage-limiting therapies and does not involve dystrophin.

Proposed Genetic System: FIMS Circuit (single therapeutic construct)
- Input sensor (context gating): composite promoter with SMAD- and NF-κB–responsive elements placed downstream of a MuSC-restricted enhancer (e.g., Pax7/Myf5 regulatory context) to ensure activation only in satellite cells experiencing pro-fibrotic/inflammatory signaling.
- Effector A (anti-fibrotic arm): nuclease-dead Cas fused to a repressive epigenetic effector (e.g., KRAB/MeCP2-class) guided to regulatory elements of key fibrogenic determinants (e.g., TCF21, PDGFRA, ACTA2/Col1 cluster, contextually tuned to human MuSC chromatin maps). Goal: durable but adjustable reduction of fibrogenic competence.
- Effector B (pro-myogenic arm): nuclease-dead Cas fused to an activating epigenetic module (e.g., p300 core or VPR-class) targeted to myogenic network nodes (e.g., PAX7 super-enhancer and early MYOD enhancers) to bias progeny toward productive myogenesis while preserving self-renewal competence.
- Memory and safety: a mild positive-feedback mini-loop (orthogonal TF → sensor promoter) to stabilize state across several divisions; drug-inducible degrons on effectors to terminate activity; microRNA target sites to de-target non-muscle lineages; and a fail-safe suicide module restricted to MuSC lineage if aberrant proliferation occurs. All elements remain within a single integrated locus to minimize recombination and simplify manufacturing.

Therapeutic Modality and Delivery
- Modality: ex vivo autologous MuSC gene therapy using epigenome-editing (no genomic double-strand breaks in therapeutic effectors). Patient-derived MuSCs receive a single integrated FIMS cassette at a characterized “safe harbor” or via a clinically validated integrating system, with clonal QC for on-target insertion, karyotype, and epigenetic setpoints.
- Administration: regional intramuscular delivery of FIMS-MuSCs to priority muscle groups (e.g., tibialis anterior, quadriceps, diaphragm-accessible bundles), with the intention to expand to multiple sites over time. Approach is compatible with repeat dosing and cryopreserved batches.
- Long-term vision: transition to in vivo FIMS delivery via next-generation muscle/satellite-tropic vectors or LNP-delivered mRNA/RNP, once specificity, dose control, and cargo constraints are resolved.

Why This Is Novel
- Prior DMD strategies target dystrophin restoration, global TGFβ blockade, or general inflammation. FIMS introduces a cell-intrinsic, pathology-sensing epigenetic switch in human MuSCs that prevents fibrogenic conversion and enforces myogenesis—a distinct, upstream control of fate commitment not previously deployed as a therapeutic gene circuit in DMD.

Specific Aims
Aim 1. Define fibrogenic and myogenic control nodes in human MuSCs under DMD-like cues.
- Use multi-omic profiling of patient-derived MuSCs exposed to TGFβ/inflammatory mimetics to nominate a minimal gRNA set for fibrogenic silencing and myogenic activation that preserves self-renewal competence.

Aim 2. Engineer and bench-validate the compact FIMS cassette.
- Build a single-locus circuit with: MuSC-restricted sensor, CRISPRi anti-fibrotic arm, CRISPRa pro-myogenic arm, tunable memory, and drug control. Validate state transitions, reversibility, and fate insulation in human MuSCs and humanized co-culture with fibro-adipogenic progenitors.

Aim 3. Demonstrate efficacy and safety in dystrophic muscle contexts.
- Evaluate engraftment, myofiber contribution, fibrosis burden, force generation, and off-target lineage outputs in relevant dystrophic models with human MuSC xenografts. Establish pharmacogenetic control windows, immune profiles to editor proteins, and genomic/epigenomic stability.

Mechanistic Success Criteria (Go/No-Go)
- ≥2-fold enhancement of myogenic colony formation and myofiber incorporation under pro-fibrotic challenge versus control cells.
- ≥30% reduction in fibrogenic gene program activation in MuSC progeny exposed to TGFβ/NF-κB stimuli, with preserved Pax7+ self-renewal pool.
- Durable epigenetic marks at targeted loci across ≥8–10 divisions, fully reversible by drug-off within a defined safety window.
- No aberrant proliferation, transdifferentiation to non-muscle lineages, or tumorigenic hallmarks; intact global chromatin architecture.

Safety, Control, and Ethics
- Epigenome editing avoids persistent double-strand breaks; effectors are drug-degradable; suicide module restricted to MuSCs provides an emergency stop.
- Cell-type restriction via enhancer logic and microRNA target sites limits ectopic activity; single-locus integration reduces insertional complexity.
- Immunogenicity managed by humanized editor variants, minimal expression outside MuSCs, and pre-release immunoprofiling of cell products.

Clinical Translation Path
- Manufacturing: GMP-compliant autologous MuSC isolation/expansion with closed-system workflows, standardized single-locus integration, and batch release assays (identity, purity, potency, genomic/epigenomic safety).
- First-in-human design: focal administration to a weight-bearing lower-limb muscle with robust clinical readouts; primary endpoints—safety, feasibility, local fibrosis reduction, and strength/functional measures; secondary—biomarkers (e.g., fibrosis imaging, serum CK trajectories).
- Scalability: banked autologous lots for staged multi-muscle treatment; potential allogeneic, hypoimmune MuSC platforms in future if safety and engraftment permit.

Anticipated Impact
By recoding the way MuSCs interpret disease signals—turning fibrotic pressure into myogenic drive—FIMS aims to slow or reverse the fibrosis-regeneration imbalance that defines DMD progression. This strategy is orthogonal to dystrophin restoration, can synergize with membrane-stabilizing or anti-inflammatory therapies, and provides a principled, cell-intrinsic lever to preserve muscle architecture and function over time.

Title
Reawakening the fetal mechano–calcium safeguard in dystrophin-deficient muscle via multiplex CRISPRa

Central question and hypothesis
Can reactivating a compact, fetal-stage sarcolemmal protection program in mature myofibers—without altering dystrophin—restore membrane stability, normalize calcium handling, and blunt fibrosis/inflammation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)? The hypothesis is that targeted CRISPRa (dCas9-VP64) activation of a defined “fetal safeguard module” will reconstitute a dystrophin-independent architecture that reduces contraction-induced damage and downstream pathology.

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Replace missing dystrophin function not by substituting its scaffold, but by reinstating the fetal mechano–calcium safeguard module—an integrated axis comprising laminin adhesion, caveolar mechanoprotection, and rapid calcium extrusion—using in situ CRISPR activation of endogenous, developmentally higher-expressed protectors in adult muscle.

Therapeutic design overview
- Modality: Non-editing, multiplex CRISPR activation (dCas9-VP64 or equivalent compact activator) targeted to endogenous promoters/enhancers.
- Target “fetal safeguard module”:
  1) ITGA7 (α7 integrin) to strengthen laminin–sarcolemma adhesion independently of the dystrophin complex.
  2) CAV3 and CAVIN1 to expand stabilized caveolae for membrane tension buffering and rapid lesion sealing.
  3) ATP2B4 (PMCA4) to augment sarcolemmal Ca2+ extrusion and prevent cytosolic Ca2+ overload.
- Optional tunable add-on if needed: ANXA6 to enhance annexin-mediated membrane repair; BIN1 (muscle isoform) to improve T-tubule integrity and excitation–contraction coupling.
- Delivery: Dual-AAV muscle-tropic vectors (e.g., AAV9 or next-gen myotropic capsid). One vector encodes muscle-restricted dCas9-VP64; the other encodes a compact gRNA array (polycistronic) for simultaneous activation of the module. Regulatable expression (drug- or ligand-inducible) to allow dose titration and safety control.
- Tissue specificity: Skeletal and cardiac muscle targeting with muscle-specific promoters and microRNA target-site de-targeting for off-tissue restriction.

Rationale and systems view
- Fetal myofibers tolerate high mechanical stress before dystrophin dependence by relying on integrin–laminin adhesion, abundant caveolae that buffer membrane tension, and dominant sarcolemmal Ca2+ extrusion pathways. In DMD, adult fibers lack this early safeguard while facing chronic membrane fragility and Ca2+ overload. Restoring this module addresses:
  - Membrane stability (adhesion + caveolae)
  - Calcium dysregulation (enhanced extrusion)
  - Downstream necrosis, inflammation, and fibrosis (by reducing primary injury signals)
  - Regeneration failure (by decreasing ongoing damage and inflammatory scarring)

Specific aims
1) Define and validate the fetal safeguard module in human-relevant muscle systems.
   - Map developmental expression trajectories of the candidate genes across fetal-to-adult transitions (human myogenesis models and available datasets).
   - Confirm that module reactivation in dystrophin-deficient myotubes improves membrane integrity and Ca2+ handling without detrimental effects on contractility.

2) Build a multiplex CRISPRa therapy and test efficacy in DMD models.
   - Engineer a compact, muscle-restricted dCas9-activator and a gRNA array targeting regulatory regions of ITGA7, CAV3, CAVIN1, and ATP2B4.
   - Evaluate in vitro (human DMD iPSC-derived myofibers) and in vivo (mdx and a cardiomyopathy-prone DMD model) for:
     - Sarcolemmal stability (dye uptake/evoked damage resistance surrogates)
     - Ca2+ homeostasis (baseline and contraction-evoked transients)
     - Muscle force, fatigue resistance, serum biomarkers, histopathology
     - Cardiac function (echocardiography, arrhythmia propensity)
     - Fibrosis/inflammation markers and macrophage polarization

3) Optimize translation, safety, and manufacturability.
   - Tune expression with inducible systems to identify therapeutic windows.
   - Assess off-target transcriptional effects and immune responses (biodistribution, anti-capsid/anti-Cas responses); implement deimmunization and re-dosing strategies as needed.
   - Advance to large-animal DMD models for dose-ranging, durability, and safety pharmacology.

Key outcomes and success criteria
- Short term (cells/tissue): Increased surface caveolae density; improved membrane repair kinetics; reduced Ca2+ overload; preserved myofiber architecture under mechanical stress.
- Preclinical (mouse): Improved specific force; reduced necrosis and fibrosis; normalized inflammatory milieu; improved cardiac function indices.
- Large-animal: Reproducible efficacy with acceptable safety margins; scalable vector yields; stable transgene control.

Safety and risk management
- Expression control: Inducible CRISPRa to mitigate overactivation (particularly CAV3, where excess expression can be harmful).
- Network balance: Staged activation (start with ITGA7 + ATP2B4; add caveola targets only if needed) to avoid membrane stiffness or conduction defects.
- Off-target and ectopic activation: High-specificity gRNAs; muscle-restricted promoters; microRNA de-targeting; transcriptome monitoring.
- Immunogenicity: Low-immunogenic capsids; transient immune modulation strategies if required; exploration of deimmunized or humanized dCas9 variants.

Clinical translation pathway
- Indication: Ambulatory and non-ambulatory DMD with skeletal and cardiac involvement; genotype-agnostic as it does not address dystrophin directly.
- Administration: Systemic infusion with weight-based vector dosing; potential regional limb perfusion for dose-sparing studies.
- Endpoints: Function (6MWT analogs, upper-limb measures), imaging (muscle MRI fat fraction), cardiac metrics, serum biomarkers, safety labs, and patient-reported outcomes.
- Manufacturing: Dual-AAV GMP production using established platforms; modular gRNA array simplifies iteration; release testing aligned with current gene therapy standards.

Differentiation and novelty
- Does not correct, restore, or re-express dystrophin or micro-dystrophin.
- Aims to reinstate a defined fetal mechano–calcium safeguard module through endogenous gene reactivation, not single-gene replacement.
- Multiplex CRISPRa enables coordinated reprogramming of a protective state that is physiologically validated during development yet absent in adult DMD muscle.

Projected impact
If successful, this strategy establishes a genotype-agnostic, developmentally informed gene therapy that addresses root biophysical vulnerabilities—membrane fragility and Ca2+ overload—thereby decompressing downstream pathology (inflammation, fibrosis, regeneration failure) and complementing any future dystrophin-directed treatments without mechanistic overlap.

Title
Hijacking Fibrosis into Mural Reinforcement: CRISPRa reprogramming of activated muscle fibroblasts into pericyte-like “myofiber sleeves” for DMD

Central question-hypothesis
If dystrophic muscle’s fibrogenic stromal cells are redirected into pericyte-like mural cells in situ, can they assemble a protective, basement-membrane–rich sleeve around myofibers and microvessels that reduces membrane injury, leakage, inflammation, and fibrosis—improving function without restoring dystrophin?

Atomic strategy
A single, transient transcriptional push: activate a mural-cell identity switch (centered on NOTCH3) specifically within periostin-high, injury-activated fibroblasts/FAPs in dystrophic muscle using in vivo CRISPRa. The goal is fate redirection (myofibroblast → pericyte-like mural cell) so that the very cells driving scarring instead build a stabilizing, compliant cuff around myofibers and capillaries.

Why this could work (system-level rationale)
- The pathologic substrate is abundant and spatially proximal: PDGFRα+ FAPs/myofibroblasts expand in DMD muscle and are major drivers of fibrosis; periostin is highly upregulated in dystrophic muscle and marks activated fibrogenic cells. Targeting this compartment leverages disease biology where it already accumulates. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8093402/?utm_source=openai))
- Pericyte/mural programs stabilize microvessels, deposit laminin- and collagen IV–rich basement membrane, and mechanically buffer adjacent tissues. NOTCH3 is a defining driver of mural fate and pericyte coverage across tissues. Redirecting fibroblasts into this lineage is predicted to convert stiff, disorganized scar into an organized, compliant reinforcement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10836734/?utm_source=openai))
- Feasible, cell-specific delivery “address”: AAV vectors using periostin regulatory elements can restrict expression to activated myofibroblast-like lineages in vivo after injury; CRISPRa has been deployed in vivo to activate lineage programs in fibroblasts, supporting translational plausibility. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/gt201620?utm_source=openai))
- Differentiation from prior art: Pericyte cell therapies in muscular dystrophy have focused on exogenous cell delivery and/or dystrophin expression, not in situ genetic reprogramming of endogenous fibrogenic cells into mural cells in DMD muscle. To our knowledge, this specific reprogramming objective has not been attempted preclinically in DMD. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6899334/?utm_source=openai))

Therapeutic design
- Modality: AAV-delivered, nuclease-dead CRISPR activation (dCas9-based transcriptional activator) targeted to NOTCH3 and a minimal set of cooperating mural genes (e.g., RGS5 or CSPG4 as accessory targets if needed for maturation). Use guide RNAs tiling endogenous promoters/enhancers to induce a pericyte-like state without genomic cuts.
- Cell-type targeting: Expression restricted by an activated-fibroblast regulatory cassette (periostin-driven), exploiting its robust induction in dystrophic muscle. To minimize expression in myofibers or liver, incorporate detargeting via post-transcriptional regulatory elements. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/gt201620?utm_source=openai))
- Dosing paradigm: Transient-on design (e.g., drug- or degron-controllable activator) to provide a finite “pulse” of fate switching, limiting sustained NOTCH3 activity once mural identity and pericellular matrix deposition are established.
- Anatomical action: Reprogrammed mural-like cells are expected to (i) ensheath capillaries adjacent to myofibers, improving perfusion and barrier function; and (ii) elaborate basement membrane components along the endomysium and myofiber surface, forming a compliant sleeve that reduces shear and microtears—indirectly alleviating calcium influx, inflammation, and downstream degeneration. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10836734/?utm_source=openai))

Key preclinical aims and decision points
- Aim 1: Establish human-relevant feasibility ex vivo.
  - Human DMD muscle stromal cells: demonstrate CRISPRa-driven upregulation of NOTCH3 program with acquisition of mural markers and matrix deposition; benchmark against fibrogenic programs to confirm fate switch rather than partial activation.
  - Go/no-go: robust induction of mural signature with concurrent suppression of profibrotic transcriptional programs relative to baseline FAPs.
- Aim 2: Demonstrate in vivo reprogramming and biomechanical benefit.
  - Models: mdx and D2-mdx mice at stages of established fibrosis.
  - Endpoints: increase in pericyte-like coverage of microvessels and myofibers; reduction in interstitial leak; decrease in fibrosis fraction; improved sarcolemmal integrity and specific force; reduced inflammatory infiltration.
  - Go/no-go: prespecified improvements in coverage, leak, fibrosis, and force versus AAV control.
- Aim 3: Specificity, safety, and reversibility.
  - Cell specificity: restrict expression to periostin+ populations; verify minimal activity in myofibers/endothelium/liver.
  - Safety: monitor for aberrant vascular constriction, neointima, or ectopic muralization; demonstrate shutdown of activator after the pulse.
  - Biodistribution/toxicology: large-animal studies to inform human dose bands and off-target risk.

Anticipated benefits across DMD pathophysiology
- Membrane stability: pericellular sleeve dampens mechanical stress, reducing microdamage and secondary calcium dysregulation.
- Vascular-inflammation axis: improved pericyte coverage reduces leakage and leukocyte trafficking, lowering chronic inflammation.
- Fibrosis remodeling: fate diversion shrinks the pool of matrix-secreting myofibroblasts, shifting deposited ECM toward organized basement membrane rather than disorganized scar.
- Regeneration support: a more permissive niche may enhance satellite cell function indirectly.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Incomplete fate conversion: prioritize NOTCH3 as the master switch; predefine minimal accessory targets if maturation markers lag.
- Off-target muralization: constrain by periostin regulatory control and transient expression; include clinical monitoring for vascular tone changes. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/gt201620?utm_source=openai))
- Heterogeneity of FAPs: stratify by single-cell profiling to identify reprogrammable subsets and refine targeting cassette to those states. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37599828/?utm_source=openai))

Path to translation
- Manufacturability: AAV supply chains and modular CRISPRa cassettes are established; periostin-targeted AAVs have precedent in vivo. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/gt201620?utm_source=openai))
- Regulatory positioning: non-nuclease CRISPRa lowers genotoxicity concerns; transient control aids risk management.
- Patient selection and endpoints: ambulatory and non-ambulatory cohorts with imaging and circulating biomarkers of fibrosis and leak; functional endpoints aligned with current DMD trial standards.

Novelty statement
This is a gene-activation therapy that does not correct or re-express dystrophin. It repurposes the fibrotic response by in situ reprogramming of endogenous activated fibroblasts/FAPs into mural cells to create a protective scaffold around myofibers and microvessels. To our knowledge, no preclinical or clinical DMD studies have attempted this specific, cell-directed fate conversion; prior pericyte strategies focused on cell transplantation and/or dystrophin delivery. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6899334/?utm_source=openai))

Milestones (18–30 months)
- Months 0–9: sgRNA and regulatory cassette optimization in human DMD stromal cells; select final vector design.
- Months 9–18: in vivo efficacy and safety in mdx and D2-mdx; finalize go/no-go.
- Months 18–30: GLP studies, human tissue transduction study, IND-enabling package.

Load-bearing references
- Periostin marks and drives fibrotic myofibroblasts in DMD muscle; periostin-targeted AAV restricts expression to activated fibroblast-like lineages in vivo. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10813341/?utm_source=openai))
- FAPs expand in DMD and are principal contributors to fibrosis; they are molecularly distinct from pericytes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8093402/?utm_source=openai))
- NOTCH3 is a defining regulator of mural (pericyte/SMC) identity and coverage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10836734/?utm_source=openai))
- In vivo CRISPRa can activate lineage programs in fibroblasts, supporting feasibility of non-nuclease gene activation for reprogramming. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42099387/?utm_source=openai))
- Existing pericyte strategies in muscular dystrophy emphasize transplantation and dystrophin, underscoring differentiation and novelty of the proposed in situ reprogramming. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6899334/?utm_source=openai))
