Title
State-modulated penetrance: a targeted blood assay and interpretable model that read out genotype-by-cell-state buffering at risk enhancers to resolve incomplete penetrance

Central hypothesis (question-as-hypothesis)
Among individuals carrying identical disease-risk SNPs, those who stay healthy exhibit protective regulatory response patterns at the risk-linked enhancers and pathways that buffer pathogenic gene programs. Measuring the per-person, genotype-conditioned stimulus–response of these enhancers in primary blood cells yields an interpretable predictor of who will develop disease and nominates protective programs that can be reinstated in susceptible individuals.

Atomic strategy
Reduce penetrance to a single measurable construct: the slope of enhancer activity at risk loci as cells traverse standardized immune states (stimuli), conditioned on SNP genotype. Protective carriers show flattened or inverted slopes (“cis-buffering”) at sensitizing states; affected carriers show steep, risk-concordant slopes. Estimate these slopes with a low-complexity, targeted multiomic assay and aggregate them into an interpretable, clinically actionable score.

Study focus and cohorts
- Initial disease domain: immune-mediated and cardiometabolic diseases (e.g., IBD, RA, T1D, CAD) where blood cell states are mechanistically relevant and accessible.
- Discovery cohort: matched discordant carrier pairs (same PRS decile and sharing prespecified risk haplotypes), one affected and one unaffected; n ≈ 200 pairs per disease.
- Validation cohort: independent carriers (n ≈ 500) followed prospectively for incident disease or flare.
- Inclusion: adults with banked genotype data; exclusion: immunosuppressive therapy at draw (discovery).

Assay: practical, integrated measurement in blood (RISK-STATE panel)
- Sample: 15–20 mL peripheral blood; isolate PBMCs.
- Standardized state panel (5 conditions): unstimulated; LPS (TLR4); IFN-β (type I IFN); IL-1β; anti-CD3/CD28 (TCR). Short stimulations (2 h for chromatin; 4 h for RNA).
- Targeted capture-ATAC-seq (per condition):
  - Hybrid-capture panel (~8–12k regions) covering fine-mapped risk SNPs and their linked enhancers/promoters across relevant cell types.
  - Reads provide both chromatin accessibility and allele-specific counts at heterozygous SNPs.
- Targeted RNA-seq (same samples, matched barcodes):
  - mRNA panel (~800–1,200 genes): sentinel cytokines, pathway reporters, and predicted target genes of the risk enhancers.
- Concurrent amplicon genotyping:
  - ~1,000 sentinel risk SNPs/haplotypes captured in the same libraries via feature barcoding to ensure per-sample genotype-state linkage (supplemented by existing array/WGS data).
- Lightweight cell-type deconvolution:
  - Either low-pass single-cell hashing in one condition or bulk marker-based deconvolution to estimate major PBMC subset proportions (monocytes, B, CD4, CD8, NK).
- Turnaround and cost targets:
  - Batched library prep; two sequencing lanes per 96 samples; per-patient consumables target <$300 at scale.

Primary features (per locus, per person)
- GxS slope: change in enhancer accessibility with stimulus intensity/dose (∆ accessibility vs baseline) signed by the risk allele’s predicted effect on TF motif(s).
- Allelic imbalance shift: deviation of risk-allele accessibility/expression from 50:50 under each stimulus (ΔAI), benchmarking expected motif disruption.
- Buffering index: observed GxS slope minus motif-predicted slope; negative values indicate protective buffering.
- State occupancy: fraction of cells (or deconvolved bulk signal) in sensitized states that expose the risk program.
- Pathway activity: targeted RNA module scores (e.g., NF-κB, JAK/STAT, AP-1, IRF).

Model: interpretable, moderate complexity
- Per-locus penetrance contribution: logistic link of disease status on [GxS slope, buffering index, ΔAI, state occupancy, pathway scores], with ridge penalty; fitted as conditional logistic regression within matched pairs.
- Subject-level Protective Regulatory Program (PRP) score: sum of per-locus contributions, grouped by pathway to yield pathway-resolved PRP components (e.g., “STAT1-axis buffering: high”).
- Output: overall risk classification (protected vs sensitized), top buffered/sensitized loci and pathways, and a minimal set of protective levers (TFs/pathways) inferred from coefficients.

Training and evaluation
- Discovery:
  - Fit the model on 70% of pairs; tune penalty by nested cross-validation minimizing pairwise misclassification; check calibration.
  - Test on held-out 30% pairs; primary metric: AUC and net reclassification improvement over PRS alone and PRS+clinical covariates.
  - Secondary: interpretability stability (concordance of top pathways across folds).
- Validation:
  - Prospective cohort; endpoints: incident diagnosis or flare within 24 months; decision-curve analysis for clinical utility.
  - Robustness checks: batch, site, and storage time; replicate subset with capillary blood microcollection.

Causal testing of protective patterns
- Nominate 2–3 top protective loci/pathways per disease from discovery.
- Patient-derived PBMCs (or iPSC-derived disease-relevant cells if needed):
  - CRISPRa/i at protective enhancers or pooled dCas9-based TF tethering to recreate buffering (flatten GxS slope).
  - Readouts: same targeted panel plus disease-relevant function (e.g., cytokine secretion, autoantibody production, foam cell formation).
  - Criterion: engineered buffering reduces pathogenic program readouts despite risk genotype.

Clinical translation plan
- Laboratory-developed test (LDT) prototype:
  - Single-tube, barcoded workflow; 5-condition mini-panel; automated library prep; CLIA-ready SOPs.
  - Report: PRP score; pathway-resolved protective deficits; suggested therapeutic axes (e.g., type I IFN dampening) aligned with approved drugs or lifestyle levers.
- Use cases:
  - Risk stratification among high-PRS carriers.
  - Monitoring: PRP dynamics pre/post therapy to detect restoration of protective buffering.
  - Trial enrichment: enroll sensitized carriers likely to benefit from pathway-specific agents.

Why this goes beyond PRS
- PRS is static; this system reads dynamic, genotype-conditioned regulatory responses that determine whether risk is realized.
- Outputs are mechanistic (locus and pathway-resolved buffering) and actionable (specific TF/pathway levers), not just aggregate allele counts.

Feasibility and complexity control
- Targeted panels keep sequencing depth, cost, and compute modest.
- Simple, regularized generalized linear models ensure interpretability and low computational load.
- Blood-based sampling and short ex vivo stimulations are routine and scalable.

Milestones
- M1 (0–6 months): finalize capture panels; pilot 40 pairs; confirm assay reproducibility; lock stimuli and timepoints.
- M2 (6–18 months): complete discovery in 200 pairs/disease; freeze model; nominate protective pathways.
- M3 (18–30 months): prospective validation (n ≈ 500); health-economic analysis.
- M4 (30–36 months): interventional CRISPRa/i validation and LDT prototype.

Risks and mitigations
- Disease where blood is a poor proxy: add minimal iPSC-derived cell module for validation; maintain blood-based predictor for clinical utility.
- Heterogeneity in stimuli response: use within-person baselines and matched pairs; include limited dose–response for two stimuli.
- Limited heterozygosity at sentinel SNPs: leverage linked enhancer targets and motif-based effect predictions; include haplotype-tagging amplicons.

Expected outcomes
- A practical, clinically translatable predictor that integrates SNP genotype with cell-state-dependent regulatory responses to explain and forecast incomplete penetrance.
- A short list of protective regulatory programs per disease, with experimental evidence that reinstating them can buffer genetic risk despite persistent risk alleles.

text:
Title
Stimulus-Resolved Allelic Imbalance to Learn and Transfer Protective Cell States (SRAIL)

Core hypothesis-question
Do resilient carriers of disease-risk SNPs exhibit stimulus-dependent, allele-specific compensatory responses at target genes that buffer pathogenic effects, and can these protective response patterns be read out from blood, scored to predict penetrance, and pharmacologically reproduced to prevent disease?

Atomic strategy
Use stimulus-resolved allele-specific expression (ASE) at genes linked to risk loci as a direct, interpretable readout of cis-regulatory buffering capacity. Resilient carriers maintain or restore balanced allelic output under defined perturbations; penetrant carriers fail to compensate. Learn the “resilient compensation signature” and design ex vivo drug nudges that shift at-risk individuals’ responses toward this resilient attractor.

Specific aims
1) Build a clinically practical assay that jointly captures genotype and induced cellular state from blood to quantify stimulus-resolved ASE at sentinel risk loci.
2) Derive an interpretable Penetrance Buffering Index (PBI) that separates resilient from penetrant carriers and identifies deficient “resilience modules.”
3) Nominate and validate preventive drug nudges that reproduce resilient compensation profiles ex vivo in at-risk carriers.

Study population
- Inclusion: Adults carrying established common risk variants for immune-mediated diseases (e.g., SLE/RA/IBD/psoriasis); oversample older unaffected carriers (putative resilient) and age/sex/ancestry-matched affected carriers.
- Discovery cohort: n=200 carriers (≈100 resilient, 100 affected).
- Validation cohort: n=300 carriers (blinded).
- Rationale for immune focus: blood accessibility, known context-specific eQTLs, and clinically relevant cytokine stimuli. The platform is general and can be reparameterized for other diseases with alternative stimuli.

Assay: integrated, moderate-complexity whole-blood platform
- Single blood draw, same tube set:
  a) Low-pass whole-genome sequencing (lpWGS, 0.5–1×) from buffy coat DNA to determine SNP genotypes and haplotypes at GWAS loci and exonic tags (cost-effective; <US$120/sample).
  b) Standardized ex vivo whole-blood challenges in duplicate wells for 0 h and 6 h with three minimal, orthogonal stimuli: TLR4 (LPS), type I IFN (IFN-β), and IL-1β. These span NF-κB and JAK/STAT axes implicated across immune diseases.
  c) Targeted UMI RNA sequencing (Capture-ASE panel; ~300 amplicons) from each condition to quantify:
     - Allele-specific expression at exonic tag SNPs in transcripts of genes mapped to ~100 sentinel GWAS loci (selected by fine-mapping + colocalized blood eQTLs).
     - Sentinel trans-regulators (e.g., STATs, NF-κB subunits, SOCS, IRF family) and druggable pathway effectors.
- “Simultaneous” genotype-state integration:
  - lpWGS provides genotype and haplotype phase per individual.
  - Capture-ASE provides state-dependent allelic readouts at time 0 h and 6 h.
  - Haplotype-aware ASE links noncoding risk alleles to exonic tags via phase, integrating genotype with induced cellular state in one analytical pass.
- Turnaround: 48 h lab workflow; sequencing on benchtop instrument; total consumables target ≤US$250/sample at scale.

Key derived features
- SRAIS (Stimulus-Resolved Allelic Imbalance Score) per locus l and stimulus s:
  SRAISl,s = logit(Alt/Ref at 6 h) − logit(Alt/Ref at 0 h), haplotype-aware.
  Interpretation: Positive magnitude indicates stress-exposed skew; resilient buffering trends toward 0.
- Transcript Response Index (TRI) per pathway p: Δlog2FC of small, curated pathway gene sets under each stimulus.
- Compact feature vector per individual: concatenation of SRAIS across loci × stimuli plus a few TRIs, yielding ≤500 interpretable features.

Modeling and interpretation
- Resilient Compensation Signature (RCS): centroid and covariance of SRAIS/TRI features learned from resilient carriers.
- Penetrance Buffering Index (PBI): 0–100 score computed as a scaled negative Mahalanobis distance to the RCS; higher = more resilient-like compensation. Provide:
  - Top deficient resilience modules (see below).
  - Locus-level contributions (waterfall chart) for clinician interpretability.
- Resilience modules: sparse factorization (nonnegative matrix factorization with k≈6–8) on SRAIS features to extract co-varying, stimulus-tuned modules mapping to TF/pathway families (e.g., IFN-STAT, NF-κB, glucocorticoid/NR3C1, PPAR/RXR, MAPK). Modules are annotated by motif enrichment at linked enhancers and by regulator expression within the panel.

Aim 1 outcomes
- Primary: Assay technical performance—allelic balance precision (binomial CI width) and replicate concordance (ICC>0.8).
- Secondary: Coverage—≥80% of participants with ≥60% sentinel loci informative for ASE via phased exonic tags.

Aim 2 outcomes
- Primary: PBI discriminates resilient vs affected carriers (AUC≥0.80 in validation; pre-registered analysis).
- Secondary: Calibration across ancestry strata; decision thresholds for “buffered,” “borderline,” “unbuffered.”
- Tertiary: Longitudinal stability of PBI (CV<15% over 3 months) and modulation by acute inflammation.

Aim 3: Learning preventive drug nudges from resilient carriers
- Drug nomination: Map deficient resilience modules to short, safe, mechanistically matched interventions (repurposed FDA-approved agents or nutraceuticals with pathway activity; e.g., low-dose JAK inhibitor, IL-1 pathway modulator, PPAR-γ agonist, RXR agonist, low-dose corticosteroid pulse, omega-3 PUFA).
- Ex vivo validation: In each at-risk, unbuffered individual (low PBI), repeat 6 h stimulation with a 10–12 compound mini-library at clinically reachable concentrations; compute Drug-Induced Resilience Shift (DIRS) = ΔPBI toward the resilient centroid and per-locus ΔSRAIS normalization.
- Down-selection: Nominate top 1–2 “resilience nudges” per person with maximal DIRS and minimal off-target TRI shifts.

Translational pilot
- Prospective observational arm: Enroll high-PRS carriers; baseline PBI; 12-month outcomes (flare rate, serologic markers). Test whether low PBI predicts events beyond PRS and clinical labs.
- Mechanistic n-of-1 crossover: In low-PBI carriers without active disease, short course (2–4 weeks) of the nominated nudge vs placebo, with pre/post ex vivo challenges. Primary endpoint: increase in PBI and SRAIS normalization ex vivo; secondary: safety and systemic biomarkers.
- Pragmatic preventive RCT (signal-finding): Low-PBI carriers randomized to standard care vs standard care plus low-risk nudge; monitor surrogate endpoints (e.g., interferon signature, CRP, flare proxies).

Design choices addressing constraints
- Moderate complexity: Whole-blood, three stimuli, targeted RNA panel, lpWGS once; simple linear statistics and sparse factorization; no single-cell required for clinical phase.
- Clinical translatability: Finger-prick or venous blood; 48 h turnaround; interpretable outputs (PBI, top deficient modules, locus-level drivers); cost target ≤US$250/sample.
- Beyond PRS: State- and allele-specific compensation readouts that are causal-proximal and actionable; PRS used only for enrichment, not as the predictive core.
- Integrated genotype-state measurement: Haplotype-aware, stimulus-resolved ASE couples risk allele context with induced cellular responses from the same sample/timepoint.

Locus and panel selection (discovery)
- Start with ~100 sentinel loci with strong fine-mapping and blood eQTL colocalization; prioritize those with:
  - Nearby exonic tag SNPs (MAF>0.1) to enable ASE phasing.
  - Established cytokine-response eQTLs.
  - Druggable regulatory context (annotated TF motifs; pathway membership).
- Update panel iteratively using discovery data to drop non-informative loci and add informative ones, keeping total amplicons ≤350.

Power and statistics
- Discovery: With n=200 and ~60 informative loci/participant, detect medium effect-size differences in SRAIS distributions between groups at FDR 5%.
- Validation: Pre-registered model; AUC with 95% CI; decision-curve analysis for clinical utility.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Limited ASE informativeness in some individuals: diversify loci; leverage phase to tag noncoding causal variants; fall back on TRI contributors where ASE sparse.
- Stimulus irrelevance for specific diseases: allow stimulus set expansion (swap IL-17A for psoriasis, GM-CSF for RA) while keeping panel count constant.
- Batch effects: UMIs, synthetic RNA standards, paired control/stim wells, and within-donor differencing (6 h − 0 h) reduce variance.

Milestones
- Month 0–6: Panel design, assay optimization, precision metrics.
- Month 7–18: Discovery cohort complete; RCS and initial PBI locked; preregistration of validation analysis.
- Month 19–30: Validation cohort complete; clinical-grade reporting; begin ex vivo drug screening.
- Month 31–42: n-of-1 crossover mechanistic study; finalize shortlist of preventive nudges.
- Month 43–60: Signal-finding preventive RCT initiation.

Deliverables
- A validated, low-cost blood assay and software that outputs PBI, deficient resilience modules, and driver loci.
- A reference Resilient Compensation Signature and open resilience modules for immune-mediated diseases.
- A ranked list of repurposable preventive drug nudges with ex vivo DIRS evidence and dosing hypotheses.

Success criteria
- PBI adds significant predictive value over PRS and clinical covariates for near-term disease activity or conversion.
- Ex vivo interventions reproducibly shift low-PBI profiles toward resilience with locus-level SRAIS normalization.
- Clinical pilot shows safety and biomarker improvement consistent with resilience induction, supporting a preventive medicine pathway.

text:
Title: Preventive Cell-State Reprogramming via Allele-Contextualized Response Profiling (ACRP)

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight):
Penetrance is governed less by static snapshots of cell state and more by how a risk-anchored regulatory module responds to brief, standardized nudges. Measuring allele-contextualized response elasticity of these modules in primary blood cell states identifies who is poised to get sick and reveals minimal, reversible interventions that restore resilience.

Hypothesis-question (merged):
Do brief, reversible perturbations reveal genotype-by-state response patterns that both (a) separate affected from unaffected risk-allele carriers and (b) nominate low-intensity interventions that shift vulnerable cells toward a resilient attractor, thereby preventing disease onset or flare?

Overview:
- Population: Carriers of fine-mapped disease-risk SNPs and matched non-carriers; both affected and unaffected carriers.
- Sample: Fresh peripheral blood (PBMCs), with rapid ex vivo derivations (e.g., monocyte-derived macrophages) where needed.
- Measurement: Single-cell targeted multi-marker expression with donor-anchored SNP genotype, under a panel of 1–2 hour reversible perturbations.
- Output: A per-individual Module Resilience Index (MRI) and an Intervention Match Score (IMS) that map to simple clinical levers (e.g., metabolic modulator, cytokine pathway nudge).
- Intervention principle: Short, reversible “nudges” that reshape response curves without permanent editing.

Specific Aims:
1) Build an allele-anchored, cell-state perturbation atlas in blood for priority risk modules.
2) Derive an interpretable Module Resilience Index (MRI) that integrates SNP genotype with state-dependent response and distinguishes affected vs. unaffected carriers.
3) Nominate and validate minimal prophylactic nudges that restore MRI in ex vivo n-of-1 assays, then test feasibility in a short prospective pilot.

Design and Methods:
- Risk module selection:
  - Curate 50–100 fine-mapped GWAS sentinel SNPs with strong blood eQTL/caQTL support and assign each to a compact “risk module” (8–12 genes) capturing the effector pathway (e.g., IL-23/STAT3 axis, PTPN22/TCR signaling, TNF/NF-κB, type I IFN, PPAR/FAO).
- Donor cohorts (n≈30/group initially):
  - Affected carriers (AC), unaffected carriers (UC), unaffected non-carriers (UN).
  - Pre-genotype donors (array/WGS). Hash-tag cells to link single cells to donors.
- Perturbation panel (brief, reversible; clinically relevant levers):
  - Cytokine cues (e.g., IL-1β, IL-23, IFN-α), TCR/BCR mimetics, metabolic nudges (2-DG, lactate, pyruvate, etomoxir-low), AHR ligand (kynurenine-low), HDACi-low (vorinostat microdose equivalent ex vivo), PPAR-δ agonist-low, mTORC1 nudge (rapa-low). Vehicle controls included.
  - 6–8 perturbations × 1–2 hours per donor; washout to verify reversibility on a subset.
- Readout (moderate complexity, interpretable):
  - Targeted single-cell RNA panel (≈150–200 genes): module genes, state markers (cell-type, activation, stress), immediate early genes, sentinel TFs; optional 20-plex oligo-tagged antibodies for phospho/activation markers in key subsets (CITE-lite).
  - Donor genotype integrated via hashing + pre-known SNPs; allele-specific expression leveraged where exonic SNPs exist.
  - 8–12k cells per donor across conditions using multiplexed droplet capture.
- Functional secondary assays (subset):
  - T cells: activation threshold, cytokine burst after standardized stimulation.
  - Monocyte/macrophage: LPS/TLR response magnitude; oxidative burst.
  - Purpose: link MRI shifts to tangible functional resilience.

Integrated modeling (simple, clinically interpretable):
- For each donor d, cell type c, module m, perturbation p:
  - Compute module activity A(d,c,m,p) as weighted sum of target genes (weights fixed from training via ridge regression).
  - Response elasticity E(d,c,m,p) = [A(d,c,m,p) − A(d,c,m,vehicle)] / dose(p).
  - Module Resilience Index MRI(d,c,m) = median_p [−|E| toward pathogenic direction] × stability factor S (variance penalty across perturbations).
  - Genotype integration: linear mixed model with fixed effects for genotype at m’s sentinel SNP(s), interaction with perturbation class, random effects for donor and batch.
- Classification:
  - Train a sparse logistic model on MRI features to separate AC vs. UC; calibrate on UN to avoid false positives.
- Intervention Match Score (IMS):
  - For each donor and module, IMS ranks perturbations that invert E toward healthy UC distribution with minimal dose and maximal reversibility.
  - IMS integrates safety priors and druggability (clinical familiarity, contraindications).

Proof-of-prevention workflow (ex vivo n-of-1):
- For donors with low MRI in specific modules, perform a 2×2 micro-dose matrix of top two IMS-ranked nudges for 2 hours, washout 2 hours:
  - Criterion for success: MRI normalization into UC range and improved functional assay readouts without residual activation post-washout.

Prospective micro-pilot (feasibility):
- Unaffected carriers with persistently low MRI randomized 1:1 to 4-week low-intensity regimen vs. placebo:
  - Examples: low-dose PPAR-δ agonist; intermittent fasting-mimetic schedule; vitamin D repletion if VDR module implicated.
  - Primary endpoint: ΔMRI toward resilient profile ex vivo at weeks 2 and 4.
  - Secondary: safety, inflammatory biomarker panel, flare proxies (disease-dependent).

Novelty beyond PRS:
- Moves from static genotype-based risk to dynamic, allele-contextualized response phenotyping that both predicts and prescribes.
- MRI and IMS are causal-leaning, mechanism-tied scores derived from controlled perturbation-response, not correlation-weighted SNP aggregates.

Clinical translatability and practicality:
- Sample: blood only. Turnaround: 48–72 hours from draw to MRI/IMS.
- Cost discipline: targeted panels, donor pooling via hashing, 6–8 perturbations, 150–200 genes; projected consumables ≈$250–$400 per donor-run at scale.
- Outputs: per-patient MRI heatmap by cell type and module; IMS-ranked, low-complexity interventions with dose guidance derived from ex vivo curves.
- Interpretability: slopes and deltas on module activity; clear linkage to known pathways.

Milestones:
- M1 (Months 0–6): Build targeted panel; validate perturbation reproducibility; technical pilot (n=15 donors).
- M2 (Months 6–18): Case-control atlas (n=90 donors); lock MRI/IMS models; preregister analysis.
- M3 (Months 18–24): Ex vivo n-of-1 rescue validation (n=40 carriers).
- M4 (Months 24–30): Micro-pilot prophylaxis (n=40 carriers); finalize clinical assay spec.

Risk management:
- Heterogeneity across diseases: start with autoimmune-leaning modules where blood is disease-proximal; extend modules iteratively.
- Batch effects: donor hashing, balanced design, mixed models; technical replicates.
- Overfitting: penalized models, nested cross-validation, external replication set.
- Safety of nudges: prioritize agents with established human safety; use ex vivo dose-response and reversibility gating before any in vivo test.

Success criteria:
- Statistical separation of AC vs. UC using MRI with AUC≥0.80 in discovery and ≥0.75 in replication.
- At least 50% of low-MRI carriers achieve MRI normalization ex vivo with top-1 IMS nudge.
- Feasibility pilot shows significant ΔMRI vs. placebo at 4 weeks with no safety signal.

Deliverables:
- An end-to-end, moderate-complexity assay that integrates genotype with state-dependent cellular response to provide two clinical outputs: (1) a mechanistically grounded penetrance-resolving risk readout (MRI), and (2) a personalized, reversible prevention lever (IMS) suitable for low-burden prophylaxis.

text:
Title
Respiratory-Entrainment to Induce a Sleep-Like Recovery State During Wakefulness Under Time-Restricted Sleep

Hypothesis/Question
Can scheduled, nasal, exhale-biased slow breathing during wakefulness induce a physiologically verifiable recovery state—approximating that achieved after sufficient sleep—across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes in individuals undergoing time-restricted sleep?

Atomic Strategy (single perturbation)
Exploit respiration as a master regulator. Impose brief bouts of nasal-only, exhale-biased slow breathing at ~0.1 Hz to synchronously:
- upshift vagal tone and downshift sympathetic/noradrenergic drive,
- increase respiration-driven cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pulsatility and perivascular exchange,
- stabilize CO2/pH-cerebrovascular dynamics,
- entrain limbic-prefrontal oscillations,
thereby engaging endogenous restoration mechanisms across the four axes without extending total sleep time.

Study Design
- Design: Randomized, counterbalanced, three-period crossover.
- Periods (7 days each; 7-day washouts):
  1) Well-rested baseline: 8 h time-in-bed (TIB) nightly (establish each participant’s “sufficient-sleep” reference).
  2) Restricted sleep + Respiratory-Entrainment (RE): 4.5 h TIB nightly + daytime RE protocol.
  3) Restricted sleep + Sham control: 4.5 h TIB nightly + time- and attention-matched sham breathing.
- Participants: n=48 healthy adults (21–45 y), habitual 7–9 h sleep, no cardiopulmonary, sleep, psychiatric, or inflammatory disorders; caffeine/alcohol standardized.
- Setting: Hybrid in-lab (days 1, 7) and ambulatory (days 2–6) with continuous compliance monitoring.

Intervention: Respiratory-Entrainment (RE) Protocol
- Breathing pattern: nasal-only; 5.5 breaths/min; 4 s inhale, 7 s exhale; no breath holds; diaphragmatic focus.
- Posture/context: lateral/semi-lateral (30–45°) or supported side-lying; eyes closed; quiet, dim environment; no napping permitted.
- Bout structure: 6 bouts/day, 7 minutes each, spaced ~2–3 h during wakefulness (total 42 min/day).
- Guidance and monitoring: metronome/pacer app; real-time respiratory inductance plethysmography; SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 spot checks in-lab.
- Prohibitions: no stimulants or naps; standardized meals and activity.
- Sham control: mouth breathing at 12 breaths/min, upright seated posture, same duration/schedule, matched expectancy/coach contact.

Primary Outcome
- Recovery State Index (RSI): mean z-score composite (relative to each participant’s well-rested baseline week) across:
  1) Neurocognitive: psychomotor vigilance test (PVT lapses), 3-back accuracy, task-switching cost, antisaccade error rate.
  2) Metabolic: 2-h OGTT incremental AUC, waking respiratory exchange ratio (RER), 24-h CGM glycemic variability (CV).
  3) Immune: 24-h plasma IL-6 AUC, high-sensitivity CRP, ex vivo LPS-stimulated TNF-α.
  4) Autonomic: high-frequency HRV (RMSSD, HF power), spontaneous baroreflex sensitivity.

Key Secondary and Mechanistic Outcomes
- Cerebrospinal/vascular dynamics: MRI phase-contrast CSF flow pulsatility index during paced breathing; internal jugular vein ultrasound (cross-sectional area/flow) pre/post bout.
- Noradrenergic/autonomic markers: pupillometry (baseline diameter and task-evoked dilation), salivary alpha-amylase diurnal slope, plasma MHPG/metanephrines.
- Neural oscillations and coupling: high-density EEG during bouts (frontal theta/delta; breathing–EEG phase coherence).
- Metabolites: plasma/urine lactate and kynurenine/tryptophan ratio.
- Subjective (secondary): Karolinska Sleepiness Scale; fatigue and mood scales.

Experimental Procedures
- Baseline week: establish individual “sufficient sleep” reference for all outcomes.
- Restricted weeks: identical sleep opportunity (4.5 h TIB) with either RE or sham; identical diet, light exposure targets, and physical activity prescriptions.
- Daily schedule (restricted weeks):
  - Morning fasted labs: glucose/insulin, cytokines, HRV, pupillometry, brief cognitive battery.
  - Midday lab (Days 1 and 7): MRI/ultrasound and EEG during a standardized breathing bout.
  - Field days (ambulatory): guided RE or sham sessions; CGM, HRV wearables; spot saliva samples.
- Safety: adverse event monitoring; protocols to abort sessions if dizziness, dyspnea, or SpO2 < 94%.

Statistical Plan
- Primary test: Mixed-effects model (participant random intercepts) comparing RSI across conditions; factors = condition (RE vs sham vs baseline), period, sequence; planned contrasts:
  1) Noninferiority of RE vs baseline (margin 0.3 SD).
  2) Superiority of RE vs sham (target Δ ≥ 0.4 SD).
- Axis-level analyses: family-wise error controlled; each axis must show directionally consistent improvement under RE vs sham.
- Mediation: proportion of RSI improvement explained by changes in HF-HRV and CSF pulsatility (path analysis).
- Power: assuming d=0.5 for RSI RE–sham, 36 completers yield 80% power (α=0.05); recruit 48 allowing attrition.

Predicted Mechanistic Chain (to be tested)
Slow nasal, exhale-biased breathing → increased vagal afferent signaling and reduced LC-noradrenergic tone → higher HF-HRV and baroreflex sensitivity; reduced cortisol/sympathoadrenal output → improved insulin action and lower glycemic variability; cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex reducing IL-6/TNF-α; enhanced respiration-driven CSF pulsatility and perivascular exchange supporting metabolite clearance → stabilized prefrontal-limbic oscillatory control and sustained attention → composite RSI approaches sufficient-sleep baseline despite restricted TIB.

Inclusion/Exclusion and Controls
- Include: BMI 18.5–30; regular diurnal schedule.
- Exclude: panic disorder, uncontrolled asthma/COPD, OSA risk (STOP-Bang ≥3), shift work, pregnancy, beta-blockers or anti-inflammatories.
- Controls: expectancy-matched coaching; identical contact time; standardize meals (isocaloric, 50/30/20 C/F/P), caffeine 0 mg, alcohol 0 g.

Criteria for Success
- Primary: RSI during RE week is within 0.3 SD of individual sufficient-sleep baseline and improves ≥0.4 SD vs sham.
- Secondary: Each axis shows significant improvement vs sham; mediation shows ≥30% of RSI improvement via HF-HRV and/or CSF pulsatility pathways.

Deliverables and Translational Path
- Open protocol, pacer software, annotated dataset.
- If successful: deploy a 40–45 min/day RE protocol as a scalable, physiology-grounded countermeasure for operational settings requiring time-restricted sleep, without pharmacological stimulants or increased TIB.

Risks and Mitigations
- Hyperventilation/dizziness: exhale bias, no holds, real-time coaching; session abort rules.
- Sleep intrusion: eyes closed but monitored; micro-sleeps flagged; sensitivity analyses excluding such bouts.
- Interindividual variability: stratify by baseline HRV and nasal patency; per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses.

Timeline
- Months 0–3: tooling, training, pilot feasibility (n=10).
- Months 4–15: main trial enrollment and completion.
- Months 16–18: analyses, dissemination.

Summary
A single, physiologically grounded perturbation—structured slow nasal, exhale-biased breathing—aims to entrain autonomic, cerebrovascular, and neural oscillatory processes that underpin sleep’s restorative functions, producing multi-axis recovery during wakefulness under restricted sleep.

text:
Title: Sleep-Mimetic Ketone Clamp (SMKC) to Induce Systemic Maintenance During Wakefulness Under Sleep Restriction

Atomic insight
A brief, daytime clamp of circulating beta-hydroxybutyrate (βHB) to deep-sleep–like levels (2.0–3.0 mM) during quiet wakefulness imposes a whole-body low-flux, high-NAD+ metabolic state that activates autophagy/mitophagy, proteostasis, anti-inflammatory pathways, and parasympathetic tilt. This single metabolic perturbation “tricks” cells across brain, immune, metabolic, and autonomic systems into executing the maintenance programs normally engaged in deep non-REM sleep, without extending total sleep time.

Hypothesis (inseparable from goal)
In adults experiencing chronic partial sleep restriction, a 60–90 minute βHB clamp delivered during wakefulness will induce a multi-system recovery state approximating sufficient sleep, normalizing neurocognitive performance, restoring metabolic and immune homeostasis, and rebalancing autonomic function.

Specific aims
1) Neurocognitive axis: Determine whether SMKC restores psychomotor vigilance, working memory, and wake EEG homeostatic markers compared with isocaloric carbohydrate control.
2) Metabolic and immune axes: Test whether SMKC improves substrate utilization and insulin sensitivity and suppresses innate inflammatory activation during sleep restriction.
3) Autonomic axis and mechanisms: Quantify SMKC effects on parasympathetic dominance and catecholamines, and identify mediators (NAD+/NADH, AMPK–mTOR signaling, autophagy, UPRmt, epigenetic acetylation) that link βHB to multi-axial recovery.

Design and methods
- Population: N=60 healthy adults (21–45 y), habitual 7–9 h sleepers, no metabolic, cardiovascular, neurologic, or sleep disorders.
- Overall design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial with two 5-night sleep-restriction blocks (time in bed 5 h/night; 00:30–05:30), separated by 10-day washout. A separate 7-night well-rested baseline (8 h TIB; 23:00–07:00) precedes the trial to define each participant’s personal “sufficient sleep” reference.
- Interventions (each block, Days 2–5):
  • SMKC: Oral d-βHB monoester titrated to reach 2.0–3.0 mM within 15 min, maintained for 60–90 min via micro-boluses every 10–15 min, guided by fingerstick βHB.
  • Control: Isocaloric, flavor-matched carbohydrate drink with identical dosing schedule.
- Timing/context:
  • Clamp window: 10:30–12:00, during quiet wakefulness in dim light. No naps, no stimulants, standardized posture and minimal movement.
  • Pre-clamp: Overnight fast from 22:00; standardized low-glycemic breakfast at 07:30 (300 kcal) to avoid severe hunger; clamp proceeds only if glucose 70–110 mg/dL and insulin <15 µU/mL.
- Safety monitoring: Cap βHB <4.0 mM; serial glucose, bicarbonate, anion gap; symptom check for GI upset or dizziness. Exclusions include diabetes, CKD, pregnancy, eating disorders, and acid–base disorders.

Outcomes and measurements
Primary endpoint
- Multi-Axis Recovery Index (MARI): composite z-score equally weighting four domains, benchmarked to the individual’s well-rested baseline.
  1) Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT lapses and median RT), 2-back d′, drift–diffusion parameters; resting wake EEG (eyes-closed) theta power and aperiodic spectral slope; Karolinska Sleepiness Scale.
  2) Metabolic: Indirect calorimetry respiratory exchange ratio (RER), mixed-meal tolerance test (MMTT) at T+2 h with glucose/insulin AUC, morning HOMA-IR, continuous glucose monitoring metrics.
  3) Immune: Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, hsCRP; ex vivo PBMC NLRP3 inflammasome activation (LPS/ATP-stimulated IL-1β release), monocyte CD14/CD16 distribution.
  4) Autonomic: 24 h HRV (RMSSD, HF power), LF/HF ratio, pupillary unrest index, baroreflex sensitivity, plasma norepinephrine/epinephrine, salivary alpha-amylase.
Secondary/mechanistic endpoints
- PBMC NAD+/NADH ratio; SIRT1/3 activity.
- AMPK–mTORC1 readouts (p-AMPKThr172, p-S6KThr389, 4E-BP1).
- Autophagy/mitophagy flux (LC3-II/I, p62 turnover with ex vivo bafilomycin; mitophagy reporter in a PBMC subset).
- UPRmt markers (ATF5, HSP60, LONP1), mitochondrial membrane potential and ROS.
- Epigenetic signaling: Histone acetylation (H3K9ac) as HDAC inhibition readout.
- Adenosine and uric acid levels; lactate, free fatty acids, cortisol/ACTH rhythm.

Assessment schedule
- Each clamp day: Pre (T−30 min), end-of-clamp (T+0–30 min), short-term (T+2 h), sustained (T+6 h) assessments for all primary outcomes; mechanistic blood draws at Pre, T+0, and T+2.
- Well-rested baseline week: identical battery on a matched day/time to define the personal “sufficient sleep” target.

Analytical plan
- Mixed-effects models with condition (SMKC vs control), day, and their interaction as fixed effects; subject as random intercept.
- Primary test: superiority of SMKC over control on MARI at T+0–2 h and T+6 h during restriction.
- Target of approximation: SMKC achieves ≥70% restoration toward the individual’s well-rested MARI at T+0–2 h, with ≥50% retained at T+6 h.
- Mediation analyses: βHB → NAD+/NADH → AMPK↓mTORC1↑autophagy/UPRmt → domain outcomes; autonomic mediation via HRV and catecholamines.
- Dose–response (exploratory): within SMKC, relate achieved βHB AUC and NAD+ change to recovery magnitude.

Predicted system-wide causal chain
- βHB clamp raises cellular NAD+/NADH and inhibits class I HDACs → activates SIRT1/3 and FOXO programs → inhibits mTORC1 and activates AMPK → increases autophagy/mitophagy and UPRmt; reduces NLRP3 inflammasome activity and proinflammatory cytokines; shifts fuel preference (lower RER) and improves insulin action; increases adenosine tone and parasympathetic dominance (higher RMSSD/HF, lower catecholamines) → stabilizes cortical networks (flatter aperiodic slope normalization, lower wake theta) and improves vigilance/working memory.

Power and sample size
- Assuming a standardized effect of 0.45 on MARI (SMKC vs control), α=0.05, 1−β=0.9, within-subject correlation 0.5, requires 52 completers; enroll 60 to allow 15% attrition.

Risk mitigation
- Monitor for hypoglycemia and acidosis; provide rescue carbohydrate if glucose <65 mg/dL or symptomatic.
- GI tolerance managed by divided micro-boluses; stop rule for persistent nausea.
- Daily medical oversight during restriction.

Falsification criteria and contingency
- If SMKC fails to move MARI ≥30% toward well-rested baseline, or if mechanistic signals (↑NAD+, ↓p-S6K, ↑LC3-II flux) are absent, the atomic premise is rejected.
- If only one axis improves, redesign focuses on βHB level/duration mapping (1.0, 2.0, 3.0 mM; 45 vs 90 min) to test temporal and dose specificity.
- If autonomic outcomes do not shift despite metabolic/immune restoration, add a mechanistically minimal vagal co-modulation (e.g., paced breathing during clamp) in a follow-up trial while keeping βHB as the sole biochemical driver.

Translational outcome
- Protocolized “maintenance pulse” deployable in shift work and operational settings: 60–90 min daytime βHB clamp during wakefulness to approximate recovery normally requiring additional sleep, without stimulants and without extending total sleep time. Success would define a physiologically grounded, single-lever strategy that restores four homeostatic axes under real-world sleep restriction.

Title
Recovery via Resonant Slow Oscillation Entrainment (ReSOE): Inducing a sleep-recovery state during wakefulness by driving the 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal–CSF oscillator

Premise
After sleep restriction, the organism executes a coordinated “recovery program” during early non-REM (NREM) sleep characterized by:
- Low noradrenergic tone and high vagal drive
- Large-amplitude 0.05–0.15 Hz neural–vascular–CSF oscillations that enhance glymphatic/lymphatic clearance
- Rebalancing of autonomic setpoints, energy metabolism, and inflammatory tone
Hypothesis and goal are inseparable: If we can selectively and safely impose the sleep-recovery control parameter—the global 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal–CSF resonance—during wakefulness, we can trigger the same restoration signals across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes without extending total sleep time.

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Drive the organism into baroreflex–vagal resonance at ~0.1 Hz to downshift central noradrenergic setpoint and synchronize low-frequency neural–vascular–CSF oscillations, thereby invoking the body’s intrinsic “recovery program” while awake.

Central hypothesis
A 20–40 minute session of closed-loop 0.1 Hz resonance breathing (extended exhalation), delivered in lateral decubitus posture and titrated to each individual’s baroreflex resonance, will:
- Neurocognitive: restore sustained attention and working memory via reduced locus coeruleus output and enhanced glymphatic clearance proxies
- Metabolic: improve insulin sensitivity and substrate switching via increased vagal efference and reduced sympathetic hepatic output
- Immune: suppress proinflammatory cytokines via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway and improved waste/antigen clearance
- Autonomic: increase vagal tone, baroreflex sensitivity, and stabilize blood pressure variability without sedation

Specific aims
1) Establish that ReSOE while awake reproduces sleep-recovery signatures
- Show induction of coupled 0.1 Hz neural (EEG slow-oscillation coupling), vascular (Mayer waves), and CSF/lymphatic (MRI/fNIRS proxies) dynamics with concurrent downshift in noradrenergic proxies (pupillometry, salivary alpha-amylase).
2) Test whole-organism restoration after acute sleep restriction
- Determine whether a single ReSOE session normalizes composite outcomes across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes vs. sham.
3) Identify mediators and dose–response
- Quantify whether vagal activation and noradrenergic downshift statistically mediate multi-axis recovery and map the minimal effective “oscillation dose” (time-in-resonance, coherence).

Study design
- Participants: Healthy adults, 18–45, undergo a standardized partial sleep restriction protocol (two consecutive nights, 4 h time-in-bed, 02:00–06:00).
- Design: Randomized, sham-controlled, crossover (washout ≥7 days).
- Intervention (ReSOE):
  - 0.1 Hz resonance breathing (6 breaths/min) with inhale:exhale ≈ 4 s:6 s, nasal, diaphragmatic
  - Posture: lateral decubitus (side-lying) to favor intracranial venous outflow and perivascular clearance
  - Closed-loop titration: continuous HRV-guided feedback to lock breathing to individual baroreflex resonance frequency (0.08–0.12 Hz), maximizing LF-HRV and baroreflex sensitivity
  - Duration: 30 minutes, eyes open, quietly awake
- Sham control:
  - Spontaneous breathing with neutral audio, seated posture; matched time and experimenter contact
- State monitoring: wakefulness verified by EEG/eye tracking; exclude microsleeps

Outcomes and measurements
Primary composite endpoint (post-session vs. pre-session, and vs. sham; standardized z-score across domains):
- Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT lapses), n-back accuracy/RT, Stroop interference; subjective sleepiness (KSS)
- Autonomic: HRV (RMSSD, HF power), baroreflex sensitivity, blood pressure variability (LF power), pupil baseline and reactivity
- Metabolic: oral glucose tolerance test (AUC glucose/insulin), HOMA-IR, fasting free fatty acids, RQ via indirect calorimetry (resting substrate use)
- Immune/inflammatory: plasma IL-6, TNF-α, hsCRP; leukocyte distribution (NLR), monocyte HLA-DR; exosomal inflammation markers
Key mechanistic/proxy measures:
- Noradrenergic setpoint: salivary alpha-amylase, resting pupil diameter, plasma NE (subset)
- Neural–vascular–CSF coupling: fMRI or fNIRS indices of low-frequency global signal; CSF inflow proxy (MRI inflow/ALPS index when feasible); transcranial Doppler (MCA velocity LFOs); respiratory–hemodynamic phase coupling; neck lymphatic Doppler (exploratory)
- Glymphatic/waste clearance proxies: plasma neurofilament light, Aβ42/40, GFAP (exploratory kinetic changes)

Procedures and timeline
- Baseline (well-rested day): characterize individual resonance frequency and response curves; establish within-subject baselines.
- Sleep restriction phase: two nights of 4 h time-in-bed.
- Intervention day (08:00–16:00): pre-test battery; 30-min ReSOE or sham; immediate post-test (T+0 h), and follow-ups at T+2 h and evening; next-morning carryover testing after a 4 h restricted sleep night to assess durability.
- Crossover after washout.

Mechanistic predictions
- ReSOE will increase LF-HRV and baroreflex sensitivity ≥25% vs. sham; reduce baseline pupil diameter and salivary alpha-amylase; strengthen 0.1 Hz neural–vascular–CSF coupling indices.
- Improvements in PVT and n-back will correlate with time-in-resonance and decreases in noradrenergic proxies.
- Insulin sensitivity (OGTT-derived) will improve acutely (reduced glucose and insulin AUC) and track with vagal indices.
- IL-6 and TNF-α will decline over 2–6 h post-intervention proportional to HF-HRV gains.

Statistical plan
- N=40 completers for 90% power to detect a 0.5 SD difference in the composite endpoint (within-subject crossover, α=0.05).
- Mixed-effects models with random intercepts for subject; mediation analysis (structural equation modeling) to test vagal and noradrenergic pathways; dose–response modeled by coherence-weighted time-in-resonance.

Safety and fidelity
- Continuous SpO2, BP, and EEG vigilance monitoring; abort if presyncope/hypocapnia.
- Training session ensures diaphragmatic technique; adherence quantified by respiratory–HRV coherence.

Falsification criteria
- Failure to induce 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory coherence and baroreflex sensitivity increase
- Absence of coupling between induced oscillations and noradrenergic downshift
- No superiority over sham on the composite endpoint and on at least three of four axes

Translational path
- If efficacious, develop an at-home protocol (guided 0.1 Hz breathing with HRV-based biofeedback) deliverable during work breaks under time-restricted sleep.
- Biomarker-guided personalization: adjust target frequency and exhale bias to maximize individual recovery index.

Why this is physiologically grounded
- Targets a single global control variable—the 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal–CSF oscillator—that coordinates neural, vascular, and clearance dynamics characteristic of early NREM recovery.
- Leverages intrinsic restoration pathways (glymphatic/lymphatic flow, noradrenergic setpoint downshift, autonomic rebalancing, cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex, metabolic parasympathetic effects) rather than masking symptoms.

Success criterion (operational)
Induction of a sustained recovery state during wakefulness, defined as a ≥0.5 SD improvement over sham in the multi-axis composite within 2 hours post-session, with concurrent evidence of neural–vascular–CSF 0.1 Hz coupling and noradrenergic downshift.

Title
Synthetic Micro-Rest via Closed-Loop Cardiorespiratory–Vagal Entrainment to Restore Multi-Axis Homeostasis During Sleep Restriction

Atomic hypothesis
Brief, repeated induction of a high-vagal/low-sympathetic “micro-rest” state during wakefulness—achieved by synchronizing resonance-frequency breathing with exhalation-locked auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) in a closed loop—will trigger the same downstream restorative programs normally engaged during non-REM slow-wave sleep (SWS), yielding multi-axis recovery of neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic function without extending total sleep time.

Rationale (single-system lever: autonomic set-point)
- The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is a master regulator that coordinates cortical arousal (locus coeruleus–noradrenergic tone), glymphatic driving forces (low-frequency vasorespiratory pulsatility), metabolic partitioning (hepatic and pancreatic vagal efferents), and immune tone (cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex).
- SWS is characterized by high vagal tone, reduced sympathetic drive, low noradrenergic signaling, enhanced low-frequency cardiorespiratory oscillations, pulsatile CSF movement, and anti-inflammatory/insulin-sensitizing shifts. Replicating this autonomic signature in ultra-brief bouts should recruit core restoration mechanisms without sleep.
- Resonance breathing (~0.1 Hz; 6 breaths/min) amplifies respiratory sinus arrhythmia and baroreflex gain; exhalation-timed taVNS phasically suppresses locus coeruleus output and activates the inflammatory reflex, jointly reproducing the SWS-like autonomic state.

Specific aims
1) Demonstrate that closed-loop resonance breathing plus exhalation-locked taVNS (RB+taVNS) induces a reproducible “micro-rest” signature: increased HF-HRV/RMSSD, elevated baroreflex sensitivity, reduced salivary alpha-amylase/pupil-indexed LC tone, and augmented intracranial low-frequency pulsatility.
2) Test whether repeated 5–7 min RB+taVNS bouts during restricted sleep restore function across four axes versus sham, matching the magnitude of restoration seen after sufficient sleep.
3) Quantify dose–response and optimize stimulation-breathing phase, duty cycle, and bout spacing to maximize recovery while preserving wakefulness and performance.

Study design
- Population: Healthy adults, 18–45, undergoing 3-night sleep restriction (time-in-bed 4 h/night) with daytime wake protocols.
- Randomized, double-blind, parallel groups (n≈40/group): RB+taVNS (active); RB+sham-taVNS; free-breathing+sham-taVNS (control). Separate sufficient-sleep reference cohort (8 h/night; no intervention) anchors “recovery equivalence.”
- Intervention schedule: 5–7 min micro-rest bouts every 60–90 min across 12 h wake, total 8–10 bouts/day, for 3 consecutive days of restriction.

Intervention (single atomic strategy)
- Closed-loop controller guides paced breathing at individualized resonance frequency determined at baseline (0.08–0.12 Hz). Photoplethysmography (PPG) and respiratory belt inform real-time phase estimation of respiratory cycle and RSA amplitude.
- taVNS delivered to cymba conchae, charge-balanced biphasic pulses, exhalation-locked (late exhale), 20–25 Hz, 200–300 μs, intensity titrated to strong-but-comfortable sensation. Stimulation is phasic (exhalation windows), not tonic, to maximize LC suppression while limiting sedation.
- Safety rails: continuous BP/HR monitoring, drowsiness checks (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale), abort criteria for hypotension or presyncopal symptoms.

Primary outcomes and measures
- Composite Recovery Index (CRI) prespecified as the mean z-score across axis-specific primary endpoints relative to baseline and sufficient-sleep reference.

Neurocognitive axis
- Primary: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) lapses and median RT; 2-back d′; task-switch cost.
- Secondary: Pupillometry (tonic diameter, cue-evoked dilation), EEG during micro-rest (frontocentral aperiodic slope, delta/theta power without sleep onset), MRS cerebral lactate pre/post-bout.

Metabolic axis
- Primary: Oral mixed-meal tolerance incremental AUC for glucose and insulin; CGM daytime mean glucose and time-in-range; fasting HOMA-IR.
- Secondary: Indirect calorimetry respiratory exchange ratio (RER) shift during/after bouts; adiponectin and free fatty acids.

Immune axis
- Primary: Plasma IL-6 and TNF-α day curves; high-sensitivity CRP.
- Secondary: Ex vivo LPS-stimulated cytokine production (TNF-α/IL-1β) from whole blood; leukocyte transcriptomic inflammatory modules.

Autonomic axis
- Primary: HF-HRV (log ms2) and RMSSD during bouts; spontaneous baroreflex sensitivity; LF/HF for completeness.
- Secondary: Salivary alpha-amylase; skin conductance level; finger temperature rebound; orthostatic BP variability.

Putative mechanistic intermediates
- Intracranial/venous pulsatility: phase-contrast MRI CSF flow (subset) or fNIRS low-frequency hemoglobin oscillations; internal jugular venous flow ultrasound.
- Catecholamine proxy: α2-agonist–like signature via decreased pupil diameter and reduced startle reactivity without subjective sedation.
- Vagal reflex engagement: IL-1RA increase; HRV–cytokine coupling.

Procedures
- Baseline day (normal sleep): determine resonance frequency; collect all measures.
- Restriction days 1–3: deliver RB+taVNS or control bouts on fixed schedule; collect repeated measures across the day; morning mixed-meal test on days 1 and 3; immune sampling at standardized times.
- Sufficient-sleep reference cohort: identical measurement cadence without intervention.

Analysis plan
- Primary: ANCOVA of CRI day 3 with baseline covariates; noninferiority margin versus sufficient-sleep reference set at Δ=0.2 SD.
- Axis-specific confirmatory tests with multiplicity control (Holm–Bonferroni).
- Mediation models linking autonomic changes (HF-HRV, BRS) to improvements in each axis.
- Dose–response: mixed models of bout count, RSA gain, and exhalation-lock precision versus CRI.

Success criteria
- RB+taVNS achieves CRI noninferior to sufficient-sleep reference (Δ≤0.2 SD) and superior to both controls (p<0.05).
- Each axis shows clinically meaningful improvement: ≥25% reduction in PVT lapses; ≥15% decrease in glucose iAUC; ≥20% reduction in IL-6; ≥0.5 SD increase in HF-HRV versus control.
- Wakefulness preserved: no increase in unintentional sleep episodes; stable or improved subjective alertness.

Feasibility and safety
- Prior human data support taVNS safety and ability to increase vagal tone; resonance breathing is low risk.
- Monitoring plan: adverse events, orthostatic vitals, near-continuous HRV; blinded safety committee.

Parameter optimization (Aim 3)
- Explore exhalation-phase timing jitter (±50–150 ms), stimulation trains (duty 30–70%), and bout spacing (45–120 min) with Bayesian adaptive design to maximize CRI and minimize sleepiness.

Potential failure modes and contingencies
- If taVNS intensity induces sleepiness: reduce duty cycle, shift to right-auricular placement, or lower frequency (5–10 Hz) while preserving exhalation locking.
- If breathing adherence is poor: biofeedback with RSA-gain target and haptic pacing; accept sub-resonant frequencies if RSA > baseline by ≥30%.
- If glymphatic proxies do not change: extend bout length to 10 min or add brief lateral recumbency during bouts while maintaining the same atomic strategy.

Translational endpoint
- A wearable, closed-loop protocol that operationalizes “synthetic micro-rest” during wakefulness for shift workers, clinicians, and military personnel under time-restricted sleep, grounded in a single physiological lever: autonomic set-point entrainment.

text:
Title
Wakeful Torpor: Inducing a reversible, parasympathetic-dominant hypometabolic state via α2A-adrenergic setpoint downshift to restore multisystem homeostasis after sleep loss

Central Hypothesis
A tonic, sub-sedative reduction of locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic output during wakefulness—achieved with selective α2A-adrenergic agonism—will recreate the permissive milieu that enables sleep’s restorative functions. This LC “setpoint downshift” will (i) normalize neurocognitive control by reducing cortical noise and enabling synaptic renormalization, (ii) lower whole-body metabolic rate and improve substrate handling, (iii) suppress proinflammatory signaling via sympathoimmune coupling, and (iv) shift autonomic balance toward vagal predominance. The resulting wakeful torpor approximates recovery attained after sufficient sleep, without adding sleep time.

Atomic Strategy (single insight)
Exploit LC-NE as a global master switch: a controlled, wake-maintaining α2A-adrenergic agonist tone places the organism into a parasympathetic-dominant, low-NE, low-metabolic “recovery mode” that unlocks the same downstream programs sleep uses to restore homeostasis.

Specific Aims
1) Neurocognitive axis: Test whether wakeful torpor restores attention and executive control after sleep restriction by reducing cortical hyperarousal and enabling network renormalization.
2) Metabolic axis: Determine whether wakeful torpor acutely reduces energy expenditure and improves insulin sensitivity and substrate utilization following sleep loss.
3) Immune axis: Assess whether wakeful torpor attenuates proinflammatory cytokines and leukocyte activation markers linked to sleep deprivation.
4) Autonomic axis: Establish whether wakeful torpor increases vagal tone, baroreflex sensitivity, and lowers sympathetic outflow during wakefulness.
Exploratory mechanistic aim: Quantify whether reduced NE tone increases surrogate markers of glymphatic/CSF dynamics compatible with clearance functions typically enhanced during NREM sleep.

Study Design
- Population: Healthy adults (n=48), 21–40 years, regular sleepers, no cardiovascular/psychiatric/metabolic disease, medication-free.
- Sleep-restriction model: Two consecutive nights of 4-hour time-in-bed (01:00–05:00).
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 3-period crossover with ≥10-day washouts.
  Arms (3-hour daytime recovery session, 13:00–16:00, enforced wakefulness):
  A) α2A-agonist (guanfacine ER, individualized sub-sedative dose determined in run-in to reduce resting pupil diameter ~10–15% without impairing psychomotor vigilance).
  B) Placebo (matched).
  C) Benchmark-nap (80-minute polysomnography-verified nap) for non-inferiority reference only; not counted toward intervention feasibility (constraint check), but informs effect size targets.
- Wakefulness assurance: Continuous EEG/EOG and psychomotor vigilance checks; Karolinska Drowsiness Scale every 30 minutes; research staff monitoring.
- Environmental controls: Dim light (<50 lux), supine or semi-recumbent posture, thermoneutral cool room (19–20°C), white noise, no caffeine/food; water ad libitum.

Intervention Rationale and Dosing Framework
- Agent: Guanfacine ER (α2A-selective) titrated in a prior familiarization session to achieve LC downshift without sedation (operationalized by stable responsiveness, PVT lapses ≤ baseline + 3, and no more than 15% slowing of simple reaction time). Typical range 0.5–1.5 mg PO, individualized; fixed per participant across study arms.
- Timing: Single oral dose at 12:00 to align peak plasma with 13:00–16:00 session.
- Safety monitoring: Continuous BP/HR, orthostatic checks pre/post; adverse events recorded; stopping rules for SBP < 90 mmHg, HR < 45 bpm, or sedation scale > 2/5.

Primary Outcomes (collected pre [12:30] and post [16:15], plus continuous where noted)
- Neurocognitive:
  - Psychomotor Vigilance Test (10-min): lapses, median RT.
  - Executive function: 2-back accuracy/RT; antisaccade error rate.
  - Cortical state: high-density EEG (eyes-closed wake): frontal theta power (4–7 Hz), aperiodic 1/f slope; slow-oscillation events during quiet wake (0.5–1 Hz) occurrence density.
  - Pupil metrics: baseline diameter and task-evoked dilations (LC proxy).
- Metabolic:
  - Indirect calorimetry: resting energy expenditure (REE), respiratory exchange ratio (RER).
  - OGTT-mini (25 g) at 11:15 with serial glucose/insulin (AUC), Matsuda index.
  - Plasma lactate, free fatty acids, β-hydroxybutyrate.
- Immune:
  - Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, hsCRP; leukocyte CD11b expression; monocyte gene expression panel (NF-κB targets).
- Autonomic:
  - HRV (RMSSD, HF power), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence method), pre-ejection period by impedance cardiography, muscle sympathetic nerve activity (subset, n=16).
  - Salivary alpha-amylase and plasma NE (catechol-O-methyltransferase–adjusted).
- Exploratory CSF/glymphatic surrogates:
  - Phase-contrast MRI aqueductal CSF stroke volume and low-frequency oscillations (subset, n=24).
  - DTI-ALPS index pre/post session.
  - Respiratory-coupled CSF flow with fast EPI (resting fMRI, subset).

Secondary/Translational Outcomes
- Subjective fatigue/sleepiness (KSS), mood (PANAS), workload (NASA-TLX).
- Safety/tolerability, orthostasis, adverse events.
- Persistence: Outcome retest at 20:00 to assess durability.

Analysis Plan
- Mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts, fixed effects for condition, period, and carryover; primary comparisons A vs B; A vs C for benchmarking.
- Composite Recovery Index: Z-scored aggregation across four axes (PVT lapses↓, REE↓, IL-6↓, RMSSD↑) with prespecified weights (0.3 neurocognitive, 0.25 metabolic, 0.25 immune, 0.2 autonomic).
- Non-inferiority margin: Wakeful torpor (A) within 20% of nap (C) for Composite Index; superiority over placebo (B) at p<0.05 (two-sided) and Bayes factor > 3.
- Mediation: LC downshift proxies (pupil baseline, HRV HF) mediating changes in immune/metabolic endpoints.

Success Criteria (Go/No-Go)
- Primary: A vs B improves Composite Recovery Index by ≥0.35 SD; each axis shows directionally supportive change with at least two endpoints significant after FDR correction.
- Benchmark: A non-inferior to C on Composite Index and on at least two axes individually.
- Tolerability: <10% sessions terminated for hypotension/sedation.

Mechanistic Predictions
- Reduced LC-NE tone (smaller baseline pupil, higher HRV HF) will:
  - Increase EEG aperiodic 1/f slope (reduced cortical excitatory drive) with stable or improved executive control metrics.
  - Lower REE by ~5–10% and shift RER toward fat oxidation.
  - Decrease IL-6/TNF-α by 15–25% from pre-session peaks induced by sleep restriction.
  - Enhance baroreflex sensitivity and shorten pre-ejection period.
  - Increase CSF stroke volume and ALPS index (subset), consistent with improved clearance permissivity.

Risk Management
- Hypotension/bradycardia: conservative titration, continuous monitoring, predefined stop criteria.
- Excess sedation: dose back-off in familiarization; auditory engagement tasks if needed while preserving low arousal.
- Interindividual variability: personalized dose targeting physiologic signature (pupil, HRV) rather than fixed mg.

Why This Satisfies the Constraints
- Targets all four axes via a single physiological lever (LC-NE setpoint), not symptom masking.
- Implemented during enforced wakefulness without increasing sleep time.
- Mechanisms map to known restorative pathways of NREM: low NE enabling clearance, parasympathetic dominance, metabolic downshift, and anti-inflammatory tone.

Milestones and Deliverables (12 months)
- Months 1–3: Dose-finding algorithms for sub-sedative LC downshift; finalize biomarkers.
- Months 4–9: Crossover trial execution; interim analysis after 24 participants.
- Months 10–12: Final analysis; define responder phenotype; dossier for Phase II in shift workers.
- Deliverable: A validated, physiologically grounded “wakeful torpor” protocol and biomarker signature enabling homeostatic recovery under time-restricted sleep.

Title
Wakeful NREM: Inducing brief “LC-off” windows to switch on sleep’s restorative program during wakefulness

Atomic Strategy
Exploit a single global control knob—tonic locus coeruleus (LC) noradrenergic output. Transiently lowering tonic LC-NE to N3-like levels during quiet wakefulness should unlock the coupled brain–body restoration program (cortical slow oscillations, glymphatic/vascular flux, synaptic renormalization, parasympathetic dominance, and immune recalibration) without extending total sleep time.

Central Hypothesis
Brief, repeated “LC-off” windows (3–5 minutes) during wakefulness, phase-aligned with cortical 0.5–1 Hz slow oscillations and supported by cardiorespiratory entrainment, will acutely and cumulatively restore neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis after sleep restriction, approximating the recovery achieved by sufficient sleep.

Specific Aims
1) Define the minimal neuromodulatory–electrophysiological code for wakeful restoration by mapping dose–state–effect relationships between tonic LC suppression, cortical slow oscillations, and downstream recovery markers across four axes.
2) Test the efficacy of a closed-loop “LC-off” protocol to normalize a preregistered composite Recovery Index spanning neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic endpoints after sleep restriction.
3) Establish mechanism by linking state transitions (NE tone, slow oscillations, CSF/hemodynamic pulsatility) to improvements on each axis, and quantify durability and dose–response across days.

Study Design
- Population: Healthy adults (n=60), 21–45 years, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover.
- Sleep manipulation: Two conditions per participant, counterbalanced:
  a) Sleep-replete baseline (8 h time-in-bed for 2 nights) → Assessment day.
  b) Sleep-restricted (5 h time-in-bed for 2 nights) → Intervention day.
- Arms on intervention day (crossover within SR condition): 
  1) LC-off protocol (active),
  2) Matched sham (placebo + non-therapeutic stimulation),
  3) Component controls (alpha-2 agonist only; slow-oscillation entrainment only; breathing only) in a subset (n=30) to identify minimal code.

Intervention: Closed-Loop “LC-off” Protocol (Wakeful, 90 minutes total)
- Primary manipulation (LC tone):
  - Microdose alpha-2A agonism to suppress tonic LC firing while preserving behavioral wake: oral or sublingual clonidine 25–50 µg (or individualized via Bayesian titration to target modest pupil constriction without sedation; continuous BP/HR monitoring).
  - Real-time pupillometry as LC proxy; algorithm adjusts session pacing to maintain target tonic state.
- Electrophysiological entrainment (thalamocortical SO):
  - Auditory closed-loop slow-oscillation stimulation (phase-locked 50 ms pink-noise clicks delivered at up-phase of endogenous 0.5–1 Hz activity detected from high-density EEG), or 0.75 Hz frontal tACS (1 mA) in those without auditory tolerance.
- Cardiorespiratory support (vascular/glymphatic pulsatility and vagal tilt):
  - Paced nasal diaphragmatic breathing at 0.1 Hz (6 breaths/min) with end-tidal CO2 monitoring to avoid hypocapnia, supine posture with mild head elevation (10–15°).
- Structure: Twelve 5-minute LC-off bouts separated by 2–3-minute light cognitive engagement (quiet reading) to maintain wakefulness; total “off” time ~60 minutes.

Mechanistic State Monitoring
- LC/NE: continuous infrared pupillometry; salivary MHPG pre/post; spectral HRV correlates of LC tone.
- Cortical state: HD-EEG delta/SO power, SO amplitude and slope, SO–spindle coupling.
- Fluid/vascular dynamics: fNIRS slow hemodynamic oscillations; carotid Doppler for pulsatility; respiratory/ cardiac coupling indices; subset (n=20) undergoes ultrafast MRI on a separate day to quantify CSF inflow and ALPS index.

Outcome Measures (Composite Recovery Index; preregistered)
- Neurocognitive:
  - Psychomotor vigilance task (PVT lapses, reaction time variability),
  - 2-back working memory accuracy,
  - Motor sequence learning (offline gain across session blocks),
  - Oculomotor fatigue markers (blink rate/velocity).
- Metabolic:
  - Plasma lactate, glucose, beta-hydroxybutyrate; targeted metabolomics (acylcarnitines),
  - HOMA-IR (fasting), subset mixed-meal tolerance test AUC glucose/insulin,
  - Resting energy expenditure and RQ via indirect calorimetry.
- Immune:
  - Serum IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1Ra, IL-10; hsCRP,
  - Ex vivo LPS-stimulated PBMC cytokine responsiveness (fold-change vs baseline),
  - Leukocyte transcriptomic NF-κB target score (subset).
- Autonomic:
  - HRV (RMSSD, HF power), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence method),
  - Resting BP/HR, pupil baseline/variance, skin conductance.
- Safety/State:
  - Karolinska Sleepiness Scale, psychometric sedation; continuous SpO2, BP, HR.

Primary Endpoint and Success Criterion
- The Recovery Index (mean of z-scored axis-specific composites) after sleep restriction + LC-off will recover ≥70% of the deficit toward the sleep-replete baseline and be superior to sham by ≥0.35 SD (noninferiority margin to full sleep set at 0.3 SD), with no performance sedation.

Analysis
- Linear mixed models with subject random effects; condition (SR+LC-off vs SR+sham vs SR+components) as fixed factor; adjust for session order, sex, and baseline values.
- Mediation analysis: extent to which changes in tonic LC proxies and SO metrics mediate improvements on each axis.
- Dose–state–effect surfaces from Bayesian hierarchical models linking NE suppression (pupil), SO amplitude, and breathing adherence to outcomes.

Mechanistic Predictions
- Lower tonic LC-NE unlocks:
  - Neurocognitive: increased SO amplitude and improved PVT/N-back via synaptic renormalization windows.
  - Metabolic: decreased plasma lactate and improved substrate flexibility; enhanced CSF/ISF exchange.
  - Immune: shift toward anti-inflammatory balance (↓IL-6/TNF-α; ↑IL-10); normalized PBMC responsiveness.
  - Autonomic: increased vagal tone (↑RMSSD/HF), improved baroreflex sensitivity, reduced sympathetic markers.
- Component controls will show partial, axis-limited effects; only the LC-off + SO + breathing triad will produce system-level recovery meeting the composite threshold.

Milestones and Go/No-Go
- Phase 1 (n=20): Tolerability/safety; establish individualized dose achieving target pupil constriction without KSS >6; confirm SO augmentation during bouts.
- Phase 2 (n=40): Efficacy on composite Recovery Index; mediation by LC/SO metrics.
- Go if safety acceptable and Recovery Index improvement ≥0.35 SD vs sham; refine toward nonpharmacologic LC modulation (e.g., mild neck suction baroreflex activation) if equivalent state signatures are achieved.

Risk Management
- Exclude cardiovascular disease, hypotension, severe OSA; continuous monitoring; predefined stop rules (SBP <90 mmHg, HR <45 bpm, SpO2 <92%, KSS ≥8).
- Maintain behavioral wakefulness with light engagement between bouts; no vehicle operation for 6 hours post-session.

Deliverables
- A validated, closed-loop, wakeful “LC-off” protocol with parameter setpoints for inducing a recovery state under time-restricted sleep.
- A mechanistic state map quantifying the minimal neuromodulator–oscillation code that generalizes across individuals.
- A translational pathway to purely nonpharmacologic implementation once the state signature is fixed.

Title
Architecture-Mimetic Sleep Compression (AMSC): Closed-loop slow-oscillation entrainment plus a REM-release micro-nap to restore multisystem homeostasis under time-restricted sleep

Core Question/Hypothesis
Can reproducing sleep architecture—rather than extending sleep duration—restore neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis under sleep restriction? We test a single physiological strategy: intensify and phase-align cortical slow oscillations during a compressed nocturnal window and discharge accumulated REM pressure via a short, circadian-timed micro-nap, without manipulating heart rate or stress pathways. Prediction: This architecture-mimetic pattern approximates the recovery state of sufficient sleep across all four axes.

Atomic Strategy (single perturbation)
Treat the thalamocortical slow oscillation as the master homeostatic lever. Use closed-loop, in-phase auditory stimulation to amplify slow-wave activity (SWA) during a short night, and reallocate a minimal fraction of minutes to a REM-permissive micro-nap timed to the circadian REM peak, preserving total sleep minutes across conditions.

Rationale
- NREM slow oscillations coordinate synaptic renormalization, glymphatic clearance, GH/prolactin pulses, and anti-inflammatory signaling while biasing parasympathetic dominance.
- REM relieves noradrenergic tone, supports emotional/mnemonic recalibration, and completes ultradian alternation.
- Under restriction, making slow waves denser and allowing a brief REM discharge should recapitulate the causal sequence of restoration with minimal minutes.

Specific Aims
1) Efficacy: Determine if AMSC improves a composite Recovery Index spanning the four axes versus restricted-sleep control without increasing total sleep time.
2) Mechanism: Test whether SWA intensity and occurrence of SOREM (sleep-onset REM) mediate improvements.
3) Benchmarking: Establish non-inferiority of AMSC to an 8-hour sufficient-sleep reference on the Recovery Index.

Design
- Participants: N=48 healthy adults (18–40y), normal BMI, regular sleepers, no sleep/psychiatric/metabolic disorders. Within-subject, randomized, 4-condition crossover; each condition lasts 5 consecutive nights with 7-day washout.
- Equal-time constraint: Total time-in-bed (TIB) per 24h fixed at 4 h 20 min for all restricted conditions. If a nap is scheduled (20–30 min), nocturnal TIB is reduced accordingly to keep TIB constant.
- Conditions:
  A) AMSC (architecture-mimetic): Night CLAS-enhanced SWA + daytime REM-release micro-nap.
  B) Restricted-Sham: Night sham stimulation + daytime eyes-closed quiet rest (no sleep) of identical duration; nocturnal TIB equals total TIB.
  C) SWA-only: Night CLAS-enhanced SWA; no nap.
  D) REM-only: Night sham + daytime REM-release micro-nap.

Interventions
- Closed-loop auditory slow-oscillation enhancement (CLAS):
  - Hardware: PSG with real-time frontal EEG detection; pink-noise pulses (~50 ms) phase-locked to upstates of 0.5–1 Hz oscillations; intensity individually titrated below arousal threshold.
  - Delivery during entire nocturnal TIB for conditions A and C.
- REM-release micro-nap (conditions A and D):
  - Timing: 12:30–13:30 local time window.
  - Duration: 20–30 min; terminate upon first detected REM epoch or at 30 min cap.
  - Environment: Dim light, thermoneutral, supine; no CLAS to permit REM; abstain caffeine ≥6 h pre-nap.
- Controls: Standardized diet, fixed caloric intake and macronutrients; fixed light schedule; no alcohol/caffeine (except standardized morning dose on test days withheld).

Outcomes (assessed morning after night 5 unless specified)
Primary Composite Recovery Index (z-scored, directionally aligned, averaged across domains):
- Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT lapses), 3-back d’, Stroop interference cost, emotion regulation (affective go/no-go accuracy), subjective sleepiness (KSS).
- Metabolic: 2-h OGTT with insulin (Matsuda index), fasting HOMA-IR, resting metabolic rate and respiratory quotient (indirect calorimetry), morning leptin/ghrelin ratio.
- Immune: Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, hsCRP, NK cell cytotoxicity assay.
- Autonomic: 10-min seated HRV (RMSSD, HF power), orthostatic baroreflex sensitivity, pupillometric unrest index.

Mechanistic/Verification Measures
- Sleep architecture (PSG): SWA power (0.5–1 Hz), spindle–slow coupling, arousals, REM latency/percentage; nap REM occurrence (yes/no).
- Endocrine: Nocturnal GH/prolactin sampling (night 5, sparse sampling) and morning cortisol awakening response.
- Brain clearance proxy: DTI-ALPS index (morning of day 6) in a 20-participant subset.
- Wake EEG theta power during PVT (sleep pressure index).

Analysis
- Mixed-effects models with condition as fixed effect and participant as random effect.
- Primary: AMSC vs Restricted-Sham superiority on Recovery Index (two-sided α=0.05).
- Mediation: SWA power (night) and nap REM occurrence (binary) mediating Recovery Index via path analysis.
- Non-inferiority: AMSC vs 8-h sufficient-sleep reference (collected in a separate baseline week) with margin Δ=10% of baseline SD on the Recovery Index.
- Equivalence of total TIB verified across restricted arms; sensitivity analyses excluding any nights with protocol deviations.

Power
- Assuming within-subject SD of 0.5 z-units and true AMSC–Sham difference of 0.35 z-units, N=40 yields >80% power; target N=48 to account for attrition.

Inclusion/Exclusion Controls
- Dim light melatonin onset assessed pre-study to confirm stable circadian phase; fixed sleep window aligned to individual chronotype.
- Actigraphy and PSG verify adherence; naps monitored to enforce duration and prevent unintended SWS in nap unless REM occurs.

Safety
- CLAS intensity titrated to avoid arousals; adverse events logged. No pharmacological stimulants or ANS-targeting devices used.

Success Criteria (Go/No-Go)
- Go: AMSC superior to Restricted-Sham on Recovery Index (p<0.05) and non-inferior to 8-h sleep (Δ≤10%).
- Mechanistic confirmation: ≥20% increase in nocturnal SWA power vs Sham and ≥50% SOREM occurrence during micro-nap under restriction.

Potential Outcomes and Interpretation
- If AMSC matches 8-h baseline: supports architecture-first compression as a viable strategy for multisystem recovery under time limits.
- If only neurocognitive improves but metabolic/immune lag: refine REM timing/dose or increase SWA drive within same TIB.
- If CLAS fragments sleep: adjust stimulus timing/intensity or abort per pre-registered fallback.

Deliverables
- Validated protocol for architecture-mimetic recovery without extending total sleep time.
- Open-source algorithms for real-time SO upstate detection and stimulus delivery.
- Composite Recovery Index and mediation model linking SWA and REM discharge to multisystem outcomes.

Ethics
- IRB approval; informed consent; right to withdraw; medical oversight for glucose tests; data privacy compliant.
