text:
Title
Inducing Sleep-Phase Physiology During Wakefulness via 0.1 Hz Cardiorespiratory Resonance (CARE) to Restore Neurocognitive, Metabolic, Immune, and Autonomic Homeostasis Under Time-Restricted Sleep

Core Hypothesis (atomic strategy)
A single oscillatory perturbation—entraining the cardiorespiratory–baroreflex system at its ~0.1 Hz resonance via paced nasal diaphragmatic breathing with prolonged exhalation—will transiently reproduce key restorative sleep-phase mechanisms during wakefulness. By lowering central noradrenergic tone, enhancing vagal activity and baroreflex gain, and amplifying respiration-driven cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and venous pulsatility, CARE will induce a multisystem “recovery microstate” that approximates the homeostatic benefits of sufficient sleep across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes without increasing total sleep time.

Rationale
- Sleep’s restorative effects co-occur with low locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC-NE) tone, high vagal drive, baroreflex dominance, and large-amplitude slow hemo/CSF pulsations that support metabolite clearance and energy reallocation.
- 0.1 Hz (6 cycles/min) breathing maximizes respiratory sinus arrhythmia, strengthens baroreflex feedback, shifts sympathovagal balance parasympathetically, entrains cortical–interoceptive networks, and augments intracranial pressure oscillations that drive CSF movement.
- A single, controllable oscillatory input can simultaneously influence arousal (LC-NE), autonomic state, glymphatic-like clearance, glucose–lipid regulation via vagal–hepatic pathways, and inflammation via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex.

Specific Aims
Aim 1: Demonstrate that distributed CARE “recovery blocks” during wakefulness after restricted sleep restore acute neurocognitive performance toward well-rested levels.
Aim 2: Determine whether CARE normalizes metabolic efficiency and substrate utilization impaired by sleep loss.
Aim 3: Test whether CARE reduces proinflammatory signaling and restores immune cell trafficking patterns altered by sleep loss.
Aim 4: Quantify autonomic normalization and mechanistic mediators (vagal tone, baroreflex sensitivity, LC-NE proxies, CSF/hemodynamic pulsatility) underlying CARE’s effects.

Study Design
- Population: Healthy adults (ages 18–45). Within-subject randomized, counterbalanced, crossover design across three conditions, each separated by ≥7-day washout:
  1) Sleep Restriction + CARE (SR+CARE),
  2) Sleep Restriction + frequency-matched control breathing at 0.27 Hz (SR+CTRL),
  3) Normal Sleep + Quiet Rest (NS+REST, benchmark).
- Sleep protocol: SR nights capped at 4 h time-in-bed (02:00–06:00). NS nights 8 h (23:00–07:00).
- Wake-day schedule: Four 15-minute recovery blocks at 09:00, 12:00, 15:00, 18:00 performed seated, eyes open, minimal external stimulation.

Intervention (single perturbation)
- CARE: Paced nasal diaphragmatic breathing at 0.1 Hz with an exhalation-dominant cycle (e.g., ~4 s inhale, ~6 s exhale) to maximize vagal recruitment and baroreflex resonance. Real-time visual biofeedback targets coherence between respiratory phase and heart-rate oscillation (RSA). Posture standardized (upright, supported), without additional devices or pharmacology.
- Control: Identical setting and biofeedback interface with nonresonant 0.27 Hz breathing; matched coach contact and expectancy.

Outcomes and Measurements
Primary endpoint (composite recovery index; morning pre- vs. evening post-intervention change, z-scored to NS+REST):
- Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Task lapses and reaction time distribution; n-back accuracy; go/no-go commission errors; sustained attention variability; pupillometry-based tonic pupil diameter (LC-NE proxy); EEG spectral markers during blocks (frontal theta/alpha power; slow vasomotor coupling via fNIRS).
- Metabolic: Oral glucose tolerance AUC; indirect calorimetry respiratory quotient and resting energy expenditure; fasting/free fatty acids; lactate; ketone bodies; HOMA-IR; CGM-derived glycemic variability (subset).
- Immune: Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10; leukocyte subset distribution and trafficking markers (e.g., CD62L, CCR7); hsCRP; ex vivo LPS-stimulated cytokine response.
- Autonomic/Mechanistic: HRV (HF power, RMSSD), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence and transfer-function methods), skin conductance, salivary alpha-amylase and cortisol diurnal slope, cerebrovascular/CSF pulsatility proxies via fNIRS/TCD (0.1 Hz power), respiratory–cardiac phase coherence.

Key Mechanistic Predictions
- CARE enhances 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory coherence, increases HF-HRV and baroreflex gain, and reduces tonic LC-NE proxies during blocks.
- CARE amplifies 0.1 Hz cerebrovascular/CSF pulsatility, supporting metabolite clearance surrogates and reducing proinflammatory tone.
- CARE shifts substrate use toward greater fat oxidation (lower RQ) and improves glucose handling despite sleep loss.
- Neurocognitive recovery emerges within-day (reduced lapses, improved response inhibition) and carries over to evening testing.

Analysis
- Mixed-effects models with condition × time interactions for each domain; composite index as primary outcome controlling for period and order effects.
- Mediation analysis testing whether autonomic/CSF pulsatility changes statistically mediate neurocognitive, metabolic, and immune improvements.
- Noninferiority analysis versus a 20-minute daytime nap comparator arm (exploratory subset) with a prespecified margin on the composite index.

Success Criteria
- Primary: SR+CARE significantly outperforms SR+CTRL and is noninferior to NS+REST on the composite recovery index at day’s end.
- Secondary: Significant frequency-specific gains in baroreflex sensitivity, HF-HRV, and 0.1 Hz hemo/CSF oscillatory power that mediate improvements across at least two other axes.

Feasibility and Safety
- Nonpharmacologic, low-risk, immediately deployable with standard biofeedback platforms.
- Adverse event monitoring limited to hyperventilation/dizziness; predefined stop criteria.

Exploratory Extensions
- Dose–response across block duration and number.
- Chronobiological alignment: clustering blocks in the biological afternoon versus distribution.
- Personalization: titrating toward each participant’s individual resonance frequency (0.07–0.12 Hz) to maximize coherence.

Impact
If successful, CARE establishes a single, physiologically grounded, sleep-mimetic perturbation that programs recovery into awake time, selectively compensating neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic impairments caused by sleep restriction—without extending total sleep duration.

text:
Title
Synthetic NREM Pacemaker: Inducing a Multi-Axis Recovery State During Wakefulness Under Sleep Restriction

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Impose a coherent 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal oscillatory state (“synthetic NREM”) during wakefulness and use it as the global pacemaker to time anabolic pituitary pulses, thereby reproducing the physiologic recovery sequence of early-night slow-wave sleep across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic axes—without increasing total sleep.

Hypothesis
A closed-loop 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal pacemaker, phase-locking respiration, heart–vessel vasomotion, and vagal afferent drive, will (i) shift autonomic balance parasympathetically, (ii) open perivascular/glymphatic clearance through enhanced low-frequency hemo- and CSF-oscillations, (iii) gate hypothalamic–pituitary anabolic pulses (via timed GHRH micropulses coupled to vagal dominance), and (iv) normalize inflammatory and metabolic tone—yielding a composite “Recovery Index” statistically indistinguishable from sufficient sleep, despite restricted sleep duration.

Rationale (first principles)
- Sleep’s earliest NREM stages are defined by slow vasomotion (~0.1 Hz), high vagal tone, cortisol nadir, and GH/prolactin pulses. The slow oscillatory milieu is the primitive organizer that coordinates clearance, repair, and energy rebalancing.
- The baroreflex–vagal loop is an accessible lever: paced breathing at 6 breaths/min entrains 0.1 Hz oscillations; vagal afferent activation engages anti-inflammatory and hypothalamic pathways; low-frequency vasomotion and respiration augment CSF/interstitial fluid exchange; parasympathetic dominance improves insulin sensitivity and reduces sympathetic catecholamines.
- If this oscillator is imposed exogenously and used to schedule pituitary anabolic pulses, the downstream multi-system “sleep outputs” can be reproduced while awake.

Study design
- Population: Healthy adults, 21–40 years, habitual 7–9 h sleepers.
- Sleep restriction model: 5 consecutive nights with 4 h time-in-bed (02:00–06:00).
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled, 2-period crossover (≥21-day washout). Each period includes baseline (habitual sleep, day −1), restriction days 1–5 with daily intervention, and follow-up (day 6).
- Arms:
  1) Synthetic NREM Pacemaker (active)
  2) Sham synthetic pacemaker (control)

Intervention: Synthetic NREM Pacemaker (90 min/day, CT 14–16)
All components are slaved to a single 0.1 Hz master oscillator and delivered during quiet wake.
- Oscillator entrainment
  - Paced respiration at 6 breaths/min with end-tidal CO2 stabilization (rebreathing titration) to avoid hypocapnia.
  - Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) phase-locked to late-exhalation (0.1 Hz cycle; duty cycle tuned by HRV feedback).
  - Cardiorespiratory biofeedback to maximize high-frequency HRV and baroreflex sensitivity (closed-loop adjustment of breathing amplitude and taVNS intensity).
- Cortico-thalamo resonance support (no sedation)
  - Prefrontal tACS at 0.75 Hz amplitude-modulated by the 0.1 Hz envelope, sub-threshold for sleep induction, to promote slow-oscillation–like cortical timing without loss of wakefulness (eyes-open, vigilance monitored).
- Endocrine pulse entrainment (anabolic gating)
  - Three IV or SC microboluses of GHRH analog (e.g., tesamorelin microdoses) at minutes 10, 30, 50 of the 90-min block, time-locked to troughs of sympathetic activity (determined by continuous HRV) to mimic early-night GH surges while minimizing hyperglycemia.
  - Dim-light environment (<10 lux) with blue-blocking eyewear during the session to reinforce a darkness cue without pharmacologic sedation.
- Safety monitoring: continuous ECG, SpO2, capnography; vigilance via auditory oddball and pupillometry to ensure maintained wakefulness.

Sham condition
- Unpaced breathing at spontaneous rate; taVNS ear-clip placed with imperceptible ramp-only; tACS sham (30 s ramp on/off); saline microboluses; room light ~100 lux with amber eyewear (placebo darkness cue). Session structure/time identical.

Outcomes
Primary endpoint
- Recovery Index: z-scored composite across domains against a well-rested reference day (day −1), preregistered weights:
  - Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Test (lapses and median RT), N-back (2-back d’), sustained attention to response task errors.
  - Autonomic: RMSSD and HF power (eyes-open), baroreflex sensitivity (sequence method), plasma/urine catecholamines.
  - Metabolic: OGTT-derived insulin sensitivity (Matsuda index), fasting HOMA-IR, RER (indirect calorimetry), resting energy expenditure.
  - Immune/inflammatory: plasma IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1ra, hsCRP, NK-cell cytotoxicity, monocyte HLA-DR.
  - Clearance proxy: respiration-coupled CSF flow amplitude by MRI (subset) or DTI-ALPS index; plasma Aβ42/40 and neurofilament light (exploratory).

Key secondary endpoints
- GH pulse metrics (deconvolution), IGF-1, prolactin.
- Subjective sleepiness (KSS) and fatigue; mood (PANAS).
- Circadian phase stability (DLMO) to ensure the method does not phase-shift the clock.
- Safety/tolerability metrics.

Mechanistic readouts (substudies)
- Microneurography (MSNA) in a subset to confirm sympathetic suppression during entrainment.
- Near-infrared diffuse optical measures of low-frequency vasomotion coherence across cortex.
- Heart–breath–BP phase coupling indices as a fidelity metric of the synthetic oscillator.

Analysis
- Mixed-effects models comparing active vs sham across restriction days; primary analysis on day 3 (peak impairment) and area-under-curve (days 1–5).
- Noninferiority test: Recovery Index (active) vs sufficient-sleep reference (day −1) with predefined margin (Cohen’s d ≤ 0.2).
- Mediation models: degree of 0.1 Hz coherence and baroreflex sensitivity as mediators of improvements in metabolic and immune outcomes; GH pulse amplitude as mediator of anabolic/metabolic recovery.
- Sample size: n=40 completers for 90% power to detect ≥0.4 SD improvement in Recovery Index (within-subject crossover).

Milestones and decision gates
- Phase 0 (feasibility, n=10): demonstrate maintenance of wakefulness and target engagement: +50% HF-HRV, +30% baroreflex sensitivity, entrained 0.1 Hz coherence across heart–breath–BP; GH pulse elicitation without hyperglycemia.
- Phase 1 (mechanism, n=24): confirm dose–response of coherence to taVNS intensity and breathing amplitude; identify optimal microdose schedule for GH pulses.
- Phase 2 (efficacy, n=40): meet primary endpoint; demonstrate noninferiority to sufficient-sleep reference on Recovery Index.

Risk management
- Avoid hypocapnia via capnography feedback.
- Monitor for taVNS adverse effects (skin irritation, bradycardia); prespecified stop criteria.
- Exclude endocrine/metabolic disorders; monitor glucose during GHRH microboluses; no exogenous GH.

Success criteria (go/no-go)
- Active vs sham difference ≥0.4 SD on Recovery Index by day 3.
- Each axis shows clinically meaningful change: ≥20% reduction in PVT lapses, ≥20% increase in HF-HRV, ≥15% increase in Matsuda index, ≥20% reduction in IL-6/TNF-α.
- No increase in daytime sleep propensity beyond baseline restricted-sleep levels; no circadian phase drift.

Why this is a single, system-wide lever
The imposed 0.1 Hz baroreflex–vagal oscillator is the singular, global control variable. All other elements (breathing pattern, taVNS phasing, cortical resonance, and hormone micropulses) are synchronized to this oscillator rather than acting independently, ensuring coherent, sleep-like recovery signaling across neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic systems during wakefulness.

text:
Title
One-oscillator recovery under short sleep: 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory entrainment to concentrate deep sleep at night and substitute REM-like functions by targeted waking replay

Question–Hypothesis (merged)
Can entraining the body’s 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory rhythm across the 24-hour cycle—used at night to intensify deep sleep and by day to run brief waking replay blocks—restore neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic homeostasis to near “well-rested” levels under time‑restricted sleep?

Atomic strategy (single perturbation)
Stabilize and amplify the 0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory–vasomotor oscillator (slow nasal breathing paced at 6 breaths/min) as a master control signal across night and day.
- Night: pre‑sleep entrainment biases early-night physiology toward high slow‑wave activity (SWA), promoting brain waste clearance and synaptic down‑selection.
- Day: brief 0.1 Hz–paced “waking replay” blocks pair memory reactivation with high‑vagal, low‑noradrenergic state that substitutes key REM-related functions without adding sleep.

Physiological rationale (mechanism map)
- Brain/glymphatic and neurocognitive: SWA couples with large, slow vascular and CSF oscillations. Lower noradrenaline and higher vagal tone favor SWA, clearance of metabolites, and synaptic homeostasis. Daytime replay during 0.1 Hz breathing promotes hippocampo‑cortical consolidation and emotional processing in a safe, low‑arousal window.
- Metabolic: Parasympathetic dominance and improved baroreflex sensitivity reduce sympathetic tone, support insulin sensitivity, enhance growth hormone pulses concentrated in early deep sleep, and normalize appetite signaling.
- Immune: The vagus–splenic anti‑inflammatory reflex attenuates pro‑inflammatory cytokines; enhanced SWA and clearance reduce neuroinflammatory drive.
- Autonomic: 0.1 Hz entrainment increases HRV (RMSSD, HF power) and baroreflex gain, stabilizing autonomic set‑points stressed by sleep loss.

Study design
- Design: Randomized, within‑subject, 3‑condition crossover; each condition 5 consecutive nights under restricted time in bed (TIB) with 9‑day washouts.
- Baseline: One week of habitual 8 h sleep to establish each participant’s “well‑rested” reference.
- Participants: Healthy adults, 21–45, regular sleepers. Exclude sleep apnea, arrhythmias, major psychiatric/medical illness, nicotine dependence.
- Restricted TIB (all arms): 4.5 h/night fixed to the early night (e.g., 23:00–03:30) to naturally concentrate deep sleep without extending total sleep time.
- Arms:
  1) Control–Restricted: No entrainment; quiet sitting pre‑sleep; daytime breaks as usual.
  2) Night‑Only Entrainment: 0.1 Hz paced nasal breathing before lights‑out and after any nocturnal awakenings.
  3) 24 h Entrainment + Waking Replay (full strategy): Night protocol plus two daytime 8‑min 0.1 Hz blocks paired with targeted memory reactivation (TMR) and emotion‑processing tasks.

Intervention protocol
- 0.1 Hz pacing: Visual or haptic pacer guides nasal inhale:exhale 4 s:6 s, relaxed tidal volume; coach to avoid hyperventilation. Sessions supervised on nights 1 and 2, then monitored remotely.
- Night block: 20 min immediately pre‑lights‑out; if awake after a nocturnal awakening >5 min, perform an additional 5‑min block.
- Waking replay blocks (Arm 3 only): Two daily 8‑min sessions (09:30 and 14:30).
  - Memory: TMR cues (sounds/odors) linked to prior learning; quiet eyes‑closed recall or brief practice (1–2 min) embedded in the 8‑min paced breathing window.
  - Emotion: Guided reappraisal of mild affective material during paced breathing to approximate REM’s affect recalibration role.
- Adherence: Wearable detects respiratory rate and HRV; app logs session timing and quality.

Outcomes
Primary endpoint (Recovery Index; assessed morning of day 6)
- Composite z‑score vs each participant’s well‑rested baseline across four axes:
  1) Neurocognitive: Psychomotor Vigilance Test lapses; N‑back d′; paired‑associate recall with TMR benefit; subjective sleepiness.
  2) Metabolic: 2 h OGTT AUC glucose; HOMA‑IR (fasting insulin/glucose); CGM mean nocturnal glucose variability.
  3) Immune: High‑sensitivity CRP; IL‑6; ex vivo LPS‑stimulated TNF‑α (Δ from baseline).
  4) Autonomic: HRV (RMSSD, HF power) during sleep and daytime; baroreflex sensitivity (sequence method).

Key secondary and mechanistic outcomes
- Sleep architecture and physiology (polysomnography, nights 1 and 5): N3 minutes per hour TIB; SWA power; slow‑oscillation slope; SO–spindle coupling; nocturnal heart–breath phase–amplitude coupling.
- Noradrenergic state: Pupil diameter variability pre‑sleep and during waking blocks; morning salivary α‑amylase.
- Glymphatic/clearance proxies: Morning plasma Aβ42/40 ratio; neurofilament light; uric acid (Δ overnight).
- Inflammation resolution: sTNFR1, IL‑10; leukocyte counts.
- Affect regulation: Emotional Stroop interference; negative affect ratings to standardized images.
- Safety/tolerability: Dizziness, dyspnea, sleep onset latency, awakenings.

Analytic plan
- Mixed‑effects models with condition and night (1 vs 5) as fixed effects; participant random intercepts.
- Non‑inferiority margin: Recovery Index within 0.3 SD of the well‑rested baseline for Arm 3; superiority of Arm 3 over Control for each axis (Holm‑adjusted).
- Mediation: Test whether night SWA and HRV changes mediate Arm 3 effects on each axis.
- Dose–response: Within Arm 3, association between achieved 0.1 Hz coherence (respiration–HR coupling) and outcomes.

Success criteria
- Arm 3 achieves non‑inferiority to well‑rested baseline on the Recovery Index and superiority to Control on each axis.
- Mechanistic confirmation: In Arm 3 vs Control, higher pre‑sleep HRV and SWA (night 1 and 5), lower noradrenergic markers, improved OGTT AUC, reduced IL‑6/CRP.

Falsification and decision rules
- If Arm 3 fails to increase SWA and HRV vs Control, or if improvements on ≥3 of 4 axes do not exceed minimal clinically important differences, reject the hypothesis.
- If daytime replay without 0.1 Hz breathing (exploratory sub‑analysis using low‑adherence participants) shows equal benefit, the breathing‑centric mechanism is disconfirmed.

Risks and mitigations
- Hyperventilation: Emphasize slow, comfortable volume; capnography spot‑checks; stop if lightheaded.
- Sleep disruption by practice: Keep night blocks pre‑sleep; no in‑sleep cues.
- Emotional tasks: Mild stimuli only; immediate debrief.

Why this is one change with system‑wide impact
A single, controllable oscillator—0.1 Hz cardiorespiratory entrainment—nudges multiple coupled systems: it deepens early‑night sleep (brain/immune/metabolic repair) and creates brief daytime windows that stand in for REM’s cognitive/affective roles. The strategy does not add sleep time or stimulants; it re‑allocates limited sleep to the highest‑leverage stage and supplies, during wake, the missing functions most tied to REM.

Deliverables and timeline
- Months 0–3: Protocol finalization, device/app validation.
- Months 4–12: Enrollment (n=60), baseline, and three crossover blocks.
- Months 13–15: Analysis and mediation modeling.
- Month 16: Pre‑registered dataset and Recovery Index metric released; manuscript submission.

Expected impact
If successful, this establishes a physiologically grounded, scalable method to approximate “fully rested” recovery under short sleep by harmonizing one rhythm across night and day—meeting neurocognitive, metabolic, immune, and autonomic goals without extending sleep.

Title
Closed-loop, Doppler-guided transabdominal focused ultrasound to cap excessive uterine sympathetic drive while preserving basal tone and systemic sympathetic function

Hypothesis and Research Question
A locally targeted, closed-loop low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) stimulus, gated by a uterine-specific hemodynamic biomarker, can selectively suppress only excessive sympathetic activity in the uterus without altering basal uterine tone or systemic sympathetic function. Can a wearable transabdominal system maintain an individual’s uterine artery perfusion within a personalized “physiologic band” during stress, with no systemic sympatholysis?

Atomic Strategy
Use a single organ-local control variable—uterine artery resistance (Doppler-derived pulsatility/resistive index)—as a real-time proxy for local sympathetic overdrive. When this index exceeds an individual’s baseline band, deliver short bursts of LIFU focused to myometrial neurovascular zones to acutely raise local sympathetic terminal thresholds and reduce norepinephrine release. Stop stimulation as soon as the index returns to band. Spatial focus and closed-loop thresholds provide specificity; gating preserves basal tone.

Rationale
- Uterine sympathetic efferents constrict uterine arteries and increase myometrial tone. Excess activation elevates Doppler resistance indices and worsens pain/ischemia.
- Peripheral nerves and terminals are mechanically sensitive; specific LIFU pulse trains can reversibly decrease excitability and transmitter release without ablation.
- Doppler of the uterine arteries is non-invasive, organ-specific, rapid, and quantifiable through the abdomen.
- A personalized band-limited controller prevents undershoot (hypotonia) and avoids systemic effects by acting only at the uterine focus.

Modality and Device Concept
- Form factor: soft abdominal belt integrating (1) a 1–1.5 MHz 2D phased LIFU/imaging array (dual-mode), (2) Doppler module to track uterine artery indices, and (3) EHG (electrohysterography) patches for auxiliary myometrial activity sensing.
- Targeting: image-guided focusing to fundus/cornua neurovascular plexuses and along uterine arteries; depth-adaptive beamforming.
- Ultrasound safety: operate within established diagnostic limits (e.g., MI ≤ 1.9; thermal index < 1.0), real-time thermal modeling, skin thermistor feedback, and duty-cycled sonication.
- Control logic: adaptive reference tracking with subject-specific baseline band (median ± allowable range). Trigger criteria = sustained excursion above band for N seconds; cessation = return to band with hysteresis guard. Rate limits prevent overtreatment.

Definition of “Excessive” and “Basal”
- Basal: resting, cycle-phase–adjusted uterine artery PI/RI and EHG activity measured during calibration sessions.
- Excessive: acute elevation of PI/RI beyond personalized band and/or concordant EHG hypertonus during standardized stress or symptomatic episodes.

Study Plan

Aim 1: Establish biomarker-band and controller in humans (non-pregnant).
- Design: observational calibration in 40 participants across two menstrual phases.
- Measures: resting and stress-challenge uterine artery PI/RI, EHG, pain scores, systemic sympathetic markers (HRV LF/HF, cold pressor response, pupillometry, skin conductance).
- Output: individualized bands; excursion dynamics; controller parameters (trigger threshold, burst duration).

Aim 2: Parameterize LIFU for selective uterine sympathetic down-modulation.
- Design: within-subject, randomized, sham-controlled crossover (n=30) during standardized stress to induce uterine sympathetic excursions.
- LIFU pulses: low-duty (e.g., 5–20%), short bursts (10–30 s), inter-burst ≥30 s; frequency 1–1.5 MHz; focal zone matched to neurovascular targets.
- Primary endpoint: ΔPI/RI reduction to within band vs. sham without undershooting below band.
- Selectivity checks: no change in systemic markers (HR, BP, HRV, pupillometry, skin conductance); preserved cold pressor reactivity.

Aim 3: First clinical application—primary dysmenorrhea with stress-exacerbated symptoms.
- Design: home-use, double-blind, randomized, sham-controlled trial (n=80; 2 cycles).
- Intervention: wearable device auto-activates when excursions occur during daily life.
- Endpoints:
  - Primary: time-in-band (%) for uterine artery PI/RI.
  - Key secondary: pain AUC per day, rescue medication use, activity impairment.
  - Safety: adverse events, menstrual characteristics, fertility biomarkers (if applicable).
  - Systemic specificity: unchanged resting and challenged systemic sympathetic indices.

Signal Processing and Control
- Sensing: continuous Doppler sampling (1–2 Hz updates) with motion artifact rejection; EHG denoised via adaptive filtering.
- Controller: proportional–integral with hard floor at lower band bound; anti-windup; refractory interval after each burst; automatic gain scheduling by cycle phase.
- Personalization: per-subject baseline learned over multiple rest windows; re-calibration monthly.

Safety and Risk Mitigation
- Acoustic dose constraints enforced in firmware; per-burst cumulative thermal dose monitored.
- “Abort on rise” rule: stop LIFU if PI/RI drops below lower band or if any systemic vital deviates beyond predefined bounds.
- Exclusions: pregnancy, uterine fibroids >5 cm distorting anatomy, bleeding disorders, implanted pelvic devices, dermatologic conditions at contact sites.

Mechanistic Substudy (optional)
- Serum/salivary catecholamine panels pre/post bursts; uterine artery flow volume quantification; pain-evoked brain responses (fNIRS) for central correlates without affecting systemic sympathetic output.

Success Criteria
- Technical: ≥70% of excursions truncated back into band within 2 minutes, without undershoot.
- Physiologic: no significant change in systemic sympathetic markers vs. sham.
- Clinical: ≥30% reduction in pain AUC and ≥25% reduction in rescue analgesic use vs. sham.
- Safety: no device-related serious adverse events; skin and tissue temperature rise <1.0°C.

Clinical Translation
- Regulatory path: non-invasive therapeutic ultrasound with integrated imaging; leverage existing acoustic safety standards and risk controls; pivotal RCT in dysmenorrhea, followed by label expansion (stress-exacerbated pelvic pain, peri-procedural uterine hypertonus).
- Manufacturing: off-the-shelf ultrasound ASICs, flexible arrays, belt form factor; cloud-based analytics for personalization.

Novelty
- First uterine-organ–specific, closed-loop neuromodulation using a direct hemodynamic proxy of sympathetic excess.
- Caps only the “excess,” preserving basal sympathetic tone and systemic function through spatial selectivity and band-limited control.

Milestones and Timeline
- Months 0–6: device engineering, phantom/thermal validation, IRB.
- Months 7–12: Aim 1 calibration; finalize controller.
- Months 13–20: Aim 2 crossover trial.
- Months 21–32: Aim 3 home-use RCT; regulatory pre-submission.

Expected Impact
A safe, non-invasive, organ-targeted therapy that normalizes uterine sympathetic overactivity only when it becomes excessive—improving pain and perfusion without systemic sympatholysis.

Title
Acoustic Stretch-Mimetics to Engage the Uterine Anti-Overdrive Reflex (ASMUAR)

Integrated hypothesis–question
If uterine intramural stretch-sensitive afferents are mechanically biased with safe, low-intensity focused ultrasound that mimics physiological distension, will this selectively downregulate excessive sympathetic drive to the uterus—without altering basal uterine tone or systemic sympathetic activity—and thereby attenuate pathologic hypercontractility and pain?

Atomic strategy
Exploit a single endogenous control point: stretch-sensitive uterine mechanosensors (e.g., Piezo/TRP-expressing intramural afferents and myocyte mechanotransducers). Brief, sub-thermal acoustic radiation force (ARF) pulses produce micrometer-scale strain that these sensors interpret as protective distension, engaging local paracrine and spinal inhibitory circuits that dampen noradrenergic efferent output and myometrial excitability. Deliver the stimulus only when uterine activity indicates excessive sympathetic drive, preserving basal tone and systemic function.

Specific aims
1) Map and validate acoustic access to uterine mechanosensor “hotspots.”
2) Demonstrate selective uterine sympatho-attenuation without systemic sympatholysis in humans.
3) Build and test a closed-loop wearable that triggers only during excessive uterine sympathetic activation.

Device concept (non-invasive, wearable, clinically translatable)
- Form factor: Soft, adjustable pelvic belt with a 2D phased-array transducer (300–700 kHz), integrated B-mode imaging for targeting, and surface EHG/IMU sensors. Battery-powered, smartphone-controlled.
- Beam strategy: Sub-thermal, low-MI focused sonication (MI ≤1.3; ISPTA ≤720 mW/cm²; 5–20 ms bursts; 50–150 Hz PRF; 5–20% duty cycle) to generate ARF-induced microstrain (target 0.1–1%) within superficial myometrium at cornua/isthmus and along arcuate vessel planes (putative mechanosensor-rich regions).
- Safety engineering: Real-time acoustic output limits, cavitation monitoring via passive acoustic mapping, thermal model with automatic cutoffs to cap ΔT ≤0.5°C; pregnancy lockout by test.

Targeting and calibration
- Step 1: Imaging-guided registration of uterine position via on-board B-mode and shear-wave elastography to estimate acoustic windows and depth.
- Step 2: Rapid “reflex-mapping” scan: deliver micro-bursts to a tiled grid and measure immediate changes in uterine EHG burst probability and uterine artery Doppler RI. Identify voxels where sonication yields transient reduction in high-frequency EHG power without systemic changes—define as mechanoreflex hotspots.
- Step 3: Personalize beamforming and intensity to the minimal effective dose producing hotspot response.

Closed-loop control (excess-only engagement)
- Sensing: Multichannel abdominal uterine EHG for myometrial burst detection; uterine artery Doppler RI; user-reported pain slider. Systemic sympathetic sentinels: HRV (LF/HF), pupillometry via smartphone camera, skin conductance.
- Trigger logic: Adaptive thresholds derived from each user’s diurnal baseline. Sonication triggers only when uterine EHG burst rate/amplitude exceeds the 90th percentile of individualized baseline for ≥30 s and systemic sentinels remain within ±10% of baseline (to avoid global sympatholysis).
- Termination: Auto-stop when uterine EHG power falls into target band for 60 s or after predefined maximum sonication time per session (e.g., 8 min).

Human studies

Aim 1: Acoustic–physiology mapping (n=30, non-pregnant, dysmenorrhea cohort)
- Design: Within-subject, randomized, sham-controlled mapping across uterine regions.
- Primary readouts: Immediate change in high-frequency uterine EHG power (1–3 Hz band), uterine artery RI, and abdominal wall M-mode strain during micro-bursts.
- Outcome: Spatial map of mechanoreflex hotspots and minimum effective acoustic parameters.

Aim 2: Selectivity and systemic preservation (n=40)
- Design: Randomized, crossover (active vs sham), with standardized sympathetic challenges (cold pressor, mental arithmetic). Sessions separated by ≥48 h.
- Primary endpoint: Percent reduction in uterine EHG burst power and event rate during challenges with active vs sham.
- Selectivity endpoints: No significant changes in HRV LF/HF, baroreflex sensitivity, pupillometry, or skin conductance vs sham; handgrip strength and peripheral vasoconstrictor responses unchanged.
- Secondary endpoints: Pain VAS reduction during menstruation (acute); uterine artery RI modulation; rescue analgesic use.

Aim 3: Feasibility of the wearable closed-loop (n=60, at-home study, 2 cycles)
- Design: Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled. Device operates autonomously using personalized thresholds.
- Primary endpoint: Time-in-excess (proportion of minutes per day with EHG above individualized excess threshold) compared between active and sham.
- Safety endpoints: Skin integrity, adverse sensations, cycle characteristics, fertility intentions unaffected.

Mechanistic substudies
- Biochemical: Non-invasive cervicovaginal fluid sampling pre/post acute sessions for NOx and catecholamine metabolites as exploratory correlates.
- Computational: Patient-specific finite-element models (from ultrasound-derived geometry and tissue property estimates) to predict microstrain distribution; correlate with hotspot efficacy.

Inclusion/exclusion
- Include: Non-pregnant women 18–45, regular cycles, moderate–severe primary dysmenorrhea or stress-exacerbated uterine pain.
- Exclude: Pregnancy or planning, IUD with ferromagnetic components, pelvic infection, known uterine malignancy, recent pelvic surgery, bleeding disorders.

Safety and risk mitigation
- Acoustic limits constrained below diagnostic ultrasound safety thresholds; continuous cavitation surveillance; thermal modeling with duty-cycle caps.
- Off-target protection: Nulls steered away from ovaries, bladder, bowel; auto-abort on motion or loss of target lock.
- Independent DSMB oversight; graded adverse event reporting; pre-registered stopping rules.

Statistical plan
- Aim 2 powered (β=0.8, α=0.05) to detect a 20% reduction in EHG power with SD=25% (n=34; enroll 40 for attrition).
- Mixed-effects models for repeated measures; equivalence testing for systemic markers (TOST within ±10%).

Clinical translation and regulatory path
- De novo 510(k)-like pathway as a wearable therapeutic ultrasound neuromodulator; predicates in diagnostic ultrasound safety and external neuromodulation.
- Manufacturing with medical-grade hydrogels, biocompatible silicone, BLE-enabled controller; cybersecurity per FDA guidance.
- Indications: Acute reduction of uterine hyperactivity and pain associated with dysmenorrhea and stress-induced exacerbations in non-pregnant adults.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Hotspot mapping reproducible in ≥80% of participants; minimum effective ISPTA ≤500 mW/cm².
- M2: ≥20% reduction in uterine EHG excess during standardized stress with no significant change in systemic sympathetic markers (equivalence margin ±10%).
- M3: At-home closed-loop reduces time-in-excess by ≥30% vs sham and lowers pain VAS by ≥1.5 points with no device-related serious adverse events.

Anticipated impact
ASMUAR leverages the uterus as both detector and controller, activating a built-in mechanoreflex only when pathologic sympathetic overdrive emerges. By targeting a single organ-specific control node with non-invasive ultrasound and closed-loop gating, the approach promises selective, drug-free relief without systemic sympatholysis and a clear path to clinical deployment.

Title: Junctional Parasympathetic Amplification to Normalize Uterine Sympathetic Excess (uJ-PA)

Central hypothesis-question (inseparable): Can non-invasive, transcutaneous, junction-focused electrical stimulation amplify pelvic parasympathetic signaling at the uterovaginal plexus to automatically constrain only stress-evoked sympathetic overdrive in the uterus, while preserving basal tone and systemic sympathetic function?

Atomic strategy: Drive a single anatomical “gate” where the calming (pelvic splanchnic; S2–S4) and stress (hypogastric; T10–L2) pathways converge—the uterovaginal plexus—by selectively upmodulating local parasympathetic/nitrergic output. Leveraging presynaptic muscarinic and nitrergic inhibition at sympathetic varicosities within the plexus, brief increases in parasympathetic activity reduce norepinephrine release only in fibers traversing this junction to the uterus. This exploits the organ’s wiring as a built-in safety system: effects are confined to axons that share the uterine junction and do not generalize systemically.

Device concept: Transcutaneous temporal interference neuromodulation for the pelvic junction (tTI-PJ)
- Hardware: Two flexible, multi-pad electrode arrays (front suprapubic belt; posterior sacral/perineal patch). A compact stimulator with real-time sensing and field-steering.
- Stimulation principle: Two kHz-range carriers (e.g., 2000 and 2020 Hz) produce a low-frequency envelope (e.g., 20 Hz) where fields spatially overlap. The envelope maximum is steered to the uterovaginal plexus by adjusting pad currents and phases.
- Intended neural effect: Preferential activation of pelvic splanchnic pre-/postganglionic elements and nitrergic interneurons within the plexus, increasing cholinergic/NO signaling that presynaptically inhibits sympathetic norepinephrine release to the uterus.
- Safety envelope: Per-pad currents within established transcutaneous limits; duty-cycled bursts; temperature and impedance monitoring; automatic shutoffs.

Closed-loop selectivity (to avoid basal sympatholysis)
- Trigger only when uterine excitability exceeds personalized thresholds derived from baseline.
- Inputs:
  1) Transabdominal uterine electromyography (EHG) features (propagation velocity, power ratios) indicating heightened myometrial excitability.
  2) Suprapubic photoplethysmography-derived surrogates of uterine artery pulsatility (relative index from diffuse optical PPG array).
- Control law: If either biomarker deviates >2 SD above individualized baseline (resting, cycle-phase matched), deliver 5–10 s envelopes at 15–25 Hz in 100–200 ms bursts; otherwise idle. This yields state-contingent suppression of spikes without shifting basal tone.

Targeting rationale and personalization
- Target: Uterovaginal (Frankenhäuser) plexus at lateral cervical fornix region, where hypogastric and pelvic splanchnic fibers mix before uterine branches.
- Field steering: Pre-session calibration uses low-amplitude “tag” pulses to map evoked uterine EHG microresponses and optimize pad weights for maximum deep-junction focus with minimal cutaneous activation.
- Anatomical guidance: Ultrasound landmarks (uterine cervix position, uterine artery course) provide subject-specific priors for solver-based field optimization.

Specific aims
1) Validate non-invasive junctional targeting in silico and on bench phantoms
- Build MRI-derived female pelvic models; optimize electrode montages for maximal envelope at uterovaginal plexus and minimal spread to bladder/rectal plexuses.
- Bench: Hydrogel pelvic phantom with embedded nerve-mimetic conductors to verify focality and heating margins.

2) Demonstrate human target engagement and state-dependent suppression (acute studies)
- Participants: Non-pregnant adults with history of stress-exacerbated uterine cramping or dysmenorrhea; cycle-phase controlled.
- Protocol: Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled, crossover. Induce sympathetic stress (cold-pressor and mental arithmetic). Run closed-loop tTI-PJ vs sham on separate days.
- Primary junctional engagement endpoints:
  - Increase in cervicovaginal NOx (non-invasive swab pre/post; safety-compliant) relative to sham.
  - Reduction in uterine artery pulsatility index (transabdominal Doppler, pre/during/post stress).
  - Reduction of stress-evoked EHG excitability metrics only during episodes exceeding baseline; no change at rest.
- Systemic specificity endpoints:
  - No significant changes in finger HRV LF/HF, skin conductance responses, or resting blood pressure during non-episode periods.
  - No changes in calf muscle oxygenation (NIRS) or hand PPG amplitude at rest.

3) Show clinical relevance in a brief home-use pilot
- Population: Individuals with stress-aggravated menstrual pain.
- Intervention: 30-minute daily wearable sessions during high-risk windows (identified from user’s symptom diary) for one cycle, closed-loop enabled.
- Outcomes: Decrease in pain area-under-curve during stressors, reduction in rescue NSAID use, stable everyday HRV and sweat indices, improved quality-of-life scores. Safety logs: skin integrity, heat, paresthesia.

Stimulation parameters (initial)
- Carriers: 2.0 and 2.02 kHz; envelope 20 Hz (titrate 10–30 Hz per responder profile).
- Current per pad: up to 3 mA rms (aggregate constrained by comfort and thermal model).
- Burst structure: 100–200 ms bursts, 10% duty cycle within 5–10 s trains, inter-train interval ≥20 s; adaptive to biomarker feedback.
- Session length: 20–30 minutes.

Mechanistic readouts (supporting)
- Non-invasive markers: salivary alpha-amylase and cortisol (systemic stress controls) unchanged between active and sham at rest.
- Uterine-specific: phase-dependent changes in EHG connectivity decrease during stress only with active stimulation.

Risk management
- Exclusions: Pregnancy, implanted electronic devices, metal pelvic hardware, active pelvic infection, severe dermatologic conditions at electrode sites.
- Real-time safety: Impedance/temperature cutoffs, skin sensors, discomfort-triggered abort, conservative SAR margins.

Criteria for success
- Aim 1: ≥2× simulated envelope intensity at uterovaginal plexus vs adjacent organs; phantom focality reproduced; <0.5°C surface temperature rise.
- Aim 2: During stress episodes, ≥15% reduction in uterine artery PI and significant dampening of EHG excitability vs sham, with no rest-state changes and no systemic sympathetic suppression.
- Aim 3: Clinically meaningful pain reduction (≥30% responder rate) without adverse events and without shifts in resting systemic sympathetic biomarkers.

Clinical translation pathway
- Final form factor: Adjustable suprapubic belt + sacral patch with embedded EHG/PPG sensors; smartphone-guided calibration and cycle-aware scheduling.
- Regulatory strategy: Non-implant neuromodulation Class II, supported by computational models, bench thermal/safety data, and acute human target-engagement evidence.
- Manufacturing: Hydrogel electrodes, medical-grade adhesive, sealed IP-rated stimulator; replaceable patches.

Why this can work now
- Uses organ-level wiring (shared junction) as the selectivity mechanism rather than systemic blockade.
- Temporal interference enables deep, steerable fields through intact skin with modest currents.
- Closed-loop, episode-triggered stimulation ensures only excessive sympathetic activity is constrained, preserving basal tone and systemic function.

Deliverables
- Open-source pelvic field models and montage solver.
- Wearable tTI-PJ prototype and calibration app.
- Blinded trial datasets linking junction-focused stimulation to selective uterine sympathetic downregulation without systemic sympatholysis.

Title
Closed-loop low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) to amplify the uterus’s endogenous adenosine “brake” and cap excessive sympathetic drive without systemic sympatholysis

Unified Hypothesis-Question
Can non-invasive, closed-loop LIFU targeted to the uterus selectively amplify a native, activity-dependent adenosine A1 receptor–mediated brake on norepinephrine (NE) signaling—via mechanically evoked ATP→adenosine transients—thereby suppressing only excessive uterine sympathetic responses while preserving basal uterine tone and systemic sympathetic function?

Atomic Strategy
Exploit a single endogenous gain-control node: presynaptic and myometrial adenosine A1 (Gi) signaling that downregulates NE release and adrenergic responsiveness in a use-dependent manner. Mechanically induce brief, local ATP efflux (via pannexin/connexin and mechanosensitive channels) with LIFU; extracellular ATP is rapidly converted by ectonucleotidases (CD39/CD73) to adenosine, which transiently engages A1 receptors. Because adenosine formation and A1 efficacy scale with activity and are rapidly cleared by adenosine kinase/deaminase, this forms a high-pass, self-limiting brake that caps peaks but spares baseline.

Specific Aims
1) Map and validate the uterine adenosine brake.
- Quantify expression/localization of CD39, CD73, A1 receptors on sympathetic varicosities and myometrial cells in human uterine tissue.
- Establish functional brake: show adenosine/A1 agonism reduces NE release and α1-adrenergic myometrial contraction; confirm activity dependence (stronger at high-frequency stimulation) and rapid reversibility.

2) Engineer LIFU parameters that maximally amplify the brake without heating or off-target effects.
- Define pulse frequency, duty cycle, and radiation force that elicit ATP→adenosine microtransients in myometrium while staying within established diagnostic-therapeutic safety indices.
- Prove mechanism: LIFU effect is abolished by A1 antagonism (e.g., DPCPX), CD73 inhibition (e.g., APCP), or pannexin/mechanosensitive channel blockade (e.g., carbenoxolone, GsMTx4), and is independent of nitric oxide (L-NAME control).

3) Demonstrate closed-loop selectivity and clinical feasibility.
- Build a transabdominal, image-guided phased-array LIFU belt with integrated B-mode imaging and surface electrohysterography (EHG) for detection; optional uterine artery Doppler module for hemodynamic triggers.
- Closed-loop algorithm: deliver short LIFU bursts only when EHG spectral-power and/or uterine artery resistive index exceed individualized thresholds indicative of sympathetic overdrive (e.g., during standardized stress challenges), then auto-terminate.
- Show preservation of systemic sympathetic function: no change in muscle sympathetic nerve activity (microneurography in a human subset), heart rate variability indices of sympathovagal balance, pupilometry, or plasma catecholamines.

Research Plan

Models and Measurements
- Ex vivo human myometrium (elective cesarean/hysterectomy tissue): organ bath with electric field stimulation (EFS) to mimic sympathetic firing; NE quantification by HPLC from superfusate; force transduction for contractility; adenosine/ATP enzymatic microelectrodes; fluorescence biosensors (if available).
- In vivo rodents (non-pregnant, then pregnant): transabdominal LIFU targeting uterine horns under ultrasound guidance; restraint/cold-pressor analog stressors; surface EHG; uterine microdialysis for NE; uterine artery Doppler; lumbar sympathetic nerve recordings (subset) to assay systemic spillover.
- First-in-human feasibility (non-pregnant, dysmenorrhea or stress-provoked hypertonus): wearable LIFU belt; EHG/Doppler-triggered bursts during cold pressor or mental stress; outcomes include EHG power reduction in the high-frequency band, uterine artery resistive index normalization, pain scores; systemic indices unchanged.

Device and Sonication Parameters
- Phased-array 1–3 MHz; electronically steered focal zone mapped to uterine fundus/body; pulse trains 10–100 ms, low duty cycle (<10%), spatial-peak temporal-average intensity within FDA obstetric/physiotherapy safety limits; real-time thermometry surrogate via backscatter/temperature model; automatic beam-shaping to avoid bowel/bladder.

Mechanism Confirmation and Selectivity Tests
- Pharmacology in ex vivo tissue: blockade of A1, CD73, pannexin/mechanosensitive channels should abolish LIFU-mediated suppression of NE release and contractile peaks.
- Frequency selectivity: LIFU reduces EFS-evoked NE and force at high frequencies (>10 Hz) but not at low frequencies (1–2 Hz), indicating high-pass braking.
- Basal preservation: no shift in resting myometrial tone or spontaneous low-amplitude EHG activity without triggers.

Safety
- Exposure below established mechanical index and thermal index thresholds; cavitation monitoring; automatic shutoff on motion or off-target reflections.
- Preclinical histopathology for tissue integrity; reproductive safety studies prior to any pregnancy application.
- Human monitoring: adverse event reporting; pain/comfort scales; no changes in menstrual regularity or fertility markers in follow-up.

Clinical Translation Path
- Indications: stress-exacerbated uterine hyperreactivity (e.g., primary dysmenorrhea, stress-triggered preterm labor risk to be evaluated later under obstetric protocols).
- Personalized calibration: per-patient acoustic window mapping and EHG/Doppler threshold setting.
- Regulatory: IDE for early feasibility as a Class II/III therapeutic ultrasound neuromodulation device; endpoints focused on safety, selectivity (uterus-only effect), and symptom reduction.

Milestones and Go/No-Go Criteria
- M1: Ex vivo proof of mechanism—≥40% reduction in high-frequency EFS-evoked NE and peak force by LIFU; abolished by A1/CD73 blockade; ≤5% change at low-frequency/basal conditions. Go if achieved.
- M2: In vivo rodent selectivity—≥30% reduction in stress-evoked EHG high-frequency power and contractile spikes with no change in systemic sympathetic readouts. Go if achieved and histology is normal.
- M3: Human feasibility—acute, on-demand reduction of stress-evoked uterine hyperactivity (≥30% EHG HF power drop and pain score improvement) with unchanged systemic sympathetic measures and zero device-related adverse events. Proceed to pivotal trial if met.

Expected Impact
A drug-free, organ-specific, activity-dependent neuromodulation that boosts a built-in uterine brake (adenosine A1 signaling) to cap sympathetic surges, preserving basal uterine function and systemic sympathetic physiology. This platform establishes a generalizable paradigm: non-invasively amplifying organ-intrinsic negative feedback to achieve precision sympatholysis only where and when it is needed.

Title
Reflex-Gated Cervical Afferent Neuromodulation to Normalize Excessive Uterine Sympathetic Drive Using Noninvasive Focused Ultrasound

Single-Insight Hypothesis
Gentle activation of low-threshold cervical mechanoreceptors can recruit a sacral spinal inhibitory reflex that suppresses excessive—but not basal—sympathetic efferent activity to the uterus. Noninvasive, closed-loop, transperineal low-intensity focused ultrasound (tiFUS) aimed at the ectocervix can trigger this local “brake” without altering systemic sympathetic function.

Specific Aims
- Aim 1: Demonstrate that brief tiFUS of the ectocervix reduces uterine sympathetic overdrive, indexed by normalization of uterine artery Doppler resistance, only when overdrive is present.
- Aim 2: Verify organ selectivity by showing no change in systemic sympathetic markers (blood pressure, pupil size, skin conductance, peripheral vascular tone, LF/HF HRV ratio).
- Aim 3: Establish safety and feasibility of repeated tiFUS sessions with real-time thermomechanical monitoring, defining exposure envelopes that preserve tissue integrity and reproductive function.

Mechanistic Rationale
- Anatomy/physiology: The cervix contains slowly adapting low-threshold mechanoreceptors (e.g., PIEZO/TRPV4-expressing endings) whose afferents project via pelvic nerves to sacral dorsal horn circuits. These circuits inhibit thoracolumbar (T10–L2) sympathetic premotor output to the hypogastric pathway and facilitate pelvic parasympathetic outflow to the uterus. Activating this pathway should relax myometrial sympathetic vasoconstriction and normalize perfusion without systemic sympatholysis.
- Control principle: A closed-loop controller triggers tiFUS only when a uterine-specific biomarker indicates excessive sympathetic tone, thereby avoiding suppression of basal tone.

Intervention Modality
- Delivery: External, transperineal low-intensity focused ultrasound (0.7–1.1 MHz) steered to the ecto-/endo-cervical junction. A slim, ergonomic perineal applicator couples through gel; no insertion or incision.
- Stimulation pattern: Quasi-static bursts (0.5–3 Hz PRF, 20–40% duty) designed to mimic gentle stretch/vibration that preferentially recruits slowly adapting mechanoreceptors while remaining subthreshold for nociceptors.
- Safety envelope: Mechanical Index ≤ 0.6; spatial-peak temporal-average intensity (ISPTA) ≤ 300 mW/cm²; modeled temperature rise < 0.4°C; real-time passive acoustic mapping plus ultrasound thermometry for shutoff if thresholds are approached.

Closed-Loop Sensing and Control
- Primary uterine biomarker: Transabdominal micro-Doppler patch (suprapubic) tracking uterine artery pulsatility index (uPI) and diastolic flow. Elevated uPI (e.g., >20% above subject-specific baseline) operationalizes “excessive sympathetic tone.”
- Secondary local perfusion: Diffuse optical spectroscopy (NIR) over lower abdomen estimates myometrial oxygenation trends.
- Systemic guardrails: Finger photoplethysmography-derived peripheral resistance, skin conductance, and pupilometry ensure no systemic sympatholysis.
- Control algorithm: Deadband controller targets a personalized uPI band (baseline ±10%). tiFUS engages only when uPI exits the band upward and ceases as it re-enters; integral anti-windup prevents overshoot.

Study Plan

Phase 0: Modeling and Bench Safety
- Finite-element simulations of acoustic fields through perineal tissues and cervix (anthropometric variability) to select transducer geometry and steering limits.
- Tissue-mimicking phantom with embedded pressure/temperature sensors to validate MI/thermal margins and beam localization.
- Go/no-go: Spatial confinement ≥ 10 mm FWHM at cervix; modeled Tmax rise < 0.5°C at duty ≤ 40%.

Phase 1a: First-in-Human, Nonpregnant Adults (n=30), Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Crossover
- Population: 18–45 years; regular menses; no pelvic floor disorders; not pregnant; no hormonal IUD; no active cervicitis; normal Pap in past 3 years.
- Provocation: Cold pressor test (hand immersion, 2 minutes) to induce systemic stress; confirm uterine-specific overdrive by rise in uPI >20% from pre-stress baseline in screening session.
- Arms: Active tiFUS vs sham (identical coupling/ultrasound imaging without neuromodulation bursts), session order randomized, 7-day washout.
- Protocol per session:
  1) Baseline: 10 min rest; record uPI, NIR myometrial oxygenation, uterine EMG, systemic vitals/HRV, skin conductance, pupil size.
  2) Stress: Cold pressor; confirm uPI overshoot.
  3) Closed-loop window (10 min): tiFUS engages only while uPI exceeds band; sham engages imaging only.
  4) Recovery: 10 min monitoring post-intervention.
- Primary endpoint: ΔuPI AUC during closed-loop window (active vs sham) normalized to baseline; superiority defined as ≥15% AUC reduction without dipping below baseline band.
- Secondary endpoints: Change in myometrial oxygenation; uterine EMG spectral shift to lower-frequency coordinated activity; pain/cramp Likert ratings (for dysmenorrhea subgroup, n=15); no change in systemic sympathovagal indices.
- Safety endpoints: Immediate and 24-hour adverse events; cervical/vaginal symptom checklist; ovulatory function markers (luteal progesterone) in a subset.

Phase 1b: Use-Case Translation (n=20) — Dysmenorrhea or Stress-Triggered Uterine Hypertonus
- Ambulatory paradigm during symptomatic episodes. Evaluate on-demand tiFUS responsiveness and durability (30–60 min follow-up), acceptability, and usability metrics.

Mechanism Confirmation Substudy (n=10)
- Capsaicin cream test on perineal skin (to control for nonspecific sensory gating) vs tiFUS; dissociate local cervical reflex effects from generalized sensory distraction.
- H-Reflex/SSR recordings and microneurography alternatives are excluded to remain noninvasive; inference relies on uterine-specific vs systemic marker dissociation.

Data and Analysis
- Crossover mixed-effects models with subject random intercept; condition (active/sham), time, and their interaction as fixed effects.
- Pre-registered uPI responder definition; hierarchical false-discovery control across secondary endpoints.
- Power: With within-subject SD of 12% for uPI, n=30 achieves 90% power to detect 10% difference at α=0.05.

Risk Mitigation
- Off-target organ effects: Real-time beam localization using concurrent B-mode imaging; geo-fencing to cervix; automatic shutdown on displacement >5 mm.
- Thermal/mechanical safety: Continuous MI/TI display; redundant cutoffs; session energy budget limits; pregnancy exclusion and pre-session urine hCG testing.
- Autonomic spillover: Continuous systemic monitoring; predefined stopping rules for BP drops or bradycardia; expected incidence low given afferent-local reflex targeting.

Translational Path
- Device: Class II pathway leveraging established ultrasound safety standards; integrated perineal emitter + suprapubic Doppler patch + controller.
- Indications trajectory: Dysmenorrhea with vasoconstrictive phenotype → uterine hypertonus in assisted reproduction cycles → stress-exacerbated pelvic pain syndromes. Pregnancy-related indications deferred to later phases after reproductive safety dossier.
- Human factors: Quiet, ergonomic, 10-minute session; privacy-compatible use; disposable gel interface.

Success Criteria and Go/No-Go
- Go: In Phase 1a, active vs sham shows ≥15% reduction in uPI AUC during stress with no significant change in systemic markers and no device-related adverse effects; ≥80% of sessions remain within thermal/mechanical safety limits with zero serious AEs.
- No-Go: Any evidence of systemic sympatholysis, persistent uterine atony below baseline band, mucosal injury, or unacceptable discomfort leading to >15% session terminations.

Expected Impact
A noninvasive, reflex-gated, cervix-targeted neuromodulation that selectively dampens pathologic uterine sympathetic overactivity while preserving basal tone and systemic autonomic function, offering a first-in-class, organ-specific therapy for uterine perfusion and spasm disorders.

text:
Title
Closed-loop “Traffic-Light” Neuromodulation to Attenuate Excess Uterine Sympathetic Surges via Presacral Focused Ultrasound

Central Question–Hypothesis (merged)
Can a closed-loop, organ-specific focused ultrasound intervention applied at the final sympathetic convergence to the uterus (superior hypogastric/presacral plexus) selectively dampen pathologic, stress-evoked sympathetic bursts—while preserving basal sympathetic tone system-wide—when triggered by a non-invasive uterine surge signature?

Atomic Strategy
Exploit the anatomical bottleneck of uterine sympathetic input (presacral/superior hypogastric plexus) with low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) to produce a brief, reversible decrease in postganglionic firing only when an on-body sensor suite detects a validated “uterine sympathetic surge” signature derived from uterine artery Doppler and abdominal electrohysterography (EHG). The intervention functions as a just-in-time traffic light at the last intersection before signals reach the uterus.

Specific Aims
1) Derive and validate a non-invasive, uterus-specific biomarker signature of excessive sympathetic activation.
2) Engineer and parameterize a transabdominal LIFU protocol that transiently reduces postganglionic sympathetic conduction at the presacral plexus without altering basal tone or off-target autonomic function.
3) Test a fully closed-loop system that triggers presacral LIFU only during detected surges, demonstrating reduction of uterine sympathetic reactivity with preserved systemic sympathetic activity in a human randomized, sham-controlled study.

Rationale and Feasibility
- Anatomy: Sympathetic fibers to the uterus converge at the superior hypogastric plexus and uterovaginal plexus (Frankenhäuser). Targeting the presacral plexus from the lower abdomen (with a comfortably filled bladder as an acoustic window) allows organ-selective access while avoiding systemic sympatholysis.
- Modality: LIFU can modulate peripheral nerve activity non-thermally with millimeter-scale focal zones, is non-invasive, and can be delivered within established diagnostic ultrasound safety indices.
- Selectivity in time: Triggering only during detected surges preserves basal tone.
- Selectivity in space: Acoustic holography and real-time image guidance confine energy to the presacral region, limiting effects on adjacent viscera.

Design and Methods

Aim 1: Uterine Surge Signature (USS)
- Population: Non-pregnant women (Phase 1) followed by pregnant participants at risk of stress-provoked uterine irritability (Phase 2; obstetric oversight).
- Provocations: Standardized acute stressors (e.g., cold pressor, validated mental stress tasks).
- Sensing (all non-invasive):
  - High-frame-rate transabdominal uterine artery Doppler (bilateral) to extract resistance index (RI), pulsatility index (PI), and beat-to-beat vasomotor variability.
  - 8-channel abdominal EHG for myometrial electrical activity; compute spectral power, propagation velocity, and EHG–Doppler coupling.
  - Diffuse optical spectroscopy over the suprapubic window for relative myometrial oxygenation as an auxiliary readout.
  - Systemic controls: heart-rate variability, finger peripheral arterial tone, and galvanic skin response to confirm absent systemic sympatholysis.
- Analysis: Define the USS as a multivariate deviation (z > 2.0 from individual baseline) combining ΔPI/ΔRI spikes with time-locked EHG spectral shifts (increase in 0.3–1.0 Hz band and coherence with PI). Classify “exaggerated responders” by reproducible USS magnitude across two sessions.
- Deliverable: A validated, individualized USS detector with sub-5 s latency and >85% precision for surge onset.

Aim 2: Presacral LIFU Parameterization
- Targeting: Ultrasound or MRI-based localization of the presacral plexus at L5–S1; bladder filling optimizes the acoustic path. Acoustic holography beamforming shapes a 3–5 mm focal zone.
- Stimulation parameters (initial bounds, safety-first):
  - Carrier: 500–700 kHz; pulse duration 0.5–1.0 ms; PRF 0.5–2 kHz; duty cycle ≤30%; sonication epochs 5–10 s; inter-epoch ≥20 s.
  - Intensity constrained to maintain TI < 0.7 and MI within diagnostic limits; real-time thermal modeling and skin surface thermography.
- Mechanistic endpoint: Reversible reduction in sympathetic efferent conduction probability at surge rates (use-dependent bias), indexed indirectly by attenuation of USS magnitude without change in resting uterine artery PI/RI.
- Off-target monitoring: Colonic motility ultrasound, bladder pressure surrogates, and lower-limb skin temperature to rule out regional autonomic spillover.

Aim 3: Closed-loop Trial (Human, Randomized, Double-Blind, Sham-Controlled)
- Device: Belt-integrated transducer array (presacral aperture) + abdominal EHG/Doppler sensors + onboard USS detector and controller.
- Arms: Closed-loop LIFU vs sham (identical audio/gel/pressure; no acoustic output).
- Procedure: Induce standardized stressors across three blocks. Controller triggers sonication only when USS threshold crossed; sham triggers “virtual” events.
- Primary endpoint: Percent reduction in stress-evoked ΔPI (mean of bilateral uterine arteries) relative to baseline in exaggerated responders.
- Key secondary endpoints:
  - Preservation of basal uterine artery PI/RI at rest (non-inferiority margin ≤5% from baseline).
  - No change in systemic sympathetic markers (HRV LF/HF, finger PAT, skin conductance) vs baseline and vs sham.
  - Safety: No pain, no cutaneous heating >1°C, no tissue dose above preset TI/MI; no urinary or bowel adverse effects.
- Sample size: n=60 exaggerated responders (30 per arm) to detect a 20% reduction in ΔPI with 80% power, α=0.05.
- Statistics: Mixed-effects models with within-subject baselines; Bayesian posterior for non-inferiority on basal tone.

Closed-loop Controller (“U-SIGNAL”)
- Detection: USS computed every heartbeat with a causal filter; surge defined as composite score crossing individualized threshold for ≥3 consecutive beats.
- Actuation: Preprogrammed sonication epoch; adaptive titration (ladder up/down duty cycle) to achieve target ΔPI attenuation while constraining a “basal integrity index” derived from resting PI/EHG.
- Fail-safes: Hard caps on duty cycle, MI/TI; lockout between epochs; auto-abort on motion or thermal rise.

Safety and Ethics
- Operate strictly within diagnostic ultrasound exposure limits; continuous thermal index monitoring.
- Pregnancy phase commences only after DSMB review of Phase 1 safety.
- Exclusions: Pelvic metal implants, coagulopathy, severe GI/urinary disorders, high-risk obstetric contraindications (Phase 2).
- Adverse event plan: Immediate cessation, clinical evaluation, and unblinding pathway.

Milestones and Go/No-Go
- M1: USS classifier AUC ≥0.85; detection latency ≤5 s.
- M2: Presacral LIFU reduces surge ΔPI ≥20% without altering resting PI (≤5% change) in ≥70% of exaggerated responders (open-label titration).
- M3: In RCT, closed-loop LIFU superior to sham on primary endpoint; non-inferiority on basal tone and systemic markers; zero device-related serious adverse events.

Translational Path
- Product concept: Wearable presacral LIFU belt integrated with Doppler/EHG sensors delivering on-demand “uterine sympathetic variance clamp.”
- Clinical use-cases: High-stress triggers in pregnancy, preterm labor risk stratification adjunct, dysmenorrhea with stress-exacerbated components.
- Regulatory: Leverage existing ultrasound safety standards; pursue de novo pathway with neuromodulation indication; human factors validation for at-home supervised use.

Novelty
- First organ-specific, event-triggered sympathetic modulation at the presacral “last intersection,” guided by a validated uterine surge signature and delivered non-invasively under diagnostic ultrasound constraints.

Expected Impact
A precise, on-demand uterine “traffic light” that reduces harmful stress-evoked sympathetic input without systemic sympatholysis, preserving physiological tone and enabling safe, clinically practical prevention of stress-linked uterine hyperreactivity.
