Title
Strain-Locked Preconditioning (SLP) to Preserve Dermal–Subcutaneous Architecture During Intentional Weight Loss

Core hypothesis and goal
If dermal and fibroseptal extracellular matrix (ECM) are photochemically cross-linked while they are held under physiologic tension from full adipocyte turgor, the tissue’s load-bearing lattice can be “strain-locked” and fibroblasts primed to reinforce it. This preconditioning will:
- Resist MMP-driven degradation during subsequent weight loss,
- Prevent fibrous septa buckling and loss of adipose support,
- Maintain skin elasticity and contour,
while leaving adipocyte lipolysis unimpaired.

Atomic strategy
Program the skin–fat composite with a single, brief intervention that combines:
- Fractional, microcontrolled injury to activate dermal and septal fibroblasts, and
- Local, light-triggered collagen/elastin cross-linking delivered while the tissue is held in a defined tensile strain field.
The cross-linking “freezes” the tensioned ECM architecture and raises its resistance to enzymatic cleavage; the injury-induced fibroblast response deposits new matrix into this pre-aligned scaffold. Lipolysis proceeds normally because no anti-lipolytic pharmacology is used and adipocyte metabolism is not targeted.

Modality
- Photo-chemistry: intratissue riboflavin (vitamin B2) as a photosensitizer for collagen/elastin cross-linking.
- Energy: interstitial 365–405 nm light via side-firing microneedle optical fibers; output calibrated for shallow dermis and superficial subcutis.
- Injury: fractional radiofrequency (RF) or ablative microneedling delivered through the same array to create ~150–300 μm microcolumns at 0.8–1.5 mm (dermis) and 2–3 mm (superficial fat septa).
- Strain field: vacuum-cup applicator imposes controlled biaxial stretch (5–12% surface strain) aligned to Langer’s lines; septal strain enhanced by alternating suction–release cycles during illumination to bias fiber alignment.
- Formulation: 0.05–0.1% riboflavin in isotonic hydrogel with collagen-binding peptide for retention; optional yellow-light quench to cap radicals and limit overt stiffening.

Treatment workflow (few-session intervention)
- Session 1 (Day −28 to −21 before caloric restriction/GLP‑1 initiation):
  1) Map target zones by ultrasound to 5–8 mm depth; register septal orientation.
  2) Prime with fractional RF microneedling (5–10% coverage) to induce controlled dermal and septal microinjury.
  3) Infuse riboflavin solution via hollow microneedles; dwell 5–7 minutes.
  4) Apply vacuum-cup strain (pre-set %strain and orientation), then deliver interstitial light:
     - Dermis: 365–405 nm, 3–9 mW/cm2 equivalent, 5–10 J/cm2 per tile.
     - Superficial septa: side-firing needles at 2–3 mm depth, 2–5 J per tract.
  5) Yellow-light cap (560–590 nm, low fluence) to terminate residual radical activity.
- Session 2 (Day −14 to −10): Repeat at lower density (2–5% coverage) to consolidate scaffold.
- Begin structured weight loss on Day 0. No further treatment needed unless touch-up at Month 3.

Mechanism of action
- Cross-linking: Riboflavin photoexcitation generates reactive oxygen species that induce covalent cross-links between collagen/elastin residues, increasing fiber stiffness, reducing susceptibility to MMP cleavage, and raising the critical buckling load of fibrous septa.
- Strain-locking: Illumination under defined tensile strain biases fiber alignment and “locks” the anisotropy of the lattice. When adipocyte volume shrinks, the pre-aligned network maintains contour and resists wrinkling.
- Regenerative priming: Fractional microinjury activates fibroblasts and adipose stromal cells to deposit collagen I/III and elastin microfibrils into the pre-stiffened scaffold, improving resilience without excessive bulk deposition.
- Selectivity: No agents inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase or ATGL; adipocytes are not thermally or chemically ablated. Effects are confined to ECM via localized light and photosensitizer placement.

Preclinical plan

Aim 1. Feasibility and dose–response (human abdominoplasty skin–fat explants)
- Groups: control, injury-only, cross-link-only (varying fluence), combined SLP ± strain.
- Readouts (Day 0, 7, 21): uniaxial tensile testing (toe-region slope, ultimate strain), AFM nanoindentation stiffness maps, second harmonic generation (SHG) imaging for collagen alignment, elastin autofluorescence quantitation, MMP-1/2/9 activity, TIMP-1/3 levels, desmosine/isodesmosine content, fibroblast myofibroblast marker (α-SMA) time course.
- Septa stability assay: compressive buckling threshold in fat-attached explants under cyclic load.

Decision gates: Identify an energy–concentration window that increases dermal modulus 20–40% and septal buckling load ≥30% without >10% loss of reversible extensibility.

Aim 2. Efficacy under weight loss (porcine model)
- N=24 pigs, stratified by zone; caloric restriction to 12–15% body weight loss over 8 weeks.
- Arms: control, injury-only, cross-link-only, SLP.
- Primary outcomes: change in skin laxity index (3D surface profilometry), dermal thickness (HF ultrasound), shear-wave elastography, septal integrity score (US/MRI), contour maintenance (sag depth under gravity), and blinded histomorphometry (collagen I/III ratio, elastin area fraction).
- Selectivity: serum glycerol/NEFA kinetics during catecholamine challenge; adipose ATGL/HSL phosphorylation; lipolysis rate in ex vivo adipocytes.
- Safety: pigmentation change, TEWL, nerve conduction in treatment field, photosensitivity, fibrosis scoring.

Success criteria: SLP improves sag depth by ≥30% vs control at equivalent fat loss; maintains or improves elastic recovery (Cutometer R7) vs baseline; no impairment of systemic or local lipolysis.

Aim 3. First-in-human pilot (single-arm, n=20; abdomen/flanks; coordinated with GLP‑1 therapy)
- Two SLP sessions completed ≥10 days before starting GLP‑1.
- Endpoints at Months 0, 3, 6: skin laxity grade, 3D photogrammetry contour retention, Cutometer elasticity (R2/R7), ultrasound dermal thickness/septa echogenicity, patient-reported outcome (BODY‑Q), safety.
- Exploratory: circulating MMP/TIMP, noninvasive ECM turnover markers.

Selectivity, safety, and risk management
- Light containment and dosimetry to avoid melanocyte/appendage injury; real-time diffuse reflectance feedback to titrate fluence.
- Limit cumulative fluence; fractional patterning preserves perfusion and mobility.
- Anti-fibrosis guardrails: cap illumination with yellow light; avoid sustained TGF‑β agonism; monitor α‑SMA; predefine retreatment ceilings.
- Photosensitizer safety: riboflavin is non-mutagenic; localized delivery via microneedles limits off-target exposure.

Manufacturability and regulatory pathway
- Device-drug combination: riboflavin gel (topical/infusible) plus a Class II/III microneedle optical RF platform with vacuum applicator.
- Precedents: corneal cross-linking (riboflavin/UVA), fractional RF microneedling, interstitial light delivery, negative-pressure tissue manipulation.
- Path: bench biophotonics/dosimetry + GLP toxicology; IDE for early feasibility under combination-product review.

Differentiation and patentable inventions
- Strain-locked photochemical cross-linking of dermal and fibroseptal ECM performed before weight loss to preserve architecture during subsequent adipocyte shrinkage.
- Integrated microneedle array that co-delivers fractional microinjury, riboflavin infusion, and interstitial side-firing light under controlled vacuum-imposed strain with real-time optical feedback.
- ECM-targeted retention chemistry for photosensitizer; yellow-light capping sequence to bound cross-link density.
- Treatment timing algorithm linked to anticipated onset of pharmacologic/dietary lipolysis.

Milestones
- M6: Dose–response map and strain–anisotropy parameters (Aim 1).
- M12: Porcine efficacy with predefined success criteria (Aim 2).
- M18: Device verification/validation; submit IDE.
- M24: Complete first-in-human pilot (Aim 3) powering a pivotal study.

Go/no-go criteria
- Demonstrate ≥30% preservation of contour metrics at equivalent fat loss without diminished lipolysis indices; maintain elastic recovery within 10% of baseline or better; no grade ≥2 adverse device effects.

Impact
SLP shifts skin tightening from reactive to proactive: a single, pre-loss, strain-programmed ECM reinforcement that preserves dermal elasticity and septal support while allowing fat to decrease as intended.

Title
Cis-anchored, trans-triggered prodrugs on living immune cells for site-selective therapy

Central question/hypothesis
Can a membrane-anchored, AND-gated small‑molecule prodrug carried by unmodified immune cells achieve selective drug release only within diseased microenvironments (inflamed tissue or tumor) while preserving native cell migration and immune functions?

Atomic strategy
Load immune cells ex vivo with a universal, cell‑membrane–inserting amphiphilic prodrug that is inert during trafficking and releases its active payload only upon simultaneous exposure to two co-localized microenvironmental cues (e.g., mild acidity AND a disease-associated protease, or high ROS AND hypoxia). This “cis-anchored, trans-cleaving” design decouples carriage from activation, preserving immune cell function and enforcing site specificity.

Innovation
- Dual-gated chemical logic on the cell surface (no heavy genetic engineering).
- Outer-leaflet insertion using endocytosis‑resistant anchors to avoid intracellular drug exposure and functional perturbation.
- Modular linker–payload library adaptable to neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and T cells and to diverse indications (acute/chronic inflammation, solid tumors).
- Clinically practical loading by brief incubation and wash; GMP-friendly small‑molecule chemistry; patentable compositions-of-matter (anchor–linker–AND-gate–payload architectures) and methods of use.

Proposed product concept
TMAPs (Tissue‑Microenvironment Activated Prodrugs): R–Anchor–Spacer–Gate1–Gate2–Self‑immolative linker–Payload
- Anchor: long-chain saturated diacyl or sterol-based anchor with hydrophilic spacer to stably partition into the outer leaflet and resist endocytosis.
- Gate1/Gate2 (examples): pH‑labile acyl/ketal; protease-cleavable peptide (MMP‑2/9, neutrophil elastase, legumain); ROS‑labile boronic/thioketal; hypoxia‑reductive nitroaromatic. Gates arranged in series to require co‑occurrence for release.
- Payload: anti-inflammatory (e.g., corticosteroid, JAK inhibitor) for inflamed tissues; cytotoxic/immune‑modulatory (e.g., microtubule inhibitor, STING agonist prodrug) for tumors.
- Optional QC tag: self‑quenched fluor that lights upon linker scission for release analytics (not present in clinical lot).

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and screen TMAP chemotypes that maximize outer‑leaflet residency and dual‑trigger specificity.
- Criteria: stable membrane insertion on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and T cells; <10% spontaneous release over relevant circulation times; ≥100‑fold faster activation under AND conditions vs single triggers; negligible internalization by the carrier cell.
- Readouts: physical retention on cells; trigger‑dependent release kinetics; serum stability; lack of complement activation or cell activation markers.

Aim 2. Demonstrate preserved immune cell function and trafficking with TMAP loading.
- Cells: primary human neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages (M0/M2‑like), and CD8+ T cells.
- Required performance: unchanged chemotaxis/transmigration to canonical chemokines; preserved phagocytosis/oxidative burst (myeloid); intact TCR signaling and cytotoxic synapse formation (T cells); normal adhesion rolling on endothelial substrates; no shift in cytokine baseline or exhaustion markers.

Aim 3. Validate site‑selective release and therapeutic benefit in disease-relevant models.
- Inflammation models (e.g., sterile lung inflammation): neutrophil or monocyte carriers bearing anti‑inflammatory TMAPs; endpoints: co-localization, on‑site release, edema reduction, cytokine normalization, off‑target exposure.
- Solid tumor models with known cue profiles (e.g., acidic/MMP‑high): macrophage or T‑cell carriers with cytotoxic or immune‑agonist TMAPs; endpoints: intratumoral payload accumulation vs plasma/healthy tissue, tumor growth delay, preservation of carrier function (tumor infiltration, antigen-specific killing), safety.

Aim 4. Establish manufacturing, safety, and regulatory path.
- Scalable closed‑system loading by short incubation and wash; release testing: anchor density window, absence of free drug, AND‑gate function.
- Safety: hematology/chemistry, cytokine panels, thrombosis/hemolysis, biodistribution, off‑target activation challenges.
- Regulatory: combination product plan (cell therapy + prodrug), CMC for small‑molecule TMAP (ICH), cell processing under cGMP with minimal manipulation relative to gene‑engineered products.

Design principles and rationale
- Function preservation: avoid receptor crosslinking by using inert lipid anchors and low surface densities; avoid intracellular payload exposure by outer‑leaflet residency and slow flip‑flop anchors; use D‑amino acid protease substrates to resist nonspecific cleavage on carrier cells; no antibody or Fc engagement to prevent opsonization.
- Spatial specificity: dual gates encode the pathophysiology of target tissues (e.g., pH 6.5–6.8 plus MMP‑9 in tumors; high ROS plus elastase in acute inflammation), minimizing premature activation in blood or healthy tissues.
- Universal chassis: the same chemical chassis applies across immune cell types; only the gate pair and payload change per indication.
- Fail‑safe: incorporate a slow “time‑lock” hydrolysis (weeks) to ensure eventual clearance if cells do not reach target.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: Lead TMAP chemotypes with ≥24 h outer‑leaflet retention on all four cell types and AND/OR selectivity ratio ≥50 in vitro.
- M2: Full preservation of migration and core functions vs untreated cells; no increase in activation/exhaustion markers.
- M3: In vivo: ≥5‑fold higher payload AUC at target vs systemic; ≥70% of total payload release occurring intralesionally.
- M4: Efficacy: statistically significant improvement over free drug and over untargeted prodrug; clean safety panel.
- M5: Scalable, closed‑system process with defined release specs; pre‑IND meeting package with regulatory feedback.

Clinical applicability
- Autologous leukapheresis for chronic indications (tumor) and rapid whole‑blood enrichment for acute indications (inflammation); short ex vivo handling fits clinical workflow.
- Broad eligibility: no HLA engineering; compatible with standard of care.
- Combination potential: TMAP‑T cells co‑administered with checkpoint inhibitors; TMAP‑macrophages with radiotherapy.

Risk mitigation
- If any cell type shows uptake or functional drift, down‑select anchors with higher flip‑flop barriers and reduce surface density.
- If dual‑gate is too stringent in vivo, rebalance kinetics by swapping one gate for a more abundant cue in the target tissue.
- If ex vivo handling limits neutrophil viability, pivot to in situ loading by brief infusion of TMAPs optimized for leukocyte‑selective insertion (backup concept).

IP strategy
- Claims on dual‑gated, outer‑leaflet–residing amphiphilic prodrugs; specific gate pairs matched to disease microenvironments; anchor–spacer scaffolds that minimize endocytosis; methods of loading living immune cells and using them as carriers for site‑specific release; QC assays linking anchor density, AND‑gated activation, and clinical release specifications.

Expected outcome and impact
A first‑in‑class, low‑engineering cell‑based delivery platform that harnesses native immune trafficking and chemical logic to confine potent therapies to diseased tissues, improving efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity and streamlining clinical translation.

Title
Phase-locked, lesion-specific chronopharmacology for rheumatoid arthritis via endogenous endocrine-ratiometric gating

Central hypothesis (atomic strategy)
A drug carrier that reads the endogenous circadian phase from the nightly melatonin:cortisol ratio (high melatonin, low cortisol) can pre-arm and then conditionally release anti-inflammatory agents only within inflamed synovium using a minimal “AND” logic with lesion signals (protease and ROS). This ratiometric endocrine gate synchronizes the carrier to patient-specific circadian phase without external clocks and triggers pre-emptive release in the late-night window preceding early-morning flares.

Specific aims
1) Build a ratiometric endocrine gate that opens only when melatonin is high and cortisol is low.
2) Add a lesion “AND” gate to confine release to inflamed joints.
3) Integrate secondary biological-phase modulators to sharpen timing (inflammatory intensity) and shut down during resolution (regeneration phase).
4) Demonstrate pre-emptive control of morning stiffness proxies and cytokine surges in ex vivo human synovial samples and in vivo arthritis models.

Design overview
- Carrier: core–shell nanoparticle (NP) or thin hydrogel depot sized for synovial retention (80–150 nm NP; or injectable depot).
- Primary circadian sensing (phase readout):
  - Melatonin gate: structure-switching melatonin-binding polymer (molecularly imprinted polymer, MIP) that swells upon melatonin binding.
  - Cortisol gate: structure-switching cortisol aptamer clamp that tightens when cortisol is present; absence of cortisol releases the clamp.
  - Ratiometric logic: two opposing gates are cross-coupled so pore opening occurs only when melatonin-bound MIP is swollen AND cortisol aptamer is unclamped (melatonin high/cortisol low, late night).
- Lesion specificity (spatial gate):
  - Stealth corona attached via peptides cleaved by synovial proteases (MMP-9/cathepsin B). Corona removal exposes tissue-binding ligands (e.g., decorin/tenascin-C–binding peptides) and opens access to pores only in inflamed synovium.
- Secondary-phase modulators (temporal sharpening):
  - Inflammatory stage: thioketal crosslinks in the shell accelerate degradation with elevated ROS, increasing release rate during active inflammation.
  - Regeneration phase off-switch: IL-10 or TGF-β aptamer-mediated re-crosslinkers tighten the shell when pro-resolving cytokines rise, halting release.
  - Optional immune-activation sensitivity: nitric-oxide–labile linkers add burst control when inducible NOS is high.
- Cargo: low-dose glucocorticoid (prednisolone) or JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib) for RA; optionally co-load IL-6R or TNF inhibitors for flare capping.
- No external timing: all triggers are endogenous hormones, proteases, ROS, and pro-resolving cytokines.

Research plan

Aim 1: Engineer the ratiometric endocrine gate
- Construct:
  - Synthesize melatonin MIP nanoparticles and embed in a porous shell to transduce melatonin binding into volumetric swelling.
  - Conjugate cortisol structure-switching DNA aptamers across pores as reversible clamps.
  - Cross-couple by tethering aptamer clamps to MIP domains so melatonin swelling physically slackens clamp tension.
- In vitro characterization:
  - Determine gate transfer function vs melatonin and cortisol (0.1–200 pg/mL melatonin; 10–300 ng/mL cortisol) across physiologic ranges.
  - Quantify opening probability and pore conductance; fit to ratiometric model (opening occurs within a defined melatonin:cortisol ratio band).
  - Check circadian entrainment fidelity under dynamic hormone waveforms mimicking human plasma profiles; measure phase-locking and pre-arming kinetics.
- Success criteria:
  - >10-fold difference in release rate between “night window” (melatonin high/cortisol low) and “day” conditions.
  - Phase-lock within 2 cycles and maintain ±1 h phase error under variable amplitudes.

Aim 2: Implement lesion “AND” gating
- Construct:
  - Attach PEG stealth corona via MMP-9/cathepsin-B cleavable linkers.
  - Under corona: expose synovial ECM-binding peptides and the endocrine gate only after proteolysis.
- Tests:
  - Protease specificity in synovial fluid vs plasma.
  - Off-target assessment in healthy cartilage explants and plasma-spiked assays.
- Success criteria:
  - >90% corona removal in inflamed synovial fluid within 2–4 h; <10% removal in matched plasma/healthy synovial fluid.
  - <5% of night-window release in protease-negative conditions.

Aim 3: Add secondary-phase modulators
- Inflammatory sharpening:
  - Incorporate thioketal crosslinks; calibrate acceleration factors at 10–100 μM H2O2 and peroxynitrite.
- Regeneration off-switch:
  - Embed IL-10 or TGF-β aptamers that, upon ligand binding, recruit multivalent crosslinkers (e.g., heparin–polycation) to re-tighten pores.
- Dynamic profiling:
  - Run time-resolved release under hormone waveforms plus step-changes in ROS and IL-10/TGF-β to emulate flare → resolution transitions.
- Success criteria:
  - ROS increases boost release rate ≥3× only during night-window and with corona removed.
  - IL-10/TGF-β addition reduces release to baseline within 1 h despite continued night-window hormones.

Aim 4: Ex vivo and in vivo validation
- Ex vivo human:
  - Use paired plasma and synovial fluid from RA patients sampled across 24 h to drive microfluidic perfusion of carriers loaded with tofacitinib.
  - Readouts: time-aligned release, blockade of IL-6/TNF in stimulated synovial explants, and prevention of pre-dawn cytokine rise.
- In vivo models:
  - Rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (robust melatonin rhythm) and a humanized cytokine RA model.
  - Dosing at afternoon; evaluate overnight arming and pre-dawn joint drug levels.
  - Outcomes: suppression of 04:00–08:00 joint cytokines, reduction of morning stiffness proxies (grip strength, gait), and histologic inflammation scores.
- Pharmacology and safety:
  - Compare AUC-normalized efficacy vs standard morning dosing and modified-release prednisone.
  - Assess systemic exposure reduction and HPA-axis perturbation.

Milestones and go/no-go
- M1 (Month 6): Endocrine gate achieves ≥10× night/day differential with ±1 h phase precision. Go if met.
- M2 (Month 12): Protease AND-gate yields ≥10× lesion vs plasma specificity; off-target release <5%. Go if met.
- M3 (Month 18): Secondary modulators deliver ≥3× ROS-boost and ≥80% IL-10/TGF-β shutoff within 1 h. Go if met.
- M4 (Month 24): In vivo pre-emptive control of morning flare proxies with ≥50% dose reduction vs standard care. Advance to scale-up.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Variability in hormone amplitudes: ratiometric gating (ratio, not absolute levels) plus broadened passband around typical night ratios; patient plasma profiling for initial tuning if needed.
- Melatonin-deficient individuals: offer cortisol-only low-nadir gate variant; or swap melatonin MIP for norepinephrine-sensing module (nocturnal drop) while retaining ratiometric logic.
- Off-target protease activity: dual-enzyme requirement (MMP-9 AND cathepsin-B in series) and inclusion of synovial ECM-binding ligands post-cleavage.
- Aptamer stability: 2′-O-methyl/PS modifications and protein coronas minimized by zwitterionic brushes.

Expected impact
- Pre-emptive, lesion-confined dosing that neutralizes the nocturnal cytokine surge driving early-morning stiffness.
- Reduced systemic exposure and side effects by releasing drug only when and where needed.
- A generalizable, clock-synchronized delivery architecture that can be retuned to other autoimmune diseases with circadian flares.

Title
Circadian phase‑locked living implants for preemptive, lesion‑specific immunomodulation in rheumatoid arthritis

Hypothesis-as-question
Can a minimal, host‑entrained genetic clock implanted into inflamed synovium convert the tissue’s own circadian phase into a fixed pre‑flare therapeutic pulse—while gating by inflammatory, immune‑activation, regeneration, and cell‑cycle states—to suppress the early‑morning flare without external timing inputs or off‑lesion release?

Atomic strategy
Exploit the peripheral clock already present in lesion tissue as the master oscillator. Build a simple, phase‑locked output in engineered cells that opens a narrow “dose window” at a defined circadian phase preceding the flare; drug release occurs only if lesion‑state gates indicate an upcoming inflammatory surge.

System concept: Circadian Phase‑Locked Therapeutic Cells (C‑PLTCs)
- Chassis
  - Encapsulated mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) or macrophage‑like cells, implanted intra‑articularly in affected joints.
  - Semipermeable, MMP‑degradable hydrogel microcapsules to confine cells to lesional synovium and bias responsiveness to inflamed extracellular matrix.

- Module 1: Host entrainment (primary sensing axis)
  - Synthetic “Circadian Phase Sensor” promoter with tandem E‑box (BMAL1:CLOCK) and RORE (REV‑ERB/ROR) elements drives a short‑half‑life timing protein (TimerTF).
  - TimerTF stability tuned by PEST/ODD degrons to sharpen a nocturnal peak; SIRT‑dependent deacetylation sites retained to couple to NAD+/redox rhythms.
  - Result: robust locking of TimerTF oscillation to the local synovial circadian rhythm without exogenous cues.

- Module 2: Phase‑advance window (pre‑flare targeting)
  - A Time‑Gate promoter (driven by TimerTF) opens a 2–3 h secretion window centered in late night (e.g., ~02:00–04:00), calibrated to precede the typical dawn cytokine rise.
  - Fine‑phase calibration via adjustable 5′UTR RNA timers and proteasomal degradation rates to set a constant phase lead relative to the tissue oscillator.

- Module 3: Lesion‑state gating (secondary biological phases; AND/NOT logic)
  - Inflammatory stage: NF‑κB‑responsive “arming latch” that records prior‑cycle inflammation amplitude. If NF‑κB activity exceeds threshold during the previous day, a transient recombinase‑based ON state (self‑erasing within one cycle) permits dosing in the upcoming Time‑Gate.
  - Immune activation: IFN‑γ/STAT1‑responsive elements add a second AND input, raising the threshold for dosing when antigen‑presenting activity is high.
  - Regeneration/resolution: IL‑10/STAT3 or TGF‑β/SMAD‑responsive NOT gate suppresses dosing during pro‑resolving or repair phases to avoid blunting regeneration.
  - Cell cycle: E2F‑responsive repressor (or miR‑targeted repression) silences output during S‑phase to minimize coupling to proliferative noise and reduce metabolic load during division.

- Module 4: Payload and release mechanism
  - Primary: secreted anti‑IL‑6R nanobody (sVHH‑IL6R) with synovial matrix‑binding peptide to enhance local retention.
  - Optional adjunct: enzyme‑mediated local prodrug activation (e.g., nitroreductase) to convert an evening‑taken, otherwise inert prodrug into active drug only within the Time‑Gate at the lesion.
  - Secretion is confined to the Time‑Gate ANDed with lesion‑state logic; outside the window or in non‑inflamed tissue, payload remains off.

- Module 5: Safety and containment
  - Dual kill switches: inducible caspase‑9 and thymidine‑kinase “suicide” responsive to clinically acceptable small molecules.
  - Auxotrophy for an essential metabolite sequestered within the capsule to prevent persistence outside the implant.
  - Insulated chromosomal landing pads to reduce insertional variability; barcoded lines for traceability.

Research plan

Aim 1. Build and calibrate the host‑entrained, phase‑advanced clock in vitro
- Construct the Circadian Phase Sensor → TimerTF → Time‑Gate axis in MSCs.
- Synchronize with serum‑shock; quantify phase locking, amplitude, and jitter of TimerTF using luminescent reporters.
- Tune phase lead (target 3–5 h) using degron strength and RNA timers; establish <30 min day‑to‑day jitter.
- Validate resilience to metabolic perturbations (NAD+/ATP fluctuations, mild temperature cycles) to confirm true entrainment rather than free‑running drift.

Deliverables and success criteria
- Stable 24 h locking to imposed circadian cues with predefined phase lead; coefficient of variation of peak timing <5%.

Aim 2. Implement lesion‑state logic and demonstrate lesion specificity
- Engineer the arming latch: NF‑κB‑responsive transient recombinase switch that decays to OFF within one circadian cycle.
- Add STAT1‑AND, SMAD/STAT3‑NOT, and E2F‑OFF gates; characterize truth‑table behavior with controlled cytokine/hypoxia pulses.
- Encapsulate cells in MMP‑degradable hydrogel; show enhanced activation only in MMP‑rich, hypoxic, inflammatory coculture with synoviocytes/macrophages.
- Quantify off‑target activation in healthy‑tissue mimics; target false‑positive rate <2% of lesional output.

Deliverables and success criteria
- Correct Boolean gating across all inputs; strong activation only under [Time‑Gate = ON] AND [NF‑κB/STAT1 = ON] AND [SMAD/STAT3 = OFF] AND [E2F = OFF].

Aim 3. Demonstrate preemptive efficacy in vivo and test re‑entrainment
- Model: collagen‑induced arthritis in mice with defined light‑dark cycles.
- Implant encapsulated C‑PLTCs intra‑articularly after disease onset.
- Endpoints:
  - Chronometry: in vivo bioluminescent tracking of TimerTF and Time‑Gate; confirm late‑night activation and stable phase lead to local cytokine peaks.
  - Pharmacodynamics: microdialysis of synovial fluid to measure nocturnal sVHH‑IL6R pulses; systemic spillover quantified in plasma.
  - Efficacy: reduction of dawn stiffness proxies (grip strength), paw swelling amplitude specifically at early morning, histologic inflammation score, and IL‑6 peak blunting.
- Re‑entrainment stress test: advance light cycle by 6 h; measure how quickly C‑PLTC output re‑locks to the new tissue phase (target <3 days).

Deliverables and success criteria
- Significant reduction of early‑morning flare metrics versus controls with equal or lower total weekly payload; maintained lesion specificity; re‑entrainment within three cycles.

Aim 4. Safety, durability, and manufacturability
- Off‑target and systemic immunosuppression assessment (infection markers, vaccine challenge response).
- Kill‑switch validation; capsule integrity under joint motion.
- Longitudinal performance for 12 weeks: stability of phase lead, amplitude, and gating thresholds; absence of fibrosis around capsules.

Integration of secondary biological phases (design summary)
- Inflammatory stage: prior‑cycle NF‑κB amplitude arms next nocturnal pulse (predictive dosing).
- Immune activation state: STAT1‑AND tightens specificity to active antigen presentation.
- Regeneration phase: IL‑10/TGF‑β‑NOT prevents dosing during resolution/repair to avoid hindering healing.
- Cell cycle: E2F‑OFF minimizes dosing during proliferation, reducing noise and metabolic stress.

Key risks and mitigations
- Risk: Disrupted circadian signaling in advanced disease reduces entrainment.
  - Mitigation: Include mild temperature‑responsive elements in the Phase Sensor as redundant zeitgebers; select chassis with robust intrinsic clocks; adjust degron kinetics to widen capture range.
- Risk: Inter‑individual variability in flare timing.
  - Mitigation: On‑device adaptive arming latch calibrates to each joint’s prior‑day inflammation amplitude, preserving preemptive timing despite phase variation.
- Risk: Immunogenicity of payload or chassis.
  - Mitigation: Use humanized nanobodies; encapsulation; local delivery reduces systemic exposure; kill switches.

Milestones and go/no‑go criteria
- M6: In vitro phase‑locked clock with <30 min jitter and 3–5 h phase lead; complete logic gating truth table.
- M12: In vivo proof of preemptive nocturnal pulses and reduction of early‑morning flare amplitude by ≥40% with ≤10% systemic spillover.
- M18: Re‑entrainment within three cycles after phase shift; 12‑week durability with no adverse events triggering kill switch.

Impact
By converting endogenous circadian phase into a lesion‑specific, pre‑flare therapeutic pulse conditioned by inflammatory and resolution biology, C‑PLTCs replace reactive sensing with predictive dosing. This single design choice—locking output to the host’s own clock—reduces sensing complexity, anticipates pathology, and minimizes off‑target immunosuppression.

text:
Title
Phase-Comparator Immunotherapy: Lesion-tethered, circadian misalignment–sensing drug release for pre-empting early-morning flares in rheumatoid arthritis

Hypothesis–Question
If a synovium-tethered drug depot releases payload only when local inflammatory oscillations enter anti-phase with the systemic glucocorticoid rhythm (high IL-6/NF-κB activity while cortisol is low), will it deliver therapy pre-emptively during the late night, blunt the pre-dawn surge that causes morning stiffness, and do so with lesion specificity and minimal off-target exposure?

Atomic strategy
Treat phase misalignment itself as the disease signal. Implement a molecular “phase comparator” that opens only under the conjunction: local inflammatory oscillator high AND systemic anti-inflammatory hormone low. All other phase relationships keep the depot closed.

Overall approach
- Disease focus: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) as exemplar autoimmune disease with robust pre-dawn symptom and cytokine rhythms.
- Primary sensing axis: endogenous circadian signals—systemic cortisol (global clock proxy) versus synovial inflammatory oscillators (local clock proxy).
- Secondary axes integrated as contextual gates: inflammatory stage (MMP/ROS/pH), immune activation state (activated macrophage markers), regeneration phase (TGF-β/M2 cues to halt release), and cell-cycle/proliferation (cathepsin B in hyperplastic synoviocytes).
- Lesion specificity: intra-articular depot or synovium-homing nanoparticles; release requires joint microenvironmental cues.

System design
1) Carrier
- Microporous PEG-based hydrogel microparticles (20–50 μm) or a thin in situ–forming hydrogel depot injected intra-articularly.
- Surface/mesh decorated with:
  a) Cortisol aptamer–mediated reversible crosslinks (global clock lock).
  b) IL-6 aptamer–gated nanopores and MMP-9–cleavable peptide crosslinks (local inflammatory gate).
  c) ROS-cleavable thioketal crosslinks and mild-acidosis–swelling polymer segments (pH ~6.6–6.9) to reinforce lesion specificity.
  d) TGF-β aptamer crosslinks that re-form to close pores during regeneration.
  e) FRβ-targeting ligands (activated macrophages) or anti–cadherin-11 peptides to concentrate depot-carrier contacts within inflamed synovium.

2) Molecular phase comparator (logic)
- Open condition (release): IL-6 high AND (cortisol low) AND (MMP/ROS/pH-inflammatory context present).
- Closed conditions (no release): any of
  a) cortisol high (time-of-day misaligned for release),
  b) IL-6 low (quiescent local oscillator),
  c) regeneration cues high (TGF-β/M2 markers) triggering re-crosslinking,
  d) healthy-tissue context (neutral pH, low MMP/ROS).
- Implementation sketch:
  a) Cortisol aptamer crosslinks: binding of cortisol increases crosslink density and reduces mesh size (kinetic lock). When cortisol falls (late night), these crosslinks loosen but do not yet permit release without local inflammatory opening.
  b) IL-6 aptamer gates: IL-6 binding disrupts duplex “caps” on nanopores, increasing local permeability. MMP/ROS simultaneously degrade supportive crosslinks to transition from permeable to releasing state.
  c) TGF-β aptamer strands re-establish crosslinks in high TGF-β/M2 contexts, halting further release to spare regeneration.

3) Payloads
- Primary: locally acting JAK inhibitor (e.g., to block IL-6 signaling) or low-dose glucocorticoid prodrug for synovial activation, optionally combined with an NF-κB pathway modulator.
- Optional sequential release: a short pre-dawn anti-inflammatory pulse followed by a daylight-window tolerogenic cue (e.g., low-dose A2A agonist) unlocked only when regeneration sensors are active.

4) Timing goal
- Auto-synchronize to patient rhythms by sensing endogenous waves; trigger a release burst 1–3 hours prior to typical symptom onset window (targeting approximately 02:00–05:00 local time in RA), without any external timers.

Research plan

Aim 1. Build the phase-comparator depot and calibrate gating thresholds
- Synthesize cortisol-aptamer crosslinked PEG hydrogels with tunable dissociation constants spanning physiological cortisol trough–peak.
- Integrate IL-6 aptamer gates, MMP-9–cleavable peptides, and thioketal linkers; quantify mesh-size changes and permeability with fluorescent tracers.
- Determine gating truth table and steepness by titrating cortisol, IL-6, MMP-9, ROS, and pH independently and in combinations. Primary metrics: on/off ratio, leak in “forbidden” states, reversibility, and fatigue over ≥30 cycles.

Milestones
- ≥10-fold increase in permeability only under the full open condition.
- <5% leakage over 12 hours in any closed condition.

Aim 2. Demonstrate pre-emptive, phase-selective release under oscillatory inputs
- Microfluidic circadian waveform bench test: drive depot with realistic, phase-staggered hormone/cytokine waveforms (cortisol low→rising; IL-6 rising pre-dawn; oscillatory pH/ROS/MMP mimics).
- Quantify phase lead (minutes) between IL-6 upswing and payload release onset; optimize aptamer affinities and crosslink densities for 60–120 min pre-flare release.

Milestones
- Stable pre-emption window (≥60 min) across ≥7 synthetic day–night cycles.
- Rapid shutoff (<30 min) when cortisol rises or IL-6 falls.

Aim 3. Achieve lesion specificity and integrate secondary biological phases
- Add targeting ligands (FRβ or cadherin-11) and test selective binding/retention in ex vivo human RA versus OA or healthy synovium explants.
- Validate regeneration-phase “off-switch”: expose depots to TGF-β, IL-10, and M2-conditioned media; require ≥80% reduction in permeability compared to inflammatory media.
- Assess proliferation-context gate with cathepsin B–sensitive elements; ensure added specificity without compromising circadian gating.

Milestones
- ≥5-fold higher retention and release in RA explants versus controls.
- Regeneration off-switch reduces release by ≥80% despite low cortisol.

Aim 4. In vivo efficacy: pre-empt morning stiffness and cytokine surge
- Model: adjuvant-induced or collagen-induced arthritis with telemetry of locomotor activity and sampling for corticosterone and IL-6 to map individual rhythms.
- Intervention: single intra-articular depot versus (a) time-programmed modified-release control and (b) conventional immediate-release control at equivalent weekly exposure.
- Endpoints: shift in joint cytokine acrophase, reduction of pre-dawn IL-6 AUC, improvement in early-morning grip strength/gait, pain behavior, synovial histology, systemic exposure profile.
- Lesion specificity: measure payload in plasma and contralateral joints; aim for >80% dose retained/released locally.

Milestones
- ≥50% reduction in pre-dawn IL-6 AUC and ≥30% improvement in early-morning function versus controls.
- Systemic exposure ≤20% of time-programmed control at matched efficacy.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Variability in individual rhythms: calibrate depot sensitivity by allowing a 24–48 h “learning” period where no payload is released while the material equilibrates to local cortisol ranges; use aptamer variants with slightly different Kd values blended to broaden capture of troughs.
- Aptamer stability/immunogenicity: use chemically stabilized backbones (2′-F/2′-OMe), minimal immunostimulatory motifs, and PEG shielding; validate nuclease resistance in synovial fluid.
- Off-target nighttime release in non-inflamed tissues: require inflammatory co-gates (MMP/ROS/pH) to be simultaneously positive; default state closed at neutral pH/low MMP.
- Species phase differences: use corticosterone-aware calibration and, where needed, light/feeding manipulations to align rodent rhythms; confirm in larger diurnal species before translation.

Success criteria
- Mechanistic: depot permeability switches governed by phase misalignment, not absolute time.
- Functional: reliable pre-emptive (≥60 min) anti-inflammatory pulses preceding early-morning flares with superior morning symptom control versus time-programmed dosing.
- Safety: strong lesion specificity, minimal systemic immunosuppression, and automatic shutoff during regeneration phases.

Deliverables
- A validated, lesion-tethered, circadian misalignment–sensing depot for RA with tunable phase thresholds.
- A generalizable framework for autoimmune diseases exhibiting clock–inflammation desynchrony, adaptable by swapping aptamer/enzyme gates to local disease rhythms.

Title: Population-Coherent Co-Reconstruction for In Situ Cryo-ET

Central insight (atomic strategy):
Replace per-tomogram reconstruction and per-particle averaging with a single, dataset-level co-reconstruction that jointly fits a physics-grounded forward model to many sparse, low-dose tilt-series acquired with intentionally diversified lamella and tilt-axis orientations. The repeated biological target acts as the global constraint; complementary missing wedges across instances close information gaps in aggregate. Reliability is certified by predictive agreement on held-out tilts/series, yielding a tomography-native validation metric.

Hypothesis:
A population-coherent co-reconstruction that exploits ensemble complementarity across many variably oriented, low-dose tilt-series can surpass the per-tomogram information ceiling, deliver reproducible in situ structures with formal tomography-native validation, and reduce barriers to adoption through standardized, resource-efficient pipelines.

Specific aims:
1) Acquisition co-design for ensemble complementarity
- Intentionally randomize lamella milling azimuth and microscope tilt-axis orientation across specimens to diversify missing-wedge directions.
- Use sparse tilt schedules (e.g., 15–25 tilts, total dose ≤60 e−/Å²) per series to increase throughput while preserving ensemble dose budget across the dataset.
- Prefer montage scouting and whole-cell area targeting to relax cryo-CLEM accuracy requirements; capture many instances per lamella rather than precise single-site targeting.

2) Population-coherent forward model and inference
- Fit a single 3D target density to all raw tilt movies simultaneously, with per-instance rigid pose, low-rank elastic deformation, per-tilt CTF, dose-weighting, and geometry.
- Optimize via MAP estimation with weak, biologically plausible priors (non-negativity, smoothness, symmetry if known), using Ewald-sphere–aware projection operators.
- Share information across instances to compensate for each instance’s missing wedge; allocate computational effort to the global model rather than many independent tomograms.

3) Tomography-native validation and resolution reporting
- Define a Predictive Cross-Wedge Agreement (PCWA) metric: correlation between measured and model-predicted projections for held-out tilts and held-out series, stratified by spatial frequency and direction.
- Convert PCWA into an anisotropic local resolution map by frequency- and direction-resolved predictive likelihood; report confidence calibrated by leave-one-lamella-out tests.
- Replace SPA-derived half-set FSC with PCWA-based maps and a per-structure reliability score that accounts for tomogram-level correlations and anisotropic sampling.

4) Accessibility and standardization
- Provide a turnkey, containerized pipeline with a single configuration schema for acquisition metadata, reconstruction, validation, and reporting; interoperate with existing formats (MRC, STAR).
- Minimize hardware burden via two-level computation: (i) local extraction of compressed sufficient statistics (Fourier slices + geometry tables) on a single mid-range GPU; (ii) optional cloud co-reconstruction.
- Release open reference datasets, standardized PCWA reports, and automated reproducibility checklists to enable small labs to benchmark end-to-end.

Approach and work plan:
- Phase 1 (months 0–6): Simulation and identifiability analysis
  - Simulate ensembles with controlled orientation distributions and dose/tilt schedules; quantify PCWA-resolved identifiability versus acquisition design.
  - Select two model targets spanning orientation behaviors (e.g., cytosolic ribosome, membrane-anchored complex).

- Phase 2 (months 6–15): Experimental proof of concept
  - Acquire 50–150 lamellae with randomized azimuths; per-lamella sparse tilt series.
  - Perform joint co-reconstruction from raw movies; compare to standard subtomogram averaging under equal total dose and microscope time.
  - Evaluate PCWA vs. independent ground-truth proxies (SPA of purified complexes; dual-axis subsets when feasible).

- Phase 3 (months 15–24): Generalization and robustness
  - Extend to complexes with partial orientation bias; test deformation modeling for flexible assemblies.
  - Validate leave-one-lab-out reproducibility using shared acquisition protocol at a partner facility.

- Phase 4 (months 18–30): Democratization and release
  - Finalize container, metadata schema, and tutorials; publish open datasets with PCWA reports.
  - Provide cloud recipes with cost caps and local-only fallbacks.

Metrics of success:
- Resolution: ≥15% improvement in directional and median resolution at fixed total dose/time versus standard STA, confirmed by PCWA and independent benchmarks.
- Reliability: High PCWA on held-out tilts/series; strong correlation between PCWA-derived maps and interpretable model features (e.g., side-chain visibility).
- Throughput: ≥2× increase in targets reconstructed per microscope day via sparse tilting and relaxed targeting.
- Reproducibility: Consistent structures and PCWA scores across labs and days from the same acquisition recipe.
- Accessibility: End-to-end run on ≤1 consumer GPU locally or <$200 cloud cost for a reference dataset.

Risk management and contingency:
- Limited orientation diversity: enforce broader azimuth randomization; add a small subset of orthogonal-tilt series for critical targets; incorporate known symmetries.
- Overfitting: monitor divergence between training-fit agreement and held-out PCWA; regularize deformation fields; increase held-out fractions.
- Computational load: use mixed-precision, blockwise Fourier operators, and multi-scale optimization; prioritize compressed statistics.

Expected outcomes and deliverables:
- A validated co-reconstruction method turning the missing wedge into a dataset-level sampling strategy.
- PCWA metric and anisotropic resolution reporting standard for tomography.
- Open-source pipeline, reference datasets, and reproducibility checklists enabling broad adoption by small laboratories.

Title: Wedge-Invariance Tomography (WIT): using deterministic missing-wedge geometry as a falsification probe for robust in situ cryo-ET

Core hypothesis and goal
- Hypothesis: The missing wedge is a deterministic, orientation-specific filter whose induced biases are predictable. By deliberately leveraging those biases as a built-in perturbation, we can separate true structural heterogeneity from reconstruction artifacts without attempting to “fill” lost information.
- Goal: Establish a wedge-aware acquisition and analysis framework that turns the missing wedge into a validation signal, producing reproducible in situ structure determination with low computational burden and standardized workflows suitable for smaller labs.

Atomic strategy
- Treat the missing wedge as a known, controllable contrast modulator. For any putative structural feature or conformational difference, test whether its measured effect is invariant to the relative orientation between the feature and the wedge. True features are wedge-invariant; artifacts show wedge-locked signatures. Build all validation around this invariance test.

Specific aims
1) Define wedge-aware metadata and lightweight estimators that predict orientation-dependent recoverability for every particle and voxel.
2) Implement “wedge-orthogonal replicates” at acquisition: minimal, practical rotations of lamella/grid azimuth across otherwise matched samples to modulate wedge orientation without extra dose or exotic hardware.
3) Replace SPA-style FSC with tomography-native, wedge-aware validation metrics that quantify wedge-invariance at map-, region-, and feature-scales.
4) Package the approach into an accessible, standardized pipeline (WedgeLab) with low storage/GPU footprints and interoperable I/O.

Aim 1: Wedge-aware recoverability modeling
- Per-particle wedge kernel: For each subtomogram i, compute its Fourier support mask Mi(k) from known tilt range, tilt geometry, CTF anisotropy, and particle pose. Represent Mi(k) in a low-order spherical harmonic basis to obtain a compact “anisotropy fingerprint.”
- Local recoverability map R(x): Propagate Mi(k) and the reconstruction filter to predict the local anisotropic point-spread function (aPSF) and a scalar recoverability score per voxel/region. R(x) upper-bounds interpretable detail; it is not a deconvolution.
- Wedge-balanced partitioning: Split data into half-sets that are balanced in wedge fingerprints and disjoint at the tomogram level to minimize shared noise and preprocessing correlations.

Aim 2: Wedge-orthogonal replicates in acquisition
- Lamella azimuth design: Prepare otherwise matched lamellae at two azimuths offset by ~90° relative to the microscope tilt axis (achieved by rotating grids before FIB milling or by loading grids in alternate azimuths). This changes wedge orientation while preserving cellular context and dose budgets.
- Orientation ladder: For a subset of targets, introduce small pre-tilt offsets (e.g., ±5–10°) across tomograms to create additional, controlled wedge orientations without resorting to dual-axis tomography.
- Minimal replication principle: Only a limited number of wedge-orthogonal tomograms are required as validation replicates per condition, keeping FIB/CLEM throughput overhead modest.

Aim 3: Tomography-native, wedge-aware validation metrics
- Wedge-Invariance Score (WIS): For any feature f (voxel cluster, domain, or eigenvolume component), compute the effect size Δf between classes/states, then regress Δf across particles against the cosine of the angle between the feature’s local normal and each particle’s wedge normal (from Mi). Report the slope and a permutation p-value under wedge-balanced resampling. Artifact if slope ≠ 0; genuine if slope ~ 0 with confidence.
- Wedge-Contrast Coefficient (WCC): A per-frequency or per-direction coefficient measuring correlation between observed amplitude fluctuations and the predicted anisotropy from Mi(k). High WCC indicates wedge-locked variance.
- Common-Support FRC (csFRC): Compute FRC between half-maps using only the intersection of their Fourier supports. Report a directional csFRC spectrum and a scalar resolution that is robust to anisotropic sampling.
- Wedge-Resolved Reproducibility (WRR): Map-wise aggregation of WIS/WCC into a reproducibility index stratified by direction. Provides a replacement for gold-standard FSC that respects tomography’s anisotropy and tomogram-level correlations.

Aim 4: WedgeLab: a standardized, low-compute pipeline
- Components:
  - Metadata: A sidecar file per particle/tomogram encoding wedge kernel parameters, CTF anisotropy, tilt geometry, and particle pose.
  - Estimators: CPU-friendly routines for Mi(k) spherical-harmonic projection, R(x) computation, WIS/WCC/csFRC/WRR, and wedge-balanced partitioning. Optional GPU kernels accelerate only FFTs; core statistics remain CPU-feasible.
  - Interop: Readers/writers for STAR/MRC/Zarr; wrappers for common packages to inject or consume wedge metadata without forking entire pipelines.
  - Reporting: Compact “Wedge Consistency Plots” showing Δf versus wedge angle, directional csFRC, and WRR heatmaps for quick, lab-to-lab comparable QC.
- Resource profile: Streaming I/O with chunked Zarr, on-the-fly feature statistics, and summary exports to keep storage and RAM demands low. No large-scale 3D classification required to validate features.

Planned experiments and validation
- Simulation benchmarks:
  - Ground-truth volumes with imposed conformational changes; generate tilt series under realistic dose/SNR and varied wedge orientations. Assess power and specificity of WIS/WCC to separate real from wedge-locked differences at different SNR and particle counts.
  - Stress tests with tomogram-level correlations (shared preprocessing, CTF, and lamella artifacts) to quantify false-positive control under wedge-balanced partitioning.
- Experimental datasets:
  - In situ ribosome: Evaluate flexible regions (e.g., stalk movements) across wedge-orthogonal lamellae. Expect WIS ~ 0 for true states and WCC low after csFRC normalization.
  - Membrane protein complexes: Test features aligned to membranes, where wedge-locking is common. Expect WCC to flag spurious anisotropic densities; WRR to improve after wedge balancing.
  - Cross-lab replication: Exchange wedge-orthogonal validation sets and confirm portability of WIS/WRR thresholds.

Success criteria
- Statistical: False-positive rate for wedge-locked artifacts ≤ 5% at preset WIS threshold on simulations; ≥ 80% power to detect true features at realistic SNR with N ≤ 5k particles.
- Reproducibility: WRR and directional csFRC stable (±0.02) across labs/lamellae; WIS distributions consistent across independent acquisitions.
- Practicality: ≤ 2× additional acquisition time for validation replicates; ≤ 1 mid-range GPU or CPU-only runtime with overnight turnaround; end-to-end pipeline reproducible from a single configuration file.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: Limited orientation diversity may confound wedge and pose effects.
  - Mitigation: Use csFRC and wedge-balanced partitioning; include orientation covariates in WIS regression; prioritize targets with known pose diversity.
- Risk: Additional azimuths increase FIB/CLEM workload.
  - Mitigation: Minimal replication principle; share validation lamellae across projects; optional pre-tilt offsets to create wedge diversity without extra lamellae.
- Risk: Over-penalization of real directional biology (e.g., membrane-parallel features).
  - Mitigation: Joint modeling of biological orientation fields (membrane normals) and wedge normals; report both wedge-locked and bio-locked components.

Deliverables
- Methods: Formal definitions of Mi(k), R(x), WIS, WCC, csFRC, WRR with reference implementations.
- Software: WedgeLab (BSD/MIT license), with CLI and notebooks; converters for major tomogram/subtomogram formats.
- Standards: A wedge-aware metadata schema and validation report template for publication and data deposition.
- Datasets: Public simulation suites and wedge-orthogonal in situ benchmarks with ground-truth annotations for features tested.

Impact
- Converts an unavoidable physical limitation (missing wedge) into a principled, low-cost validation instrument.
- Establishes tomography-native, anisotropy-aware metrics that replace misapplied SPA criteria.
- Lowers computational and operational barriers, enabling smaller laboratories to achieve defensible in situ structures with transparent, reproducible validation.

Title
Center-based, metrology-anchored in situ cryo-ET for reproducible structure determination and broad adoption

Core premise
In situ cryo-ET today lacks a unifying calibration and validation framework. We propose to convert cryo-ET from an artisanal imaging craft into a metrology-calibrated assay run by specialized imaging centers. The single system-level perturbation is to co-image a standardized, cryo-compatible 3D calibration scaffold within every lamella. This scaffold anchors acquisition, reconstruction, and validation to the same physical reference, enabling adaptive data collection, wedge-aware uncertainty quantification, and center-to-center comparability. Imaging centers will return not just images but certified evidence maps and metrics; all outputs are deposited into a public database.

Hypothesis
Embedding a sparse, inert, co-imaged 3D calibration scaffold (“metrology grid”) into each lamella allows:
- adaptive tilt/dose/defocus control to equalize information across orientations under a fixed dose budget;
- explicit estimation and correction of missing-wedge and anisotropic CTF effects during reconstruction;
- tomography-native, wedge-aware cross-validation that respects tomogram correlations;
- standardization of pipelines and compute through reference-driven QC, enabling reproducible in situ structure determination across centers and democratized access.

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Make uncertainty the primary deliverable by co-imaging a universal nanoscale metrology scaffold in every dataset; use the scaffold to calibrate acquisition, reconstruction, and validation end-to-end.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and validate a universal cryo-ET metrology scaffold co-fabricated with lamellae.
- Scaffold design: a sparse mixture of cryo-stable references with known 3D structure and spectral content, e.g., protein cages/apoferritin, 3D DNA-origami tetrahedra with angle-encoded edges, and 20–40 nm fluorescent nanodiamond/bead fiducials for CLEM registration.
- Spatial strategy: deposit on grid prior to cell seeding and/or overlay a sparse inert layer post-seeding; ensure scaffold resides in extracellular ice or lamella margins to minimize perturbation while remaining within the imaged thickness.
- Encoded functions:
  - frequency/angle bars for anisotropy readout;
  - per-tilt SNR probes for dose allocation and motion assessment;
  - focus targets for per-tilt CTF estimation;
  - FIB navigation marks (milled micro-notches) that survive thinning to quantify lamella thickness and milling quality.
- Acceptance criteria:
  - no measurable alteration of cell ultrastructure or viability proxies prior to vitrification (sentinel morphology metrics, constant lamella thickness distribution);
  - scaffold visibility across full tilt range without shadowing; stable under total dose.

Aim 2. Develop calibrant-driven adaptive acquisition and sample triage to raise information efficiency at constant dose.
- Adaptive tilt scheduling: online estimation of directional information from scaffold projections; allocate tilts and per-tilt dose to flatten the directional Fisher information spectrum given a fixed total dose.
- Eucentricity/defocus control: real-time corrections from scaffold focus/astigmatism fits; maintain per-tilt CTF targets and minimize magnification anisotropy.
- Beam-induced motion/charging monitoring: scaffold-derived motion fields trigger dose reallocation or acquisition aborts.
- Cryo-FIB QC and throughput: use milled marks and scaffold contrast to reject substandard lamellae pre-acquisition; standardized milling recipes benchmarked by scaffold-derived “Lamella Quality Index” (thickness, curtaining, residual stress).
- Cryo-CLEM targeting: scaffold fluorescent beacons provide a fixed coordinate frame for robust LM–EM registration, improving targeting accuracy and repeatability.
- Milestones:
  - ≥1.5× increase in median directional FSC within target bands (e.g., 6–10 Å) at identical total dose vs. fixed-scheme controls;
  - ≥2× reduction in failed tilt series via pre-acquisition triage;
  - targeting error ≤200 nm (median) across centers.

Aim 3. Create wedge-aware, tomography-native validation and uncertainty metrics anchored to the scaffold.
- Data model: hierarchical Bayesian framework that explicitly models within-tilt and within-tomogram correlations; scaffold provides priors for CTF, magnification, and angular coverage.
- Validation metrics:
  - Wedge-Aware Posterior Predictive Correlation (waPPC): hold out angle-stratified tilt groups; compare predictive reconstructions against held-out projections, reported locally and directionally.
  - Local Anisotropy Map (LAM): voxelwise directional information density derived from scaffold frequency bars; delivered as per-voxel confidence/evidence maps.
  - Confidence–Resolution Curve (CRC): probability that local features exceed resolution thresholds along principal directions, replacing SPA-style gold-standard FSC.
  - Subtomogram averaging validation: scaffold-grounded tilt-group cross-validation and hierarchical bootstraps across tomograms/sessions, avoiding half-set independence violations.
- Deliverables:
  - open-source implementations; standardized reporting (JSON/Zarr) with maps, masks, tilt partitions, and uncertainty fields;
  - acceptance thresholds that predict task-level success (e.g., detection of known macromolecular orientation) with ROC AUC ≥0.9 in blinded tests.

Aim 4. Build an Imaging Center network and an open, standardized database for calibrated in situ cryo-ET.
- Center operations:
  - SOPs for scaffold application, milling, adaptive acquisition, and QC;
  - automated pipelines packaged in containers/workflows; provenance capture; push-button reprocessing.
- Data products returned to users:
  - raw movies and tilt series;
  - calibrated reconstructions and per-voxel evidence maps (LAM, waPPC, CRC);
  - scaffold-derived QC (Lamella Quality Index, directional information spectra, targeting accuracy);
  - human-readable “Certificate of Evidence” summarizing confidence and limitations.
- Database (“InSitu-ET-Metrology Atlas”):
  - mandatory deposition of raw + calibrated products + metrics;
  - cross-center benchmarks and leaderboards using scaffold-ground-truth tasks;
  - compute-access layer for small labs (cloud workspaces with curated pipelines and exemplar datasets).
- Accessibility goals:
  - 80% reduction in on-prem GPU/storage burden for participating labs;
  - interoperable formats (MRC/Zarr), streaming-friendly compression, and reproducible notebooks.

Research plan and methods

R1. Scaffold fabrication and compatibility
- Produce batches of standardized scaffolds with known 3D geometry and spectral signatures; validate mechanical/chemical inertness at cryo temperatures.
- Assess biological compatibility: compare ultrastructural metrics and vitrification quality with/without scaffold across cell types; use blinded expert scoring and automated texture statistics.

R2. Simulation-to-reality loop
- Simulate tilt series with realistic noise, missing wedge, thickness gradients, and beam-induced motion; optimize scaffold geometry and adaptive policies in silico.
- Transfer policies to microscope control via center software; iterate using real-world datasets.

R3. Adaptive control algorithms
- Online estimation using scaffold ROIs per tilt: CTF, drift, SNR, and angular information.
- Constrained optimization to choose next tilt and dose increment subject to total dose and time; fallbacks for stage limits.

R4. Reconstruction and validation
- Incorporate scaffold-informed priors into tomographic reconstruction (wedge-aware regularization, directionally weighted filters).
- Implement tilt-group holdouts respecting angular neighborhoods; compute waPPC, LAM, and CRC; validate against scaffold ground truth and biological landmarks.

R5. Standardization, training, and governance
- Develop center certification program; inter-center ring trials using identical scaffolded samples.
- Establish data/metadata schema; governance board to evolve metrics, benchmarks, and SOPs.

Milestones and success criteria (years 1–3)
- Year 1: Scaffold kit finalized; adaptive acquisition prototype achieves targeted directional FSC gains on test phantoms and cells; initial waPPC/LAM/CRC released.
- Year 2: Three imaging centers pass ring trial with ≤10% variance in Lamella Quality Index and waPPC distributions on shared specimens; database publicly launches with 100+ calibrated datasets.
- Year 3: Blind community challenge demonstrates that waPPC/CRC predict task success better than SPA-style FSC (ΔAUC ≥0.1); ≥50 external labs use the centers; per-dataset failure rate halves relative to pre-scaffold baseline.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Biological perturbation by scaffold: keep sparse and spatially segregated; verify non-interference via ultrastructure metrics; provide “scaffold-outside-ROI” acquisition when needed.
- Overfitting to scaffold signatures: enforce strict separation between scaffold-driven parameter estimation and biological ROI reconstruction; validate on datasets without scaffold to confirm generalization.
- Operational complexity: encapsulate all adaptivity and validation in center software; provide fixed-schedule fallback modes with scaffold-based QC only.

Expected impact
- A single perturbation—co-imaging a universal metrology scaffold—yields global improvements across acquisition, reconstruction, and validation.
- Centers can certify evidence rather than images, enabling reproducible, comparable, and trustworthy in situ structures.
- Smaller labs gain access to high-quality, confidence-calibrated data and pipelines without capital investment, accelerating discovery and standardizing the field.

Title
Wedge-Equivariant Self-Validation (WESV) for democratized, reproducible in situ cryo-ET

Central hypothesis
The missing wedge is a known, orientation-conditioned null space. If a 3D reconstruction is correct, rotated instances of the same structure will agree within the intersection of their observed supports and will not show reproducible signal in the union of their unobserved supports. Quantifying this occlusion-consistency yields a tomography-native, reference-free validation and reconstruction control framework that is robust to anisotropy, tomogram-level correlations, and low SNR, and that can guide both data acquisition and analysis.

Specific aims
1) Define a wedge-aware occlusion-consistency metric (WESV score) and directional resolution maps that are native to tomography.
2) Use WESV to drive reconstruction, cross-validation, and early stopping via wedge-stratified splits instead of half-sets.
3) Optimize acquisition using wedge diversity as the design target to raise the effective information ceiling per specimen and session.
4) Package WESV into a lightweight, standardized, open workflow suitable for small laboratories.

Aim 1. A tomography-native, reference-free validation metric
- Forward model and masks
  - For each subtomogram i, compute an orientation-specific forward operator Fi that encodes: tilt angles, CTF per tilt (including defocus gradient and dose weighting), MTF, and binary Fourier support mask Wi for the observed region; W̄i denotes the unobserved (missing) region.
  - For a candidate reconstruction R, define Ri = Fi−1(Fi R) as the wedge-constrained estimate consistent with the observed support of i.
- WESV components
  - Intersected Masked Correlation (IMC): for paired instances (i, j) of the same motif with relative rotation Rij, compute the correlation between Wi Ri and Rij⊙Wj Rj evaluated only on Wi ∩ Rij⊙Wj. High IMC indicates agreement where both have data.
  - Null-Persistence Penalty (NPP): quantify energy in R that is reproducibly present across instances within the union of their unobserved supports, i.e., consistency on (Rij⊙W̄j) ∩ W̄i. True signal should not concentrate here; persistent features imply overfitting or bleed-through from regularizers.
  - Directional Information Capacity (DIC): estimate per-direction SNR and resolution by fitting the decay of IMC versus spatial frequency on spherical caps; report a directional resolution map and an overall anisotropy index.
- WESV score
  - A single scalar combining high-frequency IMC (reward) and NPP (penalty), normalized by DIC to account for geometry- and dose-limited information ceilings. Report with confidence intervals via wedge-stratified jackknife (see Aim 2).

Aim 2. Wedge-stratified cross-validation and reconstruction control
- Stratification
  - Partition particles by missing-wedge orientation classes (e.g., via spherical k-means on wedge normals), not by half-sets within tomograms. This reduces tomogram-level correlation and avoids information leakage through shared anisotropy.
- Training and early stopping
  - Optimize alignment, CTF refinement, and regularization hyperparameters by maximizing IMC on held-out wedge classes while minimizing NPP. Stop when improvements in IMC saturate at the DIC-predicted ceiling or when NPP increases.
- Model selection
  - Compare alternative refinement protocols and denoisers using the WESV score. Prefer models that reach higher IMC at lower NPP given the same DIC, indicating genuine signal rather than overfit anisotropic artifacts.
- Output products
  - A resolution-versus-direction curve, a voxelwise directional resolution map, and a standardized WESV report per structure.

Aim 3. Acquisition optimized for wedge diversity and information ceilings
- Wedge Diversity Design (WDD)
  - Before data collection, simulate expected DIC from lamella thickness, tilt range, increment, stage geometry, and anticipated motif orientation distribution. Choose tilt schemes and lamella milling orientation to maximize the union coverage of observed supports across particles and tomograms.
- Multi-lamella micro-rotation
  - Introduce small, controlled rotations of the grid or stage between lamellae to rotate wedge orientations relative to cellular architecture, increasing cross-dataset wedge diversity without increasing dose.
- On-the-fly stopping
  - Compute a running DIC and provisional WESV on downsampled reconstructions during collection. Stop when the predicted information ceiling is approached or when additional data fail to increase union support coverage.
- Practical constraints
  - Keep tilt ranges realistic for throughput; WDD focuses on orientation diversity rather than simply expanding tilt range. Integrate with cryo-CLEM by prioritizing targets that add complementary wedge orientations.

Aim 4. Accessible, standardized implementation
- Lightweight computation
  - Implement WESV using blockwise FFTs and binary Fourier masks; compute IMC/NPP via sparse spectral operations. Single-GPU optional; CPU-only mode supported with streaming to limit memory. Outputs are compact scalar and map products.
- Pipeline integration
  - Provide containerized plugins for common tomographic packages (e.g., RELION/EMClarity/Dynamo/Warp/M/AreTomo/IsoNet) that accept and emit open, minimal metadata: per-particle wedge masks, per-tilt CTF/dose, and alignment parameters.
- Reproducibility kit
  - Release simulated and experimental benchmark sets with ground-truth-oracle or consensus references, scripted WESV evaluation, and wedge-stratified splits to enable community comparison.
- Reporting standard
  - A simple JSON schema capturing WESV score, IMC curve, NPP, DIC map, anisotropy index, and acquisition parameters for manuscript supplements and data repositories.

Validation plan
- Simulation studies
  - Phantoms with controlled anisotropy, varying tilt ranges, dose budgets, defocus gradients, and heterogeneity. Measure calibration of DIC to known information ceilings; sensitivity and specificity of NPP to injected overfitting.
- Experimental tests
  - In situ ribosomes/proteasomes across multiple lamellae with intentional micro-rotations. Show that WESV detects over-regularization, misalignment, and CTF misestimation that elude half-map FSC. Correlate directional resolution with independent SPA controls on extracted complexes where feasible.
- Stress tests
  - Heterogeneous samples and flexible assemblies; show that classification guided by WESV improves class separation without raising NPP.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Risk: Structural heterogeneity mimics null-space persistence.
  - Mitigation: Wedge-stratified classification; compute NPP on class-consistent subsets and verify decrease post-classification.
- Risk: Mask errors from mis-modeled CTF/dose bias DIC.
  - Mitigation: Fit per-tilt CTF/dose within the WESV loop; penalize models that raise NPP despite improved IMC.
- Risk: Limited instance counts per wedge class reduce statistical power.
  - Mitigation: Adaptive class merging and Bayesian shrinkage of DIC estimates; pool across lamellae using micro-rotation diversity.

Milestones and success criteria
- Month 6: Prototype WESV metric and DIC estimator validated on simulations; open metadata schema released.
- Month 12: In situ demonstration on two cellular complexes with standardized WESV reports; external lab reproduction using the container.
- Month 18: Acquisition optimization (WDD) validated; show fewer lamellae and tilt-series achieve the same WESV score and directional resolution.
- Success criteria: Community adoption of WESV reports; improved agreement across labs on in situ structures; reduction in overfitting signatures (low NPP) at equal or better directional resolution.

Expected outcomes
- A tomography-native, reference-free validation metric that replaces half-map FSC in scenarios with anisotropy and tomogram-level correlations.
- A principled estimator of the achievable information ceiling per dataset that prevents overfitting and guides efficient acquisition.
- A lightweight, standardized toolchain that lowers compute/storage barriers and unifies fragmented steps, enabling broader, reproducible in situ structure determination.
