text:
Title
Temporal Logic-Gated Cohesin Unloader (TLCU): a 3D genome editor that selectively dissolves pathological enhancer–promoter loops while preserving normal topology

Problem and Objective
Pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops (e.g., super-enhancer–oncogene contacts) are hyper-stable, high-valency interactions that hijack structural proteins (cohesin, Mediator) and phase-separated hubs. Normal E–P loops are transient and topology-preserving. The objective is to engineer a reversible, sequence-independent molecular tool that detects the kinetic and compositional signature of pathological E–P contacts and locally unloads cohesin to break these loops without perturbing normal 3D genome architecture.

Central Hypothesis (question = goal)
Do pathological E–P loops exhibit sufficiently prolonged dwell time within BRD4/Mediator transcriptional condensates, coupled to high elongating RNAPII, to enable a logic- and time-gated recruitment of the endogenous cohesin unloader (WAPL/PDS5) that selectively dissolves these loops while sparing normal contacts?

Atomic Strategy
Exploit a kinetic discriminator: only pathological E–P contacts remain co-enriched for BRD4high–MED1–RNAPII-Ser2P for long continuous intervals. Build a molecular AND gate with an integrated dwell-time timer that, upon sustained tri-proximity, unlocks a locally acting WAPL-based cohesin unloading module. Normal loops, being short-lived or lacking this triad, never trigger the gate.

Tool Architecture (TLCU)
- Sensing triad (proximity handles)
  - E-sensor: nanobody to BRD4 bromodomain/ET interface enriched in super-enhancers.
  - Hub-sensor: nanobody to MED1 (Mediator) IDR.
  - P-sensor: nanobody to RNAPII-Ser2P (elongation mark at active promoters).
- Kinetic AND gate with built-in timer
  - Each sensor is fused to a distinct fragment of a low-affinity, ultra-slow maturing split protease (e.g., engineered split TEV/NLVM) via linkers that only permit productive assembly within ~50–100 nm.
  - The split protease reconstitutes only after continuous co-residence >τ (user-tunable, 2–10 min), implementing time integration that rejects transient normal contacts.
- Effector (local cohesin release)
  - Protease-locked WAPL activator: a minimal PDS5-interacting WAPL module (WAPLmin) rendered autoinhibited by a cleavable peptide. Upon protease reconstitution, the inhibitor is removed, exposing WAPLmin to recruit/activate endogenous PDS5–WAPL at the contact, opening the cohesin DNA exit gate and dissolving the loop.
  - Spatial confinement: WAPLmin is tethered to the sensors; activation radius is restricted to the condensate to prevent spread.
- Topology preservation and self-limiting features
  - Fast off-switch: WAPLmin carries a degron (ODC/CL1) that enforces a short half-life (t1/2 ~10–20 min), ensuring only burst-like local unloading.
  - Reload bias: an appended NIPBL/MAU2 micro-recruiter is masked by the same protease site but reveals only after contact dissolution decouples the triad, promoting physiological cohesin re-loading on nearby canonical anchors and preserving TAD insulation.
  - No DNA sequence changes; action is reversible and state-dependent.
- Optional complementary epigenetic “valency softener” (secondary)
  - A proximity-activated, condensate-confined p300-bromodomain decoy (or BRD4 BD1/2 intrabody) released by the same protease to transiently damp H3K27ac/BRD4 valency only within the pathological hub, lowering re-formation probability without genome-wide chromatin editing.

Delivery (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Vector A (AAV, LNP-mRNA, or integrase-deficient lentivirus) expressing E-sensor–ProteaseA and Hub-sensor–ProteaseB (2A-linked).
- Event 2: Vector B expressing P-sensor–ProteaseC and the protease-locked WAPLmin effector (+ optional masked NIPBL micro-recruiter).
- Event 3 (optional): Vector C expressing the optional epigenetic valency softener module.
All expression cassettes are under weak, nuclear-restricted promoters with degradation tags to minimize basal activity.

Operational Cycle
1) Only at pathological E–P hubs, sustained BRD4–MED1–RNAPII-Ser2P proximity assembles the split protease over τ minutes.
2) Protease cleaves the autoinhibitory mask on WAPLmin (and optionally unmasks the reload bias).
3) WAPLmin recruits/activates endogenous PDS5–WAPL locally, releasing trapped cohesin and dissolving the pathological loop.
4) Proteins diffuse; degrons terminate activity; NIPBL micro-recruitment biases cohesin re-loading to normal anchors, preserving global topology.
5) The system remains ready but inert until the kinetic criterion is met again.

Key Predictions
- TLCU will selectively reduce HiChIP/Micro-C contact strength at super-enhancer–oncogene pairs (e.g., MYC, TAL1, ERα targets) while leaving >95% of normal loops and genome-wide insulation scores unchanged.
- Transcriptional normalization will be confined to genes wired to the disrupted pathological loops; housekeeping and distal TAD architecture will remain stable.
- Live-cell cohesin tracking will show transient, local unloading bursts near BRD4/MED1 hubs without global residence time changes.

Research Plan and Milestones
Phase I: Build and tune components (months 0–6)
- Engineer and validate nanobody binders (BRD4, MED1, RNAPII-Ser2P) for affinity and nuclear diffusivity.
- Compare split protease variants to set τ; quantify false-positive rates using colocalization assays and FRAP.
- Map WAPLmin constructs that unload cohesin locally without global chromatin decompaction.

Phase II: In-cell selectivity and mechanism (months 6–18)
- Models: ER+ breast cancer (super-enhancer–ESR1), AML (TAL1, MYC), and matched normal cells.
- Readouts: Micro-C/HiChIP (cohesin, H3K27ac), insulation/compartment scores; RAD21/SMC3 live imaging; eRNA PRO-seq at hubs.
- Metrics:
  - Selectivity index S = Δpathological loop strength / median Δnormal loop strength; target S ≥ 10.
  - Topology preservation: <5% change in global TAD insulation; compartment eigenvector correlation >0.95 vs baseline.
  - Local cohesin dynamics: increased unloading events within 300 nm of BRD4/MED1 hubs; unchanged global cohesin residence time.

Phase III: Function and reversibility (months 18–30)
- RNA-seq for on-target transcriptional correction with minimal off-target DEGs.
- Remove tool (washout or expression off) and show re-formation of loops and phenotypes (reversibility).
- In vivo delivery (dual AAV or LNP) in xenografts; assess tumor dependence on pathologic loops and normal tissue tolerance.

Controls
- Catalytically dead protease; WAPLmin lacking PDS5 engagement; scrambled nanobodies; τ-short variants (to quantify necessity of time gating).
- Global cohesin-unloading positive control (WAPL overexpression) to benchmark safety and topology impact.

Risk Assessment and Mitigations
- Off-target unloading in active normal genes: mitigated by triad AND gating and τ tuning; use narrow-expression promoters and degrons.
- Protease leakiness: include protease inhibitor peptide in trans; engineer orthogonal cleavage site not present in human proteome.
- Condensate heterogeneity: allow alternative hub sensor (BRD4→BRD3/BRD4S or MED1→MED12) per tissue.
- Insufficient effect size: add optional local valency softener to reduce hub re-nucleation probability.

Validation Criteria for Success
- Significant selective loss of predefined pathological E–P loops (FDR < 0.05) with preserved global TAD/compartment architecture.
- Rescue of phenotype (e.g., proliferation, dependency) upon TLCU but not controls.
- Demonstrated reversibility and absence of permanent DNA sequence alteration.

Extensions
- Allele-specific deployment by coupling one sensor to an allele-specific TF or SNP-binding RNA aptamer for imprinted or fusion-driven loops.
- Non-oncologic applications (e.g., developmental disorders with neo-loops) by swapping disease TF sensors while retaining the same kinetic gate and effector.

Impact
TLCU reframes 3D genome editing as dynamic, kinetic discrimination of pathological chromatin contacts, using endogenous structural protein machinery for local, reversible correction. By targeting the lifetime and composition of disease loops—rather than DNA sequence—it promises precision topology repair with minimal collateral effects.

text:
Title
TopoFilter: Geometry-keyed decoy condensates to selectively deflect pathological enhancer–promoter loops while preserving native 3D genome topology

Summary
Pathologic enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops arise from locus-specific “geometry codes” (anchor orientation, motif spacing, occupancy, and condensate composition) that differ from healthy loops within the same topologically associating domain (TAD). TopoFilter is a 3D genome editor that reads these geometry codes and nucleates a local, reversible, high-avidity “sink” that preferentially captures the structural machinery (cohesin, CTCF, Mediator/BRD4) that sustains the diseased loop, thereby redirecting extrusion flux and coactivator residence away from the pathologic E–P pair. Normal loops are preserved by restricting the sink to the diseased microenvironment via an AND-gated assembly logic and by confining its capacity and position within the same TAD but outside native anchors.

Central hypothesis and guiding question
Hypothesis: Pathological E–P loops possess discriminable structural fingerprints that can be read to assemble a local decoy that outcompetes the disease loop for cohesin/Mediator without perturbing normal contacts. Question: What minimal, reversible, geometry-matched sink is sufficient to deflect extruders and coactivators away from the diseased E–P pair while maintaining global topology?

Atomic strategy
Exploit kinetic competition in loop extrusion by installing a single, conditionally assembling “parking-lot” decoy—geometry-matched to the pathological anchor code—at a neutral intradomain site proximal to the diseased locus, so that extruding cohesin and Mediator preferentially terminate at the decoy rather than closing the pathological E–P loop.

Specific aims
1) Define Differential Loop Fingerprints (DLFs)
- Derive a locus-resolved structural signature that distinguishes pathological from normal E–P loops: CTCF motif orientation/spacing and occupancy asymmetry; cohesin loader density; anchor stiffness (nucleosome positioning); Mediator/BRD4 condensate valency; enhancer acetylation amplitude; extrusion directionality.
- Prioritize features that create selective binding energy or kinetic traps only at the diseased site.

2) Engineer a DLF-keyed decoy that assembles only in the diseased microenvironment
- Protein-condensate decoy (primary): A modular scaffold that multivalently binds cohesin (e.g., SA2/SCC1-facing peptides), recognizes CTCF-bound DNA via tandem CTCF-DBD mimetics or CTCF-interacting nanobodies, and recruits Mediator via low-complexity repeats. Geometry (spacing/orientation) is preset to match the local DLF so avidity is maximized only for the disease code.
- DNA-scaffold decoy (alternative): A nuclear-stable DNA scaffold presenting programmed arrays of high-fidelity CTCF motifs and Mediator-recruiting aptamers at DLF-matched spacing, with minimal intrinsic promoter/enhancer activity.
- Target both decoys to a neutral “harbor” inside the same TAD but outside native anchors (selected in Aim 1), so captured complexes remain locally buffered, preserving domain-level topology.

3) Validate selective deflection and topology preservation
- Readouts: live-cell imaging of cohesin/Mediator residence; Micro-C/HiChIP for contact maps; calibrated ChIP for anchor occupancy; nascent RNA for target gene rescue; global topology metrics (boundary insulation, inter-TAD contacts) to confirm preservation.
- Criteria for success: ≥60% reduction of pathological E–P contact frequency with ≤10% change across matched normal E–P pairs within the TAD and ≤5% change in neighboring TAD insulation.

Decoy design and logic gating
- Three-signal AND gate for assembly and selectivity:
  1) Sequence proximity: programmable DNA-binding tether (e.g., dCas-based binder or designed DNA-binding proteins) brings the latent decoy to a disease-proximal neutral harbor defined in Aim 1.
  2) Chromatin state sensing: reader domains specific for the high-acetylation, high-density coactivator state typical of the disease enhancer (e.g., bromodomain-based readers) bias assembly only when that state is present.
  3) Orientation/geometry key: anisotropic binding arrays (e.g., convergent-orientation CTCF mimics at DLF-matched spacing) create an avidity advantage only for extruders approaching along the pathological axis; normal anchors with different motif phasing/orientation are not avidly captured.
- Capacity limiters: the decoy’s binding-site number is tuned to sponge only the local excess that sustains the diseased loop, avoiding depletion of cohesin/Mediator for normal loops.
- Reversibility: small-molecule- or light-switchable oligomerization domains for rapid on/off control; degron tags for emergency disassembly.

Mechanism of action (structural protein–first)
- Cohesin deflection: The decoy presents a high-avidity termination site with DLF-matched CTCF-like polarity, biasing loop-extruder stalling/retention at the decoy before the diseased enhancer reaches its promoter.
- Mediator/BRD4 redistribution: Multivalent coactivator-binding elements and local acetylation mimicry (below) create a favorable condensate that sequesters coactivators away from the pathologic E–P synapse without globally reducing availability.

Complementary epigenetic bias (secondary, reversible)
- Decoy potentiation: Install an enhancer-like acetylation cloud at the decoy harbor (e.g., catalytic recruitment of a histone acetyltransferase domain) to strengthen coactivator capture.
- Path-locus attenuation: Mild, reversible deacetylation or reader-blockade at the diseased enhancer to tip the partitioning equilibrium toward the decoy, constrained by the AND gate to avoid affecting matched normal enhancers.

Preservation of normal chromatin topology
- Intra-TAD localization limits long-range effects.
- Geometry keying and capacity limiters prevent depletion of structural proteins needed elsewhere.
- No permanent sequence alteration; all edits are protein-level assembly or reversible chromatin mark tweaks.
- Built-in kill switch to rapidly return to baseline.

Delivery plan (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Nucleic acid delivery encoding the core decoy scaffold with switchable oligomerization and reader modules.
- Event 2: Nucleic acid delivery encoding the programmable DNA-binding tethers and guide set for neutral harbors and DLF sensing.
- Event 3 (optional): A small molecule or light regimen to trigger decoy assembly and, if used, reversible chromatin biasing modules.
(Events 1–2 can be combined if vector capacity permits; omit Event 3 if constitutive assembly is acceptable in models.)

Model systems and validation sequence
- Discovery: Disease models with well-characterized pathogenic E–P loops (e.g., enhancer hijacking, boundary loss, inverted CTCF anchors).
- In silico: Polymer simulations with extrusion kinetics to optimize decoy placement/capacity before bench testing.
- In cellulo: Quantify selective loss of the targeted pathologic contact, maintenance of normal contacts, and rescue of gene expression phenotypes.
- In vivo (optional): Test tissue-delivery feasibility and durability; monitor global chromatin integrity.

Risk assessment and mitigations
- Off-target sequestration: Minimize by AND gating and local capacity; monitor with global ChIP/Hi-C dashboards. Rapid disassembly via degron/switch if unintended effects observed.
- Insufficient selectivity: Iterate DLF keying (adjust motif spacing/orientation and reader sensitivity) guided by contact-map differentials.
- Condensate spillover: Use inert scaffold backbones with low self-seeding propensity; cap valency.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: DLF atlas distinguishing diseased vs matched normal loops within the same TAD.
- M2: Decoy prototypes that assemble only under DLF-positive conditions and capture cohesin/Mediator in vitro.
- M3: In-cell demonstration of ≥60% reduction of pathologic E–P contact with ≤10% perturbation of matched normal contacts and restoration of target gene output toward baseline.
- M4: Reversibility demonstrated with full recovery of contact maps after decoy disassembly.

Novelty
Unlike approaches that cut DNA, delete anchors, or globally inhibit structural proteins, TopoFilter is a locus-restricted, geometry-keyed, reversible sink that deflects the extrusion/coactivator flux sustaining a single pathological loop, preserving normal E–P wiring and 3D genome architecture.

text:
Title
Reader-guided reactivation of endogenous loop-pruning to selectively dismantle pathological enhancer–promoter contacts (NATIVE-PRUNE)

Central hypothesis
Cells possess endogenous “loop-pruning” programs—centered on regulated cohesin release and Mediator disassembly—that preferentially dissolve high-dwell, super-enhancer–stabilized enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops during development and stress, while sparing typical, fast-exchanging contacts. By reawakening these programs only within pathological super-enhancer condensates, we can selectively disrupt disease E–P loops and preserve normal 3D genome topology.

Atomic strategy
Exploit kinetic and biophysical selectivity rather than sequence selectivity: concentrate native loop-release effectors (WAPL/PDS5–SMC3 deacetylation and Mediator un-seeding) specifically into BRD4/MED1-rich pathological condensates using chromatin “reader” domains, and gate their action with a transient, drug-inducible assembly. Pathological loops, being cohesion- and condensate-hyperstabilized, are preferentially pruned; normal contacts rapidly re-form after the brief pulse.

Specific aims
1) Define endogenous loop-pruning signatures that distinguish pathological from normal E–P contacts.
2) Build Reader-Guided Endogenous Pruning (RGEP) modules to reawaken the native pruning program only at pathological condensates.
3) Demonstrate selective E–P loop disruption with preservation of global topology in disease models.
4) Establish safety, reversibility, and delivery within ≤3 administration events.

Innovation
- Selectivity from state-sensing (condensate/kinetic features) rather than sequence targeting.
- Structural-protein–first control (cohesin, CTCF, Mediator) with epigenetic editing as a fallback stabilizer, not the primary driver.
- Single-pulse, reversible operation that corrects 3D structure without permanent DNA changes.

Approach

Aim 1: Endogenous loop-pruning atlas
- Models: differentiation (e.g., myeloid, neuronal), acute stress (heat, osmotic, oxidative), and hormone signaling that naturally remodels E–P contacts.
- Measurements:
  - Live-cell residence times: single-molecule tracking/FRAP of RAD21, WAPL, BRD4, MED1.
  - PTM maps of loop regulators: SMC3 acetylation, HDAC8 activity readouts; WAPL/PDS5 occupancy; CTCF/Mediator phospho-states (phosphoproteomics).
  - 3D maps: Micro-C/Hi-C plus H3K27ac/RAD21/BRD4/CTCF HiChIP to quantify loop half-lives and re-formation kinetics.
  - Pathological vs normal: compare disease-driving SE–P loops (e.g., MYC, TAL1, EVI1, AR-driven loci) to matched housekeeping loops.
- Output: a minimal “pruning signature” = {long dwell cohesin, high SMC3ac, high BRD4/MED1 IDR occupancy, WAPL exclusion} that predicts preferential sensitivity to transient cohesin-release/Mediator un-seeding.

Aim 2: RGEP module engineering (structural protein manipulation primary)
- Reader anchors (state-sensing):
  - SE-Reader A: BRD4-targeting nanobody or tandem bromodomain (BD1–BD2) with nuclear localization; enriched at H3K27ac/BRD4-high condensates.
  - SE-Reader B: minimal MED1-IDR docking fragment that partitions into Mediator condensates without seeding new droplets.
- Effectors (endogenous pruning reactivation):
  - Effector 1 (cohesin release): minimal WAPL release module (WAPL helix/PDS5-interaction motif) fused to FKBP.
  - Effector 2 (cohesin turnover bias): HDAC8 catalytic domain (SMC3 deacetylation) fused to FKBP.
  - Optional Effector 3 (Mediator un-seeding): short MED1-IDR competitor or CDK8/19 regulatory peptide that locally reduces Mediator dwell without global inhibition.
- Drug-gated assembly for temporal control:
  - Reader–effector dimerization via rapalog-inducible FRB–FKBP. No activity without the pulse; rapid off after drug washout.
- Rationale: Readers concentrate effectors only in pathological condensates (high H3K27ac/BRD4/MED1), eliciting cohesin release and condensate thinning where loops are hyperstabilized; typical enhancers receive sub-threshold effector levels and rapidly recover.

Aim 3: Selective pruning with global topology preserved
- In vitro disease models: leukemia (MYC/TAL1), EVI1-high AML, AR-dependent prostate lines; primary patient-derived cells where feasible.
- Assays and success criteria:
  - Loop-level: loss of target pathological E–P loops by H3K27ac/RAD21 HiChIP and Micro-C; unchanged frequencies of housekeeping E–P loops; restoration of insulated boundary usage if loop hijacking occurred.
  - Kinetics: pathological loops show delayed re-formation (>4–8 h) vs normal contacts recover promptly (<1–2 h) after a single 1–2 h pulse.
  - Topology: TAD boundary strength and compartmentalization unchanged globally; cohesin/CTCF genomic occupancy distributions return to baseline after 24–48 h.
  - Transcription: selective downshift of pathological SE target gene expression; minimal impact on housekeeping gene sets (RNA-seq, PRO-seq).
- Mechanistic validation:
  - Mutate reader acetyl-lysine binding or swap to non-SE readers to abrogate selectivity.
  - Catalytic-dead HDAC8 and WAPL-interface mutants to confirm necessity.
  - Time-resolved condensate rheology (FRAP) to show local thinning only at targeted SEs.

Aim 4: Safety, reversibility, and delivery (≤3 events)
- Delivery strategy:
  - Event 1: Single polycistronic LNP-mRNA or AAV expressing SE-Reader(FRB)-T2A-FKBP-WAPLmin-T2A-FKBP-HDAC8 under a tunable promoter.
  - Event 2: Single, timed rapalog pulse to assemble and activate RGEP at SEs.
  - Optional Event 3 (only if needed): A stabilization “antidote” small molecule that accelerates disassembly or transiently boosts NIPBL at housekeeping promoters to speed recovery.
- Off-target safeguards:
  - Activity limited by: condensate partitioning, drug-gated assembly, minimal effector domains, and short dosing window.
  - Degron fuses (e.g., dTAG) to clear RGEP components after study or therapy window.
- Reversibility: confirm restoration of baseline 3D architecture and transcription at 48–72 h post-pulse.

Complementary epigenetic stabilizer (secondary mechanism; used sparingly)
- If a pathological loop persists due to boundary erosion (e.g., hypermethylated CTCF sites), deliver a single gRNA-less reader-guided dCas9-TET1 or dCas9-KRAB transient mRNA in the same LNP to restore boundary insulation or dampen residual enhancer activity, without permanent edits.

Milestones and quantitative success criteria
- M1 (Month 12): Pruning signature identified; predictive model AUC >0.8 for loop sensitivity.
- M2 (Month 18): RGEP enriches ≥10-fold in pathological vs typical enhancers; local SMC3 deacetylation and cohesin release demonstrated.
- M3 (Month 24): ≥70% reduction of target pathological E–P loop strength with <10% change across housekeeping loops; TAD insulation score deviation <5% genome-wide.
- M4 (Month 30): In vivo PDX/CRISPR-engineered models: disease gene downregulation ≥50% with preserved animal tolerability; architecture recovery within 72 h.

Risk mitigation
- If BRD4-based readers perturb chromatin, switch to MED1-IDR–derived or AF9/YEATS readers with lower competition.
- If cohesin release is excessive, reduce pulse duration or titrate effector stoichiometry with weaker dimerizer analogs.
- If selectivity is insufficient, add a second gating layer: protease-activatable linkers cleaved only in high-acetylation microenvironments (reader-guided protease recruitment).

Expected outcomes and impact
- A reversible, state-sensing 3D genome “editor” that replays an evolutionarily encoded loop-pruning program at the precise biophysical niches that stabilize disease loops.
- High selectivity from endogenous-state recognition plus kinetic bias, preserving normal topology and contacts.
- A generalizable platform to correct 3D structural pathologies across cancers and inflammatory diseases without permanent DNA alteration and within ≤3 delivery events.

Title
LATCH: a loop-activated, AND-gated chromatin husher that selectively collapses pathological enhancer–promoter loops while preserving normal 3D topology

One-sentence hypothesis/goal
Pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops are uniquely characterized by prolonged enhancer–promoter dwell time within BRD4/Mediator-dense condensates; an AND-gated proximity sensor that requires (i) sustained enhancer–promoter proximity and (ii) high local condensate valency can reconstitute structural effectors to unload cohesin and dismantle Mediator only at these loops, while a self-limiting repressive tag locks the enhancer, thereby correcting 3D structure without altering DNA sequence or perturbing normal loops.

Atomic strategy
Exploit a kinetic/valency threshold that distinguishes disease loops from normal loops: only contacts that are both long-lived and within high-valency coactivator condensates trigger effector assembly. This converts a pathological 3D state into a local, self-extinguishing program of cohesin unloading and enhancer silencing.

System design (modular architecture)
- Enhancer Sensor (ES)
  - Targeting: multivalent reader array that binds enhancer chromatin with high acetylation density and enhancer identity (e.g., tandem low-affinity bromodomains + H3K4me1-preferring reader + short MED1-IDR interaction peptide).
  - Payload: split-Protease A (slow-reconstituting), masked WAPL/PDS5 recruiter (primary structural), and a caged minimal H3K27 methyltransferase microdomain (secondary epigenetic), each behind orthogonal protease-cleavable linkers.
  - Fail-safe: degron that renders ES effectors unstable unless retained in condensates (condensate-dependent stabilization tag).

- Promoter Sensor (PS)
  - Targeting: bind engaged promoters via Pol II CTD pSer2/pSer5 and a Mediator-subunit docking peptide.
  - Payload: split-Protease B (complements A), plus a proximity-limited E3 ligase recruiter targeting MED1/RAD21 when uncaged.
  - Fail-safe: identical condensate-dependent degron.

- AND gate and kinetic discrimination
  - The split protease pair (A+B) has deliberately slow association kinetics (t1/2 ≈ minutes) and requires multivalent co-assembly (coiled-coil assist) so that only prolonged ES–PS proximity within dense condensates reconstitutes activity; normal, brief E–P touches fall below threshold.
  - Upon reconstitution, the protease cleaves:
    1) a “lid” on the WAPL/PDS5 recruiter to locally unload cohesin at the active loop anchor (primary mechanism).
    2) a “lid” on the E3 recruiter to transiently ubiquitinate MED1/RAD21 at that specific junction, dismantling Mediator/cohesin bridging.
    3) a “lid” on the enhancer-anchored H3K27 methylation microdomain to deposit a small, spatially restricted, self-limiting repressive patch that reduces acetylation rebinding and prevents rapid loop re-formation (secondary mechanism).
  - As cohesin unloads and Mediator disassembles, ES and PS separate; loss of condensate retention exposes degrons, auto-extinguishing residual effectors.

Selectivity rationale
- Feature 1 (time): Cancer super-enhancers and hijacked E–P pairs exhibit longer contact dwell times than normal regulatory passes. Slow protease reconstitution makes time the primary discriminator.
- Feature 2 (valency): High-density BRD4/Mediator condensates supply the local avidity needed for ES/PS co-assembly. Normal enhancers/promoters rarely exceed this threshold.
- Dual-feature AND logic yields orders-of-magnitude selectivity over either feature alone; collateral action at normal loops is minimized because either contacts are too brief or valency too low.

Mechanism-of-action sequence (local only)
1) ES and PS co-reside in a pathological condensate/loop long enough to reconstitute protease activity.
2) Protease uncages the WAPL/PDS5 recruiter and E3 module; cohesin unloading and Mediator/RAD21 dampening occur at that specific loop.
3) Protease uncages the enhancer-anchored H3K27 writer microdomain; a small repressive patch forms, reducing BRD4 rebinding.
4) Loss of the pathological bridge disperses ES/PS; effectors degrade; cohesin extrusion proceeds to pre-existing CTCF boundaries, restoring normal topology.

Compliance with constraints
- Primary mechanism: manipulation of structural proteins (cohesin unloading via WAPL/PDS5; Mediator/RAD21 dampening).
- Secondary mechanism: localized, transient epigenetic tagging (H3K27me3 micro-patch) to maintain off-state without DNA edits.
- No DNA sequence mutation; actions are protein-level and reversible.
- Normal topology preserved by confining action to the pathological junction and using self-extinguishing modules.

Delivery plan (≤3 events)
- Single-event preferred: one LNP mRNA cocktail encoding ES and PS on separate transcripts (2A-linked variants as backup) under cancer-selective or ubiquitous promoters with post-translational gating.
- Optional second event (only if needed for temporal control in vivo): a small-molecule “arming key” that stabilizes ES/PS coiled-coil assist for a limited window, then is withdrawn.
- No third event planned.

Key experiments and readouts
Phase I: Build and calibrate the AND gate
- Live-cell single-molecule tracking of ES/PS and FRAP within enhancer condensates to tune slow reconstitution half-times.
- Proximity biosensor assay (split-luciferase) to quantify activation only under prolonged, high-valency contacts.
- Off-target baseline: confirm no activation at typical active genes with short E–P dwell times.

Phase II: Structural efficacy and specificity
- Acute assays in cancer cell models with known oncogenic E–P loops:
  - Micro-C/HiChIP (cohesin, Mediator) to show selective loss of target E–P contact with intact neighboring loops/TADs.
  - RAD21/MED1 ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN to verify local cohesin unloading/Mediator dampening without global depletion.
  - Live imaging of loop dynamics (CRISPR-tagged loci) to demonstrate dwell-time reduction at targeted pairs.

Phase III: Functional silencing and topology preservation
- ChIP-seq for H3K27ac↓ and focal H3K27me3↑ at the targeted enhancer with confined spread.
- RNA-seq/PRO-seq: loss of oncogene transcription; housekeeping genes and global transcription profiles remain stable.
- Hi-C at 5–10 kb resolution: unchanged compartments/TADs; selective correction at pathological loops only.

Controls and falsification
- Catalytically dead protease, WAPL/PDS5 recruiter-null, and E3-null variants.
- Fast-reconstituting protease variant (should increase off-target effects; used to demonstrate necessity of kinetic gating).
- If normal loops are disrupted or global cohesin is perturbed, reject the design; iterate by lowering reader affinities and slowing protease kinetics further.

Risk mitigation
- Reader domain choice emphasizes low-affinity multivalency to avoid sequestration.
- Spatial restrictors: short flexible linkers, degrons, and condensate-dependent stabilization minimize spread.
- Reversibility: add an inducible degradation tag to ES/PS for rapid shutdown if needed.

Success criteria (go/no-go)
- ≥80% reduction of pathological E–P contact frequency with ≤5% change in non-targeted loop frequencies genome-wide.
- ≥70% reduction in target gene transcription with ≤10% change in median expression of housekeeping gene set.
- No significant shift in A/B compartments or TAD boundary insulation scores.

Novelty statement
The core innovation is a loop-conditional, kinetic/valency-gated reconstitution of structural effectors that converts a disease-specific 3D state into a local cohesin/Mediator disassembly event, followed by a self-limiting repressive tag. This exploits dwell-time and condensate thresholds as the selectivity code, rather than sequence-directed recruitment or global cohesin perturbation, enabling precise correction of pathological chromatin loops while preserving normal topology.

Title
Cohesin-QC: a mechanosensitive cohesin variant that selectively resolves pathologic enhancer–promoter loops

Summary
Pathologic enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops display sustained abnormal mechanical strain arising from dysregulated extrusion, torsional stress, and anchor instability. Cohesin-QC is a 3D genome editor that senses this excess mechanical load and triggers local, reversible loop release while leaving normally loaded loops intact. It operates by embedding a calibrated force-sensing switch in cohesin’s kleisin interface that exposes an endogenous release-docking epitope only under sustained over‑tension. A coupled “reset” module restores physiological topology and, upon repeated triggering at the same enhancer, transiently dampens enhancer drive to prevent immediate relapse—without altering DNA sequence.

Central hypothesis (research question as hypothesis)
If cohesin is endowed with an intrinsic, tunable mechanosensitivity that converts sustained over‑tension in a loop into selective recruitment of loop‑release and reset factors, then pathologic E–P loops can be autonomously dissolved while preserving normal contacts and higher‑order topology.

Atomic strategy
Recode cohesin from a passive topological entrapment ring into an adaptive mechano-logic gate: “IF local loop tension is high for long enough, THEN expose a native release cue; ELSE remain inert.” This single global change—adding a tension-gated exposure switch to cohesin—enables stress-based (not sequence-based) discrimination across the entire 3D genome.

Mechanistic design
- Sensor (tension gate)
  - Insert a compact, reversible tension-sensing module (TSM) within the kleisin–SMC gate such that:
    - Normal loop forces keep TSM folded, masking a short linear motif (SLiM).
    - Sustained over‑tension unfolds TSM, unmasking the SLiM.
  - The SLiM is selected to bind endogenous release regulators (e.g., WAPL/PDS cofactors) with low basal affinity and high avidity only when multivalently displayed upon TSM unfolding, creating a built‑in kinetic filter for sustained, not transient, tension.

- Effector (selective release)
  - Unmasked SLiM recruits native release machinery at that ring only, transiently opening the kleisin gate to disengage the high‑tension loop while leaving other cohesin complexes unaffected.

- Reset (topology preservation)
  - A second masked SLiM (“reset motif”), revealed only after release, recruits a loader/cohesin‑stabilizer complex to rapidly re‑establish extrusion competence nearby, minimizing long‑range topological side effects.

- Recurrence brake (optional, epigenetic and reversible)
  - If the same enhancer triggers repeated TSM unfolding within a time window, a low‑duty epigenetic dampener is co‑recruited (e.g., a scaffold that transiently favors reduced enhancer acetylation via endogenous readers/writers). This decreases enhancer drive just enough to prevent immediate re‑formation of the pathological loop, without permanent editing.

Selectivity logic
- Physical discriminator: pathologic loops are enriched for chronically elevated tension/torque due to hyper‑enhancer output, stalled extrusion, or improper anchor orientation; normal loops exhibit adaptive loading with shorter, subthreshold bursts.
- Temporal discriminator: the TSM’s unfolding/refolding kinetics impose a built‑in persistence requirement so that only prolonged strain exposes the SLiM.
- Spatial discriminator: effector recruitment occurs on the strained ring only; neighboring rings with folded TSMs remain invisible to release machinery.
- Functional safeguard: the reset motif accelerates re‑loading to preserve TAD integrity and compartment structure post‑release.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and calibrate cohesin‑QC
- Construct a panel of kleisin‑embedded TSMs with graded unfolding thresholds; map a regime where normal chromatin dynamics keep the module folded while pathologic contexts unfold it.
- Validate that TSM insertion preserves essential cohesin functions (viability, cell cycle cohesion) by targeting interphase loop‑extrusion isoforms preferentially.

Aim 2. Build tension-to-release coupling with kinetic filtering
- Optimize SLiM identity, copy number, and spacing to ensure negligible basal binding but robust recruitment under sustained TSM unfolding.
- Quantify “persistence time” required for effector recruitment and ensure rapid disengagement once tension normalizes.

Aim 3. Demonstrate selective dissolution of pathological E–P loops with topology preservation
- In disease-relevant models harboring well‑characterized hijacked/super‑enhancer loops, test whether Cohesin‑QC:
  - Specifically reduces contact frequency at pathological E–P pairs.
  - Preserves global TAD boundaries, insulation scores, and compartmentalization.
  - Normalizes target gene overexpression without broad transcriptional collapse.

Aim 4. Implement the recurrence brake (optional module)
- Configure a repeat‑trigger counter using cooperative exposure of a second, weaker SLiM that engages endogenous chromatin‑modifying scaffolds only upon repeated unfolding events.
- Show that this transient dampening reduces rapid loop relapse while remaining reversible and locus‑nonspecific.

Delivery plan (≤3 events total)
- Event 1: Deliver Cohesin‑QC (engineered kleisin or cohesin subunit) as a replace-or-supplement transgene under interphase‑biased regulation.
- Event 2: Transiently down‑tune endogenous wild‑type subunit (e.g., degrader/ASO) to favor incorporation of Cohesin‑QC into extrusion-competent rings.
- Event 3 (optional): Provide the recurrence‑brake scaffold if not encoded on Event 1.

Readouts and success criteria
- Mechanics: sensor operational window where normal loops remain below exposure threshold; pathological contexts cross it persistently.
- Structure: selective loss of pathological E–P contacts; preserved genome-wide insulation and compartments.
- Function: correction of misregulated target expression with minimal off‑target transcriptional changes.
- Reversibility: loop release and topology reset without DNA sequence alteration; phenotype tracks with Cohesin‑QC presence/activity.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: global weakening of loops. Mitigation: narrow TSM thresholds; include reset motif to speed re‑loading; restrict expression to extrusion‑dominant cohesin isoforms.
- Risk: interference with cohesion during mitosis. Mitigation: interphase‑restricted promoters and/or isoform choice; dose titration.
- Risk: unintended widespread chromatin dampening by recurrence brake. Mitigation: require repeated triggers; use weak, rapidly reversible interactions; default off in Event 1.

Innovation
- Introduces mechanosensitive, persistence‑filtered cohesin as a universal “quality inspector” acting on the physics of loop strain rather than sequence or static marks.
- Couples autonomous tension sensing to endogenous release and rapid reset, enabling precise, reversible 3D genome correction.
- Adds a minimal, optional epigenetic brake that only engages upon pathological recurrence, maintaining specificity without permanent edits.

Expected outcome and impact
Cohesin‑QC will selectively dismantle disease‑driving E–P loops while preserving normal chromatin topology, establishing a class of 3D genome editors that operate by reading and correcting mechanical stress states rather than altering DNA sequence.

text:
Title: ChromaVAC—A PTM‑gated “vaccine” decoy that dissolves pathological enhancer–promoter loops while preserving normal 3D genome topology

Central question/hypothesis:
Can a decoy, loop‑mimicking minichromosome that selectively attracts and transiently reconditions abnormally post‑translationally modified (PTM) cohesin/CTCF/Mediator complexes deplete the pathogenic pool sustaining disease E–P loops, allowing those loops to collapse while sparing normal chromatin architecture?

Atomic strategy:
Exploit a PTM‑defined biochemical difference between pathological and normal loop‑forming complexes to drive selective partitioning of the pathological complexes into engineered “decoy looplets” that (i) capture them with high avidity only when the disease‑PTM signature is present and (ii) enzymatically remove those PTMs so the complexes lose affinity and re‑enter the normal pool—thus correcting 3D structure without permanently mutating DNA.

Mechanism of action (conceptual):
- Pathology: a subpopulation of cohesin/CTCF/Mediator acquires a disease‑specific PTM signature (e.g., SUMOylated/ADP‑ribosylated/hyper‑acetylated combinations) that stabilizes aberrant E–P loops.
- Intervention: introduce PTM‑gated decoy minichromosomes that mimic loop anchors and locally present multivalent PTM “reader‑traps.” Pathological complexes partition to decoys, reducing their on‑target residence at disease loops; normal complexes (lacking that PTM signature) ignore the decoys.
- Reconditioning: while tethered, site‑specific “erasers” on the decoy remove the disease PTMs from the trapped complexes, which then disengage and rejoin the physiological pool, preventing global depletion of structural proteins and preserving normal topology.

Tool architecture (modular):
1) LoopMimic episomal minichromosome (20–40 kb)
   - DNA scaffold: arrays of high‑affinity CTCF sites arranged in convergent pairs (10–16 anchors) spaced 1–2 kb to approximate strong anchor valency; interspersed cohesin loader–recruiting sequences (e.g., NIPBL‑tethering aptamer docking sites via CRISPR‑RNA handles).
   - Tethering and insulation: sequences for lamina‑association and CTCF‑insulator buffers to minimize inadvertent transcription; no strong promoters.
   - RNA scaffold: Pol III–driven noncoding RNA (e.g., 12× MS2/PP7 hairpins) to nucleate protein reader‑traps on the episome without genomic integration.

2) TAG‑Catcher reader‑trap (single mRNA expression)
   - Localizer: MS2/PP7 coat protein to dock on LoopMimic RNA scaffold; optional dCas tether to specified episomal sites.
   - PTM gate (AND logic): multivalent domains that collectively yield high avidity only for pathological complexes, e.g. SIM×3 (SUMO), WWE/PBM (PAR), tandem bromodomains (Ac‑Lys). Affinities are tuned so single‑mark binding is transient; co‑occurrence enables stable capture.
   - Structural‑protein interface: low‑affinity peptides for RAD21/Scc1 or CTCF to bias encounters without sequestering unmodified complexes.
   - Reconditioning cassette (detox‑and‑release): catalytically active SENP (deSUMOylase), PARG (anti‑PAR), and a recruited class‑I HDAC microdomain positioned to deacetylate bound factors; activities are restricted to the decoy via proximity.
   - Self‑limits: an inducible degron and small‑molecule “off‑switch” to rapidly disperse traps if global architecture perturbs.

3) Optional valency booster (encoded on LoopMimic)
   - Low‑level MED1‑IDR or SH3/PRM lattice to enhance selective condensation only when TAG‑Catcher is PTM‑occupied, preventing indiscriminate droplet formation.

Selectivity features:
- PTM‑gated avidity ensures capture only when the disease signature is present.
- Spatial segregation (lamina‑tethered episomes) minimizes interference with endogenous loci.
- Reconditioning releases normalized complexes, preventing global cohesin/CTCF depletion.
- Transcriptional inertness of LoopMimic avoids ectopic gene activation.

Delivery plan (≤3 events):
1) Event 1: Delivery of LoopMimic episome(s) as minicircle DNA (AAV or non‑integrating vector).
2) Event 2: LNP‑mRNA for TAG‑Catcher (single polyprotein with self‑cleaving linkers to assemble domains).
3) Optional Event 3: Orally available small molecule to toggle degron/dimerizer for temporal control (arm/disarm).

Research plan and milestones:

Aim 1. Define PTM signature(s) of pathological loop‑forming complexes at target disease loci.
- System: human cell models with well‑characterized pathogenic E–P loops (e.g., MYC or TAL1 super‑enhancer addiction; a cohesinopathy line).
- Methods: CUT&Tag/CUT&RUN‑ChIP for CTCF/RAD21/MED1 coupled to SUMO, PAR, and Ac‑Lys PTM mapping (proximity‑biotinylation with PTM‑aware mass spec).
- Output: combinatorial PTM “barcode” that distinguishes pathological from housekeeping loops; parameterize reader‑trap affinities.

Milestone: Identify at least one two‑or‑three‑mark combination enriched ≥3‑fold at disease E–P anchors versus housekeeping anchors.

Aim 2. Build PTM‑gated LoopMimic + TAG‑Catcher and demonstrate selective partitioning.
- Engineering: create a small library varying reader valency, inter‑domain linkers, and detox enzyme activities.
- Assays:
  - Live‑cell imaging (Halo‑RAD21/CTCF) to quantify partitioning to LoopMimic foci ± pharmacologic modulation of PTMs.
  - FRAP to measure residence times of modified vs unmodified complexes at decoys.
  - Proteomics of decoy‑bound complexes to confirm PTM enrichment and reconditioning kinetics.

Milestone: ≥5× enrichment of disease‑PTM complexes at decoys; normalized PTM status (≥60% loss of disease PTMs) within 30–60 minutes and complex release.

Aim 3. Test functional loop dissolution with preservation of normal topology.
- Readouts:
  - HiChIP/PLAC‑seq for E–P contacts at disease loci: ≥60–80% reduction in pathogenic loop contact frequency.
  - In parallel, genome‑wide insulation score, TAD strength, and aggregate loop counts: <5–10% deviation from baseline.
  - RNA‑seq: correction of disease‑driver gene expression toward normal with minimal impact on housekeeping gene sets.
  - Time‑course reversibility on disarming the system.

Milestone: Achieve target loop suppression and expression normalization with preserved global metrics; effects reversible within 24–48 h off‑switch.

Aim 4. In vivo proof‑of‑concept and safety.
- Model: xenografts or patient‑derived organoids matching Aim 1 signatures.
- Delivery: Event 1 (episome) by AAV to target tissue; Event 2 (mRNA) by LNP; Event 3 optional on‑demand control.
- Endpoints: reduction of disease‑loop signal (HiChIP on biopsies), restoration of transcriptional programs, absence of widespread architectural collapse (insulation/compartment scores), and tolerability.

Controls:
- Reader‑trap lacking one PTM domain (tests AND‑gate stringency).
- Catalytically dead “erasers” (tests detox necessity).
- Episome without CTCF arrays (tests loop‑mimic valency).
- Decoy positioned without lamina tether (tests spatial insulation).

Quantitative success criteria:
- Selectivity index = (decoy capture of disease‑PTM complexes)/(capture of unmodified complexes) ≥10.
- Pathogenic E–P loop contact frequency ↓ ≥70%; global TAD/loop metrics within ±5% of baseline.
- Driver gene overexpression ↓ ≥50% with ≤10% median change in housekeeping genes.
- Full reversibility within 48 h of disarming; no increase in DNA damage markers (γH2AX) or replication stress.

Risk analysis and mitigations:
- Risk: global cohesin titration. Mitigation: PTM‑AND gate; detox‑and‑release cycle; rapid degron off‑switch.
- Risk: ectopic transcription from LoopMimic. Mitigation: insulators, promoterless design, lamina tethering.
- Risk: insufficient PTM separation between normal and pathological pools. Mitigation: expand reader palette (e.g., O‑GlcNAc, phospho‑readers), increase combinatorial logic, or pivot to locus‑proximal recruitment of decoys via dCas tethering near disease anchors.

Scope of novelty:
- Introduces PTM‑gated, loop‑mimicking episomal “vaccines” that transiently sequester and biochemically recondition aberrant structural protein complexes, correcting 3D genome structure without genome edits or permanent sequence changes.

Projected timeline:
- Months 0–6: Aim 1 (PTM mapping), initial reader‑trap design.
- Months 6–12: Aim 2 (partitioning and detox kinetics), select lead construct.
- Months 12–18: Aim 3 (3D topology/rescue in cells), reversibility tuning.
- Months 18–24: Aim 4 (in vivo feasibility), delivery optimization.

Deliverables:
- Lead ChromaVAC construct (LoopMimic + TAG‑Catcher) with validated PTM‑gate parameters.
- A quantitative framework linking PTM barcodes to selective 3D genome correction.
- Data package demonstrating pathologic loop dissolution with topology preservation and reversibility.

text:
Title: Guard-and-Prune 3D Genome Editor (GaP-3D): Proximity-gated protection of native enhancer–promoter loops with context-targeted cohesin unloading to erase pathological contacts

Central hypothesis and research goal
- Hypothesis-question: Can a two-phase “protect-then-prune” intervention that (i) kinetically locks native enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops and (ii) broadly unloads loop-extruding complexes in suspicious chromatin contexts eliminate cancer-specific E–P loops while preserving normal 3D genome topology?
- Goal: Build a reversible, non-mutagenic 3D genome editor that distinguishes and preserves developmentally encoded E–P contacts and selectively collapses oncogenic E–P loops, using structural protein manipulation as the primary mechanism and epigenetic editing as a stabilizing complement.

Atomic strategy
- Single global lever: Exploit loop lifetime. Normal E–P loops formed during development are long-residence, motif-constrained, and co-factored; many pathological E–P loops are shorter-lived and cofactor-misaligned. A proximity-gated “LoopShield” forms only across contacts that persist beyond a kinetic threshold, thereby locking native loops. A subsequent, region-focused cohesin unloading (“LoopShear”) prunes unprotected loops. Protection is contact-first and agnostic to locus identity, turning heterogeneity into a feature.

Design overview
- Module 1: LoopShield (protect)
  - A bivalent, proximity-gated anchor clamp that engages only when two anchors dwell in contact beyond a preset time window.
  - Input logic (AND gate): anchor-bound CTCF/cohesin presence + E–P cofactor signature (e.g., YY1/Mediator enrichment or promoter/enhancer histone code) + sustained proximity.
  - Output: a reversible trans-anchor “latch” that (a) increases local cohesin residence (WAPL antagonism) and (b) retains Mediator/Pol II scaffolding. Locked loops become unload-resistant.
- Module 2: LoopShear (prune)
  - A cohesin-unloading actuator tuned to operate broadly over suspicious chromatin (e.g., hyperacetylated super-enhancer fields, boundary-erosion zones) via reader-guided targeting, or globally at moderated strength.
  - Mechanism: promote cohesin release (e.g., WAPL recruitment or processivity dampening) and reduce Mediator residency. Unprotected loops collapse; LoopShielded loops persist.
- Module 3: Epigenetic stabilizer (optional, complement)
  - Reader-writer tethers docked to LoopShielded anchors to reinforce normative enhancer/promoter marks and erase ectopic activation in pruned regions, consolidating the corrected 3D state without altering DNA sequence.
- Reversibility and safety
  - LoopShield latches include a built-in disassembly trigger (external cue–responsive) to return to baseline if needed.
  - No permanent sequence edits; operations act on protein complexes and chromatin states.

Specific aims and milestones
- Aim 1: Engineer and validate LoopShield’s kinetic and biochemical selectivity for native E–P loops.
  - Build a proximity-gated, reversible anchor clamp that engages only under sustained contact.
  - Encode cofactor- and mark-sensitivity so locking requires CTCF/cohesin plus E–P cofactor signatures.
  - Success criteria: In reporter and genome-wide assays, LoopShield occupancy is enriched at developmentally conserved E–P contacts, with minimal engagement at ectopic or transient interactions; protected loops retain cohesin/Mediator after mild unloading challenge.
- Aim 2: Develop LoopShear to unload cohesin in suspicious chromatin while sparing LoopShielded contacts.
  - Construct a reader-guided cohesin-unloading actuator that concentrates in hyperacetylated and boundary-erosion regions, with adjustable global background activity.
  - Success criteria: Post-LoopShear, unprotected E–P loops (including oncogenic rewires) collapse; global TAD/compartment metrics and promoter capture contact maps for housekeeping/lineage genes remain within normal bounds due to LoopShield.
- Aim 3: Consolidate corrected topology and function with epigenetic stabilization and demonstrate reversibility.
  - Attach enhancer/promoter-specific read–write tethers to LoopShield to preserve normative marks; deploy context-matched erasers in pruned regions to prevent re-engagement.
  - Demonstrate on–off control of LoopShield to revert to pre-intervention topology if needed.
  - Success criteria: Stable maintenance of corrected E–P wiring after removal of LoopShear activity; rapid reversal upon LoopShield disassembly without sequence changes.

Mechanism-of-action details
- Selectivity arises from three orthogonal filters that together favor normal E–P loops:
  1) Kinetic filter: The latch forms only across contacts with dwell times above threshold, biasing toward developmentally encoded loops.
  2) Structural filter: Engagement requires anchor-bound CTCF/cohesin features and appropriate motif polarity/cofactor occupancy characteristic of canonical E–P loops.
  3) Contextual filter (during pruning): Cohesin unloading is focused where oncogenic rewiring concentrates (e.g., hyperacetylated enhancer fields), raising the likelihood that pathological loops are unprotected and thus pruned.
- Topology preservation: Locked loops provide a “load-bearing skeleton” that maintains local TAD integrity and promoter connectivity while extraneous or hijacked loops are removed.

Evaluation plan
- Structure-first readouts: Micro-C/Hi-C, promoter capture, and multi-contact assays to quantify loop persistence/erasure; insulation and compartment scores to assess topology integrity.
- Protein occupancy: CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for CTCF, cohesin, Mediator to confirm protection vs unloading.
- Function: nascent transcription and RNA profiles to verify restoration of normal enhancer targeting and suppression of oncogenic rewiring, without widespread expression collapse.
- Safety: DNA replication timing, replication stress markers, and genome stability metrics; reversibility tests by disassembling LoopShield.

Delivery strategy (≤3 events)
- Event 1: Delivery of LoopShield (single vector encoding both halves under controllable expression).
- Event 2: Delivery of LoopShear (context-targeted cohesin-unloading actuator).
- Event 3 (optional): Delivery of epigenetic stabilizer module; alternatively co-encode with LoopShield to reduce to two events.
- All modules are designed for transient, controllable expression; no permanent genome edits.

Risk analysis and mitigation
- Risk: Stable oncogenic loops could meet the kinetic threshold and be inadvertently protected.
  - Mitigation: Tighten LoopShield’s AND-logic to require E–P cofactor signatures enriched at physiological, not hijacked, contacts; incorporate boundary-violation sensing (e.g., loss of insulation cues) to veto latching across aberrant spans.
- Risk: Excess unloading perturbs higher-order topology.
  - Mitigation: Calibrate LoopShear strength; bias targeting to suspicious chromatin; rely on LoopShield skeleton to preserve essential architecture.
- Risk: Off-target latching or chromatin rigidity.
  - Mitigation: Use reversible latches with timed auto-release; cap occupancy to avoid excessive crosslink density.

Why this is novel
- Inverts the usual “find-and-destroy” paradigm by first globally protecting functionally correct loops using a contact-kinetics gate, then broadly pruning with structural-protein manipulation. The kinetic AND contextual selectivity at the level of 3D contact formation—combined with reversible, protein-centric locking and unloading—constitutes a distinct, non-mutagenic mode of 3D genome editing.

Expected outcomes and impact
- Selective elimination of pathological E–P loops with preservation of normal contacts and topology.
- A generalizable, reversible framework for 3D genome correction that leverages endogenous structural machinery, with optional epigenetic reinforcement to maintain repaired architecture without altering DNA sequence.

Title
SELECT: A self-selecting 3D genome editor that unloads cohesin only on kinetically fragile enhancer–promoter loops

Central research question and hypothesis
Question: Can loop-intrinsic instability serve as the sole selector to disrupt pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) contacts while preserving normal chromatin topology?
Hypothesis: Pathological E–P loops are kinetically fragile—exhibiting short residence time of cohesin/Mediator and a bias toward unacetylated Smc3—whereas homeostatic E–P loops are kinetically robust and Smc3-acetylated. An engineered, single-chain protein that (i) detects E–P proximity and (ii) actuates cohesin unloading only when unacetylated cohesin is present will dissolve fragile (pathological) loops but spare robust (normal) loops, restoring global 3D topology without altering DNA sequence.

Atomic strategy
Convert loop kinetic fragility into a local biochemical trigger: “state-sensing cohesin unloading.” The tool engages only where two conditions are simultaneously true in real time: enhancer–promoter juxtaposition AND unacetylated cohesin. This two-key gating implements a physical selectivity filter rather than a sequence- or disease-catalog-based target list.

Tool design: SELECT protein (Selective E–P Loop Editing by Cohesin Turnover)
Single polypeptide with three tightly coupled modules:

1) E–P proximity gate (context gate)
- Enhancer reader: low-affinity bromodomain variant recognizing H3K27ac-enriched enhancer chromatin.
- Promoter reader: PHD finger variant recognizing H3K4me3 at promoters.
- Geometry constraint: a calibrated flexible linker enforces avidity only when enhancer and promoter surfaces are within ~10–50 nm, i.e., during an actual E–P contact. Outside juxtaposition, readers disengage due to sub-saturating affinity.

2) Cohesin state sensor (fragility gate)
- Conformation/state-specific binder that preferentially recognizes unacetylated Smc3 (e.g., an engineered binder or nanobody selective for the unacetylated K105/K106 epitope) on loop-anchoring cohesin.
- Rationale: unacetylated cohesin displays higher turnover and lower gate-closing stability; stable architectural loops are enriched for Smc3 acetylation. Thus, the sensor reports loop kinetic fragility.

3) Unloading actuator (action module)
- Minimal WAPL/PDS5-recruiting motif that catalytically increases local cohesin unloading only when both gates are engaged.
- Autoinhibition: an intramolecular latch occludes the WAPL-recruiting surface unless dual engagement (E–P AND unacetylated Smc3) induces a conformational release. Therefore, no action at isolated enhancers, isolated promoters, or E–P contacts bearing acetylated cohesin.

Optional, secondary stabilization (epigenetic nudge)
- A weak, delay-integrated HDAC mini-module tethered behind the same dual gate that transiently reduces H3K27ac only if a site is repeatedly targeted across time (i.e., persistently fragile loops). This discourages rapid re-formation without permanently rewriting marks or DNA. The epigenetic nudge is off by default and rate-limited to avoid spreading.

Operating principle
- Normal E–P loops: readers bind, but Smc3 is acetylated → fragility gate remains closed → actuator stays off → loop preserved.
- Pathological fragile E–P loops: readers bind during brief contacts and encounter unacetylated cohesin → dual gate opens → local WAPL/PDS5 recruitment increases cohesin unloading → loop dissolves. Repeated attempts to re-form are met with the same kinetic veto, optionally reinforced by the slow, local acetylation nudge.

Delivery
- Single delivery event preferred: mRNA or AAV expressing SELECT under a cell-type-restricted promoter. Up to three total deliveries allowed; optional second event can provide a ligand-controlled degron for temporal control; an optional third event can deliver a fluorescent reporter for pharmacodynamics only in preclinical studies.

Research plan

Aim 1: Build and calibrate the dual-gated SELECT architecture
- Construct SELECT variants spanning an affinity matrix for the enhancer and promoter readers to set the E–P avidity window.
- Engineer Smc3 state-sensor binders with differential preference for acetylated vs unacetylated epitopes; benchmark selectivity in cells using acetyl-mimic and acetyl-dead Smc3 alleles (non-genomic, transient expression controls).
- Quantify autoinhibition stringency and gate logic using live-cell FRET reporters fused to SELECT.

Milestone: A variant exhibiting ≥10-fold activation difference between unacetylated vs acetylated cohesin within E–P juxtaposition, and <5% baseline activity elsewhere.

Aim 2: Test selective disruption on model systems with engineered loop fragility
- Use inducible systems that modulate cohesin residence (e.g., transient WAPL upshift or ESCO inhibition) at reporter E–P pairs to create “fragile” vs “robust” contacts without changing DNA sequence.
- Readouts: Micro-C/Hi-C for contact frequency; live-cell cohesin residence tracking; targeted 3C at reporters; transcriptional response by RT-qPCR and nascent RNA-seq focused on the reporter locus.

Milestone: SELECT reduces contact frequency and reporter output only in the fragile condition, with ≤5% effect in the robust condition and no detectable perturbation of compartment/TAD structure.

Aim 3: Apply SELECT to disease-relevant miswiring that is kinetically fragile
- Choose systems where pathological activation is supported by labile E–P contacts (e.g., enhancer hijacking events exhibiting short-lived Mediator/cohesin occupancy).
- Metrics: differential E–P contact decay kinetics pre/post-SELECT; restoration of native expression profiles; preservation of global 3D metrics (A/B compartments, CTCF loops, insulation scores).

Milestone: Pathological target gene downshift to physiologic range with maintenance of global topology metrics within ±5% of baseline.

Aim 4 (optional): Evaluate the epigenetic nudge as a re-formation suppressor
- Enable the slow HDAC mini-module and assess whether rebound of pathological contacts is further reduced without spreading hypoacetylation beyond the E–P window (CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag footprinting).

Milestone: Additional ≥20% reduction in contact rebound with unchanged enhancer/promoter mark landscapes outside the E–P window.

Selectivity safeguards and failure modes
- Triple-context gating: E–P juxtaposition AND unacetylated cohesin AND autoinhibitory release are all required; any single failure prevents action.
- Kinetic containment: actuator is catalytic but locally gated; no genome-wide cohesin depletion.
- Topology preservation: biasing unloading to short-lived E–P contacts avoids CTCF-anchored architectural loops, minimizing TAD/compartment distortion.
- Off-target risks: If some normal E–P loops carry unacetylated cohesin, SELECT could act there. Mitigation: tighten E–P avidity window, reduce actuator potency, or add a Mediator-tail valency sensor that requires low Mediator dwell time to open the latch.

Readouts and success criteria
- Structural: targeted Micro-C/Hi-C shows selective loss of pathological E–P contacts; insulation scores and loop strength at CTCF–CTCF anchors unchanged.
- Biochemical: increased local WAPL/PDS5 signal and decreased unacetylated Smc3 at targeted E–P sites only.
- Functional: correction of misregulated gene expression toward baseline without broad transcriptional repression.
- Safety: no increase in DNA damage markers; cell fitness maintained.

Why this is novel
- The core novelty is a state-sensing, dual-gated actuator that reads a physical property of a loop (kinetic fragility via cohesin acetylation state) only within the E–P geometric context to trigger unloading. It does not require prior knowledge of disease-specific sequences, motifs, or catalogs; selectivity emerges from biophysics and chromatin state.
- Unlike prior epigenome editors or sequence-guided tethers, SELECT edits 3D structure transiently by modulating cohesin turnover rather than mutating DNA or installing durable chromatin marks.

Anticipated outcomes and impact
- A generalizable, self-selecting 3D genome editor that preferentially dissolves pathological E–P loops while preserving normal topology.
- A blueprint for future “kinetic-logic” chromatin therapeutics that act at the level of chromatin physics, not sequence.

Title: Kinetic-Topology Whitelisting to Correct Pathological Enhancer–Promoter Loops

Central hypothesis
A brief, global “reset” of loop-maintaining proteins, followed by a boundary-first reassembly of cohesin guided by a high-stringency CTCF loader and a transient depletion of super-enhancer coactivator capacity, will allow normal chromatin topology to re-form while selectively preventing re-nucleation of pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops.

Atomic strategy
Exploit an order-of-return dependency: normal 3D architecture is scaffolded first by CTCF-anchored TAD boundaries and only then refined by enhancer-driven contacts, whereas pathological E–P loops over-rely on Mediator-rich transcriptional hubs. A staged reconstitution that (i) seeds boundary-cohesin loading with high sequence-stringency and rapid cohesin turnover, and (ii) transiently reduces Mediator-driven condensate availability, creates a kinetic “whitelist” funnel in which healthy loops reassemble and disease loops fail to nucleate.

Tool concept: 3D Genome Editor (3DGE-KTW)
A two-payload, three-phase system operating entirely at the protein/epigenetic level with no permanent sequence edits.

Phase 0 (baseline characterization)
- Map “keystone” boundary CTCF sites and candidate pathological E–P loops in the target cell type using Micro-C/Hi-C, CTCF/Cohesin/Mediator CUT&RUN, and H3K27ac/BRD4 profiles.
- Define a small whitelist (100–300 keystone boundaries conferring most insulation) and a blacklist (10–50 disease E–P anchors).

Phase 1: Global, synchronous reset (minutes–hours)
- Mechanism: transient proteolysis of RAD21 (cohesin), CTCF, and MED1 (Mediator) via mRNA-delivered nanobody–E3 fusions (TRIM21-based) targeting endogenous proteins; optional dimerizers for fast on/off.
- Objective: collapse existing loops and hubs uniformly without DNA damage or lasting edits.

Phase 2: Boundary-first scaffold reassembly (6–12 h)
- Mechanism A (primary, structural): express a transient, high-stringency CTCF variant fused to a minimal cohesin-loader (CTCFHiFi–NIPBLmini). The zinc-finger tuning increases affinity for canonical, high-information CTCF consensus and reduces binding at degenerate, disease-gained sites. NIPBLmini promotes local cohesin loading where CTCFHiFi binds.
- Mechanism B (structural kinetics): co-express WAPL transiently to increase cohesin turnover, favoring long-range extrusion to strong CTCF barriers over short-range enhancer capture during scaffold formation.
- Expected effect: rapid restoration of TAD boundaries and normal compartmental constraints without reactivation of enhancer hubs.

Phase 3: Selective suppression of pathological E–P re-nucleation during release (12–36 h)
- Mechanism C (structural-to-epigenetic interface, transient): a Mediator-IDR “sponge” (MED1-IDR binding peptide array fused to a cytosolic sequestration tag with an inducible degron) modestly reduces available Mediator for condensate formation at super-enhancers.
- Mechanism D (complementary, optional): multiplexed dCas9-KRAB mRNA plus a minimal gRNA pool targets only blacklist enhancers to keep them inactive during reassembly.
- Tuning: withdraw WAPL overexpression; degrade CTCFHiFi–NIPBLmini and the Mediator sponge using orthogonal small-molecule/optogenetic degrons to return the endogenous proteome. Normal E–P loops requiring modest coactivator levels recover; disease loops that require high, cooperative Mediator density remain selectively impaired.

Delivery plan (≤3 events)
- Delivery 1 (Reset): LNP-encapsulated mRNAs encoding anti-RAD21/anti-CTCF/anti-MED1 nanobody–TRIM21 fusions with a small-molecule–controlled safety switch.
- Delivery 2 (Reassembly and guardrails): a single LNP co-encapsulating mRNAs for CTCFHiFi–NIPBLmini (light- or ligand-degron), WAPL (short-lived), Mediator-IDR sponge (auxin- or dTAG-degron), and optional dCas9-KRAB with a compact blacklist gRNA set.
- Delivery 3 (optional for in vivo timing precision): a pharmacologic pulse (auxin/dTAG/photostimulation) to remove the transient effectors and complete return to native protein composition. In many settings, this can be combined with Delivery 2 (e.g., light control), keeping total events at 2.

Selectivity rationale
- Sequence stringency: CTCFHiFi preferentially occupies canonical, high-affinity boundary motifs that anchor normal topology, while sparing lower-affinity, context-dependent sites more common at disease-gained anchors.
- Kinetic sieving: transiently high cohesin turnover (WAPL) disfavors stable short-range enhancer capture during early reassembly, biasing loop extrusion toward boundary-anchored structures.
- Hub desaturation: a modest, time-limited decrease in effective Mediator availability reduces the probability of pathological condensate nucleation without abolishing basal transcription needed for normal loops to resume later.
- Spatial whitelist: seeding only keystone boundaries is sufficient to reconstruct the global scaffold; healthy local contacts follow passively under restored constraints.

Validation plan
- Structure
  - Micro-C/Hi-C time course across Phases 1–3 to track TAD insulation recovery and E–P contact frequencies at blacklist loci.
  - HiChIP/CUT&RUN for CTCF, RAD21, MED1 to verify boundary-first loading and reduced Mediator at disease enhancers during Phase 3.
- Function
  - PRO-seq/RNA-seq to confirm restoration of housekeeping and lineage programs with selective reduction of oncogenic/pathogenic transcripts.
  - Single-cell ATAC/RNA multiome to ensure cell-state preservation and absence of global chromatin silencing.
- Specificity and reversibility
  - Turn off transient effectors; re-measure architecture and expression to confirm durable correction of pathological loops and intact normal topology.
  - Off-target assessment of replication dynamics and DNA damage markers (EdU, γH2AX).

Controls
- No-reset control (skip Phase 1) to show necessity of the global reset for selectivity.
- CTCFWT–NIPBLmini vs CTCFHiFi–NIPBLmini to quantify the benefit of increased sequence stringency.
- Sponge-minus and WAPL-minus arms to deconvolve contributions of condensate desaturation and kinetic sieving.
- Non-targeting dCas9-KRAB gRNAs for epigenetic control specificity.

Milestones and success criteria
- M1: ≥80% restoration of TAD insulation scores within 12 h of Phase 2 with minimal enhancer hub activity (MED1 foci count reduced ≥50%).
- M2: ≥60% reduction in contact frequency at predefined pathological E–P pairs (Capture-C) with ≤10% change at matched normal E–P pairs.
- M3: ≥50% reduction of pathogenic transcript output with preserved global transcriptional complexity (Shannon index change ≤5%) and no increase in DNA damage markers.
- M4: After effector withdrawal, maintenance of corrected architecture and expression for ≥5 cell doublings without genome sequence changes.

Risk mitigation
- Excessive transcriptional suppression: tune sponge expression and ensure rapid degron off-switch; prioritize blacklist-only CRISPRi if broad effects observed.
- Incomplete reset: increase nanobody–E3 dosage or add a short proteasome pulse; verify by proteomics.
- Boundary over-stabilization: throttle NIPBLmini activity or duration; reduce WAPL to normalize cohesin residence time.

Translational note
All components operate transiently at the protein/epigenetic level. For in vivo use, payloads can be formulated as LNP-delivered mRNAs with orthogonal, clinically tractable switches (e.g., small-molecule degrons, light for accessible tissues). No permanent DNA sequence edits are required.

Outcome
3DGE-KTW provides a globally minimal yet system-level intervention—reset, boundary-first scaffold, guarded release—that distinguishes pathological from normal E–P loops by protein dependency and assembly order, achieving selective disruption of disease loops while preserving and restoring native 3D genome topology.
