Title
LoopClutch: A time-integrating, condensate-gated “3D genome editor” that selectively unlocks pathological enhancer–promoter loops while preserving normal topology

Central Hypothesis and Reframed Goal
Pathological enhancer–promoter (E–P) loops differ from physiological loops not only by anchor identity but by three emergent properties: (i) prolonged residency of cohesin/loop-stabilizing complexes (reduced turnover), (ii) high-density, multivalent enhancer condensates (Mediator/BRD4-rich, hyperacetylated chromatin), and (iii) aberrant cofactor composition at both anchors (e.g., enhancer condensate at one anchor abnormally paired with promoter complexes at the other). If a molecular system reads this composite “loop-state fingerprint” and integrates it over time before acting, it can discriminate diseased loops from normal ones and trigger local, reversible loop release without altering DNA sequence or disturbing global 3D architecture.

Atomic Strategy
Exploit loop persistence and condensate multivalency as the discriminative signal: build a proximity- and density-gated timer that only matures when two anchors remain abnormally close within a high-valency enhancer microenvironment long enough to exceed a preset dwell-time threshold; once matured, it briefly recruits endogenous cohesin-release machinery to that single loop, causing local disassembly. Loss of proximity immediately resets the system, sparing normal, transient contacts.

System Architecture
1) Sensing Layer: Multivalent Fingerprint Reader
- Structural readouts: low-affinity binders to cohesin/CTCF/Mediator surfaces and IDRs; these accumulate only where those factors are locally enriched.
- Chromatin-state readouts: distributed bromodomain-like readers for dense H3K27ac and enhancer-associated marks that require multivalent binding to engage.
- Promoter-engagement readouts: weak Pol II/TFIID-interface binders that register promoter-side occupancy.
- Logic: All sensor interactions are intentionally weak; only when two anchors co-reside within a dense enhancer–promoter microenvironment do sufficient avidity and colocalization occur to assemble a functional complex (AND gate across density at both anchors and their proximity).

2) Temporal Integrator: Proximity-Dependent Slow Maturation
- A slow-maturing, proximity-requiring molecular timer (e.g., a reconstitution or maturation event with minutes-scale kinetics) that only completes if the two anchors remain in contact beyond normal loop lifetimes. Normal, short-lived contacts fail to complete the timer and thus remain untouched.

3) Effector Layer: Local, Reversible Loop Release
- Upon timer completion, an effector transiently biases endogenous cohesin dynamics toward release at that specific loop by recruiting native release cofactors (e.g., WAPL/PDS5) or by momentarily reducing cohesin processivity via allosteric engagement. The action radius is constrained by the assembled sensor, limiting activity to the matured loop.
- Auto-reset: Loop opening disrupts proximity and condensate density, dismantling the sensor and terminating effector recruitment.

4) Safeguards and Boundaries
- Multi-input gating (enhancer density AND promoter occupancy AND cohesin enrichment AND time) enforces selectivity.
- Failsafe cap: maximal duty cycle and refractory period limit cumulative action.
- Optional boundary insurance: a weak, global bias that mildly stabilizes canonical boundary CTCF–cohesin interactions to preserve TAD insulation while diseased loops are corrected, without changing normal loop patterns.

Proposed Effectors and Complementary Epigenetic Nudges
- Primary (structural): transient recruitment of endogenous cohesin-release modulators (e.g., WAPL/PDS5 bias) or brief disruption of Mediator–cohesin bridging via competitive, low-affinity interfaces. No DNA cutting or permanent edits.
- Secondary (epigenetic, optional): locally constrained de-acetylation or phase-modulating peptides that slightly reduce enhancer condensate valency only after the structural release has occurred, preventing immediate re-formation but avoiding broad chromatin changes.

Selectivity Rationale
- Residence-time discrimination filters out physiological loops (fast turnover) and targets pathological ones (prolonged dwell).
- Multivalency thresholding requires dense enhancer condensates uncommon at typical enhancers.
- Bi-anchored logic prevents action at single high-density sites lacking an aberrant partner.
- Local-only effector action preserves neighboring loops and global topology.

Research Plan and Milestones
Aim 1: Map disease-evolving loop fingerprints
- Define longitudinal changes in loop dwell-time distributions, condensate density, and anchor cofactor composition across disease initiation to progression.
- Derive quantitative thresholds for the sensor’s density and time gates that best separate pathological from healthy loops.
Deliverable: A minimal multi-feature “fingerprint” that robustly classifies diseased E–P loops.

Aim 2: Engineer LoopClutch modules and validate logic in cell systems
- Build modular readers for cohesin/CTCF/Mediator and enhancer/promoter states using weak, multivalent interfaces.
- Implement a slow, proximity-requiring maturation timer and couple it to a minimal, reversible cohesin-release effector.
- Demonstrate AND-gated activation only under high-density, prolonged contacts; verify rapid auto-reset after loop release.
Success criteria: >20-fold on/off activation ratio between pathological versus physiological loop states; immediate disassembly after loop opening.

Aim 3: Demonstrate selective loop correction with topology preservation
- In disease-relevant models, show loss of targeted pathological E–P loops with minimal impact on normal loops and TAD insulation.
- Confirm constrained transcriptional normalization at corrected target genes while preserving genome-wide expression homeostasis.
Success criteria: ≥80% reduction of selected pathological loops; ≤5% perturbation of non-target loops within the same TAD; restoration of local gene regulation without global dysregulation.

Aim 4: Durable correction via minimal interventions (≤3 delivery events)
- Evaluate one- or two-component delivery formats for the sensing–timer–effector system; optionally add a single boundary-insurance component if required.
- Test durability, reversibility, and retreatment feasibility without genomic alteration.
Success criteria: Stable maintenance of corrected topology over disease-relevant timescales with no accumulation of permanent edits.

Risk Analysis and Mitigations
- Risk: High-density physiological super-enhancers might be targeted. Mitigation: enforce the bi-anchored promoter-engagement requirement and dwell-time threshold; cap effector duty cycle.
- Risk: Broad cohesin perturbation. Mitigation: local effector recruitment tethered to matured sensor; employ weakest effector that yields reliable single-loop release.
- Risk: Adaptive re-formation of pathological loops. Mitigation: optional, tightly localized epigenetic nudge post-release; iterative threshold tuning.

Validation Readouts
- Structural: genome-wide contact profiling and targeted, time-resolved proximity assays to quantify loop loss and topology preservation.
- Molecular: occupancy and turnover metrics for cohesin/CTCF/Mediator before and after LoopClutch action.
- Functional: expression normalization of disease-driving genes without broad transcriptional collateral effects.

Novelties
- Uses loop persistence and condensate multivalency as a composite, time-integrated fingerprint rather than genomic address.
- Implements a slow, proximity-gated maturation timer to enforce discrimination by dwell-time—an emergent physical property—before engaging a minimal, reversible cohesin-release clutch.
- Achieves topology correction without DNA sequence editing, with built-in auto-reset and boundary insurance.

Expected Impact
LoopClutch provides a principled, systems-level means to correct disease-causing 3D genome wiring by reading and normalizing emergent physical states of chromatin, offering selective, reversible intervention that preserves healthy architecture.

Title
FILP switch: Field‑Induced Locus Pairing for reversible, locus‑specific chromatin looping and gene control

Central hypothesis
A uniform magnetic field can reversibly bias the proximity of two preselected genomic loci by inducing attractive dipole–dipole interactions between magnetizable “seeds” that are CRISPR‑tethered to those loci. This physical, non-chemical actuation will toggle enhancer–promoter contact probability and thereby switch transcription ON when the field is applied and OFF when it is removed.

Atomic strategy (single perturbation)
Use a single external magnetic field to modulate the material state and relative distance of two chromatin sites via induced magnetic dipoles on locus‑anchored seeds. No light‑activated protein dimerization or oligomerization is used; the sole control knob is the presence or absence (or strength) of the magnetic field.

Design overview
- Targeting: Catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) guided to two DNA elements (e.g., an enhancer and its cognate promoter). Each dCas9 carries an orthogonal recruitment handle (distinct peptide/epitope or RNA aptamer).
- Locus‑anchored MagSeeds: Biocompatible superparamagnetic nanoscale seeds bearing matching binders that attach to the handles at each locus. Seeds are designed to be monovalent with respect to cellular binders to avoid unintended crosslinking in the OFF state.
- Field actuation: A spatially uniform, low‑frequency magnetic field polarizes the seeds, generating short‑range, pairwise dipole–dipole attraction along the field lines. This biases the two tagged loci into proximity, stabilizing a chromatin loop that enhances (or blocks) transcription depending on genomic context.
- Reversibility: Removing the field eliminates the induced dipoles, allowing thermal and chromatin dynamics to dissipate the enforced contact and return expression toward baseline. Multiple ON↔OFF cycles are feasible without altering genome sequence.

Mechanistic novelty vs optogenetic dimerizers
- No light-responsive protein domains, photoswitchable heterodimers, or opto‑oligomerization modules are used.
- Looping is driven by field‑induced physical forces between artificial dipoles rather than protein–protein dimerization scaffolds.
- The actuator is a single, deep‑tissue‑penetrant magnetic field, avoiding phototoxicity, spectral crowding, and scatter limitations.
- The output emerges from biasing 3D genome mechanics (contact probability landscape) rather than building new biochemical tethers.

Target gene–cell system to demonstrate utility
- Primary human erythroid progenitors (CD34+‑derived) and K562 erythroleukemia cells targeting the β‑globin locus control region (LCR).
- Use case: ON switching of fetal γ‑globin (HBG1/2) by enforced looping between LCR HS2 and the HBG promoter to model a noninvasive, reversible approach to elevate fetal hemoglobin—a clinically meaningful axis for hemoglobinopathies. K562 provides tractable screening; primary erythroid cells demonstrate physiological relevance.

Specific aims
1) Build a CRISPR‑addressable, reversible MagSeed platform at selected loci.
   - Engineer two dCas9 constructs with orthogonal recruitment handles.
   - Validate locus‑specific MagSeed occupancy and absence of spurious bridging in the OFF state.

2) Demonstrate reversible loop control and transcriptional switching.
   - Target HS2 and HBG promoter with paired guides; apply magnetic field to induce looping (ON), remove to dissolve (OFF).
   - Readouts: live‑cell dual‑color locus tracking for co‑localization dynamics; 3C/Hi‑C derivative for contact enrichment; nascent RNA measurements for rapid transcriptional responses; steady‑state mRNA/protein to assess amplitude and kinetics.
   - Show multiple ON/OFF cycles without loss of dynamic range or genomic integrity.

3) Map system parameters and mechanism of action.
   - Titrate field strength/duty to establish a transfer function from physical input to contact probability and transcriptional output.
   - Perturb loop‑extrusion machinery (e.g., cohesin loader/blocker) to test whether MagSeed proximity synergizes with or bypasses extrusion.
   - Benchmark against a representative dCas9‑CRY2 loop‑inducing system for speed, reversibility, spatial cross‑talk, and cell health under actuation.

Key design choices and controls
- Monovalent seed display and orthogonal handles to minimize OFF‑state crosslinking.
- Genomic specificity controls: scrambled guides; single‑locus seeding; nonpolarizable control seeds.
- Polarity control: rotate the field to verify vectorial dependence of locus coalescence; confirm dissolution kinetics when the field is removed.
- Genomic context inversion: As a counterexample, target an enhancer to an insulating element (e.g., CTCF‑rich boundary) to show field‑induced OFF switching for a gene where insulation reduces expression.

Readouts and success criteria
- Rapid, reversible increase in enhancer–promoter colocalization probability under field, decaying upon field removal.
- Concordant, stimulus‑locked changes in nascent transcription with minimal latency.
- Cycle stability across multiple ON/OFF rounds with consistent amplitude.
- Minimal global chromatin disruption and negligible off‑target contact changes by genome‑wide contact mapping.

Why this will work
- Superparamagnetic seeds polarize only under the applied field, providing clean OFF states without persistent magnetization.
- The nucleus operates in a viscoelastic regime where modest, short‑range forces meaningfully bias contact probabilities without requiring large displacements.
- Enhancer–promoter transcriptional output scales with contact frequency; modest proximity bias can yield measurable ON/OFF expression differences.

Risk mitigation
- Insufficient force/valency: increase local seed valency via multiepitope recruitment at each locus while keeping seeds monovalent to cellular binders; select loci with favorable baseline mobility.
- Off‑target aggregation: restrict seed size/coating to prevent nonspecific interactions; implement degron‑based clearing of unbound seeds.
- Biological buffering: choose enhancers with strong quantitative influence (e.g., HS2) and assess multiple guide placements to optimize capture radius.

Milestones
- M1: Verified, orthogonal seeding at two chosen loci with no OFF‑state bridging.
- M2: Field‑dependent, reversible colocalization of targeted loci in K562.
- M3: Reversible ON switching of HBG transcription with defined input–output curve.
- M4: Replication in primary erythroid progenitors and benchmarking against optogenetic dimerizers.

Potential extensions
- Multiplexed control of several genes using frequency‑ or handle‑encoded seed populations.
- Therapeutic ex vivo application during cell manufacturing (e.g., transiently elevating fetal hemoglobin), leveraging the noninvasive, single‑stimulus actuation.

Deliverable
A CRISPR‑addressable, magnetic‑field‑actuated chromatin‑loop switch that is reversible, modular, and mechanistically distinct from optogenetic dimerizers, with proof‑of‑concept control of the β‑globin program in human erythroid cells.

text:
Title: LoopValve—A light-reversible CRISPR roadblock that captures and releases enhancer–promoter loops by gating cohesin extrusion in neurons

Hypothesis and goal
A single optical stimulus can reversibly gate endogenous loop extrusion to form or dissolve defined chromatin loops at preselected loci, enabling on/off control of neuronal gene expression without forced protein–protein tethering. The question is whether toggling extrusion “barriers” at two anchors is sufficient to switch an activity-regulated enhancer–promoter contact and its transcriptional output in intact neurons.

Atomic strategy
Instead of bridging DNA with optogenetic dimerizers, place light-gated, CRISPR-targeted extrusion barriers (pSEBs) that act as reversible “valves” for cohesin. When pSEBs are ON, loop extrusion stalls at the selected anchors, capturing a loop that juxtaposes enhancer and promoter; when pSEBs are OFF, barriers lift, cohesin translocates past the anchors, and the loop dissolves.

System overview (single stimulus: light)
- Targeting scaffold: dCas9 directed by sgRNAs to two genomic anchors flanking a distal enhancer and its promoter.
- Light-gated barrier: a photoswitchable extrusion barrier (pSEB) module that toggles its ability to block cohesin in response to light. Two alternative realizations are envisioned; either is sufficient and both avoid opto-dimerization:
  1) Photo-switchable anti-CRISPR gating (global switch): A light-responsive anti-CRISPR (Acr) that binds dCas9 and disables DNA binding in one light state and releases in the other, globally turning all pSEBs ON or OFF.
  2) Photo-responsive sgRNA (local switch): A reversibly photo-switchable sgRNA architecture whose conformation alternates between dCas9-competent and incompetent states with different wavelengths, modulating dCas9 occupancy at each anchor.
- Orientation logic: Guides are positioned so that when pSEBs are ON, extrusion is halted on the inward faces of both anchors, maximizing capture of the defined enhancer–promoter loop; OFF-state removes the barriers, allowing loop relaxation.
- Readout coupling: The loop state directly modulates target gene transcription via enforced or released enhancer proximity; no exogenous activators or repressors are required.

Clear differentiation from dimerizer-based chromatin looping
- No forced tethering: Does not use CRY2/CIBN, PhyB/PIF, or any hetero-/homo-dimerization to bridge loci.
- Mechanism-level novelty: Exploits endogenous cohesin loop extrusion by toggling extrusion barriers, rather than creating synthetic protein bridges or condensates.
- Single actuator, many targets: One light input simultaneously gates any number of CRISPR-programmed anchors, enabling multiplexed loop control without wiring distinct opto-dimer pairs.
- Reversible without reassembly: Looping/delooping follows barrier occupancy, not assembly/disassembly of multimeric scaffolds.

Biologically appropriate target cell type and locus
- Cell type: Post-mitotic excitatory neurons in mouse hippocampus (e.g., CA1 pyramidal neurons), where long-range enhancer–promoter contacts drive immediate-early gene (IEG) programs central to plasticity.
- Demonstration locus: An activity-regulated IEG such as Arc or Bdnf (e.g., Bdnf exon IV promoter with its distal enhancer). These loci undergo stimulus-coupled looping and exhibit robust transcriptional outputs, offering sensitive readouts for ON/OFF control.

Specific aims
1) Engineer and validate pSEB function at single anchors
- Aim: Show that light toggles dCas9 occupancy (via Acr or photo-sgRNA) and correspondingly gates cohesin passage at an anchor site, evidenced by altered local insulation and contact bias.
- Success criterion: Light-state–dependent changes in contact insulation and cohesin enrichment at the anchor; rapid reversibility across multiple cycles.

2) Program a light-gated enhancer–promoter loop
- Aim: Place inward-facing pSEBs at an enhancer and its promoter to create a LoopValve. Demonstrate light-dependent formation/dissolution of the specific contact and concordant changes in nascent transcription of the target gene.
- Success criterion: In the ON-state, increased enhancer–promoter contact frequency and elevated nascent RNA; in the OFF-state, return to baseline; both reversible over repeated toggles with minimal drift.

3) Establish neuronal utility and specificity
- Aim: In hippocampal neurons, test LoopValve control over activity-inducible transcription bursts without altering upstream signaling (e.g., calcium influx). Demonstrate locus specificity and minimal off-target topology disruption.
- Success criterion: Precise temporal gating of IEG bursts with light, preserved native activity signaling, and no broad chromatin compaction or global transcription perturbation.

Design principles and rationale
- Leverage endogenous motors: Cohesin already extrudes loops; providing reversible barriers requires less energy and fewer synthetic parts than building protein bridges.
- Modularity via CRISPR: sgRNA retargeting selects any enhancer–promoter pair without re-engineering the photoswitch.
- Bistability with a single knob: Light provides a universal “remote” to engage or release multiple loops synchronously or, with orthogonal photo-sgRNAs, in patterned subsets.
- Independence from native control: Looping is forced by barrier geometry, not by hijacking native transcription factors, providing a clean separation between remote control and endogenous signaling.

Key performance considerations
- Temporal resolution: Barrier occupancy switching is expected to follow photostate kinetics of the Acr or sgRNA conformer; transcriptional response follows enhancer contact (~minutes scale). Repeated ON/OFF cycles should maintain amplitude with minimal photofatigue.
- Spatial precision: Light enables subcellular targeting; patterned illumination can confine switching to selected neurons or nuclear regions if desired.
- Reversibility: Photostates are intrinsically reversible; removing light or toggling wavelength returns barriers to baseline without degradation or turnover.
- Safety and orthogonality: No exogenous dimerizers, no clustering domains, and minimal interference with non-targeted loci by restricting anchors to CTCF-depleted windows or enhancer–promoter–specific anchor points.

Validation readouts (conceptual)
- Topology: Changes in specific contact frequencies and insulation at anchors.
- Cohesin dynamics: State-dependent cohesin accumulation at barriers and release upon OFF.
- Transcription: Nascent RNA and reporter readouts from the targeted promoter; single-cell responsiveness and reversibility in neurons.
- Specificity: Genome-wide contact and expression profiling to ensure local, not global, remodeling.

Milestones and risk mitigation
- If single anchors show weak barrier effects, increase local barrier avidity by multiplexing closely spaced guides at each anchor (still no inter-molecular dimerization).
- If neuronal phototoxicity limits duty cycles, use red/far-red photopharmacology for the Acr/sgRNA switch to minimize energy load.
- If cohesin bypass occurs, refine anchor placement and orientation to maximize inward-facing stall probability without encroaching on essential regulatory elements.

Expected impact
LoopValve establishes a mechanistically fresh, reversible, and programmable way to write and erase specific chromatin loops in neurons with a single optical input, transforming enhancer–promoter topology into a true, noninvasive gene expression switch independent of the cell’s native controllers.

Title
SonoLoop-WORM: An ultrasound-programmable, reversible chromatin loop writer/eraser for stateful gene control at defined loci

Central hypothesis
A short, locus-targeted “SET” pulse of focused ultrasound can write a cohesin-acetylation state at selected genomic anchors that nucleates and self-maintains enhancer–promoter looping and gene activation after the stimulus ends; a distinct “RESET” pulse can erase this state to dissolve loops and silence the gene. This stateful, ultrasound-only control will reveal whether cardiac stress-response loops are self-sustaining through biochemical memory or require ongoing signaling.

Atomic strategy
Control the biochemical lifetime of loop-stabilizing cohesin directly—by acoustically toggling SMC3 acetylation and cohesin loading/unloading at pre-specified CRISPR-dCas9–addressed anchors—rather than forcing physical proximity via stimulus-dependent dimerization.

System overview
- External modality: Focused ultrasound (FUS) as the single stimulus.
- Addressing: CRISPR/dCas9 with guide RNAs to two anchors (enhancer and promoter or boundary) flanking the target gene.
- Acoustic actuation: Two populations of size-tuned perfluorocarbon nanodroplets (NDs) that release orthogonal, cell-permeant ligands at distinct acoustic thresholds/pulse codes:
  - U-SET ligand: covalently binds a “DockA” tag on dCas9 at both anchors to recruit a NIPBL–ESCO1 writer complex and a CTCF stabilization module.
  - U-RESET ligand: covalently binds a distinct “DockB” tag on the same anchors to recruit an HDAC8–WAPL eraser/unloader module.
- Memory substrate: SMC3 acetylation on cohesin (promotes cohesin residency and loop stability) and context-appropriate histone marks at the enhancer (e.g., H3K27ac for activation or H3K27me3 for repression, selectable by effector choice).
- Readout: Loop topologies (Capture-C/HiChIP), cohesin/SMC3ac occupancy (CUT&RUN), and gene expression (RNA-seq).

What is novel vs existing optogenetic dimerizers
- State writing, not stimulus-bound proximity: Instead of light-triggered dimerization (CRY2/CIBN, PhyB/PIF) that requires continued stimulus or reverses within minutes, SonoLoop-WORM writes a biochemical state (SMC3ac and associated factors) that persists after ultrasound ceases, enabling “write once, read many” operation until explicitly reset.
- Mechanism targets endogenous loop maintenance: Direct regulation of cohesin loading/acetylation/unloading at specific anchors, rather than synthetic scaffolding of two sites.
- Modality and depth: Ultrasound affords millimeter-to-centimeter penetration and spatial selectivity without phototoxicity or chromophore constraints; control is encoded in acoustic pulse parameters addressing ND subtypes, not in multispectral light or exogenous chemicals administered systemically.
- Bistable programmability: Two ultrasound pulse codes (SET vs RESET) select between orthogonal, covalent ligand–dock interactions to establish or erase loops with hysteresis.

Biologically appropriate target cell type and locus
- Cell type: Human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) and engineered cardiac microtissues. Rationale: Cardiomyocytes exhibit long-lived “stress memory” in gene regulation; ultrasound penetrates cardiac tissues; and the model directly addresses how pathological gene programs persist in heart failure.
- Demonstration locus: The NPPA/NPPB locus (atrial/ventricular stress-response hormones) with well-characterized stimulus-coupled enhancer–promoter interactions. Secondary loci: MYH6/MYH7 switch and ANKRD1 stress enhancers to generalize across activation and repression contexts.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Build an ultrasound-gated, locus-anchored cohesin writer/eraser
- Engineer two dCas9 fusions per anchor: dCas9-DockA and dCas9-DockB. DockA binds U-SET to recruit a NIPBL–ESCO1 complex and a CTCF stabilization module; DockB binds U-RESET to recruit HDAC8 and WAPL.
- Formulate two ND populations carrying U-SET and U-RESET ligands with distinguishable release thresholds/pulse codes, enabling orthogonal acoustic addressing with a single stimulus modality.
- Validate that brief SET pulses increase SMC3ac and cohesin residence at targeted anchors; RESET pulses decrease SMC3ac and increase unloading, without global chromatin disruption.

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible chromatin loop control and gene ON/OFF switching in hiPSC-CMs
- Target guides to the NPPA distal enhancer and promoter. After a transient SET pulse, assay for enhancer–promoter loop formation, BRD4/H3K27ac enrichment, and NPPA transcriptional upregulation. After a RESET pulse, test loop dissolution and transcriptional downregulation.
- Quantify spatial precision (off-target loops), temporal dynamics (minutes-to-days), and dose–response with varying pulse codes.
- Compare to controls: non-targeting guides, writer-only or eraser-only recruitment, and an optogenetic dimerizer benchmark; evaluate persistence after stimulus withdrawal.

Aim 3. Test “memory” and hysteresis in cardiac stress programs
- In 3D cardiac microtissues exposed to transient catecholamine or stretch stress, use SET to write loops at NPPA/NPPB and measure whether loops/genetic activation persist absent ongoing stress.
- Use RESET to determine if erasure of SMC3ac/cohesin is sufficient to extinguish pathological gene expression and loops, probing whether loop memory is autonomous or needs reinforcing transcriptional feedback.

Key design choices enabling reversibility and specificity
- Orthogonal covalent docking: U-SET and U-RESET form selective covalent bonds with DockA and DockB, limiting crosstalk and allowing durable recruitment that outlives ligand clearance, yet remains erasable by recruiting endogenous erasers/unloaders.
- Endogenous process leverage: Cohesin acetylation (ESCO1) and deacetylation (HDAC8) directly tune loop lifetime; WAPL provides an unloading lever to actively dissolve loops during RESET.
- Single-modality control: Both SET and RESET are ultrasound-triggered releases; orthogonality arises from ND physical properties and pulse coding, not additional external inputs.

Success criteria
- SET increases local SMC3ac and cohesin occupancy at anchors and creates a new enhancer–promoter loop detectable by Capture-C/HiChIP, with ≥10-fold higher frequency than controls; associated gene expression rises concordantly.
- The induced loop and expression persist hours–days after SET without further stimulation, demonstrating “write–read” behavior.
- RESET reduces SMC3ac and cohesin occupancy and abolishes the loop and expression to baseline, demonstrating reversibility.
- Minimal off-target loop formation and no global cohesin perturbation outside targeted sites.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Insufficient persistence: If loops decay rapidly, augment memory by co-recruiting a modest H3K27ac writer (e.g., p300 core) only during SET to reinforce enhancer activity without hardwiring dependence on the effector.
- Off-target cohesin effects: Constrain recruitment stoichiometry via low-copy Dock tags and use guide tiling to identify minimal anchor sets.
- Acoustic crosstalk between ND populations: Increase release orthogonality by tuning ND core composition and shell stiffness; encode SET vs RESET in both frequency and duty-cycle domains.

Expected outcome and impact
SonoLoop-WORM will establish a stateful, ultrasound-programmable chromatin loop switch at specified loci in cardiomyocytes. By writing and erasing cohesin acetylation at defined anchors, the system will disentangle whether cardiac stress-response loops self-maintain through biochemical memory or require ongoing cues. The mechanistic focus on cohesin’s lifetime at anchors—rather than light-driven proximity—provides a fresh, reversible path to test and therapeutically steer durable gene programs deep in tissues.

text:
Title
US-RESET: An ultrasound-gated, locus-specific “melt-and-rebuild” chromatin loop switch for reversible control of gene expression

Central question
Does transiently melting locus-restricted chromatin interactions with ultrasound, then allowing endogenous rebuilding, produce superior cell-fate fidelity and memory compared with systems that forcibly impose loop geometry?

Atomic strategy (single insight)
Exploit a thermosensitive, multivalent protein scaffold that nucleates bridging-induced attraction between two CRISPR-targeted genomic anchors at baseline temperature, but acousto-thermally melts under brief, mild focused ultrasound. When ultrasound stops, the scaffold re-condenses and loops reform autonomously. The external modality is only ultrasound.

Mechanistic novelty and differentiation from optogenetic dimerizers
- Stimulus physics: mechanical/acousto-thermal vs. photon-driven. No light, chromophore, or photoswitch.
- Actuation logic: ultrasound transiently lowers local interaction strength (“reset”) rather than externally gluing two loci together (“force”). Loop re-formation leverages endogenous dynamics and self-assembly.
- Bidirectional reversibility without complex timing optics: ON at rest, OFF under ultrasound; invertible by tuning scaffold transition temperature.
- Deep-tissue applicability: ultrasound focuses noninvasively in vivo; avoids scattering/phototoxicity constraints of light-based dimerizers.

System design (modular, CRISPR-compatible)
- Targeting module: dCas9 with sgRNAs tiling two predefined genomic anchor windows (e.g., promoter-proximal and distal enhancer) of a chosen gene. A SunTag or equivalent multivalent recruiter amplifies local scaffold density.
- Acousto-thermolabile scaffold (“SonoMELT”): paired, heterotypic coiled-coil/low-complexity domains engineered with a transition near physiological temperature (UCST-like behavior). At baseline, the scaffold hetero-oligomerizes across anchors to increase contact probability (loop “formed” state). A brief ultrasound exposure raises temperature by a few degrees within the focal volume, dissolving scaffold interactions (loop “melted” state). Cooling restores the formed state.
- Optional acoustic concentrator (safety/efficiency knob): an intranuclear, genetically encoded acoustically responsive nanoassembly (e.g., a compact, nucleus-targeted protein assembly that enhances local acousto-thermal conversion) co-recruited via peptide–peptide affinity. This remains under the same single external stimulus (ultrasound) and is only used if actuation thresholds require margin.
- Readout module (for assays only): CRISPR-based live-locus tagging and reporter transcription unit positioned within the looped domain for rapid expression readout. This does not alter the stimulus.

Biological use case and target cell type
Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) undergoing directed differentiation to cardiomyocytes. Rationale: cardiac lineage commitment depends on enhancer–promoter loops at key loci (e.g., cardiac TFs/structural genes). Comparing “reset-and-rebuild” vs. “force-and-hold” at the same loci allows testing whether transient melting improves epigenetic reprogramming fidelity and long-term identity.

Proposed target loci (illustrative)
- Loop pairs flanking super-enhancer contacts to a cardiogenic transcription factor (e.g., GATA4/MEF2C/TBX5 neighborhood) or a structural gene under developmental control. Locus selection guided by prior accessibility and CTCF motif orientation maps; final choice based on robust differentiation sensitivity.

Research plan and milestones
Aim 1. Engineer and validate the SonoMELT loop switch at a safe-harbor reporter locus.
- Construct: dCas9–SunTag recruiting two complementary, thermosensitive multivalent partners targeted to flanking sites of a reporter gene.
- Validation endpoints: reversible changes in 3D proximity (live CRISPR-locus imaging/Capture-C), synchronized transcription toggling (nascent RNA reporter), and kinetics/retention (on/off half-times, fatigue across many cycles). Criteria: ≥5–10× change in contact frequency and ≥3× change in reporter output with full recovery after ≥50 ultrasound cycles; minimal global transcriptome perturbation.

Aim 2. Deploy US-RESET at endogenous cardiogenic loci in hiPSCs and benchmark against optogenetic forcing.
- Conditions: identical genomic targets across three arms—(i) US-RESET (reset-and-rebuild), (ii) optogenetic dimerizer forcing (canonical dCas9-CRY2/CIBN or PhyB/PIF implementation), (iii) neutral dCas9 controls.
- Protocol logic: apply US pulses at defined stages of differentiation to transiently melt loops, then allow reassembly; in forcing arm, impose sustained loop formation during the same windows.
- Readouts: gene expression trajectories (time-resolved RNA-seq), chromatin accessibility and histone marks (ATAC-seq, ChIP-profile panels), 3D genome architecture (Capture-C/Hi-C at target neighborhoods), and cardiomyocyte maturation metrics (electrophysiology/contractility phenotypes).
- Primary outcomes: (a) efficiency and synchrony of lineage gene activation, (b) fidelity of terminal cardiomyocyte identity, (c) persistence (“memory”) of correct chromatin state after stimulus removal. Success if US-RESET yields higher maturation fidelity and stable chromatin marks with less ectopic looping than forcing.

Aim 3. Mechanistic dissection of rebuild dynamics and endogenous factor engagement.
- Test whether rebuild recruits cohesin/CTCF in native orientation and restores TAD integrity faster/more faithfully than forced contacts.
- Quantify damage/stress safeguards: heat-shock response markers, DNA damage indices, and nuclear mechanics. Optimize scaffold transition window to minimize collateral effects while retaining robust toggling.

Key controls
- Non-thermosensitive scaffold variant (constitutively bridged) to isolate ultrasound-specific effects.
- Scrambled sgRNAs and single-anchor targeting to separate bridging from mere local compaction.
- Temperature-matched, ultrasound-free controls (global mild warming) to distinguish mechanical vs. thermal contributions of ultrasound focusing.

Risk mitigation and alternatives
- If thermal thresholds prove too close to stress responses, shift the scaffold transition slightly below global stress activation and employ the optional acoustic concentrator to reduce required field intensity.
- If bridging overcompacts chromatin, lower valency (SunTag repeat reduction) or shorten dwell-time via degron-tagged scaffold with slow turnover to preserve epigenomic health.
- If rebuild is sluggish, append cohesin loader/recycling motifs to the scaffold to bias native loop restoration without externally forcing geometry.

Why this matters
- Conceptual advance: replaces externally imposed topology with a reversible, self-healing, acoustically gated reset that respects endogenous genome physics.
- Practical advance: a single, clinically compatible stimulus provides deep, multiplexable, and noninvasive locus control.
- Biological insight: directly tests whether transiently erasing local 3D memory enables cleaner fate transitions than coercively pinning new structures.

Deliverables and success criteria
- A validated, ultrasound-only, CRISPR-targetable loop switch with reversible on/off gene control at user-defined loci.
- Benchmarked evidence that reset-and-rebuild improves differentiation fidelity and long-term identity compared with optogenetic forcing.
- An open, modular toolkit (targeting guides, scaffold designs, response models) enabling broader adoption for developmental reprogramming and therapeutic genome topology control.

text:
Title: LiNEL: Light-inducible Nuclear Eviction of Loop-locks for reversible control of endogenous chromatin loops and gene expression

Core idea (atomic strategy):
Replace “build-a-loop” actuation with “release-the-lock” actuation. Pre-position a multivalent, chromatin-compacting LoopLock at chosen loci to stabilize naturally repressive loops (OFF). A single light input transiently evacuates the LoopLock from the nucleus, allowing endogenous polymer dynamics and loop extrusion to relax the loop (ON). Removing light restores nuclear LoopLock, re-clamping the loop (OFF). This is subtractive control (photo-eviction) rather than additive assembly and is mechanistically distinct from optogenetic dimerizer systems.

Hypothesis:
Locus-restricted nuclear eviction of a multivalent chromatin-compacting factor is sufficient to reversibly dissolve pre-existing repressive enhancer–promoter loops and activate transcription of silenced metabolic genes in hepatocytes. Re-accumulation of the factor reinstates local compaction and restores repression.

System overview:
- Targeting scaffold: dCas9-SunTag(10x) (constitutive, light-insensitive) bound to paired CRISPR guides flanking endogenous loop anchors (e.g., promoter-proximal CTCF sites and distal silencers).
- LoopLock effector (light-responsive): scFv(GCN4)-HP1αCSDx2-IDR-LEXY-NLS
  - HP1α chromoshadow domain (CSD) tandem + short low-complexity IDR: multivalent bridging/compaction without relying on H3K9me3 reader function, minimizing epigenetic spreading.
  - LEXY: blue-light–exposed NES for rapid nuclear export; in darkness the NES is masked and NLS-driven nuclear accumulation predominates.
  - scFv(GCN4): constitutive, moderate-affinity recruitment to SunTag to ensure fast off-rates compatible with photo-eviction.
- Single stimulus: Pulsed blue light (∼450–480 nm) toggles nuclear residence of the LoopLock; no light-gated dimerization or oligomerization is used.
- Readouts: rapid loop relaxation (minutes) and gene activation (tens of minutes to hours) on light; reversal in darkness.

Why hepatocytes (biological fit):
Adult human hepatocytes maintain numerous developmentally silenced or diet-state–repressed metabolic loci via insulated neighborhoods and repressive loops. Releasing pre-existing restraints should unmask endogenous enhancer potential without needing to build synthetic bridges. The liver’s rapid transcriptional plasticity and well-annotated chromatin architecture enable clear mechanistic attribution.

Primary demonstration loci (examples):
- Oncofetal/metabolic genes normally silent in adult liver: AFP, CYP3A7.
- Diet/circadian-repressed modules with poised enhancers: select cytochrome P450 cluster elements or lipogenic nodes (e.g., SREBF1 neighborhood) where repressive looping has been mapped.
Multiple loci enable generalization and specificity tests.

Experimental plan:

Aim 1. Build and validate the subtractive “LoopLock” switch
- Construct dCas9-SunTag(10x) and scFv-HP1αCSDx2-IDR-LEXY-NLS (LiNEL effector).
- Design paired gRNAs to bracket endogenous loop anchors at chosen loci (one set at promoter-proximal CTCF site, one at distal repressor/silencer or boundary).
- Quantify dark-state repression:
  - Reporter-free: nascent RNA (PRO-seq), RT-qPCR, and Pol II ChIP for target genes vs. matched control loci.
  - Architecture: Capture-C/HiChIP to verify strengthened anchor–anchor contacts and reduced promoter–enhancer engagement in dark.
  - Accessibility: ATAC-seq for local compaction signature.

Milestones/success criteria:
- Dark-state: enhanced anchor–anchor contact frequency and reduced transcription vs. non-targeting gRNA control without broad heterochromatin spreading (H3K9me3 ChIP confined to ≤5–10 kb of targeted anchors).
- Light-state (photo-eviction): ≥50% reduction in target loop contact within 5–15 min of blue light; ≥2–5x induction of nascent transcription within 30–120 min.

Aim 2. Kinetics and reversibility of loop dissolution and re-clamping
- Apply brief blue-light pulses (e.g., 30–120 s every 3–5 min for 15–30 min), then dark recovery.
- Live tracking of anchor distances with CRISPR-Sirius or dCas9-MS2 fluorescent tags to measure polymer relaxation and re-compaction.
- Time-resolved HiChIP/Capture-C and single-molecule RNA FISH to map architecture–transcription coupling.
- Repeat light/dark cycles to test fatigue and hysteresis.

Milestones/success criteria:
- Bidirectional switching across ≥5 light/dark cycles with minimal drift (<15% change in amplitude).
- Half-times: loop relaxation t1/2 ≤5 min; re-locking t1/2 ≤10–20 min in dark.
- Transcription matches architecture with expected lag (10–30 min).

Aim 3. Locus specificity and genome-wide innocuity
- Off-target profiling: RNA-seq and Hi-C with and without targeting gRNAs to confirm locus-restricted effects.
- Titrate SunTag valency and scFv affinity to balance occupancy (dark) and rapid washout (light).
- Negative controls: LEXY-dead mutant; HP1αCSD mutant lacking oligomerization; dCas9-SunTag without effector.

Milestones/success criteria:
- Differential expression largely confined to targeted loci (FDR <0.05; |log2FC| >1 primarily at targets).
- Hi-C changes enriched within targeted TADs; no global heterochromatinization.

Aim 4. Functional phenotypes in hepatocytes
- Use primary human hepatocytes or iPSC-derived hepatocyte-like cells; benchmark with HepG2 for screening.
- Assess metabolic outputs: e.g., bile acid intermediates or xenobiotic metabolism changes when activating CYP3A7/cluster elements, or AFP re-expression as a binary switch readout.
- Test environmental context (fasting-mimetic vs. fed-mimetic media) to show that releasing the lock unmasks pre-existing enhancer competence.

Milestones/success criteria:
- Light-triggered phenotypic changes concordant with target gene activation; reversal in darkness.

Mechanistic novelty versus existing optogenetic looping systems:
- Subtractive control: We do not assemble loops with opto-dimerizers (e.g., CRY2/CIBN, PhyB/PIF). LiNEL pre-installs a compaction Lock and uses light solely to change nuclear localization (eviction), letting endogenous forces dissolve loops.
- No light-gated hetero-dimerization at DNA: Recruitment is constant (SunTag–scFv), light only toggles nuclear residence of the effector.
- Uses endogenous loop relaxation/extrusion rather than synthetic bridging to create contacts.
- Reads out the natural “spring” of chromatin by removing restraints, aligning perturbation with physics of polymer decompaction.

Key design safeguards and failure-mode mitigations:
- Eviction efficiency: Use moderate-affinity scFv–SunTag and fast-exchange IDR design; add PEST tag to increase nuclear free-pool turnover so export drains occupancy.
- Over-compaction risk: Limit SunTag valency (6–10x), use HP1αCSD-only plus tuned IDR to avoid spreading; insulator-adjacent targeting to confine effects.
- Phototoxicity: Low-duty-cycle blue pulses; red-shifted LEXY variants or two-photon illumination as needed.
- Incomplete reversibility: Add strong NLS and nuclear retention motif for dark-state recovery; calibrate light dose–response.

Compatibility and extensibility:
- CRISPR guide programmability allows rapid retargeting to any locus.
- Alternative loop-lock chemistries are plug-and-play: cohesin-retention motifs, condensin II fragments, or designed multimeric scaffolds in place of HP1αCSD to test distinct compaction mechanisms.
- Same subtractive logic can be ported to ultrasound or magnetogenetic nuclear export modules if developed, preserving the core eviction concept.

Validation metrics (go/no-go):
- Architecture: ≥50% reversible change in target anchor–anchor contact by Capture-C/HiChIP.
- Expression: ≥2–5x reversible change in nascent RNA; minimal off-target transcriptome impact.
- Kinetics: minute-scale loop and hour-scale expression switching with stable multi-cycle performance.

Deliverables:
- A generalizable, single-input, reversible ON/OFF chromatin switch that activates endogenous genes by releasing locus-tethered restraints.
- Mechanistic maps linking restraint removal to polymer relaxation and transcription.
- A hepatocyte use-case demonstrating control over clinically relevant metabolic programs without synthetic loop assembly.

Outcome:
LiNEL establishes a new control axis—photo-eviction of loop locks—that complements and clearly diverges from dimerizer-based chromatin engineering. It probes how “letting go” of locus-specific restraints licenses endogenous architecture and transcription, delivering a compact, reversible, CRISPR-retargetable gene switch in liver cells.

text:
Title: MaGISTER — A magneto-mechanical, CRISPR-targeted switch to reversibly break and remake specific chromatin loops to control gene expression

Core hypothesis and question
- Hypothesis-question: For developmentally regulated genes in cortical progenitors, is the rate-limiting step in transcriptional state-switching the mechanical destruction of pre-existing CTCF–cohesin loops rather than their construction?
- Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight): Apply picoNewton-scale, locus-specific mechanical tension via magnetically actuated, CRISPR-tethered nanoparticles at loop anchors to force-release cohesin and open loops on demand; on stimulus withdrawal, allow endogenous loop extrusion to passively reclose the loop. One stimulus modality controls both states.

Modality and differentiator
- Single external stimulus: Magnetic field only.
- Mechanistic novelty vs optogenetic dimerizers (dCas9-CRY2/CIBN, PhyB/PIF):
  - Mechanism: Force-gating of the physical loop (mechano-epigenetics), not light-driven recruitment or protein dimerization.
  - Actuation target: CTCF–cohesin anchor stability and chromatin mechanics, not effector occupancy.
  - Directionality: “Field ON” dissolves the loop; “Field OFF” permits intrinsic extrusion to reform it—bidirectional, reversible, and independent of photoswitch cycles or chromophore availability.
  - State variable: Tension at anchors, not proximity of synthetic dimers.

Use case and target cell type
- Cell type: Human iPSC-derived dorsal forebrain neural progenitor cells (radial glia–like NPCs), where enhancer–promoter loops gate maintenance vs differentiation.
- Primary locus: SOX2 super-enhancer ↔ promoter loop (robust, developmentally salient). Secondary loci for generalization: FEZF2 and BDNF.

System architecture
1) CRISPR locus targeting
- Guide RNAs direct dCas9 to two predetermined CTCF/cohesin-enriched anchors flanking a chosen enhancer–promoter pair (e.g., SOX2).
- To ensure a stable “loop-on” baseline, anchors are pre-validated for strong CTCF occupancy (either native or mildly strengthened via sequence tuning during cell line engineering).

2) Magneto-mechanical actuator (single modality)
- At each anchor, dCas9 carries a high-affinity tag that binds biocompatible, superparamagnetic nanoparticles (SPMNs) designed for nuclear access.
- Under a weak, oscillatory or rotating magnetic field, SPMNs undergo coordinated micro-rotations/torques that transmit picoNewton forces through dCas9 to local chromatin, destabilizing CTCF–cohesin interactions and opening the loop.
- Field withdrawal removes torque, allowing cohesin-driven loop extrusion and CTCF rebinding to re-establish the loop. A low-gradient static field (same modality) can be optionally applied to bias re-encounter and accelerate refolding.

3) Optical independence and compatibility
- No light-gated dimerization; no phototoxicity; compatible with standard fluorescent imaging.
- Fully CRISPR-addressable: multiplexable gRNA sets enable simultaneous, orthogonal control of different loops.

Readouts and decision metrics
- Loop state: Capture change in contact probability at the targeted anchors by locus-focused 3C derivative (e.g., targeted HiChIP) and live CRISPR imaging of the two loci with orthogonal fluorescent tags.
- Transcriptional kinetics: Quantify nascent RNA at the promoter using an integrated reporter (e.g., MS2/PP7 cassette) or intronic smFISH to extract on/off dwell times.
- Chromatin mechanics: Monitor local chromatin mobility and compaction by single-locus MSD analyses before/during/after field application.

Experimental aims

Aim 1 — Build and validate MaGISTER at SOX2 in cortical NPCs
- Establish robust “loop-on” baseline and confirm CRISPR addressability of both anchors.
- Demonstrate magnetic-field–dependent, rapid loop dissolution with full reversibility across many cycles.
- Define the minimal actuation regime that toggles loop state without detectable DNA damage or global transcriptional stress.

Aim 2 — Measure gene switch kinetics: breaking (OFF) vs remaking (ON)
- OFF kinetics: Apply field to dissolve the loop and measure time-to-silencing (nascent transcript decay and promoter bursting suppression).
- ON kinetics: Withdraw field and measure time-to-reactivation as loops passively reform; optionally apply a gentle static gradient (same modality) to test whether mechanical bias speeds re-encounter.
- Fit a two-state kinetic model to extract transition rates; compare OFF vs ON rate constants to identify the dominant bottleneck.

Aim 3 — Specificity, generality, and causal controls
- Specificity: Scrambled gRNAs; nonmagnetic nanoparticles; off-target loci controls; cohesin/CTCF perturbation epistasis (genetic or small-molecule) to confirm that observed effects require loop mechanics.
- Generalization: Repeat at FEZF2 and BDNF to test locus-to-locus variability and developmental-context dependence.
- Multiplexing: Independent actuation of two loops with spectrally distinct nanoparticle coatings recognized by orthogonal tags yet controlled by the same field.

Predicted outcomes and interpretation
- If OFF (breakage) is the bottleneck for developmental silencing, MaGISTER will show:
  - Rapid loop opening and faster decline in nascent transcription upon field ON.
  - Slower recovery of transcription upon field OFF due to rate limits in cohesin loading/extrusion or re-acquisition of insulated neighborhoods.
- Alternatively, if ON (formation) is the bottleneck, recovery will lag substantially behind OFF decay, even when re-encounter is mechanically biased by a static field.

Risk and mitigation (within single-modality constraint)
- Insufficient force transmission at single anchors: Increase local actuator valency by recruiting several SPMNs per anchor via multitag clustering; distribute tags along a short chromatin segment flanking the anchor to amplify torque without altering modality.
- Incomplete reversibility: Reduce duty cycle or adopt brief burst actuation to avoid anchor remodeling; verify that loop re-formation kinetics stabilize across multiple cycles.
- Off-target mechanical effects: Limit actuation to brief, low-amplitude windows and include nuclear mechanics reporters to ensure local, not global, perturbation.

Why this is the right biological context
- Cortical NPCs rely on insulated enhancer–promoter communication to maintain progenitor identity; SOX2 and FEZF2 represent decisive developmental switches. A force-gated, locus-specific breaker/remaker directly probes the physical determinism of these loops in controlling transcriptional transitions relevant to neurodevelopment.

Deliverables
- A magneto-mechanical, CRISPR-addressable switch (MaGISTER) that toggles specific chromatin loops and gene output with a single external stimulus.
- Quantitative kinetics comparing loop destruction (OFF) vs passive loop re-formation (ON) at neurodevelopmental loci.
- A generalizable framework for dissecting how mechanical integrity of chromatin loops, not merely factor recruitment, sets the tempo of gene-state transitions.

Title
SonoLoop: An ultrasound-gated CRISPR roadblock that harnesses cohesin to reversibly form or dissolve chromatin loops at chosen loci

Atomic strategy (single conceptual insight)
Rather than forcing DNA together with synthetic bridges, place a tunable “roadblock” at precise genomic coordinates so cohesin’s native loop-extrusion halts or proceeds on command. Make the roadblock’s steric bulk reversible with a single external input—low-intensity focused ultrasound (US)—by fusing dCas9 to a thermoresponsive elastin-like polypeptide (ELP). Ultrasound transiently raises local temperature to trigger an ELP coil–globule transition, switching the roadblock between weak (permissive, loops dissolve) and strong (insulating, loops form) states without dimerizers or exogenous bridging.

Hypothesis and research goal
A US-tuned, CRISPR-targeted ELP roadblock positioned at CTCF-adjacent sequences will reversibly control where cohesin stops, thereby toggling formation of specific enhancer–promoter loops and switching gene expression on/off. Because this acts upstream of transcription by restoring or relaxing native insulation, it will more faithfully rescue pathogenic 3D genome defects than synthetic loop-tethering systems.

System design
- Effector: dCas9–ELP “Sono-Barrier,” nuclear-localized. The ELP is composition-tuned so mild, reversible US-induced hyperthermia toggles its phase state and hydrodynamic radius.
- Targeting: sgRNAs tile 1–3 sites immediately adjacent to endogenous CTCF motifs (or engineered convergent motifs) that define loop anchors around the gene of interest. Orientation is chosen to favor convergent extrusion when the barrier is strong.
- Single stimulus: Pulsed ultrasound is the only external input. When US is ON, ELP collapses and self-associates, amplifying steric hindrance at the bound site to create a high-occupancy boundary that stalls cohesin and forms the intended loop. When US is OFF, ELP re-expands and becomes permissive; cohesin reads through to distal boundaries, dissolving that loop.
- Readouts: Live-cell locus imaging (dCas9–MS2/MCP tagging), targeted 3C/Hi-C, Micro-C, DNA/RNA FISH, and RNA-seq to quantify loop state and transcriptional switching.

Target cell type and locus
- Primary demonstration: Human iPSC-derived cortical neurons modeling MEF2C TAD-boundary disruption (a neurodevelopmental disorder with well-documented enhancer miswiring). Install Sono-Barrier at newly chosen convergent CTCF-adjacent sites that re-insulate MEF2C from ectopic enhancers when US is ON, normalizing MEF2C and neighboring gene expression; switch OFF dissolves the rescue for reversible validation.
- Secondary demonstration (generalizability): HUDEP2 erythroid progenitors at the β-globin locus to toggle LCR–HBB contacts bidirectionally, illustrating precision control in a lineage with strong enhancer–promoter dependency.

Why this is mechanistically novel and distinct from optogenetic dimerizers
- No synthetic bridging: Unlike dCas9–CIBN/CRY2 or PhyB/PIF, SonoLoop does not tether distal sites. It modulates the physical stop-signal for cohesin, letting the endogenous machine build or relax loops.
- Single tunable obstacle, not heterodimer assembly: A monovalent, sequence-addressable obstacle whose steric profile alone is US-gated; no multicomponent light-activated complexes.
- Stimulus orthogonality: Ultrasound, not light. Deeply penetrant, non-phototoxic, and compatible with 3D tissues.
- Reversibility without epigenetic memory: Switching relies on ELP conformational state, avoiding persistent chromatin marks that slow reversibility.

Specific aims

Aim 1. Engineer and calibrate the ultrasound-gated roadblock
- Construct dCas9–ELP fusions with tunable transition temperatures near physiological range; select variants showing large, rapid, reversible hydrodynamic changes in the nucleus.
- In reporter cell lines harboring barcoded sgRNA landing pads, quantify US-dependent occupancy and steric effects using single-molecule tracking of cohesin (e.g., RAD21-Halo) and polymer simulations constrained by imaging.

Success criteria: Reversible change in cohesin pause time and extrusion stall probability at Sono-Barrier sites with minimal global chromatin perturbation.

Aim 2. Rebuild and switch disease-relevant insulation in neurons
- Introduce Sono-Barrier and sgRNAs into hiPSC-derived cortical neurons carrying MEF2C boundary loss (patient-derived or engineered).
- Place barriers at designed convergent positions flanking MEF2C to reconstitute a TAD-like boundary when US is ON.
- Measure: (i) restoration of insulation (Micro-C/Hi-C insulation score, contact decay), (ii) guided enhancer routing (Capture-C from MEF2C promoter), (iii) reversible normalization of MEF2C and miswired neighbors (smFISH, RNA-seq), and (iv) functional neuronal outputs (activity assays) to link 3D rescue to phenotype.

Success criteria: US-ON increases local boundary strength and corrects enhancer targeting with concordant gene expression rescue; US-OFF returns to the miswired state within one to two cohesin residence times, demonstrating on/off control.

Aim 3. Kinetics, specificity, and safety envelope
- Kinetics: Determine switching latencies and hysteresis across multiple US duty cycles; correlate with cohesin turnover and transcriptional bursting dynamics.
- Specificity: Map off-target binding and off-target loop changes (Hi-C at moderate depth); implement gRNA narrowing and PAM selection to confine effects.
- Safety: Establish thermal and mechanical operating windows that avoid heat-shock responses or membrane perturbation; verify that repeated cycles maintain neuronal health and chromatin integrity.

Controls and comparators
- ELP-null dCas9 and ELP with shifted transition temperature as negative controls.
- sgRNAs targeting non-CTCF regions to show dependence on boundary context.
- “Classical” light-driven dimerizer loopers (run in parallel, not integrated) to demonstrate that SonoLoop achieves comparable loop control without synthetic bridges and with improved reversibility and locus specificity.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Slow dCas9 off-rate could limit reversibility if occupancy change were required. Mitigation: The barrier toggles steric magnitude while remaining DNA-bound, so switching does not rely on unbinding.
- Potential stress responses to US-induced heating. Mitigation: Use brief pulses within mild hyperthermia range; monitor stress transcripts; employ ELP variants with sharp transitions to minimize exposure.
- Incomplete insulation: If single-site barriers are insufficient, deploy 2–3 closely spaced sgRNAs to create a distributed obstacle without multimeric tethers.

Expected outcomes and impact
- A reversible, single-input gene control switch that edits 3D genome traffic rules rather than forcing contacts, providing cleaner causal tests of loop extrusion in living human neurons.
- A therapeutic conceptual advance: temporary restoration of boundary function to correct enhancer miswiring in cohesinopathy-like states, with spatiotemporal precision and no need for permanent genome edits or light delivery.

Compatibility and modularity
- Fully CRISPR-addressable: swap sgRNAs to retarget any locus with characterized boundary logic.
- Modality upgrades: the same framework can adopt alternative US-responsive polymers or mechanosensitive domains as they emerge, retaining the single-stimulus, roadblock-centered design.

Title
LUMINEL: a light-gated, locus-tethered microcondensate switch that rewires enhancer–promoter looping to control gene expression

Central hypothesis
A single-component, CRISPR-tethered scaffold whose light exposure increases local “valency” for weak, multivalent interactions will nucleate a reversible transcriptional microcondensate at a chosen genomic address. This condensate will recruit endogenous coactivators/RNAPII and wet nearby acetylated chromatin, shortening effective genomic distance and capturing cognate promoters into transient loops that switch transcription on; darkness dissolves the condensate and releases loops, switching transcription off.

Atomic strategy
Instead of mechanically tethering two DNA sites, modulate the local nuclear “solvent quality” at one site with a light-gated, multivalent sticker–spacer scaffold. Turning on light increases sticker exposure and mesh connectivity above a percolation threshold, converting the site into a selective coactivator-rich droplet that exerts capillary attraction on compatible regulatory DNA and factors.

System design
- Stimulus: blue light (single modality), reversible on/off with intensity-tunable thresholds.
- Targeting: nuclease-dead CRISPR (dCas12a) to enable compact, multiplexed gRNA arrays that tile a chosen enhancer (and optionally promoter).
- Opto-phase scaffold (LUMINEL core; single fusion protein):
  - dCas12a–NLS–[LOV2-caged “stickers”]n–spacers–Reader/Recruit modules.
  - Stickers: short, low-complexity, tyrosine/arginine-enriched and acidic activation peptides whose interaction strength is masked by AsLOV2 in the dark and exposed in light. Multiple copies raise effective valency without hard oligomerization.
  - Readers/Recruiters (modest-affinity to bias reliance on condensates): tandem MED1-IDR fragment and a single BRD4 BD1 module to enhance co-condensation with Mediator/BRD4 at H3K27ac-rich DNA while avoiding strong, constitutive activation.
  - No heterodimerizers or pairwise tethering domains; one polypeptide per locus suffices.
- Mechanism
  1) Dark: stickers are caged; the locus remains in the dilute phase; enhancer–promoter distances remain baseline; low transcription.
  2) Light: sticker uncaging raises local network connectivity; a microcondensate nucleates at the targeted enhancer seed. Endogenous Mediator/BRD4/RNAPII partition in, the droplet wets acetylated chromatin, and loop capture of the cognate promoter occurs via capillary attraction plus cohesin-driven extrusion. Transcription rises.
  3) Light off: stickers re-cage; the condensate dissolves below percolation; loops relax; transcription falls.

Why this is mechanistically novel vs dCas9–CIBN/CRY2 or PhyB/PIF tethers
- Physical principle: wetting-driven capture by a multi-valent mesh, not forced pairwise bridging. No engineered enhancer–promoter “rope”; loops self-organize when the condensate exists.
- Single-component locus nucleator: no two-part dimerizers; no requirement to target both ends.
- Endogenous machinery first-class: activation emerges from selective partitioning of Mediator/BRD4/RNAPII into a condensate whose composition is set by weak interactions, not by bolting on strong synthetic activators.
- Reversibility from phase boundary crossing: light simply tunes valency across a percolation threshold; dissolution retraces the same path without lingering heterodimers.
- Programmable capture radius: light intensity and gRNA tiling density tune condensate size and, hence, loop reach—impractical with discrete tethers.

Biologically appropriate testbed
- Cell type: human erythroid progenitors (HUDEP-2). Rationale: long-range, acetylation-rich super-enhancer architecture; robust, well-mapped enhancer–promoter dynamics; strong clinical relevance.
- Locus: β-globin cluster (HBB) and its LCR. The LCR–HBB loop is a canonical, quantitatively assayable, developmentally regulated interaction.

Aims and experiments
Aim 1. Engineer a reversible, light-tuned condensate at a chosen enhancer
- Construct: dCas12a–LUMINEL core with n=6–8 LOV2-caged stickers, MED1-IDR(1–100), and BD1. Nuclear localization and minimal degron for turnover.
- gRNAs: dCas12a array tiling HS2/HS3 of the β-globin LCR (± optional promoter seeding).
- Readouts:
  - Live-cell fluorescence of scaffold and BRD4/MED1 knock-in tags to confirm co-condensation upon light; FRAP to show liquid behavior; reversibility with dark recovery cycles.
  - Threshold mapping: condensate nucleation probability vs light intensity and sticker copy number.

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible chromatin loop capture and transcriptional control
- Structural assays: targeted 3C/HiChIP for Mediator and RNAPII; distance distributions by live Oligopaint-FISH for LCR–HBB ± light.
- Functional assays: nascent transcription (smFISH of HBB introns), PRO-seq, and time-resolved MS2 reporter integrated at HBB.
- Dynamics:
  - On-kinetics: latency from condensate nucleation to loop proximity and to nascent RNA.
  - Off-kinetics: condensate dissolution, loop relaxation, and transcriptional decay after light-off.
- Reversibility: multi-cycle on/off showing minimal hysteresis and stable baselines.

Aim 3. Establish specificity, mechanism, and superiority to tethering
- Specificity:
  - Non-enhancer control sites and scrambled gRNAs show condensates without loop capture or activation.
  - Off-target profiling by ATAC/ChIP-seq ± light to ensure local effects.
- Mechanism:
  - Partitioning dependence: acute BRD4 or MED14 degradation reduces activation without abolishing condensate formation.
  - Cohesin dependence: RAD21 depletion diminishes loop capture amplitude more than condensate formation, decoupling structure from phase nucleation.
  - Wetting: modulate H3K27ac (p300 inhibition) to reduce promoter capture, implicating acetylation-dependent wetting.
- Benchmark vs dCas9–CRY2 tethering:
  - Build a standard two-site dCas9–CRY2/CIBN bridge between LCR and HBB.
  - Compare onset time, peak transcription, reversibility, noise, and off-target chromatin interactions.
  - Prediction: LUMINEL achieves faster, higher, and more reversible activation with lower ectopic contacts because it recruits function before forcing geometry.

Validation criteria and success metrics
- Condensate nucleation is light-dose dependent and reversible (≥5 cycles) with liquid-like FRAP recovery.
- Median LCR–HBB distance shortens ≥30% on light with return to baseline in dark; HiChIP shows increased contact frequency specifically between targeted enhancer–promoter.
- HBB nascent RNA increases ≥5-fold upon light and returns to within 20% of baseline after dark.
- Loss-of-function perturbations (BRD4/Mediator/cohesin/acetylation) shift structural vs transcriptional phenotypes as predicted by condensate-driven looping, not by forced tethering.
- Benchmarking shows superior reversibility and lower ectopic looping than dimerizer bridges at matched illumination.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Potential constitutive activation: use modest-affinity reader/recruit modules and optimize sticker copy number to place operation near the light-dependent percolation threshold.
- Phototoxicity: low-duty-cycle pulses; blue-light–stable LOV2 variants; confirm viability and transcriptional integrity at operating doses.
- Droplet overgrowth: include weak PEST degron; tune sgRNA tiling density to limit nucleator multiplicity.
- Locus heterogeneity: test a second locus with super-enhancer logic (e.g., MYC in K562) to generalize.

Milestones
- M1: Light-reversible nuclear condensates with MED1/BRD4 co-partitioning (month 3).
- M2: LCR–HBB loop shortening and reversible HBB activation with dose–response curves (month 6).
- M3: Mechanistic dissection (Mediator/BRD4/cohesin/acetylation) and wetting signatures (month 9).
- M4: Head-to-head with dCas9–CRY2/CIBN tethering; deliver design rules for capture radius and responsiveness (month 12).

Extensions
- Red-shifted LOV variants for deeper penetration and multiplexing.
- Ultrasound/thermo-switchable variant by replacing LOV2 with an ELP LCST block for in vivo applications, preserving the same condensate-first principle.

Outcome
LUMINEL establishes a single-stimulus, single-component, CRISPR-addressable switch that controls gene expression by reversibly creating and erasing a transcriptionally competent microenvironment. By letting geometry follow phase behavior, it turns enhancer–promoter looping from a forced connection into a self-assembling, stimulus-gated state change.

label: elements_bypass
text:
Title
Light-Scissor: Reversible, locus-tethered photo-unloading of cohesin to dissolve chromatin loops and shut off target genes in human iPSC-derived neurons

Central hypothesis
A single, locus-tethered, light-activated “unloader” of cohesin is sufficient to reversibly dissolve a specified enhancer–promoter loop and acutely silence the associated gene in neurons. When light is removed, endogenous loop extrusion restores the loop and gene expression.

Atomic strategy
Convert loop “bridges” into light-breakable fasteners by locally increasing cohesin ring opening at a chosen CTCF/cohesin anchor. Achieve this with a CRISPR-tethered, single-component, allosterically photoswitched WAPL (the endogenous cohesin release factor). No synthetic bridging, no inter-locus dimerization.

System architecture
- Targeting module: Nuclease-dead Cas9 (dCas9) directed by pooled gRNAs to one or both anchors (CTCF sites) flanking a disease-relevant enhancer–promoter loop.
- Light-gated unloader: Photo-allosteric WAPL (paWAPL), a WAPL variant bearing an intramolecular photoswitch (e.g., LOV2 insertion) that sterically blocks its PDS5-facing unloader interface in the dark and unmasks it upon illumination. paWAPL is fused to dCas9 for cis-restricted action at the bound locus.
- Optional avidity booster: A cohesin hinge–binding nanobody or PDS5 peptide tethered in cis to paWAPL to increase local encounter rate without catalytic activity in the dark.
- Single stimulus: Visible light (blue) toggles paWAPL activity ON; darkness returns it OFF. The same light also drives a fluorescent reporter to read out dosing history.

Mechanism of action
- Dark (ON gene): Cohesin remains stably engaged at the anchor; the enhancer–promoter loop persists; transcription is maintained.
- Light (OFF gene): paWAPL unmasking locally accelerates cohesin ring opening/release at the targeted anchor, dissolving the loop and shutting down transcription.
- Reversal: When light ceases, paWAPL re-masks; endogenous NIPBL-mediated loading and extrusion re-establish the loop and gene expression.

Why this is mechanistically novel (vs. optogenetic dimerizer loop-formers)
- Function reverses direction: actively dissolves existing loops instead of creating synthetic ones.
- Enzymatic principle: harnesses the endogenous unloading reaction (WAPL/PDS5–cohesin gate opening) rather than hetero-dimerization-driven DNA bridging.
- Single-component photoswitch at the locus: intramolecular allostery gates activity; no light-induced inter-molecular binding pairs (e.g., CRY2/CIBN, PhyB/PIF).
- Uses native topology dynamics for recovery: loop re-formation leverages natural extrusion after stimulus removal; no synthetic bridge persists.

Biological context and target cell type
- Cell type: Human iPSC-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
- Disease rationale: Alpha-synuclein (SNCA) overexpression contributes to Parkinson’s disease; persistent enhancer–promoter contacts and super-enhancers near SNCA can maintain elevated transcription. Being able to dissolve SNCA-associated loops on command allows causal tests of whether “failure-to-release” sustains pathogenic expression and offers a precision downregulation modality.

Primary locus and guide design
- Primary target: CTCF/cohesin anchors delimiting the SNCA super-enhancer–promoter loop(s).
- Secondary test loci (for generality): Activity-dependent loops at BDNF (e.g., promoter IV–enhancer) and ARC in cortical neurons derived from the same iPSC lines.
- Guides: Multiplexed gRNA tiling across anchor CTCF motifs to maximize paWAPL occupancy while minimizing off-targets (computationally filtered).

Key innovations for specificity and reversibility
- Cis restriction: paWAPL is dCas9-tethered; a cryptic NLS and a rapid self-degron keep any unbound paWAPL short-lived, preventing global unloading.
- Activity windowing: Light duty cycles tune unloading bursts; darkness restores paWAPL autoinhibition and allows re-extrusion to baseline.
- Two-key control (optional): Require coincident occupancy at both loop anchors (AND logic) by splitting paWAPL into two allosterically gated fragments that only complement when co-localized at adjacent anchors on the same loop.

Experimental Aims

Aim 1. Build and optimize paWAPL-dCas9
- Engineer LOV2 insertions or light–oxygen–voltage domain fusions at WAPL surfaces predicted to control PDS5/cohesin engagement; screen for light/dark activity ratios using a reporter for cohesin release at a synthetic array.
- Validate on-target cis action: show rapid, light-dependent depletion of RAD21/SMC1 ChIP signal specifically at gRNA-targeted anchors without genome-wide cohesin loss.

Aim 2. Demonstrate reversible loop dissolution at endogenous loci
- Measurements: targeted 3C/5C/HiChIP at SNCA anchors; live-cell two-color CRISPR imaging of anchor–promoter distances; quantify dissolution and re-formation kinetics across light on/off cycles.
- Criteria for success: ≥2-fold reduction in contact frequency and ≥150–300 nm increase in inter-anchor distance within minutes of illumination; full or near-full recovery in darkness on comparable timescales.

Aim 3. Achieve reversible ON/OFF control of target gene transcription and protein
- Readouts: Nascent transcription (intronic qPCR or smFISH), steady-state mRNA (RNA-seq), and alpha-synuclein protein levels (immuno-quantification).
- Function: Assess neuronal phenotypes linked to SNCA dosage (e.g., synaptic vesicle dynamics) in light-on versus light-off states; demonstrate rescue upon loop re-formation.

Controls and differentiation tests
- Non-targeting gRNAs and catalytically silenced paWAPL (interface-dead) to control for phototoxicity and recruitment effects.
- Head-to-head with dCas9-CRY2/CIBN loop-formers: show that Light-Scissor reduces enhancer–promoter contact and gene output when loop-formers would increase them, highlighting opposite directionality and distinct mechanisms.

Risk analysis and mitigations
- Risk: Global cohesin unloading. Mitigation: cis tethering, fast off-target degradation, paWAPL activity attenuation (partial unloader variants), and short, low-duty illumination.
- Risk: Re-formation failure. Mitigation: transient NIPBL co-boost targeted to anchors only in the dark phase to bias recovery without affecting genome-wide loading.
- Risk: Light delivery in neurons. Mitigation: in vitro neuronal cultures tolerate blue light well; red-shifted single-component photoswitch variants can be engineered in later phases.

Milestones and quantitative success criteria
- M1: paWAPL variant with ≥5:1 light/dark unloading activity at a reporter array.
- M2: At SNCA, light induces ≥50% local cohesin ChIP reduction and ≥2-fold drop in enhancer–promoter contact within 5–10 minutes; darkness restores ≥80% of baseline within 60 minutes.
- M3: Reversible ≥60% reduction in SNCA transcription and ≥40% reduction in alpha-synuclein protein over repeated light/dark cycles without global transcriptional dysregulation.

Scope for generalization
- Apply the same Light-Scissor to activity-dependent neuronal genes (BDNF, ARC) and to other disease-relevant loop-stabilized loci (e.g., super-enhancer-driven oncogenes in glia), enabling a unifying “release-the-loop” paradigm.

Expected impact
Light-Scissor establishes a conceptually new control axis for gene regulation: dissolving, not building, chromatin bridges with a single, reversible, locus-tethered stimulus. It directly tests whether hyper-stable loops maintain pathogenic states in neurons and provides a precise, rapidly reversible means to turn disease-driving genes OFF and back ON without genomic cuts or synthetic inter-locus tethers.
