Title: Breaking the neurogenic cartilage-damage loop in osteoarthritis via selective MRGPRX2 antagonism

Atomic strategy (single perturbation):
- Systemic, peripherally restricted antagonism of MRGPRX2 on synovial mast cells to uncouple nociceptor antidromic neuropeptide signaling from chondrocyte/synoviocyte catabolism. This normalizes sensitization without blocking baseline nociception and is expected to improve pain rapidly while secondarily slowing cartilage loss.

Mechanistic hypothesis:
- In a subset of OA patients, nociceptor activity drives structural progression via a mast cell–protease–PAR2 axis. Inhibiting MRGPRX2 will (1) reduce neuropeptide-triggered mast cell degranulation and tryptase release, (2) downshift PAR2→MAPK/NF-κB signaling in chondrocytes/synoviocytes, (3) suppress MMP13/ADAMTS5 and angiogenic/neurotrophic factors, and (4) diminish peripheral input that maintains central sensitization. Pain thus improves first; structure follows.

Causal pathway (explicit, bidirectional):
- Structural→nociceptive: Cartilage fibrillation/subchondral bone marrow lesions→exposed nociceptors/mechanonociception/acidic milieu→PAR2/TRPV1 phosphorylation on nociceptors (by tryptase/proteases)→heightened firing.
- Nociceptive→structural (pathologic loop): Nociceptor activation→antidromic SP/CGRP release→MRGPRX2 activation on synovial mast cells→rapid degranulation (tryptase, chymase, histamine, heparin) and cytokines→PAR2 activation on chondrocytes/synoviocytes/endothelium→MMP13/ADAMTS5/VEGF↑, cartilage ECM breakdown, angiogenesis/nerve ingrowth→more nociceptor access/sensitization.
- Intervention node: MRGPRX2 antagonism breaks SP/CGRP→mast cell→tryptase→PAR2 feed-forward loop, normalizing peripheral/central sensitization and decelerating structural loss.

Why MRGPRX2 fits constraints:
- Not an IL-1, broad MMP, or NGF blockade.
- Normal tissue homeostasis avoidance: MRGPRX2 primarily mediates neuropeptide/drug-induced (pseudo-allergic) mast cell activation; IgE/FcεRI pathways and essential host defense remain intact.
- Sensitization normalization: Reduces exaggerated neuroimmune amplification rather than silencing nociception.
- Systemic modality; no intra-articular injection.

Modality and joint specificity narrative:
- Modality: Oral, peripherally restricted small-molecule MRGPRX2 antagonist, optionally as a pH-activated prodrug to exploit inflamed joint acidosis for local unmasking.
- Joint specificity despite systemic dosing: Inflamed OA joints show (a) high mast cell density, (b) elevated local neuropeptides, (c) acidic pH and leaky vasculature that favor prodrug activation/accumulation, and (d) enriched PAR2 expression. Thus, target engagement and pharmacodynamic effects concentrate within diseased joints.

Prospective responder selection (pre-specified):
- Clinical/physiologic: Large capsaicin-induced neurogenic flare area (intradermal forearm microdose), heightened pressure pain sensitivity around index joint, impaired conditioned pain modulation.
- Fluid/tissue biomarkers: Elevated baseline serum/synovial tryptase; synovial SP/CGRP; low synovial pH; high urinary CTX-II and serum COMP; synovial biopsy immunostaining for MRGPRX2+ mast cells and PAR2 on lining cells (when available).
- Ex vivo functional assay: Whole-blood or PBMC-derived mast cell SP challenge with tryptase release readout; inclusion threshold defined by standardized z-score.
- Imaging: Power Doppler ultrasound synovitis; MRI-detected bone marrow lesion volume; qMRI T2/T1ρ cartilage comp heterogeneity (progression risk enrichment).
- Genomic/transcriptomic: MRGPRX2 promoter variants or synovial transcriptomic “Mast cell–PAR2–MMP13 high” signature from minimally invasive biopsy or blood-derived surrogates.

Translational validation package (run-in before trial randomization):
- Human OA synovium/chondrocyte co-culture challenged with SP±antagonist: outcomes = tryptase, PAR2 internalization, pERK/p65, MMP13/ADAMTS5, sulfated GAG release from cartilage explants.
- Microfluidic tri-culture (human DRG neurons–mast cells–chondrocytes) to confirm that antagonist breaks antidromic SP-driven catabolism and reduces neuronal hyperexcitability.
- PopPK/target occupancy modeling anchored to synovial fluid levels in a short lead-in cohort.

Clinical trial (Phase 2a proof-of-mechanism with enrichment):
- Design: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 1:1:1 (low/high dose/placebo).
- Population: 150 adults with knee OA (Kellgren–Lawrence 2–3) or symptomatic hand OA; enriched by the responder signature (above). Stable background analgesics allowed but capped (no IA steroids/HA within 3 months).
- Dosing: Oral BID, 24 weeks; peripherally restricted exposure confirmed by CSF:plasma ratio ≤0.05 in a sentinel subset.
- Primary endpoint (pain improvement preceding structure): Change from baseline in daily NRS pain (weekly averaged) at Week 4; key co-primary = WOMAC Pain at Week 12.
- Key secondary (structure and mechanism):
  - qMRI: Cartilage T2/T1ρ mapping and dGEMRIC at Weeks 12 and 24; bone marrow lesion volume change.
  - Biochemical: Serum tryptase and synovial fluid tryptase (subset) at 48 h, Week 2, Week 12; urinary CTX-II and serum C2C at Weeks 4, 12, 24.
  - Ultrasound: Power Doppler synovitis score change at Weeks 12 and 24.
  - Sensitization: Pressure pain threshold at joint margin; temporal summation; conditioned pain modulation; patient Global Impression of Change.
- Mechanistic PD milestones (placebo-exceeding anchors):
  - ≥30% reduction in serum tryptase at 48–72 h predicts ≥1.5-point NRS reduction at Week 4 and ≥20% reduction in BML volume at Week 24 (pre-registered mediation).
  - PAR2 activity score (soluble PAR2 fragments or ex vivo PAR2 internalization on patient-derived chondrocytes) declines ≥25% by Week 2.

Statistical and causal inference plan:
- Hierarchical Bayesian model linking early PD (tryptase↓) → pain↓ (Week 4) → structure stabilization (Week 24), with pre-specified causal mediation analysis (natural indirect effects through tryptase/PAR2).
- Placebo mitigation: Biomarker-enriched sampling, centralized ePRO with daily capture, short single-blind run-in, objective PD anchors, and qMRI endpoints less prone to expectation bias.
- Powering: 80% power to detect Δ=1.0 NRS vs placebo at Week 4 (SD 1.8), and standardized effect d=0.45 on T2 relaxation heterogeneity at Week 24; FDR control across secondary endpoints.

Safety and homeostasis considerations:
- Preserve IgE/FcεRI mast cell functions; monitor infection rates, wound healing, and vaccine responses.
- Screen out patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria requiring high-dose antihistamines (confounding).
- Off-target surveillance: hemodynamics, hepatic tests, dermal reactivity. CNS AEs minimized by peripheral restriction.

Exploratory extensions:
- Polyarticular OA: Hand OA stratum with identical enrichment and endpoints (MRI synovitis and cartilage thickness by HR-pQCT, pain on hand-specific scales).
- Digital twin modeling to personalize dose based on baseline tryptase, synovitis PD signal, and qMRI maps.

Go/no-go criteria:
- Go if all three achieved: (1) ≥1.0 NRS separation at Week 4; (2) ≥25% mean tryptase reduction at 48–72 h correlating with pain improvement; (3) significant slowing of BML growth or improvement in cartilage compositional MRI at Week 24 with concordant uCTX-II decline.
- No-go if PD uncouples from clinical or structural outcomes, or if safety signals indicate interference with essential homeostasis.

Why this will exceed placebo:
- Prospective enrichment for an activated neuropeptide–mast cell axis; immediate, objective PD readouts (tryptase) precede and predict pain changes; structural endpoints tied mechanistically to the same axis (PAR2→MMP/ADAMTS), reducing noise and placebo susceptibility.

Contingencies and falsification:
- If pain improves without PD change, analgesia is off-target (reject mechanism).
- If PD improves without structural effect, refine selection to higher PAR2/MMP13 signature or extend duration; alternatively test combination with a PAR2-biased antagonist while maintaining a single causal axis.
- If safety limits exposure, pivot to an antibody fragment with joint-tropic, pH-activated masking that maintains peripheral restriction.

Deliverables and timeline:
- Year 1: Preclinical human explant validation; first-in-human SAD/MAD with PD readouts.
- Year 2: Enrichment assay qualification (tryptase/SP challenge, capsaicin flare); Phase 2a initiation.
- Year 3: Phase 2a completion with integrated causal mediation results to confirm the “pain-first, structure-follows” hypothesis and select dose for Phase 2b.

text:
Title
Closed‑loop, joint‑sound–guided focused ultrasound to normalize subchondral remodeling at overloaded loci, reduce bone‑marrow lesions, and relieve pain in knee/polyarticular osteoarthritis

Integrated hypothesis-question
If focal mechanical overload is continuously detected and treated in real time, can closed‑loop, non‑thermal focused ultrasound (FUS) that induces osteoclast quiescence in overloaded subchondral bone reduce bone‑marrow lesion (BML) volume, slow cartilage degeneration, and durably lower pain by cutting the bone‑to‑nerve nociceptive drive and allowing peripheral/central desensitization?

Atomic strategy
Correct the mechanosensory set‑point of overloaded subchondral bone—by delivering targeted, pulsed ultrasound that biases osteocyte/osteoclast signaling toward low resorption—thereby reducing BML‑driven nociceptive input and secondarily preserving cartilage.

Causal pathway (pre‑specified, testable)
1) Overload bursts → microcrack accrual in subchondral trabeculae → osteocyte danger signaling (e.g., RANKL↑/OPG↓) → osteoclast recruitment and edema → BML and plate porosity.
2) BML/porosity → aberrant angiogenesis and CGRP+/TrkA+ sensory fiber ingrowth across the osteochondral junction → elevated spontaneous and mechanically evoked nociception.
3) Persistent nociception → peripheral sensitization (lowered thresholds) → central sensitization (temporal summation↑, CPM↓) → reflex co‑contraction → higher joint loads → cartilage shear and proteoglycan loss.
4) Intervention: pulsed, low‑thermal‑rise FUS at overloaded loci engages mechanotransduction (e.g., integrins/Piezo/TRPV channels on osteocytes/osteoclast precursors), shifting OPG:RANKL upward, reducing osteoclast activity and marrow edema, stabilizing the stiffness gradient, and regressing angiogenesis/nerve sprouting; concurrent reduction of aberrant afferent firing enables re‑normalization of peripheral and central sensitization.
5) Outcome: less BML volume and osteochondral porosity → lower nociceptive input → decreased pain; restored load transfer and reduced fluid‑pressure pulses → slower cartilage loss.

Intervention (device and control)
- Wearable system: knee sleeve or joint‑specific wraps with (a) IMUs + pressure insoles to estimate joint load vectors (e.g., KAM surrogates), (b) bone‑conducted contact microphones to capture joint acoustic emissions, (c) steerable multi‑element ultrasound patch (0.5–1.5 MHz, pulsed; spatial peak temporal‑average intensity within diagnostic safety limits; modeled to concentrate at subchondral targets 1–3 cm deep), (d) cloud inference engine.
- Sensing-to-therapy loop: algorithm flags overload epochs and unhealthy vibroacoustic motifs (trained against MRI‑defined BML maps) and triggers brief FUS bursts to affected coordinates; weekly blood chemistry (finger‑stick) of cartilage damage markers modulates dose (see below).
- Sham: identical wearables with sensing, sounds, and skin‑level vibrations but sub‑threshold defocused ultrasound energy.

Mechanism‑specific dosing logic
- Initiation: 3 sessions/week for 6 weeks, then algorithmic taper to event‑triggered bursts only.
- Up‑titration when any two of: serum/urine CTX‑II↑ ≥20% from baseline, COMP↑ ≥15%, or sustained overload percentile >85th for compartment; down‑titration if systemic bone resorption marker TRAP5b or CTX‑I falls >15% below baseline (normal tissue homeostasis guardrail).
- Thermal rise limited <1.0°C by duty‑cycle and active thermistors; cavitation sensors abort if thresholds exceeded.

Prospective responder selection (enrichment)
- Inclusion: (a) MRI BML volume ≥1.5 cm3 in index compartment; (b) gait‑derived overload signature (top quartile medial or lateral load metric); (c) serum CTX‑II or PRO‑C2 above age/sex‑adjusted 60th percentile; (d) pain localized to BML compartment by palpation/functional tasks; (e) QST showing peripheral sensitization (reduced PPT at index joint).
- Exclusion: predominant neuropathic pain phenotype, inflammatory arthropathy, osteoporosis requiring antiresorptives, or deep joints beyond acoustic reach without safe windows.

Why this avoids normal tissue homeostasis disruption
- No systemic drug exposure; osteoclast effects are focal, time‑locked to overload events; systemic bone turnover markers are monitored and bounded by pre‑specified guardrails; formation indices (P1NP, bone‑specific ALP) preserved.

Why analgesia exceeds placebo
- Objective, rapidly responsive structural driver (BML) is directly targeted and quantifiable; closed‑loop targeting reduces heterogeneity; sham preserves expectancy without subchondral energy deposition; enrichment ensures strong signal by aligning mechanism with patient biology.

Joint specificity narrative
- Spatial specificity arises from beam focusing to MRI‑mapped BML coordinates and real‑time load/acoustic triggers unique to each joint and compartment; other joints do not cross trigger thresholds and receive no therapeutic sonication.

Study plan

Phase 0 (mechanistic feasibility, n=30)
- Single‑arm, adaptive. Primary PD: Δ BML T2* and volume at 6 weeks; Δ serum TRAP5b (safety), Δ CTX‑II/PRO‑C2 (on‑target). Secondary: pain VAS during standardized overload task; acoustic biomarker reproducibility. Go/No‑Go: ≥20% mean BML reduction with no >15% fall in systemic TRAP5b.

Phase 2b multicenter RCT (enriched, knee OA; n=220; 1:1 FUS vs sham; 24 weeks + 12‑month extension)
- Population: KL 2–3, inclusion as above; stratify by medial vs lateral compartment overload and baseline BML volume.
- Intervention: closed‑loop FUS as specified; sham identical without focal energy.
- Co‑primary endpoints (24 weeks):
  1) Structural: percent change in total BML volume in index compartment (qMRI).
  2) Pain: KOOS Pain responder rate (≥20 points and ≥30% from baseline).
- Key secondary (hierarchical control of alpha):
  - Cartilage: Δ cartilage thickness (qDESS/3D spoiled GRE) at 12 months; Δ T2/T1ρ at 24 weeks.
  - Sensitization normalization: Δ pressure pain threshold at index vs remote site; Δ temporal summation; Δ conditioned pain modulation.
  - Nociceptive drive: change in osteochondral junction porosity (UTE MRI) and synovial fluid NGF (optional subset) as mechanistic biomarkers.
  - Function: 6‑minute walk, stair‑climb test, daily activity load without pain flare.
  - Rescue medication‑adjusted pain days.
- Mediation analysis (pre‑specified): proportion of pain improvement mediated by Δ BML volume and Δ sensitization metrics (SEM/causal mediation), testing the structural→nociception pathway.
- Imaging core lab, blinded adjudication; device telemetry verifies actual subchondral acoustic dose delivered.

Polyarticular sub‑study (n=80 within RCT)
- Simultaneous monitoring of contralateral knee and ipsilateral ankle/hip; therapy delivered only when joint‑specific thresholds are met. Endpoint: joint‑level within‑person correlation between overload‑triggered dose and Δ BML/pain per joint, testing generalizability.

Safety monitoring
- Real‑time temperature and cavitation sensing; quarterly DXA to confirm no global bone loss; systemic turnover markers (CTX‑I, P1NP, TRAP5b) bounded; neuro exam for neuropathic adverse events; vascular ultrasound when deep windows used.

Statistical considerations
- Power: 90% to detect 15% between‑arm difference in BML reduction and 12‑point KOOS Pain difference (two‑sided α=0.05), accounting for 25% placebo responder rate.
- Missing data: multiple imputation; estimand addresses treatment policy with rescue allowed but modeled.
- Interim futility at 50% information based on joint Bayesian predictive probability of success.

Assays and biomarker panel
- On‑target bone: TRAP5b, CTX‑I, OPG:RANKL ratio (serum); acoustic emission burden; overload time‑above‑threshold.
- Cartilage: CTX‑II (serum/urine), PRO‑C2, COMP; MRI T2/T1ρ.
- Sensitization: PPT, TS, CPM; sleep and catastrophizing (to stratify, not to treat).

Operational notes
- Training dataset to link acoustic motifs and load spikes to BML geography built from baseline MRI and week‑1 supervised walking tasks.
- Standardized footwear and activity diaries to control mechanical confounding; allowed stable background NSAIDs/acetaminophen, rescue tracked.

Success criteria for advancement
- Co‑primary success at 24 weeks and ≥50% mediation of pain via structural/sensitization pathways; 12‑month cartilage loss rate reduced by ≥30% vs sham without systemic bone turnover suppression beyond guardrails; safety profile non‑inferior to sham.

Innovation summary
A single perturbation—normalizing subchondral mechanobiology only where and when overload occurs—breaks the bone‑BML‑nerve sensitization loop that links structure to pain. Closed‑loop, joint‑specific FUS offers a mechanistically matched, homeostasis‑sparing, placebo‑resistant path to concurrent structural and analgesic benefit in osteoarthritis.

Title
Resolution-Deficit–Guided Systemic Pro-resolving Agonism for Concurrent Structural and Pain Improvement in Knee and Polyarticular Osteoarthritis

Atomic Strategy
Amplify endogenous resolution—not suppression—of post-injury synovitis by systemically activating a single pro-resolving receptor axis (ChemR23 or FPR2/ALX) in patients prospectively identified to have a synovial fluid “resolution deficit,” thereby halting cartilage catabolism and normalizing nociceptive sensitization.

Central Hypothesis
In OA patients with a quantified synovial resolution deficit, short-acting, orally administered selective agonists of ChemR23 or FPR2/ALX will (a) restore macrophage-led inflammatory resolution and chondroprotection, (b) reduce osteochondral angiogenesis/nerve ingrowth, and (c) desensitize joint-innervating nociceptors, leading to simultaneous slowing of structural progression and clinically meaningful pain reduction beyond placebo.

Causal Pathway (explicit, testable)
1) Systemic ChemR23/FPR2 agonist exposure → 2) preferential uptake/action in inflamed joints where receptor expression and vascular permeability are upregulated → 3) macrophage reprogramming to pro-resolving phenotype, enhanced efferocytosis, and cessation of neutrophil recruitment → 4) suppression of catabolic mediators (e.g., COX2/PGE2, aggrecanases) and promotion of chondrocyte anabolism/survival → 5) reduced generation of cartilage/bone DAMPs and decreased osteochondral angiogenesis and aberrant nerve ingrowth → 6) lowered local nociceptor sensitizing milieu (PGE2, protons, cytokines), downregulation of TRPV1/Nav1.8 signaling on joint afferents → 7) reduced peripheral input to dorsal horn → 8) normalization of central sensitization (improved conditioned pain modulation, reduced temporal summation) → 9) sustained pain relief linked to slowed cartilage loss and fewer bone marrow lesions.

Why Systemic Yet Joint-Selective
- Pathology-anchored selectivity: inflamed synovium/subchondral bone exhibit increased receptor density (ChemR23, FPR2) and higher permeability, concentrating ligand action locally.
- Demand-driven pharmacology: drug effect size scales with resolution deficit and inflammatory tone, both greatest in symptomatic joints.
- Pharmacodynamic selectivity: resolution agonism requires inflammatory context to exert large effects; minimal impact in non-inflamed tissues.

Normal Tissue Homeostasis Avoidance
- Targets (ChemR23/FPR2) are resolution switches, not primary mediators of basal homeostasis; agonism is time-limited and non-immunosuppressive.
- Intermittent, pulse dosing mimics physiological resolution bursts, reducing off-target chronic modulation.

Prospective Responder Selection (pre-specified)
Define a Resolution Deficit Index (RDI) from synovial fluid and plasma at screening:
- Lipid mediator panel: low resolvins/protectins/maresins (e.g., RvD1/RvD2/RvE1/MaR1/PD1) relative to precursors (17-HDHA, 18-HEPE).
- Cellular signature: high synovial M1/M0 ratio; low expression of resolution enzymes (ALOX15) and/or low ChemR23/FPR2 receptor density on synovial macrophages/fibroblasts (flow cytometry or RNA).
- Structural-inflammatory phenotype: MRI synovitis and bone marrow lesion burden.
Eligibility requires RDI-low (below pre-validated threshold) and receptor-positive status.

Intervention
- Modality: Oral, short-acting, selective small-molecule agonist of ChemR23 (RvE1-mimetic) or FPR2/ALX (RvD1/MaR1-mimetic). No intra-articular injections.
- Dosing: Once daily, 12 weeks induction, then maintenance to 52 weeks; pulse strategy (evening dosing) to align with endogenous resolution rhythms.
- Comparator: Matching placebo.

Study Design
- Phase 2, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, biomarker-enriched trial with an enriched-enrollment/randomized-withdrawal (EERW) component to exceed placebo effects.
- Population A (primary): Knee OA with inflammatory phenotype (KL 2–3), symptomatic ≥6 months, RDI-low, receptor-positive.
- Population B (exploratory): Polyarticular hand/knee OA with RDI-low to assess generalizability.
- Randomization: 2:1 active:placebo after a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in with digital pain diary compliance gating.
- Duration: 52 weeks; interim mechanistic readouts at weeks 4 and 12.

Endpoints
Primary (co-primary, hierarchical to ensure structural-pain linkage):
1) Structural: Change in medial tibiofemoral cartilage thickness by quantitative 3T MRI (segmented morphometry) at 52 weeks.
2) Pain: Change in 24-hour average knee pain (0–10 NRS, eDiary) at week 12 sustained through week 24.

Key Secondary
- MRI synovitis and bone marrow lesion scores (weeks 12 and 52).
- dGEMRIC/T2 mapping for cartilage composition.
- Serum and synovial biomarkers: ARGS-aggrecan, uCTX-II, hsCRP, PGE2 metabolites, lipid mediator class switching (increase in SPMs).
- Peripheral/central sensitization: QST (pressure pain threshold), temporal summation, conditioned pain modulation; optional fMRI nociceptive network activity.
- Function and quality: WOMAC function, KOOS-PS, PGIC, actigraphy-measured activity.
- Innervation/angiogenesis: contrast-enhanced MRI perfusion metrics; circulating VEGF/NGF as ancillary biology (not targeting NGF directly).

Mechanistic Substudies
- Synovial biopsies (optional): macrophage phenotype shift (CD206+/MerTK+), receptor occupancy assays.
- Single-cell transcriptomics on synovial aspirates: resolution pathway activation signatures.
- Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic modeling: exposure vs. synovial SPM restoration vs. outcomes.
- Mediation analysis: test pre-specified chain—drug → synovitis reduction → cartilage preservation → pain reduction.

Placebo-Exceeding Design Features
- Biomarker enrichment (RDI-low, receptor-positive).
- Placebo run-in and adherence gating; centralized eDiary with compliance algorithms.
- Objective imaging co-primary; centralized blinded reads.
- EERW: responders at week 12 re-randomized to continue vs. withdraw to quantify drug-dependent effect beyond placebo.

Safety
- Monitor infection rates, wound healing, leukocyte profiles to confirm non-immunosuppressive profile.
- Safety labs and AE adjudication focused on bleeding risk, hepatic enzymes, and cardiovascular profile typical for small-molecule GPCR agonists.
- Stopping rules for infection clusters or systemic hypersensitivity.

Statistics
- Powering assumes: 0.08–0.12 mm between-group difference in cartilage thickness loss at 52 weeks; 1.2-point NRS pain difference at week 12 sustained to week 24; alpha-split for co-primaries.
- Enrichment expected to increase effect sizes by ≥30% vs. unselected OA.
- Bayesian interim analysis (week 12) to adapt sample size within pre-specified caps.

Prospective Validation and Preclinical Bridge
- Resolution Atlas: longitudinal lipid mediator profiling in post-ACL injury cohorts distinguishing “healers” vs. “progressors” to select the dominant human-relevant SPM axis (ChemR23 vs. FPR2) before dosing.
- Human ex vivo synovium and osteochondral organoids to confirm chondroprotection and nociceptor desensitization signatures with candidate agonists.

Success Criteria (Go/No-Go)
- Biological: ≥2-fold increase in synovial SPMs and ≥30% reduction in MRI synovitis at week 12.
- Clinical: ≥1.0-point NRS reduction vs. placebo at week 12, maintained at week 24.
- Structural: ≥30% reduction in rate of cartilage thickness loss vs. placebo at 52 weeks.
- Mechanistic: Demonstrated mediation from synovitis reduction to pain/structure outcomes.

Why This Meets Constraints
- Excludes IL-1/MMP/NGF blockade and pain-only suppression; targets resolution GPCRs.
- Systemic, non–intra-articular modality.
- Explicit causal chain from structure to nociception with sensitization normalization.
- Minimizes homeostatic disruption via context-dependent resolution agonism and pulse dosing.
- Prospective biomarker selection (RDI and receptor expression) to enrich responders and surpass placebo rates.
- Joint specificity arises from pathology-anchored receptor upregulation/permeability and demand-driven pharmacodynamics.

Deliverables
- Validated RDI assay and receptor expression panel for clinical screening.
- Proof-of-mechanism and proof-of-concept for systemic pro-resolving agonism in OA with concurrent structural and analgesic benefits.
- A scalable precision-medicine framework for polyarticular extension.

text:
Title
Rate-limiting blockade of disease-activated aggrecanase to simultaneously prevent cartilage loss and extinguish nociceptor-activating DAMPs in osteoarthritis

Atomic strategy (single causal lever)
Identify a specific aggrecan-derived fragment that directly excites/sensitizes joint-innervating nociceptors, map its obligate rate-limiting cleavage to ADAMTS-5 in diseased cartilage, and systemically inhibit ADAMTS-5 with a highly selective agent to (a) halt aggrecan structural breakdown and (b) prevent generation of the nociceptive fragment. One enzyme, two outcomes.

Central hypothesis
In knee and polyarticular OA, aggrecanase-5 (ADAMTS-5)–dependent cleavage of the aggrecan interglobular domain generates a defined 32–amino-acid DAMP peptide that activates TLR2 on nociceptors and drives peripheral and secondary central sensitization. Selective systemic inhibition of ADAMTS-5 in patients with high baseline “aggrecan-DAMP load” will (i) reduce production of this fragment, (ii) normalize nociceptor excitability and central sensitization, and (iii) slow cartilage thickness loss beyond placebo.

Explicit causal pathway
Mechanical/biochemical stress in OA cartilage → ADAMTS-5 activation on pericellular aggrecan → aggrecan interglobular domain cleavage → release of a defined 32-mer DAMP into synovial milieu → TLR2 engagement on peptidergic nociceptors (and synovial macrophages) → increased nociceptor firing, neuropeptide release, spinal dorsal horn facilitation → pain and activity-evoked hyperalgesia. ADAMTS-5 inhibition removes the source DAMP, reducing TLR2 drive, thereby normalizing sensitization rather than blocking conduction.

Why this avoids crowded spaces
- Not IL-1 pathway targeting.
- Not broad MMP inhibition; ADAMTS-5 is a specific aggrecanase with non-overlapping catalytic profile.
- Not NGF blockade; upstream DAMP removal reduces NGF induction secondarily without ligand sequestration.
- Not pain-only suppression; primary structural protection plus removal of a nociceptive driver.

Joint-selective effects under systemic dosing
- Disease-restricted target activation: ADAMTS-5 is upregulated and activated in OA cartilage/synovium but low in most healthy adult tissues.
- Substrate restriction: high aggrecan concentration is unique to cartilage; kinetic selectivity concentrates pharmacodynamic effect where enzyme and substrate co-localize.
- Microenvironmental amplification: OA cartilage/synovium (acidic, high GAG density) enhances residence of cationic small molecules or basic-side-chain biologics without intra-articular delivery.

Prospective responder selection
- Baseline aggrecan DAMP burden: synovial fluid or plasma ARGS-aggrecan neoepitope and LC–MS quantification of the aggrecan 32-mer; responders defined as top tertile of DAMP load.
- Target activation signature: ex vivo ADAMTS-5 activity assay in plasma/synovial fluid; transcriptomic signature of ADAMTS5-high from peripheral blood extracellular vesicles.
- Nociceptor pathway engagement: whole-blood TLR2-responsive cytokine signature after ex vivo DAMP stimulation; QST profile consistent with peripheral drive (pressure pain thresholds at the index joint disproportionately reduced vs remote sites).

Specific aims

Aim 1. Identify and validate the nociceptor-activating aggrecan fragment and its enzyme-of-origin in human OA.
- Discovery peptidomics: fractionate synovial fluid from painful OA vs. asymptomatic radiographic OA; LC–MS/MS to map aggrecan peptides; prioritize interglobular-domain fragments.
- Functional triage: apply fractions/peptides to human iPSC-derived nociceptors; measure Ca2+ influx, action potential firing; TLR2 reporter assays and pharmacologic/CRISPR TLR2 loss-of-function.
- Enzyme mapping: generate fragments with recombinant ADAMTS-4/5 ± MMP-3 sequential cleavage; kinetic modeling to identify the rate-limiting step; neoepitope antibody mapping to confirm in human fluids.

Milestones: A single peptide that (i) reproducibly excites nociceptors via TLR2, (ii) is elevated in painful OA, and (iii) requires ADAMTS-5 as the rate-limiting cleavage.

Aim 2. Develop or repurpose a highly selective systemic ADAMTS-5 inhibitor optimized for cartilage engagement and homeostasis sparing.
- Chemistry/biologic selection: downselect from existing ADAMTS-5–selective small molecules or antibodies with >100-fold selectivity vs ADAMTS-4/other ADAMTS/MMPs.
- Cartilage engagement: prioritize cationic, GAG-interacting chemotypes or basic isoelectric point biologics that exhibit high cartilage partitioning in ex vivo human cartilage.
- Homeostasis screen: verify minimal inhibition of versican cleavage in vascular smooth muscle assays; normal wound-closure assays in fibroblasts; no effect on bone turnover markers in osteoblast/osteoclast co-culture.
- PK/PD modeling: target trough concentrations achieving ≥80% ADAMTS-5 occupancy in cartilage; PD readouts include plasma/synovial ARGS and 32-mer suppression.

Milestones: Candidate with clean selectivity, predicted joint PD coverage at clinically feasible exposures, and no disruption of essential homeostatic readouts.

Aim 3. Demonstrate dual structural–analgesic efficacy and sensitization normalization in preclinical disease and a biomarker-enriched clinical study.
Preclinical
- Models: mouse DMM and rat MMT with systemic dosing.
- Outcomes:
  - Structure: histomorphometry (OARSI), μMRI T2/dGEMRIC for GAG content.
  - Pain/sensitization: weight bearing, mechanical/thermal thresholds, conditioned place aversion; dorsal horn wind-up and c-Fos; DRG TLR2 pathway downregulation.
  - Mechanism: synovial fluid/plasma 32-mer and ARGS suppression; loss of nociceptor TLR2 activation by ex vivo perfusates.
- Stringency: compare vs inactive analog; include Tlr2−/− and neuron-specific Tlr2 conditional KO to confirm pathway dependence.

Clinical (Phase 1b/2a, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 24–52 weeks)
- Population: knee OA (Kellgren–Lawrence 2–3) or polyarticular hand+knee OA with:
  - Baseline NRS pain ≥5/10,
  - Top-tertile plasma or synovial 32-mer and/or ARGS levels,
  - QST indicating peripheral sensitization predominant (index-joint pressure pain threshold low with near-normal remote site thresholds).
- Intervention: systemic selective ADAMTS-5 inhibitor (oral or SC), two dose levels targeting 80% vs 95% modeled occupancy.
- Co-primary endpoints:
  - Structural: change in medial femorotibial cartilage thickness by quantitative MRI (qMRI) at 24/52 weeks.
  - Pain: WOMAC Pain and daily NRS AUC weeks 12–24; activity-evoked pain (6MWT effort-normalized).
- Key secondary/mechanistic endpoints:
  - DAMP suppression: change in plasma/synovial 32-mer and ARGS (confirm causal link).
  - Sensitization normalization: increase in index-joint pressure pain threshold; reduction in temporal summation; reduction in fMRI dorsal horn/supraspinal pain-facilitation signals.
  - Function: KOOS-ADL, performance-based tests.
- Enrichment/analysis:
  - Hierarchical testing: co-primaries then mechanistic biomarker suppression.
  - Bayesian adaptive enrichment: ongoing inclusion weighted to highest baseline 32-mer strata.
  - Placebo mitigation: centralized rating, objective activity-evoked pain, biomarker-confirmed target engagement.
- Safety: monitor vascular/dermal healing, blood pressure, bone turnover markers; ECG and lab panel. Stop rules tied to any off-target versican PD signal.

Addressing constraints

Causal pathway specified and testable
- Single chain from enzyme activation → specific aggrecan fragment → TLR2 on nociceptors → sensitization and pain; each node has an assayable biomarker (ADAMTS-5 activity, 32-mer/ARGS, nociceptor TLR2 signaling, QST/fMRI).

Avoiding essential homeostatic disruption
- ADAMTS-5 selectivity; adult redundancy with ADAMTS-4 minimizes risk; preclinical homeostasis panel gates progression. Systemic exposure is acceptable because functional PD requires high aggrecan substrate density, largely confined to cartilage.

Sensitization normalization rather than blockade
- By removing the DAMP that drives TLR2-dependent hyperexcitability, peripheral input and central facilitation recede; sodium channel function and conduction remain intact.

Prospective patient selection
- Use quantitative 32-mer and ARGS thresholds plus ADAMTS-5 activity; optional composite “AggreDAMP score” for screening and stratification.

Placebo-exceeding effect size strategy
- Biomarker enrichment, objective activity-evoked endpoints, early proof of mechanism (DAMP drop), and adaptive randomization to high-DAMP strata increase assay sensitivity and reduce placebo dilution.

Joint specificity narrative under systemic dosing
- Spatial coincidence of high target activation (ADAMTS-5) with abundant substrate (cartilage aggrecan) in diseased joints yields preferential pharmacodynamic effect without intra-articular dosing.

Experimental details and deliverables

Key assays
- LC–MS/MS absolute quantification of 32-mer; ARGS neoepitope ELISA.
- Recombinant protease kinetics to define rate-limiting step; selective inhibitor confirmation.
- Human nociceptor (iPSC) electrophysiology; TLR2 loss-of-function; synovial fluid challenge.
- qMRI cartilage mapping; QST and temporal summation; pain-evoked fMRI.

Go/no-go criteria
- Aim 1: Single aggrecan fragment meeting functional criteria; correlation with pain severity (r > 0.4).
- Aim 2: ≥100-fold selectivity vs off-target proteases; ≥60% 32-mer suppression in ex vivo human cartilage explants at clinically reachable concentrations.
- Aim 3 (preclinical): concurrent ≥30% pain reduction and ≥30% protection of cartilage thickness vs vehicle with ≥70% fragment suppression.
- Aim 3 (clinical): at 24 weeks, ≥0.3 mm reduction in qMRI cartilage loss rate vs placebo and ≥1-point NRS improvement vs placebo in high-DAMP stratum, with ≥50% median 32-mer suppression.

Impact
A single, mechanism-anchored intervention that unifies structure modification and analgesia by eliminating a validated nociceptor-activating DAMP at its enzymatic source. If successful, it establishes a biomarker-driven, disease-modifying analgesic paradigm for OA that generalizes to polyarticular disease while maintaining joint-selective pharmacodynamics under systemic therapy.

text:
Title: Restoring neuro–osteochondral repulsion to re‑establish joint “volume control” of pain and slow structural progression in osteoarthritis

Atomic strategy (single insight):
- Normalize the joint’s antinociceptive “volume control” by blocking osteoclast-derived netrin‑1 that drives aberrant sensory nerve/vessel ingrowth and lowers nociceptor thresholds in subchondral bone. This single perturbation simultaneously:
  - Reduces peripheral input that fuels central sensitization (pain improvement).
  - Stabilizes subchondral remodeling and load distribution, reducing downstream cartilage loss (structural benefit).

Hypothesis and goal:
- In early OA, microdamage activates osteoclasts that secrete netrin‑1, attracting and stabilizing nociceptive fibers and angiogenesis within subchondral bone. This collapses the healthy joint’s anti-innervation “repulsion gate,” creating acidic, vascularized, hyperinnervated niches that sensitize afferents and provoke neurogenic inflammation.
- Systemic, bone-seeking netrin‑1 neutralization will restore neuro–osteochondral repulsion, reduce aberrant innervation and acidification, normalize pain processing, and secondarily attenuate cartilage loss by correcting subchondral mechanics.

Mechanism with explicit causal pathway (pre-specified):
1) Intervention: Anti–netrin‑1 biologic accumulates at high-turnover subchondral surfaces.
2) Primary structural node: Reduced osteoclast–netrin‑1 signaling decreases (a) sensory and sympathetic sprouting and (b) angiogenic invasion at the osteochondral junction; also diminishes focal acidification at resorption pits.
3) Nociceptive input: Lower intraosseous sprouting + less acidification raise nociceptor activation thresholds, decreasing CGRP/Substance P release and neurogenic inflammation → normalization of peripheral and central sensitization (QST/CPM improve).
4) Structure → pain linkage: Fewer bone marrow lesions (BMLs) and normalized subchondral plate stiffness/load transfer reduce cartilage shear and tidemark advancement → slower cartilage thickness loss → sustained reduction in nociceptive drive.
5) Net result: Pain reduction exceeding placebo and measurable slowing of structural progression.

Modality and agent:
- Agent: Humanized anti–netrin‑1 IgG1 (or Unc5B‑Fc decoy), conjugated to a bone‑seeking bisphosphonate via an acid‑ and cathepsin‑K–cleavable linker (systemic IV or SC dosing q4–8 weeks).
- Rationale for format: 
  - Netrin‑1 is not an essential adult homeostatic ligand; partial/compartmental inhibition is tolerated.
  - Bone-homing and disease-activated release restrict on‑target activity to high‑turnover subchondral niches, minimizing systemic exposure to non-joint tissues.

Why joint‑selective effects despite systemic dosing:
- Pharmacokinetic/physiochemical targeting: Bisphosphonate confers hydroxyapatite affinity and concentrates drug at actively remodeling subchondral bone typical of OA BMLs.
- Pathophysiologic activation: Acidic pH and cathepsin‑K activity at osteoclast lacunae cleave the linker to liberate active antibody locally.
- Biological selectivity: Elevated netrin‑1 and aberrant neurovascular growth are enriched in diseased joints, creating a pharmacodynamic sink.

Avoidance of excluded/undesirable spaces:
- Not IL‑1 axis, not broad MMP, not NGF blockade, and not nociception-only suppression. The mechanism restores gating and desensitization set‑points by removing an aberrant sprouting cue.

Responder identification (prospective enrichment):
- Imaging:
  - MRI: Large/worsening BMLs (semiquantitative score or volumetric segmentation).
  - 18F‑NaF PET: Elevated subchondral bone formation/turnover (SUVmax/SUVmean threshold).
  - DCE‑MRI or CE‑ultrasound: Subchondral/periosteal neovascular signal.
- Blood biomarkers:
  - High osteoclast activity (TRAP5b, CTX‑I) and low osteoblast coupling (P1NP/CTX‑I ratio).
  - Elevated circulating netrin‑1 (ELISA) and/or Unc5B+ monocyte signature.
- Sensory phenotype:
  - Local mechanical hyperalgesia at the index joint with preserved conditioned pain modulation (CPM) reserve, indicating a gate weakened but not broken.
- Composite enrollment rule: BMLhigh/NaFhigh/TRAP5bhigh with CPM reserve → predicted responders.

Primary outcomes and powering (placebo-exceeding effect size):
- Primary pain endpoint: Change in daily numeric rating scale (NRS) pain averaged over weeks 12–24 with hierarchical testing at week 12, 24, and 52; target placebo-adjusted effect ≥1.0 NRS at week 24 in enriched cohort.
- Key structural endpoint: 
  - MRI BML volume change at 6 and 12 months (co‑primary at 12 months).
  - Cartilage thickness loss (3D MRI) at 12–18 months as a ranked secondary with alpha preservation.
- Sensitization normalization:
  - QST: ↑ Pressure pain thresholds (PPT) at joint and ↓ temporal summation.
  - CPM: Improvement toward normal range.
- Mechanism readouts:
  - Serum CGRP/Substance P decrease.
  - 18F‑NaF PET reduction in subchondral turnover correlating with pain change.
- Mediation plan (pre-specified):
  - Path a: Treatment → ΔBML/ΔNaF.
  - Path b: ΔBML/ΔNaF → ΔPPT/ΔCPM → ΔNRS.
  - Proportion mediated quantified to link structure to pain.

Trial design:
- Phase 2, multicenter, randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled, adaptive enrichment.
  - N=~240; 2:1 randomization; interim at week 12 for sample re‑estimation and enrichment tightening.
  - Population: Knee OA (KL2‑3) and/or polyarticular hand/knee OA with BMLhigh/NaFhigh and CPM reserve.
  - Dosing: Anti–netrin‑1‑BP IV/SC q4–8 weeks for 48 weeks.
  - Concomitants: Stable background analgesics allowed; rescue acetaminophen only during assessment windows.
- Digital phenotyping to reduce placebo noise:
  - Daily ePRO pain, activity‑adjusted pain (step‑normalized), and passive wearable metrics.
  - Run‑in to identify high day‑to‑day placebo reactivity; exclude extreme placebo responders.

Safety and homeostasis:
- Minimized systemic exposure via bone targeting and disease‑site cleavage.
- Monitor for angiogenesis‑related healing signals, autonomic effects, and bone turnover suppression; adjudicate wound/infection healing events and BMD.
- Immunogenicity tracking; PK/PD modeling ties circulating free netrin‑1 to effect.

Joint‑specific narrative:
- OA joints with active subchondral turnover act as physiological “magnets” for the conjugate and present the biochemical conditions for payload release. Joints without these features will see little exposure, explaining joint‑selective benefits from systemic dosing.

Go/no‑go gates:
- At 12 weeks: ≥0.6 NRS placebo‑adjusted improvement and ≥10% reduction in 18F‑NaF SUV in target regions.
- At 24 weeks: ≥1.0 NRS improvement with concordant QST/CPM normalization; safety acceptable.
- At 12 months: Significant BML volume reduction and directional cartilage‑loss slowing.

Extensions and generalizability:
- Polyarticular OA: Same enrichment (joint‑level NaF/BML signatures) predicts which joints benefit within the same patient.
- Companion Dx: Plasma netrin‑1 + NaF PET composite to prospectively select responders and guide dose.

Deliverables:
- A mechanism-anchored therapy that restores the joint’s pain‑gating “volume control” and mechanistically links structural correction (subchondral remodeling and neurovascular exclusion) to durable pain relief, with prospective selection to surpass OA placebo response.

text:
Title
Marrow-confined, logic‑gated opsonization to replace myeloablation: a selective, non‑genotoxic allo‑HSCT platform that eradicates leukemia stem cells and preserves donor HSC engraftment

Central hypothesis (atomic strategy)
A single, spatially confined intervention—logic‑gated opsonization of LSCs within bone marrow that simultaneously recruits complement, unlocks phagocytosis, and locally blocks inhibitory checkpoints—will convert protected, immune‑evasive LSCs into universally recognizable targets for donor innate and adaptive immunity, restoring and surpassing the anti‑leukemia effect of MAC without systemic genotoxicity.

Therapeutic concept (M‑LOT: Marrow‑Logic Opsonization Therapy)
- Molecule: a tri‑functional biologic delivered on a marrow‑homing carrier.
  1) Dual‑antigen AND‑gate: two low‑affinity binders (e.g., CD123 AND CLL‑1; patient‑specific 2‑of‑N panels permitted: TIM‑3, GPR56, CD93) that achieve high avidity only on LSCs, sparing normal HSCs.
  2) Effector recruitment: a C1q‑recruiting and Fc‑engineered domain to drive classical complement deposition (C3b/MAC) and potent ADCP/ADCC.
  3) Conditional immune‑evasion release: a masked anti‑CD47 plus anti‑PD‑L1 scFv that unmask only upon dual‑antigen engagement and/or leukemic niche protease cleavage (e.g., MMP‑9/cathepsin), ensuring activity only on LSCs in marrow.
- Spatial confinement: bone‑targeted nanoparticles (bisphosphonate or Asp8‑decorated) and/or intra‑osseous dosing to restrict exposure to marrow, limiting GVHD risk and off‑tissue effects.

Overall study objective
Demonstrate that non‑genotoxic allo‑HSCT using M‑LOT plus niche‑disruptive, antibody‑only conditioning and GVHD‑inert graft engineering yields relapse rates ≤ MAC while maintaining low GVHD and preserving donor HSC engraftment.

Specific aims
Aim 1. Engineer and validate M‑LOT selectivity and potency against human LSCs while sparing normal HSCs.
- Design: Build a modular, recombinant tri‑functional opsonin with swappable antigen binders; formulate on marrow‑homing carriers.
- In vitro: Patient‑matched AML LSC vs CD34+CD38− HSC co‑cultures; endpoints: (i) dual‑antigen thresholding, (ii) complement deposition, (iii) macrophage/NK‑mediated clearance, (iv) apoptosis, (v) clonogenicity (CFU‑HSC preservation).
- Ex vivo human marrow: assess spatial activation (protease‑dependent unmasking) and bystander safety (erythrocytes/platelets/endothelium).
- Off‑switches: evaluate protease‑resistant mutants and dose‑titrated masks to ensure donor HSC safety.

Aim 2. Establish non‑genotoxic conditioning that creates space and dismantles LSC niche protection.
- Conditioning backbone: anti‑CD117 (CD117 mAb) for host HSC depletion and niche opening (no busulfan/TBI).
- Niche disruption: brief, peri‑opsonin blockade of CXCR4 (plerixafor) and E‑selectin (uproleselan) to (i) dislodge quiescent LSCs, (ii) expose them to opsonization/complement, (iii) prevent rapid re‑sequestration.
- Marrow‑confined dosing: M‑LOT on days −3 and −1 by intra‑osseous injection; pharmacokinetics and biodistribution via PET‑label.
- Endpoints: host HSC space (flow/single‑cell), LSC depletion (MRD by ddPCR/flow), absence of systemic cytopenias beyond hematopoietic compartment.

Aim 3. Enhance GVL while minimizing GVHD using graft engineering that complements M‑LOT and defeats LSC immune‑evasion.
- Graft composition: αβ T‑cell–depleted peripheral blood stem cell graft to lower GVHD; add back:
  - Memory‑like NK cells (IL‑12/15/18 primed) for missing‑self killing of HLA‑loss variants.
  - Polyclonal γδ T cells (MHC‑independent cytotoxicity).
  - Optional iNKT cells (GVHD attenuation and APC re‑education).
- Temporal sequencing: infuse innate effectors on day 0 immediately after final M‑LOT dose to exploit fresh opsonization and complement tags; infuse αβ‑depleted CD34+ graft thereafter.
- Post‑transplant control: marrow‑only re‑dosing of M‑LOT for MRD surveillance; local checkpoint control via the built‑in anti‑PD‑L1 domain without systemic CPI exposure.
- Endpoints: (i) acute/chronic GVHD rates, (ii) time to neutrophil/platelet engraftment, (iii) donor chimerism, (iv) LSC eradication/MRD− durability.

Translational plan and study design
- Preclinical
  - Patient‑derived xenografts (PDX) engrafted intra‑tibially with AML LSCs; compare RIC alone vs RIC+M‑LOT vs MAC; readouts: LSC frequency (ELDA), marrow imaging, systemic toxicity, donor HSC engraftment after human CD34+ infusion.
  - Nonhuman primate feasibility: anti‑CD117 conditioning + intra‑osseous M‑LOT analog + autologous HSC rescue; endpoints: biodistribution, hematopoietic recovery, complement consumption, off‑target safety.
- Phase 1 (safety/PK/PD; single‑arm)
  - Adults with AML/MDS indicated for allo‑HSCT; RIC/NMA backbone replaced by anti‑CD117 ± low‑dose serotherapy (non‑genotoxic).
  - Dose‑escalate M‑LOT (−3, −1 intra‑osseous); plerixafor/uproleselan window; αβ‑depleted graft + NK/γδ T addback.
  - Primary: DLTs, engraftment by day +28, grade II–IV aGVHD by day +100. Secondary: MRD− CR at day +100, complement/ADCP biomarkers, off‑target cytopenias.
- Phase 2 (efficacy; randomized)
  - M‑LOT platform vs institutional MAC.
  - Primary: 1‑year relapse‑free survival; key secondaries: non‑relapse mortality, GRFS, chronic GVHD, MRD conversion rates, quality of life.

Key mechanistic assertions mapped to constraints
- Compensate for loss of MAC anti‑leukemia effect: complement‑driven cytotoxicity + ADCP/ADCC within marrow; innate effector addback (NK/γδ T) amplifies killing independent of HLA.
- Exclude non‑selective genotoxic agents: conditioning via anti‑CD117 mAb ± serotherapy; no busulfan/TBI.
- LSC‑selective targeting with preserved HSC engraftment: dual‑antigen AND‑gate avoids HSC antigens; protease‑ and proximity‑gated anti‑CD47 avoids donor HSC opsonization; timing separates opsonization from graft infusion as needed.
- Overcome marrow niche sanctuary: CXCR4/E‑selectin blockade dislodges LSCs; intra‑osseous, marrow‑retained M‑LOT paints residual niche‑resident LSCs; complement/ADCP do not require cell cycling.
- Counter multiple immune‑evasion mechanisms simultaneously: 
  - HLA loss—addressed by NK missing‑self responses and HLA‑independent complement killing.
  - Checkpoint upregulation—local anti‑PD‑L1 within M‑LOT.
  - Anti‑phagocytic CD47—conditional blockade built into M‑LOT.
- Enhance GVL without exacerbating GVHD: marrow‑confined effector engagement and αβ T‑cell–depleted graft reduce systemic alloreactivity; iNKT and γδ T addbacks bias toward GVL with low GVHD.

Safety and risk management
- On‑target hematologic toxicity: staggered dosing; complement consumption monitored; eculizumab rescue plan for uncontrolled complement activation.
- Donor HSC protection: ensure anti‑CD47 unmasking requires dual‑antigen engagement; if needed, delay graft infusion ≥24–48 h post‑last M‑LOT or use rapid‑clearance carrier; confirm no binding to CD34+ HSCs ex vivo.
- Off‑marrow exposure: bone‑targeting ligands/intra‑osseous delivery; whole‑body PET‑PK to confirm confinement; predefined stopping rules if systemic deposition > prespecified threshold.

Biomarkers and endpoints
- Pharmacodynamics: C3b/MAC deposition on LSCs, FcγR engagement, local PD‑L1/CD47 occupancy, single‑cell protease activity maps.
- MRD: high‑sensitivity flow and error‑corrected NGS at days +30, +100, +180, +365.
- Immune profiling: NK/γδ T expansion, missing‑self signatures, macrophage activation markers in marrow aspirates.
- Clinical: engraftment kinetics, GVHD (a/c), GRFS, NRM, RFS/OS.

Statistics (Phase 2 outline)
- Superiority margin: 1‑year relapse rate reduction from 30% (MAC historical) to ≤15% with M‑LOT; α=0.05, power 80%; stratify by ELN risk and MRD status pre‑HSCT; interim futility at 50% enrollment.

Milestones and go/no‑go
- Go to first‑in‑human if: (i) ≥2‑log LSC reduction with HSC CFU preservation in PDX, (ii) marrow confinement >85% AUC, (iii) no grade ≥3 non‑hematologic toxicity in NHP.
- Advance to Phase 2 if: (i) engraftment by day +28 in ≥90%, (ii) grade II–IV aGVHD ≤20% by day +100, (iii) MRD− rate ≥70% at day +100.

Deliverables
- A non‑genotoxic, marrow‑confined, logic‑gated opsonization platform (M‑LOT) integrated with antibody‑only conditioning and GVHD‑inert graft engineering, designed to achieve relapse rates equal to or lower than MAC while preserving donor HSC engraftment and minimizing GVHD.

text:
Title
Antigen-triggered “Lure-and-Liquidate” allogeneic HSCT: niche-ejection and immune-unmasking of leukemia stem cells with HSC-sparing, non-genotoxic conditioning

Central Hypothesis
Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) can be eradicated after reduced-intensity/nonmyeloablative (RIC/NMA) allogeneic HSCT by (i) forcing LSCs to disengage from marrow sanctuaries and enter a proliferative, drug- and immune-sensitive state, and (ii) simultaneously stripping their immune-evasion shields—provided these actions are executed only on LSCs and only within marrow, while sparing healthy hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and avoiding non-selective genotoxic conditioning.

Atomic Strategy
Create donor-derived, marrow-homing CAR-NK cells that, upon encountering LSC antigens, secrete a single, LSC-tethering “cis‑LURE” protein that (on the same LSC surface) blocks retention/dormancy and unmasks the cell to multi-modal immune attack. This antigen-triggered, locally tethered lure converts the niche from a shield into a spotlight, exposing LSCs to graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) without collateral damage to engrafting donor HSCs.

Specific Aims
1) Engineer and validate the cis‑LURE: an LSC-anchored, multi-domain biologic that dismantles niche protection and immune evasion only on target cells.
2) Build inducible LURE-secreting, multi-kill CAR-NK effectors (LURE-NK) that home to marrow, operate independent of HLA, and do not cause GVHD.
3) Establish a non-genotoxic RIC/NMA platform that preserves donor HSC engraftment while maximizing LURE-NK access to LSCs.
4) Test overall strategy in humanized bone marrow niche systems and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, then advance to a phase 1/2 trial targeting relapse rates ≤ myeloablative conditioning (MAC).

Innovation
- Single perturbation at system’s leverage point: antigen-triggered, LSC-surface–tethered “lure” that simultaneously (a) ejects from the niche, (b) awakens from dormancy, and (c) removes immune cloaks—without altering the niche globally.
- GVL without GVHD: HLA-independent CAR-NK plus local, on-LSC checkpoint and anti-phagocytic blockade.
- Conditioning without genotoxicity: targeted host HSC/CD117 antibody and lymphodepletion, not alkylators/TBI.

Approach

Aim 1: Engineer cis‑LURE (LSC-tethered niche-ejection and immune-unmasking protein)
- Architecture
  - Anchor: bispecific high-avidity scFv module recognizing CLEC12A (CLL‑1) and CD123 to bind LSCs and avoid HSCs (CLL‑1 absent on HSCs; CD123 low on HSCs).
  - Niche-ejection/dormancy exit (cis on LSC):
    - CXCR4 blockade domain (e.g., high-affinity EPI‑X4 derivative or anti‑CXCR4 sdAb) to disable CXCL12 retention.
    - VLA‑4 (α4β1) blockade sdAb to prevent VCAM‑1–mediated adhesion.
    - TGF‑β trap (scTβRII) microdomain to release quiescence brake locally.
  - Immune unmasking (cis on LSC):
    - High-affinity SIRPα D1 variant to block CD47 (“don’t eat me”).
    - Anti‑PD‑L1 scFv to block checkpoint upregulation on LSCs.
- Control elements
  - Marrow-restricted stability tag cleaved by MMP‑9/MT1‑MMP (abundant in leukemic niches) to minimize peripheral activity.
  - Fc‑silenced backbone to avoid off-target effector function.
- Bench validation
  - Binding selectivity to primary human LSCs vs CD34+CD38−CD90+ HSCs.
  - Loss of adhesion to human BM stromal/endothelial co-cultures (E‑selectin/VCAM‑1 substrates), time-lapse egress assays.
  - Single-cell RNA-seq: reversal of dormancy/quiescence signatures without HSC impact.
  - Safety: no apoptosis or colony-forming impairment in healthy CD34+ HSCs.

Aim 2: Build LURE-NK effectors (antigen-inducible secretion and multi-modal kill)
- Cell chassis: donor-derived memory-like NK cells (preactivated IL‑12/15/18), edited to express:
  - CAR(OR) targeting CLL‑1 or CD123 for broad LSC coverage.
  - SynNotch/NFAT promoter controlling cis‑LURE secretion strictly upon CAR engagement.
  - Homing: enforced CXCR4 and HECA‑452–positive glycoengineering to enhance E‑selectin ligand presentation for marrow entry.
  - Intrinsic resilience: PD‑1 knockout; NKG2A blockade via membrane-tethered scFv to resist HLA‑E–mediated inhibition.
  - Multi-kill: constitutive NKG2D signaling domain to sense stress ligands; CD16 maintained for ADCC against opsonized blasts (augmented by LURE-enabled macrophage opsonization).
  - Safety: inducible caspase‑9 suicide switch.
- Functional readouts
  - Antigen-gated LURE release kinetics; bystander-sparing in mixed cultures.
  - Killing of quiescent vs cycling LSCs within 3D human BM niche organoids.
  - Macrophage co-cultures: increased phagocytosis via CD47 blockade.
  - HLA-loss variants: retained killing (CAR, NKG2D, missing-self).
  - No alloreactive TCR (not present) and no GVHD in hu-mouse skin/gut models.

Aim 3: Non-genotoxic transplant platform preserving donor HSC function
- Conditioning (no busulfan/TBI/PTCy):
  - Lymphodepletion: fludarabine + alemtuzumab (anti‑CD52) to permit donor cell and LURE-NK engraftment.
  - Host HSC niche access: anti‑CD117 (c‑KIT) antibody (e.g., JSP191) to selectively deplete host HSCs and open niche without DNA damage.
- Graft and cell therapy sequence
  - Day 0: infusion of CD34+ donor HSCs.
  - Day +3 to +5: first LURE-NK dose (after donor HSC homing), then weekly x3; optional boost at MRD signal.
  - GVHD prophylaxis: calcineurin inhibitor + abatacept; no genotoxic agents.
- Guardrails
  - Time-gated LURE-NK dosing to avoid early displacement of donor HSCs.
  - Pharmacovigilance: rapid iCasp9 activation criteria for cytokine toxicity or cytopenias.

Aim 4: Efficacy in advanced models and early-phase clinical trial
- Preclinical
  - Human AML PDX with traceable LSC fraction in NSG-SGM3, with humanized BM niches.
  - Endpoints: LSC frequency by limiting dilution, MRD by flow/ngs-MRD, marrow imaging of egress, scRNA-seq of residual cells.
  - Safety: donor HSC engraftment (chimerism, multilineage CFU, serial transplantation).
- Clinical (phase 1/2, single-arm with matched historical MAC controls; expansion randomized vs RIC alone)
  - Population: adults with AML/MDS in CR/CRi with MRD+ or high-risk features eligible for allo-HSCT.
  - Primary endpoints: 1-year relapse incidence ≤ MAC benchmarks; GRFS improvement; absence of excess grade II–IV GVHD.
  - Key secondaries: MRD clearance by day +60; donor chimerism; cytopenia duration; infectious complications; NK persistence; LURE in marrow fluid.

How this compensates for reduced-intensity conditioning
- Replaces MAC cytotoxicity with targeted, multi-axis LSC control:
  - Physical sanctuary dismantling (CXCR4/VLA‑4/TGF‑β) converts protected LSCs into exposed, cycling targets.
  - HLA-independent elimination via CAR-NK/NKG2D and macrophage phagocytosis (CD47 blockade) addresses HLA loss.
  - Local PD‑L1 blockade restores effector function where antigen is present, not systemically.
  - OR-gated antigen recognition (CLL‑1/CD123) limits antigen escape while sparing HSCs.

GVL without exacerbating GVHD
- NK chassis lacks alloreactive TCR; CAR engagement and synNotch-gated LURE confine effector functions to LSC sites.
- Checkpoint and CD47 blockade are cis-tethered to LSCs, minimizing off-tumor immune activation.

Selectivity for LSCs and preservation of donor HSC engraftment
- Antigen anchors (CLL‑1/CD123) absent/low on HSCs ensure LURE acts in cis on LSCs only.
- Dosing post–donor HSC homing avoids niche disruption for engrafting cells.
- Preclinical CFU/serial transplant assays confirm HSC function.

Key Experiments and Milestones
- M1: cis‑LURE shows ≥80% reduction in LSC adhesion to human BM stroma with no effect on healthy HSC CFU (in vitro).
- M2: In 3D niche organoids, LURE-NK induces ≥2-log LSC depletion and ≥70% macrophage phagocytosis of residual blasts.
- M3: In PDX, LSC frequency ↓ ≥10-fold vs RIC-only; MRD negativity in ≥60% by day +60; no impairment of donor HSC reconstitution.
- M4: Phase 1 safety (DLT rate <25%); phase 2 efficacy (1-year relapse ≤20% and non-inferior to institutional MAC historicals with improved GRFS).

Risk Mitigation
- Antigen heterogeneity: OR-gated CAR plus dual-anchor LURE; add-on BiKE (CD16×CD33) if needed.
- Off-target adhesion effects: marrow-cleavable stability tag; suicide switch; step-up dosing.
- Cytopenias from bystander myeloid hit: transient effect anticipated; manage with G‑CSF; predefined iCasp9 triggers.
- Insufficient NK persistence: encode IL‑15 sushi domain with membrane tether; consider repeat dosing.

Manufacturing and Translation
- Donor apheresis split: CD34+ selection for graft; CD34− fraction to NK manufacturing under closed, feeder-free conditions; CRISPR edits (PD‑1 KO), lentiviral CAR/synNotch; release testing for potency and inducible LURE secretion; on-demand cryobanked doses for MRD-triggered boosts.

Success Criterion
Achieve relapse incidence and MRD clearance at or better than MAC benchmarks with:
- No use of non-selective systemically genotoxic agents.
- Preserved donor HSC engraftment and function.
- Demonstrable LSC-selective niche ejection and immune unmasking.
- Enhanced GVL without increased GVHD.

text:
Title
Graft-embedded, marrow‑tethered, logic‑gated immune engagers (GEM-LINK) to eradicate leukemia stem cells after antibody-only RIC allogeneic HSCT

Core hypothesis
Programming donor HSCs to secrete marrow‑anchored, LSC‑restricted, multi‑modal immune engagers will (a) restore and sustain graft-versus-leukemia after non‑genotoxic reduced‑intensity conditioning, (b) overcome marrow‑niche sanctuary and HLA‑independent immune evasion, and (c) preserve normal donor HSC engraftment and avoid GVHD by spatial, antigenic, and protease‑dependent restriction of immune activation.

Atomic strategy
Convert the allogeneic graft into a site‑restricted “immune synapse factory”: donor HSCs continuously deposit bone‑marrow‑anchored, logic‑gated engager proteins that only assemble functional immune synapses on cells co‑displaying LSC antigens, thereby creating durable, HLA‑independent surveillance without systemic activation.

Design overview
- Platform: GEM-LINKs are secreted, ECM‑anchoring, multi‑arm biologics expressed from engrafted donor HSC progeny.
- Target logic: high‑avidity AND gate to LSCs (e.g., CD123 AND CLL-1), with NOT gate against normal HSC markers (e.g., CD34/EPCR) via low‑affinity decoy arms that divert binding when HSC antigens are present.
- Effector recruitment: masked anti‑CD3ε minibody (T cells) plus anti‑CD16a nanobody (NK cells) to provide HLA‑independent killing and missing‑self sensing.
- Innate checkpoint reversal: SIRPα variant domain to block CD47 (“don’t‑eat‑me”) and promote macrophage phagocytosis.
- Checkpoint blockade: anti‑PD‑L1 VHH fused within the scaffold for local PD‑(L)1 axis inhibition.
- Marrow localization: collagen/osteonectin‑binding domain tethers GEM-LINKs to bone‑marrow ECM, limiting systemic diffusion.
- Protease activation: LSC‑enriched protease‑cleavable masks on CD3 and CD16 arms prevent off‑target crosslinking; masks are removed only in the leukemia milieu.

Conditioning and peri‑transplant regimen (non‑genotoxic)
- Host HSC clearance: anti‑CD117 antibody‑based conditioning ± targeted anti‑CD45 biologic; no busulfan, TBI, or alkylators.
- Lymphodepletion: anti‑CD52–based regimen to permit engraftment while reducing GVHD risk.
- GVHD prophylaxis: abatacept (CTLA4‑Ig) plus ruxolitinib; optional third‑party Treg add‑back; no post‑transplant cyclophosphamide.

Niche‑sanctuary disruption and timing
- Mobilization pulses: CXCR4 antagonist administered peri‑graft and scheduled post‑engraftment pulses (e.g., weekly × 4, then MRD‑triggered) to dislodge LSCs from SDF‑1 niches into GEM‑LINK–rich marrow/blood, synchronizing peak mobilization with maximal local engager deposition.
- Adhesion interference: transient VLA‑4/VCAM‑1 blockade during early pulses to counter physical sequestration without chemotherapy.

Transgene control to preserve engraftment
- Expression gating: GEM‑LINK cassette placed in a hematopoietic safe harbor under a promoter active in committed myeloid/monocytic progeny; embedded microRNA target sites (e.g., miR‑126) suppress expression in primitive HSCs, delaying onset until stable donor engraftment.
- Kill‑switch/antidote: an extracellular capture epitope enables rapid systemic neutralization of GEM‑LINKs by a clinically supplied antibody if toxicity emerges.

How constraints are met
- Compensate for reduced GVL with RIC/NMA: persistent, local GEM‑LINK production drives multi‑arm cytotoxicity and phagocytosis long after lymphodepletion wanes, creating durable, vaccine‑less surveillance.
- Exclude non‑selective genotoxins: antibody‑based conditioning and biologic GVHD prophylaxis; no busulfan/TBI/alkylators.
- LSC‑selectivity with preserved HSC engraftment: AND/NOT antigen logic, marrow tethering, and delayed expression protect donor HSCs and early progenitors.
- Overcome marrow sanctuary: ECM anchoring concentrates effectors in marrow; CXCR4/VLA‑4 disruption flushes protected LSCs.
- Counter multiple evasion modes: HLA loss (CD3/CD16 engagement), checkpoint upregulation (local PD‑L1 blockade), anti‑phagocytosis (CD47 blockade).
- Enhance GVL without exacerbating GVHD: spatial tethering, protease‑masked CD3, and CTLA4‑Ig/ruxolitinib prophylaxis restrict activation to leukemia sites; absence of systemic cytokine drivers limits off‑target alloresponses.

Preclinical plan
Aim 1: Engineering and specificity
- Construct modular GEM‑LINKs with swappable LSC binders; quantify AND/NOT gate behavior on primary AML/LSC vs donor HSC/progenitors.
- Test protease masking and marrow‑ECM anchoring in co‑culture with human marrow stromal cells; measure off‑target activation in mixed hematopoietic panels.

Aim 2: Multi‑effector synergy and evasion blockade
- Parse contributions of CD3, CD16, SIRPα, and PD‑L1 arms using domain‑dropout variants; metrics: T/NK cytotoxicity, ADCP, cytokine profiles, and bystander sparing.

Aim 3: In vivo efficacy with RIC substitute
- Humanized AML PDX with allogeneic HSC grafts expressing GEM‑LINKs; conditioning with anti‑CD117±anti‑CD52 only.
- Endpoints: LSC frequency by limiting‑dilution xenografts, MRD by NGS, marrow drug levels, and chimerism; mobilization pulses vs none.

Aim 4: Safety and engraftment
- Engraftment kinetics, lineage reconstitution, cytopenias, organ histology, and GVHD scoring.
- Antidote antibody reversal studies and recovery of hematopoiesis after neutralization.

Translational study (Phase 1/2)
Population
- Adults with high‑risk AML/MDS undergoing first allo‑HSCT, MAC‑ineligible, with ≥1 LSC antigen pair (e.g., CD123/CLL‑1) confirmed pre‑transplant.

Intervention
- Antibody‑only RIC; infusion of engineered donor HSCs; standardized GVHD prophylaxis (abatacept+ruxolitinib); scheduled CXCR4 antagonist pulses.

Primary endpoints
- Cumulative incidence of relapse at 1 year ≤ historical MAC benchmarks, adjusted for risk.
- Non‑relapse mortality and grade II–IV acute GVHD at day 100.

Secondary/exploratory endpoints
- MRD negativity at day +100 and +180; LSC burden by functional xenograft readout from marrow aspirates.
- Time to neutrophil/platelet engraftment; immune repertoire reconstitution; serum/bone‑marrow GEM‑LINK levels; anti‑drug antibodies.

Safety monitoring and stopping rules
- Continuous cytokine and organ toxicity monitoring; pre‑specified halt for grade ≥3 unexpected marrow‑independent toxicities.
- On‑demand GEM‑LINK neutralization with capture antibody; protocolized taper of ruxolitinib if delayed immune reconstitution.

Risk mitigation and contingency
- Antigen heterogeneity: patient‑specific binder selection (CD123/CLL‑1 default; alternatives include TIM‑3, CD70); cocktail permitted if dual expression is mosaic.
- Off‑tumor myeloid effects: NOT‑gate tuning and marrow tethering; temporary antidote if cytopenias exceed thresholds.
- Immunogenicity: central tolerance via hematopoietic expression reduces ADA risk; monitor and swap to humanized domains if needed.

Go/no‑go milestones
- Preclinical: ≥2‑log LSC reduction vs controls with antibody‑only RIC; preserved donor HSC engraftment; no excess GVHD in PDX models.
- Phase 1: DLT rate ≤25% through day +100; MRD negativity ≥60% by day +100.
- Phase 2 signal: 1‑year relapse ≤20% in high‑risk cohort with TRM and GVHD not exceeding contemporary RIC allo‑HSCT.

Success criteria relative to MAC
- Achieve equal or lower relapse than MAC while avoiding non‑selective genotoxic conditioning, maintaining timely engraftment, and not increasing GVHD—validating graft‑embedded, marrow‑localized immune synapse engineering as a self‑sustaining, selective LSC eradication strategy.

text:
Title: Niche-Inversion Conditioning (NIC) to Enable Genotoxin-Free Allo-HSCT with LSC Eradication

Atomic strategy (single insight):
Convert the marrow niche into an LSC-incompatible, HSC-supportive microenvironment before transplant by transiently implanting engineered niche “inverter” cells that deposit extracellular-matrix–tethered effector cues. These cues detach and kill LSCs while simultaneously preserving and priming spaces for donor HSC engraftment, thereby replacing the anti-leukemia function of myeloablative conditioning without systemic genotoxicity.

Hypothesis:
A short-lived, marrow-confined effector field created by engineered stromal cells will (i) break LSC sanctuary and induce local, antigen-restricted death; (ii) amplify marrow-restricted graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) while damping graft-versus-host disease (GVHD); and (iii) maintain or enhance engraftment niches for donor HSCs under reduced-intensity or nonmyeloablative (RIC/NMA) regimens.

Specific aims:
1) Build a marrow-confined “detach-and-die” field that overcomes LSC niche sanctuary while sparing HSCs.
2) Install multipronged, local immune pressure that bypasses HLA loss, neutralizes checkpoint signaling, and removes anti-phagocytic shields—without exporting activation to GVHD target tissues.
3) Preserve and expand donor HSC engraftment capacity under RIC/NMA by locally restoring key trophic and homing cues.
4) Test safety, efficacy, and immunologic correlates in staged models, then in a phase 1/2 trial comparing NIC+allo-HSCT (RIC/NMA) to historical MAC outcomes for relapse.

Design overview:
- Cell chassis: Hypoimmunogenic, short-lived bone marrow stromal “NIC cells” (derived from mesenchymal/endothelial progenitors) administered by intraosseous injection to major marrow sites. Persistence window: 2–4 weeks with a drug-inducible suicide switch. HLA-E/G expression protects from NK clearance; costim blockade minimizes off-target T cell activation.
- Localization: All secreted biologics carry collagen/heparan-binding domains for ECM tethering; vesicle-anchored or membrane-tethered formats further limit diffusion. This confines activity to marrow and minimizes systemic exposure/GVHD risk.

Effector modules (tethered and logic-gated):

A. Detach-and-die module (overcome sanctuary; selective LSC kill)
- Antigen-restricted anti-adhesion: An AND-gated bispecific that neutralizes CXCR4/VLA-4 only when co-engaged with an LSC antigen (e.g., CLEC12A, TIM-3, IL1RAP). This mobilizes LSCs off protective VCAM-1/E-selectin niches while leaving HSC retention intact.
- ECM-tethered TRAIL/DR5 agonism: Local death-receptor engagement biases to LSCs (typically more TRAIL-sensitive) while sparing quiescent HSCs.
- E-selectin antagonism (tethered): Disrupts LSC–endothelial adhesive refuges without global vascular effects.
- Oxidative-vulnerability tilt: Matrix-bound inhibitors of LSC redox buffering (e.g., local GSH-cycle modulation) co-released only in antigen-positive proximity, sensitizing to death-receptor signaling.

B. Anti–immune-evasion module (amplify GVL, avoid systemic activation)
- CD47 blockade in place: ECM-tethered high-affinity SIRPα decoys strip “don’t-eat-me” signals on nearby opsonized LSCs, boosting local phagocytosis.
- Checkpoint micro-traps: Marrow-tethered PD-1/PD-L1 and TIGIT ligands traps prevent inhibitory synapses within marrow while avoiding systemic checkpoint blockade.
- HLA-loss bypass: NIC cells display NKG2D ligands and secrete matrix-bound IL-15/IL-15Rα for in situ NK licensing; missing-self target recognition persists even if LSCs lose HLA.
- Opsonization independent of HLA: ECM-tethered, Fc-optimized opsonins against LSC antigens (dual-antigen AND gating to spare HSCs) drive ADCC/ADCP locally.

C. HSC-support module (preserve engraftment under RIC/NMA)
- Gradient shaping: Matrix-tethered SCF (membrane kit ligand), CXCL12, and low-dose TPO presentation near endosteal niches to retain and prime donor HSCs post-infusion.
- Anti-inflammatory buffering: Local TGF-β neutralization micro-islands away from HSC zones and transient IL-33/TSLP pulses to condition niche without systemic skewing.
- Space creation without genotoxins: Systemic anti-CD117 (c-Kit) monoclonal antibody for host HSC depletion; NIC cells preserve niche integrity and reconstitute homing cues for incoming donor HSCs.

D. Traffic and containment controls (enhanced GVL, attenuated GVHD)
- Marrow-homing bias for donor effectors: NIC cells deposit CXCL9/10 and CCL19/21 microgradients to recruit NK/central memory T cells into marrow. Concurrent systemic CCR9/CCR10-sparing keeps gut/skin homing low.
- Local costimulation bias: ECM-tethered 4-1BBL/OX40L at low density enhances cytotoxicity in marrow; absence elsewhere reduces GVHD.

Transplant schema (no non-selective genotoxic agents):
- Day −10 to −8: Bilateral intraosseous NIC cell delivery (pelvis/sternum) to establish the effector field.
- Day −7: Single-dose anti-CD117 antibody conditioning for host HSC depletion. Optionally add targeted anti-CD45 immunotoxin if disease burden is high (non-genotoxic).
- Day −5 to −3: Short window donor NK cell infusion (KIR-mismatch prioritized) to capitalize on local IL-15 licensing and opsonization.
- Day 0: Allogeneic HSCT with TCRαβ-depleted graft plus memory T cells and/or γδ T cells to favor GVL over GVHD.
- Day +7 and +21: Intraosseous NIC “boost” if minimal residual disease (MRD) persists; suicide-switch activation after MRD negativity or by Day +35.

Preclinical plan:
- Models: Humanized AML xenografts with primary LSCs; syngeneic and MHC-mismatched models for GVL/GVHD balance; intraosseous imaging for cell localization.
- Readouts:
  - LSC metrics: Limiting-dilution transplantation, serial MRD (flow and targeted sequencing), LSC frequency in endosteal vs vascular niches.
  - Engraftment: Donor chimerism, long-term repopulating unit assays, multilineage recovery.
  - Immunity: NK/T-cell infiltration in marrow, checkpoint occupancy, ADCP/ADCC rates, cytokine spillover.
  - Safety: Off-target opsonization of HSCs/progenitors, serum cytokines, organ histology for GVHD, clearance kinetics of NIC cells.
- Comparators: RIC/NMA alone; RIC/NMA + systemic checkpoint blockade; MAC controls (historical in xenografts).

Clinical phase 1/2 blueprint:
- Population: Adults with AML/HR-MDS in CR1/CR2 with MRD+ or high relapse risk; fit for allo-HSCT but poor MAC tolerance.
- Primary endpoints: Safety (DLTs including GVHD grade ≥III, off-target cytopenias), NIC-related SAEs, NIC cell persistence window.
- Key efficacy endpoints: MRD conversion at Day +30/+90, relapse at 1 year, non-relapse mortality, GVHD-free/relapse-free survival (GRFS).
- Correlatives: Marrow-local vs systemic cytokine ratios; NK/T cell activation restricted to marrow; occupancy of PD-1/PD-L1 traps; phagocytosis indices; HSC niche factor levels.

How NIC meets constraints:
- Compensates for reduced MAC anti-leukemia effect: Local detach-and-die field plus NK/T-cell amplification replaces debulking with marrow-confined cytotoxicity and opsonophagocytosis.
- Excludes non-selective systemically genotoxic agents: Conditioning is antibody-based (anti-CD117 ± targeted immunotoxin); NIC is non-genotoxic and local.
- Achieves LSC selectivity with HSC preservation: Dual-antigen AND gating for detachment/opsonization; death-receptor bias; HSC trophic-factor presentation and homing gradients.
- Overcomes niche sanctuary: LSC-restricted CXCR4/VLA-4 blockade, E-selectin antagonism, and local redox-tilt dismantle protective adhesion and survival signals.
- Counters multiple immune-evasion tactics: CD47 blockade, checkpoint traps, HLA-loss–agnostic NK licensing, and antibody-mediated opsonization act in parallel in the marrow.
- Enhances GVL without exacerbating GVHD: ECM tethering and intraosseous delivery confine activation; marrow-homing gradients recruit effectors locally; graft selection (TCRαβ-depletion/γδ T cells) reduces systemic alloreactivity.

Risk analysis and mitigations:
- Risk: Off-target harm to HSCs if antigen gating fails. Mitigation: Boolean AND gating with antigens absent on HSCs; HSC-proximal zones display only supportive ligands; real-time MRD and HSC marker monitoring.
- Risk: Spillover immune activation and GVHD. Mitigation: ECM tethering, intraosseous delivery, absence of systemic checkpoint blockade; predefined cytokine thresholds to trigger NIC suicide switch.
- Risk: LSC antigen heterogeneity/escape. Mitigation: Use 2–3 LSC antigens per patient (CLL-1, TIM-3, IL1RAP, CD123) with modular opsonins; post-transplant NIC boosts re-targeted by updated MRD phenotype.
- Risk: Insufficient host HSC depletion with anti-CD117 alone. Mitigation: Add targeted anti-CD45 immunotoxin or repeat dosing; verify niche opening via donor chimerism kinetics.

Go/no-go criteria:
- Preclinical go: ≥1-log reduction in functional LSC frequency vs RIC alone; preserved LTC-ICs from healthy HSCs; marrow-restricted immune activation (systemic:marrow IL-15 ratio >1:5); no grade ≥II GVHD in models.
- Phase 1 proceed: DLT rate <20%; MRD conversion Day +30 ≥50%; no unexpected prolonged aplasia attributable to NIC.
- Phase 2 success threshold: 1-year relapse ≤ MAC historical controls with non-relapse mortality not increased; GRFS improved vs RIC historical benchmarks.

Deliverables and milestones (24 months preclinical → 24 months clinical pilot):
- Year 1: Validate ECM confinement, logic gating, and detach-and-die efficacy; select antigen panels; finalize safety switches.
- Year 2: IND-enabling tox, GMP NIC cell manufacture; complete NK/T recruitment optimization.
- Years 3–4: Phase 1 dose/field-defining study; expansion cohort with adaptive antigen targeting based on MRD phenotypes.

Outcome:
If successful, NIC replaces systemic genotoxins with a marrow-local, logic-gated effector field that makes LSCs nonviable while improving donor HSC engraftment and restraining GVHD—achieving relapse rates at or below MAC with reduced toxicity.
